Seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The basmala: we have already discussed it many times, and we said that the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is dependent on an omitted element, and this omitted element is estimated as a suitable verb placed later. So when you say "bismillah" while you want to eat, how do you estimate the verb? "Bismillah, I eat" (bismillahi akulu).

We said that it must be estimated as dependent on an omitted element. Why? Why do we not say that it is not dependent? Because the prepositional phrase must have something it depends on:

"There is no escape for the prepositional phrase from depending on a verb or its meaning, such as 'murtaqi' (the one who ascends)."

Because the prepositional phrase is a governed element (ma'mul); it has the status of a direct object, so it needs a governing element ('amil).

Why did we estimate it as a verb placed later? For two benefits. The first benefit: seeking blessing by placing the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, first. The second benefit: restriction (hasr), because placing the governing element later gives restriction. It is as if you are saying: "I do not eat in the name of anyone, seeking blessing and help, except in the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Why did we estimate it as a verb? Because the original in governing is verbs, and grammarians know this: the original in governing is verbs. That is why nouns do not govern except under conditions. The active participle (ism al-fa'il) governs like a verb under conditions, the verbal noun (masdar) governs like a verb under conditions, and the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul) governs like a verb under conditions. Does the verb govern under conditions? No, because it is the original in governing; therefore we estimate it as a verb.

Why did we estimate it as specific? Because it is more indicative of the intended meaning. We could estimate: "Bismillah, I begin," but begin what? We do not know: begin eating, begin drinking, begin ablution, begin work. When you say "Bismillah, I eat," and you specify the verb, it is more indicative of the intended meaning. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah," or he said: "upon the name of Allah," specifying the verb.

So we say: the prepositional phrase depends on an omitted element, placed later, a verb suitable to the context.

As for Allah, it is a proper name for the Essence of Allah, glorified and exalted, for the Holy Essence; it is not applied except to Him, and it is the origin of the names. That is why the names come following it: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," they follow it.

Al-Rahman: possessor of vast mercy; that is why it is in the pattern fa'lan, which indicates fullness and vastness.

Al-Rahim: the one who conveys mercy to whomever He wills of His servants; that is why it came in the pattern fa'il, which indicates the occurrence of the act. So here, mercy is His attribute, indicated by "Al-Rahman," and mercy is His act, meaning the conveying of mercy to the one shown mercy, indicated by "Al-Rahim."

"Al-Rahman al-Rahim" are two names of Allah that indicate the Essence, the attribute of mercy, and the effect or ruling indicated by that meaning. Is that right or not? So in these two names is gathered everything that must be related to faith in the name of Allah, because faith in the name of Allah requires that you believe in the name, and what else? And the attribute, and the effect that is the ruling resulting from it. So we say: Allah is Rahman, possessor of mercy, who shows mercy. All of these are present in the Qur'an. Al-Rahman, as you see, means possessor of mercy: "And your Lord is the Rich, the possessor of mercy" (Al-An'am: 133). "He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills" (Al-Ankabut: 21).

"Al-Rahman" is a name indicating mercy, and it is true mercy, indicated by both revelation and reason. Do I not know whether this is Arabic language speech or not? It is Arabic. It is indicated by revelation and reason. And what is meant by revelation? The texts: the Book and the Sunnah. Reason: reflection and consideration. The evidence of revelation for Allah's mercy is countless. The evidence of reflection is that we say: how many blessings are there in the world? And what is the answer? They cannot be counted: "And if you count the blessings of Allah, you cannot enumerate them" (An-Nahl: 18). Is that right? They cannot be counted in their types and kinds, let alone their individual instances. These blessings indicate what? They indicate that the Bestower is merciful, and had there been no mercy, the blessing would not have come about. And how many averted calamities are there in the world? Is that not so? By what? By the effects of mercy: had there been no mercy, calamity would not have been averted.

It is strange that some people who claim reason say: mercy is not indicated by reason; rather reason indicates its opposite. I seek refuge in Allah! Why? They say: because mercy is tenderness, softness, submission, and gentleness, and this is not fitting for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Look at Satan! Is it not fitting? We say: mercy in this sense is whose mercy? The mercy of the created being. But the mercy of the Creator is not like the mercy of the created being. Furthermore, we deny that mercy, as you claim, is so even in the created being. A king of complete authority who fears no one except Allah comes and shows mercy to this poor man. Do we say that his mercy contradicts the authority and the fitting greatness he has? Never. It does not contradict it, nor does one say: "By Allah, this is a contemptible king who shows mercy to the poor and the weak." No, rather this is counted among his perfection.

Then we say to them: reason indicates it. We deny your statement that reason does not indicate it. Rather we say reason does indicate it. If you ask a common man in the market after rain fell at night and people went out walking in the rain, with the dust settled by the rain, the air and humidity of the rain, and you meet a common man and say: "Masha'Allah, it rained last night," he will say to you: "Yes, by Allah, praise be to Allah, the mercy of Allah is vast." And how does he know that this rain came from where? From mercy.

But they say: will (irada) was established by reason. Allah's will was established by reason. By what? They say: it was established by specification: He specified this to be a sky, and this to be an earth, and this a cow, and this a sheep, and this a camel, and this a donkey, and so on. Who specified this from that? The will. So there is will in Allah indicated by specification. Ask a student of knowledge, not a common man: how do you infer by reason the will of Allah? What will he say to you? He cannot. Perhaps he can say: I infer the will of Allah, for this whole universe is by the will of Allah. But he will not say to you that specification is what indicates the will. Is that right or not? Yet despite that, they hold that mercy is not indicated by reason, while will is indicated by reason. We say that both will and mercy are indicated by reason, and there is no doubt in this.

We mentioned earlier that the basmala is a verse of the Qur'an, without doubt, independent, not a continuation of what precedes it or what follows it, independent. But it is recited at the beginning of the surah. Every surah begins with the basmala except one surah, which is Bara'ah (At-Tawbah), for it was not established among the Companions that the Messenger ﷺ began it with the basmala. That is why they placed a separator between it and Al-Anfal and did not write a basmala, because they were uncertain whether it was part of Al-Anfal or independent. So they said: we place the separator and do not place the basmala. The basmala is recited as an independent verb that begins every surah, even Al-Fatihah, which is the first surah, is begun with it.

Is it part of the surah? We say: no. Accordingly, what is found now in the mushaf, numbered in Al-Fatihah specifically, with the number one, counting it as the first verse of Al-Fatihah, is a less preponderant view, and the preponderant view is that it is not a verse of Al-Fatihah, and the explanation of the preponderance of this view has passed before us. Yes.

* Student: (...)
* The Shaykh: Yes, he asks, saying: we ask Allah to grant us victory over the disbelieving people, and we do not have weapons with which to resist them? We say: victory over the disbelieving people is that Allah prepares for us weapons with which to resist, or destroys their weapons. Is the destruction of their weapons a victory for us or not?
* Student: Allah the Glorified and Exalted says: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardian" (Al-Hijr: 9). The disagreement of the scholars over whether the basmala is a verse of the verses of Allah or not, does that count as diminishing this verse?
* The Shaykh: No, no. Was it removed from the mushaf? Yes, it is preserved. No, no, they say it is a verse, but is it a verse? By agreement it is a verse. The disagreement concerns whether it belongs to the surah that follows it or not; the disagreement is about the count.

Student: Seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif Lam Mim (1). Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting (2). He has sent down to you the Book with truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel (3) before, as guidance for mankind. And He sent down the Criterion. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Mighty, the Owner of Retribution (4) [Al 'Imran: 1-4].

* The Shaykh: Seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. We have discussed the basmala grammatically, semantically and in its position, and we have also discussed the disjointed letters with which some surahs begin.

The disjointed letters with which Allah began some surahs: it has been said that they are symbols and indications of things, and some exegetes specified them. It has also been said that they are letters whose meaning we do not know, and Allah knows best what He intended by them. It has further been said that they are simply alphabetic letters with no meaning, and this last view is the correct one, because this Qur'an was revealed in clear Arabic language, and the Arabic language does not give these alphabetic letters a meaning. Since it gives them no meaning, by the requirement of its revelation in it, they should have no meaning. But some of the discerning scholars said: they have a purpose (maghza), meaning these letters have a purpose, which is that this Qur'an, which made the eloquent pure Arabs incapable, came with the letters they know and compose their speech from. Despite that, it defeated them. Had it come in a non-Arabic language, they would have said: we are incapable of it. But it came in the Arabic language, which they use to form their speech from these letters. He said: that is why you will hardly find a surah begun with these alphabetic letters without the mention of the Qur'an after them. This is what al-Zamakhshari, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and a group of scholars said.

As for His saying: "Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting": this is a sentence composed of a subject and predicate. "Allah" is the subject, and the sentence "there is no god but He" is the predicate of the subject. This sentence is itself a sentence, but grammarians call it a minor sentence (jumla sughra), because when the predicate is a sentence, it is a minor sentence, and the major sentence is the whole of the subject and predicate. "Al-Hayy al-Qayyum" are two further predicates: "al-Hayy" is a second predicate of "Allah," and "al-Qayyum" is a third predicate.

So His saying "Allah" is a proper name for the Holy Essence, a proper name for the Lord, Mighty and Majestic. Its origin is al-Ilah, in the sense of "the one worshipped" (al-ma'luh), and the hamza was dropped for lightness, as the hamza was dropped from khayr and sharr in the saying of the Messenger ﷺ: "The best of the rows of men is the first of them, and the worst of them is the last of them," meaning the best (akhyaruha) and the worst (ashharuha). The hamza was also dropped from "al-nas" (people), whose origin is "unas."

Allah is a proper name for the Holy Essence, and it is the most definite of the designations absolutely. Its meaning is the one worshipped with love and veneration. It is on the pattern fi'al in the sense of maf'ul, and how often fi'al comes in the sense of maf'ul, like ghira, meaning maghrus (planted), and bina, meaning mabni (built).

As for His saying "there is no god but He," that is, there is no true object of worship except Him. So "ilah" is the noun of "la," the negation of the genus, and its predicate is omitted, estimated as "haqq" (true). There are false gods, but they are gods only in that names have been placed upon them without right, as Allah the Exalted said: "You worship besides Him only names which you and your fathers have named" (Yusuf: 40). And He the Exalted said: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other? Is the male for you and the female for Him? That would be an unjust division. They are not but names you have named, you and your fathers; Allah has not sent down for them any authority" (An-Najm: 19-23).

With this estimation of the predicate in "la ilaha illa Huwa," the difficulty disappears, which is how the godhead can be negated in such a sentence and affirmed in His saying: "So their gods which they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything" (Hud: 101). The reconciliation is that those gods are false. As for the ilah in "la ilaha illa Allah," or "la ilaha illa Huwa," it is a true god: "That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood" (Al-Hajj: 62).

His saying "Huwa" is a pronoun, not a noun. It is a pronoun and not a noun, as evidenced by His saying: "So know that there is no god except Allah" (Muhammad: 19). Is this a proper noun or a pronoun? A proper noun. And as evidenced by His saying: "And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me" (Al-Anbiya: 25), where "Ana" is a pronoun. So in "la ilaha illa Ana" and "la ilaha illa Huwa," both are separate nominative pronouns. Just as the one who remembers Allah does not say "la ilaha illa ana," or just as the one who remembers Allah does not make "ana" a name of Allah, so it is not permissible to make "Huwa" a name of Allah. By this we know the falsehood of the remembrance of the Sufis who remember Allah with the phrase "Huwa Huwa," considering this remembrance the best of remembrances, though it is a false remembrance.

His saying "al-Hayy": the alif and lam here are for comprehensiveness, meaning the one whose life is complete. The life of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is complete in its existence and complete in its duration. He is Living with no beginning and no end. His life was not preceded by non-existence and will not be followed by cessation. Its existence is complete, and no deficiency enters it in any respect. He is complete in His hearing, knowledge, power and all His attributes. When we look at a human being, indeed when we look at anything other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic, we find it deficient in its life in duration and existence: its life is preceded by what? By non-existence, and followed by what? By cessation and annihilation. Its existence is also deficient. Is the living one complete in hearing? The living is not complete in hearing, nor in sight, nor in knowledge, nor in power. Every living thing is deficient. So its life is deficient in existence and duration: in duration it is preceded by non-existence and followed by cessation, and in existence it is deficient in all attributes.

(...) on the pattern fay'ul, derived from standing (al-qiyam), and its meaning is: the one who subsists by himself and the one who sustains others. He subsists by himself, so He needs no one, and He sustains others, so everyone needs Him.

In combining the two noble names, al-Hayy al-Qayyum, their combination comprehends all that Allah is described with of all perfections: in al-Hayy is the perfection of attributes, in al-Qayyum is the perfection of actions, and in both together is the perfection of the Essence. Al-Hayy is the perfection of attributes, al-Qayyum is the perfection of actions, and with their combination is the perfection of the Essence. He is perfect in His attributes, actions and Essence.
