* Shaykh: Allah knows best; for Allah says: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾ [al-A'raf 145]. And there has come in a hadith: "Verily Allah wrote the Torah with His own hand" [narrated by Abdullah in al-Sunnah (576) from Zayd ibn Aslam as a mawquf report; and in Sahih Muslim (2652/15): "How much did you find that Allah had written the Torah before I was created?" in the debate of Adam and Musa, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. So I withhold judgment on this, but the statements of the Salaf are clear: they say that the Torah and the Gospel are the speech of Allah, and the Psalms. But there is no doubt that they are sent down by Allah, and this must be believed; it suffices that we believe they were sent down from Allah.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan. ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah (5). He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but He, the Almighty, the All-Wise (6). He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise (muhkamat), which are the foundation of the Book, and others that are allegorical (mutashabihat). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is allegorical in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation, and none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firm in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran 5–7].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him.﴾
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution﴾ [Al 'Imran 4]. We have already mentioned that might (al-'izzah) has three categories. From this noble verse is derived the affirmation of one of Allah's names: He is al-'Aziz, in the three meanings mentioned earlier.
* Among the benefits of the verse: Allah the Exalted is described with retribution (intiqam), as shown by His saying: ﴿Owner of Retribution﴾. But this is not on an absolute basis; rather, He takes retribution against those who deserve it, who are the criminals, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution against the criminals﴾ [as-Sajdah 22]. For this reason, al-Muntaqim (the Avenger) is not reported among Allah's names in an absolute form; what is reported is in a restricted form: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution against the criminals﴾, or it occurs as an indefinite attribute such as ﴿Owner of Retribution﴾, meaning one who possesses retribution. This does not indicate, or does not signify, an absolute attribute that He is described as al-Muntaqim, because retribution is praiseworthy in its proper place, but outside its proper place it is not praiseworthy. So if retribution is called for by wisdom, it becomes praiseworthy; otherwise, it is not.
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you (1). And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the defective for the good, and do not consume their property into your own. Indeed, that is ever a great sin﴾ [an-Nisa' 1–2].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾.
This surah is Surat an-Nisa', and it is Medinan. According to the majority, the Medinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah, and the Meccan is what was revealed before the Hijrah. So the Medinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah even if outside Madinah, and the Meccan is what was revealed before the Hijrah even if outside Makkah. Accordingly, the criterion for determining the Meccan and Medinan is time, not place.
The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have mentioned criteria for the Meccan and Medinan, and have mentioned well-known distinguishing features of the Meccan and Medinan in the science of the principles of tafsir (usul al-tafsir). Among them: the predominant feature of the Meccan verses is brevity and strength, the strength of style, and their subject is generally monotheism (tawhid) and what relates to it.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah.﴾

This sentence, as we see, is a declarative sentence emphasized by (inna), and its predicate is negated: ﴿nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Him﴾. Al-khafa' (concealment) is the opposite of al-zuhur (manifestness). In it, (shay') (thing) is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it encompasses everything. ﴿On earth or in the heavens﴾ is connected to ﴿is hidden﴾. The meaning is: ﴿nothing is hidden from Him﴾, neither in this nor in that. By "the earth" and "the heavens" is meant the genus, so it includes all the earths and all the heavens. In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informs that nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Him. This is a negative attribute whose purpose is to demonstrate the perfection of His knowledge, because negated attributes are not intended to be mere negation, as we went over in the study of 'aqidah, but are intended to demonstrate the perfection of the opposite of that which is negated. So when He says ﴿nothing is hidden from Him﴾, why? For the perfection of His knowledge, nothing is hidden from Him. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has perfect knowledge: ﴿nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Him﴾. The purpose of this sentence is to train a person in himself to comply with Allah's command and avoid His prohibition, and that you should not think your deed is hidden from Allah, rather it is known to Him. So you must obey Him and avoid His disobedience. Do not say: "I am in my house, I am in a room, I am in a chamber where no one can see me," because Allah is watching you. ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah.﴾

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against disobeying Allah. And how so? Out of fear that He will know of your disobedience to Him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, who say that Allah does not know what the servant does until after it occurs. Their extremists are as previously mentioned.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Most High, knows both universals and particulars, derived from His saying ﴿thing (shay')﴾, the indefinite noun in a negative context, which encompasses everything.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the earth and the heavens, which is a known matter. But if someone says: Does anything other than the earth and the heavens remain hidden from Allah? The answer: No, but He specified the earth and the heavens because they are what is witnessed by us; we only witness the earth and the heavens, and everything beyond that we know only through the unseen. So the mention of the earth and the heavens... Can we say that among the benefits of the verse is that the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are either negative or positive?

Answer: Yes, and we have previously discussed this division in (Tawhid). We said that the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are either positive (thubutiyyah) or negative (salbiyyah). The positive ones are called thubutiyyah and the negative ones are called salbiyyah. We said that negative attributes necessarily include an affirmation, but they negate a deficiency in that affirmed attribute. So, for the perfection of His knowledge, nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Him.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾. This is among His knowledge, which is hidden from many people, yet it is known to Him. ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾. ﴿Forms you﴾, i.e., makes you into a particular form which He chooses and wills. As for His saying ﴿in the wombs﴾: al-arhām (wombs) is the plural of raḥim, which is the container of the fetus in its mother's belly. Allah the Exalted has explained in another verse that the fetus in its mother's belly is in three darknesses: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta. The placenta means the watery sac in which the fetus is contained, and among the common people it is called (al-qumqum).

As for His saying ﴿however He wills﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of ﴿wills﴾, meaning that He forms us in whatever manner He wills. As for His saying ﴿in the wombs﴾: it is a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun in ﴿you﴾ (kum) in ﴿forms you﴾, meaning: while you are in the wombs. And His saying ﴿however He wills﴾ means that we have no choice in selecting a particular form for the fetus in the belly.

Then He said: ﴿There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. This declarative sentence is negated and affirmed, containing the restriction (ḥaṣr) whose method is negation and affirmation. The word ilāh (god) means maʾlūh (one who is worshipped). His saying ﴿but He﴾: the pronoun (huwa) is a substitute for the omitted predicate; that is, there is no true god except He. It is not one of Allah's names, as claimed by the Ṣūfiyya, who assert that (Huwa) is one of Allah's names and call upon Allah by it, saying: (Huwa, Huwa, Huwa). This is among their ecstatic utterances (shaṭaḥāt). ﴿The Mighty, the Wise﴾: al-ʿAzīz (the Mighty) has already been explained shortly before, and that He possesses perfect might, and that the might of Allah Mighty and Majestic is of three kinds: might of rank (qadr), might of subjugation (qahr), and might of inaccessibility (imtināʿ). And al-Ḥakīm (the Wise) is on the pattern of faʿīl in the sense of mufʿil, and faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil. As for faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, it is common in the Arabic language, such as qadīr in the sense of qādir, samīʿ in the sense of sāmiʿ. As for samīʿ in the sense of musmiʿ (one who causes to hear), it is also attested in the Arabic language. The poet said:

Is it from Rayḥāna, the caller who causes to hear (al-samīʿ), that my sleeplessness comes, while my companions are asleep?
Amin Rayḥāna al-dāʿī al-samīʿ: al-samīʿ here means al-musmiʿ, the one who makes me hear, who keeps me awake while my companions lie in slumber. Thus ḥakīm here means muḥkim (one who makes firm) and also ḥākim (judge). Allah Mighty and Majestic is a judge and firmly establishes what He decrees. His judgment is divided into two kinds: the cosmic judgment (kawnī) and the legislative judgment (sharʿī). The cosmic judgment is what Allah has decreed upon His servants in creation, and to this everyone submits—believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked—and no one can ever escape it. The legislative judgment is what Allah has decreed upon His servants by way of law, and this is what people differ over: some are disbelievers and some are believers; some submit to this legislative judgment and perform what is obligatory upon them concerning it, and others are arrogant toward it, deny it, and pay it no heed. Is this clear? What did we say?
* Student: (...) to people.

* Shaykh: No. First: judgment?

* Student: Judgment means decree.

* Shaykh: Judgment?

* Student: Its meaning is (...) the judge.

* Shaykh: We mentioned that judgment has two kinds.

* Student: The judge (...) means the one who makes firm.

* Shaykh: No, no, my brother, no.

* Student: Legislative judgment is what He decides among His servants.

* Shaykh: Legislative judgment, and the second?

* Student: Cosmic judgment.

* Shaykh: Cosmic judgment. Good, do you understand? Come on, what is legislative judgment?

* Student: Legislative judgment: it is the rulings of Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Shaykh: What He has decreed upon His servants by way of law. And the cosmic?

* Student: The cosmic: what Allah, glorified and exalted, has decreed upon all His servants, believer and disbeliever.

* Shaykh: Cosmic judgment is something everyone submits to, and no one can escape it. And the legislative?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. People are divided regarding it into two groups: a group that is responsive to this judgment and carries it out, and a group that is neither responsive to it nor carries it out. Is this clear?

We said that it derives from (ḥākim) and from (muḥkim), in the sense of (mutqin, one who perfects). Here it means (dhū al-ḥikma, possessor of wisdom), that is, one who perfects everything He decrees. So everything Allah decrees, whether cosmic or legislative, is in its most complete and perfect and best form. ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful. Return your gaze; do you see any flaw? Then return your gaze twice; your gaze will return to you humbled, and it will be fatigued﴾ [al-Mulk 67:3–4]. ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of ignorance? Who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Mā'ida 5:50]. This legislative or cosmic judgment is firm and perfected, free of any defect or deficiency. Moreover, it is also firm in its attribute and form in which it is, and perfected in its intended end. Wisdom may be formal, that is, in a particular form that conforms to wisdom, and it may be final, that is, its aim is benefit, advantage, the repelling of harms, and the like; the important thing is that the aim be praiseworthy. So wisdom is present in the cosmic judgment and in the legislative judgment, and it is either formal, in that the thing is in a form that corresponds to wisdom, or final, in that its purpose and end is a praiseworthy goal. Is this clear?

All of this is included in our saying (muḥkim). For example, if we look at the Sharīʿa, all the prescribed acts are in a form that corresponds to wisdom, such as prayer, zakat, fasting, and pilgrimage; and their purpose also accords with wisdom: their purpose is the reform of hearts, the reform of deeds, the reform of the individual, and the reform of society. All of these are praiseworthy ends. All of this is included in His saying the Exalted: ﴿the Wise﴾.

* This verse contains several benefits:

* First: the demonstration of Allah's power, in that He forms created beings in the wombs: ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs﴾.

* Second: Among the benefits of the verse is also that the forming of images is by Allah's command and permission, however He wills: this one is white and that one black, this one beautiful and that one ugly, this one tall and that one short, this one thick and that one thin, and so on. Indeed, one may even say that it includes: this one male and this one female, since the form of the male differs from the form of the female.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's mercy, in that He takes charge of the affairs of the fetus and forms it. It does not emerge unformed. Had Allah willed, the fetus would have emerged unformed, and then it would have been formed little by little as its mind develops. But by the wisdom and mercy of Allah, it does not emerge except in the form which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed, only in the form which Allah willed. If someone says: ﴿however He wills﴾: it is inferred from it that this formation does not return to the action of the servant, but returns to the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that is so. Yet this does not preclude that the form be close to that of the father, or the mother, or the grandfather, or the grandmother; that is, that this fetus may have inherited a trait (ʿirq) from its fathers, mothers, and relatives. This does not prevent it, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made a cause for everything. This is shown by the story of the man who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my wife has given birth to a black boy." (They were both white, so he was implying something about his wife, and who brought the black one to her?) The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Do you have camels?" He said: Yes. "What are their colours?" He said: Red. "Are there any grey (awrad) among them?" The awrad is the silvery one between white and black. He said: Yes. He said: "How did that come about?" He said: Perhaps a trait (ʿirq) pulled it. The Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "Then this son of yours perhaps has a trait that pulled it."[[Agreed upon. Related by al-Bukhari (5305) and Muslim (1500/18) from Abu Hurayra.]] The man was convinced, because this is a clear and evident analogy. The point of the matter is his saying: "Perhaps a trait pulled it." It is inferred from this that this form which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills in the wombs does not preclude that a trait from his fathers, mothers, grandfathers, or grandmothers may have pulled it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of will, from His saying ﴿however He wills﴾. It has already been stated that when will is mentioned without qualification, it is coupled with wisdom; nothing is willed by Allah except for a wisdom.

If someone says: Is there in the verse evidence that it is not permissible for a person to undergo cosmetic surgery, from His saying ﴿however He wills﴾, where He made the forming dependent upon His will alone?

* The students: It may be said.

* The Shaykh: It may and it may not. That is, it may be said, and it may not be said; it may not be said. For Allah, the Exalted, has informed in many verses that He extends provision to whom He wills, He constricts and extends, does He not? He decrees and extends, that is, He decrees constriction. Do we say that a person is forbidden from doing the means by which provision is extended?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: Because extension returns to the will of Allah? No, we do not say so. But we say that there is a difference between the matter of extending provision and seeking extension, and this matter; for the texts have come forbidding cosmetic alteration. It has been established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he cursed the woman who plucks (nāmiṣa) and the woman who has her eyebrows plucked (mutanammiṣa), the woman who makes hair-extensions (wāshira) and the one who has them made (mustawshira), and the tattooer (wāshima) and the one who is tattooed (mustawshima).[[Agreed upon. Related by al-Bukhari (4886) and Muslim (2125/120) from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, without the phrase "wāshira wa-l-mustawshira"; Ṣāḥib Kanz al-ʿUmmāl attributed this addition to Ibn Jarīr.]] This shows that a person is forbidden from cosmetic alteration that is permanent. As for temporary beautification, such as a woman adorning herself with henna and the like, there is no harm in it.

If someone says: Is there in the verse anything that indicates the prohibition of repairing and removing defects, from His saying ﴿however He wills﴾?

* A student: (...) not (...).

* The Shaykh: If this boy comes out with six fingers on each hand, is it permissible for us to cut off the extra finger?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: The brother (...) says: No. Who formed him?

* Students: Allah.

* The Shaykh: Allah. Then "however He wills": leave this to the will of Allah.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is said that this is not a matter of cosmetic alteration; cutting off this finger is not a matter of beautification, but of removing a defect.

* A student: Improvement and beautification.

* The Shaykh: Improvement and beautification are one thing, O shaykh; but the removal of a defect has been permitted by the Sunna. "The man whose nose was struck off and cut, the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, permitted him to make a nose of silver" (i.e., of silver), "but it became foul-smelling, so he permitted him to make a nose of gold."[[Related by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4232) and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami (1770) from ʿArfaja ibn Asʿad.]] So that his nose would not remain cut off with a disfigurement. This shows that removing a defect is not like acquiring beauty: beautification is not permissible, while removing a defect is permissible, because it is contrary to the original state. On that basis we say that it is permissible to cut off an extra finger. However, some scholars explicitly stated its prohibition, saying that it is forbidden, but they gave as the reason that one whose finger is cut off may fear dying from bleeding; this reason no longer applies in our present time, and accordingly it is permissible to cut off the extra finger.

Suppose there were an extra piece of flesh in the ear, or on the head, or on the neck: is it permissible to remove it? Yes, we say it is permissible, like the finger.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, alone possesses divinity, from His saying ﴿There is no god but He﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the two noble names ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾, and what they comprise of attributes. It has already passed that every name of Allah indicates the Essence and the attribute derived from it. Every name: if it is transitive, there is a third indication, namely the effect that results from it. Thus al-Samīʿ (the All-Hearing), for example, includes the affirmation of hearing, namely He is the All-Hearing; the attribute, which is hearing; and the effect, which is that He hears. Likewise al-ʿAlīm. As for names that are not transitive to others, they include only the affirmation of the name and the attribute, such as al-Ḥayy (the Living), al-ʿAẓīm (the Great), al-ʿAlī (the Most High); these are not transitive to others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 1 of 4):

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾. ﴿It is He who﴾: the pronoun in "huwa" (He) refers back to Allah. Reflect here on how the verses are linked to one another. When Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned that He is the One who fashions (al-musawwir), and that this is the beginning of creation, He then mentioned the sending down of the Book, through which guidance comes, as in: ﴿The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an. Created man. Taught him the explanation﴾ [Ar-Rahman 1-4]. Sometimes Allah mentions the religious blessing first, and sometimes He mentions the worldly blessing first. So here He began with the fashioning, then mentioned the sending down of the Qur'an. However, in ﴿The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an﴾ He mentioned the teaching of the Qur'an before the creation of man. Then He said: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾, and what is meant by it is the Qur'an. The meaning of its being a Book has already been mentioned: that it is written in the Preserved Tablet, in the scrolls held by the angels, and in the scrolls in our hands. Then Allah divided this Book, saying: ﴿In it are clear verses (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others﴾, meaning: and in it are others, ﴿ambiguous (mutashabihat)﴾. Here it is necessary to say "and in it are others" so that the division is complete.

His saying ﴿clear verses (muhkamat)﴾: "ayat" is the plural of "aya", which means a sign, and every verse of the Qur'an is a sign of the One who sent it down because of its inimitability and its challenge. His saying ﴿muhkamat﴾ means: perfected in indication, in ruling, and in report; that is, their reports and rulings are firm and known, with no difficulty in them. ﴿And others ambiguous (mutashabihat)﴾ means that their rulings or their reports are not known. So the muhkam is that which is firm and perfected in indication, whether it is a report or a ruling. The mutashabih is that whose indication is not clear, whether it is a report or a ruling.

Then He said: ﴿they are the foundation of the Book﴾. He mentioned the description of these muhkamat and the explanation of their status first, so that what comes first to the mind is that the mutashabihat must be referred back to the muhkamat, because they are the "umm" (foundation), and the umm of a thing is its source and origin. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and confirms, and with Him is the Foundation of the Book﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 39], meaning the source, which is the Preserved Tablet to which all writings are returned. From this, al-Fatiha is called "Umm al-Kitab" (the Foundation of the Book), because the Qur'an returns to it. Therefore these muhkamat must be the reference to which the mutashabihat are returned.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and others ambiguous﴾. Ambiguous in what? In indication, whether it is a ruling or a report. For this reason we find that some verses do not clearly indicate the ruling for which they are cited as evidence, and some reports also do not clearly indicate the report for which they are cited. So what do we do? He said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts there is deviation...﴾ and so on. With regard to these mutashabihat, people divide into two groups. One group follows the mutashabih, puts it before people, and presents it to them, saying: "How is this, and how is that?" The other group says: ﴿We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord﴾, and if all of it is from our Lord, it cannot contradict or conflict; rather it is unified and consistent. So the mutashabih is referred back to the muhkam, and all of it becomes muhkam. Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾. Zaygh means inclination, and from it comes the saying: "the sun deviated (zaghat) when it leaned away from the middle of the sky."

﴿Those in whose hearts is deviation﴾ means: inclination away from the truth, not desiring the truth. They follow the mutashabih, and you find them, may Allah protect us, taking the Qur'anic verses that have ambiguity and striking some against others. This is very common among the Christians. The Christians now introduce many doubts to the Muslims based on the mutashabih. For example, they say: "God is the third of three; we have evidence: do you not read in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾ [Al-Hijr 9], and ﴿And when We took from the prophets﴾ [Al-Ahzab 7]?" The form of the pronoun is plural, so Allah is more than two, three. And so they bring things with which they deceive people, because there is deviation in their hearts. Likewise, some verses appear to contradict, such as His saying: ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [An-Nisa 42]. Here He said: ﴿they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾, and in another verse He says: ﴿Then their discourse will not be but that they say: By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am 23]. So did they conceal or not?

* The students: They concealed.

* The Shaykh: They concealed. They said: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾; they concealed, they denied being polytheists. Likewise, he comes to you and says: ﴿On the Day when some faces will be white and some faces will be black﴾ [Ali 'Imran 106], and in another verse He says: ﴿And We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾ [Ta-Ha 102]. Then he comes to you and says: ﴿And they will not be permitted, so they will not make excuse﴾ [Al-Mursalat 36], and in another verse: they make excuses, saying that if they were returned to the world they would reform and their conditions would be set right, so they make excuses. The point is that those in whose hearts is deviation bring these ambiguous verses in order to turn people from the way of Allah and to cast doubt among people about the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. As for those who have no deviation in their hearts, they are the firmly grounded in knowledge, who have enough knowledge to reconcile the ambiguous verses and to understand their meaning. These do not experience this ambiguity: ﴿They say: We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7], and so they see nothing in the Qur'an that is contradictory or conflicting.

* A student: Regarding His saying ﴿He fashions you﴾, can actual rulings be derived from it that are connected to fashioning, such as prayer and other things?

* The Shaykh: From what?

* The student: From prayer, meaning the prayer upon him before he is fashioned; and before fashioning he is nothing. His saying ﴿He fashions you﴾.

* The Shaykh: Can this be derived from it? He asks: can it be derived from His saying ﴿He fashions you﴾ that if a fetus in its mother's womb falls before it is fashioned, it has no ruling?

* A student: It cannot be derived, Shaykh, it cannot be derived.

* The Shaykh: It cannot be derived.

* The student: It cannot be derived, because the fetus has stages, and at its beginning the name "form" does not apply to it.

* The Shaykh: By Allah, it is not clear, it is not clear.

* A student: Shaykh, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾ and called it "the Book" while it was still among the angels; it does not exist in our hands until it reaches us.

* The Shaykh: By what is going to be. Have you not read the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf 36]? Wine is not what he is pressing; he presses grapes, which become wine after being pressed.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. Suppose a man has, for example, a slight tilt in his nose, or his teeth vary, some longer and some shorter, or slightly different. Is it permissible for him to have a procedure to correct this slight tilt?

* The Shaykh: Yes. A tilt that is a defect, there is no doubt that it is permissible.

* The student: Especially if it causes harm.

* The Shaykh: No, no, how would it cause harm? Harm!

* The student: No, no, I mean: it is permissible, especially if it causes harm.

* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning especially if it causes harm. Yes. Likewise with the teeth: if their difference is disfiguring, there is no harm in adjusting them. But if their difference is slight, yet they want them to be like one tooth, as some women do now, then this is not permissible; this is of the kind of tattooing, this is tattooing.

* A student: Shaykh, regarding the hadith you mentioned a moment ago, the man who came to the Messenger ﷺ and whose nose was cut off, and he ordered him to take a nose of gold.

* The Shaykh: Yes, of silver first, then it stank.

* The student: So this man's nose was not born that way; his nose was cut off, meaning this was an accident. It was not originally so; he was born with six fingers.

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no difference. I say: there is no difference. The aim is removing the defect, whether the defect is acquired or original.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. We said that the sixth finger is removed and there is no harm in that, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic said about Satan: ﴿And I will surely command them, and they will change the creation of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 119], and this sixth finger is part of the creation of Allah.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but not everything forbidden is forbidden. A change that is commanded is commanded. Circumcision, for example, is a change to the creation of Allah and it is commanded. Removing the moustache is a change to the creation of Allah and it is commanded.

* The student: But he did not order him to remove the sixth one.

* The Shaykh: Yes, we find that the Lawgiver does not prohibit a person from removing something that people consider a defect. The story of the man with the nose is the main basis for this issue.

* The student: But the Prophet ordered the man with the nose to place something, not to remove, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: What was placed on his nose, is it not a completion for him?

* The student: But he had no nose.

* The Shaykh: Yes, his nose was cut off, so he was given a completion. If he removes it, it is a completion for him, because people now consider what has an extra part a defect, so it removes a defect.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good, Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven﴾. Do you say that ﴿on earth﴾ is attached to ﴿is hidden﴾?

* The Shaykh: No, it is attached to (شيء, "thing") as a qualifier of "thing".

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you, regarding someone who begins a surah or any word with "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Gracious" (reversing ar-Rahman ar-Rahim)?

* The Shaykh: What is the case?

* The student: He reverses "ar-Rahman ar-Rahim": when he begins a surah he says "bismillah ar-Rahim ar-Rahman". Is there a prohibition in this?

* The Shaykh: Is his intention recitation; recitation of the Qur'an, or not?

* The student: If his intention is recitation, and if it is other than that.

* The Shaykh: If his intention is recitation, then it is haram, because the Qur'an is arranged in its words and arranged in its verses too. Yes. The correct view is that the arrangement of the surahs is by ijtihad.

* The student: So the basmala is considered a verse of the Qur'an?

* The Shaykh: Known, yes.

* The student: I mean the basmala that is at the beginning of the surah.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you. Some have said that ﴿and others ambiguous﴾ refers to attributes (...)?

* The Shaykh: This will come to us, Allah willing, in the benefits (fawa'id).

* The student: Shaykh, also a question: the one who brings verses, does he have (...)?

* * *

* Student: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are clear verses, they are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous. As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation, and none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say: We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord. And none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are clear verses, they are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous﴾. We have already explained that Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that He divided the Qur'an into two parts: clear verses (muhkamat), meaning verses whose meaning is plain, which no one fails to understand; and the second, ambiguous verses (mutashabihat), in which there is obscurity in indication, or apparent contradiction between them and others, or other causes of ambiguity. People divided regarding these ambiguous verses into two groups. One group, in whose hearts is deviation, meaning inclination from the truth, follows the ambiguous, and they bring the ambiguous, confusing people with it, and seeking discord. Likewise, ﴿seeking its interpretation﴾ means seeking its interpretation according to what they want, not according to what Allah the Mighty and Majestic wants. This is common: all the people of innovation, such as the Rafidah, the Khawarij, the Mu'tazilah, the Jahmiyyah and others, all of them followed what is ambiguous of it, some with little and some with much. These follow the ambiguous for these two purposes, or one of them. What are they? ﴿Seeking its interpretation﴾, that is, turning people away from the religion of Allah, because discord in the sense of turning away from the religion of Allah is as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and did not repent will have the punishment of Hellfire﴾ [Al-Buruj 10]. "Fatanu" means they turned them away from the religion of Allah. ﴿Then they did not repent, so for them is the punishment of Hellfire﴾. And ﴿seeking its interpretation﴾: that is, seeking its interpretation according to what they want; they explain it according to their own purpose, not according to the purpose of Allah the Exalted.

We have also already explained that His saying ﴿and others﴾ is not conjoined to His saying ﴿clear verses﴾ in ﴿in it are clear verses﴾, because the meaning would be corrupted, and that "others" (akhar) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: and in it are others that are ambiguous. We mentioned a parallel to this, His saying the Exalted: ﴿So among them is wretched and fortunate﴾ [Hud 105]. Here "fortunate" is not conjoined to "wretched", because if it were conjoined, the division would be corrupted. Rather the implied meaning is: among them is wretched, and among them is fortunate. Likewise: in it are clear verses, and in it are others that are ambiguous.

We said that ambiguity may be in meaning, where the meaning is not clear, or in apparent contradiction, where a person supposes that the Qur'an contradicts itself. We mentioned examples of that earlier.

* The student: Did we not mention them?

* The Shaykh: May Allah guide you, we mentioned them, we mentioned examples and answered them, and we said: it is absolutely impossible that there be anything contradictory in the Qur'an, it is impossible, because the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa 82]. That is, since it is from Allah, there is no contradiction in it; it confirms one part with another. But the apparent contradiction that some people understand arises either from deficiency of knowledge, or deficiency of understanding (this is two), or neglect in reflection (this is three), or ill assumption, or ill intention, such that one assumes the Qur'an contradicts itself. When one holds this assumption, he is not granted success in reconciling the texts, and he is deprived of good, because he has assumed what does not befit the Qur'an. These are the causes of supposing contradiction in one who supposes it: four causes, namely: deficiency of knowledge, or deficiency of understanding, or neglect in reflection, or bad intention. When one of these four matters is present, ambiguity arises. But as for the one whom Allah has given knowledge, understanding, and good intention, the fourth?

* The students: Good assumption, five.

* The Shaykh: And good assumption. He does not experience contradiction in the noble Qur'an, because he has perfection in knowledge, perfection in understanding, vigor in reflection, and good intention and purpose. Such a person is granted success; Allah the Exalted grants him success, so he knows how to reconcile what appears contradictory, or how to recognize this ambiguity.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 2 of 4):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."﴾ Regarding this noble verse, the early scholars (al-salaf) differed over where to pause. Most of the early scholars paused at His saying ﴿except Allah﴾ and considered the pause here obligatory (lazim), meaning that you must pause, saying: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾, and then begin: ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it"﴾. On this reading, the waw in His saying ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ is for resumption (isti'naf), ﴿those firmly rooted﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿say﴾ is the predicate of the subject. This is what most of the early scholars held: that the ambiguous (mutashabih) text, its interpretation is known only to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and those firmly rooted in knowledge, who do not know it, do not seek by it sedition, but say: ﴿We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord﴾, and there is no contradiction or conflict in the words of our Lord. They entrust the matter to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because He is the One who knows what He intended. Thus people are divided into two categories: ﴿those firmly rooted in knowledge, who say, "We believe in it"﴾ and ﴿those in whose hearts is deviation, who follow what is ambiguous of it﴾.

Some of the early scholars joined the words and did not pause, that is, they recited: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾, so the waw is conjunctive (lil-'atf), and ﴿those firmly rooted﴾ is coordinated with the word "Allah"; meaning: none knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly rooted in knowledge, unlike those in whose hearts is deviation and who have no knowledge, for these do not know. The truth is that the apparent meaning of the two readings appears to conflict, because the first reading implies that none knows the interpretation of this ambiguous text except Allah, while the second reading implies that this ambiguous text's interpretation is known to Allah and those firmly rooted in knowledge. So the apparent meaning of the two views is contradictory; but the correct position is that there is no contradiction between them, and that this disagreement rests on the difference over the meaning of "interpretation" (ta'wil) in His saying: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾. If by ta'wil is meant tafsir (explanation), then the reading with joining is preferable, because those firmly rooted in knowledge know the tafsir of the ambiguous Qur'an, and nothing is hidden from them, given their rootedness in knowledge and their reaching the depth of knowledge; for the one firmly rooted in a thing is the one established and settled in it. Because of their firmness and the steadiness of their feet in knowledge and their depth in it, they know what is hidden from others. So if we take ta'wil to mean tafsir, the reading with joining is preferable. But if we take ta'wil to mean the outcome and the unknown end, then pausing at ﴿except Allah﴾ is preferable, because the outcome of this ambiguous text and what it leads to is an unknown matter to all creation. If someone says: "Now we seek two points: the first is that ta'wil means tafsir, and the second is that ta'wil means the unknown outcome known only to Allah," the answer is: yes, this is necessary, and it exists in the Qur'an. First, ta'wil in the sense of tafsir, such as the words of the two companions of the prison to Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿One of them said, "Indeed I see myself pressing wine," and the other said, "Indeed I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its ta'wil"﴾ [Yusuf 36], meaning: explain the interpretation of this dream, and what does it mean? So he explained it to them. And from this is the saying of the Messenger ﷺ to Ibn 'Abbas: "O Allah, grant him understanding in religion and teach him ta'wil"[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (2397) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. In al-Bukhari (143) and Muslim (2477/138) without his words: "and teach him ta'wil."]], meaning: the tafsir of speech and knowledge of its meaning. As for ta'wil in the sense of outcome, from it is His saying: ﴿Do they await except its ta'wil? The day its ta'wil comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth"﴾ [al-A'raf 53]. So His saying ﴿Do they await except its ta'wil﴾ means its outcome and what it leads to; ﴿the day its ta'wil comes﴾ means its promised outcome comes; ﴿those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth."﴾ And from it is His saying: ﴿That is better and more excellent in ta'wil﴾ [an-Nisa' 59], meaning: better in outcome and final result. Thus it becomes clear that the word "ta'wil" is suitable for both meanings together: tafsir and outcome. So if we take it to mean tafsir, there is no doubt that those firmly rooted in knowledge know the tafsir of the Qur'an, and nothing is hidden from them, and it is not possible under any circumstances that Allah, glorified and exalted, would send down to His servants a Book about which He would question them on the Day of Resurrection while they do not know its meaning. Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: It is impossible at all that He would send down to them a Book about which He would question them on the Day of Resurrection while they do not know its meaning. It is true that some may not know it, but those firmly rooted in knowledge must know it, or else the proof would be void. So it is necessary to know this Book sent down upon the Messenger ﷺ. But if we say that ta'wil is what the matter ends up as, and what it actually is in reality, which is unknown to us, then here it is necessary to pause at His saying: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾.

Know that many people who spoke about creed explained the ambiguous text as the verses of the attributes. They said: the ambiguous verses are the verses of the attributes. But there is no doubt that explaining the ambiguous verses as the verses of the attributes absolutely is neither correct nor sound, because the verses of the attributes are known and unknown at once: in terms of meaning they are known, and it is not possible that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, would address us and speak to us about Himself with a matter unknown from which we gain nothing, and for us it would be no more than the letters of the alphabet, which have no meaning. This is absolutely impossible. Yes, they are unknown from another aspect, which is the reality and the modality (kayfiyyah) they have. This is unknown to us. We do not know how the hand of Allah is, and we do not grasp its reality. We do not know how the face of Allah is, and we do not grasp its reality. We do not grasp the reality of Allah's knowledge, and we do not grasp the realities of all His attributes, because Allah says: ﴿and they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha 110]. Whoever claims that the verses of the attributes are ambiguous in an absolute sense has erred, and the obligatory position is what? The obligatory position is detail. We say: if you mean by their being ambiguous the ambiguity of the reality they have, then you are correct; but if you mean by ambiguity the ambiguity of meaning, that their meaning is unknown to us, then you are gravely mistaken. Some people have gone to this view and said: the verses and hadiths of the attributes are unknown; we do not know them, and the Messenger ﷺ did not know them, nor Abu Bakr, nor 'Umar, nor 'Uthman, nor 'Ali, nor Ibn Mas'ud, nor Ibn 'Abbas, nor the jurists among the Companions, nor the jurists among the Successors, nor the imams of Islam; all of them do not know what they mean. You say to him: What is the meaning of "istawa 'ala al-'arsh" (He rose over the Throne)? He says: "Allah knows best." What is the meaning of the hand of Allah in His saying: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ [al-Ma'idah 64]? He says: "Allah knows best." What is the meaning of: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [ar-Rahman 27]? Allah knows best. Everything: Allah knows best. Everything related to the attributes of Allah, he says: Allah knows best. Strangely, this view is at the extreme of falsehood, even though some people think it is the madhhab of Ahl al-Sunnah, or the madhhab of the early scholars, to the point that the matter led them to this false statement: "The way of the early scholars is safer, and the way of the later scholars is more knowledgeable and wiser." This statement and this claim are among the most false claims: that the way of the early scholars is safer while the way of the later scholars is more knowledgeable and wiser. Rather we say: the way of the early scholars is safer, more knowledgeable, and wiser. The point is that some people think the madhhab of the early scholars is delegation (tafwid), not knowing the meaning, and not speaking about it, even the Prophet ﷺ, according to their claim, says: "Allah laughs at two men, one of whom kills the other, and both enter Paradise"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2826) and Muslim (1890/128) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. If you asked him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the meaning of 'laughs'?" He would say: "I do not know!" "Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1145) and Muslim (758/168) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. If you asked: "What is the meaning of 'descends'?" He would say: "I do not know." I am amazed how the tongue of a person can be sound who claims that this is the madhhab of the Companions, the Successors, and their followers until the Day of Resurrection! This is far from the truth!

So we say: the verses of the attributes are ambiguous in the reality and modality they have, because a human being is a mortal who cannot grasp these magnificent attributes; but in meaning they are clear and known, hidden from no one. We all know the meaning of knowledge, we all know the meaning of istiwa', we all know the meaning of the face, the meaning of the hand. For this reason, Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, stated his well-known saying transmitted from his teacher: "Istiwa' is not unknown, the modality (kayf) is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."
* A student: O Shaykh, ambiguous in reality and not ambiguous, how is it ambiguous in reality? Do you mean in terms of indication (dalalah)?
* The Shaykh: How many questions remain?
* The student: No, it is not a question, just a comment on the same verse.
* The Shaykh: Yes! I said: if you understood, say yes.
* A student: Yes, O Shaykh, we do not want this type, but there are some things as he mentioned.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but if I say: Did you understand? and one of you says: yes, and the rest remain silent, it means they all understood. The one who does not understand must, no... If I say: I understood, it means my speech has ended. So if I say: Did you understand? and you did not understand, you must make it clear. I say for example: do we know the meaning of "eye" or not? But the reality of Allah's eye and its modality, is it known or unknown? Unknown. We do not know: our eyes are known, composed of multiple layers and veins, and such and such, known; but Allah's eye, you cannot say about it like that, it is unknown to you, right? So its reality is unknown; but the meaning of "eye," which is what sight and seeing occur through, is a known matter. Is the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, known to us in reality? No. The hand is known and the fingers are known, and grasping with the hand is known, and taking with the hand is known. Is that correct or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: But the reality of this hand and its modality, you cannot speak about it, and whoever claims knowledge of it is a liar. This is the meaning of realities: realities are one thing and meanings are another. Be assured that if we said we do not know the meanings of the verses of the attributes, we would lose thirty percent or more of the meanings of the Qur'an, because you hardly find a verse without a name of Allah or an attribute of His in it.

He says: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾. Who are those firmly rooted in knowledge? Those who are established and have reached its depth, the depth of knowledge; because rootedness originally means firmness and settledness. ﴿They say, "We believe in it"﴾, that is: we affirm it, the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih). As for the clear, it is evident that they believe in it, because they know its meaning and are at peace with it. As for the ambiguous, their belief in it is submission, and for this He said of it: ﴿all of it is from our Lord﴾, and it is absolutely impossible that there be any contradiction or conflict in it.

Here Allah divided the Qur'an into two categories, but in another place He made it one category, saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and paired (mathani), at which the skins shiver of those who fear their Lord﴾ [az-Zumar 23]. He said in another verse: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. This is the Book whose verses are made firm and then detailed﴾ [Hud 1], and He did not mention ambiguity. We say: this is also ambiguous, is it not? Because how can the Qur'an be described with attributes whose apparent meaning is contradictory? We say: those firmly rooted in knowledge know that there is no contradiction. They say: the ambiguity by which the Qur'an is described, when not paired with the clear, is meant to indicate ambiguity in perfection, excellence, and guidance; so it is ambiguous, all its verses are similar, all of them perfect in eloquence, all of them perfect in report, perfect in command and prohibition. So it is ambiguous in terms of what? In perfection, excellence, rulings, reports, and so on; clear. When the clear is mentioned without mention of the ambiguous, the matter is obvious: it is precise, free of contradiction, conflict, falsehood in reports, or injustice in rulings. When both clarity and ambiguity are mentioned, each is understood in a different sense: clarity is understood as what? As evidentness. When ambiguity is mentioned alongside clarity, the counterpart of ambiguity is what? The evident, the clear and manifest in meaning. So ﴿of it are clear verses (muhkamat)﴾, that is, manifest and plain; ﴿and others ambiguous (mutashabihat)﴾, whose counterparts are their opposites. Is it clear now?

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And none remembers except those of understanding﴾. The word "ma" is negating; ﴿yadhdhakkaru﴾ originally is "yatadhakkaru," but the ta was changed to dhal and assimilated into the other dhal, becoming ﴿yadhdhakkaru﴾. That is, none is admonished and benefits from the Qur'an except those of understanding, that is, the people of intellect, because "albab" is the plural of "lubb," and lubb is intellect. The intellect meant here is the intellect of perception or the intellect of conduct, or both?
* The students: It includes both.
* The Shaykh: It includes both, but the more important is the intellect of conduct. The intellect of perception, whose opposite is madness, and the intellect of conduct, whose opposite is foolishness. The one who is reminded by the Qur'an is the person whom Allah has given intellect by which he perceives things, and whom Allah has given right guidance by which he conducts himself well; this is the one who remembers. As for the one whom Allah has given intellect by which he perceives things, which is the intellect opposed to madness, but has not given him intellect by which he conducts himself well, which is the intellect opposed to foolishness, this one does not benefit from the Qur'an. Only the person of both perceptive intellect and practical intellect benefits.

In this noble verse there are many great benefits. First: that this Qur'an is the speech of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾. If someone said: this is challenged by ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [al-Hadid 25], and ﴿He sent down from the sky water﴾ [al-An'am 99]; do you say that iron is the speech of Allah, and that water is the speech of Allah?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No? All of you say no?
* The students: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: Why did you make this indicate that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah? We say: because speech is an attribute that does not subsist on its own; it subsists only in a speaker, unlike water and unlike iron, which are a self-subsisting entity, and thus are created. The Qur'an, however, is not created, because it is an attribute of the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, and the created is something separate from the Creator, distinct from Him. But speech is an attribute which is His act, so it is not created.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the loftiness (uluww) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since sending down can only be from above to below. If the Qur'an is His speech and it was sent down, then Allah is above, and so He is; this is the madhhab of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, indeed the madhhab of all the messengers, that Allah, the Exalted, is above everything. Have you not seen how Pharaoh said: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways (al-asbab) — the ways of the heavens — and look at the God of Moses﴾ [Ghafir 36-37]; and this indicates that Moses told him that Allah is above.
* The students: In the sky.

**Shaykh:** Exalted-ness (al-'uluw) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is established by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the consensus (ijma') of scholars, reason ('aql), and innate nature (fitrah). These are five types of evidence: the Book, the Sunnah, ijma', reason, and fitrah. As for the Book, its evidences are too numerous to count. They are varied: sometimes by mention of exalted-ness (al-'uluw), sometimes by mention of being above (al-fawqiyyah), sometimes by the descent of things from Him, sometimes by the ascent of things to Him, and sometimes by the mention of (fi) as in "in the heaven." The Sunnah is likewise widely transmitted (mutawatir) regarding the exalted-ness of Allah, and it is varied: sometimes by the words of the Messenger (ﷺ), sometimes by his actions, and sometimes by his tacit approval. As for his words: he used to say in every prayer, "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High" [Muslim (772/203) from the hadith of Hudhayfah]. As for his actions: he pointed to the sky on more than one occasion. He pointed to the sky when supplicating, raising his hands toward the sky. He also pointed to the sky when he called Allah to witness over his Ummah that they had acknowledged his conveying of the message. When was that?

**Students:** On the Day of 'Arafah.

**Shaykh:** On the Day of 'Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage, at the greatest gathering of the Muslims in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). As for his tacit approval: he asked the slave girl, "Where is Allah?" She said, "In the heaven." He said, "Free her, for she is a believer" [Muslim (537/33) from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam]. As for ijma': the righteous predecessors (al-salaf) from among the Companions, the Successors, and the leaders of guidance after them agreed that Allah, exalted is He, is above everything. None of them is reported to have said, "Allah is in every place," nor to have said, "Allah cannot be described as being above the world, nor beneath it, nor within it, nor outside it, nor connected to it, nor separate from it, nor distinct from it, nor in a direction." Never did anyone say this. As for reason: if we asked any person, "What do you say about exalted-ness: is it a attribute of perfection or of deficiency?" he would say, "It is an attribute of perfection." And reason says: every attribute of perfection is affirmed for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So exalted-ness is established for Allah by the evidence of reason from this aspect, or not?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** As for fitrah, speak and there is no blame. A person who has not learned and does not know what the scholars say about this, when he asks Allah, where does he raise his hands?

**Students:** To the sky.

**Shaykh:** To the sky. We have never seen anyone, when he wished to supplicate, place his hands on the ground, not ever, nor move them to the right or left. He raises them to the sky. For this reason, Abu al-A'la al-Hamadhani argued against Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni with this innate evidence (fitri), until al-Juwayni could not contain himself, cried out, struck his head, and said, "He has bewildered me." For Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni, may Allah forgive us and him, used to tell people, "Allah was, and nothing else was." Correct? Is this correct?

**Students:** Yes, correct.

**Shaykh:** "Allah was, and nothing else was," correct. He is the First, with nothing before Him, and He is now as He was. Look at this phrase, it is misleading. What does he mean by "and He is now as He was"? That is, He is not established upon the Throne, because the Throne did not exist, and Allah was when nothing else was. And He is now as He was. Therefore He did not istawa (rise/settle) over the Throne. So Abu al-'Ala al-Hamadhani said to him, "O Master, leave aside mention of the Throne, for istiwa' upon the Throne has a non-rational evidence; it is neither rational nor innate. The istiwa' upon the Throne has a textual (sam'i) evidence, because had Allah not informed us that He istawa upon the Throne, we would not have known that, nor would we know about the Throne all that we know of it. Inform us about this necessity that we find in our souls. No one who knows Allah has ever said, 'O Allah!' without finding in his heart a necessity to seek exalted-ness. Everyone who asks Allah says, 'O Allah!' Where does his heart go? To exalted-ness." Then al-Juwayni cried out, struck his head, and said, "He has bewildered me," because he had no answer to this innate nature (fitrah).

So the exalted-ness of Allah, all praise is His, is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, ijma', reason, and fitrah. Were it not for the statements of those whom the devils have led astray, a person would never dream or think that Allah, exalted is He, is in everything, in every place. Never! It would not even cross his mind. Nor would he think that we deny Allah every attribute, saying, "Not above the world, nor beneath it, nor to the right of the world, nor to its left, nor within the world, nor outside the world, nor connected to the world, nor separated from the world." Where would He go? Nowhere, I seek refuge with Allah! What is strange is that these people think they are glorifying Allah, yet if they were told, "Describe for us nothingness," they would find no better description than this. We ask Allah not to make our hearts swerve. So the exalted-ness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is established by five types of evidence. These are not individual items, whose instances cannot be counted; rather, their types are five: the Book, the Sunnah, ijma', reason, and fitrah.

**Student:** Among the mutashabih (ambiguous verses) are the opening letters of the surahs (...)?

**Shaykh:** What do you all say about this? He says: among the mutashabih are the opening letters of the surahs?

**Student:** I say: some of them are.

**Student:** That is not correct.

**Shaykh:** Yes, I say this is incorrect.

**Student:** Are not all the surahs' openings mutashabih?

**Shaykh:** No, he says: all the openings of the surahs are mutashabih. The openings of surahs that are the alphabetic letters.

**Student:** The disjointed letters (al-muqatta'at).

**Shaykh:** Yes. We say this is incorrect, because we know that these letters have no meaning in themselves. We know this from the Qur'an. Allah says: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in clear Arabic speech﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193–195]. Clear Arabic speech does not give these letters a meaning. Therefore they have no meaning; they are clear.

**Student:** Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding His words ﴿seeking discord﴾, we said: meaning turning people away from the way of Allah. What is meant by ﴿seeking its interpretation (ta'wil)﴾?

**Shaykh:** The scholars said: the meaning of ﴿its ta'wil﴾ is its tafsir (interpretation) contrary to what Allah intended. That is, they want to interpret it in a way Allah did not intend, whether or not people were thereby led into discord. This leads to doubts in their own souls; they themselves also become doubtful about it.

**Student:** Would its meaning not also be according to the two views? That is, either "seeking its ta'wil" means the goal, or the interpretation is among them in disagreement, from His words: ﴿and none knows its ta'wil except Allah﴾.

**Shaykh:** Yes, it is known necessarily. It cannot be interpreted except in this sense. That is, my intention is that they seek its ta'wil, which none knows except Allah. They say about what none knows except Allah: we say nothing about it, we refrain from it. Not "yes, we will interpret it" even if they interpret it contrary to what Allah intended. Never! Rather, they follow the mutashabih so that they can tell people, "Look, the Qur'an contradicts itself!" Or they bring verses whose meaning is not clear, then interpret them as they wish.

**Student:** Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, if we say that "seeking its ta'wil" means they distort it contrary to the intention of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, do we not take from this verse that ta'wil comes with distortion?

**Shaykh:** That will come to us, God willing, in the benefits.

**Student:** Allah says: ﴿Say: none in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [al-Naml 65]. Here, is the exception connected (muttasil)?

**Shaykh:** The exception? There is no doubt. This is an exhaustive exception (istithna' mufarragh), because ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject.

**Student:** An exception from whom?

**Shaykh:** He says: none knows except Allah, like: there is no god except Allah. This is an exhaustive exception; that is, no one knows except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Student:** (...) Shall we say it is an exception (...) none knows from whom except Allah?

**Shaykh:** The exhaustive exception is meant to restrict.

**Student:** The ta'wil here, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** It seems to you that there is confusion about ﴿whoever is in the heavens﴾. Even if we said ﴿whoever is in the heavens﴾, Allah is in the heaven as He said about Himself, so Allah is above everything. It is exhaustive, not a connected exception. That is, it is not an exception from a connected stated antecedent. "None knows the unseen except Allah." ﴿Say: none in the heavens and the earth knows...﴾ No, this is not an exception. I said "exhaustive" incorrectly. This is a correct exception, an exception from a complete negated statement. So the meaning is: none in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah. This is a substitute (badal) for (man). The badal, as the grammarians said, is the follower that is the intended object of the ruling. When it is the follower that is the intended object of the ruling, the meaning of the verse becomes: none knows the unseen except Allah. That is the analysis of this.

**Student:** So (Allah) is excepted from (man)?

**Shaykh:** From (man). But since it is a badal, and it is in the nominative case now, it is a badal. Since it is a badal, it is the intended object of the ruling. So it is as if: none knows the unseen except Allah. This is the explanation.

**Student:** Ta'wil, Shaykh, and tafsir: does the knowledge of Allah equal the knowledge of ﴿those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ regarding tafsir?

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** Ta'wil and tafsir?

**Shaykh:** No, no. They are not equal, but they know from the tafsir what they cannot do without.

**Student:** So then, none knows it except Allah.

**Shaykh:** Or they may not know the tafsir of everything. Even scholars now: you find some of them derive two benefits from a verse, some three, and some more. But what they cannot do without from these mutashabih, they know.

**Student:** So the Qur'an says ﴿they do not know﴾, meaning the knowledge Allah knows.

**Shaykh:** What they cannot do without, they must know. But the realities (al-haqa'iq), they do not know.

**Student:** Shaykh, istiwa' in the Arabic language is known. But if a person wanted to translate it into another language for people who do not know Arabic, would tashbih (likening Allah to creation) occur?

**Shaykh:** No, it is for clarification. There is no objection. That is, if we do not know, or if we want to make clear that istiwa' means exalted-ness, we point to someone and say: like something above something, like a person's istiwa' upon a camel, in meaning only, not in modality (kayfiyyah). There is nothing wrong with it.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. We raised an objection to this, namely that Allah said: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾ [al-Hadid 25], and He said: ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah 22]. We answered this, did we not?

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this Qur'an is divided into muhkam (clear) and mutashabih (ambiguous) verses, based on His words: ﴿In it are clear verses, they are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous﴾ [Al 'Imran 7]. We mentioned that this division raises an issue, since Allah mentions in another verse that the whole Qur'an is mutashabih, and in another verse that all of it is muhkam. We mentioned the reconciliation. Right?
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to refer the mutashabih to the muhkam, based on His words: ﴿they are the mother of the Book﴾, meaning: its reference. This, that is, referring to the muhkam when the mutashabih exists, is not specific to the Qur'an; it applies even to the Sunnah. If there are ambiguous hadiths and clear hadiths, it is obligatory to return the ambiguous to the clear so that all becomes clear. Whether the ambiguity is in the meanings of wording or in the authenticity of a report. The latter applies specifically to the Sunnah, because the Qur'an has no ambiguity regarding its authenticity. Or the ambiguity may be in the statements of the scholars, meaning that most of the scholars hold one view while it is ambiguous to you regarding the evidences. The truth is generally with the one who is most trustworthy and closest to the Book and the Sunnah, whether by knowledge, by trustworthiness, or by number.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in making the Qur'an divided into two categories. The wisdom is that by this, trial and testing occur. The believer is not misled by this division, but the one in whose heart is deviation is misled. This is like how Allah tests His servants with commands and prohibitions; He also tests them with evidences. He makes this clear and that ambiguous, so that the believer is distinguished from the non-believer. If the whole Qur'an were muhkam, no trial would occur. If the whole Qur'an were mutashabih, no clarification would occur. Allah, glorified and exalted, made the Qur'an a clarification, and made it muhkam and mutashabih for testing and examination. Have you understood now?
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the signs of deviation is that a person follows the mutashabih of the Qur'an, whether he follows it in his own understanding, to the point that he raises ambiguous verses for himself, or he follows it by presenting the Qur'an to others. He says to people, for example, "What do you say about such and such?" and brings ambiguous verses without resolving them. For this reason, it is a great danger to present to students or to the general public ambiguous verses without clarifying the resolution of their difficulty, because by doing so you cast them into bewilderment and doubt, and you become like one who throws a person into a sea he cannot escape, and does not rescue him. This happens with some of the pretentious students of knowledge: they present ambiguous verses and then stop. They stop and do not explain to people the aspect of this ambiguity, so they throw people into bewilderment without realizing it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those who follow the mutashabih sometimes seek discord and turning people away from their religion, and removing trust from their hearts regarding the Qur'an, based on His words: ﴿seeking discord﴾. And sometimes they intend by this, that is, by presenting this ambiguity, to distort it into the meaning they want. That is because if they wanted to distort the muhkam, they would not be accepted. Right? But they bring the mutashabih in order to be able to distort it as they wish. Because if it is ambiguous, the one they address may be confused about the matter and accept the distortion they bring. By this, the difficulty that may arise for a person in His words ﴿and seeking its ta'wil﴾ [Al 'Imran 7] disappears. Because seeking the ta'wil in the intended way is a required matter, and it is not the concern of those with deviation; it is the concern of people of faith. But those with deviation bring this mutashabih in order to distort it as they wish, because it is not clear and muhkam, so that people could refute them. Rather, it is ambiguous, and by that they achieve their distortion.

And here is a question: many speakers of kalam (theology) said that the verses of the attributes are among the mutashabih, and they said that the mutashabih's ta'wil is known only to Allah. The result was that the meanings of the verses of the attributes are not known. Therefore they said that the correct position regarding the verses of the attributes is tafwid (delegation of meaning). Pay attention to the meaning. Their claim that the truth is tafwid, and that you should not speak about them with anything, results from two matters: first, that the verses of the attributes are mutashabih; second, that the mutashabih's ta'wil is known only to Allah. The result is that we should not delve into the meanings of the verses of the attributes, because they are mutashabih and their ta'wil is known only to Allah, and what cannot be reached by knowledge may not be delved into. But we say: this position is false. First, we say: what do you mean by the mutashabih, or what do you mean by the ambiguity in the verses of the attributes? If they say, "We mean ambiguity of meaning," which is what they intend, we say: this is wrong. Why? Because the meanings of the verses of the attributes are clear and known, and there is no ambiguity in them at all. As Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The istiwa' is not unknown." It is not unknown to anyone; rather it is known, known to everyone. "He istawa upon the Throne" means He rose above it. There is no difficulty. If they mean by ambiguity the ambiguity of the reality and modality, they are truthful, but they do not mean this. Because if they said, "We know the meaning but are ignorant of the reality and modality," we would say: this is a correct position. But they say: we are ignorant of the meaning, the modality, and the reality. For this reason they are called "the people of delegation" (ahl al-tafwid) and "the people of ignorance" (ahl al-tajhil), because they say that all verses and hadiths of the attributes are unknown to anyone, and that our reading of them is like a non-Arabic speaker reading Arabic discourse, or an Arab reading a non-Arabic discourse, or like reading the alphabetic letters (alif, ba', ta', tha') to the end. This is their view regarding what? Regarding the verses of the attributes. And it is, without doubt, a mistaken view. How could we know the meaning of the verses of ablution, prayer, and sale, and similar matters that are nothing compared to the attributes of Allah, yet be ignorant of the meanings of the verses of the attributes, which are more deserving of knowledge than others, and without which worship cannot truly be fulfilled except through knowing the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?

Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on Sūrah Āl ʿImrān, verse 7 (part 4 of 4)

We say: If you mean that the reality (ḥaqīqah) of these attributes, the way they actually are, cannot be known, then we say: You are right. But if you say that their meaning cannot be known and that they are unintelligible, then this is an error. So if someone asks, "Are the verses about the divine attributes among the ambiguous (mutashābih) verses?", we say: It is not correct to answer with an unqualified yes or no. Yet you will find in the books of usūl al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that when they want to give an example of the ambiguous, they say, "Like the verses about the attributes." This is an error, because a distinction is necessary. If they mean semantic ambiguity (al-tashābuh al-maʿnawī), then this is wrong. Rather, these verses are among the clear, decisive (muḥkam) verses. If they mean that the reality is unknown, in that we do not know the modality (kayfiyyah) of these attributes and cannot encompass it, then this is true. But they do not mean this; they mean the first.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of being firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rusūkh fī al-ʿilm). And what is the meaning of "firmly grounded in knowledge"?
* The students: Steadfastness.
* The Shaykh: Steadfastness in it, and going deep into it until one reaches its roots, based on His saying: ﴿And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it"﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:7). The opposite of being firmly grounded in knowledge is superficiality in knowledge, and how much superficiality there is among us today. Most people today have superficial knowledge. That is why, when they author or write, you find them quoting excessively, saying "So-and-so said, and so-and-so said, and so-and-so said," because they do not have a real grasp of the subject. A person who lacks a firm grasp cannot express himself, so he gives himself license in speech, cites "so-and-so said," and argues for you one full aspect or more. But if you return to the people of knowledge, the true people of knowledge, you will find that they speak from knowledge within their own hearts without quotation. That is why you sometimes find their expressions differing from the expressions of other scholars. Among the clearest and most evident examples are the books of Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah and his student Ibn al-Qayyim. You will find that they speak from firmly rooted knowledge, and their like is many. But the point is that this is among the clearest things I have come across: firm knowledge makes a person as if knowledge springs forth from his heart. As for the superficial one, who is merely a shade over the head, the benefit to his student is small.

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: a person should be eager to be firmly grounded in knowledge, not merely to accumulate much of it, because what counts is firmness in knowledge. When a person has firm knowledge, he acquires a faculty by which he can bring parts of knowledge close to one another and analogize what has not been explicitly stated to what has been stated, and knowledge becomes for him like a settled nature.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: those firmly grounded in knowledge know that what comes from Allah contains no contradiction, based on His saying: ﴿They say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord"﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:7).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is part of the requirement of Lordship (rubūbiyyah) that Allah, exalted is He, send down to His servants a Book in which there is no discrepancy that would cause them doubt and confusion, based on their saying: ﴿all of it is from our Lord﴾. Whatever comes from the Lord who cares for His servants through His lordship will not contain anything contradictory or discordant.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: no one takes heed from this Qurʾān or from anything else except people of intellect, based on His saying: ﴿And none will be mindful except those of understanding﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:7).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the more a person's intellect increases, the more he takes heed from the speech of Allah, exalted is He. And whenever his remembrance of the Qurʾān diminishes, that indicates a deficiency in his – what – intellect? Because if Allah has restricted remembrance to those of understanding, this implies that such remembrance is absent from one who lacks understanding.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: intellect is not the same as intelligence (dhakāʾ).
