"And You take sovereignty away from whom You will." His saying "You take away sovereignty" (tanzi'u al-mulk) may have two meanings. The first: removal after established possession. The second: prevention, in the sense of withholding. On the first meaning, it indicates that Allah grants sovereignty to whomever He wills among His creatures and then takes it away from him. How many kings have ruled and then their sovereignty ended, either by being overcome, or by death, or otherwise? It may also mean prevention: You give sovereignty to whom You will and You withhold it from whom You will. Both meanings are correct. Allah may withhold sovereignty from a person, and He may take it away after it was established for him. Both are correct.

So sovereignty is in Allah's hand. He gives it to whom He wills; this one He makes a ruler, and that one He does not. This one is made a ruler and then deprived of it, and this one is made a ruler and remains so until Allah takes him in death.

"And You take sovereignty away from whom You will." But this also happens by wisdom. It may be that the one from whom sovereignty is taken was unfit for rule, being among those who spread corruption in the land, so that someone is empowered over him to remove it from him. Or it may be that this ruler was weak, not desiring corruption, but weak and unable to establish reform, so someone is empowered over him to remove his sovereignty. This is common in history, if you reflect on it. Allah the Exalted does nothing except for a wisdom.

"You honour whom You will, and You humble whom You will." Here "honour" (i'zāz) means strengthening: You make him mighty and strong, overcoming others. Likewise "You humble whom You will." Is this necessarily tied to sovereignty, so that You honour whichever kings You will and humble whichever kings You will, or is it general? It is general. Allah may honour a person through his religion, knowledge, and faith even if he is not a king, and He may honour him through his kingship. Likewise in humbling: He may humble a person through sin or through being overcome. Humbling through sin is the opposite of honour through faith, and humbling through being overcome is the opposite of honour through kingship. The point is that honour and humiliation do not necessarily entail kingship, and kingship does not necessarily entail them.

Who does Allah honour? Allah honours the one whom He mentioned in His saying: "And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers" [al-Munafiqun 8]. So honour belongs to Allah, but this has no bearing on the verse here. Yet those whom Allah honours are the messengers and their followers, as Allah said: "Allah has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail. Indeed Allah is Powerful and Mighty" [al-Mujadila 21]. So among the causes of honour is faith, whether the person is a king or not. Among the causes of honour are readiness, caution, resolve, strength, and vigour. All of these are causes of honour, but these are material, sensory causes, while faith is a spiritual cause. Faith may also have as its fruit and result that a person becomes strong and resolute, looking at affairs through the lens of wisdom, and thus honour is obtained for him.

He said: "You honour whom You will, and You humble whom You will." Allah humbles whom He wills, among those to whom He gave sovereignty and among those to whom He did not give it. Perhaps a person is a king but is humble, weak, and afraid, fearing everything, with no resolve, strength, or vigour. Allah the Exalted may humble a person even in his kingship, and He may humble one who is not a king.

Among the causes of humiliation is that a person is self-admiring and exposes himself to what he cannot repel. These are two things: self-admiration may forsake him and humble him, and exposing himself to what he cannot repel may also be a cause of his humiliation and abandonment. Many people fall into both. Many people speak or act without attention to seeking help from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and so they are forsaken. Many people expose themselves to matters they cannot repel, great matters beyond their level, and then they are forsaken and humiliated. For this reason it has been reported in a narration: "It does not befit any of you to humble himself." They said: "How does one humble himself?" He said: "By speaking of what he cannot repel" [al-Tirmidhi (2254) and Ibn Majah (4016) from the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman], or words to this effect. A person should not expose himself to humiliation through a reasonable cause, or a moral cause, or otherwise. The first is being self-admiring, saying a statement or doing an act without attention to seeking help from Allah. The second is exposing oneself to matters one cannot repel, matters greater than one's level. Suppose someone speaks of jurisprudence while not knowing jurisprudence, speaks of grammar while not knowing grammar, or speaks of the principles of jurisprudence while not knowing them; his humiliation will appear before people. For this reason a person should be careful in his speech, so that he does not fall into the net of humiliation.

"And You humble whom You will. In Your hand is all good." Good is in the hand of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Good is everything that contains benefit and advantage for the servant, whether in the matters of this world or of the Hereafter. So provision, health, and knowledge are good, and righteous deeds are also good. Everything from which a person benefits in his religion and his worldly life is good, and all of this is in Allah's hand, as He said: "Whatever blessing you have is from Allah" [al-Nahl 53].

Here He mentioned that good is in His hand, and He did not mention evil, although good is from Allah and evil is from Allah. Some exegetes said that this is from the category of omitting the known counterpart, like His saying: "And He made for you garments to protect you from the heat" [al-Nahl 81]. They claimed that the implied meaning of the verse is: "In His hand is good and evil." But this is a false notion, and this is not a context of omission, restriction, or economy. The context is one of praise, and in praise it is appropriate to expand and elaborate. Omission is inappropriate in wording and false in meaning, because evil is not attributed to Allah. It is not permissible to say: "In His hand is evil," because it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "And evil is not attributed to You" [Muslim (771/201) from the hadith of 'Ali]. So evil is not attributed to Allah, either in speech or in act. Allah speaks the truth, He guides to the way, He does good, and He does not do evil. When evil is found in created things, it is evil from one aspect and good from another aspect. But Allah's bringing into existence these evil things is not evil; rather it is good, pure good. So Allah's act contains no evil at all. Evil is in the things made, not in the acts. Good is in both the things made and the acts, and therefore it is attributed to Allah. One does not say "In His hand is good" and then also say "evil is to Allah."

Let us give an example of this: beasts of prey and venomous creatures. Beasts of prey have evil in them, and stinging and biting creatures have evil in them without doubt, and satans are all evil. Yet Allah's bringing these things into existence is good, a good that is unavoidable, which wisdom requires. For one cannot know the full extent of Allah's power except by creating opposing things. Furthermore, in creating these things there is the reform of the servant, his turning to his Lord, and his seeking refuge in Him from these evil matters, which is abundant good. Moreover, good is only known by its opposite. Good cannot be known except when its opposite is known, so that the measure of good may be understood.

Furthermore, creation must undergo a test. It must undergo a test. If it were always in good, the test would cease, because it would always be in good. When evil exists, the test becomes clear. If a person were always in health, always wealthy, always sensible, and always in ease, no test would occur, and he would not know the value of blessing or thank Allah for it. But when he is afflicted with illness, he knows the value of health; with poverty, he knows the value of wealth; with fear, he knows the value of security; and so on.

So the existence of these things has great benefits, and their bringing into existence is therefore good and not evil. Yet in themselves they contain evil. Likewise, the existence of destructive things like earthquakes, storms, floods, and similar things is evil in themselves, but they contain great good, so their bringing into existence is good and not evil. Therefore we must keep the verse on its apparent meaning without estimation, namely His saying: "In Your hand is all good," and no evil is attributed to Allah. As for created things, there is no doubt that they contain good and evil.

"Indeed, You are over all things competent." Indeed You are over all things competent. Among Your power is the changing of these great matters: giving sovereignty, removing it, honouring, and humbling. All of these are great matters that none can accomplish except the One who is capable of them, the Glorified and Exalted.

His saying "Indeed, You are over all things competent" is general. He is competent over all things, over what He wills and over what He does not will. He is competent over what He wills and over what He does not will. He is competent to bring into existence what He does not will, and He is competent to bring into existence what He wills if it is restricted to a time, and to annihilate it if it exists. The point is that Allah is competent over all things, over bringing the non-existent into existence and annihilating the existent, whether He wills it or does not will it. From this we know that restricting God's power by His will, as some people do, is an error. Those who say "He is competent over what He wills" are wrong, because Allah is competent over what He wills and over what He does not will, but what He wills cannot be beyond His ability. With this last estimation, that what He wills cannot be beyond His ability, the answer to His saying the Exalted becomes clear: "And He is, when He wills, competent to gather them" [al-Shura 29]. The will here does not refer to the power, but to the gathering. That is, if He wills to gather them and wills their gathering, He is competent over it and cannot be incapable of it.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. "You cause the night to enter the day, and You cause the day to enter the night. You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living. And You provide for whom You will without account" (27). "Let not the believers take disbelievers as allies rather than believers. And whoever does that has nothing with Allah, except when you fear from them a precaution. And Allah warns you of Himself, and to Allah is the destination" (28). "Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it. And He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and Allah is over all things competent" (29). [Ali 'Imran 27–29.]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 26–27 (part 2 of 3):

* Among the benefits of this verse, firstly: Allah, mighty and majestic, teaches His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to entrust the matter to Him in His saying: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty"﴾. The address directed to the Messenger (ﷺ) is also directed to his community, either through emulation (ta'assi), or because he is the imam (leader), and address to the imam is address to him and to those who follow him, unless evidence indicates that it is specific to him, in which case it is specific to him.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the complete dominion and authority of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, in His saying: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty"﴾. Every kingdom belongs to Allah, its Owner. It has already been mentioned to us that the word "mulk" (sovereignty) is meant either as the thing possessed or as the class of sovereignty.
* Also among its benefits: that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, gives sovereignty to whom He wills, in His saying: ﴿You give sovereignty﴾.
  Also among its benefits: that the sovereignty of created beings is not independent sovereignty, but is by way of grant; as indicated by His saying: ﴿You give sovereignty﴾. Sovereignty that is by way of grant is undoubtedly less than the sovereignty of the One who grants it. And there has come in the authentic hadith: "The upper hand is better than the lower hand"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1427) and Muslim (1034/95), from the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam.]].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's will in His saying: ﴿whom You will﴾. Every matter that Allah has coupled with His will is founded upon wisdom whenever it calls for it, and He wills it. The evidence for this is the saying of the Most High: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the complete dominion and authority of Allah also lies in His making sovereignty humiliated whom He wills and removing it, after it has been established, from whom He wills; as in His saying: ﴿And You remove sovereignty from whom You will﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: also a demonstration of the complete dominion and authority of Allah in that might is from Him: He honours whom He wills. But it has already been mentioned to us in the exegesis that might has causes, among them faith, as the saying of Allah, the Most High, states: ﴿And to Allah belongs might, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [Al-Munafiqun 8].
* Also among its benefits: that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, has complete dominion and authority in that He humbles whom He wills, however far human might may reach. Indeed, the hand of Allah is above him, however much a person may attain of honour; Allah is able to humble him. There are many examples of this, among them the story of Pharaoh: Pharaoh transgressed and oppressed, and said, "I am your lord, the Most High," and boasted of the rivers he possessed; so Allah destroyed him by the very thing he boasted of, water, and he drowned. As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land and said, "Who is stronger than us?" So Allah destroyed them by the wind, which is among the gentlest of things, yet among the most severe of things despite its gentleness. So Allah, mighty and majestic, humbles whom He wills.
  It follows from this benefit that, when we know that honouring and humiliating are in the hand of Allah, we do not seek might except from Him, mighty and majestic. For this reason we say: whoever seeks might from other than Allah is humiliated; might is sought only from Allah.
  It also follows from this: that a person should always seek refuge in Allah from physical and moral humiliation, because Allah, the Most High, is the One in whose hand is humiliation; He humbles whom He wills and honours whom He wills.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, has good in His hand.
  It follows from this benefit: since good is in His hand, one should seek good only from Him, for no one holds good in hand except Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala; so it is He from whom good is sought.
* Among its benefits: that evil is not attributed to Allah, although He, mighty and majestic, is the One who created everything. But evil is not attributed to Allah. Why? Because all His actions are good, and evil lies in the things that are affected (al-maf'ulat). Then this evil in the affected things may itself be good even in those things: how many an illness has become a cause of the body's health, and how many blights in crops and other things have become causes of economic growth from another angle, for example. The essential point is that evil is not attributed to Allah, because all His acts are good, subhanahu wa ta'ala.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's power, in His saying: ﴿indeed, You are over all things Competent﴾. This includes both His actions and the actions of creation. In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, who say that Allah does not create the actions of His servants nor will them, and that man is independent in his will and his deeds. We say: is this by the power of Allah or not? If they say: not by the power of Allah, then they have denied the generality of the saying of the Most High: ﴿indeed, You are over all things Competent﴾. And if they say: by the power of Allah, we say: then it must follow that it is what? Willed and created by Allah; for since the matter is by His power, it must be created by Him and willed by Him.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of a statement made by some exegetes, including Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, in the saying of the Most High: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things Competent﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 120], where he said: "[The verse] specifies His Essence, so He is not Competent over it." This is a false statement. He intended a meaning, and Allah knows best, but the expression is wrong. We say: Allah, the Most High, is Competent over everything that relates to His action or the action of His servants. Everything Allah does is by His power, subhanahu wa ta'ala; everything the servants do is also by His power. This exception or specification is not correct; rather, reason itself testifies to Allah's perfection, or to the generality of His power, and that He is over all things Competent.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: sufficiency of praise in place of supplication. For if you reflect on this verse, you will not find in it a supplication, that is, a request. But praise is something by which one draws near to Allah. It has already passed for us that supplication is sometimes by mentioning the condition of the one supplicating, sometimes by praising Allah, sometimes by both, and sometimes by request alone, and all of this has come in the Sunnah. Here, praise includes what these sentences indicate: when you say, "You are the One who honours and You are the One who humbles," the meaning, or the implication, of this is that you are asking Allah to honour you and not to humble you. For this reason the poet said:
  When a man praises you one day, / his praise suffices him from asking you [the poet's line].
  That is: his praise of you suffices instead of his seeking and asking.
  Then Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾. He said: ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾, that is, You cause the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night; meaning that the night enters upon the day, so the night increases and the day decreases; ﴿You cause the day to enter into the night﴾, conversely, the day enters upon the night, so the day lengthens and the night shortens. This act is one of those that none can do except Allah alone; He is the One who causes the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night.
  Yet this entering is with wisdom, gradually: it comes little by little until it ends, then returns. What would you think if the night leapt from the shortest night to the longest? The order of the world would be disrupted and the world corrupted, and its times would be spoiled. But Allah, mighty and majestic, makes it gradual so that people may know their times. Also following from this entering is the change of seasons: when the day lengthens, the time the sun is on the surface of the earth lengthens, and the atmosphere becomes hot; and the sun's rays are also perpendicular, so they have a stronger effect on heat than when they are not perpendicular. The reverse is true for winter. Thus the seasons' times result from this entering.
  And from the mercy of Allah, mighty and majestic, is that this seasonal change does not come all at once. What would you think if people moved from the hottest day of the year to the coldest day? Great harm! Or the reverse? But the Merciful Lord, mighty and majestic, the Wise, brings this about gradually. Who can add an hour to the night or an hour to the day? No one can. Even if the whole nation, all creatures, gathered to add an hour to the night or an hour to the day, they would not find a way to do so.
  As for His saying: ﴿You bring the living out of the dead﴾: ﴿al-mayyit﴾ in both places has two readings: ﴿al-mayt﴾ and ﴿al-mayyit﴾, that is, with and without shaddah.
  ﴿You bring the living out of the dead﴾: is the intended meaning "the living" (al-hayy) sensory life, or moral life, or both? The third is the intended meaning, because the word is suitable for both meanings; and when a word is suitable for both meanings without contradiction between them, it is obligatory to take it in both senses.
  "The living" in sensory life has many examples: man is created from a drop (nutfah), which is dead in the linguistic sense, and then becomes living from inanimate matter. Hence the Most High said: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then give you life again﴾ [Al-Baqarah 28]. You were in your fathers' loins as dead, having no spirits; then the spirit was breathed into man and he became living.
  So: the living comes out of the dead, that is, He makes the dead living, as the Most High said: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 14]; or He brings forth a living, growing, moving thing from something that does not grow, which is dead, like the chick emerging from the egg, for the egg is dead and a living chick emerges from it. This is sensory death and sensory life.
  Moral: the living comes out of the dead, that is, the believer from the disbeliever, because the believer is living with heart-life, and the disbeliever is dead. The living, the one who knows, comes out of "the dead," the ignorant, as the Most High said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness and cannot emerge from it?﴾ [Al-An'am 122]. The first is the knowledgeable, the second the ignorant. This is moral life and sensory life.
  He said: ﴿And You bring the dead out of the living﴾. The dead out of the living, in terms of sensory life, like the egg from where? From the hen: dead from living. And what else?
* A student: Semen from the man.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: If it falls...
* The Shaykh: The dead from the living, yes, and it may refer to the dead when it falls from a living thing; that is, a woman who miscarries a dead fetus, which comes out, although this fetus does not move, but it comes out by the power of Allah, who drives it until it emerges.
* A student: Grain from the tree.
* The Shaykh: Grain? Yes, grain from the tree. Grain does not grow while the tree grows, and this is a particular life, vegetative life.
  Moral: the disbeliever comes out of the believer, and the ignorant comes out of the scholar. Is that right?
  He said: ﴿And You provide whom You will without account﴾. ﴿You provide﴾: You give. ﴿whom You will without account﴾: that is, without return, for accounting only occurs with exchange; one who does not want a return is not held to account. But one who wants a return is the one who is held to account, so that he knows whether what he took is in exchange for what he gave or not. As for one who does not need a return, or who takes no return, he is not held to account.
  So ﴿You provide whom You will﴾ without return; but the accounting that implies exchange, or whose consequence is exchange, is denied. Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, gives without return. How numerous are the blessings He has bestowed upon us, yet He does not hold us to account; He gives us of His bounty and generosity. And if He commands us to give thanks and we thank Him, this is a second gift: a person's thanks to his Lord for His blessing is itself one of His blessings. For this reason the poet says:
  If my thanks is a blessing from Allah / upon me, for which thanks is due in return for a like of it...
  How, then, can thanks be fulfilled except by His bounty, / even though days lengthen and life continues?
  Let me repeat the two lines:
  If my thanks is a blessing from Allah / upon me, for which thanks is due in return for a like of it...
  How, then, can thanks be fulfilled except by His bounty, / even though days lengthen and life continues?
  And the third time:
  If my thanks is a blessing from Allah / upon me, for which thanks is due in return for a like of it...
  How, then, can thanks be fulfilled except by His bounty, / even though days lengthen and life continues?
  Let us hear it.
* A student:
  If my thanks is a blessing from Allah / upon me, for which thanks is due in return for a like of it...
  How, then, can thanks be fulfilled except by His bounty, / even though days lengthen and life continues?
* The Shaykh: The meaning of the two lines is clear: that if Allah enables you to thank for His blessing, this blessing needs thanks; when you thank for it, that thanks needs further thanks, and when you thank for the third, it needs a fourth, and so on. For this reason he said: How, then, can thanks be fulfilled except by His bounty, even though days lengthen and life continues?
  So He says: ﴿You provide whom You will without account﴾, that is, You give whom You will without account. Know that the provision of Allah, mighty and majestic, is of two kinds: provision by which the body is sustained, and provision by which the heart and spirit are sustained. The first includes the believer and the disbeliever, the righteous and the sinner, the obedient and the wicked, and even animals. What is it? The provision by which the body is sustained. This is common to everyone; even the disbeliever is provided for. Does it include the unlawful? Yes, it includes the unlawful: even one who eats and drinks only unlawfully is provided for by Allah. It is provision, but it is provision by which the body is sustained.
  The second is that by which the heart and spirit are sustained, and this is specific to people of faith and knowledge. Allah provides them with what sustains their hearts and spirits, which is knowledge, for knowledge is to the heart what water is to a tree: it cannot grow without it. Faith is likewise: the heart cannot stand or be set right except by faith, and the more the heart increases in faith in Allah, the more it is set right.
  So provision is of two kinds: general and specific. The general is that by which the body is sustained; the specific is that by which the heart and spirit are sustained. Thus whoever Allah provides with what sustains the heart and spirit has also been provided with what sustains the body; but not everyone provided with what sustains the body has been provided with what sustains the heart and spirit.
  He said: ﴿You provide whom You will without account﴾, and the phrase ﴿whom You will﴾ is to be understood as stated before: that is, whom Your wisdom requires You to provide.
  The causes of provision are many: either an action by the person, or a supply from Allah. Action itself benefits only with a supply from Allah. But sometimes a person is provided without earning or working, such as when a relative dies and he inherits from him, or when he goes out to the desert and gathers firewood, though this too is a kind of work. Sometimes work and trade must be practised; all of these are causes of provision.
  Indeed, among the causes of provision is the fear of Allah (taqwa). Taqwa does not mean that you sit confined in the mosque and worship; taqwa is more general than that. One who strives on behalf of the widow and the needy, going and seeking provision for them and looking after them: the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "The one who strives for the widow and the needy is like the one who fights in the way of Allah"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5353) and Muslim (2982/41), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. So is this religion or not? Striving for the widow and the needy: he goes into the land of Allah seeking provision for these widows and needy. Everyone who does not earn is a needy person, even if he is one of your children; even if you are rich and this son does not earn, he is needy, and when you strive on his behalf, you are like the one who fights in the way of Allah. He said, and I think he said: "like one who fasts without breaking his fast, and like one who stands in prayer without tiring"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5353) and Muslim (2982/41), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
  So the fear of Allah is not that a person clings to the mosques; the fear of Allah is that a person performs obedience to Allah of whatever kind it may be, and even seeking provision for those whose support is obligatory upon you counts as the fear of Allah, mighty and majestic.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the completeness of Allah's power and authority, mighty and majestic, in that He causes the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 26–27 (part 3 of 3):

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of God's wisdom, for this interchange (iljaj) carries a great wisdom upon which the interests of creation cannot be sustained except by it. For there results from this interchange, as we have said, the difference of the seasons of the year, upon whose difference the growth of bodies and plants depends. Among plants there are those that are winter plants, and among them those that are summer plants.
* Among the benefits of this also: a person recognizes through it his weakness and his need for his Lord. If cold comes, he seeks what will warm him; if heat comes, he seeks what will cool him. So he is in need of his Lord in both states. Is it clear? And this is among the benefits of the difference of heat and cold.
* Among its benefits also, and this branches off from it: there are harmful things, which is what is referred to in medical science as germs (jarathim), which only the intensity of cold kills, and others which only the intensity of heat kills. This is something observed. This too is among the wisdoms of Almighty God that result from the interchange of night into day and day into night.
* Among the benefits of that (i.e., the interchange of night into day and day into night): this interchange indicates the perfection of power, as we mentioned at first, for no one can add an hour of the night to the day or the reverse, but God Most High is the One who has power over this.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the completeness of God's power and sovereignty in bringing forth the living from the dead and bringing forth the dead from the living. The reason for this is evident, for the one who is able to bring a thing out of its opposite is proof that his power is complete and his dominion is effective, glorified and exalted is He.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that provision is in God's hand, based on His saying: ﴿And You provide for whom You will﴾. And from this follows that it is fitting for the intelligent person, let alone the believer, not to seek provision from people's hands, but to seek it from Almighty God. For this reason the texts have come with the virtue of chastity (iffah), that a person abstain from what is in people's hands and not ask.
"Among the things the Companions, may God be pleased with them, pledged to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was that they would not ask people for anything. So a whip of one of them would fall from his camel, and he would dismount to the ground to pick it up and would not say: 'Hand it to me.'"[[Recorded by Muslim (1043 / 108) from the hadith of 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i.]] Because they pledged not to ask people for anything, and this undoubtedly leads a person to turn to whom? To God Almighty, he turns to God, (...) a person asks what is permissible for him to ask; rather, the completeness of chastity is not to ask people for anything, but to leave the matter entrusted to God Almighty.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that God's giving is without return, based on His saying: ﴿without reckoning﴾. So Almighty God does not sell you the fruit you eat, or the garment you wear, or the house you dwell in. No, rather He provides and gives without reckoning. Every blessing we have is from God.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of God's will (mashi'ah), in His saying: ﴿whom You will﴾. It has already passed with us in the study of tawhid that God has will and volition (iradah), that will (mashi'ah) admits no division, while volition is divided into cosmic (kawniyyah) and legislative (shar'iyyah). As for will, it is cosmic, for God Most High wills everything.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 28 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾. ﴿Let not take﴾: (*lā*) is a prohibitive particle (*nāhiyah*). The evidence that it is prohibitive is that the verb after it is in the jussive mood (*majzūm*), is it not? But why is the verb vowelled with a kasra? It is vowelled with a kasra because of the meeting of two consonants at rest (*iltiqā' al-sākinayn*), so that the tongue can move from the vowelled letter to the resting letter easily. For this reason, the most suitable vowel when two resting consonants meet is the kasra. The kasra is most suitable in ﴿let not take﴾, because the kasra involves a lowering, so that the tongue can rise from the vowelled letter to the resting one.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies﴾, meaning: let them not make them allies and so take them. The word (*ittakhadha*, "to take") indicates adopting a thing, inclining towards it and seeking refuge in it, like your saying: "I have taken this as a companion", meaning: I made him my companion, adopted him and chose him. So the meaning is: the believers should not choose the disbelievers as allies apart from the believers.

As for His saying ﴿the believers, the disbelievers﴾, how does (*al-kāfirīn*, "the disbelievers") take the accusative when it comes after a nominative noun?

* Students: It is an object (*maf'ūl bihi*).

* Shaykh: Can it not be an adjective (*na't*)? No, it cannot be; the meaning would differ enormously. ﴿The disbelievers﴾ is the first object of (*ittakhadha*), and ﴿allies﴾ is the second object.

As for His saying ﴿the believers﴾ and ﴿allies﴾: do they take them as allies from above, or as allies from below, or both? It includes both, meaning: they should neither support them nor seek support from them. They should not make the disbelievers their allies, nor give the disbelievers authority over them. The prohibition covers both, except, as will come, Allah willing, in what is excepted.

However, when the matter is one of ease and the believers are strong, it is still not permissible for them to take from among the disbelievers someone who will support them, because the disbelievers, however hostile they may be to the Muslims, ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than yourselves; they will not spare you [from] ruin. They wish you would suffer; hatred has appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 118]. So we have no right to seek help from the disbelievers except when need calls for it. We may then seek their help, by taking weapons and similar things, and even by a covenant with them. For the Prophet (ﷺ) borrowed armour from Safwān ibn Umayyah, and he said to him: "Is it seizure, O Muhammad?" He said: "Rather, it is a loan that will be returned." [Reported by Abū Dāwūd (3562) and al-Ḥākim in al-Mustadrak (2332) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās.] This indicates the permissibility of seeking help from a polytheist with weapons. For example, if we take weapons, what is it to us and him? We are the ones who use the weapons and train with them.

Likewise, the Prophet (ﷺ) made an alliance with Khuzāʿah, as in the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyyah. [Reported by Ibn Abī Shaybah in his Muṣannaf (37899) from the hadith of ʿIkrimah.] He made an alliance with them. But at that time the people were not in a position of strength. Therefore it is also permissible for the Muslims to make an alliance with the disbelievers when need calls for it, because this may be in the interest of the Muslims. If the Muslims are weak, other disbelievers will dominate them; so if they make an alliance with strong disbelievers, they gain support through them, and there is benefit in that.

The essence of the prohibition on allying with the disbelievers is so that Islam is not humiliated before them. Therefore, when such matters serve the interest and strength of the Muslims, they become permissible. This is with regard to seeking support through them.

This is with regard to seeking support through them. We have mentioned that His saying ﴿allies﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 28] includes both aspects. As for supporting them, this is never permissible: it is not permissible under any circumstances for us to support a disbeliever against a believer. But is it permissible to support a disbeliever against a disbeliever when the interest requires it?

We say: the believers rejoiced when the Romans overcame the Persians, though both were disbelievers, a victory of disbelievers over disbelievers, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah. He grants victory to whom He wills﴾ [al-Rūm 4–5]. So if there is an enemy common to us and to this group of disbelievers, and we know that if we do not support the disbelievers against this disbeliever he will overcome them and then destroy us, then aiding them in that need is permissible. We are aiding them not for their own sake because they are disbelievers, but for the interest of the Muslims. All of this returns to the interest. But if we see a disbeliever asking us for help against a Muslim, this is not permissible under any circumstances. For this reason He said: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 28], meaning: those other than the believers who oppose the believers and ally with the disbelievers. This is impossible. This is why the verse says ﴿Let not the believers take﴾ and does not say "Do not take," because Allah distinguished between His saying ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾ and the case where the believers take the disbelievers as allies not apart from the believers. In the second case, He addressed the believers directly, not in the first: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies﴾ [al-Mā'idah 51]; ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 1]. So He addressed them directly. But here He said: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾. Thus He differentiated between them. Some scholars have said this, and they said: Allah did not address the believers directly here, because this is a shameful matter, and in a shameful matter direct address would be a severe shock. This is why Allah said to the Messenger: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him﴾ [ʿAbasa 1–2], and He did not say "you frowned." This view is what a person first thinks is good. But a difficulty arises from His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. Do you want to give Allah a clear case against you?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 144]. Here He addressed them directly, although He said ﴿rather than the believers﴾. Accordingly, the explanation mentioned by some contemporary scholars is open to question. We say: Allah used the third-person form here, ﴿Let not the believers take﴾, instead of direct address, for an eloquence known to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which we may or may not know.

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾. Have I answered the questions?

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, I say: the question of useful books from some of the brothers...

* Shaykh: Your question. Delete the *mīm* here, delete the *mīm*, may Allah reward you with good.

* Student: I say, may Allah be good to you: the question of useful books from some of the brothers, does it contradict complete chastity (*ʿiffah*)?

* Shaykh: If he is saying: asking for books on loan, borrowing, what about that?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Borrowing, or possession?

* Student: Borrowing, to read them.

* Shaykh: No, borrowing is permissible, there is no problem with it.

* Student: But I take it, photograph it for example, or read it and return it?

* Shaykh: It appears that photocopying is of the category of borrowing. Taking it, reading it and returning it is borrowing. But asking for it as one's own property, that is what is blameworthy. As for borrowing, the Muslims have always borrowed. The Prophet (ﷺ) borrowed armour from Safwān ibn Umayyah. [Reported by Abū Dāwūd (3562), and Aḥmad (15302, 27636) from the hadith of Safwān ibn Umayyah.]

* Student: But if, for example, he has several copies and I do not have one, and in the market it is not available, and I buy it?

* Shaykh: Buy it.

* Student: Yes?

* Shaykh: Buy it from him.

* Student: If he says, "I will not sell"?

* Shaykh: Say: "Lend it to me."

* Student: Meaning, a loan?

* Shaykh: Yes, a loan, there is nothing wrong with that.

* Student: But I do not take it for a day or two; it is a large travel book that I need to keep as a reference to benefit from, and so on?

* Shaykh: I do not see that.

* Student: But the Prophet, Shaykh, said: "Seek help from Allah and be eager for what benefits you"? [Reported by Muslim (2664/34) from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.]

* Shaykh: What?

* Student: I say...

* Shaykh: Yes, and among what benefits you is that you do not ask people for anything.

* Student: But what benefits me is not in this book.

* Shaykh: Even the thief says: "By Allah, I only steal because it benefits me."

* Student: Shaykh, the context of His saying "without reckoning"?

* Another student: Shaykh, there are people among the Muslims now who take American citizenship?

* Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. Taking the citizenship of disbelievers is forbidden, because what this citizenship requires is: that you be allied to those they ally with, hostile to those they oppose, and that you support them in everything, even against the Muslims. This is forbidden and never permissible.

* Student: Shaykh, His saying: ﴿And You take the living from the dead﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 27]. We said, Shaykh, that it brings the knowledgeable out of the ignorant. And His saying, Exalted: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ [al-Anʿām 122]? But His saying ﴿and You bring the dead out of the living﴾: bringing the ignorant out of the knowledgeable, the reverse. How is that? Does it mean that he forgets the knowledge?

* Shaykh: No, its meaning is: a man who is a scholar whose children are ignorant.

* Student: No, in the first meaning, ﴿Is one who was dead﴾, what is that?

* Shaykh: In the first meaning, that he was dead, this is not rejected. It is not rejected, and perhaps it is possible. No, the apparent meaning is not rejected.

* Student: Shaykh, in His saying, Exalted: ﴿You cause the night to enter the day and You cause the day to enter the night﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 27], does it include benefits such as the interest of plants and fruit, that some fruit only develops in winter, and the reverse as well?

* Shaykh: Did we not say this?

* Students: We said that this is an established benefit.

* Shaykh: We mentioned it.

* Student: Shaykh, if we seek help from the disbelievers...

* Shaykh: If what?

* Student: If we seek help from the disbelievers in terms of equipment and weapons, is seeking help from them permissible, correct or not?

* Shaykh: (...)

* Student: If the disbelievers seek help from us, knowing that Islam... we cannot say they are divided into Sunnis and Shiites. If they seek help from us, and we have no equipment to give to the Shiites, is it permissible?

* Shaykh: This requires consideration. If the Shiites are of a kind that makes them disbelievers, then it is permissible. If they are not of a kind that makes them disbelievers, it is not permissible, because a Muslim, however sinful he may be, is not permitted to help a disbeliever against him.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. And whoever does that has nothing with Allah, except when you fear from them a fear. And Allah warns you of Himself, and to Allah is the destination. Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it. He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and Allah is over all things competent. On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between it and that were a great distance. And Allah warns you of Himself, and Allah is kind to the servants﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 28–30].

* Shaykh: Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿You cause the night to enter the day and You cause the day to enter the night, and You bring the living out of the dead﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 27]. What is meant here by *al-walāyah* (guardianship, allegiance)?

We said: He does not seek support through them, nor for them. As for the prohibition of supporting them, the matter is clear. But the prohibition of seeking support through them is problematic, because the Prophet (ﷺ) made an alliance with Khuzāʿah, who were disbelievers.

* Student: If the interest requires defending the Muslims, for example against a neighbour, and the interest requires seeking their help, we seek help.

* Shaykh: Yes. We say: when the interest or necessity requires seeking help through them, there is no harm in it. Let us complete this discussion because it is important. Suppose someone says: if seeking help through them is not for the interest of Islam, but because these people are enemies of whoever wants to attack the Muslims, so they support the Muslims because this is a common enemy; that is, they did not support the Muslims for the sake of God or to establish the religion of God, but because the enemy is common. Is it permissible for us to seek their help in this case?

* Student: Yes, we seek their help, but not for the sake of supporting the disbelievers, rather for the interest of the Muslims.

* Shaykh: We say: yes. If they support us, whether that is for God or not for God, definitely, or because our enemy and theirs is one common enemy, understood? Nevertheless, it is not permissible for us to make this seeking of help through them at the expense of our religion; that is, to flatter them and allow them to commit their ugly acts in our lands, the lands of Islam. No, because this is flattery (*mudāhanah*), and flattery in the religion of God is forbidden and not permissible.

He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾. This is the reality: a believer cannot ally himself with a disbeliever rather than with the believers. Later, Allah willing, in the benefits (*fawā'id*) it will come that those who do this are the hypocrites. ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. Do they seek honour with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 139].

Then He said: ﴿And whoever does that﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 28]. The referent of "that" is the taking, and the reference here returns to what is understood from the verb, because the verb indicates an event and an agent, the event and its agent. The event here is the taking, and the agent is the believer. So we say: the pronoun refers back to the taking understood from what? From (*yattakhidh*, "takes"). Like His saying: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [al-Māʾidah 8], where it refers back to justice understood from the word ﴿Be just﴾. ﴿And whoever does that﴾, meaning: who takes them as allies rather than the believers, ﴿then he has nothing with Allah﴾, meaning: Allah is free of him, because Allah, Exalted, does not approve that any of the believers should ally with any of the disbelievers, since the disbeliever is an enemy of Allah; indeed, he is also an enemy to you. ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 1]. Whatever the case, the disbeliever can never harbour love or allegiance for you, and he can never support you except for his own interest, because he is an enemy, and an enemy cannot want the benefit of his enemy. For this reason He said: ﴿then he has nothing with Allah﴾, meaning: Allah is free of him, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Then He said: ﴿except when you fear from them a fear﴾. The word (*illā*, "except") here is undoubtedly a particle of exception, but is this exception connected (*muttaṣil*) or disconnected (*munqaṭiʿ*)? The correct view is that it is disconnected, indeed it is required, because in a state of *taqiyyah* (fear-based precaution) we do not take them as allies, but we agree with them outwardly and oppose them inwardly. Also, look at ﴿except when you fear﴾: it means that these disbelievers have control, power and capability that we fear, so we guard ourselves against them, that is, we take a shield against their violence and their punishment of us. But this is outwardly only, not inwardly. So be aware: this is not permissible except in a state of fear for oneself, and when the Muslims are weak and the disbelievers are strong.

Second: this allegiance must be only with the tongue, outwardly. As for inwardly, we must hold enmity and hatred towards them and not be allied to them. His saying ﴿except when you fear from them a fear﴾ contains a shift (*iltifāt*) from the third person to the second person, and the address is to those present, because without the shift He would have said: "except when they fear from them a fear." The shift has been mentioned before, and it has benefits. Who will mention them?

* A student: A general benefit of every shift is alerting the listener, and a specific benefit for each context...

* Shaykh: Yes. The general benefit is alerting the listener. This means alerting the one being addressed, because when speech follows one pattern, a person keeps going along with it without paying attention. When the pattern changes, he pays attention. This applies to every kind of movement, whether mental or physical. If you are walking and find a pit in the road, you notice it. If you find a raised step in the road, you notice it. Isn't that so? The same applies to speech. If you were speaking in one unvarying pattern as a preacher, your sermon would put people to sleep. But if the sermon includes commands, prohibitions, questions, presentations, and urgings, this creates an alert, an alert for the listener. Likewise, in the Qur'an, God, glorified and exalted be He, sometimes shifts from the first context to a new context in order to alert the listener. As for the second benefit, it is restricted according to the contextual indicators.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. ﴿Believers should not take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Whoever does that has nothing to do with God, unless you are protecting yourselves against them out of caution. God warns you about Himself, and to God is the final destination (28). Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, God knows it. He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and God has power over everything (29). On the Day when every soul will find what it did of good present before it, and what it did of evil, it will wish there were a vast distance between it and that. God warns you about Himself, and God is Kind to His servants﴾ [Al 'Imran 28–30].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Believers should not take disbelievers as allies instead of believers﴾. Here, is (lā) a negation particle or a prohibition particle?

* Student: (lā) is a negation particle.

* Shaykh: A negation particle?

* Student: A prohibition particle.

* Shaykh: A prohibition particle? What is the evidence?

* Student: The evidence for jazm (apocope/jussive) is that it put the verb in the jussive, and it changed the jazm into sukūn because of the meeting of two sukūns.

* Shaykh: It changed the jazma into sukūn?!

* Student: It changed the sukūn into a kasra because of the meeting of two sukūns.

* Shaykh: Wrong.

* Student: It changed the sukūn into a kasra because of the meeting of two sukūns.

* Shaykh: Wrong.

* Student: The dhāl was vowelled with a kasra because of the meeting of two sukūns.

* Shaykh: Wrong.

* Student: It was vowelled with a kasra because of the meeting of two sukūns.

* Shaykh: It was vowelled with a kasra because of the meeting of two sukūns.

* Student: I say: there is no dispute over terminology!

* Shaykh: No, no, there is no dispute over an error! Because when we say of ﴿lā yattakhidh﴾ that it was vowelled with a kasra, it means that this kasra is not a kasra of i'rāb (grammatical inflection). It is not a substitute for sukūn. Rather, it was vowelled only phonetically, for the ease of moving from a vowelled letter to an unvowelled one, because moving from one sukūn to another sukūn is an abbreviation (ikhtiṣār).

* Student: But, Shaykh, it was replaced (ubdilat). Is that not correct?

* Shaykh: No, no. Because ibdāl (replacement) means that it actually and judicially takes the place of the original. Its ruling is sukūn, but it was vowelled only for vocalization.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿ʾawliyāʾ min dūni l-muʾminīn﴾. What made ʾawliyāʾ (allies) accusative?

* Student: It is the object of ﴿yattakhidh﴾.

* Shaykh: The word al-kāfirīn is the object of ﴿yattakhidh﴾. ﴿Believers should not take the disbelievers﴾.

* Student: It is the second object of ﴿yattakhidh﴾.

* Shaykh: It is the second object of ﴿yattakhidh﴾, yes. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿min dūni l-muʾminīn﴾. What does dūn mean here?

* Student: Other than the believers.

* Shaykh: Other than the believers. I think we did not complete the verse?

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does that has nothing to do with God﴾. What is its meaning? What is the meaning of the sentence ﴿wa-man yafʿal dhālika fa-laysa mina llāhi fī shayʾ﴾?

* Student: That is, whoever takes disbelievers as allies instead of believers, God, glorified and exalted be He, is not pleased with him, so he is not among His allies, that is.

* Shaykh: Yes. What required the particle fa- in His saying ﴿fa-laysa﴾?

* Student: That it is the apodosis of a conditional.

* Shaykh: How?

* Student: ﴿Whoever does that has nothing to do with God﴾ is the apodosis of a conditional.

* Shaykh: And in the apodosis of a conditional, is the fa- omitted?

* Student: Shaykh, the joining of fa- with the apodosis of a conditional.

* Shaykh: Is the joining of fa- with the apodosis of a conditional obligatory?

* Student: If it is laysa (...).

* Shaykh: That is, if he were reciting the Qur'an, it would be permissible to omit the fa-?

* Student: Shaykh, it is a nominal sentence.

* Shaykh: It is not a nominal sentence.

* Student: Shaykh, because the apodosis here is a rigid (jāmid) verb, so it is obligatory to join it with fa-.

* Shaykh: That is, it begins with a rigid verb, and when the apodosis begins with a rigid verb.

* Student: It is obligatory to join it with fa-.

* Shaykh: Fine. Do you have a witness or a well-known statement on this?

* Student: Some of them said, reconciling the requirement of joining fa- with:

*Nominal, imperative, and with a rigid verb,
and with mā, qad, lan, and with the tanfīs (sa/sawfa).*

* Shaykh:

*Nominal, imperative, and with a rigid verb,
and with mā, qad, lan, and with the tanfīs.*

Fine. Which of the seven types is this?

* Student: The rigid verb, this is the rigid one.

* Shaykh: Rigid, that is to say.

* Student: Yes, a rigid verb that does not inflect.

* Shaykh: Yes, it does not inflect. Well done. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿illā an tattaqū minhum tuqāh﴾. What is the meaning of His saying ﴿tattaqū minhum tuqāh﴾?

* Student: That is: that you protect yourselves from their harm.

* Shaykh: Except that you say something by which you protect yourselves from their harm. Is the exception here disjunct (munqaṭiʿ) or connected (muttaṣil)?

* Student: Disjunct.

* Shaykh: Disjunct, yes, correct. That is to say, but if you protect yourselves from them with some caution, like one forced into disbelief whose heart remains firm in faith, this is nothing and does no harm.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿illā an tattaqū minhum tuqāh﴾. It is said tuqāh and it is said taqiyyah. As for tuqiyyah, it is a common lahn (grammatical error) in their saying tuqiyyah. This is a common lahn, because if we said tuqiyyah, it would have to be changed into tuqāh according to the well-known morphological rule. On this basis, we say: the correct form is tuqāh or taqiyyah.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿wa-yuḥadhdhirukumu llāhu nafsah﴾. In ﴿yuḥadhdhirukum﴾ there is a verb and an object. The word Allah is the subject, and ﴿nafsahu﴾ is the second object. ﴿yuḥadhdhirukumu llāhu nafsah﴾ means: He frightens you about Himself, glorified and exalted be He, and warns you of His punishment if you take them as allies, except in the situation where your alliance with them is out of caution and not by choice and intention.

﴿wa-yuḥadhdhirukumu llāhu nafsahu wa-ilā llāhi l-maṣīr﴾: That is, the return (al-marjiʿ). This sentence, as you can see, is a nominal sentence in which the predicate was placed first for the purpose of restriction: that is, to God and not to anyone else. Al-maṣīr means the return. And what return is this? Is the intended meaning the return in the Hereafter, or the return in all matters?

The answer: the return in all matters, as God, the Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿wa-ilā llāhi turjaʿu l-umūr﴾ [Al 'Imran 109]. So to God is the maṣīr, meaning after departing from this world. And to God is the return in all states and all matters.

In this noble verse there are the following benefits:

First: the prohibition of taking disbelievers as allies, by His saying: ﴿Believers should not take disbelievers as allies instead of believers﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the requirement of true faith is that a person takes disbelievers as enemies. His saying ﴿Believers should not take﴾ attaches this ruling to the believers, and this is evidence that the requirement of their faith is that they should not take them as allies, but rather that they should take them as enemies. For these disbelievers are the partisans and allies of Satan, and God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party to be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fāṭir 6].

* Among its benefits: that taking disbelievers as allies is contrary either to faith at its root, or to the perfection of faith. That is, it contradicts either the essence of faith or its completeness. Why? Because when a ruling is attached to an attribute, it follows that attribute in strength and weakness. Whenever faith is perfected, hostility is perfected and loyalty is removed. When loyalty exists, faith weakens, and when faith weakens, loyalty also exists.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that believers must take allies from among the believers, by His saying here: ﴿min dūni l-muʾminīn﴾. There is no doubt that this is the requirement of faith. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Tawbah 71]. So it is obligatory for the believer to take allies from among the believers.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that taking disbelievers as allies is one of the major sins (kabāʾir). The basis of this inference: God disassociated Himself from them, and attaching a ruling, or attaching disassociation to a ruling, indicates that it is one of the major sins. Kabāʾir is the plural of kabīrah. The best of what has been said in defining it is: that for which a specific punishment has been prescribed. This is because prohibited acts are of two types: either they are forbidden, but there is no specific punishment for the one who does them, so these are minor sins (ṣaghāʾir); or a specific punishment is prescribed for doing them, and in that case they are major sins. But just as minor sins vary, so that some of them approach the major ones, so too major sins vary. Severing ties of kinship between an uncle and his nephew is not like disobedience to one's parents, even though each of them is one of the major sins. The important point is that major sins vary, and so do minor sins.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that God, glorified and exalted be He, is the Ally of the believers. Its basis: whoever takes disbelievers as allies and abandons the believers, God disassociates Himself from him, because he is not among the believers in any way, so God has nothing to do with him. This has witnesses in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Your ally is only God, His Messenger, and those who believe﴾ [al-Mā'idah 55], and His saying: ﴿God is the Ally of the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 68], and His saying: ﴿God is the Ally of those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 257]. The verses with this meaning are many: God, the Exalted, is the Ally of the believers, so He allies with whoever allies with them, and He opposes whoever opposes them. It is authentically related in a hadith from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he related from his Lord that God, glorified and exalted be He, said: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him."[[Narrated by al-Bukhārī (6502) from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.]]

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the ease and facility of Islam, for it lifted hardship from the Ummah. This is by permitting taqiyyah (protective dissimulation) when there is need for it, by His saying: ﴿except that you protect yourselves from them out of caution﴾.

Among the benefits of the verse: that it is not permissible to flatter the enemies of God or to show approval of what they are doing, by His saying: ﴿except that you protect yourselves from them out of caution﴾. It is well known that taqiyyah is not permitted except in cases of necessity, and even then, the person must intend by it what? That it is a protection against what is feared from them, not approval of what they have done or reassurance in it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that God, the Mighty and Majestic, despite His perfect mercy, its comprehensiveness, and His love for repentance, in the context of warning uses severe and strong expressions, by His saying: ﴿God warns you about Himself﴾. This is because the situation calls for severity in this matter, for it is among the gravest things that believers take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. For this reason He said: ﴿God warns you about Himself﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the application of the word nafs (self) to the essence (dhāt), because the meaning of nafsahu is His essence: ﴿God warns you about Himself﴾, that is, His essence. Expressing it with nafs is better than expressing it with dhāt, although expressing it with dhāt is the well-known usage among the scholars. But using dhāt to mean nafs is not from classical Arabic, as Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah said. Rather, it is borrowed from a conventional (ʿurfī) terminology. Its origin is that dhāt is used in construct form, so one says: dhāt jamāl (possessing beauty), dhāt dīn (possessing religion), dhāt māl (possessing wealth), and similar expressions. They express by dhāt the entity characterized by attributes. Then they removed it from the construct and used the word dhāt unattached. This is the origin of the usage of the word dhāt. Otherwise, it is not purely Arabic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to return matters to God, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿and to God is the maṣīr﴾.

And among its benefits also: the repetition of the warning. When the situation calls for it, its repetition is among the highest kinds of eloquence, because His saying ﴿God warns you about Himself﴾ is a warning, and ﴿and to God is the maṣīr﴾ is also a warning, for it is a threat and a warning to whoever opposes what God has warned against.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

Then He said: ﴿Say: If you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾. ﴿Say﴾ is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), but there is no harm in someone who needs it saying it, even if he is not the Messenger, peace be upon him. ﴿What is in your breasts﴾: what is in the breasts is what the hearts harbour. He placed it in the breasts because the hearts are in the breasts, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts﴾ [al-Hajj 46].

His words ﴿If you conceal what is in your breasts﴾: concealing what? Everything: good or evil, enmity or loyalty, or other things. Everything that a person conceals in his breast, or reveals to whom? To people.

He said: ﴿or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾. ﴿Knows it﴾ is in the jussive mood as the answer to the condition in His words ﴿If you conceal﴾: Allah the Mighty and Majestic knows it. He, glorified and exalted is He, knows it before the breasts and what is in them were created, but He also knows it after it occurs in the breasts with knowledge of occurrence. As for His prior knowledge, it is knowledge of what will be. As for after a thing has occurred, it is knowledge of the thing after it has come into being. So with respect to what happens, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has two considerations concerning knowledge:
The first consideration: in terms of what will be. The second: in terms of what has been. With this explanation, the problem that occurs to the mind, and that many people raise, disappears regarding His words: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those who strive among you and the steadfast﴾ [Muhammad 31]. They say: Has not Allah the Mighty and Majestic known the strivers and the steadfast from others from eternity? The answer: Yes, but His knowledge from eternity is knowledge of what will be, and His knowledge after a thing has come into being is knowledge of it as existing, and there is a difference between the two. This is one aspect.

Another aspect: His eternal knowledge does not entail reward or punishment, whereas His knowledge of a thing after it has come into being is what entails reward and punishment. So the meaning of ﴿until We know﴾ is: knowledge that entails reward and punishment; otherwise Allah knew before He tested us.

He said: ﴿Allah knows it, and He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾. ﴿Knows﴾ (ya'lamu) is in the nominative case (raf') as a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), and the implied meaning is: and He knows. In such a construction the jussive is not permissible as a conjunction with ﴿Allah knows it﴾, unlike His words, the Exalted: ﴿And if you show what is in yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives﴾ [al-Baqarah 284], where it is permissible to say (fa-yaghfiru li-man yasha') and it is also permissible to say (fa-yaghfira), three possibilities. But in this verse only the nominative is permissible. Why? Because if we made it jussive, the knowledge of Allah of what is in the heavens and what is in the earth would become restricted by His words: ﴿Say: If you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it﴾; because what is conjoined to the answer of a condition has the ruling of the answer of the condition, and the answer of the condition is conditioned by what? By the verb of the condition. Accordingly, with His words ﴿and He knows﴾, the resumptive sentence and the nominative are required, and the jussive is not permissible.

﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾. ﴿What (ma)﴾ is one of the forms of the relative pronoun, or one of the relative nouns (al-asma' al-mawsulah). Every relative noun conveys generality, whether it is a plural form like ﴿those who (alladhina)﴾ and ﴿those (allati)﴾ [feminine plural], or a singular form like ﴿the one who (alladhi)﴾ and ﴿the one (allati)﴾ [feminine singular], or a common form like ﴿what (ma)﴾ and ﴿who (man)﴾. Accordingly, all relative nouns in their three categories convey generality. Have you not considered the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the one who brings the truth and confirms it﴾ [al-Zumar 33]. And where is the predicate? ﴿Those are the righteous﴾ [al-Zumar 33]. He made the predicate plural even though the subject is singular, because it is singular in form but general in meaning.

Here, ﴿what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾: I say that ﴿what (ma)﴾ is a relative noun conveying generality. So everything that is in the heavens is known to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and everything that is in the earth is known to Allah the Mighty and Majestic by His eternal, ancient knowledge. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven﴾ [Ali 'Imran 5]. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed: "Allah wrote the decrees of all things fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth"[[Recorded by Muslim (2653/16) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]]. And only what is known to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, is written.

﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and Allah is over all things competent﴾. He concluded the verse by stating the generality of His power, as an indication that Allah the Exalted has encompassed all things in knowledge and power, and that He is able to take vengeance upon you if you conceal what does not please Him, but in His wisdom He may delay the vengeance.

His words ﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾: the wording is general, as you can see: ﴿over all things competent﴾, whether that is among His actions or among the actions of the servants. He is competent over everything, whether He wills that thing or does not will it. He is competent over everything He wills and everything He does not will. And everything He wills, He is competent over. So we now have two generalities: the first generality is in power, so we say: He is competent over everything, whether He wills it or not. The second generality is in will: everything Allah wills, He is competent over, as came in the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi): "Indeed, I am competent over whatever I will"[[Recorded by Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]].

From this verse are the following benefits. First: the obligation to inform people that Allah the Exalted knows what is in their breasts, based on His words: ﴿Say: If you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾.

Among its benefits also: the generality of the knowledge of Allah the Mighty and Majestic regarding what a person conceals and what he reveals.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the intellect is in the heart, the reasoning is in the heart, and the will is in the heart, because He said: ﴿If you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it﴾. This matter is one on which the people of kalam (theology) differed: is the intellect in the heart or in the brain? But whoever reflects upon the Quranic verses finds that the intellect is in the heart. Indeed, whoever reflects upon the Quranic verses and the prophetic hadiths will find it; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth so that they would have hearts by which to reason?﴾ [al-Hajj 46] and ﴿For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts﴾ [al-Hajj 46]. This verse is an explicit text that the intellect is in the heart, and an explicit text that the word "heart" here does not mean the immaterial faculty in the brain. Rather, what is meant by the heart is, what? The true heart, the piece of flesh in the chest. For this reason He said: ﴿which are within the breasts﴾. And this speech is the speech of whom? The speech of the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, and the Creator knows best what He has created. However, there is no doubt that the brain has an influence, because the brain conceives a thing, arranges it and prepares it, then sends it to the heart and waits for orders. Then the heart issues orders to where? To the brain, not to the intellect; the intellect is in the heart. It sends to the brain, and the brain is a servant, a prince, obedient at all times, directing the orders to the soldiers, the limbs. Do not be surprised at this matter. How can you say that at this moment there is an issuing of orders and a reception? We say: Allah the Mighty and Majestic is competent over all things. So the brain conceives and arranges things, then sends them to the heart, and the heart commands or forbids. Then this brain executes immediately, without delay. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107) from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]].

As for what has become well known among physicians now, that the heart is merely a pump that purifies the blood and sends it out, receiving corrupt blood, cleansing it and sending it to the veins and arteries, this is not correct. For we say to them: Are you more knowledgeable or is Allah? There is no doubt that Allah is more knowledgeable, because He is the Creator. But we agree with you that the brain has an influence; however, the nature of its influence is that, by the permission of Allah, it is responsive to everything the heart commands.

* A student: Shaykh, do we want the Sunnah?
* The Shaykh: The Sunnah is this hadith we pointed to.
* A student: Those who bring in servants from the disbelievers, does this count as allegiance (muwalah) to them?
* The Shaykh: The question: those who bring in servants from the disbelievers, does this count as allegiance to them or not?
* A student: It depends on the person's intention, some people.
* The Shaykh: The apparent view is that it depends on this. If the intention of that employment is to exploit them and humiliate them, then it is humiliating them. If the purpose is to benefit them, that they benefit, then this without doubt is allegiance, because it is considered supporting them. These dirhams that leave our pockets for these disbelievers are taxed by them for their disbelieving states, so the states benefit from them and consequently use them to strike the Muslims. So the matter is in reality dangerous. But most Muslims today do not look at these issues with this careful scrutiny. They want only to get their worldly affairs going. But if they reflected on where these dirhams go! Then, you do not bring in a disbeliever except that you deprive a Muslim in place of the disbeliever. Bring a Muslim, and let the Muslim be less productive than the disbeliever. The matter is easy: "I benefit him and a family behind him that is Muslim and longing to find a loaf of bread." But we ask Allah to guide our brothers to consider these matters.
* A student: Shaykh, His words ﴿Say: If you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾: does it mean that whatever comes into my breast I will be held accountable for it in the verse?
* The Shaykh: No. Nothing indicates this except what a person inclines to and is at rest with.
* The student: How so?
* The Shaykh: That he insists upon it, resolves upon it, and intends to do it. But mere passing thought, no.
* A student: Shaykh, His words: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾. Some say it is with an omitted element: that Allah warns you of the punishment of Himself, because the essence itself cannot be feared. So if I say to a person, "He feared himself," and now we say: it cannot be conceived from himself, but from his actions?
* The Shaykh: When I say: "I warn you of yourself," everyone knows that it does not mean that the person (...) to the other. This is to make him stop. The meaning is: He warns you of what is in Himself of punishment. But this is more eloquent. Attributing the warning to the self is more eloquent than attributing it to the act. So if we say "the punishment of Himself," the warning is intensified, and if we say "Himself," it becomes stronger.
* A student: Shaykh, we said that allegiance to the disbelievers is among the major sins. Allah, glorified and exalted, says in the Noble Quran: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah 51]. So is this disbelief or one of the major sins?
* The Shaykh: We have said: it may be disbelief and it may be less than that.
* The student: How is the form that is less than that?
* The Shaykh: It may be that he takes them as allies in a worldly matter that is not for the sake of their religion, and not to assist them in their religion and disbelief. Then this is not disbelief; it is not disbelief. Suppose someone wishes to be kind to this disbeliever, wishes to honour him and give him money. This is not considered disbelief. And if we consider it allegiance, it does not remove him from Islam. But allegiance in the sense of support and assistance, whether he assists them against the believers, and we have previously mentioned that if they assist them against the disbelievers, the enemies of the Muslims, then there is no harm.
* The student: Shaykh, when I give a person money, does a bond of affection form between me and them?
* The Shaykh: No, not at all. They do not claim this.
* The student: Shaykh, so is it possible for me to give him without any affection or anything?
* The Shaykh: No, not at all. This is kindness, mere kindness (...). And Allah said: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being righteous toward them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 8].
* A student: Shaykh, some people dress in the manner of Christians or Jews. Does this count as allegiance?
* The Shaykh: He says: If I dress in the manner of Jews or Christians or other disbelievers, is this allegiance?
It is without doubt imitation (tashabbuh), which is agreed upon. But if by that he intends to honour them and raise their status, then it is allegiance, because he may imitate them in order to honour them and display their particular clothing and dress, and so this becomes allegiance.
* A student: They are doing heart transplant operations, Shaykh, from one person to another. Does the second person not get affected after the heart is transplanted to him, so that his creed changes and his thoughts change?
* Another student: You mean an artificial heart?
* The Shaykh: And what about the will? We raised this before and answered it, and an intelligent person understands the answer from my words.
* A student: (...) I say: what is transferred is the body, not the soul, and the accountability is in the heart, which is the soul in the heart, not the body.
* The Shaykh: No, he is not referring to the matter of accountability. He says: a person's thoughts do not change.
