As for the family of ʿImran: scholars differed about who is meant. It is said: the family of ʿImran, the father of Musa, because Musa is the most excellent of the prophets of the Children of Israel. And it is said: the family of ʿImran, the father of Maryam: ﴿and Maryam daughter of ʿImran﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:12]. He mentioned the family of ʿImran because among them is the last of the messengers before Muhammad ﷺ, namely Isa son of Maryam, to whom the Christians attribute themselves. He singled them out in this way, that is, He singled out the family of ʿImran, because the context also requires it. This Surah's beginning was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran, who were Christians. Whether this or that is the case, it indicates that Allah chose this lineage, the lineage of Abraham. So he is chosen from among the chosen: ﴿chose Adam and Noah﴾ is the first choosing; ﴿and Noah﴾ is the second; ﴿and the family of Abraham﴾ is the third; ﴿and the family of ʿImran﴾ is the fourth. These noble people of mankind were the ones He chose.

The meaning of choosing (istifaʾ) is that Allah selected them and preferred them over many of His creation with preference, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam and carried them on land and sea and provided for them of the good things and preferred them over much of what We have created, with [definite] preference.﴾ [al-Isra 17:70]. It is not over everything We have created, but ﴿over much of what We have created, with [definite] preference.﴾ I say: istifaʾ means ikhtiyar (choosing), because its root is from safwah (the best of something), and the safwah of something is its best part, and istafa means he took its best part.

As for His saying: ﴿over the worlds.﴾ Which worlds? Is it all of the world, or the worlds of animals? The first is the original meaning: that by "the worlds" is meant everything other than Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:2]. What follows from this difference will come, God willing, in the benefits.

As for His saying: ﴿offspring, one descended from another.﴾ "Offspring" (dhurriyyah) is in the accusative as a substitute for ﴿Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran.﴾ "Offspring" means these four categories are offspring, one descended from another. Dhurriyyah is derived from (dhara'a), meaning to create, as in His saying: ﴿He multiplies you through it﴾ [al-Shura 42:11], that is, He creates you. It is also said to be derived from (wadhara), meaning to leave. According to the first, dhurriyyah includes both ancestors and descendants, because the ancestors are created and the descendants are also created. But if we derive it from (wadhara), meaning to leave, then it refers only to descendants. This is the common understanding among people: that dhurriyyah are descendants, that is, those who arise from a person and whom he leaves behind after him. Is there anything in the Qur'an indicating that dhurriyyah is applied to ancestors? What?

**Student:** ﴿We will join them with their offspring﴾ [al-Tur 52:21].

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them﴾ [al-Tur 52:21].

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** The offspring of Adam and those whom We carried...

**Shaykh:** No. ﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ [al-Isra 17:3].

**Student:** His saying, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾

**Shaykh:** Yes, this one: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. (41) And We created for them from the like of it...﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:41–42]. Those who were carried as offspring were the ones who believed with Noah, and they were the foremost.

As for His saying: ﴿one descended from another.﴾ Is this in the kind of creation? Or ﴿one descended from another﴾ in deeds, manners, and morals?

**Student:** It includes both.

**Shaykh:** The apparent meaning is that it includes both. That is, all human beings are of one kind. There is no human who was originally a monkey, as the "brothers of the apes" say, and those who have confessed about themselves that they are apes. The human is originally human. Allah created his father with His own hand from the beginning. But they refused except to make themselves of the apes. So ﴿one descended from another﴾ refers to creation. From Adam until our day, creation has not changed except in the strength and bulk of the body. "Because Adam's height in Paradise was sixty cubits, and his breadth was also seven cubits, according to many hadiths" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3326), Muslim (2841/28), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (7933) from Abu Hurayrah]. This creation has diminished, decreasing until it reached this nation, and it ended there, because this nation is the last of nations.

It is not objected to that in some regions the human race is large and in others it is less. This is due to climate and heredity. But the principle is that we consider the last stage of the children of Adam, because we are the last of nations.

Likewise, ﴿one descended from another﴾ applies to manners, morals, and religions, except for those among them who were unjust and departed from this origin, for they go out by what they went out by.

﴿Offspring, one descended from another, and Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ He concluded the verse with hearing and knowledge, as a sign that everything these chosen ones say or do is known to Allah. He hears what they say and knows what they do. Indeed, He knows what they do not do of what is in their hearts. He even knows what they will do, even if it is not in their hearts, because Allah the Exalted knows what has happened, and what would happen if it were to happen, how it would be.

* In these two verses there are benefits.
* In the first: an explanation that Allah chose these creations over the rest of creation.
* Among its benefits also: that Allah may choose from His creation whatever He wills, as He said: ﴿Your Lord creates what He wills and chooses. They do not have the choice. Glory be to Allah, and exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ [al-Qasas 28:68].
* Among its benefits: just as preference exists in deeds, it also exists in essences. Just as preference exists in deeds and qualities, it also exists in persons. For this reason we say: the Arab race is more excellent than other races. But if this excellent race combines with it piety, it attains absolute excellence. If piety is absent, its origin is good but its deeds are wicked, and it becomes more wicked, because its origin was good and then it fell by itself to the lowest level. Whoever had a good origin and then descended by himself to the lowest level is more blameworthy than one who was not like that. Is this not so?

* **The students:** Yes.

* **Shaykh:** Therefore, if a free woman commits fornication, she is lashed one hundred lashes if she is unmarried, and stoned if she is married. If a slave woman commits fornication, she is not stoned even if she is married, and she is lashed fifty lashes, not one hundred, because there is a difference between a person whose origin is noble and honorable who then debases himself, and a person who was originally otherwise. This is indicated by the fact that people differ in their races, and Allah said in His Book: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:124]. Allah placed it among the Arabs in Muhammad ﷺ. So if Muhammad was the best and most noble of creation, it follows that the Arab race is the best, most excellent, and most noble of races. And this is so. It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The best of you in the pre-Islamic period are the best of you in Islam, if they gain understanding." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3374) and Muslim (2378/168) from Abu Hurayrah].

If someone says: What is the answer to His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:13]?

The answer: As for the answer to this noble verse, Allah the Exalted intended to erase what the people of pre-Islamic ignorance were accustomed to, namely boasting of lineage. He says: "I am from such-and-such tribe, I am from such-and-such tribe." So Allah clarified that these peoples and tribes were made by Allah for the purpose of mutual recognition, not for boasting, and that your boasting does not bring you closer to Allah. What brings you closer to Allah is piety: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.﴾ This does not negate that the Arab race is more excellent than others, as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah verified in his book Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim Mukhalafat Ashab al-Jahim, and his evidences are what you have heard.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse is what some scholars mentioned: that the righteous among mankind are more excellent than the angels. He said: because of His saying "over the worlds," and the angels are a world. So those chosen from among mankind are more excellent than whom?

* **The students:** The angels.

* **Shaykh:** Than the angels.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah Al 'Imran, verses 33–34 (part 2 of 2):

They cited other evidences, such as God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam, and others. In my view, inquiry into this question is among the superfluous (fudul) kinds of knowledge. What benefit do we gain if we say: "So-and-so is better than Jibril (Gabriel), or Jibril is better than so-and-so?" Or: "The righteous among the children of Adam are better than the angels, or the angels are better than the righteous?" We know that the angels are drawn near to God, ﴿They glorify Him night and day, and they never tire﴾ [al-Anbiya' 20], and that they are noble, ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording﴾ [al-Infitar 10–11], ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it. In scrolls honored, exalted and purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ [Abasa 11–16]. As for whether they are better than the righteous children of Adam, or the righteous children of Adam are better than them, this is something we have not been obligated to know. For this reason, the Sunnah did not come to distinguish between these and those, or to prefer one over the other. It gave each group its virtue. Had this been among the matters that must be believed, without which faith is not complete, God and His Messenger would have explained it. But if we are afflicted with someone who says, "Clarify which of them is better," we say: the scholars differ on this. Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah), may God have mercy on him, reconciled these two positions and said: the angels are better in terms of their beginning (al-bidayah), and the righteous of mankind are better in terms of their end (al-nihayah). How so? He said: Yes, because light is better than clay. The angels were created from light, from a luminous, shining, beloved substance, unlike clay. As for the end, Paradise is for the righteous among the children of Adam and among the jinn, according to the preponderant view. God, Mighty and Majestic, has mentioned that the angels enter upon the people of Paradise from every gate, saying, ﴿Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured﴾ [al-Ra'd 23–24], congratulating and gladdening them.

Nevertheless, I see that refraining from this is better, and that we should know the virtue of the angels and the virtue of the messengers whom God chose from the children of Adam. As for which of them is best, this is a matter we have not been obligated to address.

* Student: (...) that Allah, glorified and exalted, created the angels without desire: light, intellect without desire. And He also created desire without intellect, and created man from desire and intellect. If his intellect overcomes his desire, he is better than the angels; and if his desire overcomes his intellect, he is worse than them. Does this have any basis?
* Shaykh: Not at all. It has no basis.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, some people say this. But we say: who told you that the angels have no desire? If you mean by desire sexual intercourse, this does not apply to the angels, because the angels are ṣamad (free of need), and they do not marry, eat, or drink. If you mean by desire volition (al-irada), then they certainly have volition. They desire good, glorify God, and carry out His command.
* Student: Is this a hadith?
* Shaykh: No, not at all. This is a classification by some people. He was permitted to make this division. Yes indeed. As for animals too, do they not have intellect? The animal?
* Student: They have intellect.
* Shaykh: They have intellect according to their nature. They know what harms them and what benefits them. They protect themselves from the sun and the cold, they seek water, they seek food, they yearn for their young. They have intellect, but suited to them. If an animal had an intellect like the intellect of a human being, when someone came to ride it, it would say, "Get away from me!" True. But God did not make its intellect like the intellect of a human being. He made its intellect suitable to it.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding the statement (...), there is an objection to this: the "worlds" mentioned among human beings, based on God's saying, ﴿Do you approach males among the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 165]. Did they not approach females (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, this will come to us; we have not reached it yet.
* Student: What is the connection, Shaykh, between this verse and the verse before it?
* Shaykh: It is the beginning of a new topic (...), with the beginning of speech. We do not know the connection between each verse and the next.
* Student: May God reward you with good, Shaykh. Regarding the theory of evolution in the rest of the animals, is it correct?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: The evidence?
* Shaykh: The evidence is observation. We have nothing but observation. We see this is a hen, this is a camel, this is a cow, and this is a donkey.
* Student: So the theory of evolution is wrong?
* Shaykh: Wrong, yes. Who said it? And what is the origin of the hen?
* Student: A bird.
* Shaykh: A small bird. Then it grew. Perhaps after ten years it becomes an ostrich.
* Student: Who are the Al (family), Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Al are those who belong to a person. The term "Al" may also be applied to followers. Like: "O God, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the Family of Muhammad," meaning his followers, according to the preponderant view.
* Student: Shaykh, is our father Adam, peace be upon him, the father of the jinn?
* Shaykh: The father of the jinn is Satan. The father of the jinn is Satan. God, Exalted, says: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me, while they are enemies to you?﴾ [al-Kahf 50].
* Student: It is related that the angels took him from the earth as a child and raised him with them to heaven?
* Shaykh: No, no, that is an Israelite narration (israiliyyat). Satan was originally created from fire, and the angels were created from light. He was created from fire. God is capable of all things. Just as He created man from clay, He created Satan from fire.
* Student: Among the jinn there are Muslims. How can they be the offspring of Iblis, the Satan?
* Shaykh: Are there not among the children of Adam those who are the offspring of human satans? ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am 112]. Among mankind there are devils, even though their origin is from dust. God is capable of all things.
* Student: What is mentioned about the lineage of the Prophet ﷺ back to Adam, is it correct?
* Shaykh: Historians mention this. But it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that when he reached 'Adnan he said: "The genealogists have lied." That is, we only know the lineage up to 'Adnan, and beyond that, God knows best.
* Student: Shaykh, which of the two opinions is stronger regarding the family of 'Imran: is it Abu Musa or Abu Maryam?
* Shaykh: By God, each has a valid aspect. Every opinion has a valid aspect, as we have mentioned.
* Student: Shaykh, is this (Surah) al-An'am not sent down from heaven?
* Shaykh: Al-An'am? 
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: The Qur'an does not say that it was sent down from heaven, ﴿He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar 6], only that.
* Student: It indicates that it...
* Shaykh: We do not know. God did not specify it. God says: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ [al-A'raf 26]. From where is the clothing? From trees. It is made from trees, from the earth.

* * *

* Student: ﴿The wife of 'Imran said, "My Lord, I have dedicated to You what is in my womb, consecrated, so accept it from me. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing." (35) And when she delivered her, she said, "My Lord, I have delivered her as a female," and God was most knowing of what she delivered, "and the male is not like the female. And I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan." (36) So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good growth, and He entrusted her to Zakariya. Every time Zakariya entered upon her in the sanctuary (al-mihrab), he found with her provision. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from God. Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Al 'Imran 35–37].
* Shaykh: ﴿offspring, some of them from others, and God is Hearing and Knowing﴾. In this verse is a clarification that human beings are one kind, some of them from others, based on His saying: ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who claim that human beings evolved from one species into another, from apes to human beings. It is fitting that we call this speaker an ape, because he was content for himself that his origin be the ape. As for us, we say: our origin is Adam, peace be upon him, whom God created with His own hand from dust, and that he is a species standing independently, not evolved.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming two of God's names, ﴿al-Sami'﴾ (the Hearing) and ﴿al-'Alim﴾ (the Knowing). ﴿al-Sami'﴾ relates to sounds, and ﴿al-'Alim﴾ relates to everything: sounds, states, and entities, everything. It has already passed with us that belief in God's names, Glorified and Exalted, includes three things if they are transitive (muta'addiyah), and two things if they are intransitive (lazimah). If they are transitive, belief in them includes three things. First, affirming them as names of God, meaning you affirm them as one of God's names and do not deny them. Second: affirming the attribute they contain or imply (ma tadammanathu aw istalzamathu). Third: affirming the ruling resulting from this attribute. How many are these? What are they?
* Student: Affirming the name of God, Majestic and Exalted.
* Shaykh: Affirming this name as one of God's names.
* Student: Yes, and affirming the ruling.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Affirming the attribute, unless it is the implied one, or...
* Shaykh: Affirming what it contains or implies of the attribute.
* Student: Affirming the ruling, if they are transitive.
* Shaykh: Affirming the ruling if they are transitive. We say: what it contains or implies. Is there a difference between tadammun (inclusion) and istilzam (implication)?
Yes. Tadammun is part of what the name indicates by its wording. This is tadammun: part of what it indicates by its wording. For example, the name al-Khaliq (the Creator) includes indication of the Essence of God, Mighty and Majestic, and indication of the attribute of creation. This is tadammun. It also implies knowledge and power by way of necessary implication (iltizam), because there is no creation except with knowledge and power. The point is that the name is not complete for you except by affirming these three things: first, affirming it as one of God's names; second, affirming the attribute it contains or implies; third, the resulting ruling. For example, the name (al-Khaliq), the contained attribute (creation), the implied attributes (knowledge and power), and the effect or ruling that He creates. So He is Creator by creating.
Al-Rahman is a name; its inclusion of mercy is an attribute; He shows mercy is the ruling or effect. As for when a name is intransitive, belief in it is not complete except by affirming it as one of God's names and affirming the attribute it contains. For example, al-Hayy (the Living) does not transitively extend to other than God. We affirm it as one of God's names and affirm the attribute it contains, which is life. This is the rule for affirming God's names and attributes. If we apply this rule to the two names before us, al-Sami' includes belief in it as one of God's names, belief in the attribute it indicates, which is hearing, and the effect or ruling that He hears. The same applies to al-'Alim.

**Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImran over the worlds, (33) offspring, one descended from another. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing. (34) When the wife of ʿImran said: "My Lord, I have dedicated to You what is in my womb, as a devoted servant, so accept it from me. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing." (35) And when she gave birth to her, she said: "My Lord, I have given birth to a female," and Allah knew best what she had delivered, "and the male is not like the female. I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan."﴾ [Ali ʿImran 3:33–36].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImran over the worlds.﴾

First: I think we have completed the earlier benefits (fawa'id), and nothing remains.

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah.﴾ This sentence, as we see, is emphasized with (inna), because the context requires it, since the purpose is to explain that Allah the Exalted chooses whom He wills from among people. ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind.﴾ [al-Hajj 22:75], meaning: and from among mankind. So Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam.﴾ Adam is the father of mankind. Allah created him as a separate creation, and not evolved from another kind or species before him, as the atheists claim. Whoever claims this has disbelieved in Allah, because Allah the Exalted informed us in His Book in several places that Allah created Adam from earth: ﴿from clay like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman 55:14], ﴿from clay﴾ [Sad 38:71]. He created him with His own hand, breathed into him from His spirit, and commanded His angels to prostrate to him. Whoever claims otherwise is a disbeliever, a believer in other than Allah and a denier of Allah, may Allah protect us. Moreover, no one can speak about Adam and the beginning of his creation and how he was created without relying on revelation, and his words are not accepted. Why? Because he did not witness it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of themselves.﴾ [al-Kahf 18:51]. Allah the Exalted also says: ﴿Has there not come to you the report of those before you: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows except Allah?﴾ [Ibrahim 14:9]. Whoever claims to know anything about those who came before is a liar, unless he has proof. And Adam, as we know, is separated from us by very long periods of time, so we cannot accept any statement about him except through sound revelation.

Adam was named, it is said, after his ʾudmah (complexion), meaning that his color was neither pure white nor deep black, but between the two. Allah created him in His image, that is, in the image of Allah the Exalted, as an honor to him. Being created in the image of Allah does not necessarily mean that he resembles Him, because Allah says: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing.﴾ [al-Shura 42:11]. We must believe in all the texts: we believe that He created him in His image, and we believe that there is nothing like Him.

If you say: How can he be in His image and not like Him?

The answer is: This is possible. It is possible in the created, so what about the Creator? The Prophet ﷺ informed us that: "The first group to enter Paradise will be in the form of the full moon on its night." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3246) and Muslim (2834/14) from Abu Hurayrah]. It is known that resemblance is not required. That is, their form is not exactly like the form of the full moon, but in general terms of beauty and radiance, like the moon on the night of the full moon. Moreover, the Qur'an and the Sunnah do not contradict one another. If it is possible for created things to share a likeness without resembling one another, that is, for one thing to be in the form of another without being identical to it, then it is more fitting that this is possible between the Creator and the created, because there is nothing like Him. As for his saying: "and Allah created him in His image," and "He commanded His angels to prostrate to him," it is an honor for him. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down in prostration to him.﴾ [al-Hijr 15:29]. He commanded them to prostrate, so He commanded the angels to prostrate to him as an honor.

Adam, peace be upon him, received revelation, as stated in the Noble Qur'an. There is no doubt that revelation came to him also by reason, because he cannot independently know how to worship Allah except through revelation from Allah, and he was created for worship: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:56]. So both the transmitted texts and reason indicate that he received revelation.

But was he a messenger? No, he was not a messenger, according to the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah. As for the Book, it is in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾ [al-Nisa 4:163]. He made the prophets come after Noah. And He said: ﴿And We sent Noah and Abraham and placed in their offspring prophethood and the Scripture.﴾ [al-Hadid 57:26]. As for the Sunnah, in the authentic long hadith of intercession: "People will come to Noah and say to him: You are the first messenger whom Allah sent to the people of the earth." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3340) and Muslim (194/327) from Abu Hurayrah]. Accordingly, Adam was a prophet to whom revelation was sent with a law (shariʿah), and by which he worshiped Allah. The people remained upon this law because they were few, and no disagreement arose among them. When they disagreed: ﴿Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between people concerning that over which they differed.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213].

As for His saying: ﴿Adam and Noah.﴾ Allah mentioned Noah after Adam because he is the second father of mankind. When his people denied him, except for a few, Allah destroyed them by drowning, and made his offspring the remaining ones, as in Surah al-Saffat: ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors.﴾ [al-Saffat 37:77]. So he became the second father of mankind, and he was the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth. He remained among his people for a thousand years minus fifty years, calling them to Allah, and only a few believed with him. A thousand years, and only a few believed with him! When we call ten people and they hesitate a little, and then one of the ten responds, we say: "Our call was not accepted," and we grow weary of calling to Allah and despair. This was a messenger who remained a thousand years minus fifty years among his people, and only a few believed with him. Yet Allah said in His Book: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding.﴾ [Yusuf 12:111].

﴿And the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran over the worlds.﴾ The family of Abraham: there is no doubt that Abraham is included among them, with even greater priority, but the family was specified because of the large number of messengers among them, especially since the best of messengers, Muhammad ﷺ, is among them. Muhammad ﷺ is from the family of Abraham.

As for the family of ʿImran: scholars differed about who is meant. It is said: the family of ʿImran, the father of Musa, because Musa is the most excellent of the prophets of the Children of Israel. And it is said: the family of ʿImran, the father of Maryam: ﴿and Maryam daughter of ʿImran﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:12]. He mentioned the family of ʿImran because among them is the last of the messengers before Muhammad ﷺ, namely Isa son of Maryam, to whom the Christians attribute themselves. He singled them out in this way, that is, He singled out the family of ʿImran, because the context also requires it. This Surah's beginning was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran, who were Christians. Whether this or that is the case, it indicates that Allah chose this lineage, the lineage of Abraham. So he is chosen from among the chosen: ﴿chose Adam and Noah﴾ is the first choosing; ﴿and Noah﴾ is the second; ﴿and the family of Abraham﴾ is the third; ﴿and the family of ʿImran﴾ is the fourth. These noble people of mankind were the ones He chose.

The meaning of choosing (istifaʾ) is that Allah selected them and preferred them over many of His creation with preference, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam and carried them on land and sea and provided for them of the good things and preferred them over much of what We have created, with [definite] preference.﴾ [al-Isra 17:70]. It is not over everything We have created, but ﴿over much of what We have created, with [definite] preference.﴾ I say: istifaʾ means ikhtiyar (choosing), because its root is from safwah (the best of something), and the safwah of something is its best part, and istafa means he took its best part.

As for His saying: ﴿over the worlds.﴾ Which worlds? Is it all of the world, or the worlds of animals? The first is the original meaning: that by "the worlds" is meant everything other than Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:2]. What follows from this difference will come, God willing, in the benefits.

As for His saying: ﴿offspring, one descended from another.﴾ "Offspring" (dhurriyyah) is in the accusative as a substitute for ﴿Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran.﴾ "Offspring" means these four categories are offspring, one descended from another. Dhurriyyah is derived from (dhara'a), meaning to create, as in His saying: ﴿He multiplies you through it﴾ [al-Shura 42:11], that is, He creates you. It is also said to be derived from (wadhara), meaning to leave. According to the first, dhurriyyah includes both ancestors and descendants, because the ancestors are created and the descendants are also created. But if we derive it from (wadhara), meaning to leave, then it refers only to descendants. This is the common understanding among people: that dhurriyyah are descendants, that is, those who arise from a person and whom he leaves behind after him. Is there anything in the Qur'an indicating that dhurriyyah is applied to ancestors? What?

**Student:** ﴿We will join them with their offspring﴾ [al-Tur 52:21].

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them﴾ [al-Tur 52:21].

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** The offspring of Adam and those whom We carried...

**Shaykh:** No. ﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ [al-Isra 17:3].

**Student:** His saying, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾

**Shaykh:** Yes, this one: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. (41) And We created for them from the like of it...﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:41–42]. Those who were carried as offspring were the ones who believed with Noah, and they were the foremost.

As for His saying: ﴿one descended from another.﴾ Is this in the kind of creation? Or ﴿one descended from another﴾ in deeds, manners, and morals?

**Student:** It includes both.

**Shaykh:** The apparent meaning is that it includes both. That is, all human beings are of one kind. There is no human who was originally a monkey, as the "brothers of the apes" say, and those who have confessed about themselves that they are apes. The human is originally human. Allah created his father with His own hand from the beginning. But they refused except to make themselves of the apes. So ﴿one descended from another﴾ refers to creation. From Adam until our day, creation has not changed except in the strength and bulk of the body. "Because Adam's height in Paradise was sixty cubits, and his breadth was also seven cubits, according to many hadiths" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3326), Muslim (2841/28), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (7933) from Abu Hurayrah]. This creation has diminished, decreasing until it reached this nation, and it ended there, because this nation is the last of nations.

It is not objected to that in some regions the human race is large and in others it is less. This is due to climate and heredity. But the principle is that we consider the last stage of the children of Adam, because we are the last of nations.

Likewise, ﴿one descended from another﴾ applies to manners, morals, and religions, except for those among them who were unjust and departed from this origin, for they go out by what they went out by.

﴿Offspring, one descended from another, and Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ He concluded the verse with hearing and knowledge, as a sign that everything these chosen ones say or do is known to Allah. He hears what they say and knows what they do. Indeed, He knows what they do not do of what is in their hearts. He even knows what they will do, even if it is not in their hearts, because Allah the Exalted knows what has happened, and what would happen if it were to happen, how it would be.

* In these two verses there are benefits.
* In the first: an explanation that Allah chose these creations over the rest of creation.
* Among its benefits also: that Allah may choose from His creation whatever He wills, as He said: ﴿Your Lord creates what He wills and chooses. They do not have the choice. Glory be to Allah, and exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ [al-Qasas 28:68].
* Among its benefits: just as preference exists in deeds, it also exists in essences. Just as preference exists in deeds and qualities, it also exists in persons. For this reason we say: the Arab race is more excellent than other races. But if this excellent race combines with it piety, it attains absolute excellence. If piety is absent, its origin is good but its deeds are wicked, and it becomes more wicked, because its origin was good and then it fell by itself to the lowest level. Whoever had a good origin and then descended by himself to the lowest level is more blameworthy than one who was not like that. Is this not so?

* **The students:** Yes.

* **Shaykh:** Therefore, if a free woman commits fornication, she is lashed one hundred lashes if she is unmarried, and stoned if she is married. If a slave woman commits fornication, she is not stoned even if she is married, and she is lashed fifty lashes, not one hundred, because there is a difference between a person whose origin is noble and honorable who then debases himself, and a person who was originally otherwise. This is indicated by the fact that people differ in their races, and Allah said in His Book: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:124]. Allah placed it among the Arabs in Muhammad ﷺ. So if Muhammad was the best and most noble of creation, it follows that the Arab race is the best, most excellent, and most noble of races. And this is so. It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The best of you in the pre-Islamic period are the best of you in Islam, if they gain understanding." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3374) and Muslim (2378/168) from Abu Hurayrah].

If someone says: What is the answer to His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:13]?

The answer: As for the answer to this noble verse, Allah the Exalted intended to erase what the people of pre-Islamic ignorance were accustomed to, namely boasting of lineage. He says: "I am from such-and-such tribe, I am from such-and-such tribe." So Allah clarified that these peoples and tribes were made by Allah for the purpose of mutual recognition, not for boasting, and that your boasting does not bring you closer to Allah. What brings you closer to Allah is piety: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.﴾ This does not negate that the Arab race is more excellent than others, as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah verified in his book Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim Mukhalafat Ashab al-Jahim, and his evidences are what you have heard.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse is what some scholars mentioned: that the righteous among mankind are more excellent than the angels. He said: because of His saying "over the worlds," and the angels are a world. So those chosen from among mankind are more excellent than whom?

* **The students:** The angels.

* **Shaykh:** Than the angels.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah Al 'Imran, verses 33–34 (part 2 of 2):

They cited other evidences, such as God's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam, and others. In my view, inquiry into this question is among the superfluous (fudul) kinds of knowledge. What benefit do we gain if we say: "So-and-so is better than Jibril (Gabriel), or Jibril is better than so-and-so?" Or: "The righteous among the children of Adam are better than the angels, or the angels are better than the righteous?" We know that the angels are drawn near to God, ﴿They glorify Him night and day, and they never tire﴾ [al-Anbiya' 20], and that they are noble, ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording﴾ [al-Infitar 10–11], ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it. In scrolls honored, exalted and purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ [Abasa 11–16]. As for whether they are better than the righteous children of Adam, or the righteous children of Adam are better than them, this is something we have not been obligated to know. For this reason, the Sunnah did not come to distinguish between these and those, or to prefer one over the other. It gave each group its virtue. Had this been among the matters that must be believed, without which faith is not complete, God and His Messenger would have explained it. But if we are afflicted with someone who says, "Clarify which of them is better," we say: the scholars differ on this. Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah), may God have mercy on him, reconciled these two positions and said: the angels are better in terms of their beginning (al-bidayah), and the righteous of mankind are better in terms of their end (al-nihayah). How so? He said: Yes, because light is better than clay. The angels were created from light, from a luminous, shining, beloved substance, unlike clay. As for the end, Paradise is for the righteous among the children of Adam and among the jinn, according to the preponderant view. God, Mighty and Majestic, has mentioned that the angels enter upon the people of Paradise from every gate, saying, ﴿Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured﴾ [al-Ra'd 23–24], congratulating and gladdening them.

Nevertheless, I see that refraining from this is better, and that we should know the virtue of the angels and the virtue of the messengers whom God chose from the children of Adam. As for which of them is best, this is a matter we have not been obligated to address.

* Student: (...) that Allah, glorified and exalted, created the angels without desire: light, intellect without desire. And He also created desire without intellect, and created man from desire and intellect. If his intellect overcomes his desire, he is better than the angels; and if his desire overcomes his intellect, he is worse than them. Does this have any basis?
* Shaykh: Not at all. It has no basis.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, some people say this. But we say: who told you that the angels have no desire? If you mean by desire sexual intercourse, this does not apply to the angels, because the angels are ṣamad (free of need), and they do not marry, eat, or drink. If you mean by desire volition (al-irada), then they certainly have volition. They desire good, glorify God, and carry out His command.
* Student: Is this a hadith?
* Shaykh: No, not at all. This is a classification by some people. He was permitted to make this division. Yes indeed. As for animals too, do they not have intellect? The animal?
* Student: They have intellect.
* Shaykh: They have intellect according to their nature. They know what harms them and what benefits them. They protect themselves from the sun and the cold, they seek water, they seek food, they yearn for their young. They have intellect, but suited to them. If an animal had an intellect like the intellect of a human being, when someone came to ride it, it would say, "Get away from me!" True. But God did not make its intellect like the intellect of a human being. He made its intellect suitable to it.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding the statement (...), there is an objection to this: the "worlds" mentioned among human beings, based on God's saying, ﴿Do you approach males among the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 165]. Did they not approach females (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, this will come to us; we have not reached it yet.
* Student: What is the connection, Shaykh, between this verse and the verse before it?
* Shaykh: It is the beginning of a new topic (...), with the beginning of speech. We do not know the connection between each verse and the next.
* Student: May God reward you with good, Shaykh. Regarding the theory of evolution in the rest of the animals, is it correct?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: The evidence?
* Shaykh: The evidence is observation. We have nothing but observation. We see this is a hen, this is a camel, this is a cow, and this is a donkey.
* Student: So the theory of evolution is wrong?
* Shaykh: Wrong, yes. Who said it? And what is the origin of the hen?
* Student: A bird.
* Shaykh: A small bird. Then it grew. Perhaps after ten years it becomes an ostrich.
* Student: Who are the Al (family), Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Al are those who belong to a person. The term "Al" may also be applied to followers. Like: "O God, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the Family of Muhammad," meaning his followers, according to the preponderant view.
* Student: Shaykh, is our father Adam, peace be upon him, the father of the jinn?
* Shaykh: The father of the jinn is Satan. The father of the jinn is Satan. God, Exalted, says: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me, while they are enemies to you?﴾ [al-Kahf 50].
* Student: It is related that the angels took him from the earth as a child and raised him with them to heaven?
* Shaykh: No, no, that is an Israelite narration (israiliyyat). Satan was originally created from fire, and the angels were created from light. He was created from fire. God is capable of all things. Just as He created man from clay, He created Satan from fire.
* Student: Among the jinn there are Muslims. How can they be the offspring of Iblis, the Satan?
* Shaykh: Are there not among the children of Adam those who are the offspring of human satans? ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am 112]. Among mankind there are devils, even though their origin is from dust. God is capable of all things.
* Student: What is mentioned about the lineage of the Prophet ﷺ back to Adam, is it correct?
* Shaykh: Historians mention this. But it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that when he reached 'Adnan he said: "The genealogists have lied." That is, we only know the lineage up to 'Adnan, and beyond that, God knows best.
* Student: Shaykh, which of the two opinions is stronger regarding the family of 'Imran: is it Abu Musa or Abu Maryam?
* Shaykh: By God, each has a valid aspect. Every opinion has a valid aspect, as we have mentioned.
* Student: Shaykh, is this (Surah) al-An'am not sent down from heaven?
* Shaykh: Al-An'am? 
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: The Qur'an does not say that it was sent down from heaven, ﴿He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar 6], only that.
* Student: It indicates that it...
* Shaykh: We do not know. God did not specify it. God says: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ [al-A'raf 26]. From where is the clothing? From trees. It is made from trees, from the earth.

* * *

* Student: ﴿The wife of 'Imran said, "My Lord, I have dedicated to You what is in my womb, consecrated, so accept it from me. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing." (35) And when she delivered her, she said, "My Lord, I have delivered her as a female," and God was most knowing of what she delivered, "and the male is not like the female. And I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan." (36) So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good growth, and He entrusted her to Zakariya. Every time Zakariya entered upon her in the sanctuary (al-mihrab), he found with her provision. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from God. Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Al 'Imran 35–37].
* Shaykh: ﴿offspring, some of them from others, and God is Hearing and Knowing﴾. In this verse is a clarification that human beings are one kind, some of them from others, based on His saying: ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who claim that human beings evolved from one species into another, from apes to human beings. It is fitting that we call this speaker an ape, because he was content for himself that his origin be the ape. As for us, we say: our origin is Adam, peace be upon him, whom God created with His own hand from dust, and that he is a species standing independently, not evolved.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming two of God's names, ﴿al-Sami'﴾ (the Hearing) and ﴿al-'Alim﴾ (the Knowing). ﴿al-Sami'﴾ relates to sounds, and ﴿al-'Alim﴾ relates to everything: sounds, states, and entities, everything. It has already passed with us that belief in God's names, Glorified and Exalted, includes three things if they are transitive (muta'addiyah), and two things if they are intransitive (lazimah). If they are transitive, belief in them includes three things. First, affirming them as names of God, meaning you affirm them as one of God's names and do not deny them. Second: affirming the attribute they contain or imply (ma tadammanathu aw istalzamathu). Third: affirming the ruling resulting from this attribute. How many are these? What are they?
* Student: Affirming the name of God, Majestic and Exalted.
* Shaykh: Affirming this name as one of God's names.
* Student: Yes, and affirming the ruling.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Affirming the attribute, unless it is the implied one, or...
* Shaykh: Affirming what it contains or implies of the attribute.
* Student: Affirming the ruling, if they are transitive.
* Shaykh: Affirming the ruling if they are transitive. We say: what it contains or implies. Is there a difference between tadammun (inclusion) and istilzam (implication)?
Yes. Tadammun is part of what the name indicates by its wording. This is tadammun: part of what it indicates by its wording. For example, the name al-Khaliq (the Creator) includes indication of the Essence of God, Mighty and Majestic, and indication of the attribute of creation. This is tadammun. It also implies knowledge and power by way of necessary implication (iltizam), because there is no creation except with knowledge and power. The point is that the name is not complete for you except by affirming these three things: first, affirming it as one of God's names; second, affirming the attribute it contains or implies; third, the resulting ruling. For example, the name (al-Khaliq), the contained attribute (creation), the implied attributes (knowledge and power), and the effect or ruling that He creates. So He is Creator by creating.
Al-Rahman is a name; its inclusion of mercy is an attribute; He shows mercy is the ruling or effect. As for when a name is intransitive, belief in it is not complete except by affirming it as one of God's names and affirming the attribute it contains. For example, al-Hayy (the Living) does not transitively extend to other than God. We affirm it as one of God's names and affirm the attribute it contains, which is life. This is the rule for affirming God's names and attributes. If we apply this rule to the two names before us, al-Sami' includes belief in it as one of God's names, belief in the attribute it indicates, which is hearing, and the effect or ruling that He hears. The same applies to al-'Alim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 35–37 (part 1 of 5):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran 35]. That is: remember when she said. This construction is found very often in the Qur'an, and the governing verb has been omitted because the context indicates it. This is a well-known rule among the grammarians (nahwiyyun), which Ibn Malik alluded to in his Alfiyya when he said:
"The omission of what is known is permissible, as when you say, 'Zayd' in reply to someone who asks, 'Who denied [it]?'"
So here the omitted governing verb is known from the context: "remember when she said." That is: remember this circumstance in which this statement was uttered by the wife of 'Imran. ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾. Who is the wife of 'Imran?
She is the mother of Maryam, that is, the grandmother of 'Isa ibn Maryam. ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said: My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated, so accept it from me﴾ [Al 'Imran 35].
﴿Rabb﴾ (My Lord) is a vocative from which the ya' of address has been dropped; the original is "ya Rabbi." The ya' of address is dropped in such a construction for brevity, due to its frequent use. The ya' of the first person (the pronoun of the speaker) has also been dropped from it; the original is "Rabbi, inni," and it was elided for lightness.
Her words: ﴿My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated﴾. ﴿Nadhartu﴾ (I have vowed) means: I have bound myself that what is in my womb be freed from my service and devoted to it, so that it becomes a servant of the mosque, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. It was their custom to do this; that is, one of them would vow his child to be standing in service of the Al-Aqsa Mosque, out of reverence for it. So she says: ﴿My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated﴾. Her words ﴿what is in my womb﴾ is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) that conveys generality, so it includes whether she gives birth to one or two, and male or female.
If someone says: How can you say that it includes what she might bear as two, when she says: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated﴾, and "dedicated" is singular, and she did not say "dedicated (dual)"?
The answer: the shared relative pronouns, that is, those which suit the singular and others, may be treated according to their wording (lafz) as singular, or according to their meaning: singular if the singular is intended, dual if the dual is intended, and plural if the plural is intended, whether masculine or feminine. Accordingly, there is nothing to prevent her saying ﴿dedicated﴾ from including what she bears even if there were more than one, because it is singular in consideration of what? In consideration of the wording. Likewise the conditional (man) allows treatment according to wording and treatment according to meaning. Have you not seen the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds, He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾ [At-Taghabun 9]. In consideration of what?
The singular here is in consideration of the wording: ﴿He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾; he mentioned it in consideration of the wording. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is in consideration of the meaning.
﴿Allah has certainly made good for him a provision﴾ [At-Talaq 11] is in consideration of the wording.
You say: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb﴾ is general, including everything in her womb, whether males or females, one or more; ﴿dedicated﴾ from what? From the bond of my service to the service of the Al-Aqsa Mosque.
﴿So accept it from me﴾ means: accept from me this drawing near to You by vowing this child, who will serve Your House.
﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) sentence giving the reason; that is, I asked You to accept from me because You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. "All-Hearing" here includes both hearing of perception and hearing of response, meaning that You hear my supplication and answer it. It has already passed that As-Sami' (the All-Hearing) is one of Allah's names and includes both hearing of perception and hearing of response, and that (sami'a) comes with the meaning of (istajaba, responded), as in the words of the one praying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him," i.e., responds. So here, ﴿Hearer of supplication﴾: which is more appropriate, perception or response?
* The students: Response... it includes both.
* The Shaykh: It includes both, but what is the benefit of the one who supplicates? By response.
Her words ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing﴾ mean: the hearer of my supplication, who responds to it, the All-Knowing of what is good, and of everything. But the mention of knowledge here is because a person may ask for something that is not good for him to obtain, so he attributes the matter to the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
It is known that when a supplicant supplicates, one of three things happens to him: either Allah responds to his supplication, or He stores it up for him for the Day of Resurrection, giving him the like of what he asked for, or He averts from him an evil greater than it. Besides this, supplication itself is an act of worship for which a person is rewarded. ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. ﴿So when she delivered her﴾; she did not say "when she delivered him." In consideration of what?
* The students: In consideration of the meaning.
* The Shaykh: In consideration of the meaning, because she delivered a female. So when she delivered her, and she had vowed her as dedicated on the assumption that it was a male, when she delivered her she made an excuse to her Lord: ﴿She said: My Lord, I have delivered her a female﴾ [Al 'Imran 36]. This is an excuse from her to Allah that she delivered a female, and a female is not customarily one who serves the mosque, so she is, as it were, excusing herself to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for this vow.
He said: ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾. In another reading: ﴿And Allah knows best what I delivered﴾, which is a canonical (sab'i) reading. We explain it according to both readings. As for her words ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female﴾, you know that the purpose of this sentence is what?
* The students: The excuse.
* The Shaykh: The excuse, not informing Allah of what she delivered, since He is the All-Knowing, the Mighty and Majestic. He is the One who created her, and she was delivered by His permission and command, so the matter is not hidden from Him. But she mentioned it as an excuse. Accordingly, on the reading ﴿And Allah knows best what I delivered﴾, the sentence is a precautionary insertion (ihtiras), lest it be thought that she believed Allah did not know. So she said: "My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what I delivered." I am not informing Allah of a matter hidden from Him; rather I believe that He knows what I delivered. This is on the reading with the damma on the ta'. As for the reading with the sukun: ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾, the speech is from Allah, and in it is a defence of this woman, that Allah the Exalted knows that she did not say ﴿I have delivered her a female﴾ as information to Allah, because He, glorified and exalted, attested to her by His words: ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾. This is one aspect. Another aspect: to show that her words ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female﴾ do not mean that Allah does not know what she delivered; rather He knows, even if she said: ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what she delivered﴾.
"Knows best" (a'lam) is a comparative form indicating that the one preferred exceeds the one compared in this attribute, as if you say: "So-and-so is more generous than so-and-so," meaning that this one preferred, who is so-and-so, exceeds the other in generosity. So "a'lam" here means: more knowing than anyone of what she delivered. This affirms knowledge to Allah with excess. By this explanation we know the weakness of the view of those who said that the comparative here carries the meaning of the active participle, and that the meaning of His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ is "and Allah is knowing of what she delivered." That view is without doubt deficient, a deficiency in explaining the speech of Allah, because affirming knowledge without comparison is less than affirming knowledge with comparison. Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because when you say "so-and-so is knowing," it does not prevent that another might be equal to him in knowledge; but when you say "so-and-so is more knowing than so-and-so," the one is superior to the other in knowledge, and the other is inferior. And I do not know, glory be to Allah, how some scholars flee from affirming comparison between Allah, glorified and exalted, and His creation, even though comparison does not indicate any deficiency. Rather, the expression that implies sharing is what may admit deficiency and similarity, but the expression that indicates comparison contains no deficiency in any way. So Allah is more knowing than anyone, whether this knowledge is restricted or unrestricted.
His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ contain a point of inquiry: "ma" is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun requires a returning pronoun (a'id). Where is the returning pronoun? ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾, or: ﴿what I delivered﴾. The question again: where did your thought go?
* A student: (...) "delivered" (wada'at) and "I delivered" (wada'tu) is a reading (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the returning pronoun is omitted: an omitted object pronoun. The estimate is: "what I delivered it" or "what she delivered it," on both readings.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾. The male is not like the female. Is this from her speech or from the speech of Allah?
As for the reading ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾, it is apparent that it is from the speech of Allah; that it is from the speech of Allah is more likely, because His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ are from the speech of Allah.
As for the reading ﴿And Allah knows best what I delivered﴾, that it is from her speech is more likely, so that the sentences do not scatter. Let us recite the verse: ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what I delivered, and the male is not like the female, and I have named her Maryam﴾, which is now coherent and well-joined. But if we make ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ part of the speech of Allah, then His words ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ fit with His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾. Therefore the scholars differed over whether this sentence is from the speech of Allah or from the speech of the wife of 'Imran.
We say: both possibilities exist in any case, but on the reading ﴿what I delivered﴾ it is more likely to be from the speech of whom? The wife of 'Imran; and on the reading ﴿what she delivered﴾ it is more likely to be from the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
In any case, this sentence makes clear that the male is not like the female. It is as if a person speaks to himself and says: the situation would require the phrase to be "and the female is not like the male," since the custom is that the lesser is compared to the greater. Here, "the female is not like the male" seems closer at first glance than "and the male is not like the female."
For this reason some scholars claimed that there is an inversion (qalb) in the comparison, and the inverted comparison is a style of the Arabic language, especially among the poets of the middle ages, to the extent that some exaggerate in inverted comparison until one says:
"When the morning appears, its brightness is as if it were the face of the caliph when he is praised."
The morning, which fills the horizon and lights the world, is as if its brightness (its whiteness) were the face of the caliph when praised. And what is the caliph's whiteness? That is, the whiteness of his face. This is, in truth, a repugnant exaggeration. The point is that some said it is an inverted comparison, and some said it is a comparison in its original and proper form: the male is not like the female, and the superiority of the male over the female is known from other proofs and other indications. But the male in his service of Bayt al-Maqdis is not like the female. Is the male higher, or lower? Higher.
* A student: Will the story of "Abu Maryam" not be explained to us?
* The Shaykh: Abu what?
* The student: (...) Abu Maryam.
* The Shaykh: Between them are long periods of time. This was raised against the Messenger ﷺ, regarding his words: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾ [Maryam 28]: Maryam daughter of 'Imran, and Harun. He said: they used to name people after their prophets. The wife of Maryam's father cannot be a sister of Musa ibn 'Imran, because the Messenger ﷺ said: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾, "They used to name themselves after their prophets" [recorded by Muslim (2135/9) with the wording: "They used to name themselves after their prophets and the righteous before them," from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, may Allah be pleased with him]; that is, between them are many centuries, and Musa ibn 'Imran.
* The student: Yes indeed, she is the sister of Harun, daughter of Harun, sister of Harun.
* The Shaykh: The sister of Harun is not the sister of Musa.
* A student: Shaykh, when the mother of Maryam, peace be upon her, vowed, was there a reason (...) the female in this way?
* The Shaykh: Not at all; it was out of their desire to serve the mosque.
* A student: Shaykh, we said that "the worlds" (...) Shaykh, and we also mentioned that there was a difficulty in the words of Allah: ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds?﴾, from this lesson?
* The Shaykh: Yes, did we raise this difficulty?
* A student: Honored Shaykh, because here (...) creation (...).
* The Shaykh: Sometimes the general is specified by an indicator, either the indicator of the situation or the indicator of speech. That is, it may be a situational indicator or a verbal indicator; if it is verbal, it is an indicator of speech, and if it is situational, it is an indicator of the situation. Allah mentioned that He preferred the Children of Israel over the worlds, and it is known that the community of Muhammad is better than them. Allah said about the Children of Israel: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 32]. So the intended meaning is "over the worlds of their time."
* * *
* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿So when she delivered her, she said: My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what she delivered, and the male is not like the female, and I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan﴾ (36). ﴿So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow up with a good growth and entrusted her to Zakariyya. Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her at the prayer niche, he found with her provision. He said: O Maryam, from where is this for you? She said: It is from Allah; indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾ (37). ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord. He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring; indeed You are the Hearer of supplication﴾ (38). ﴿And the angels called him while he stood in prayer in the prayer niche: Indeed Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a master, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran 36–39].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ means the male is not equal to the female. When equality between the male and the female is negated, equality of the female with the male is negated too, because equality is between two things; if equality is absent in one of them, it must be absent in the other. So there is no equality between male and female; rather each has its own distinctive features. The female surpasses the man in some things, and the man surpasses the female in some things. But the one generally suited to serve the mosques is the man, because he is stronger, more intelligent, more sensible, and more enduring in work. A female, when she menstruates, for example, cannot serve the mosque, since she would have to leave it and not sit in it. This is if their law is like ours. Also, the female cannot bear the arduous tasks; rather she is weaker than the man. Although she may have more endurance and patience than a man in dealing with people, not in bearing calamities, since the woman in bearing calamities is far below the man, as is well known. He said: ﴿And the male is not like the female, and I have named her Maryam﴾. Who says it? Her mother says: I have named her Maryam. This name either was well known among them, or she chose it for a matter that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, intends.
In any case, I cannot explain why she chose this name, since this is a matter specific to her, and Allah knows best what was the reason she chose this name. She said: ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You﴾. "I seek refuge for her" means: I ask You for protection on her behalf, since seeking refuge (isti'adha) means seeking protection (istijara) from a disliked matter. That is why we seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan, and we seek refuge in Allah from the punishment of Hell and the punishment of the grave, the trial of life and death, and the trial of the false Messiah. The lexicographers said: "al-'iyadh" is seeking refuge from what is disliked, and "al-liyadh" is seeking shelter in hope of what is loved, seeking shelter in hope of what is loved; and they cited in support of this the verse of the poet:
