* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. Some people now, Shaykh, criticize the mihrabs (the niche-shaped markers in mosque carpets). They say it is an innovation (bid'ah)?

* Shaykh: That is not correct. Some people do not understand the meaning of bid'ah (innovation in religion) from the Sunnah, because they do not distinguish between a means (wasilah) and what is intended for its own sake. The Muslims who approved them, from hundreds of years ago, were eminent scholars, and they were further from innovation than these people. They knew that they did not adopt them in order to worship Allah by adopting them, but to guide the Muslims to the direction of the qiblah. If a commoner entered a mosque with no mihrab, where would he face? I saw with my own eyes, when the carpets first came to Riyadh, the carpet-layer who laid them had, at the beginning, a picture of mihrabs on them. Do you not remember?

* The students: They are still there. They are still there until now.

* Shaykh: There is a picture of mihrabs on them. The carpet-layer laid them, and the face of the mihrab came behind the qiblah, the reverse way. A man entered, saw the mihrab, and did not realize it was the qiblah of the mosque. He said "Allahu Akbar" and began to pray behind it. So there is a benefit in them. They are intended for something else, not for their own sake. The Muslims do not say: "We did it following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," or "We did it to draw near to Allah." They say: "We did it so that the ignorant person may be guided to the qiblah by them."

* * *

* Student: "There Zechariah called upon his Lord, saying: 'My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication.' (38) So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the mihrab: 'Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a noble leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous.' (39) He said: 'My Lord, how can I have a boy when old age has already reached me and my wife is barren?' He said: 'So it is; Allah does what He wills.' (40) He said: 'My Lord, appoint for me a sign.' He said: 'Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days except by gestures. And remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning.'" [Al 'Imran 38–41].

* Shaykh: "Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning." Indeed Allah provides. Provision (rizq) means giving, and giving is divided into two kinds: universal giving (kawni, that which occurs by the cosmic decree of Allah) and legislative giving (shar'i, that which is by the revealed law). Universal giving is what Allah provides to all living creatures: humans and animals, the lawful and the unlawful. This is universal giving, what is it?

* The students: Universal (kawni).

* Shaykh: Universal. It is not specific to the believers, nor to good provision. The second is legislative giving, which is what the believer is given of lawful provision. It is the specific provision that carries no accountability. It also includes legislative giving, which is what has been given according to the requirement of the law, such as giving to the poor from zakat, for example, and giving to those who share in the spoils from the booty. This is legislative giving. Its evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near of kin and the orphans and the needy and the traveler, so that it does not circulate only among the rich among you. And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it" [al-Hashr 7]. The giving here (ītā') is it legislative or universal?

* The students: Legislative.

* Shaykh: Legislative. And His saying, the Exalted: "And if they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and said: 'Allah is sufficient for us; Allah will give us of His bounty, and His Messenger. Indeed we are toward Allah desiring.' (59) The zakat is only for the poor..." [at-Tawbah 59–60], and so on to the end. This too is legislative giving.

So provision is either universal or legislative. What is for enjoyment in this world, or what sustains the body, is universal. What sustains the soul and the heart, or what is by permission of the law, is legislative. Knowledge and faith: are they legislative or universal?

* The students: Legislative.

* Shaykh: This is legislative, because the soul and heart are sustained by it.

As for His saying: "whom He wills," there is no doubt that this refers to the will of Allah. Provision only occurs by the will of Allah. But do you think the will is absolute and unrestricted? No, rather it is tied to wisdom. He gives whom He wills for a wisdom, and withholds from whom He wills for a wisdom. The proof that whatever Allah attributes to His will is accompanied by wisdom is His saying: "And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise" [al-Insan 30]. So He does not will except what the requirement of wisdom wills.

As for His saying: "Indeed Allah provides whom He wills," we have said that it must be accompanied by wisdom.

"Without reckoning" means without recompense. He feeds and is not fed, He provides and is not provided for. "I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me. Indeed Allah is the Provider, Possessor of strength, the Firm" [adh-Dhariyat 57–58]. Unlike others, who may give in order to be given to. Is that not so? As for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He gives not in order to be given to, but provides without reckoning, meaning without recompense. He does not ask anyone for recompense. As for the reckoning concerning what Allah has given of provision, what a person earned, where he spent it, and the like, this will occur. Allah said: "Then you will be asked that Day about pleasure" [at-Takathur 8]. So the reckoning intended here is what? Recompense? Meaning He does not reckon with creatures in order to repay them, but He reckons with them in order to see, or in order to know, the Mighty and Majestic, what they spent of what He gave them.

In these verses there are benefits. I think we should begin from His saying: "When the wife of 'Imran said..." or not?

* Some benefits of these verses:

First: the glorification of this story, because Allah commanded His Messenger to explain it to the people. The implied meaning is: "Mention when the wife of 'Imran said..."

Another benefit: the permissibility of vowing (nadhr) about an unknown matter, due to her saying: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated." Does this mean that the speaker may say: "I owe Allah a vow to give in charity what is in the belly of this sheep or this camel," and the vow is carried out?

* Another benefit of the verse: the permissibility of a woman giving charity without her husband's permission. Its basis? She vowed to free or dedicate this child without the husband's permission. If someone says: "What is your evidence that it was without her husband's permission? Is it not possible that she sought his permission?"

The answer: Yes, that is possible, but it is not mentioned. If someone says: "Non-mention is not a mention of non-existence," there is a difference between my remaining silent about a matter and my negating it. Negating a thing is a mention of its non-existence, but silence about it is not a mention of non-existence. We say: this is not in every place. Rather we say: this applies when there are general texts, and then someone claims their specification or restriction or the like. This is what we say to him: non-mention is not a mention of non-existence. But when an unrestricted account comes and no conditions are mentioned in it, the original position is what?

* The students: The absence of conditions.

* Shaykh: The original position is the absence of conditions. The Islamic law has come supporting this, meaning that a woman disposes of her wealth freely. The evidence: "That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he addressed the women on the day of 'Id and said: 'O assembly of women, give charity,' they began to throw their rings and earrings into the cloth of Bilal." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (304) and Muslim (80), with the wording of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] Did the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Seek your husbands' permission"? Did they say: "We will seek permission"? No.

Take also from the Qur'an: "And give the women their dowries graciously. But if they give you of it willingly, then consume it with satisfaction and pleasure" [an-Nisa' 4]. Who are "they" (tibna)?

* The students: The women.

* Shaykh: The women. "Consume it with satisfaction and pleasure." So the woman is free to dispose, and her husband has no right to prevent her from any disposal she wishes, except in one matter. It may be said that he prevents her from disposing of it, such as if he buys her jewelry and clothes of adornment to beautify herself for him. Here we may say he has the right to prevent her from disposing of these clothes and this jewelry by sale or gift, because that harms his purpose. Is that not so?

* Man: Yes.

* Shaykh: So if she now sells this jewelry and this beautiful clothing, and goes out to her husband with no jewelry, and wears poor, shabby clothes, he is between two situations: either he has intercourse with her while disliking her, or he does not accept this state. Then she says: "Come, give me," and he buys for her. When he buys for her, another woman comes to her complaining of the situation, and she says: "Take," and on the second day she goes out to him with nothing again. The matter continues in a chain. In this situation we may say that the husband has the right to prevent her from disposing of what he gave her, because that harms him, either financially or in his enjoyment.

From the benefits of this noble verse: a child serves his parent, whether mother or father. Do you agree with this?

* The students: Yes, yes indeed.

* Shaykh: How?

* The students: Because she said: "I have vowed him."

* Shaykh: Because she said: "I have vowed him dedicated," meaning freed from service, such that I do not employ him and do not exploit his life.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: suppressing self-admiration (ujb). That is, when a person does an act, he does not boast about it before Allah, saying: "I did, I did." Rather he acts and feels that he is in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the acceptance of that act. For this reason she said: "So accept from me" [Al 'Imran 35]. Ibrahim and Isma'il, while raising the foundations of the House, said: "Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing" [al-Baqarah 127]. When a person knows that he is in need of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, in the deed and in its acceptance, self-admiration leaves him. When self-admiration leaves him, he becomes worthy that Allah accepts from him and rewards him.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-Samī' (the All-Hearing) and al-'Alīm (the All-Knowing). We have already discussed al-Samī' and what it indicates of the attribute, and that it means responding to supplication, and it means perceiving what is heard. As for al-'Alīm, it was also discussed earlier. Al-'Alīm is the perception of a thing as it is. Whoever does not perceive is not knowing, and whoever perceives it contrary to what it is, is not knowing. The first is simple ignorance (jahl basīt), and the second is compound ignorance (jahl murakkab). Which of them is in a better state?

* The students: The simple one.

* Shaykh: The simple one. The simple one is in a better state than the compound one, because the compound one is ignorant and is ignorant that he is ignorant, so he remains as if he were knowing while he is ignorant. But the simple one says: "I do not know," so he is ignorant. We give an example of this: a man asked another, saying: "Tell me, when was the Battle of Badr?" He said: "Upon the expert it has fallen," [a play on Qur'an: "And none informs you like one who is expert" (Fatir 14)]. The Battle of Badr was in the sixth year of the Hijrah, in the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. What do you say about this?

* The students: This is compound ignorance.

* Shaykh: This is compound ignorance. He says: "Upon the expert it has fallen, and none informs you like one who is expert"? And this too is from his ignorance.

* Student: Let him review!

* Shaykh: In any case, this is compound ignorant. The second, when we asked him he said: "I do not know." This is simple ignorance. The second: if we tell him it was in the second year in Ramadan before, because he has nothing to oppose it with. But that first one opposes, saying: "Not at all. I am certain, and I am an expert on the subject."

It is related that a man called (Tuma) who styled himself "the wise," and a poet composed about him in the voice of his donkey, which he rode:

The donkey of the wise Tuma said,
"If time were just, I would be the rider,
For I am simple ignorant, and my companion
Is compound ignorant."

The donkey says: "If time were just," in any case the donkey's speech here is not good. He says: "If time were just, I would be the one riding, because I am simply ignorant and my companion is compoundly ignorant." And from the ignorance of Tuma, the poet pointed to it by his saying:

Whoever seeks the sciences without a shaykh
Goes astray from the straight path.
And the sciences become confused for him,
Until he is more astray than Tuma the wise.
He gave his daughters in charity to men
Seeking by that the gardens of bliss.

Is this knowledge or ignorance?

* The students: Ignorance.

* Shaykh: Ignorance. Daughters are not given in charity. Daughters are married off under known conditions and a dowry: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth" [an-Nisa' 24]. And what comes after it? "That you seek with your wealth." A dowry is necessary.

In any case, we have mentioned that knowledge is the perception of a thing as it is. The knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is vast, all-encompassing, complete. It is not preceded by ignorance, nor is it followed by forgetfulness. Allah said, through the tongue of Musa: "In a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets" [Ta-Ha 52]. "Neither errs" means He does not not-know. "Nor forgets" means He does not forget what He knew. Rather He, the Mighty and Majestic, knows what will happen, and how it would happen if it did, and knows what has occurred and does not forget it, and encompasses everything. Read, if you wish, His saying: "With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. And not a leaf falls but that He knows it" [al-An'am 59]. "Not a leaf falls" means any leaf that falls. For this reason the emphatic "min" (from) came: "And not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor a grain within the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry but that it is in a clear Record" [al-An'am 59]. This great generality, vastness and comprehensiveness indicates the perfection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

What is the fruit of our belief in Allah's knowledge and hearing? The fruit of our belief in that is great when we believe in it with true belief. As for the first: when we believe that He is the All-Hearing in both senses, responding and perceiving, we are cautious not to let Him hear what He does not approve, because He hears. So we beware of letting Him hear what He does not approve. And when we know that He is the All-Hearing in the sense of "responding," we insist upon Him in supplication. And of His generosity, the Mighty and Majestic, He loves those who persist in supplication. Rather He commands: "Call upon Me; I will respond to you" [Ghafir 60], and He descends in the last part of the night and says: "Who supplicates to Me that I may respond to him? Who asks Me that I may give to him? Who seeks forgiveness from Me that I may forgive him?" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1145) and Muslim (758/168) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. O Allah, grant us success. The conclusion is that this is among the fruits of belief in the All-Hearing.

Al-'Alīm: when you believe in Him with true belief, you fear that He hears from you a word, or sees from you an action, or knows from you what is neither speech nor action, such as the whispers of the soul. You fear all of this, because Allah knows it. "And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than the jugular vein. When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left" [Qaf 16–17].

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: "So when she delivered it, she said: 'My Lord, I have delivered it a female,' and Allah was most knowing of what she delivered."

From the benefits of this noble verse: the mother bears the burden of pregnancy, as the word "wadha'tha" (she delivered it) suggests, that she carries it. And that is certainly so: she bears the burden of pregnancy. If we assume that this child in her belly will remain nine months while she carries him within her body, in the most delicate part of the body, standing and sitting, awake and asleep, what suffering can we imagine? For this reason Allah said: "His mother carried him in hardship and delivered him in hardship" [al-Ahqaf 15], "His mother carried him, weakness upon weakness" [Luqman 14]. Furthermore, is this child motionless in the womb? No, he is not motionless. He moves and she feels him. Had it not been for Allah's kindness to His servants, she could not have borne this. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, helps her.

Consequently, another benefit follows from this one: the great right that a mother has over her child. Whoever has been good to you and has suffered for you has the greatest claim on your kindness. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) made the mother the person most deserving of good companionship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person's apologizing to his Lord, or before his Lord, when a matter turns out contrary to what he wished, based on His saying: ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾. This is in effect an apology, like her earlier words: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb to be devoted﴾, and in their view a female cannot serve in the mosques. That is why she apologized.

Another of its benefits is seeking nearness to Allah, the Exalted, through His lordship (*tawassul bi-rububiyyah*). From where is this derived? From ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is part of the perfection of eloquence to guard against (*al-ihtiraz*, or with the letter sīn if you prefer, *al-ihtiras*), meaning to take precaution against anything that might suggest a wrong matter. A person should take precaution against anything that might suggest a wrong matter, whether in speech or in action. From where is this derived?

* Students: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾, on both readings. On the reading with a *ḍamma* it is clear: ﴿And Allah knows best what I gave birth to﴾. We have said that a person apologizes whether what occurs from him is in speech or in action. In speech, as you have seen. In action, such as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he went out with Ṣafiyyah, may Allah be pleased with her, escorting her home when she came to him while he was in seclusion (*iʿtikāf*), and she talked with him and then stood up and left at night. The Prophet (ﷺ) went out with her, and suddenly two men of the Anṣār passed by and hurried on. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Slow down, both of you, indeed she is Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy." They said: "Glory be to Allah!" That is, there was no problem in the matter that would require an apology. He said: "Indeed Satan flows through the son of Adam like the blood, and I feared that he would cast evil into your hearts," or he said, "something."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2035) and Muslim (2175/24), from the hadith of Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy, may Allah be pleased with her.]]

This is true. Without doubt, the one furthest from entertaining bad suspicion is the Messenger (ﷺ), and especially his companions could not possibly suspect him of anything bad. Yet he feared for them. He feared that Satan would cast evil or something into their hearts. A person should likewise ward off suspicion (*al-ghībah*, or rather the suspicion that invites backbiting) from himself as far as he can. He should not say, "I do not care what people think, sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." That is fine, but take the means that ward off evil from you so that people do not think ill of you.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of superlatives in the attributes of Allah. Yes?

* Students: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿Knows best what she gave birth to﴾, contrary to those who prohibit that and interpret *aʿlam* (most knowing) as *ʿālim* (knowing). In reality, that is fleeing from one thing and falling into something worse. When one says *ʿālim*, he has not excluded sharing, because "knowing" can be applied to Him and to others. But when he says *aʿlam*, he excludes sharing. Why? Because the form of comparison (*ism al-tafḍīl*, the elative) requires that the one preferred be at the peak, with no one equal to him. Is that not so?

So *aʿlam* is more appropriate than *ʿālim*. Indeed, Allah says: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest example﴾ [An-Naḥl 60], meaning the most perfect attribute. Would you say, "To Allah belongs the lofty example"? That is not correct; it must be *al-aʿlā* (the highest). They say that when you say *aʿlam*, the comparison between two things, the high and the low, makes the high one low, as the poet said:

*Have you not seen that the sword's worth diminishes*
*When it is said: the sword is sharper than the staff?*

We reply: there is a difference between the elative used for two things that share the attribute or its root, and the elative used for two things that do not share it. The staff has no sharpness, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said that game killed by it is *waqīdh* (beaten to death, and forbidden) because it does not let blood flow and has no sharpness, whereas the sword has sharpness.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2054) and Muslim (1929/3, 4), with the wording "If it strikes with its edge, eat; if it strikes with its flat side and kills, do not eat, for it is *waqīdh*," from the hadith of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, may Allah be pleased with him.]] If you came to a person who is paralyzed (*zamin*) and a young, strong man, and you said, "So-and-so is faster in his running than so-and-so," meaning the paralyzed one, would that diminish him or not?

* Students: It would diminish him.

* Shaykh: It would diminish him, because the paralyzed one has no running. *Zamin* means the one who is paralyzed and cannot move. People call him *maḥrūl* or *muqaṣmal* in colloquial speech, words with this meaning. In any case, the correct view without doubt is that the elative is permissible in the attributes of Allah: ﴿knows best what she gave birth to﴾.

* A student: Shaykh, some people are alone with a woman, and when we tell them that this is not permitted, [he says], "My heart is clean." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No man should be alone with a woman except in the presence of a *dhū maḥram* (a mahram relative)."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5233) and Muslim (1341/424), the wording being al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] He also said: "No man is alone with a woman except that Satan is the third of them."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2165).]] Satan flows through the son of Adam like blood. This is observable and perceptible, even with righteous, committed people: when one is alone with a woman, Satan will inevitably put something into his heart, even if it is clean. Tell him, when he says "my heart is clean," we say: this seclusion has soiled it.

* A student: Shaykh, it is understood from the verse that vowing an unknown thing is permissible. If a person vows an unknown thing, and then it turns out that there was nothing and he obtained nothing, is he obligated to give a substitute?

* Shaykh: No, he is not obligated. He is not obligated.

* The student: Is this derived from the verse?

* Shaykh: Yes, because this actually happened.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, we have spoken about the benefits before. Shaykh, could this not be specific to their law?

* Shaykh: Did you hear the question?

* Students: No, we did not hear it.

* Shaykh: He says: the benefits we have drawn from the story of Maryam can be nullified with a quarter of a word, by saying: this is specific to them, which is not correct. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Certainly in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yūsuf 111]. It is a lesson in everything: in what they did of laws and transactions, and in what befell them of Allah's punishments, in everything. Otherwise, what would be the benefit of the story?

* The student: Shaykh, what about the suspicion that some of our brothers in da'wah are in, such as entering places of immorality and places where wine is drunk, with the intention of calling to Allah? Is it obligatory for them, Shaykh, to remove suspicion?

* Shaykh: What?

* The student: That they remove suspicion from themselves.

* Shaykh: Yes, no. They entered to call them and to forbid them from evil. For what does "forbidding evil" mean without entering upon them? But if they entered, for example, places of amusement, and no one saw them denouncing wrong, perhaps they could be accused. But people who entered among a group drinking wine and said: "O servants of Allah, fear Allah, this is forbidden and not permitted," there is no problem with that.

* Student: Could it be (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, well done. If this corruption is feared, one should not enter. They write letters, or they enter in a state where they are not present, and they tell the owner of the place: beware of this matter.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, how can a wife give away a child when he is not her possession but her husband's?

* Shaykh: What did we say, everyone?

* Student: *Istaʾthara* (she has the right of preference).

* Shaykh: Is it not her right that he serve her?

* The student: Her husband likewise has the right that she serve him.

* Shaykh: Yes, there is no harm: he has the right that she serve him. But she has freed him from her service, meaning regarding her service, she freed him. As for what she does not possess, she cannot dispose of it.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿There Zechariah prayed to his Lord, saying: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring. Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication. (38) Then the angels called him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: Indeed Allah gives you good news of Yaḥyā, confirming a word from Allah, and a leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous. (39) He said: My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren? He said: Thus Allah does what He wills. (40) He said: My Lord, appoint a sign for me. He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture. And remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning. (41)﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 38–41].

* Shaykh: He said: ﴿So when she had given birth to her, she said: My Lord, I have given birth to a female, and Allah knows best what she gave birth to, and the male is not like the female﴾, to the end. In this is evidence for the use of *iḥtirās* (precaution) in speech: that is, when a person says something that might cause suspicion, he must mention a precaution that removes this suspicion. From her words: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾, on both readings. Just as precaution may be by speech, it may also be by action, such as when a person displays a permissible, lawful action but fears that people will suspect it is forbidden, so he does something that shows it was permissible, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did when two men passed him while he was escorting Ṣafiyyah to her house, and he said: "Slow down, both of you, indeed she is Ṣafiyyah."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the perfection of Allah's knowledge, and that it is above every knowledge, based on His saying: ﴿Most knowing﴾, for the elative indicates that the one preferred possesses the most perfect degree of the attribute by which he is preferred.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: males and females are not equal: ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾, neither in nature, nor in character, nor in treatment, and even at times not in rulings. The male is not like the female, and if the male is not like the female, then the female is not like the male either.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse:
Among the benefits of this noble verse: naming the newborn at the time of birth, based on her saying: ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 36]. This is the Sunnah: that a person be named at birth, unless a name has not been prepared, in which case he is named on the seventh day. Thus the evidences are reconciled: when the Prophet (ﷺ) had Ibrāhīm, he said: "A son has been born to me tonight, and I have named him Ibrāhīm."[[Recorded by Muslim (2315/62), from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik, with the wording: "A boy was born to me tonight, and I named him after my father Ibrāhīm."]] In the hadith about the ʿaqīqah he said: "It is slaughtered on its seventh day, and the head is shaved, and it is named."[[Recorded by Abū Dāwūd (2838) and al-Tirmidhī (1522), from the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub.]] So the reconciliation is that whoever has prepared a name before birth, it is better to name him at birth, and whoever has not prepared one, it is better to delay it until the seventh day.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that naming belongs to the mother.

* A student: No.

* Shaykh: Why?

* Student: Because here there is no (...).

* Shaykh: Did she not say: ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾?

* Student: He has no father.

* Shaykh: How has he no father? This one has a father. There is a possibility, but the closest thing to say is that this is evidence for the permissibility of *taṣarruf al-fuḍūlī* (unauthorized disposal), meaning that a person acts upon another's right and it takes effect if the other party agrees to it. Is that not so?

* Students: Indeed.

* Shaykh: You know *taṣarruf al-fuḍūlī*. For example, a man sells another man's watch without his permission, and the owner of the watch approves and agrees to the sale. We say the sale is valid because he approved it. Here it is possible that the agreement was already in place between the mother and the father about the naming, or that the mother saw that the father would not object, so she named him. Otherwise the default is that naming belongs to the father, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A son has been born to me and I have named him Ibrāhīm."[[Already cited.]] But it is better that the parents not dispute over naming the child, and that they agree. Sometimes the mother insists that her son be named so-and-so or her daughter so-and-so, and sometimes the father insists on the opposite. What is appropriate is that this should not become a point of contention between them, and that they agree on the name. If they disagree, one refers to the best names. If the mother says, "I want my son named after his grandfather, and his grandfather's name is Nāṣir," and the father says, "I would love for him to be named ʿAbdullāh," then the right belongs to the father, and his side is also stronger, because "the most beloved names to Allah are ʿAbdullāh and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān."[[Recorded by Muslim (2132/2) and al-Tirmidhī (2833), from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, the wording being his.]] But in case of dispute and lack of a preference regarding the name, there is no doubt that the right belongs to the father.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the legitimacy of a person seeking refuge for his children in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from the accursed Satan and from the evil of creation, based on her saying: ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of supplicating for one who does not yet exist. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿and her offspring﴾, for her offspring had not yet come into being; she was a small girl, a child. But it is permissible to say: "May Allah set you right and your offspring," "May Allah forgive you and your offspring," and similar.

Can it be said that in this verse there is a *karāmah* (miraculous favor) for the wife of ʿImrān?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Yes, how?

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: Nothing other than this: from His saying ﴿and her offspring﴾. She anticipated that she would have offspring, and she did have offspring, namely ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. Otherwise, one might say: how can she say ﴿and her offspring﴾? Does she know that this little girl will survive and will have children? She certainly has no knowledge of that. But because she says it so confidently, and the matter then comes to pass as she anticipated, this is a kind of *karāmāt* (miracle).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Satan is an enemy of the children of Adam, since a person asks Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to protect him from him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power, the Glorified and Exalted, over everything, and among that, protection from Satan. Otherwise, seeking refuge in Him from Satan would be futile.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and caused her to grow up in a goodly growth﴾, to the end. Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is All-Hearing, Near, and Responsive, for she supplicated and Allah heard her, and she supplicated and Allah answered her. In the Noble Qur'an: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah 186].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the atheists who deny the existence of the Lord. What is its aspect?

* Student: (...) refutation of the atheists.

* Shaykh: What is the refutation of the atheists, and where are the atheists?

* Student: Her saying, "Indeed You..."

* Shaykh: But who mentioned refutation of the atheists?

* Student: You did.

* Shaykh: I did?

* Student: The aspect of refutation of the atheists, because they deny the existence of Allah. She said: "Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication," and only something that exists hears supplication.

* Shaykh: Did I say it like this?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Did I say there is a refutation of the atheists in her saying "Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication"?

* Student: You said to us that there is a refutation of the atheists who deny the existence of Allah. You did not say (...).

* Shaykh: Alright, from where is this derived?

* Student: From her saying, "Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication."

* Shaykh: No... where did this come before?

* Student: You did not say (...).

* Shaykh: But from where? Now I will say it.
* Student: We take (...) her words: ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾
* Shaykh: What you mentioned in what she said, ﴿Hearer of supplication﴾, is in ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.
* Student: ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾
* Shaykh: This was covered in a previous lesson, and we took its benefits.
* Student: Yes indeed, we take from her words: ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾
* Shaykh: There is no god but Allah.
* Student: Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance﴾; because when she supplicated, He said: ﴿So He accepted her﴾. This fa' (fa, the particle of sequence) is conjunctive, indicating causation, sequence, and immediacy.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed upon this young girl two things: good acceptance and good growth, and in that there is development of her character and her body and physique.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person's development in life is by the command of Allah; from His saying: ﴿and caused her to grow well﴾. Nourishment and care for the child are only a means, while Allah, Exalted is He, is the Causer, the One who creates the human being and causes him to grow.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may facilitate for a person someone from the people of goodness to sponsor him, and this is among the causes of his protection from the accursed Satan; from His saying: ﴿and Zechariah became her guardian﴾.
* And among its benefits also: the establishment of hadanah (custody of a child) for the child. The evidence? His saying: ﴿and Zechariah became her guardian.﴾ Can it be taken from this that guardianship belongs to the father and not the mother? The answer: this is not apparent, because kafalah (guardianship) here may mean guardianship of discipline, upbringing, and providing maintenance, without the direct physical custody (hadanah). For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the mother of a child: «You have more right to him as long as you do not marry»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (2276) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that this young girl became one of the worshipful devoted ones; from His saying: ﴿Whenever Zechariah entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found with her provision﴾.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may facilitate for a person provision that he did not expect; from His saying: ﴿He said, "O Mary, from where is this for you?"﴾.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that for every weakness there is a gentle kindness. This weak woman, whom Allah favored with occupation in worship, had Allah facilitate for her someone who brings her provision.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that things are attributed to Allah even though they have a cause; from His saying: ﴿It is from Allah﴾. Attributing things to their causes is merely attributing an effect to its cause, not to its originator; otherwise the true originator is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the prophets do not know the unseen; from His saying: ﴿O Mary, from where is this for you?﴾.
And among its benefits: the establishment that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, provides without recompense and without expecting any reward; from her saying: ﴿Indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 35–37 (part 1 of 5):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran 35]. That is: remember when she said. This construction is found very often in the Qur'an, and the governing verb has been omitted because the context indicates it. This is a well-known rule among the grammarians (nahwiyyun), which Ibn Malik alluded to in his Alfiyya when he said:
"The omission of what is known is permissible, as when you say, 'Zayd' in reply to someone who asks, 'Who denied [it]?'"
So here the omitted governing verb is known from the context: "remember when she said." That is: remember this circumstance in which this statement was uttered by the wife of 'Imran. ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾. Who is the wife of 'Imran?
She is the mother of Maryam, that is, the grandmother of 'Isa ibn Maryam. ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said: My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated, so accept it from me﴾ [Al 'Imran 35].
﴿Rabb﴾ (My Lord) is a vocative from which the ya' of address has been dropped; the original is "ya Rabbi." The ya' of address is dropped in such a construction for brevity, due to its frequent use. The ya' of the first person (the pronoun of the speaker) has also been dropped from it; the original is "Rabbi, inni," and it was elided for lightness.
Her words: ﴿My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated﴾. ﴿Nadhartu﴾ (I have vowed) means: I have bound myself that what is in my womb be freed from my service and devoted to it, so that it becomes a servant of the mosque, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. It was their custom to do this; that is, one of them would vow his child to be standing in service of the Al-Aqsa Mosque, out of reverence for it. So she says: ﴿My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated﴾. Her words ﴿what is in my womb﴾ is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) that conveys generality, so it includes whether she gives birth to one or two, and male or female.
If someone says: How can you say that it includes what she might bear as two, when she says: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated﴾, and "dedicated" is singular, and she did not say "dedicated (dual)"?
The answer: the shared relative pronouns, that is, those which suit the singular and others, may be treated according to their wording (lafz) as singular, or according to their meaning: singular if the singular is intended, dual if the dual is intended, and plural if the plural is intended, whether masculine or feminine. Accordingly, there is nothing to prevent her saying ﴿dedicated﴾ from including what she bears even if there were more than one, because it is singular in consideration of what? In consideration of the wording. Likewise the conditional (man) allows treatment according to wording and treatment according to meaning. Have you not seen the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds, He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾ [At-Taghabun 9]. In consideration of what?
The singular here is in consideration of the wording: ﴿He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾; he mentioned it in consideration of the wording. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is in consideration of the meaning.
﴿Allah has certainly made good for him a provision﴾ [At-Talaq 11] is in consideration of the wording.
You say: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb﴾ is general, including everything in her womb, whether males or females, one or more; ﴿dedicated﴾ from what? From the bond of my service to the service of the Al-Aqsa Mosque.
﴿So accept it from me﴾ means: accept from me this drawing near to You by vowing this child, who will serve Your House.
﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) sentence giving the reason; that is, I asked You to accept from me because You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. "All-Hearing" here includes both hearing of perception and hearing of response, meaning that You hear my supplication and answer it. It has already passed that As-Sami' (the All-Hearing) is one of Allah's names and includes both hearing of perception and hearing of response, and that (sami'a) comes with the meaning of (istajaba, responded), as in the words of the one praying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him," i.e., responds. So here, ﴿Hearer of supplication﴾: which is more appropriate, perception or response?
* The students: Response... it includes both.
* The Shaykh: It includes both, but what is the benefit of the one who supplicates? By response.
Her words ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing﴾ mean: the hearer of my supplication, who responds to it, the All-Knowing of what is good, and of everything. But the mention of knowledge here is because a person may ask for something that is not good for him to obtain, so he attributes the matter to the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
It is known that when a supplicant supplicates, one of three things happens to him: either Allah responds to his supplication, or He stores it up for him for the Day of Resurrection, giving him the like of what he asked for, or He averts from him an evil greater than it. Besides this, supplication itself is an act of worship for which a person is rewarded. ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. ﴿So when she delivered her﴾; she did not say "when she delivered him." In consideration of what?
* The students: In consideration of the meaning.
* The Shaykh: In consideration of the meaning, because she delivered a female. So when she delivered her, and she had vowed her as dedicated on the assumption that it was a male, when she delivered her she made an excuse to her Lord: ﴿She said: My Lord, I have delivered her a female﴾ [Al 'Imran 36]. This is an excuse from her to Allah that she delivered a female, and a female is not customarily one who serves the mosque, so she is, as it were, excusing herself to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for this vow.
He said: ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾. In another reading: ﴿And Allah knows best what I delivered﴾, which is a canonical (sab'i) reading. We explain it according to both readings. As for her words ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female﴾, you know that the purpose of this sentence is what?
* The students: The excuse.
* The Shaykh: The excuse, not informing Allah of what she delivered, since He is the All-Knowing, the Mighty and Majestic. He is the One who created her, and she was delivered by His permission and command, so the matter is not hidden from Him. But she mentioned it as an excuse. Accordingly, on the reading ﴿And Allah knows best what I delivered﴾, the sentence is a precautionary insertion (ihtiras), lest it be thought that she believed Allah did not know. So she said: "My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what I delivered." I am not informing Allah of a matter hidden from Him; rather I believe that He knows what I delivered. This is on the reading with the damma on the ta'. As for the reading with the sukun: ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾, the speech is from Allah, and in it is a defence of this woman, that Allah the Exalted knows that she did not say ﴿I have delivered her a female﴾ as information to Allah, because He, glorified and exalted, attested to her by His words: ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾. This is one aspect. Another aspect: to show that her words ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female﴾ do not mean that Allah does not know what she delivered; rather He knows, even if she said: ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what she delivered﴾.
"Knows best" (a'lam) is a comparative form indicating that the one preferred exceeds the one compared in this attribute, as if you say: "So-and-so is more generous than so-and-so," meaning that this one preferred, who is so-and-so, exceeds the other in generosity. So "a'lam" here means: more knowing than anyone of what she delivered. This affirms knowledge to Allah with excess. By this explanation we know the weakness of the view of those who said that the comparative here carries the meaning of the active participle, and that the meaning of His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ is "and Allah is knowing of what she delivered." That view is without doubt deficient, a deficiency in explaining the speech of Allah, because affirming knowledge without comparison is less than affirming knowledge with comparison. Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because when you say "so-and-so is knowing," it does not prevent that another might be equal to him in knowledge; but when you say "so-and-so is more knowing than so-and-so," the one is superior to the other in knowledge, and the other is inferior. And I do not know, glory be to Allah, how some scholars flee from affirming comparison between Allah, glorified and exalted, and His creation, even though comparison does not indicate any deficiency. Rather, the expression that implies sharing is what may admit deficiency and similarity, but the expression that indicates comparison contains no deficiency in any way. So Allah is more knowing than anyone, whether this knowledge is restricted or unrestricted.
His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ contain a point of inquiry: "ma" is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun requires a returning pronoun (a'id). Where is the returning pronoun? ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾, or: ﴿what I delivered﴾. The question again: where did your thought go?
* A student: (...) "delivered" (wada'at) and "I delivered" (wada'tu) is a reading (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the returning pronoun is omitted: an omitted object pronoun. The estimate is: "what I delivered it" or "what she delivered it," on both readings.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾. The male is not like the female. Is this from her speech or from the speech of Allah?
As for the reading ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾, it is apparent that it is from the speech of Allah; that it is from the speech of Allah is more likely, because His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ are from the speech of Allah.
As for the reading ﴿And Allah knows best what I delivered﴾, that it is from her speech is more likely, so that the sentences do not scatter. Let us recite the verse: ﴿My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what I delivered, and the male is not like the female, and I have named her Maryam﴾, which is now coherent and well-joined. But if we make ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾ part of the speech of Allah, then His words ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ fit with His words ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered﴾. Therefore the scholars differed over whether this sentence is from the speech of Allah or from the speech of the wife of 'Imran.
We say: both possibilities exist in any case, but on the reading ﴿what I delivered﴾ it is more likely to be from the speech of whom? The wife of 'Imran; and on the reading ﴿what she delivered﴾ it is more likely to be from the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
In any case, this sentence makes clear that the male is not like the female. It is as if a person speaks to himself and says: the situation would require the phrase to be "and the female is not like the male," since the custom is that the lesser is compared to the greater. Here, "the female is not like the male" seems closer at first glance than "and the male is not like the female."
For this reason some scholars claimed that there is an inversion (qalb) in the comparison, and the inverted comparison is a style of the Arabic language, especially among the poets of the middle ages, to the extent that some exaggerate in inverted comparison until one says:
"When the morning appears, its brightness is as if it were the face of the caliph when he is praised."
The morning, which fills the horizon and lights the world, is as if its brightness (its whiteness) were the face of the caliph when praised. And what is the caliph's whiteness? That is, the whiteness of his face. This is, in truth, a repugnant exaggeration. The point is that some said it is an inverted comparison, and some said it is a comparison in its original and proper form: the male is not like the female, and the superiority of the male over the female is known from other proofs and other indications. But the male in his service of Bayt al-Maqdis is not like the female. Is the male higher, or lower? Higher.
* A student: Will the story of "Abu Maryam" not be explained to us?
* The Shaykh: Abu what?
* The student: (...) Abu Maryam.
* The Shaykh: Between them are long periods of time. This was raised against the Messenger ﷺ, regarding his words: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾ [Maryam 28]: Maryam daughter of 'Imran, and Harun. He said: they used to name people after their prophets. The wife of Maryam's father cannot be a sister of Musa ibn 'Imran, because the Messenger ﷺ said: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾, "They used to name themselves after their prophets" [recorded by Muslim (2135/9) with the wording: "They used to name themselves after their prophets and the righteous before them," from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, may Allah be pleased with him]; that is, between them are many centuries, and Musa ibn 'Imran.
* The student: Yes indeed, she is the sister of Harun, daughter of Harun, sister of Harun.
* The Shaykh: The sister of Harun is not the sister of Musa.
* A student: Shaykh, when the mother of Maryam, peace be upon her, vowed, was there a reason (...) the female in this way?
* The Shaykh: Not at all; it was out of their desire to serve the mosque.
* A student: Shaykh, we said that "the worlds" (...) Shaykh, and we also mentioned that there was a difficulty in the words of Allah: ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds?﴾, from this lesson?
* The Shaykh: Yes, did we raise this difficulty?
* A student: Honored Shaykh, because here (...) creation (...).
* The Shaykh: Sometimes the general is specified by an indicator, either the indicator of the situation or the indicator of speech. That is, it may be a situational indicator or a verbal indicator; if it is verbal, it is an indicator of speech, and if it is situational, it is an indicator of the situation. Allah mentioned that He preferred the Children of Israel over the worlds, and it is known that the community of Muhammad is better than them. Allah said about the Children of Israel: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 32]. So the intended meaning is "over the worlds of their time."
* * *
* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿So when she delivered her, she said: My Lord, I have delivered her a female, and Allah knows best what she delivered, and the male is not like the female, and I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan﴾ (36). ﴿So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow up with a good growth and entrusted her to Zakariyya. Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her at the prayer niche, he found with her provision. He said: O Maryam, from where is this for you? She said: It is from Allah; indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾ (37). ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord. He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring; indeed You are the Hearer of supplication﴾ (38). ﴿And the angels called him while he stood in prayer in the prayer niche: Indeed Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a master, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran 36–39].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾ means the male is not equal to the female. When equality between the male and the female is negated, equality of the female with the male is negated too, because equality is between two things; if equality is absent in one of them, it must be absent in the other. So there is no equality between male and female; rather each has its own distinctive features. The female surpasses the man in some things, and the man surpasses the female in some things. But the one generally suited to serve the mosques is the man, because he is stronger, more intelligent, more sensible, and more enduring in work. A female, when she menstruates, for example, cannot serve the mosque, since she would have to leave it and not sit in it. This is if their law is like ours. Also, the female cannot bear the arduous tasks; rather she is weaker than the man. Although she may have more endurance and patience than a man in dealing with people, not in bearing calamities, since the woman in bearing calamities is far below the man, as is well known. He said: ﴿And the male is not like the female, and I have named her Maryam﴾. Who says it? Her mother says: I have named her Maryam. This name either was well known among them, or she chose it for a matter that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, intends.
In any case, I cannot explain why she chose this name, since this is a matter specific to her, and Allah knows best what was the reason she chose this name. She said: ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You﴾. "I seek refuge for her" means: I ask You for protection on her behalf, since seeking refuge (isti'adha) means seeking protection (istijara) from a disliked matter. That is why we seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan, and we seek refuge in Allah from the punishment of Hell and the punishment of the grave, the trial of life and death, and the trial of the false Messiah. The lexicographers said: "al-'iyadh" is seeking refuge from what is disliked, and "al-liyadh" is seeking shelter in hope of what is loved, seeking shelter in hope of what is loved; and they cited in support of this the verse of the poet:
