* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. Some people now, Shaykh, criticize the mihrabs (the niche-shaped markers in mosque carpets). They say it is an innovation (bid'ah)?

* Shaykh: That is not correct. Some people do not understand the meaning of bid'ah (innovation in religion) from the Sunnah, because they do not distinguish between a means (wasilah) and what is intended for its own sake. The Muslims who approved them, from hundreds of years ago, were eminent scholars, and they were further from innovation than these people. They knew that they did not adopt them in order to worship Allah by adopting them, but to guide the Muslims to the direction of the qiblah. If a commoner entered a mosque with no mihrab, where would he face? I saw with my own eyes, when the carpets first came to Riyadh, the carpet-layer who laid them had, at the beginning, a picture of mihrabs on them. Do you not remember?

* The students: They are still there. They are still there until now.

* Shaykh: There is a picture of mihrabs on them. The carpet-layer laid them, and the face of the mihrab came behind the qiblah, the reverse way. A man entered, saw the mihrab, and did not realize it was the qiblah of the mosque. He said "Allahu Akbar" and began to pray behind it. So there is a benefit in them. They are intended for something else, not for their own sake. The Muslims do not say: "We did it following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," or "We did it to draw near to Allah." They say: "We did it so that the ignorant person may be guided to the qiblah by them."

* * *

* Student: "There Zechariah called upon his Lord, saying: 'My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication.' (38) So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the mihrab: 'Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a noble leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous.' (39) He said: 'My Lord, how can I have a boy when old age has already reached me and my wife is barren?' He said: 'So it is; Allah does what He wills.' (40) He said: 'My Lord, appoint for me a sign.' He said: 'Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days except by gestures. And remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning.'" [Al 'Imran 38–41].

* Shaykh: "Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning." Indeed Allah provides. Provision (rizq) means giving, and giving is divided into two kinds: universal giving (kawni, that which occurs by the cosmic decree of Allah) and legislative giving (shar'i, that which is by the revealed law). Universal giving is what Allah provides to all living creatures: humans and animals, the lawful and the unlawful. This is universal giving, what is it?

* The students: Universal (kawni).

* Shaykh: Universal. It is not specific to the believers, nor to good provision. The second is legislative giving, which is what the believer is given of lawful provision. It is the specific provision that carries no accountability. It also includes legislative giving, which is what has been given according to the requirement of the law, such as giving to the poor from zakat, for example, and giving to those who share in the spoils from the booty. This is legislative giving. Its evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near of kin and the orphans and the needy and the traveler, so that it does not circulate only among the rich among you. And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it" [al-Hashr 7]. The giving here (ītā') is it legislative or universal?

* The students: Legislative.

* Shaykh: Legislative. And His saying, the Exalted: "And if they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and said: 'Allah is sufficient for us; Allah will give us of His bounty, and His Messenger. Indeed we are toward Allah desiring.' (59) The zakat is only for the poor..." [at-Tawbah 59–60], and so on to the end. This too is legislative giving.

So provision is either universal or legislative. What is for enjoyment in this world, or what sustains the body, is universal. What sustains the soul and the heart, or what is by permission of the law, is legislative. Knowledge and faith: are they legislative or universal?

* The students: Legislative.

* Shaykh: This is legislative, because the soul and heart are sustained by it.

As for His saying: "whom He wills," there is no doubt that this refers to the will of Allah. Provision only occurs by the will of Allah. But do you think the will is absolute and unrestricted? No, rather it is tied to wisdom. He gives whom He wills for a wisdom, and withholds from whom He wills for a wisdom. The proof that whatever Allah attributes to His will is accompanied by wisdom is His saying: "And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise" [al-Insan 30]. So He does not will except what the requirement of wisdom wills.

As for His saying: "Indeed Allah provides whom He wills," we have said that it must be accompanied by wisdom.

"Without reckoning" means without recompense. He feeds and is not fed, He provides and is not provided for. "I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me. Indeed Allah is the Provider, Possessor of strength, the Firm" [adh-Dhariyat 57–58]. Unlike others, who may give in order to be given to. Is that not so? As for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He gives not in order to be given to, but provides without reckoning, meaning without recompense. He does not ask anyone for recompense. As for the reckoning concerning what Allah has given of provision, what a person earned, where he spent it, and the like, this will occur. Allah said: "Then you will be asked that Day about pleasure" [at-Takathur 8]. So the reckoning intended here is what? Recompense? Meaning He does not reckon with creatures in order to repay them, but He reckons with them in order to see, or in order to know, the Mighty and Majestic, what they spent of what He gave them.

In these verses there are benefits. I think we should begin from His saying: "When the wife of 'Imran said..." or not?

* Some benefits of these verses:

First: the glorification of this story, because Allah commanded His Messenger to explain it to the people. The implied meaning is: "Mention when the wife of 'Imran said..."

Another benefit: the permissibility of vowing (nadhr) about an unknown matter, due to her saying: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated." Does this mean that the speaker may say: "I owe Allah a vow to give in charity what is in the belly of this sheep or this camel," and the vow is carried out?

* Another benefit of the verse: the permissibility of a woman giving charity without her husband's permission. Its basis? She vowed to free or dedicate this child without the husband's permission. If someone says: "What is your evidence that it was without her husband's permission? Is it not possible that she sought his permission?"

The answer: Yes, that is possible, but it is not mentioned. If someone says: "Non-mention is not a mention of non-existence," there is a difference between my remaining silent about a matter and my negating it. Negating a thing is a mention of its non-existence, but silence about it is not a mention of non-existence. We say: this is not in every place. Rather we say: this applies when there are general texts, and then someone claims their specification or restriction or the like. This is what we say to him: non-mention is not a mention of non-existence. But when an unrestricted account comes and no conditions are mentioned in it, the original position is what?

* The students: The absence of conditions.

* Shaykh: The original position is the absence of conditions. The Islamic law has come supporting this, meaning that a woman disposes of her wealth freely. The evidence: "That the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he addressed the women on the day of 'Id and said: 'O assembly of women, give charity,' they began to throw their rings and earrings into the cloth of Bilal." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (304) and Muslim (80), with the wording of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] Did the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Seek your husbands' permission"? Did they say: "We will seek permission"? No.

Take also from the Qur'an: "And give the women their dowries graciously. But if they give you of it willingly, then consume it with satisfaction and pleasure" [an-Nisa' 4]. Who are "they" (tibna)?

* The students: The women.

* Shaykh: The women. "Consume it with satisfaction and pleasure." So the woman is free to dispose, and her husband has no right to prevent her from any disposal she wishes, except in one matter. It may be said that he prevents her from disposing of it, such as if he buys her jewelry and clothes of adornment to beautify herself for him. Here we may say he has the right to prevent her from disposing of these clothes and this jewelry by sale or gift, because that harms his purpose. Is that not so?

* Man: Yes.

* Shaykh: So if she now sells this jewelry and this beautiful clothing, and goes out to her husband with no jewelry, and wears poor, shabby clothes, he is between two situations: either he has intercourse with her while disliking her, or he does not accept this state. Then she says: "Come, give me," and he buys for her. When he buys for her, another woman comes to her complaining of the situation, and she says: "Take," and on the second day she goes out to him with nothing again. The matter continues in a chain. In this situation we may say that the husband has the right to prevent her from disposing of what he gave her, because that harms him, either financially or in his enjoyment.

From the benefits of this noble verse: a child serves his parent, whether mother or father. Do you agree with this?

* The students: Yes, yes indeed.

* Shaykh: How?

* The students: Because she said: "I have vowed him."

* Shaykh: Because she said: "I have vowed him dedicated," meaning freed from service, such that I do not employ him and do not exploit his life.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: suppressing self-admiration (ujb). That is, when a person does an act, he does not boast about it before Allah, saying: "I did, I did." Rather he acts and feels that he is in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the acceptance of that act. For this reason she said: "So accept from me" [Al 'Imran 35]. Ibrahim and Isma'il, while raising the foundations of the House, said: "Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing" [al-Baqarah 127]. When a person knows that he is in need of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, in the deed and in its acceptance, self-admiration leaves him. When self-admiration leaves him, he becomes worthy that Allah accepts from him and rewards him.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-Samī' (the All-Hearing) and al-'Alīm (the All-Knowing). We have already discussed al-Samī' and what it indicates of the attribute, and that it means responding to supplication, and it means perceiving what is heard. As for al-'Alīm, it was also discussed earlier. Al-'Alīm is the perception of a thing as it is. Whoever does not perceive is not knowing, and whoever perceives it contrary to what it is, is not knowing. The first is simple ignorance (jahl basīt), and the second is compound ignorance (jahl murakkab). Which of them is in a better state?

* The students: The simple one.

* Shaykh: The simple one. The simple one is in a better state than the compound one, because the compound one is ignorant and is ignorant that he is ignorant, so he remains as if he were knowing while he is ignorant. But the simple one says: "I do not know," so he is ignorant. We give an example of this: a man asked another, saying: "Tell me, when was the Battle of Badr?" He said: "Upon the expert it has fallen," [a play on Qur'an: "And none informs you like one who is expert" (Fatir 14)]. The Battle of Badr was in the sixth year of the Hijrah, in the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. What do you say about this?

* The students: This is compound ignorance.

* Shaykh: This is compound ignorance. He says: "Upon the expert it has fallen, and none informs you like one who is expert"? And this too is from his ignorance.

* Student: Let him review!

* Shaykh: In any case, this is compound ignorant. The second, when we asked him he said: "I do not know." This is simple ignorance. The second: if we tell him it was in the second year in Ramadan before, because he has nothing to oppose it with. But that first one opposes, saying: "Not at all. I am certain, and I am an expert on the subject."

It is related that a man called (Tuma) who styled himself "the wise," and a poet composed about him in the voice of his donkey, which he rode:

The donkey of the wise Tuma said,
"If time were just, I would be the rider,
For I am simple ignorant, and my companion
Is compound ignorant."

The donkey says: "If time were just," in any case the donkey's speech here is not good. He says: "If time were just, I would be the one riding, because I am simply ignorant and my companion is compoundly ignorant." And from the ignorance of Tuma, the poet pointed to it by his saying:

Whoever seeks the sciences without a shaykh
Goes astray from the straight path.
And the sciences become confused for him,
Until he is more astray than Tuma the wise.
He gave his daughters in charity to men
Seeking by that the gardens of bliss.

Is this knowledge or ignorance?

* The students: Ignorance.

* Shaykh: Ignorance. Daughters are not given in charity. Daughters are married off under known conditions and a dowry: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth" [an-Nisa' 24]. And what comes after it? "That you seek with your wealth." A dowry is necessary.

In any case, we have mentioned that knowledge is the perception of a thing as it is. The knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is vast, all-encompassing, complete. It is not preceded by ignorance, nor is it followed by forgetfulness. Allah said, through the tongue of Musa: "In a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets" [Ta-Ha 52]. "Neither errs" means He does not not-know. "Nor forgets" means He does not forget what He knew. Rather He, the Mighty and Majestic, knows what will happen, and how it would happen if it did, and knows what has occurred and does not forget it, and encompasses everything. Read, if you wish, His saying: "With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. And not a leaf falls but that He knows it" [al-An'am 59]. "Not a leaf falls" means any leaf that falls. For this reason the emphatic "min" (from) came: "And not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor a grain within the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry but that it is in a clear Record" [al-An'am 59]. This great generality, vastness and comprehensiveness indicates the perfection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

What is the fruit of our belief in Allah's knowledge and hearing? The fruit of our belief in that is great when we believe in it with true belief. As for the first: when we believe that He is the All-Hearing in both senses, responding and perceiving, we are cautious not to let Him hear what He does not approve, because He hears. So we beware of letting Him hear what He does not approve. And when we know that He is the All-Hearing in the sense of "responding," we insist upon Him in supplication. And of His generosity, the Mighty and Majestic, He loves those who persist in supplication. Rather He commands: "Call upon Me; I will respond to you" [Ghafir 60], and He descends in the last part of the night and says: "Who supplicates to Me that I may respond to him? Who asks Me that I may give to him? Who seeks forgiveness from Me that I may forgive him?" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1145) and Muslim (758/168) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. O Allah, grant us success. The conclusion is that this is among the fruits of belief in the All-Hearing.

Al-'Alīm: when you believe in Him with true belief, you fear that He hears from you a word, or sees from you an action, or knows from you what is neither speech nor action, such as the whispers of the soul. You fear all of this, because Allah knows it. "And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than the jugular vein. When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left" [Qaf 16–17].

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: "So when she delivered it, she said: 'My Lord, I have delivered it a female,' and Allah was most knowing of what she delivered."

From the benefits of this noble verse: the mother bears the burden of pregnancy, as the word "wadha'tha" (she delivered it) suggests, that she carries it. And that is certainly so: she bears the burden of pregnancy. If we assume that this child in her belly will remain nine months while she carries him within her body, in the most delicate part of the body, standing and sitting, awake and asleep, what suffering can we imagine? For this reason Allah said: "His mother carried him in hardship and delivered him in hardship" [al-Ahqaf 15], "His mother carried him, weakness upon weakness" [Luqman 14]. Furthermore, is this child motionless in the womb? No, he is not motionless. He moves and she feels him. Had it not been for Allah's kindness to His servants, she could not have borne this. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, helps her.

Consequently, another benefit follows from this one: the great right that a mother has over her child. Whoever has been good to you and has suffered for you has the greatest claim on your kindness. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) made the mother the person most deserving of good companionship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person's apologizing to his Lord, or before his Lord, when a matter turns out contrary to what he wished, based on His saying: ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾. This is in effect an apology, like her earlier words: ﴿I have vowed to You what is in my womb to be devoted﴾, and in their view a female cannot serve in the mosques. That is why she apologized.

Another of its benefits is seeking nearness to Allah, the Exalted, through His lordship (*tawassul bi-rububiyyah*). From where is this derived? From ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is part of the perfection of eloquence to guard against (*al-ihtiraz*, or with the letter sīn if you prefer, *al-ihtiras*), meaning to take precaution against anything that might suggest a wrong matter. A person should take precaution against anything that might suggest a wrong matter, whether in speech or in action. From where is this derived?

* Students: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾, on both readings. On the reading with a *ḍamma* it is clear: ﴿And Allah knows best what I gave birth to﴾. We have said that a person apologizes whether what occurs from him is in speech or in action. In speech, as you have seen. In action, such as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he went out with Ṣafiyyah, may Allah be pleased with her, escorting her home when she came to him while he was in seclusion (*iʿtikāf*), and she talked with him and then stood up and left at night. The Prophet (ﷺ) went out with her, and suddenly two men of the Anṣār passed by and hurried on. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Slow down, both of you, indeed she is Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy." They said: "Glory be to Allah!" That is, there was no problem in the matter that would require an apology. He said: "Indeed Satan flows through the son of Adam like the blood, and I feared that he would cast evil into your hearts," or he said, "something."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2035) and Muslim (2175/24), from the hadith of Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy, may Allah be pleased with her.]]

This is true. Without doubt, the one furthest from entertaining bad suspicion is the Messenger (ﷺ), and especially his companions could not possibly suspect him of anything bad. Yet he feared for them. He feared that Satan would cast evil or something into their hearts. A person should likewise ward off suspicion (*al-ghībah*, or rather the suspicion that invites backbiting) from himself as far as he can. He should not say, "I do not care what people think, sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." That is fine, but take the means that ward off evil from you so that people do not think ill of you.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of superlatives in the attributes of Allah. Yes?

* Students: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿Knows best what she gave birth to﴾, contrary to those who prohibit that and interpret *aʿlam* (most knowing) as *ʿālim* (knowing). In reality, that is fleeing from one thing and falling into something worse. When one says *ʿālim*, he has not excluded sharing, because "knowing" can be applied to Him and to others. But when he says *aʿlam*, he excludes sharing. Why? Because the form of comparison (*ism al-tafḍīl*, the elative) requires that the one preferred be at the peak, with no one equal to him. Is that not so?

So *aʿlam* is more appropriate than *ʿālim*. Indeed, Allah says: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest example﴾ [An-Naḥl 60], meaning the most perfect attribute. Would you say, "To Allah belongs the lofty example"? That is not correct; it must be *al-aʿlā* (the highest). They say that when you say *aʿlam*, the comparison between two things, the high and the low, makes the high one low, as the poet said:

*Have you not seen that the sword's worth diminishes*
*When it is said: the sword is sharper than the staff?*

We reply: there is a difference between the elative used for two things that share the attribute or its root, and the elative used for two things that do not share it. The staff has no sharpness, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said that game killed by it is *waqīdh* (beaten to death, and forbidden) because it does not let blood flow and has no sharpness, whereas the sword has sharpness.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2054) and Muslim (1929/3, 4), with the wording "If it strikes with its edge, eat; if it strikes with its flat side and kills, do not eat, for it is *waqīdh*," from the hadith of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, may Allah be pleased with him.]] If you came to a person who is paralyzed (*zamin*) and a young, strong man, and you said, "So-and-so is faster in his running than so-and-so," meaning the paralyzed one, would that diminish him or not?

* Students: It would diminish him.

* Shaykh: It would diminish him, because the paralyzed one has no running. *Zamin* means the one who is paralyzed and cannot move. People call him *maḥrūl* or *muqaṣmal* in colloquial speech, words with this meaning. In any case, the correct view without doubt is that the elative is permissible in the attributes of Allah: ﴿knows best what she gave birth to﴾.

* A student: Shaykh, some people are alone with a woman, and when we tell them that this is not permitted, [he says], "My heart is clean." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No man should be alone with a woman except in the presence of a *dhū maḥram* (a mahram relative)."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5233) and Muslim (1341/424), the wording being al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] He also said: "No man is alone with a woman except that Satan is the third of them."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2165).]] Satan flows through the son of Adam like blood. This is observable and perceptible, even with righteous, committed people: when one is alone with a woman, Satan will inevitably put something into his heart, even if it is clean. Tell him, when he says "my heart is clean," we say: this seclusion has soiled it.

* A student: Shaykh, it is understood from the verse that vowing an unknown thing is permissible. If a person vows an unknown thing, and then it turns out that there was nothing and he obtained nothing, is he obligated to give a substitute?

* Shaykh: No, he is not obligated. He is not obligated.

* The student: Is this derived from the verse?

* Shaykh: Yes, because this actually happened.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, we have spoken about the benefits before. Shaykh, could this not be specific to their law?

* Shaykh: Did you hear the question?

* Students: No, we did not hear it.

* Shaykh: He says: the benefits we have drawn from the story of Maryam can be nullified with a quarter of a word, by saying: this is specific to them, which is not correct. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Certainly in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yūsuf 111]. It is a lesson in everything: in what they did of laws and transactions, and in what befell them of Allah's punishments, in everything. Otherwise, what would be the benefit of the story?

* The student: Shaykh, what about the suspicion that some of our brothers in da'wah are in, such as entering places of immorality and places where wine is drunk, with the intention of calling to Allah? Is it obligatory for them, Shaykh, to remove suspicion?

* Shaykh: What?

* The student: That they remove suspicion from themselves.

* Shaykh: Yes, no. They entered to call them and to forbid them from evil. For what does "forbidding evil" mean without entering upon them? But if they entered, for example, places of amusement, and no one saw them denouncing wrong, perhaps they could be accused. But people who entered among a group drinking wine and said: "O servants of Allah, fear Allah, this is forbidden and not permitted," there is no problem with that.

* Student: Could it be (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, well done. If this corruption is feared, one should not enter. They write letters, or they enter in a state where they are not present, and they tell the owner of the place: beware of this matter.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, how can a wife give away a child when he is not her possession but her husband's?

* Shaykh: What did we say, everyone?

* Student: *Istaʾthara* (she has the right of preference).

* Shaykh: Is it not her right that he serve her?

* The student: Her husband likewise has the right that she serve him.

* Shaykh: Yes, there is no harm: he has the right that she serve him. But she has freed him from her service, meaning regarding her service, she freed him. As for what she does not possess, she cannot dispose of it.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿There Zechariah prayed to his Lord, saying: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring. Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication. (38) Then the angels called him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: Indeed Allah gives you good news of Yaḥyā, confirming a word from Allah, and a leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous. (39) He said: My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren? He said: Thus Allah does what He wills. (40) He said: My Lord, appoint a sign for me. He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture. And remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning. (41)﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 38–41].

* Shaykh: He said: ﴿So when she had given birth to her, she said: My Lord, I have given birth to a female, and Allah knows best what she gave birth to, and the male is not like the female﴾, to the end. In this is evidence for the use of *iḥtirās* (precaution) in speech: that is, when a person says something that might cause suspicion, he must mention a precaution that removes this suspicion. From her words: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾, on both readings. Just as precaution may be by speech, it may also be by action, such as when a person displays a permissible, lawful action but fears that people will suspect it is forbidden, so he does something that shows it was permissible, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did when two men passed him while he was escorting Ṣafiyyah to her house, and he said: "Slow down, both of you, indeed she is Ṣafiyyah."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the perfection of Allah's knowledge, and that it is above every knowledge, based on His saying: ﴿Most knowing﴾, for the elative indicates that the one preferred possesses the most perfect degree of the attribute by which he is preferred.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: males and females are not equal: ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾, neither in nature, nor in character, nor in treatment, and even at times not in rulings. The male is not like the female, and if the male is not like the female, then the female is not like the male either.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse:
Among the benefits of this noble verse: naming the newborn at the time of birth, based on her saying: ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 36]. This is the Sunnah: that a person be named at birth, unless a name has not been prepared, in which case he is named on the seventh day. Thus the evidences are reconciled: when the Prophet (ﷺ) had Ibrāhīm, he said: "A son has been born to me tonight, and I have named him Ibrāhīm."[[Recorded by Muslim (2315/62), from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik, with the wording: "A boy was born to me tonight, and I named him after my father Ibrāhīm."]] In the hadith about the ʿaqīqah he said: "It is slaughtered on its seventh day, and the head is shaved, and it is named."[[Recorded by Abū Dāwūd (2838) and al-Tirmidhī (1522), from the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub.]] So the reconciliation is that whoever has prepared a name before birth, it is better to name him at birth, and whoever has not prepared one, it is better to delay it until the seventh day.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that naming belongs to the mother.

* A student: No.

* Shaykh: Why?

* Student: Because here there is no (...).

* Shaykh: Did she not say: ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾?

* Student: He has no father.

* Shaykh: How has he no father? This one has a father. There is a possibility, but the closest thing to say is that this is evidence for the permissibility of *taṣarruf al-fuḍūlī* (unauthorized disposal), meaning that a person acts upon another's right and it takes effect if the other party agrees to it. Is that not so?

* Students: Indeed.

* Shaykh: You know *taṣarruf al-fuḍūlī*. For example, a man sells another man's watch without his permission, and the owner of the watch approves and agrees to the sale. We say the sale is valid because he approved it. Here it is possible that the agreement was already in place between the mother and the father about the naming, or that the mother saw that the father would not object, so she named him. Otherwise the default is that naming belongs to the father, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A son has been born to me and I have named him Ibrāhīm."[[Already cited.]] But it is better that the parents not dispute over naming the child, and that they agree. Sometimes the mother insists that her son be named so-and-so or her daughter so-and-so, and sometimes the father insists on the opposite. What is appropriate is that this should not become a point of contention between them, and that they agree on the name. If they disagree, one refers to the best names. If the mother says, "I want my son named after his grandfather, and his grandfather's name is Nāṣir," and the father says, "I would love for him to be named ʿAbdullāh," then the right belongs to the father, and his side is also stronger, because "the most beloved names to Allah are ʿAbdullāh and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān."[[Recorded by Muslim (2132/2) and al-Tirmidhī (2833), from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, the wording being his.]] But in case of dispute and lack of a preference regarding the name, there is no doubt that the right belongs to the father.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the legitimacy of a person seeking refuge for his children in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from the accursed Satan and from the evil of creation, based on her saying: ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of supplicating for one who does not yet exist. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿and her offspring﴾, for her offspring had not yet come into being; she was a small girl, a child. But it is permissible to say: "May Allah set you right and your offspring," "May Allah forgive you and your offspring," and similar.

Can it be said that in this verse there is a *karāmah* (miraculous favor) for the wife of ʿImrān?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Yes, how?

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: Nothing other than this: from His saying ﴿and her offspring﴾. She anticipated that she would have offspring, and she did have offspring, namely ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. Otherwise, one might say: how can she say ﴿and her offspring﴾? Does she know that this little girl will survive and will have children? She certainly has no knowledge of that. But because she says it so confidently, and the matter then comes to pass as she anticipated, this is a kind of *karāmāt* (miracle).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Satan is an enemy of the children of Adam, since a person asks Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to protect him from him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power, the Glorified and Exalted, over everything, and among that, protection from Satan. Otherwise, seeking refuge in Him from Satan would be futile.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and caused her to grow up in a goodly growth﴾, to the end. Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is All-Hearing, Near, and Responsive, for she supplicated and Allah heard her, and she supplicated and Allah answered her. In the Noble Qur'an: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah 186].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the atheists who deny the existence of the Lord. What is its aspect?

* Student: (...) refutation of the atheists.

* Shaykh: What is the refutation of the atheists, and where are the atheists?

* Student: Her saying, "Indeed You..."

* Shaykh: But who mentioned refutation of the atheists?

* Student: You did.

* Shaykh: I did?

* Student: The aspect of refutation of the atheists, because they deny the existence of Allah. She said: "Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication," and only something that exists hears supplication.

* Shaykh: Did I say it like this?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Did I say there is a refutation of the atheists in her saying "Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication"?

* Student: You said to us that there is a refutation of the atheists who deny the existence of Allah. You did not say (...).

* Shaykh: Alright, from where is this derived?

* Student: From her saying, "Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication."

* Shaykh: No... where did this come before?

* Student: You did not say (...).

* Shaykh: But from where? Now I will say it.
* Student: We take (...) her words: ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾
* Shaykh: What you mentioned in what she said, ﴿Hearer of supplication﴾, is in ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.
* Student: ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾
* Shaykh: This was covered in a previous lesson, and we took its benefits.
* Student: Yes indeed, we take from her words: ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾
* Shaykh: There is no god but Allah.
* Student: Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance﴾; because when she supplicated, He said: ﴿So He accepted her﴾. This fa' (fa, the particle of sequence) is conjunctive, indicating causation, sequence, and immediacy.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed upon this young girl two things: good acceptance and good growth, and in that there is development of her character and her body and physique.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person's development in life is by the command of Allah; from His saying: ﴿and caused her to grow well﴾. Nourishment and care for the child are only a means, while Allah, Exalted is He, is the Causer, the One who creates the human being and causes him to grow.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may facilitate for a person someone from the people of goodness to sponsor him, and this is among the causes of his protection from the accursed Satan; from His saying: ﴿and Zechariah became her guardian﴾.
* And among its benefits also: the establishment of hadanah (custody of a child) for the child. The evidence? His saying: ﴿and Zechariah became her guardian.﴾ Can it be taken from this that guardianship belongs to the father and not the mother? The answer: this is not apparent, because kafalah (guardianship) here may mean guardianship of discipline, upbringing, and providing maintenance, without the direct physical custody (hadanah). For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the mother of a child: «You have more right to him as long as you do not marry»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (2276) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]].
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that this young girl became one of the worshipful devoted ones; from His saying: ﴿Whenever Zechariah entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found with her provision﴾.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may facilitate for a person provision that he did not expect; from His saying: ﴿He said, "O Mary, from where is this for you?"﴾.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that for every weakness there is a gentle kindness. This weak woman, whom Allah favored with occupation in worship, had Allah facilitate for her someone who brings her provision.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that things are attributed to Allah even though they have a cause; from His saying: ﴿It is from Allah﴾. Attributing things to their causes is merely attributing an effect to its cause, not to its originator; otherwise the true originator is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that the prophets do not know the unseen; from His saying: ﴿O Mary, from where is this for you?﴾.
And among its benefits: the establishment that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, provides without recompense and without expecting any reward; from her saying: ﴿Indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿There did Zakariya call upon his Lord﴾ [Ali 'Imran 38], and this is the beginning of the lesson.

﴿There﴾: this is a demonstrative noun indicating a place. The lam is said by the scholars to indicate distance, and the kaf is a particle of address. It means: at that time. The indication here may refer to the time, i.e. at that time, or to the place, which is the niche (mihrab) of Maryam. ﴿There﴾ means: in that place and at that time. ﴿Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾. The name ﴿Zakariya﴾ has two recitations: the madd (long) and the qasr (short). ﴿Zakariyā'u﴾ is the madd, and ﴿Zakariya﴾ is the qasr.

﴿He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾. ﴿Grant me﴾ means: give me. Hibah (gift) is the donating of a thing without compensation. But the scholars said: there is hibah, hadiyyah and sadaqah. How many? Three things. Sadaqah is that by which the reward of the Hereafter is intended; hadiyyah is that by which affection and drawing closer between the giver and the recipient is intended; and hibah is that which is intended merely for the benefit of the one given to. Here, ﴿My Lord, grant me﴾ means: give me a gift without price.

﴿From Yourself a good offspring﴾. ﴿From Yourself﴾ means: from Your presence. He attributed it to the presence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to make it more eloquent and greater, because the gift of the Generous is most noble. His words ﴿offspring﴾ mean: that which is created (madhru'ah), i.e. created. His words ﴿good﴾ mean: good in its words and deeds, and likewise in its bodies; so it encompasses sensory goodness and moral goodness.

﴿Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication﴾, i.e. the One who answers it. Du'a (supplication) is the servant's asking his Lord for his need, either by bringing about a benefit or by repelling a harm.

He said: ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾. In another recitation: ﴿Then the angel called to him﴾. As for the recitation of the plural, ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾, the feminine in the verb is evident, because ﴿the angels﴾ is a plural, and every plural may have its verb made feminine, every plural except the sound masculine plural, which is feminine only very rarely. An example of the feminine in the plural even for the masculine is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah 253]; here ﴿the messengers﴾ is feminine. What is the proof? The demonstrative is in the feminine form. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Bedouins say: We have believed﴾ [al-Hujurat 14]; He said "qalat al-a'rab" and did not say "qala al-a'rab", because it is a plural. As for the sound feminine plural, it must be made feminine, and the sound masculine plural must be made masculine. For this reason Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

*And the ta' with a plural other than the sound masculine*
*Is like the ta' with "one of the bricks"*

The meaning is that the ta' with the plural is like the ta' with "iḥdā al-labin" (one of the bricks). What is "iḥdā al-labin"? A brick (labinah). Labinah is feminine, but its femininity is metaphorical, so it is permissible to make its verb masculine or feminine: you say "inkasarat al-labinah" and "inkasara al-labinah". The apparent meaning of his words is that even the sound feminine plural need not be made feminine; but the correct view is that the sound feminine plural must be made feminine. The sound plural, whether masculine or feminine, is [governed] accordingly: the masculine must be made masculine and the feminine must be made feminine, and all other plurals may be made masculine or feminine.

Here ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾ poses no difficulty regarding the feminine verb, why? Because it is a plural, since the subject is plural. But on the recitation ﴿Then the angel called to him﴾, is there a difficulty? We say: there is no difficulty in it either. Why? Because "al-malā'ikah" is a broken plural, and a broken plural may have its verb masculine or feminine: you say "qama al-rijal" and "qamat al-rijal". It is possible that "the angels" refers to one, namely Jibril, who called to him, and it is expressed in the plural in terms of the category, since he is one of them.

﴿The angels called to him while he was standing praying in the mihrab﴾. The clause ﴿while he was standing﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), the hal referring to the pronoun in His words ﴿called to him﴾. His words ﴿standing praying in the mihrab﴾: the mihrab is the place of prayer or place of worship, and it was so named because it is the place of the war against the devils, for worship is a war against the devils. The mihrab here does not mean the niche of the qiblah as some people think, so they interpret the verse by it and say: these mihrabs have existed since ancient times. Do you not hear His words: ﴿Whenever Zakariya entered upon her the mihrab﴾, and His words: ﴿The angels called to him while he was standing praying in the mihrab﴾? But this is not correct.

﴿That Allah gives you good news﴾. The particle ﴿that﴾ has a recitation with fat-hah and a recitation with kasrah. As for the kasrah reading ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, it is because calling is speech, and the content of speech, when introduced by ﴿inna﴾, requires the kasrah of ﴿inna﴾, like the words of Allah: ﴿He said: Indeed I am the servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam 30]; and you may not say: "He said: that I am the servant of Allah". Fine. As for the fat-hah reading, it is by the implied preposition: "the angels called to him that Allah gives you good news", i.e. with glad tidings: Allah's glad tidings of this son, Yahya.

Also in His words ﴿gives you good news﴾ there are two recitations, ﴿yabshuruka﴾ and ﴿yubashshiruka﴾, and both are among the seven recitations. So in this verse there are three words each of which has two recitations: ﴿fa-nādat-hu﴾, ﴿fa-nādā-hu﴾, ﴿anna Allāha yubashshiruka﴾, ﴿inna Allāha yubashshiruka﴾, ﴿inna Allāha yabshuruka﴾, ﴿inna Allāha yubashshiruka﴾, yes. Bishārah is informing of what pleases, and it was so named because the skin (bashrah) is affected by the news; for when a person is given good news of what pleases him, he rejoices and that shows on his face. Have you not seen the face of the Prophet ﷺ when Mujazziz al-Mudlaji entered upon Usamah ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Harithah while they were wearing a cloak that did not reveal anything of them except their feet? He looked at their feet and said: "These feet are part of one another." Then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, entered upon 'Aishah, and the lines of his face were radiant[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3555) and Muslim (1459/38), from 'Aishah.]]: he was affected by what? By the pleasing news. Fine. If someone says: if you say this, then consider the informing of what is displeasing to be glad tidings too, since the skin is affected by that; when you inform a man of what displeases him, his face darkens and changes, so call it glad tidings? What is the answer? We say: this may be called that, i.e. informing of what displeases may be called bishārah, and from it is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran 21], ﴿Give the hypocrites the tidings that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [an-Nisa' 138], because this affects the skin.

* The Student: Yes, because she was vowed and he did not...
* The Shaykh: By Allah, it is not far-fetched.

* The Shaykh: And also Zakariya was her guardian, yes. So this is good: that her father was not present, yes, he does not take her, and then the problem disappears.

* The Shaykh: Her age when?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: By Allah, historians must mention that, but the apparent is that she was an adult young woman, because she carried him and withdrew with him to a remote place.

* The Shaykh: Allah knows best; but there is no doubt she was mature and energetic, she had not reached the age of old age nor the young age at which one cannot bear.
* Student: Shaykh, (...), I say: if you mentioned that the name is prepared, then it is at the time of birth, and if it was not prepared, then on the seventh day. May Allah reward you well: if it becomes prepared a day or two after birth, is it named immediately or...?
* The Shaykh: No, it is better to delay.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The Shaykh: If this is for the purpose of teaching, then there is no doubt it is permissible, for teaching. If it is for the purpose of recitation, some scholars permitted that, among them Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and some did not permit it and said: if you recite according to one reader's recitation, persist in it. But what appears is that the Qur'an is one thing, and it is permissible to recite one word by one reader's recitation and the second word by another's.

* Student: Shaykh, can one not cite His words, glorified be He, ﴿And He made Zakariya her guardian﴾ as evidence that this verse supports the story of the dispute between Ja'far and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib?
* The Shaykh: How so?

* The Shaykh: But is there a dispute in this? We do not know whether there is a dispute in this or not.

* The Shaykh: We cannot say there is a dispute, and it is not mentioned in the story; and the apparent, as the brother mentioned, is that her father had died, Maryam's father apparently died, and perhaps he died before she was born, as evidenced by Maryam disposing of her and naming her.
* Student: It would not be support.
* The Shaykh: Support for what?
* Student: For the Prophet ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: No, there is no support, there is no dispute; who disputed with Zakariya?

* * *

* Student: ﴿Then the angels called to him while he was standing praying in the mihrab: that Allah gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a master, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾ (39) ﴿He said: My Lord, how can I have a boy when old age has reached me and my wife is barren? He said: Thus Allah does what He wills﴾ (40) ﴿He said: My Lord, appoint for me a sign. He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture; and remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning﴾ [Ali 'Imran 39–41].
* The Shaykh: Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿gives you good news of Yahya﴾. This is the one given the good news. We have bishārah, as we mentioned, and mubashshir, and mubashshar bihi, and mubashshar: how many are these?
* The Students: Four.
* The Shaykh: Four; all of them are contained in His words: ﴿gives you good news of Yahya﴾. Yahya is said to be from life (hayah), and that Allah named him thus as an indication that he will live and remain. On this view he is diptote for being a proper noun and having the form of a verb. Others said: rather it is a foreign name, and foreign names are not derived, because they are not Arabic; on this view the preventing factors from declension are proper noun and foreignness, since being a proper noun and foreignness are two causes preventing declension. We will now mention the preventing factors of declension incidentally: nine, gathered in a verse. You?
* Student: I do not memorize it.
* The Shaykh: You do not memorize the verse? Yes?
* Student:
*Mawani'u al-sarfi tis'un in aradta bi-ha ∗∗∗ 'awnan li-tablugha fi i'rabika al-amalā*
*Ijma' wa-zin 'adlan anna th bi-ma'rifatin ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-zid 'ujmatan fa-l-wasfu qad kamalā*
* The Shaykh: Well done.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is it?
* Student:
*Jam'un wa-'adlun zada wazn wasfuhu ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-anni'thu 'ujmatan (...)*
* The Shaykh: Yes, fine.
* Student: Let us hear it.
* The Shaykh: Yes, recite it.
* Student: Jam'un wa-'adlun zada wazn wasfah.
* The Shaykh: Wait, but we want you to recite it to us on condition that you memorize it. Come on.
* Student: I will say it from the beginning.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student:
*Jam'un wa-'adlun zada wazn wasfah ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-anni'th 'ujmatan (...)*
* Student: As (...) best.
* The Shaykh: Did you hear?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: We will come to the second round, God willing. The first verse, from memory, is well known:
*Ijma' wa-zin 'adlan anna th bi-ma'rifatin ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-zid 'ujmatan fa-l-wasfu qad kamalā*
These nine are divided: three of them need only one cause; three need two causes, one of which is proper-noun status together with another cause; and three need two causes, one of which is proper-noun status or descriptiveness together with another cause. So these nine causes fall into three categories: a category in which one cause suffices, a category of two causes one of which is proper-noun status, and a category of two causes one of which is proper-noun status or descriptiveness. What we have here is proper-noun status and foreignness; foreignness is not produced by descriptiveness. Foreignness is not produced by descriptiveness; proper-noun status and the verbal pattern (wazn al-fi'l) are produced by descriptiveness, because descriptiveness and the verbal pattern are two causes preventing declension, and proper-noun status and the verbal pattern are two causes preventing declension.

Now: ﴿gives you good news of Yahya, confirming﴾: ﴿confirming﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿Yahya﴾. ﴿a word from Allah﴾ is 'Isa ibn Maryam, meaning confirming 'Isa; because 'Isa is a word from Allah, or the word of Allah. He was so named because he was by the word of Allah: he had no father, as humans do, but was by the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed the likeness of 'Isa before Allah is like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he is﴾ [Ali 'Imran 59], i.e. Adam. Therefore 'Isa was called the word, the word of Allah, because he was by His word, and he is not the word of Allah itself; why? Because "the word of Allah" is an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and speech is an attribute of the one described, and it is not possible that an attribute of Allah be a separate entity distinct from Him. Rather, its meaning necessarily is that being a "word" means that he was by what? By the word of Allah: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾.

And His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾ indicates the origin of the matter, and it is not partitive. The word is not a part of Allah; rather, it originates from Him. So ﴿min﴾ (from) here denotes origin, because the Word originates from Allah, since He is the One who spoke it.

﴿And chief﴾ is coordinated with ﴿confirming﴾, so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). It is in the accusative as a ḥāl, it is in the accusative as a ḥāl. ﴿Chief﴾: who is the chief? The chief is one who excels over others and is superior to them in knowledge, religion, character and conduct. Our saying "character" includes every trait by which a person surpasses others, such as generosity, courage, self-sacrifice and other qualities. The point is that the chief is one who surpasses others in perfections, meaning he is superior to them and exceeds them, so he combines all the perfect attributes possible for a created being.

Likewise, He also described him as ﴿chaste﴾, coordinated with ﴿confirming﴾, so it is in the accusative as a ḥāl. ﴿Chaste (ḥaṣūr)﴾ is on the pattern fa‘ūl in the sense of fā‘il, meaning one who restrains himself from base morals. Thus this announced one is described with the attributes of perfection indicated by what? ﴿Chief﴾, one who is free from deficiency and bad character, indicated by ﴿chaste﴾. So he combines in himself both negation and affirmation. This is because a person is not perfected except by the presence of the attributes of perfection and the absence of the attributes of deficiency. Note, brothers, that the attributes of perfection and deficiency here do not mean absolute deficiency and absolute perfection, which belong to no one but Allah. Rather, they are relative matters. A person may have perfection in some attributes but have a flaw in another respect, and this is deficient. He may have a flaw and deficiency in perfection, and this is more deficient. He may have perfection in perfection and be free of deficiency, and this is what? The perfection with which Yaḥyā, peace be upon him, was described.

As for those among the exegetes (mufassirūn) who said that ḥaṣūr means one who is prevented from approaching women, meaning he is not able to be with women, there is clearly a problem with this, because a person's inability to approach women is not a perfection. It is not something he acquires by discipline; rather it is a defect, isn't it? It is a defect, yes. There is another opinion: that he does not approach women who are not lawful to him, and thus it describes him with what? With the perfection of chastity, which a person is praised for. This is praised. But what we said is more comprehensive than this opinion, more comprehensive. It is known that when a more comprehensive meaning exists, it takes precedence over a lesser meaning, because the lesser is included within the more comprehensive, and not the reverse. The point is that ﴿ḥaṣūr﴾ is one who restrains himself from bad and base morals, so the verse describes him with perfection of character and absence of bad qualities, and this is the utmost perfection.

﴿And chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾: this is also coordinated with ﴿confirming﴾, so he is a confirmer and a prophet. His confirming of Jesus does not necessarily mean that he follows him. Does Muhammad ﷺ, who confirms all the prophets, follow them? No. They follow him and he does not follow them. For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If my brother Moses were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me" [Narrated by Aḥmad in al-Musnad (15156) and al-Dārimī (449) from the hadith of Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh]. For this reason he became their imam on the night of the Ascension (al-Miʿrāj). And for this reason, when Jesus descends at the end of time, he will rule by the Sharia of the Prophet, peace be upon him. The point is that his confirming of Jesus son of Mary does not contradict his being a prophet. He is a prophet who confirms the prophets. For this reason He said: ﴿and a prophet from among the righteous﴾. ﴿From among the righteous﴾ means: from among them, one of them. We say this because prophethood is a higher attribute than righteousness, but he is among the righteous. Prophethood is righteousness plus more. The evidence for this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 69]. The righteous are in the fourth rank, and everyone before them is included among them, isn't that so? So every prophet is righteous, but not vice versa. Every truthful one is righteous, but not vice versa. Every martyr is righteous, but not vice versa. Is that right? Every righteous person is righteous, correct, every righteous person is righteous.

* A student: "But not vice versa."
* The Shaykh: "But not vice versa" what?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: The converse is what? That is, every corrupt person is corrupt, or what?
* A student: The converse of "every righteous person is righteous."
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. In any case, His saying ﴿from among the righteous﴾ means from among them, because the prophet combines the attribute of prophethood and righteousness, so he is one of them.

﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has already overtaken me and my wife is barren?"﴾ He said this when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave him the good news. ﴿How can I have a son, when old age has already overtaken me?﴾ That is, how? He says this not out of disbelief or denial, but out of seeking certainty. Otherwise, we know that Zakariyyā, peace be upon him, had believed in what Allah gave him good news of, and he could not possibly consider it unlikely. Rather, he said this for what reason? Seeking certainty. A person is an imperfect human in perception and knowledge, and needs something that confirms matters for him. Abraham, peace be upon him, undoubtedly believed with perfect faith, with no doubt, that Allah gives life to the dead, yet he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest"﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. This is because news is not like seeing with one's own eyes. If a person informs you of something, however truthful he may be, his report will never be to you like seeing it directly. So Zakariyyā, peace be upon him, asked Allah: ﴿How can I have a son, when old age has already overtaken me?﴾ with the intention of what? Seeking certainty and confirming this matter, not considering Allah's power unlikely, nor doubting His report, Exalted is He. Rather, he believed in that and believed in Allah's power, Glorified and Exalted is He, and that when He wills something He says to it "Be" and it is. Especially since he had seen with Mary the provision, and so he said: ﴿Where has this come to you from?﴾ She said: ﴿It is from Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 37].

﴿How can I have a son?﴾ He said "a son" even though the child had not yet been born. But this is in view of what will be. Expressing a thing by what it will be is a valid usage in the language and occurs in the Qur'an: ﴿One of them said: "I see myself pressing wine"﴾ [Yūsuf 36]. That is, pressing grapes which will become wine, because wine itself is not pressed; what is pressed is grapes, and their juice turns into wine. So he expressed the thing by what it will become. Now here, ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ How can there be a son when he has not yet been born? We say: in view of what will be.

Then he said: ﴿when old age has already overtaken me﴾. The wāw here, the scholars call it the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), meaning that it indicates that the clause following it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier: that is, "while in fact old age has already overtaken me." It is a circumstance of what? Of the yā' in His saying: ﴿to me﴾?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, brother, it is a circumstance of the yā' in His saying ﴿to me﴾, in ﴿How can I have a son?﴾. So it is in the accusative position as a circumstance of the yā' in His saying ﴿to me﴾.

﴿Old age has overtaken me﴾ means old age has reached me. In reality, it may appear to a person that there is a reversal in the meaning: did old age reach you, or did you reach old age? Or both are permissible? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and I have indeed reached extreme old age﴾ [Maryam 8]. So he became the one who reached old age. And here he says: ﴿old age has already overtaken me﴾. So the expression is correct in both cases: if you reach old age, then old age has overtaken you, and if old age has overtaken you, then you have reached it. ﴿Old age has already overtaken me﴾ means it has befallen me. It is customary that when an old person has not had children in his youth, he will not see children, because begetting and fertility occur only in youth. The more advanced a person's age, whether a man or a woman, the less their ability to have children becomes. So he says: how is it that when I was young no child came to me, and now a child is coming to me? Likewise the woman: his wife is barren. ʿAqir (barren) is masculine in form but feminine in meaning here, and it is applied to both male and female. One says "a barren man" and "a barren woman," meaning one who cannot have children. So now each of the spouses is not in a state of bearing children. But Allah is over all things capable: when He wills something He says to it "Be" and it is. For this reason He said: ﴿He said: "Thus Allah does what He wills."﴾ ﴿Thus Allah﴾ ("thus") here, in my view, admits of two possibilities. The first: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied meaning is: "the matter is thus," meaning that old age has overtaken you and your wife is barren, but Allah does what He wills. The second: it is in the position of an accusative of absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), meaning: Allah does an action like that, because He does what He wills. Both possibilities are correct. He will indeed have a son even though old age has overtaken him and even though his wife is barren. Why? Because Allah does what He wills. Whatever Allah wills, He does, because He, Mighty and Majestic, is not prevented by anything, as we say at the end of every prayer: "O Allah, there is no preventer of what You have given, and no giver of what You have withheld" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (6330) and Muslim (593/137) from the hadith of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba]. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does what He wills, because He has absolute sovereignty over His creation, so no one prevents Him and no one asks Him: why did You do that? ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 23]. ﴿Thus Allah does what He wills.﴾

So when he became certain that Allah, the Exalted, would grant him a child, he said: ﴿My Lord, make for me a sign﴾, that is: appoint for me a sign that indicates this child, as if he is saying: when will this sign come? My Lord, make for me a sign that indicates the coming of this child, and that the child has begun to develop. Why? In order to increase in what? In tranquillity. To increase in tranquillity regarding what Allah had given him good news of. ﴿Make for me a sign﴾ by which I may know that the child has begun to develop, or ﴿make for me a sign﴾ by which I may increase in tranquillity regarding what You have given me good news of. The word āyah in the language means sign. The signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are cosmic and legislative. The prophets, peace be upon them, were supported with what? With signs that indicate their truthfulness: cosmic signs and legislative signs. Many people call the prophets' signs "miracles" (muʿjizāt). Although this name has become common on tongues, it has a deficiency, and the correct and sound expression is to call them signs, as Allah named them. We call the extraordinary events that occur at the hands of the prophets "signs." For this reason you will not find any verse in the Qur'an in which Allah called these extraordinary events "miracles" at all; rather He called them signs, indicators of truthfulness. As for "miracles," the term is deficient, because if we took it literally it would include what the sorcerers bring, or what the jinn bring, because what the sorcerers and jinn bring is also miraculous, isn't it? It is miraculous, but is it a sign? No. For this reason the expression found in the Qur'an is better than the expression some scholars used when they called the extraordinary events that Allah causes at the hands of the prophets "miracles."

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days,"﴾ meaning: the sign that informs you. He attributed it to Zakariyyā even though he was not the one who brought it into being, but because it is a sign for him. ﴿That you will not speak to the people for three days.﴾ I would like to understand the grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of ﴿Your sign that you will not speak﴾?
* A student: ﴿Your sign﴾ is the subject (mubtada').
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: And the kāf is a pronoun in the genitive position, and the interpreted infinitive from "an" (that) and (...) is in the nominative position as the predicate.
* The Shaykh: "An" and what it contains is interpreted as an infinitive?
* The student: In the nominative position as the predicate.
* The Shaykh: In the nominative position, or interpreted as an infinitive predicate? Or not in the nominative position?
* The student: Predicate.
* The Shaykh: A predicate, because it is a single word, and what is said "in the position of" applies to a clause. Good. Now estimate it?
* The student: The sign (...).
* The Shaykh: Excellent, perfect. ﴿Your sign﴾ means the sign I give you, ﴿that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture﴾. ﴿That you will not speak to the people﴾ means you will not address them. ﴿Except by gesture.﴾ ﴿For three days﴾: three days with their nights? Yes, by the evidence of the Exalted's saying in Sūrat Maryam: ﴿that you will not speak to the people for three nights, sound﴾ [Maryam 10]. His sign was that he would not speak to the people for their nights. He said: ﴿except by gesture﴾. ﴿Except﴾ is a particle of exception. But I would like to understand whether this exception is connected (muttaṣil) or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ).
* A student: Disconnected.
* The Shaykh: Disconnected?
* The student: Because what follows "except" is not of the same kind as what precedes it.
* The Shaykh: Is gesture not speech? Speech or not speech?
* The students: No, not speech.
* The Shaykh: Good. Yes?
* A student: The context shows it is connected, because He said ﴿that you will not speak to the people﴾, then said to him ﴿except by gesture﴾. He counted it as speech, meaning it is connected.
* The Shaykh: Connected. These are two opinions.
* A student: The grammarians do not call it speech, but the rhetoricians do call it speech.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is a detailed view. In reality the exegetes differed over whether the exception is connected, so that gesture is a kind of speech, since speech is what expresses what is in the soul, whether by word, gesture or writing. Some exegetes say the exception is disconnected, because gesture is not speech. For this reason, if a person gestures during prayer his prayer is not invalidated, but if it were speech it would be invalidated, due to the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "Nothing of human speech is fitting in this prayer" [Muslim (537/33) from the hadith of Muʿāwiya ibn al-Ḥakam]. Whoever looks at the meaning says: gesture is speech, because it conveys what is in the soul, and the Lawgiver has taken it into account. The Lawgiver took gesture into account. Did not the Prophet, peace be upon him, kill the Jew by the gesture of the Anṣārī slave-girl? The Anṣārī slave-girl, when they said to her: "Who killed you? Was it so-and-so, so-and-so?" she gestured: "Yes" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (5295) and Muslim (1672/15) from the hadith of Anas]. So he took the gesture into account. There is no doubt that a gesture expresses what is in the soul, but it is not the speech that is sound, and there is no doubt about this either. Whoever considers the meaning says the exception is connected, and whoever considers the wording, that speech is sound, says the exception is disconnected. But on both opinions the meaning is one: he will not be able to speak with his tongue to the people, but will gesture to them. The way this is a sign is that he was unable to speak to people though he was sound, and he was unable to speak with people but not with Allah. This is a strange thing. A person who speaks, saying "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest," a sound person with no affliction or illness in his tongue, and yet cannot speak to people? This is a sign: inability in a state of ability, and ability in a state of inability. He is unable to speak to people though he has the ability to speak, and he has the ability to speak with Allah through glorification and other forms, and unable to speak with people. So this is one of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to show him that He, Glorified and Exalted, is capable of everything. Speech, which I and others know is the lightest movement of the body, isn't it? A person can speak for how long, when Allah gives him support in the meaning?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Until (...). By Allah, (...) about this, but he speaks much and does not tire. But walking tires, and grasping tires. As for this light speech, which everyone can do, this man is prevented from it, so he cannot speak to the people except by gesture. But with Allah He said: ﴿And remember your Lord much﴾. The time has run out.
* A student: Shaykh, the preferred view on the first question...
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* The student: The one we mentioned before?
* The Shaykh: What is it?
* The student: That speech, meaning gesture, is speech.
* The Shaykh: If you wish the preferred view to be that the exception is disconnected, then it is disconnected, and if he who said it is connected wishes it to be connected, then it is connected. If the one who wants the detailed view makes a distinction, then let us distinguish. The matter has no consequence.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: By Allah, there is a possibility of the reality.
* A student: Shaykh...
* The Shaykh: Yes?
* The student: We said that one of the conditions for the answering of supplication is firm resolve in the supplication, that the person be certain of being answered. And here Zakariyyā, when he said ﴿My Lord, how can I have a son, when old age has already overtaken me?﴾, although he had previously supplicated, it was as if he was not certain of the answer.

**Shaykh:** There is no god but Allah! This would apply if the interrogative were meant to express astonishment, but the interrogative is not expressing astonishment at what has occurred. It is an interrogative of confirmation. If I now said to you, "I will give you twenty riyals," and you could see that I was being sincere, you would say, "You will give me twenty riyals? And what do you mean by that?" You mean confirmation, not astonishment or doubt.

* * *

**Student:** ﴿And glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning (41). And when the angels said: "O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds (42). O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate and bow with those who bow (43). That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to determine] which of them would be responsible for Maryam, nor were you with them when they disputed (44). When the angels said: "O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, ʿIsā son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near (45). And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and he is among the righteous"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 41–46].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And remember your Lord much﴾. Allah commanded him to remember his Lord much, because by the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest, faith increases, and the heart is illuminated. For this reason Allah commanded him to remember his Lord much. The benefit of remembering much here, or of the command to remember much, is that when Allah informed him that He would prevent him from speaking with people, He gave him the good news that he would not be prevented from the remembrance of Allah, which is greater and more honourable than addressing and speaking with people. So He said: ﴿And remember your Lord much﴾. This is because it may occur to his heart, when Allah said to him: ﴿That you will not speak to people for three nights, except by gesture﴾, that he might be prevented from speaking. So Allah the Exalted wished to console him and remove from him what might have occurred to his heart, and He said to him: ﴿Remember your Lord much﴾. Here He did not say to him, "You will remember your Lord," but rather He said: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾. He commanded him to remember Allah so that his remembrance of Allah the Exalted, at a time when speaking with people is prevented, would be a specific act of worship that he is commanded to perform. When he was prevented from addressing people, he became free, so he was commanded to fill this free time with what? With the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is better for him and more beneficial for him than if Allah had said to him, "You will remember your Lord much." Its meaning, as I told you, is that when he is commanded to do something, it becomes an act of obedience, even though remembrance is in its origin an act of obedience. However, this becomes a particular act of obedience in this state in which he refrains from speaking with people.

As for His saying: ﴿Remember your Lord much﴾, is ﴿much﴾ an adjective of an omitted time noun, meaning "a long time," or of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a great remembrance"? The second, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance (41), and glorify Him morning and afternoon﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 41–42]. Here He said: ﴿And glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾. Al-ʿashiyy is the late part of the day, and al-ibkār is the early part of the day. Allah has commanded remembrance of Him at these two times, as He said: ﴿And glorify with the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ [Qāf 39]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾ here, and: ﴿with the evening and the sunrise﴾ [Ṣād 18]. The verses on this are numerous, because at sunrise is the beginning of the day, and in the evening is the end of the day, so a person fills his time, at its beginning and its end, with what? With the remembrance of Allah. From where does the evening begin? The evening begins from the decline of the sun, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ led us in one of the two evening prayers"[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhārī (1229) and Muslim (573/97), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. That is either the Ẓuhr prayer or the ʿAṣr prayer. It has been said that the evening is from after the ʿAṣr prayer until midnight, but the first view is more correct. Yes, al-masāʾ (the night) is applied from the ʿAṣr prayer until midnight, but al-ʿashiyy is the late part of the day.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿wal-ibkār﴾, al-ibkār is not the plural of bakar, because the plural of bakar is abkār, like sabab and asbāb. Rather, it is a verbal noun or a name for this specific time, which is the early part of the day.

As for His saying: ﴿Glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾, it includes the declaring of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, free of everything that does not befit Him. It has passed with us that glorifying Allah is concerning three matters: the attribute of defect, deficiency in His perfection, and resemblance to created beings. Pay attention, (al-mushābahah, resemblance) is something you should remove from your tongues. Say: mumāthalah (likeness), because this is the term that the Qur'an used. So Allah is glorified from these three matters. What are they? Deficiency, deficiency in perfection, and likeness to the created.

Deficiency is like His saying: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾ [al-Furqān 58]. Deficiency in perfection is like His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], and ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qāf 38]. Likeness to the created is like His saying: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shūrā 11], ﴿Do you know of any equal to Him?﴾ [Maryam 65], and ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlāṣ 4].

Glorification occurs by speech and by action. So whoever worships Allah has glorified Him. Whoever worships Allah has glorified Him. By speech or by action? By action, even if the word "subḥān" (glory be to Him) is not in it, because the worshipper's worship necessarily implies that the one worshipped is perfect, since a deficient being cannot be worshipped by a sensible person. So his worshipping Allah necessitates that he affirms Allah's perfection and glorifies Him above deficiency. Is that clear, brothers?

﴿And glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾. The particle "bi" in His saying ﴿bil-ʿashiyy﴾ may be for comprehensiveness, meaning throughout the entire time, or it may be for time, meaning "during the evening." If we take it to indicate time, it does not follow that the glorification must cover the whole time, because of His saying: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning (137) and at night﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 137–138]. Do they pass by them every night, travelling at night to them? No. They pass in its beginning, its end, and its middle. But if it is for comprehensiveness, then the meaning is that Allah commanded him to cover both of these times entirely, with what? With glorification.

Now let us return to the benefits. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring"﴾, to the end. From this noble verse it is derived that all creation is in need of Allah, and even the prophets do not do without calling upon Allah, because of His saying: ﴿Zakariyya called upon his Lord﴾.
