* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of analogy (qiyās, reasoning by analogy). From where? Because when he saw that Allah provides this woman with sustenance without any known cause, he knew that the One who brings her provision, while she is a woman cut off from earning in her sanctuary, is able to grant him a child. So this is a transition from one thing to its counterpart, and this is the very essence of analogy, correct? So he derived from this story a lesson, which is that one may ask Allah for something even if it seems unlikely.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the form of address used in supplication is the name al-Rabb (the Lord). This is because of His saying: ﴿his Lord﴾, and He did not say "Allah." For this reason you will find most supplications begin with "al-Rabb." Because the answering of the supplicant is a requirement of lordship (rubūbiyyah). Is that not so? Because it is an act, and all acts are a requirement of lordship. Therefore the supplicant always seeks nearness to Allah by the name al-Rabb. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "He raises his hands to the sky, saying: 'O Lord, O Lord'"[[Narrated by Muslim (1015/65), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, reached an advanced age without a child being granted to him. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿And indeed old age has overtaken me﴾.

* Student: Teacher, shall we say it in your opinion: ﴿morning and evening﴾ and ﴿in the evening and the morning﴾, "morning and evening" means (...) all of it, and "evening and morning" means (...).

* Shaykh: If we take the "bi" as indicating time, then there is a difference between them. If we take it as comprehensiveness, there is no difference.

* Student: That comprehensiveness only...

* Shaykh: No, comprehensiveness means the entire time, covering the entire time. The meaning is not "to the exclusion of other times," but these two times are specifically singled out for mention. Is it not that anyone else may glorify Allah? But this matter is the most important.

* Student: (...) specifically together, or...?

* Shaykh: No, not together. For this reason, the most frequent glorifications and declarations of Allah's oneness occur at the beginning and end of the day.

* Student: ﴿He said: "Thus Allah does what He wills"﴾. Who is the speaker to whom Zakariyya responded?

* Shaykh: Read: who called out to Zakariyya?

* Student: The angels.

* Shaykh: Then the speaker is still a matter of inference; we have not reached the reality. This is an open question.

* Student: Glorification, we said, includes action and speech. Does what one who glorifies silently in his heart include that?

* Shaykh: You mean inner speech (ḥadīth al-nafs)? Inner speech is included in this, but it is one of the actions, because he spoke to himself.

* Student: Shall we say: "Our master Muhammad ﷺ"?

* Shaykh: "Our master Muhammad"? Indeed Allah has made Muhammad our master. But did the Companions say such things?

* Student: "The Messenger of Allah."

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: He was raised by two polytheist parents, whereas Yahya, peace be upon him, was from two righteous parents. Is it derived from His saying: ﴿and a prophet from among the righteous﴾ that prophethood and righteousness are combined?

* Shaykh: You mean that he was born of righteous people?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: That is not the apparent meaning. This is a description of the state of Yahya.

* Student: Teacher, some people say "Ya sayyidī" (my master). Is there anything wrong with it?

* Shaykh: "Ya sayyidī," to whom?

* Student: I mean, when he speaks he says "Ya sayyidī."

* Shaykh: If the man is worthy of being a master, there is no harm. For example, if someone came to a wicked, sinful person and said to him "Ya sayyidī," that is not permissible. But for one who is worthy of mastership, there is no harm.

* Student: Analogy, Teacher. Is it valid for a person, if he sees anything, for example a supplication, to make an analogy from it?

* Shaykh: If there is no transgression in that, there is no harm. If there is no transgression, there is no harm. But, for example, if someone comes and supplicates Allah, saying: "O Allah, make me a prophet and messenger," that is forbidden. Now, we were discussing with the brother who asked, who said "sayyidī," "sayyidunā Muhammad." Does that mean it is forbidden for a person to say "Sayyidunā Muhammad said"?

* Student: It is not forbidden.

* Shaykh: It is not forbidden.

* Student: Because he is the master of the first and the last.

* Shaykh: And because we ought to show good manners like the manners of the Companions. The Companions, when they related hadith from the Messenger, did not say "Our master said," "The Messenger of Allah said," "The Prophet of Allah said."

* Student: Teacher, (...) "Ya sayyidī, ya mawlāy"...

* Shaykh: If the description is true, there is no harm. If the freed slave said to the one who freed him, "Ya mawlāy" (my master), it is correct.

* * *

**Student:** ﴿And when the angels said: "O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds (42). O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate and bow with those who bow (43). That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to determine] which of them would be responsible for Maryam, nor were you with them when they disputed (44). When the angels said: "O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, ʿIsā son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near (45). And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and he is among the righteous"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 42–46].

**Shaykh:** Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication"﴾. We have derived from it four benefits?

* Student: The first: that all creation is in need of Allah, even the prophets. Second: the affirmation of analogy, because when he saw that Allah provides this woman with sustenance without any known cause, he knew that the One who brings her provision, while she is a woman cut off from earning in her sanctuary, is able to grant him...

* Shaykh: To grant him a child, is it not? Yes.

* Student: The third: that the form of address used in supplication is the name al-Rabb. The fourth: that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, reached an advanced age without a child being granted to him.

* Shaykh: Good. The third?

* Student: That the form of address used in supplication is the name al-Rabb.

* Shaykh: Usually. The fourth?

* Student: The fourth: that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, reached an advanced age without a child being granted to him. Because of His saying: ﴿And indeed old age has overtaken me﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes.

Among the benefits of the verse is what is derived from His saying: ﴿Grant me from Yourself﴾, where He attributed the giving to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The gift of the Generous is great. A parallel to this is the Prophet's ﷺ saying, when he taught Abu Bakr the supplication that he should recite in his prayer, He said: "So forgive me with a forgiveness from You and have mercy upon me"[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhārī (6326) and Muslim (2705/48), from the hadith of Abu Bakr.]]. As we have pointed out, something from the Generous is great.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person should not ask for offspring in general, because offspring may be a source of distress and trial. Rather, one should ask for good offspring.

And among the benefits of this noble verse that it alludes to: a person should take the means by which his offspring will be good, and among them is supplication, the supplication to Allah, which is among the greatest means. Allah the Exalted has mentioned about the man who reaches maturity that he says: ﴿Make righteous for me my offspring. Indeed, I have repented to You, and indeed I am of the Muslims﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 15]. There is no doubt that the righteousness of offspring is something sought, because righteous offspring benefit you in life and after death, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: an ongoing charity, knowledge from which benefit is gained, or a righteous child who prays for him"[[Narrated by Muslim (1631/14), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: seeking nearness to Allah the Exalted by His names that suit the need, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication﴾, meaning: the One who answers it. Likewise, the names by which a person seeks nearness to Allah in his supplication should be suited to what? To the matter for which he supplicates. So one who supplicates for forgiveness seeks nearness by the name al-Ghafūr (the Forgiving), and for mercy by al-Raḥīm (the Merciful), and for provision by al-Razzāq (the Provider), and so on. This is also indicated by His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 180]. His saying: ﴿call upon Him by them﴾ encompasses supplication of request and supplication of worship. It includes supplication of request, by making them a means for your supplication, and supplication of worship, by worshipping Allah according to their requirements. So if you know that He, glorified be He, is Forgiving, then present yourself for His forgiveness, and if you know He is Merciful, likewise, and so on. So His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿call upon Him by them﴾ includes this and that.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's hearing, Allah's generosity, and Allah's power. From where is this derived?

* Student: ﴿Thus Allah does what He wills﴾.

* Student: ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication﴾.

* Shaykh: What is the connection?

* Student: That He heard the supplication and answered it.

* Shaykh: Good, that is one. The affirmation of power?

* Student: Power to answer.

* Shaykh: Power to answer, yes. The third?

* Student: That He does not give except to the generous.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 38–41 (part 4 of 6):

* The Shaykh: Yes, this establishes that Allah is Generous, since He, may He be exalted, is shy to turn away one who calls upon Him. If someone says: sometimes a person calls upon Allah and Allah does not answer his supplication? And here Zakariyya (ﷺ) says: ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication﴾, and Ibrahim said: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39]. So what is the answer? The answer is that if Allah does not answer a supplication, it is either because of the presence of an obstacle, or because of the benefit of the one supplicating, or because a condition is missing. As for when the conditions are fulfilled and the obstacles are absent, and the benefit does not require the opposite of what the supplicant asked for, then Allah, may He be exalted, certainly answers the supplication, because Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir 60]. So when a person calls upon his Lord while his heart is heedless, saying: "O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings me closer to it of words and deeds," but in the time of testing his heart wanders among the pages of the book, is this person heedless or present?
* The students: Heedless.
* The Shaykh: Heedless? Yes. He does not answer a supplication from a heedless heart. How can you ask Allah, glorified and exalted is He, while He knows what is in your soul, and you whisper to Him: "O Lord, give me such and such," while your heart is occupied with something else? By Allah, this is a lack of good manners. Here the answer to the supplication is delayed due to the absence of the condition, due to the non-fulfilment of the condition, because his heart was not present. It may also be due to the presence of an obstacle, and among them (i.e., among the obstacles) is that a person consumes what is unlawful, and we seek refuge in Allah. Consuming the unlawful is one of the greatest obstacles to the answering of supplication, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is Good and accepts only what is good, and indeed Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the Messengers. So He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾, and He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you and be grateful to Allah﴾." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned a man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, who stretches his hands toward the sky, saying: "O Lord, O Lord," (four causes for the answering of supplication) "and his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, and he is nourished with the unlawful; so how could his supplication be answered?"[[Narrated by Muslim (1015/65) from Abu Hurayrah.]] (We seek refuge in Allah.) He considers it unlikely that Allah would answer such a supplicant. So here the answer to the supplication was delayed. Why? Because of the presence of an obstacle.
And it may be due to the benefit of the one supplicating: Allah keeps for him with Him something greater than what he asked for, or Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows that if He answered him, harm would come to his religion, such as his being answered in a way that would become a trial for him in his religion. So by the mercy and wisdom of Allah, He does not answer that supplication. For whose benefit?
* The students: The supplicant's.
* The Shaykh: For the benefit of the supplicant. For this reason, a person should not become impatient if he calls upon Allah and is not answered, nor should he grow weary and feel exhausted, saying: "I have called upon Him, then I called again, and He has not answered me," for if he says that, he will not be answered. Has the problem now been resolved? The problem that might arise from His saying: ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication﴾ has been resolved. But another problem remains, which is that someone might say: there is no benefit in supplication, because what is written for you will come to you without supplication, and if it is not written for you, it will not come to you even if you supplicate. Some people say this. So how do we answer? First, we say: this statement is false from its very root, because it implies the foolishness of the Messengers, the Prophets and the righteous. Rather, it implies that Allah, may He be exalted, commands something that has no benefit. For Allah said: ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me﴾. So how would He, may He be exalted, command a matter that has no benefit?! That is impossible. So this statement is false from its root. Then we say: a thing is written for you, but with a cause. If Allah has decreed for you a good offspring because of your supplication, then when the supplication is absent, the good offspring is absent, because Allah decreed it—that is, the good offspring—linked to what? To supplication. Would a sensible person say: "I will not marry; if Allah has willed for me a child, it will come without marriage, and if He has not willed for me a child, it will not come even if I marry"? Would a sensible person say this? No, he would not say it. We say: Allah has decreed for you a child through marriage; marry, and the child will come to you.
And would a sensible person say: "I will not marry; if Allah has willed for me a child, it will come without marriage, and if He has not willed for me a child, it will not come even if I marry"? Would a sensible person say this? No, he would not say it. We say: Allah has decreed for you a child through marriage; marry, and the child will come to you. Likewise is supplication.
So there is no doubt that supplication is among the strongest causes for obtaining what is desired and removing what is disliked, and this is a known matter. Allah, may He be exalted, has decreed this thing, which is the attainment of what you desire or the removal of what you dislike, linked to what? To this cause, supplication. So the supplication is decreed and what is supplicated for is decreed by Allah, may He be exalted. But you do not know. It is incumbent upon you to perform the cause that you know, which is supplication, and what lies beyond that is not in your hands. This objection applies to all decreed matters, but it is answered by this answer: that Allah decreed these things linked to their causes.
Furthermore, we say: supplication itself is an act of worship. The very act of supplication is worship. When you raise your hands to your Lord, saying: "O Lord," this is humility and submission before Allah, may He be exalted, and it is among the greatest acts of worship. So supplication itself is worship, whether you are answered or not. So why not supplicate more? What? What did you say?
* A student: Supplication is worship in itself, so a person calls upon Allah, glorified and exalted is He, even if not...
* The Shaykh: And he should increase in supplication.

He said: ﴿Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Al 'Imran 38]. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the chamber﴾ [Al 'Imran 39].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of angels. Some discussion of them has already preceded, and they are an unseen world, created from light. Allah, may He be exalted, created them for what He prepared them for, and they carry out what their Creator, may He be exalted, wills, such as ﴿They glorify Him night and day, they do not slacken﴾ [Al-Anbiya 20]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) informed, saying: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2312) and Ibn Majah (4190) from Abu Dharr.]] Al-atit (الأطيط) is the sound heard from the creaking of a saddle on a camel loaded with a heavy burden.
* A student: Is it al-sarih (الصريح), O Shaykh, or al-sarir (الصرير)?
* The Shaykh: Al-sarir (الصرير). "There is no place of four fingers' breadth in which there is not an angel standing for Allah, or bowing, or prostrating."
In this verse, ﴿the angels called to him﴾ is an affirmation of angels. What is the ruling on denying the angels?
Its ruling is disbelief, because it is a denial of the Qur'an.
If someone says: I do not deny them, and I say: there are angels, but the angels are forces of good and the devils are forces of evil, so I make them meanings, not beings.
We say: this is also a denial of them, because Allah said: ﴿Who made the angels messengers having wings, two, three, or four﴾ [Fatir 1]. How can they be forces? ﴿Having wings, two, three, and four﴾.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that the angels speak with an audible voice, due to His saying: ﴿So the angels called to him﴾ [Al 'Imran 39].
* And from its benefits: the permissibility of addressing one who is praying, due to His saying: ﴿called to him while he was standing in prayer in the chamber﴾. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to speak to one another during prayer, but the speaker, while praying, would not address the other directly; rather, he would understand what the other said and respond with a gesture. But is this absolute as regards the permissibility of speaking to one who is praying?
The answer: it is better to leave it, except for a need, because when you speak to him while he is praying, you disturb him, and perhaps he forgets and addresses (someone), as this often happens.
* From the benefits of the noble verse: the legislated nature of giving good news to a person about what pleases him, due to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that Allah gives you good news of Yahya﴾ [Al 'Imran 39]. This matter is conditioned in its kind and its genus. As for its kind: it has already been mentioned that Allah, may He be exalted, informed about the angels giving good news to Ibrahim of Isma'il and of Ishaq. Concerning Isma'il Allah said: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾ [As-Saffat 101], and concerning Ishaq: ﴿And they gave him good news of a knowing boy﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 28].
Is it among the good news that which is established in the Sahih, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A child was born to me tonight, and I named him Ibrahim"[[Narrated by Muslim (2315/62) from Anas.]]? Or is this from the category of speaking of Allah's blessing?
* A student: The second.
* The Shaykh: This is the original principle: the second, that it is from the category of speaking of Allah's blessing, this is the original principle.
And from the benefits of the noble verse...
* A student: Good news in its genus.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Another student: Its kind and its genus.
* The Shaykh: Good news in its genus means that a person may give good news of any good, of anything that the Sunnah has brought, from the understanding of His (ﷺ) saying: "Two should not confide in one another privately excluding a third, until they mix with the people, because that would grieve him."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (6290) and Muslim (2184/37) from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] This indicates bringing joy to a Muslim, and it is so, whether it is by good news or by other means.
He said: ﴿That Allah gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 39], to the end. From this is also derived: the permissibility of naming a newborn before the seventh day. This is so: it is permissible for a person to name his child, male or female, before the seventh day, and this applies when the name is ready. But if the name is not ready, it is better to delay it until the seventh day.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: praise for one who confirms the Messengers, due to His saying: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾. Allah said this as praise of Yahya. There is no doubt that whoever is confirmed by clear proofs is praiseworthy, even in worldly matters. If you confirm one whose truthfulness is established by proof, this is undoubtedly good. But if you confirm one whose truthfulness is not established by proof, this is hastiness. And if you confirm one whose lying is established by proof, this is folly: that you confirm one whose lying is established.
So there are three states: one whose lying is established by proof, confirming him is folly, foolishness in intellect and error in religion. One whose truthfulness is established by proof, confirming him is perfection for which a person is praised. And one for whom neither truthfulness nor lying is established by proof, confirming him is hastiness, because such news requires a person to be patient about it. For this reason Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, if a sinful person brings you news, verify it﴾ [Al-Hujurat 6]. He, may He be exalted, did not say: "reject it" or "accept it." Investigate until you examine it, because it may be true.
* From the benefits of the noble verse: that Yahya, peace be upon him, will be a master, because he is one of the Prophets, and the Prophets are the masters of creation and the best of creation.
* And from its benefits also: that Yahya, peace be upon him, although possessing the attributes of perfection, having the mastery, was in addition to that protected from bad character, due to His saying: ﴿and chaste﴾ [Al 'Imran 39]. The most sound and most comprehensive of what has been said about it is that he was protected from the evils of character.
* And from its benefits also: that Yahya was among the Prophets, due to His saying: ﴿and a Prophet﴾. Every one described in the Qur'an with the attribute of prophethood is a Messenger. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Nuh and the Prophets after him, and We revealed to Ibrahim﴾ [An-Nisa 163], to the end. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We have certainly sent Messengers before you; among them are those We have related to you﴾ [Ghafir 78]. And what Allah has related to us about them, He relates mostly with the word "Prophet." So every one mentioned in the Qur'an with the attribute of prophethood is a Messenger.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that the Prophets are among the righteous, indeed they are at the highest levels of righteousness. The levels of righteousness are four: prophethood, truthfulness (siddiqiyyah), martyrdom, and righteousness. When they are all mentioned together, they become levels; when they are not all mentioned together, righteousness becomes general, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When you say that—O servants of Allah, the righteous—you have greeted every righteous servant in the heaven and the earth."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (831) and Muslim (402/55) from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]
﴿He said: My Lord, how can I have a boy when old age has overtaken me﴾ [Al 'Imran 40], to the end.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: there is no blame upon a person in seeking what will set his soul at rest, because Zakariyya, peace be upon him, did not doubt the news of Allah, but he wanted the joy and happiness to come to him with the strength of proofs, because the news of Allah is undoubtedly a proof. But the more the proofs increase, the more the certainty increases. So here he asked: ﴿How can I have a boy when old age has overtaken me﴾, meaning in astonishment at the power of Allah, may He be exalted: that he should have a boy when old age has overtaken him. For usually when a person reaches old age, his fertility decreases, and it may cease altogether, and barrenness is more likely to be found in women than in men. For this reason a woman may be barren before a man is barren.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse, we say: does a person own his child?
Students: ﴿li﴾ (لي)...
Other students: The lam.
* The Shaykh: The lam. Consider this.
* A student: Ownership (اختصاص, specificity).
* The Shaykh: Or do we say: the lam is not necessarily for ownership?
* A student: No mistake.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is not necessarily for ownership. It may be for specificity, because a person does not own his child as he owns his slave. If he wanted to sell his child, it would not be valid. As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You and your wealth belong to your father,"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3530) and Ibn Majah (2291) from Jabir ibn Abdullah, and the wording is his.]] the intended meaning there is the benefits, or that the intention is exaggeration, because this man came to complain to the Messenger (ﷺ) that his father had seized his wealth, meaning he had taken it, and he said to him: "You and your wealth belong to your father." So this is either from the category of exaggeration, or that your benefits belong to your father as your wealth belongs to your father.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of describing a person with what he dislikes, when the intention is mere clarification, not disparagement or defamation, due to His saying: ﴿and my wife is barren﴾ [Al 'Imran 40]. For if you described a woman as barren, would she be upset or pleased? She would be upset, obviously. If you said to her: "You are forty years old," well, how is it that you say "you are barren"? But if the intention is to state the matter as it is, without blame or disparagement, this is not objectionable. The proof of this is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As for Abu Jahm, he never puts down his staff from his shoulder,"[[Narrated by Muslim (1480/36) from Fatimah bint Qays.]] but this is from the category of counsel, and the Messenger (ﷺ) did not intend to defame the man, but intended to make clear his condition so that a person would be with him with insight.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's action, due to His saying: ﴿Thus Allah does what He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran 40].
The position of the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah is the affirmation of Allah's voluntary actions, those connected to Him and those transitive to others. Allah's voluntary actions, meaning those that occur by His will, and nothing among Allah's actions occurs except by His will. But among them are some connected to Him, such as istiwa' (settling), descent, laughter and rejoicing, and some connected to others, such as creating, for creating is transitive to others. So the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah affirm both kinds: the action specific to Him, may He be exalted, which does not extend to others, and the action which extends to others. And they say, without doubt: the Lord who does what He wills is more perfect than the Lord who is unable to act.
Most of the Ash'arites, if I do not say all of them, and the Mu'tazilites and those who resemble them, say: Allah has no voluntary actions. He does not settle, nor descend, nor come, nor laugh, nor rejoice, nor love, nor dislike... and so on, to the end of what they say in denying voluntary actions.

Their reasoning is weaker than any other argument. They say: "Events cannot subsist except in something that is itself an event, and Allah, may He be exalted, is eternal and everlasting." So it is said to them: First, who told you this, that events cannot occur except through an event? Who said this?! Do you have revelation for it, or is it merely a corrupt rational analogy you have put forward?!

The truth is that this is a corrupt rational analogy. It does not follow that events cannot subsist except in something that is itself an event. For it is well known that the one who causes an event (the agent) precedes the event, and if the agent precedes the event, it does not follow that the agent must be an event. You are now eating lunch today, and today's lunch, relative to you, is an event, since when? Since the time of its occurrence, and you existed before it. So the Lord, may He be exalted, performs these acts at the time of their performance, and He has always existed. But according to your claim and your false doctrine, it would follow that Allah, glorified and exalted, does not perform any act, is idle with respect to acts. Is this a defect or a perfection? It is a defect, because the one who acts is more perfect than the one who does not act, by the agreement of people. And there is no imperfection whatsoever that befalls Allah, may He be exalted, from affirming action in His regard, in any respect.

The verses affirming Allah's action are numerous: ﴿Thus does Allah do what He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran 40], ﴿Doer of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj 16], ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ibrahim 27]. The texts on this are numerous, and praise be to Allah, and the People of the Sunnah and the Community believe in them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the use of the plural for the singular, or is it something else? His saying: ﴿Thus said He: Allah does what He wills﴾. Who is the speaker? Is it Allah? If it is Allah, then this benefit is void. If it is the angels, then this verse indicates that the speaker is one and that His saying ﴿the angels called to him﴾ [Ali 'Imran 39] means one of them. The difference of opinion on this has already been mentioned in the tafsir.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming the will (mashi'ah) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying:
* Student: ﴿Thus does Allah do what He wills﴾.
* The Shaykh: And where?
* The student: ﴿what He wills﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿what He wills﴾, correct. But every thing that Allah has restricted by His will is?
* Student: It is with wisdom.
* The Shaykh: Accompanied by wisdom. What is your evidence for this?
* Student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30].
* The Shaykh: Yes. He said: ﴿except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, which shows that He wills only what wisdom requires, and so it is.

If someone says: This raises a difficulty: Allah has willed both good and evil, so what is the wisdom in evil? Reflect on it until the next lesson, if Allah the Exalted wills.

* Student: O Shaykh, there is a benefit here (...) He answered his supplication, because He said: ﴿the angels called to him﴾ (...) the supplication?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he says: among its benefits is the swiftness of Allah's answering supplication, from His saying: ﴿called to him﴾, for the fa' indicates sequence and immediacy. And Muhammad al-Wasil has a benefit here. What is it?
* Student: In His saying: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾, the permissibility of applying the single word (kalimah) to a large speech, because Yahya, peace be upon him, did not confirm a single word, but rather confirmed all of Allah's speech.
* The Shaykh: What is the word by which Yahya confirmed?
* Student: The word by which he confirmed?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...) in the story of 'Isa.
* The Shaykh: What is the word in the story of 'Isa?
* Student: I have forgotten it; it is the verse in Surah Ali 'Imran.
* Another student: We say, O Shaykh: the word is indeed a word, because the word is: ﴿Be﴾.
* The Shaykh: Correct. He says: the word is His saying, exalted is He, about 'Isa: ﴿Be﴾. However, applying "word" (kalimah) to speech is the original usage in the Arabic language, that a word is meant to denote speech. ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind. No! It is but a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun 99-100]. How many words did he say? Four words, four sentences as well, and he is the one who said them. And the Prophet ﷺ said: «The truest word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid: Certainly everything except Allah is vain» [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3841) and Muslim (2256/3) from Abu Hurayrah].
("Certainly everything except Allah is vain") is it a word or words? Words. So the saying of Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him:
............................. ∗∗∗ "And kalimah is that by which speech is formed, qad yu'am"
meaning according to the terminology of the grammarians, not according to the requirement of the Arabic language. The Arabic language applies "word" only to meaningful speech, but the grammarians, may Allah have mercy on them, applied "word" to a single utterance.
* Student: May Allah reward you with good. Some people say that one who consumes usury does not supplicate to Allah, because there is no benefit in his supplication, since even if he supplicates it will not be answered for him (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, by Allah, this is a difficulty, as if it were great. I say: this is a difficulty, indeed a real difficulty. But the Messenger ﷺ regarded it as unlikely and did not say that it is certain. He said: «How could such a one be answered?» [Related by Muslim (1015/65) from Abu Hurayrah], meaning he considered answering unlikely; it does not mean it is definitely not answered. But to the one who consumes usury we say: Do you wish that Allah forgive you?
* The student: He will say: Yes.
* The Shaykh: He says yes, but "I am not one who supplicates, by Allah He will not answer me." We say: Leave usury, just as the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, said regarding the sinful traveler who is compelled to eat carrion, whether he eats from it or dies. They said: He dies and does not eat from it. But Allah has not made carrion lawful for the compelled? They say: It is impossible, and it is not permitted for him. And what does he do? Does he die? They say: He dies. But here there is something before death that he can determine, which is that he repent. We say: Repent and eat. If you are definitely holding a ticket to travel to a country where you will commit adultery, throw away the ticket and eat.
Does he pray the full four-rak'ah prayer or not? He does not pray the full four; there is disagreement, in any case, among those who say it is not permissible. He says: What should I do, folks? I am a traveler. We say: Repent and pray two rak'ahs.
He nearly died of thirst in Ramadan while traveling and said: Shall I break the fast? What do we tell him? Do not break the fast. He says: Folks, I am dying of thirst. We say: Die. And what is the way out?
Students: Repent to Allah.
* The Shaykh: We say: Repent and drink.
* Student: O Shaykh, should it be said to them: Repent and then supplicate?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he says: repent and supplicate to Allah.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. Some people, may Allah be good to you, when they enter the mosque while people are sitting in the mosque, they greet them. Many people are unaware of (...) returning the greeting by gesture. And some people, when they enter an empty place such as a room or the like where no one is present, say the greeting and say: I am greeting the angels?
* The Shaykh: Both have no basis. But greeting one who is praying is not objectionable at times, because the Companions used to do this with the Prophet ﷺ and he did not forbid them.
* Student: Shaykh, but people do not know how to return it..?
* The Shaykh: In any case, sometimes, not always.
* * *
* Student: ﴿And when the angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds. O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord and prostrate and bow with those who bow. That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you, and you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would be entrusted with Maryam, nor were you with them when they disputed﴾ [Ali 'Imran 41-44].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. I think there remain for us benefits from...?
* Student: That Allah wills good and evil...
* The Shaykh: Yes. The affirmation of Allah's will in His saying: ﴿Thus does Allah do what He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran 40]. We have explained that absolute will is restricted by wisdom, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30]. It is not mere will, but will accompanied by wisdom. We mentioned that from the generality of ﴿what He wills﴾ it is derived that it includes both good and evil, but evil is not attributed to Allah, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «And evil is not attributed to You» [Related by Muslim (771/201) from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib], and for this reason in praise of Allah it is said: «In His hand is the good» [Related by al-Tirmidhi (3428) and Ibn Majah (2235) from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab], and it does not say "and the evil", because evil is not ascribed to Him. Evil exists in the effects separate from Him. As for His action itself, meaning the act itself, there is no evil in it, because Allah does not do anything containing evil except for a good purpose. For example, Allah the Mighty and Majestic wills evil, and His willing it is not evil but good, for several reasons. The first: good cannot become clear except when evil exists, since things are not distinguished except by their opposites. Were all of Allah's effects good, good would not be recognized, and evil would not exist at all. So goodness and its being good are only known through the existence of its opposite, which is evil. This is part of the wisdom.

Among the other wisdoms is the testing and trial of people, for if the path were entirely good, there would be no test or trial in it. Testing and trial occur only when there are two paths: one good, which people are told to take, and the other evil, which people are told not to take. Through this the truthful is distinguished from the liar, and testing is impossible without it.

Among them, from the wisdoms in the existence of evil, is that the commanding of good and forbidding of evil, by which this Ummah was distinguished, cannot be realized without the existence of evil, so that good opposed to it is commanded and evil, which is corruption, is forbidden. If all matters were good and right, there would be no enjoining of good and forbidding of evil, for a person has no path except this good, and one cannot be commanded to something for which he has no path but that.

Among the wisdoms also: the establishment of jihad in the way of Allah, for jihad would not be established without good and evil, since jihad is a struggle between the friends of Allah who uphold good and the enemies of Allah who uphold evil, and without this jihad in the way of Allah would not occur.

Among the wisdoms in this: the demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by creating opposites, for the creation of opposites is undoubtedly evidence of the power of Allah, and without these opposites being created and brought into existence, the perfection of power would not be manifest, since creating a thing together with its opposite is more eloquent in power than creating a thing that has no opposite.

Among the wisdoms in the existence of evil: it is a motive for a person to turn to his Lord. Often the existence of evil moves people to turn to Allah, to litanies and to precautions. Were there no evil, people would not turn to Allah, because they would be in good.

Among them, that is, among the wisdoms in the existence of evil, is that a person thereby knows the measure of Allah's blessing upon him, for he finds many people of evil and corruption, while Allah has graced him with goodness, righteousness and reform. Thereby he knows the measure of Allah's blessing upon him, so he thanks Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, for this blessing which He has bestowed upon him by loving good and striving for it. Then he praises Allah again that He has saved him from evil and corruption and its people, and deliverance from evil and corruption and its people is undoubtedly a great blessing: ﴿So when you have settled, you and those with you, upon the ship, say: Praise be to Allah, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Mu'minun 28].

Among the wisdoms in creating evil: the manifestation of human weakness and helplessness before the forces of evil. A person may be kept from sleep and have his rest disturbed by a mosquito, a mosquito, one of the weakest of creatures, preventing him from sleep. If he is a heavy sleeper, it deprives him of the pleasure of sleep. He may be able to sleep, but he is bitten: once on the hand, once on the leg, once on the face, and it deprives him of the sweet sleep. And what is it? Something weak, a mosquito. Thereby a person knows his own measure, and that he is weak before the forces of evil, so that he does not become arrogant and proud.

It is mentioned that a tyrant among the tyrannical kings was speaking with his people, mocking and saying: What is the wisdom in creating flies? The fly carries germs and carries diseases and the like, so what is its wisdom? One of those present said: Its wisdom is to humiliate, or to rub the noses of tyrants like you in the dust. Yes, for this contemptible fly alights on the nose of this mighty man, whom no one may enter upon except with permission, and who has a chamberlain behind a chamberlain, and this contemptible fly comes and alights on his nose, and perhaps soils him with its droppings too. Yes, if it comes to him while he is asleep and he is a heavy sleeper, the fly can settle on him.

In any case, this is also from the wisdom of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, in creating evil, and there are wisdoms in which much may become apparent to the one who reflects.

Thereby we know the perfection of Allah's wisdom and lordship, and whoever knows Allah increases in His worship, as it is said: The one who knows Allah more is more fearful of Him and more obedient to Him.

He said: ﴿Thus said He: Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran 40]. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿He said: My Lord, make for me a sign. He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture﴾ [Ali 'Imran 41].

From the benefits of this verse: the permissibility of seeking that by which faith may increase, even if faith is already present. Indeed, we may even say: it is obligatory to seek that by which faith may increase, because a person is required to strengthen his faith by every means.

Among its benefits, from the benefits of this noble verse: the completeness of Allah's power, the Glorified and Exalted, through extraordinary events. For Zakariya, peace be upon him, not speaking to the people except by gesture, yet his tongue being loosened in glorification, is one of the signs of Allah. Hence He said: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the sign may be the reverse of what it was sought for. It was sought to confirm the existence of what he was given glad tidings of, but the sign was the reverse, it was the cancellation of something existing, namely speech. He was able to speak, but was prevented from speaking. Previously he was an elderly man and his wife was barren, then a son was given to him. So the sign, and what was a sign for him, between them is what? Opposition. This is existence and that is non-existence.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a gesture takes the place of expression. From where is this derived?
* Student: ﴿except by gesture﴾.
* The Shaykh: How, I mean, from where is it derived?
* The student: That you will not speak to the people except by gesture.
* The Shaykh: What is the benefit we mentioned?
* The student: He speaks to the people by gesture.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: That a gesture takes the place of expression.
* The Shaykh: That a gesture takes the place of expression, from His saying: ﴿that you will not speak to the people... except by gesture﴾. And this benefit is based on what?
* Student: A benefit (...)
* The Shaykh: Yes, but based on what, with respect to the interpretation of the verse?
* The student: It is based on His saying: ﴿that you will not speak to the people three nights, sound﴾ [Maryam 10].
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: ﴿three days except by gesture﴾ [Ali 'Imran 41].
* Student: On the basis that the exception is continuous.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is based on the exception being continuous, so the gesture is considered a form of speech.

Another benefit: that a gesture takes the place of expression when one is unable to express himself. From where is this derived?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From where is it derived, before we see the basis of derivation afterward?
* Student: His saying: ﴿except by gesture﴾.
* The Shaykh: What is the basis of derivation?
* The student: We take the second opinion, that the exception here is disconnected, so it is not speech.
* The Shaykh: So it is not speech, but it takes its place when?
* The student: When unable.
* The Shaykh: When unable to do it. Both matters are true: a gesture takes the place of expression in conveying meaning, especially when one is unable. We mentioned in the tafsir examples where a gesture departs from speech and examples where a gesture agrees with speech. Do you recall them now?
An example of a gesture departing from speech?
* Student: (...)

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 38–41 (part 6 of 6):

* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning that it is not speech.
* The student: Like when one gestures during prayer.
* The Shaykh: Yes, like when one gestures during prayer; for a gesture does not invalidate the prayer, whereas speech does invalidate it. Good. An example?
* The Shaykh: An example of a gesture taking the place of speech?
* A student: In the words of Maryam (...): ﴿So she pointed to him﴾ [Maryam 29] (...) she pointed to him; the gesture here..
* The Shaykh: When they insinuated slander against her, she pointed to him. And others?
* A student: The hadith of the woman whom the Jew killed[[Recorded by Abu 'Awana in his Musnad (6134) from the hadith of Anas.]], when they asked her, and she gestured toward the Jew.
* The Shaykh: She did not gesture toward the Jew.
* The student: She signaled.
* The Shaykh: She gestured when his name was mentioned.
* A student: In the story of Dhu al-Yadayn, when the Prophet said: "Is what Dhu al-Yadayn says true?", and they signaled that yes.
* The Shaykh: Some of them did, and some of them said: yes.
So we say: the verse, on both interpretations, indicates that a gesture takes the place of speech either absolutely or when there is need for it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when a person is cut off from people, he should occupy his time with the remembrance of Allah, from the words of the one who was prevented from speaking with people and could only communicate by gesture. It is well known that a person who speaks to people only by gesture will not be eager to converse with them, lest he tire or be tired; so Allah commanded him: ﴿And remember your Lord much and glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾ [Ali 'Imran 41].
* Among its benefits: the virtue of glorification and remembrance at these two times: al-'Ashi, the end of the day, and al-Ibkar, the beginning of the day. From the same is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ [Qaf 39].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: remembrance should be coupled with glorification, except where a text specifies separating one from the other; for He said: "remember your Lord and glorify," but for remembrance He said: ﴿much﴾, and for glorification He said: ﴿in the evening and the morning﴾. So do we say that remembrance is not restricted to the evening and the morning, or that it is restricted but one should increase in it?
Both are possible; but other verses indicate that a person is commanded to remember Allah much. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance, and glorify Him morning and afternoon﴾ [al-Ahzab 41–42], and He the Exalted described the righteous: ﴿and the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember﴾ [al-Ahzab 35]. Accordingly, remembrance is more frequent than glorification; yet joining the two together also has a benefit, which is that it combines praise of Allah with declaring Him free of imperfections.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿There did Zakariya call upon his Lord﴾ [Ali 'Imran 38], and this is the beginning of the lesson.

﴿There﴾: this is a demonstrative noun indicating a place. The lam is said by the scholars to indicate distance, and the kaf is a particle of address. It means: at that time. The indication here may refer to the time, i.e. at that time, or to the place, which is the niche (mihrab) of Maryam. ﴿There﴾ means: in that place and at that time. ﴿Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾. The name ﴿Zakariya﴾ has two recitations: the madd (long) and the qasr (short). ﴿Zakariyā'u﴾ is the madd, and ﴿Zakariya﴾ is the qasr.

﴿He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾. ﴿Grant me﴾ means: give me. Hibah (gift) is the donating of a thing without compensation. But the scholars said: there is hibah, hadiyyah and sadaqah. How many? Three things. Sadaqah is that by which the reward of the Hereafter is intended; hadiyyah is that by which affection and drawing closer between the giver and the recipient is intended; and hibah is that which is intended merely for the benefit of the one given to. Here, ﴿My Lord, grant me﴾ means: give me a gift without price.

﴿From Yourself a good offspring﴾. ﴿From Yourself﴾ means: from Your presence. He attributed it to the presence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to make it more eloquent and greater, because the gift of the Generous is most noble. His words ﴿offspring﴾ mean: that which is created (madhru'ah), i.e. created. His words ﴿good﴾ mean: good in its words and deeds, and likewise in its bodies; so it encompasses sensory goodness and moral goodness.

﴿Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication﴾, i.e. the One who answers it. Du'a (supplication) is the servant's asking his Lord for his need, either by bringing about a benefit or by repelling a harm.

He said: ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾. In another recitation: ﴿Then the angel called to him﴾. As for the recitation of the plural, ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾, the feminine in the verb is evident, because ﴿the angels﴾ is a plural, and every plural may have its verb made feminine, every plural except the sound masculine plural, which is feminine only very rarely. An example of the feminine in the plural even for the masculine is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah 253]; here ﴿the messengers﴾ is feminine. What is the proof? The demonstrative is in the feminine form. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Bedouins say: We have believed﴾ [al-Hujurat 14]; He said "qalat al-a'rab" and did not say "qala al-a'rab", because it is a plural. As for the sound feminine plural, it must be made feminine, and the sound masculine plural must be made masculine. For this reason Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

*And the ta' with a plural other than the sound masculine*
*Is like the ta' with "one of the bricks"*

The meaning is that the ta' with the plural is like the ta' with "iḥdā al-labin" (one of the bricks). What is "iḥdā al-labin"? A brick (labinah). Labinah is feminine, but its femininity is metaphorical, so it is permissible to make its verb masculine or feminine: you say "inkasarat al-labinah" and "inkasara al-labinah". The apparent meaning of his words is that even the sound feminine plural need not be made feminine; but the correct view is that the sound feminine plural must be made feminine. The sound plural, whether masculine or feminine, is [governed] accordingly: the masculine must be made masculine and the feminine must be made feminine, and all other plurals may be made masculine or feminine.

Here ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾ poses no difficulty regarding the feminine verb, why? Because it is a plural, since the subject is plural. But on the recitation ﴿Then the angel called to him﴾, is there a difficulty? We say: there is no difficulty in it either. Why? Because "al-malā'ikah" is a broken plural, and a broken plural may have its verb masculine or feminine: you say "qama al-rijal" and "qamat al-rijal". It is possible that "the angels" refers to one, namely Jibril, who called to him, and it is expressed in the plural in terms of the category, since he is one of them.

﴿The angels called to him while he was standing praying in the mihrab﴾. The clause ﴿while he was standing﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), the hal referring to the pronoun in His words ﴿called to him﴾. His words ﴿standing praying in the mihrab﴾: the mihrab is the place of prayer or place of worship, and it was so named because it is the place of the war against the devils, for worship is a war against the devils. The mihrab here does not mean the niche of the qiblah as some people think, so they interpret the verse by it and say: these mihrabs have existed since ancient times. Do you not hear His words: ﴿Whenever Zakariya entered upon her the mihrab﴾, and His words: ﴿The angels called to him while he was standing praying in the mihrab﴾? But this is not correct.

﴿That Allah gives you good news﴾. The particle ﴿that﴾ has a recitation with fat-hah and a recitation with kasrah. As for the kasrah reading ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, it is because calling is speech, and the content of speech, when introduced by ﴿inna﴾, requires the kasrah of ﴿inna﴾, like the words of Allah: ﴿He said: Indeed I am the servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam 30]; and you may not say: "He said: that I am the servant of Allah". Fine. As for the fat-hah reading, it is by the implied preposition: "the angels called to him that Allah gives you good news", i.e. with glad tidings: Allah's glad tidings of this son, Yahya.

Also in His words ﴿gives you good news﴾ there are two recitations, ﴿yabshuruka﴾ and ﴿yubashshiruka﴾, and both are among the seven recitations. So in this verse there are three words each of which has two recitations: ﴿fa-nādat-hu﴾, ﴿fa-nādā-hu﴾, ﴿anna Allāha yubashshiruka﴾, ﴿inna Allāha yubashshiruka﴾, ﴿inna Allāha yabshuruka﴾, ﴿inna Allāha yubashshiruka﴾, yes. Bishārah is informing of what pleases, and it was so named because the skin (bashrah) is affected by the news; for when a person is given good news of what pleases him, he rejoices and that shows on his face. Have you not seen the face of the Prophet ﷺ when Mujazziz al-Mudlaji entered upon Usamah ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Harithah while they were wearing a cloak that did not reveal anything of them except their feet? He looked at their feet and said: "These feet are part of one another." Then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, entered upon 'Aishah, and the lines of his face were radiant[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3555) and Muslim (1459/38), from 'Aishah.]]: he was affected by what? By the pleasing news. Fine. If someone says: if you say this, then consider the informing of what is displeasing to be glad tidings too, since the skin is affected by that; when you inform a man of what displeases him, his face darkens and changes, so call it glad tidings? What is the answer? We say: this may be called that, i.e. informing of what displeases may be called bishārah, and from it is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran 21], ﴿Give the hypocrites the tidings that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [an-Nisa' 138], because this affects the skin.

* Student: Shaykh, what about Maryam... that her mother vowed her, then...?
* The Shaykh: Maryam — you mean her father died before she was born?
* The Student: Yes, because she was vowed and he did not...
* The Shaykh: By Allah, it is not far-fetched.
* The Student: Then she named her.
* The Shaykh: And also Zakariya was her guardian, yes. So this is good: that her father was not present, yes, he does not take her, and then the problem disappears.
* Student: How old was Maryam?
* The Shaykh: Her age when?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: By Allah, historians must mention that, but the apparent is that she was an adult young woman, because she carried him and withdrew with him to a remote place.
* Student: Middle-aged.
* The Shaykh: Allah knows best; but there is no doubt she was mature and energetic, she had not reached the age of old age nor the young age at which one cannot bear.
* Student: Shaykh, (...), I say: if you mentioned that the name is prepared, then it is at the time of birth, and if it was not prepared, then on the seventh day. May Allah reward you well: if it becomes prepared a day or two after birth, is it named immediately or...?
* The Shaykh: No, it is better to delay.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The Shaykh: If this is for the purpose of teaching, then there is no doubt it is permissible, for teaching. If it is for the purpose of recitation, some scholars permitted that, among them Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and some did not permit it and said: if you recite according to one reader's recitation, persist in it. But what appears is that the Qur'an is one thing, and it is permissible to recite one word by one reader's recitation and the second word by another's.

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no harm. No — do you mean repeating the word twice?
* Student: No, no, I mean he reads...
* The Shaykh: For example you read ﴿inna Allaha yubashshiruka﴾ and ﴿anna Allaha yabshuruka﴾, like that?
* Student: No, no, I mean he reads the verse by one recitation, for example Hafs, and the next verse by another reader's recitation, the verse that follows.
* The Shaykh: At the same time, or the second verse following?

* The Shaykh: No harm; that is the one in which the difference lies, this is the one with the difference.
* Student: Shaykh, can one not cite His words, glorified be He, ﴿And He made Zakariya her guardian﴾ as evidence that this verse supports the story of the dispute between Ja'far and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib?
* The Shaykh: How so?
* Student: When they disputed over a daughter... the Messenger ﷺ gave her to Ja'far because her maternal aunt (...), and Maryam's maternal aunt was under Zakariya?
* The Shaykh: But is there a dispute in this? We do not know whether there is a dispute in this or not.
* Student: Perhaps...
* The Shaykh: We cannot say there is a dispute, and it is not mentioned in the story; and the apparent, as the brother mentioned, is that her father had died, Maryam's father apparently died, and perhaps he died before she was born, as evidenced by Maryam disposing of her and naming her.
* Student: It would not be support.
* The Shaykh: Support for what?
* Student: For the Prophet ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: No, there is no support, there is no dispute; who disputed with Zakariya?
* Student: Regarding her custody, for example that the guardianship goes to the aunt's husband.
* The Shaykh: Basically the father does not exist.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And her mother exists, and she is with her mother.

* * *

* Student: ﴿Then the angels called to him while he was standing praying in the mihrab: that Allah gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a master, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾ (39) ﴿He said: My Lord, how can I have a boy when old age has reached me and my wife is barren? He said: Thus Allah does what He wills﴾ (40) ﴿He said: My Lord, appoint for me a sign. He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture; and remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning﴾ [Ali 'Imran 39–41].
* The Shaykh: Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿gives you good news of Yahya﴾. This is the one given the good news. We have bishārah, as we mentioned, and mubashshir, and mubashshar bihi, and mubashshar: how many are these?
* The Students: Four.
* The Shaykh: Four; all of them are contained in His words: ﴿gives you good news of Yahya﴾. Yahya is said to be from life (hayah), and that Allah named him thus as an indication that he will live and remain. On this view he is diptote for being a proper noun and having the form of a verb. Others said: rather it is a foreign name, and foreign names are not derived, because they are not Arabic; on this view the preventing factors from declension are proper noun and foreignness, since being a proper noun and foreignness are two causes preventing declension. We will now mention the preventing factors of declension incidentally: nine, gathered in a verse. You?
* Student: I do not memorize it.
* The Shaykh: You do not memorize the verse? Yes?
* Student:
*Mawani'u al-sarfi tis'un in aradta bi-ha ∗∗∗ 'awnan li-tablugha fi i'rabika al-amalā*
*Ijma' wa-zin 'adlan anna th bi-ma'rifatin ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-zid 'ujmatan fa-l-wasfu qad kamalā*
* The Shaykh: Well done.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is it?
* Student:
*Jam'un wa-'adlun zada wazn wasfuhu ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-anni'thu 'ujmatan (...)*
* The Shaykh: Yes, fine.
* Student: Let us hear it.
* The Shaykh: Yes, recite it.
* Student: Jam'un wa-'adlun zada wazn wasfah.
* The Shaykh: Wait, but we want you to recite it to us on condition that you memorize it. Come on.
* Student: I will say it from the beginning.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student:
*Jam'un wa-'adlun zada wazn wasfah ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-anni'th 'ujmatan (...)*
* Student: As (...) best.
* The Shaykh: Did you hear?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: We will come to the second round, God willing. The first verse, from memory, is well known:
*Ijma' wa-zin 'adlan anna th bi-ma'rifatin ∗∗∗ rakkib wa-zid 'ujmatan fa-l-wasfu qad kamalā*
These nine are divided: three of them need only one cause; three need two causes, one of which is proper-noun status together with another cause; and three need two causes, one of which is proper-noun status or descriptiveness together with another cause. So these nine causes fall into three categories: a category in which one cause suffices, a category of two causes one of which is proper-noun status, and a category of two causes one of which is proper-noun status or descriptiveness. What we have here is proper-noun status and foreignness; foreignness is not produced by descriptiveness. Foreignness is not produced by descriptiveness; proper-noun status and the verbal pattern (wazn al-fi'l) are produced by descriptiveness, because descriptiveness and the verbal pattern are two causes preventing declension, and proper-noun status and the verbal pattern are two causes preventing declension.

Now: ﴿gives you good news of Yahya, confirming﴾: ﴿confirming﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿Yahya﴾. ﴿a word from Allah﴾ is 'Isa ibn Maryam, meaning confirming 'Isa; because 'Isa is a word from Allah, or the word of Allah. He was so named because he was by the word of Allah: he had no father, as humans do, but was by the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed the likeness of 'Isa before Allah is like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he is﴾ [Ali 'Imran 59], i.e. Adam. Therefore 'Isa was called the word, the word of Allah, because he was by His word, and he is not the word of Allah itself; why? Because "the word of Allah" is an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and speech is an attribute of the one described, and it is not possible that an attribute of Allah be a separate entity distinct from Him. Rather, its meaning necessarily is that being a "word" means that he was by what? By the word of Allah: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾.

And His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾ indicates the origin of the matter, and it is not partitive. The word is not a part of Allah; rather, it originates from Him. So ﴿min﴾ (from) here denotes origin, because the Word originates from Allah, since He is the One who spoke it.

﴿And chief﴾ is coordinated with ﴿confirming﴾, so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). It is in the accusative as a ḥāl, it is in the accusative as a ḥāl. ﴿Chief﴾: who is the chief? The chief is one who excels over others and is superior to them in knowledge, religion, character and conduct. Our saying "character" includes every trait by which a person surpasses others, such as generosity, courage, self-sacrifice and other qualities. The point is that the chief is one who surpasses others in perfections, meaning he is superior to them and exceeds them, so he combines all the perfect attributes possible for a created being.

Likewise, He also described him as ﴿chaste﴾, coordinated with ﴿confirming﴾, so it is in the accusative as a ḥāl. ﴿Chaste (ḥaṣūr)﴾ is on the pattern fa‘ūl in the sense of fā‘il, meaning one who restrains himself from base morals. Thus this announced one is described with the attributes of perfection indicated by what? ﴿Chief﴾, one who is free from deficiency and bad character, indicated by ﴿chaste﴾. So he combines in himself both negation and affirmation. This is because a person is not perfected except by the presence of the attributes of perfection and the absence of the attributes of deficiency. Note, brothers, that the attributes of perfection and deficiency here do not mean absolute deficiency and absolute perfection, which belong to no one but Allah. Rather, they are relative matters. A person may have perfection in some attributes but have a flaw in another respect, and this is deficient. He may have a flaw and deficiency in perfection, and this is more deficient. He may have perfection in perfection and be free of deficiency, and this is what? The perfection with which Yaḥyā, peace be upon him, was described.

As for those among the exegetes (mufassirūn) who said that ḥaṣūr means one who is prevented from approaching women, meaning he is not able to be with women, there is clearly a problem with this, because a person's inability to approach women is not a perfection. It is not something he acquires by discipline; rather it is a defect, isn't it? It is a defect, yes. There is another opinion: that he does not approach women who are not lawful to him, and thus it describes him with what? With the perfection of chastity, which a person is praised for. This is praised. But what we said is more comprehensive than this opinion, more comprehensive. It is known that when a more comprehensive meaning exists, it takes precedence over a lesser meaning, because the lesser is included within the more comprehensive, and not the reverse. The point is that ﴿ḥaṣūr﴾ is one who restrains himself from bad and base morals, so the verse describes him with perfection of character and absence of bad qualities, and this is the utmost perfection.

﴿And chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾: this is also coordinated with ﴿confirming﴾, so he is a confirmer and a prophet. His confirming of Jesus does not necessarily mean that he follows him. Does Muhammad ﷺ, who confirms all the prophets, follow them? No. They follow him and he does not follow them. For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If my brother Moses were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me" [Narrated by Aḥmad in al-Musnad (15156) and al-Dārimī (449) from the hadith of Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh]. For this reason he became their imam on the night of the Ascension (al-Miʿrāj). And for this reason, when Jesus descends at the end of time, he will rule by the Sharia of the Prophet, peace be upon him. The point is that his confirming of Jesus son of Mary does not contradict his being a prophet. He is a prophet who confirms the prophets. For this reason He said: ﴿and a prophet from among the righteous﴾. ﴿From among the righteous﴾ means: from among them, one of them. We say this because prophethood is a higher attribute than righteousness, but he is among the righteous. Prophethood is righteousness plus more. The evidence for this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 69]. The righteous are in the fourth rank, and everyone before them is included among them, isn't that so? So every prophet is righteous, but not vice versa. Every truthful one is righteous, but not vice versa. Every martyr is righteous, but not vice versa. Is that right? Every righteous person is righteous, correct, every righteous person is righteous.

* A student: "But not vice versa."
* The Shaykh: "But not vice versa" what?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: The converse is what? That is, every corrupt person is corrupt, or what?
* A student: The converse of "every righteous person is righteous."
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. In any case, His saying ﴿from among the righteous﴾ means from among them, because the prophet combines the attribute of prophethood and righteousness, so he is one of them.

﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has already overtaken me and my wife is barren?"﴾ He said this when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave him the good news. ﴿How can I have a son, when old age has already overtaken me?﴾ That is, how? He says this not out of disbelief or denial, but out of seeking certainty. Otherwise, we know that Zakariyyā, peace be upon him, had believed in what Allah gave him good news of, and he could not possibly consider it unlikely. Rather, he said this for what reason? Seeking certainty. A person is an imperfect human in perception and knowledge, and needs something that confirms matters for him. Abraham, peace be upon him, undoubtedly believed with perfect faith, with no doubt, that Allah gives life to the dead, yet he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest"﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. This is because news is not like seeing with one's own eyes. If a person informs you of something, however truthful he may be, his report will never be to you like seeing it directly. So Zakariyyā, peace be upon him, asked Allah: ﴿How can I have a son, when old age has already overtaken me?﴾ with the intention of what? Seeking certainty and confirming this matter, not considering Allah's power unlikely, nor doubting His report, Exalted is He. Rather, he believed in that and believed in Allah's power, Glorified and Exalted is He, and that when He wills something He says to it "Be" and it is. Especially since he had seen with Mary the provision, and so he said: ﴿Where has this come to you from?﴾ She said: ﴿It is from Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 37].

﴿How can I have a son?﴾ He said "a son" even though the child had not yet been born. But this is in view of what will be. Expressing a thing by what it will be is a valid usage in the language and occurs in the Qur'an: ﴿One of them said: "I see myself pressing wine"﴾ [Yūsuf 36]. That is, pressing grapes which will become wine, because wine itself is not pressed; what is pressed is grapes, and their juice turns into wine. So he expressed the thing by what it will become. Now here, ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ How can there be a son when he has not yet been born? We say: in view of what will be.

Then he said: ﴿when old age has already overtaken me﴾. The wāw here, the scholars call it the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), meaning that it indicates that the clause following it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier: that is, "while in fact old age has already overtaken me." It is a circumstance of what? Of the yā' in His saying: ﴿to me﴾?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, brother, it is a circumstance of the yā' in His saying ﴿to me﴾, in ﴿How can I have a son?﴾. So it is in the accusative position as a circumstance of the yā' in His saying ﴿to me﴾.

﴿Old age has overtaken me﴾ means old age has reached me. In reality, it may appear to a person that there is a reversal in the meaning: did old age reach you, or did you reach old age? Or both are permissible? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and I have indeed reached extreme old age﴾ [Maryam 8]. So he became the one who reached old age. And here he says: ﴿old age has already overtaken me﴾. So the expression is correct in both cases: if you reach old age, then old age has overtaken you, and if old age has overtaken you, then you have reached it. ﴿Old age has already overtaken me﴾ means it has befallen me. It is customary that when an old person has not had children in his youth, he will not see children, because begetting and fertility occur only in youth. The more advanced a person's age, whether a man or a woman, the less their ability to have children becomes. So he says: how is it that when I was young no child came to me, and now a child is coming to me? Likewise the woman: his wife is barren. ʿAqir (barren) is masculine in form but feminine in meaning here, and it is applied to both male and female. One says "a barren man" and "a barren woman," meaning one who cannot have children. So now each of the spouses is not in a state of bearing children. But Allah is over all things capable: when He wills something He says to it "Be" and it is. For this reason He said: ﴿He said: "Thus Allah does what He wills."﴾ ﴿Thus Allah﴾ ("thus") here, in my view, admits of two possibilities. The first: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied meaning is: "the matter is thus," meaning that old age has overtaken you and your wife is barren, but Allah does what He wills. The second: it is in the position of an accusative of absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), meaning: Allah does an action like that, because He does what He wills. Both possibilities are correct. He will indeed have a son even though old age has overtaken him and even though his wife is barren. Why? Because Allah does what He wills. Whatever Allah wills, He does, because He, Mighty and Majestic, is not prevented by anything, as we say at the end of every prayer: "O Allah, there is no preventer of what You have given, and no giver of what You have withheld" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (6330) and Muslim (593/137) from the hadith of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba]. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does what He wills, because He has absolute sovereignty over His creation, so no one prevents Him and no one asks Him: why did You do that? ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 23]. ﴿Thus Allah does what He wills.﴾

So when he became certain that Allah, the Exalted, would grant him a child, he said: ﴿My Lord, make for me a sign﴾, that is: appoint for me a sign that indicates this child, as if he is saying: when will this sign come? My Lord, make for me a sign that indicates the coming of this child, and that the child has begun to develop. Why? In order to increase in what? In tranquillity. To increase in tranquillity regarding what Allah had given him good news of. ﴿Make for me a sign﴾ by which I may know that the child has begun to develop, or ﴿make for me a sign﴾ by which I may increase in tranquillity regarding what You have given me good news of. The word āyah in the language means sign. The signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are cosmic and legislative. The prophets, peace be upon them, were supported with what? With signs that indicate their truthfulness: cosmic signs and legislative signs. Many people call the prophets' signs "miracles" (muʿjizāt). Although this name has become common on tongues, it has a deficiency, and the correct and sound expression is to call them signs, as Allah named them. We call the extraordinary events that occur at the hands of the prophets "signs." For this reason you will not find any verse in the Qur'an in which Allah called these extraordinary events "miracles" at all; rather He called them signs, indicators of truthfulness. As for "miracles," the term is deficient, because if we took it literally it would include what the sorcerers bring, or what the jinn bring, because what the sorcerers and jinn bring is also miraculous, isn't it? It is miraculous, but is it a sign? No. For this reason the expression found in the Qur'an is better than the expression some scholars used when they called the extraordinary events that Allah causes at the hands of the prophets "miracles."

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days,"﴾ meaning: the sign that informs you. He attributed it to Zakariyyā even though he was not the one who brought it into being, but because it is a sign for him. ﴿That you will not speak to the people for three days.﴾ I would like to understand the grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of ﴿Your sign that you will not speak﴾?
* A student: ﴿Your sign﴾ is the subject (mubtada').
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: And the kāf is a pronoun in the genitive position, and the interpreted infinitive from "an" (that) and (...) is in the nominative position as the predicate.
* The Shaykh: "An" and what it contains is interpreted as an infinitive?
* The student: In the nominative position as the predicate.
* The Shaykh: In the nominative position, or interpreted as an infinitive predicate? Or not in the nominative position?
* The student: Predicate.
* The Shaykh: A predicate, because it is a single word, and what is said "in the position of" applies to a clause. Good. Now estimate it?
* The student: The sign (...).
* The Shaykh: Excellent, perfect. ﴿Your sign﴾ means the sign I give you, ﴿that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture﴾. ﴿That you will not speak to the people﴾ means you will not address them. ﴿Except by gesture.﴾ ﴿For three days﴾: three days with their nights? Yes, by the evidence of the Exalted's saying in Sūrat Maryam: ﴿that you will not speak to the people for three nights, sound﴾ [Maryam 10]. His sign was that he would not speak to the people for their nights. He said: ﴿except by gesture﴾. ﴿Except﴾ is a particle of exception. But I would like to understand whether this exception is connected (muttaṣil) or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ).
