Third: if a person fears self-purification when he says "if Allah wills," or fears that he will be left to himself if self-admiration appears in him, because a person, may Allah protect us, when he is impressed by his deed, is left to himself and his blessing is removed. If he fears this, what is the ruling?
* A student: Obligatory.
* The Shaykh: The exception is obligatory. How? Was the exception not forbidden?
* A student: Obligatory, obligatory.
* The Shaykh: Did we not say a moment ago: if the motive for it is doubt, it is forbidden? This is the reverse; the exception is obligatory, obligatory for what reason? So that he does not purify himself or become self-admiring, thinking he is a believer, as the poet says:
"I am the son of Jala and the one who ascends the peaks; when I take off my turban, you will know me."

This view we mentioned, or this distinction we described, is the correct view, and if you reflect on the reasons of the two previous views, you will find that this view or this distinction brings together the positions.

He said: ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and we have followed the Messenger, so write us down among the witnesses﴾.

* From the benefits of this verse: the virtue of the disciples in their turning to Allah, mighty and majestic, as they said: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾, for after they called their prophet to witness, they turned to their Lord, mighty and majestic.
* And from the benefits of the verse: seeking nearness to Allah, exalted is He, through His lordship, for lordship revolves around three things: creation, dominion, and management, and answering supplication falls within these three. For this reason the callers to Allah often invoke His lordship, as in the authentic hadith: "He raises his hands to the sky: O Lord, O Lord." [Muslim (1015/65), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him.]
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that faith must encompass everything Allah has sent down: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾.
* And also from its benefits: the careful precision in the disciples' saying ﴿what You have sent down﴾, and they did not simply state faith in, for example, the Torah, because the Torah in the hands of the Jews is altered and changed, they show some things and conceal others. For this reason they said ﴿what You have sent down﴾, and we say: we believe in what Allah has sent down of the Torah and the Gospel, not in the altered Torah in the hands of the Jews, nor in the altered Gospel in the hands of the Christians.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that faith must have following ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾; for this reason Allah, mighty and majestic, joins faith with righteous deeds in many verses, because bare faith does not benefit. Righteous deeds are like watering a tree: if you do not water it, it dies. Therefore when we speak of Islam, we should not try to make Islam mere creed; rather it is creed and action. Creed alone is not sufficient, because now everyone claims to hold a creed: the Jews and Christians say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day." Now they say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day, we believe there is a Lord who manages creation, that He, mighty and majestic, is the Creator, and we believe in resurrection." But this is not faith, even if they hold this creed; this is a corrupt creed. So creed must be joined with righteous deeds, lest people rely on the creed they have and say, "What need is there for action?" For this reason He said: ﴿We have believed﴾ and then? ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾. This is necessary.

Consider His saying: ﴿We have believed﴾ ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾. Can it be derived from it that belief in every book Allah has sent down is obligatory, while following is specific to the particular Messenger?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is this possible?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because they said, ﴿We have believed in what You have sent down﴾ is general, and ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾ is specific, and that is so. Faith is obligatory in all that Allah has sent down: ﴿Say: I believe in what Allah has sent down of Book, and I have been commanded to be just among you﴾ [al-Shura 15]. But following is specific to the Messenger sent to you. As for a messenger who was not sent to you, you are not commanded to follow him unless your sharia indicates following him.

* From the benefits of the verse: if there are two attributes, and one of them is more specific than the other in action or in the situation you are in, then it is preferable to take the more specific one, as in His saying ﴿the Messenger﴾; for the Messenger is sent to us. They did not say "and we followed the Prophet," but ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾, because the Messenger is sent to us and dispatched. But a prophet is not commanded to convey, according to the view of the majority of scholars. Here, regarding following, which of the two is more closely tied to the mission: the messengership or the prophethood? The messengership. For this reason they chose the attribute of Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 52–53 (part 3 of 3):

If someone says: In the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib concerning the mention of sleep, when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited, when he mentioned the sleep that a person experiences at the end [of the day], he said, among what he said: "I believe in Your Book which You have sent down, and in Your Prophet whom You have sent." When al-Bara' repeated it, he said: "and in Your Messenger whom You have sent," and he (ﷺ) said: "Say: and in Your Prophet whom You have sent" [[A hadith agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (247) and Muslim (2710 / 56), from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. It is known that the context is one of following [the wording], so why, when he said "Your Messenger whom You have sent," did he [the Prophet] correct it to "Your Prophet," when messengership includes prophethood?

The answer to this is in two respects. The first respect: the indication of "messenger" for "prophet" is by implicational signification (dalalat al-iltizam), while the indication of "prophet" for "prophet" is by literal signification (dalalat al-mutabaqah, correspondence). The literal signification is undoubtedly stronger, because in implicational signification the opponent may contest it; he may say: "This is not a necessary implication." Therefore he chose the attribute of prophethood, even though "whom You have sent" came after messengership.

The answer to this is in two respects. The first respect: the indication of "messenger" for "prophet" is by implicational signification, and the indication of "prophet" for "prophet" is by...?
* The students: Correspondence (mutabaqah).
* The Shaykh: Correspondence (mutabaqah). The literal signification is undoubtedly stronger, because in implicational signification the opponent may contest it; he may say: "This is not necessary." Therefore he chose the attribute of prophethood, even though "whom You have sent" came after messengership. If he had said "Your Messenger whom You have sent," by what way does it indicate prophethood?
* The students: By implicational signification.
* The Shaykh: By implicational signification, because every messenger is a prophet. But if he says "Your Prophet whom You have sent," it indicates prophethood by literal signification, because he stated it explicitly with its own word. It is known that signification by correspondence is stronger than signification by implication, because the implication may be denied. The second respect: if he says "Your Messenger whom You have sent," it is not a specifying attribute for Muhammad (ﷺ), since it may refer to Jibril, for example. Jibril is a sent messenger, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, [possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne, [and] obeyed there [in the heavens] and trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir 19–21]. So Jibril is one who was sent. If he said "Your Messenger whom You have sent," he would not have specified that this faith is in Muhammad (peace be upon him). But if he says "Your Prophet whom You have sent," by whom is the attribute specified? By the Messenger, Muhammad (ﷺ), because Jibril is not called a prophet but is called a messenger. By this, the difficulty we pointed to is removed, namely that the attribute corresponding to the speaker's state should be mentioned. Because in the hadith of al-Bara', prophethood was chosen over messengership for these two reasons.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: eagerness for the company of the righteous. From where do we take this?
* The students: ﴿So record us among the witnesses﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿So record us among the witnesses.﴾ There is no doubt that the company of the righteous is good, to the extent that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave it the example of the bearer of musk. He said: "The likeness of the good companion is like the bearer of musk: either he will give you some, or you will buy from him, or you will find from him a pleasant fragrance." All of this is good. "The bad companion is like the one who blows the bellows." Do you know the one who blows the bellows?
* A student: Yes, we know him.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, it seems that none of you know him? Therefore it would be good for you to go to the craftsmen's market in Riyadh so that you can see the bellows, because I think there is nothing here. In any case, the bellows is like a skin, like the ghurb. The ghurb is the bucket for a camel used to raise water. This existed a year or two ago, they put "sawani" [water-wheel buckets]... yes, this is the ghurb. The point is that it is like the ghurb: it has an open end, and an end connected to a pipe that leads to the place of light, the place of the fire. He opens it like this, then closes it, then pushes it. When he pushes it, he has carried air through this pipe. We said this pipe comes to the place of the fire; the fire blazes, blazes intensely. Usually there are two, one here on the man's right and one on the left, and it is always like this, always, and the light is always blazing. The one who blows the bellows: the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Either he will burn your clothes, or you will find from him a foul smell" [[Agreed upon; recorded by al-Bukhari (2101) and Muslim (2628 / 146), from Abu Musa; the wording is al-Bukhari's.]]. When will he burn your clothes? When sparks fly from it onto you, or you find a foul smell. Therefore a person should choose the best of companions, because the good companion is all good, and the bad companion is all evil. So choose good companions for yourself. If you are deceived by someone and then sit with them time after time, and it becomes clear that they neither help you in obedience nor prevent you from disobedience, then seek someone better than them. A person sometimes associates with friends, and is deceived by them, for example, and then they benefit him not but harm him. Therefore a person's gatherings should be filled with beneficial research and with questions that open the mind, not with a person's main preoccupation in gatherings being "So-and-so said, and so-and-so said, where did so-and-so go, where did so-and-so come, so-and-so erred in this, so-and-so was right in that, so-and-so has knowledge, so-and-so has no knowledge, so-and-so is tall and so-and-so is short, so-and-so is rich and so-and-so is poor." This is not correct. This is a waste of time, and perhaps it involves backbiting, which becomes harm. "No people sit in a gathering in which they do not mention Allah except that it will be a regret for them on the Day of Resurrection" [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra (10170), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]], because they have missed the good.
* A student: We have mentioned: ﴿and record us among the witnesses﴾: everyone who bears witness to the messengers with the truth [is included]. Does this include some disbelievers who bore witness to some prophets with the truth, such as Abu Talib, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: If his testimony had been true, he would have followed him.
* The student: Yes, but he testified to him with the truth?
* The Shaykh: His testimony was not beneficial.
* A student: May Allah be good to you, Shaykh. You distinguished between the messenger and the prophet: that the messenger is one to whom revelation is sent and who is commanded to convey it, and the prophet is one to whom revelation is sent but who is not commanded to convey it. [There is] his saying (ﷺ) in Sahih Muslim: "There is no prophet except that it is a duty upon him to explain to his community the best of what he explains to them, and to warn them against evil" [[Recorded by Muslim (1844 / 46), from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]]. So this shows that the prophet likewise explains to his community what the messenger explains to them. Does this not show that there is no difference between the prophet and the messenger?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not show that, because if we say that this [explanation] was by the command of Allah, then it is?
* Students: A messenger.
* The Shaykh: Then it is a messenger. And if we say he explained voluntarily, without being obliged to do so, but out of love for good, then it is a prophet. Although the one meant in this hadith you mentioned is the prophet who is the messenger. This is why Allah often mentions the prophets without the messengers and the messengers without the prophets: ﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra' 55], and in another verse: ﴿Those messengers – We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah 253].
* A student: The signification of "prophet" for prophethood, is it by correspondence or by inclusion?
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: The signification of "prophet" for prophethood, is it by correspondence or by inclusion?
* The Shaykh: Correspondence.
* The student: Which one exactly?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this "exactly" is subsidiary.
* A student: May Allah be good to you. We said, in explaining Allah's words ﴿al-Hawariyyun﴾, that it comes from "hawr," which is intense whiteness, and the disciples' hearts are white and pure, not defiled by sins. Shaykh, the verse that is coming: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that will come to us. These who schemed are other than the disciples.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 52–53 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said, "Who are my helpers toward Allah?"﴾ And in another reading: ﴿"Who are my helpers toward Allah?"﴾ with the yā' of the first person pronounced with a fatḥah (ya'). This is because the yā' of the speaker (yā' al-mutakallim) may be used in three dialectal forms: with fatḥah as a built form (binā'), with sukūn as a built form, and with deletion for lightness (takhfīf). So you say: hādhā ghulāmī, hādhā ghulāmiya, hādhā ghulām, but it is clear that it is an addition (muḍāf).

He says here: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them﴾. ﴿Aḥassa﴾ means he perceived it with his senses and became certain that they had disbelieved, despite these great signs that they witnessed, they did not believe — and Allah forbid. This is because when Allah seals the heart, its owner never believes: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their eyes is a veil, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah 7]. What precedes it is: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾ [al-Baqarah 18]. And the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them﴾ [Yunus 96–97]. So they did not believe even with these signs. When he sensed disbelief from them, perceived it, and it became clear to him, he resorted to choosing and selecting the capable ones, and said: ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ ﴿Who are my helpers?﴾ meaning: since belief has become impossible from all of you, then who will be my helpers?

And his saying: ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ — ﴿ilā﴾ (toward) here indicates the endpoint (lil-ghāyah), and he did not say "in Allah" so that the support would be founded on sincerity; because ﴿ilā﴾ indicates the endpoint, so he wants the support to be a means leading to whom?
* The students: To Allah.
* The Shaykh: To Allah the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Said: Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ Here "man" (who) is the subject (mubtada'), "anṣārī" (my helpers) is the predicate (khabar), and "ilā Allāh" (toward Allah) is attached to "anṣār" (helpers).

He said: ﴿The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah﴾. "Al-ḥawāriyyūn" (the disciples) is the plural of "ḥawārī" with the yā' doubled, and it derives from "al-ḥawar," which means whiteness. They were called ḥawāriyyūn because their hearts were free from the trace of sins, since sins — we ask Allah for well-being — are black spots that form on the heart. Whenever a person disobeys, a black spot is added to his heart; if he repents, it is polished and returns to brightness; if he does not repent and commits another sin, another spot is added, and so on until the heart is sealed. So the ḥawāriyyūn are those who made their religion sincere and were not stained by sins.

﴿The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah﴾. ﴿We are the helpers of Allah﴾ means: not others than us. The basis of our saying "not others than us" is that this sentence here consists of a subject and a predicate; it is a nominal sentence whose two parts are definite, and a nominal sentence whose two parts are definite conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). But there is no doubt that the restriction it conveys is weak, not like the force of "innamā" (only) or of negation and affirmation.

﴿The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah; we believed in Allah﴾. ﴿Āmannā﴾: belief (īmān) in the language is more specific than taṣdīq (affirmation of truth), because it is affirmation with acknowledgement; for this reason it is transitive with "bi" (in), so one says "āmantu bihi." We cannot make it mean taṣdīq, because when one word is a synonym of another — that is, having the same meaning — it takes the same complements and is restricted by the same restrictions. It is known that "āmana" takes complements that "ṣaddaqa" does not take: one says "ṣaddaqa bil-khabar" (he affirmed the report), and one does not say "ṣaddaqa lahu," and one says "ṣaddaqa Zaydan" but does not say "āmana Zaydan"; rather "āmana bihi" and "āmana lahu." So when the two differ in their complements, existentially and in absence, it is known that they are not one meaning, although many who know belief in the language say: belief in the language is what? Affirmation of truth. This needs examination; rather it is more specific than affirmation of truth.

As for belief in the Sharia, it is: taṣdīq (affirmation of truth). Or if you wish, say: acknowledgement that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. Is it taṣdīq, or acknowledgement that necessarily entails what? Acceptance and submission. Affirmation alone is not sufficient; there must be acceptance of what the Messenger brought and submission to him. You know that Abu Talib affirmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and openly declared on the assembly that he affirmed him, saying in his famous rhyming ode:

"Indeed they know that our son is not a liar among us, and he is not concerned with the words of falsehoods."

Look: "not a liar among us," and that he is not concerned with the words of falsehoods, nor pays heed to them. He says:

"And indeed I know that the religion of Muhammad is, of the best religions of mankind, a religion."

This is affirmation, but there was no acceptance and submission from him — we seek Allah's protection — he did not follow the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, nor submitted to him. Rather his last words were that he was upon the creed of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, upon disbelief. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, interceded for him, because he had shown a good trial in defending the Messenger ﷺ, not because he was his uncle; for if the motive for the Messenger's intercession had been kinship, he would have interceded for Abu Lahab. But the motive for the intercession was that he showed a good trial in defending the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, as is well known. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "He was in a shallow fire, and upon him were two sandals, from which his brain boils" — we seek Allah's well-being, O Allah, save us from the Fire — and he said: "And had it not been for me, he would have been in the lowest level of the Fire."[[A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayhi); al-Bukhari (3883), and Muslim (209/357), from the hadith of al-ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

The point is that the messengers, peace be upon them, call to what? To the path of Allah. ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah? The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah; we believed in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. And that belief is not realized except by affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and what afterward? Submission. As for without acceptance or submission, it is not belief in the Sharia.

They said: ﴿We believed in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾: they called their Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to witness their Islam, although he is a witness over them, whether they asked him to witness or not, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That you may be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah 143]. Every messenger is a witness over his nation that Allah the Exalted sent him to them and that he conveyed the message to them. So their saying: ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ is by way of emphasis and declaring Islam.

Then they said: ﴿Our Lord, we believed in what You sent down, and we followed the Messenger﴾. This also is from their saying, may Allah be pleased with them: ﴿Our Lord, we believed in what You sent down﴾, which is the Gospel brought by Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿And we followed the Messenger﴾: the definite article "al" in "al-rasūl" here is for mental (dhihnī) reference, namely Jesus, peace be upon him, because there was no messenger for these people of the Children of Israel except Jesus. So what specifies that by "the Messenger" Jesus is meant is the mental reference which was known to them. It is possible that "the Messenger" is meant generically, i.e., "and we followed everyone who was a messenger from You," and then this is an acknowledgement that they believed in all the messengers, because every later nation must believe in all the earlier messengers. So we, for example, as the last of the nations, must believe in all the messengers: ﴿The Messenger believes in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers; each believes in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers; we make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah 285], regarding the basis of belief; though we distinguish between the messengers in terms of following, for we follow only Muhammad ﷺ and what he permitted us of the law of those before. As for belief, belief in all of them is obligatory.

* A student: O Shaykh, you mentioned to us a benefit which is (...) — is this a consistent rule always, or in some cases only?
* The Shaykh: No, in some cases. In the vocative it is consistent; outside the vocative it is sometimes deleted and sometimes not deleted.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What do you say about this? The difficulty: how is it that Allah said to ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥarām, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed I have decreed that they will not return to it" [recorded by al-Tirmidhi (3010), Ibn Majah (190), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (14881), the wording being his, from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him], and here it is mentioned that He gave life to the dead for Jesus? The answer?
* A student: That this is the original rule, as long as...
* The Shaykh: That it be specified?
* The student: That it be specified.
* The Shaykh: But this is problematic, since He said: "Indeed I have decreed that they will not return to it." Does the divine decree (al-qaḍāʾ al-qadarī) not preclude this?
* A student: Shaykh, perhaps he is revived and dies, and returns dead at the same time; that is, he returns alive and then returns dead.
* The Shaykh: Fine.
* A student: That was a law of those before us.
* The Shaykh: No, this is the decree of Allah, general.

Apparently — and Allah knows best — ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥarām sought to return for the sake of work, whereas what occurred as a sign for Jesus, they did not return in order to work. Moreover, the matter also has a point of difficulty in one respect: when the thunderbolt seized the companions of Moses who were with him, Moses called upon Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and He raised them up after their death, and they remained and worked. So the meaning is: if there is no cause, such as there being a sign, then there is no objection; but as for ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥarām, there was no cause.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path﴾ [51]. ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said: Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ He expressed with ﴿aḥassa﴾ (sensed) rather than saying "ʿalima" (knew). Why?
* A student: Because he perceived and became certain.
* The Shaykh: What? He perceived and became certain, so the matter became perceptible to him.

His saying: ﴿The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah﴾ — who are the disciples?
* A student: The disciples are the followers of Jesus, peace be upon him; they are his elite from among his people.
* The Shaykh: They are the elite of his people. From where is this word derived?
* A student: The elite (ṣafwa).
* The Shaykh: No, is it "al-ḥawar" or "al-ḥawāriyyūn"?
* The student: From "al-ḥawar," which is beauty.
* The Shaykh: Beauty of what?
* The student: The black-eyed maidens (ḥūr al-ʿayn).
* The Shaykh: Which?
* The student: Their beauty.
* The Shaykh: That is, their beauty is their purity.

In this verse there is evidence that the Christians are Muslims: they said ﴿We believed in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. What do you say, is this deduction correct?
* A student: Yes, correct, if you intend their sharia (...).
* The Shaykh: We say: are they Muslims in the general sense? Because every person who follows a messenger whose law is still in force is a Muslim; every person who follows a messenger whose law is still in force is a Muslim. Do you understand? As for when there is nothing that abrogates it, whoever remains on the earlier religion is a disbeliever, if the messenger was sent to him. Clear? Based on this: there is no Muslim after the sending of the Messenger ﷺ except one who follows him alone, and whoever else is a disbeliever. On this basis, the Christians are disbelievers, and the Jews are disbelievers, among the people of the Fire. Whoever says that they are Muslims in the specific sense by which they enter Paradise today is a disbeliever, because he contradicts the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Ali ʿImran 85], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Ali ʿImran 19].

* Among the benefits of these verses: the arrogance of the Children of Israel, and that despite these great signs brought by Jesus, none of them believed; by His saying: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them﴾.
* And among its benefits also — among the benefits of these verses — that when a matter becomes unclear, the caller should call for sincerity by saying: Who is sincere? That is, he should single out the elite of the people; by His saying: ﴿He said: Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ He, seeing that the people had rebelled and perceived disbelief from them and that it had become evident, called upon those he considered to be among their elite.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that the messengers, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them, call to Allah and not to themselves; by His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾
* And among the benefits of the noble verse also: that the messengers need those who support them; by His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers?﴾ And Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿He it is who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal 62].
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of the disciples, may Allah be pleased with them, in that they declared themselves the helpers of Allah despite the disbelief of their people; by His saying: ﴿The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah﴾. Thus a person should declare his following of the Messenger before the leaders of disbelief, so that he does not flatter in the religion of Allah; for flattery (mudāhana) in the religion of Allah and concealment (taqiyya) are in reality hypocrisy, hypocrisy. Rather, a person must be forthright in the religion of Allah. We have already mentioned the difference between mudāhana and mudārā: mudāhana is to approve them in the falsehood they are upon; mudārā is to disapprove of them but to be gentle with them, so that they do not prevent him from the truth.

* * *

* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said: Who are my helpers toward Allah? The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah; we believed in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims (52). Our Lord, we believed in what You sent down, and we followed the Messenger, so write us among the witnesses (53). And they schemed, and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers (54). When Allah said: O Jesus, I will take you in death and raise you to Me and purify you from those who disbelieve, and make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ (55). As for those who disbelieved, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers (56). And as for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full; and Allah does not love the wrongdoers (57). That which We recite to you of the verses and the wise reminder﴾ [Ali ʿImran 52–58].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. We have already spoken about some of the verses he recited: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said: Who are my helpers toward Allah? The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah; we believed in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾.
﴿Our Lord, we believed in what You sent down, and we followed the Messenger, so write us among the witnesses﴾ The ones who say this are the disciples; they say: ﴿Our Lord, we believed in what You sent down﴾. The grammar of this verse is clear: the saying ﴿Our Lord﴾ is a vocative from which the yā' of address has been deleted for two reasons. The first reason: the frequent use of this noble name in supplication. The second: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, since "al-Rabb" (the Lord) is one of Allah's names. The saying ﴿what You sent down﴾ contains a deleted returning pronoun referring to the relative, and the estimate is: "what You sent it down."

As for his saying: ﴿and we followed the Messenger﴾, is the "al" here for prior mention (dhikrī) or mental reference (dhihnī)?
* The students: Prior mention... mental reference.
* The Shaykh: Did they not say: ﴿and a messenger to the Children of Israel﴾ [Ali ʿImran 49]? Then it is prior mention, because it was previously mentioned.

The commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin on Surah Al 'Imran, verses 52–53 (part 2 of 3):

And His saying: ﴿Write us down among the witnesses﴾. The particle (maʿa, "with") here denotes accompaniment, and accompaniment does not require mixing or being contemporaneous in time. Accompaniment may be with people who preceded you, yet in the end they will be with you. These disciples (al-Hawariyyun), when they declared their submission and called their prophet to witness it, turned to Allah, mighty and majestic, with full affirmation, saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾. Faith (al-iman) in the linguistic sense is affirmation that includes acceptance and submission (idhʿan), and not mere assent. Rather, it includes compliance and submission. For this reason it does not match assent (tasdiq) in its transitive and intransitive usage: one says "amantu bihi" and "sadaqtu bihi," and one says "amantu lahu" and "sadaqtu lahu," but one does not say "amantuhu," as one says "sadaqtuhu." Thus the two differ.

They say: ﴿We have believed﴾, and the meaning of faith here is everything that came in the Qur'an. Thus it refers to faith in its legal reality (al-haqiqa al-shar'iyya), not its linguistic reality. Faith in the legal reality is affirmation of what Allah has made obligatory to believe in, together with acceptance and submission, meaning full compliance. For this reason, if someone says, "I believe in Allah," but does not submit to Him or comply, he has not become a believer in the legal sense.

And their saying: ﴿what You have sent down﴾. Here (ma) is a relative pronoun that encompasses everything sent down. Apparently it includes the Gospel which was sent down to Jesus and what preceded it, namely the Torah which was sent down to Moses. Indeed, it is more general than that, covering everything their prophet informed them of that Allah had sent down.

And their saying: ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾. This is in reality the fruit of faith: following. Whenever a person's faith is stronger, his following is more intense toward the one in whom he believes, and whenever faith diminishes, following diminishes. Is that so? Could we also say: whenever following diminishes, faith diminishes? Or we may say: it is a sign, a sign of deficiency in faith, because faith in truth must lead a person to seek to reach what he believes in, and this requires that he exert every effort in the work that leads him there.

And His saying: ﴿So write us down among the witnesses﴾. Who are "the witnesses"? Some scholars said: the intended witnesses are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, because absolute witnessing belongs only to them, since they are the last of the nations. They are witnesses over all the messengers and over all the nations, whereas the witnesses who came before them were witnesses only over those who preceded them. Absolute, general witnessing belongs to whom? To the community of Muhammad ﷺ, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah 143]. So their saying ﴿write us down among the witnesses﴾ means: write us down with the community of Muhammad ﷺ.

If someone says: this interpretation faces the objection that they preceded the community of Muhammad, so how could they ask to be written with them? The answer: Jesus, peace be upon him, gave them good news of Muhammad ﷺ, saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming what was before me of the Torah and giving good news of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff 6]. So they had knowledge of this community through the good news that Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon him, conveyed to them.

The second view: the intended "witnesses" are those who bore witness to Your messengers with the truth. Does this include whom? It includes those who preceded them, without doubt, and it includes the community of Muhammad if that occurred after he informed them of it and gave them good news of it. This second view is more general than the first and less problematic. The point is that the correct view is: everyone who bore witness to the messengers with the truth.

* From the benefits of this verse, and the verse before it, and the first verse also: that a person calling others to witness his faith, his Islam, or the like, is not considered showing off (riya'), especially in the context of following, because there is a benefit in it, which is strengthening the one who is followed. If he says, "Bear witness that I am a Muslim, or a believer, or one who follows you," there is undoubtedly a benefit in it, namely strengthening the one followed. This is not considered what? 
* The students: showing off.
* The Shaykh: showing off.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: that messengers do not know the unseen, as shown by their saying: ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, for if he had knowledge of that he would not need the witnessing, except as a form of their outward affirmation.

Can it be derived from this noble verse that a person may say, "I am a believer," from their saying: ﴿bear witness that we are Muslims﴾?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Perhaps it may be derived that a person may say, "I am a believer," and there is no doubt that this is permissible. But what has been subject to disagreement among the scholars is whether one may make an exception in faith by saying, "I am a believer, if Allah wills." Is this permissible? On this there is disagreement among the scholars. Some said it is not permissible; some said it is obligatory; some said it is permissible under two considerations.

As for those who said it is not permissible, they said: this exception suggests doubt, that he is doubtful. Otherwise, how could he say "if Allah wills"? So as long as faith has settled in his heart, he should not say "if Allah wills." Then they said, supporting their reasoning: Consider if someone prayed and was asked, "Did you pray?" and he said, "If Allah wills." That would be considered nearly idle speech. If he were asked, "Did you wear your garment?" and he said, "I wore it, if Allah wills," while he was wearing it, that is idle speech, idle talk. So if he is certain of his faith, why would he say "if Allah wills"? Therefore the exception is forbidden on this basis, because it implies doubt, and if it does not, it is idle speech.

The second view: he must say "if Allah wills," it is obligatory, obligatory. If he said, "I am a believer," and remained silent, that would be forbidden for him. They gave two reasons: first, that beneficial faith is that with which a person dies. Whatever a person dies upon, and does the person know or not know?
* The students: He does not know.
* The Shaykh: He does not know, he does not know what he will die upon. "O Allah, keep us firm upon the truth until death." He does not know. How many a person's heart has swerved, may Allah protect us, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed one of you may act with the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is between him and it only a cubit, then the decree overtakes him, and he acts with the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3208), Muslim (2643/1), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.] Since this is so, he must say "if Allah wills," obligatorily. This is one reason.

The second reason: one says, this is not correct, this reason is not valid, it is not a valid basis, because a person speaks only of his present. His present: does he know that he is a believer or not? He knows that he is a believer. The future, its knowledge is with Allah. Yes, if he said, "I will die upon faith," we would say to him: say "if Allah wills." But the correct ground is that if he says, "I am a believer," and affirms it with certainty, there is in that a kind of self-praise (tazkiyat al-nafs), there is a kind of self-purification claimed, and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not claim yourselves as pure; He knows best who fears Him﴾ [al-Najm 32]. For this reason we say to him: the implication of your certainty in faith is that you are certain you are among the people of Paradise, so you have testified for yourself that you are among the people of Paradise. No one is testified to for Paradise by name except one whom the Messenger ﷺ testified for. At that point you must say "if Allah wills," not because you do not know what you will die upon, but in order not to purify yourself. It follows from your purifying yourself that you bear witness for yourself to Paradise, and this is forbidden.

Some scholars distinguished in this matter and said: the exception may be forbidden, may be obligatory, and may be permissible, depending on circumstances. If a person says, "I am a believer, if Allah wills," intending by that blessing (tabarruk) or to show that what has occurred of his faith was by the will of Allah, this is permissible. If he says it not out of doubt nor out of self-purification, but says "if Allah wills" meaning that his faith occurs by the will of Allah, or says it seeking blessing, we say: the exception here is permissible; if you wish, say "if Allah wills," and if you wish, do not say it.

The exception with the will (mashiyya) regarding an event that has occurred is permissible, legally permissible. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills﴾ [al-Fath 27]. He said "if Allah wills," although they would certainly enter it. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, at the Treaty of Hudaybiyya: "Indeed you will come to it and circumambulate it." Do you know the story? When the treaty was concluded between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Quraysh, among its terms was that the Prophet ﷺ would return without completing his 'umrah. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, came to him disputing this matter and said: "Did you not tell us that we would come to the House and circumambulate it?" He said: "Yes. But did I tell you that you would come to it this year?" He said: "No." He said: "Indeed you will come to it and circumambulate it." [al-Bukhari (2731), from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Marwan ibn al-Hakam.] Although Allah said "if Allah wills." And in visiting graves, a person passes by them and says: "And indeed we, if Allah wills, will join you," although our joining them is certain. But this is a matter of clarifying that our joining them is conditioned by what? By the will of Allah.

If the motive for the exception is doubt, it is obligatory to make the exception, or is it forbidden?
* The students: Forbidden.
* The Shaykh: It is forbidden to make the exception if he says "if Allah wills," because he is wavering; this is forbidden, because doubt in faith contradicts faith, since faith must be certainty.

But beware, brothers, lest Satan toy with you in the matter of whisperings (waswas), the whisperings with which many doubters are afflicted regarding what Allah has bestowed upon them of turning to Him. When the youth have now turned toward religion, Satan comes to them with whisperings, with doubts, in order to loosen their faith. But this, praise be to Allah, is a scheme that returns upon the one who devised it, as the hadith says: "Praise be to Allah who has turned his scheming into whispering." [Abu Dawud (5112), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.] The Prophet ﷺ informed that this is the clear sign of faith, that one should be sincere, with no doubt in it. Otherwise Satan comes, among what he whispers, what the Messenger ﷺ informed of: "People will continue asking: Who created this? Who created that? until they say: Who created Allah? When they reach that, let him seek refuge in Allah and let him desist." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3276), Muslim (134/214), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him.] Say: "I seek refuge in Allah," desist, turn away, go about your task, do not pay attention to this.

So the point is that when a person says "if Allah wills," if the motive for saying "if Allah wills" is doubt, what is the ruling?
* A student: Forbidden.
* The Shaykh: The exception is forbidden; it is forbidden to say "if Allah wills," because certainty is obligatory.

Third: if a person fears self-purification when he says "if Allah wills," or fears that he will be left to himself if self-admiration appears in him, because a person, may Allah protect us, when he is impressed by his deed, is left to himself and his blessing is removed. If he fears this, what is the ruling?
* A student: Obligatory.
* The Shaykh: The exception is obligatory. How? Was the exception not forbidden?
* A student: Obligatory, obligatory.
* The Shaykh: Did we not say a moment ago: if the motive for it is doubt, it is forbidden? This is the reverse; the exception is obligatory, obligatory for what reason? So that he does not purify himself or become self-admiring, thinking he is a believer, as the poet says:
"I am the son of Jala and the one who ascends the peaks; when I take off my turban, you will know me."

This view we mentioned, or this distinction we described, is the correct view, and if you reflect on the reasons of the two previous views, you will find that this view or this distinction brings together the positions.

He said: ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and we have followed the Messenger, so write us down among the witnesses﴾.

* From the benefits of this verse: the virtue of the disciples in their turning to Allah, mighty and majestic, as they said: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾, for after they called their prophet to witness, they turned to their Lord, mighty and majestic.
* And from the benefits of the verse: seeking nearness to Allah, exalted is He, through His lordship, for lordship revolves around three things: creation, dominion, and management, and answering supplication falls within these three. For this reason the callers to Allah often invoke His lordship, as in the authentic hadith: "He raises his hands to the sky: O Lord, O Lord." [Muslim (1015/65), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him.]
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that faith must encompass everything Allah has sent down: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾.
* And also from its benefits: the careful precision in the disciples' saying ﴿what You have sent down﴾, and they did not simply state faith in, for example, the Torah, because the Torah in the hands of the Jews is altered and changed, they show some things and conceal others. For this reason they said ﴿what You have sent down﴾, and we say: we believe in what Allah has sent down of the Torah and the Gospel, not in the altered Torah in the hands of the Jews, nor in the altered Gospel in the hands of the Christians.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that faith must have following ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾; for this reason Allah, mighty and majestic, joins faith with righteous deeds in many verses, because bare faith does not benefit. Righteous deeds are like watering a tree: if you do not water it, it dies. Therefore when we speak of Islam, we should not try to make Islam mere creed; rather it is creed and action. Creed alone is not sufficient, because now everyone claims to hold a creed: the Jews and Christians say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day." Now they say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day, we believe there is a Lord who manages creation, that He, mighty and majestic, is the Creator, and we believe in resurrection." But this is not faith, even if they hold this creed; this is a corrupt creed. So creed must be joined with righteous deeds, lest people rely on the creed they have and say, "What need is there for action?" For this reason He said: ﴿We have believed﴾ and then? ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾. This is necessary.

Consider His saying: ﴿We have believed﴾ ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾. Can it be derived from it that belief in every book Allah has sent down is obligatory, while following is specific to the particular Messenger?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is this possible?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because they said, ﴿We have believed in what You have sent down﴾ is general, and ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾ is specific, and that is so. Faith is obligatory in all that Allah has sent down: ﴿Say: I believe in what Allah has sent down of Book, and I have been commanded to be just among you﴾ [al-Shura 15]. But following is specific to the Messenger sent to you. As for a messenger who was not sent to you, you are not commanded to follow him unless your sharia indicates following him.

* From the benefits of the verse: if there are two attributes, and one of them is more specific than the other in action or in the situation you are in, then it is preferable to take the more specific one, as in His saying ﴿the Messenger﴾; for the Messenger is sent to us. They did not say "and we followed the Prophet," but ﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾, because the Messenger is sent to us and dispatched. But a prophet is not commanded to convey, according to the view of the majority of scholars. Here, regarding following, which of the two is more closely tied to the mission: the messengership or the prophethood? The messengership. For this reason they chose the attribute of Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 52–53 (part 3 of 3):

If someone says: In the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib concerning the mention of sleep, when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited, when he mentioned the sleep that a person experiences at the end [of the day], he said, among what he said: "I believe in Your Book which You have sent down, and in Your Prophet whom You have sent." When al-Bara' repeated it, he said: "and in Your Messenger whom You have sent," and he (ﷺ) said: "Say: and in Your Prophet whom You have sent" [[A hadith agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (247) and Muslim (2710 / 56), from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. It is known that the context is one of following [the wording], so why, when he said "Your Messenger whom You have sent," did he [the Prophet] correct it to "Your Prophet," when messengership includes prophethood?

The answer to this is in two respects. The first respect: the indication of "messenger" for "prophet" is by implicational signification (dalalat al-iltizam), while the indication of "prophet" for "prophet" is by literal signification (dalalat al-mutabaqah, correspondence). The literal signification is undoubtedly stronger, because in implicational signification the opponent may contest it; he may say: "This is not a necessary implication." Therefore he chose the attribute of prophethood, even though "whom You have sent" came after messengership.

The answer to this is in two respects. The first respect: the indication of "messenger" for "prophet" is by implicational signification, and the indication of "prophet" for "prophet" is by...?
* The students: Correspondence (mutabaqah).
* The Shaykh: Correspondence (mutabaqah). The literal signification is undoubtedly stronger, because in implicational signification the opponent may contest it; he may say: "This is not necessary." Therefore he chose the attribute of prophethood, even though "whom You have sent" came after messengership. If he had said "Your Messenger whom You have sent," by what way does it indicate prophethood?
* The students: By implicational signification.
* The Shaykh: By implicational signification, because every messenger is a prophet. But if he says "Your Prophet whom You have sent," it indicates prophethood by literal signification, because he stated it explicitly with its own word. It is known that signification by correspondence is stronger than signification by implication, because the implication may be denied. The second respect: if he says "Your Messenger whom You have sent," it is not a specifying attribute for Muhammad (ﷺ), since it may refer to Jibril, for example. Jibril is a sent messenger, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, [possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne, [and] obeyed there [in the heavens] and trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir 19–21]. So Jibril is one who was sent. If he said "Your Messenger whom You have sent," he would not have specified that this faith is in Muhammad (peace be upon him). But if he says "Your Prophet whom You have sent," by whom is the attribute specified? By the Messenger, Muhammad (ﷺ), because Jibril is not called a prophet but is called a messenger. By this, the difficulty we pointed to is removed, namely that the attribute corresponding to the speaker's state should be mentioned. Because in the hadith of al-Bara', prophethood was chosen over messengership for these two reasons.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: eagerness for the company of the righteous. From where do we take this?
* The students: ﴿So record us among the witnesses﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿So record us among the witnesses.﴾ There is no doubt that the company of the righteous is good, to the extent that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave it the example of the bearer of musk. He said: "The likeness of the good companion is like the bearer of musk: either he will give you some, or you will buy from him, or you will find from him a pleasant fragrance." All of this is good. "The bad companion is like the one who blows the bellows." Do you know the one who blows the bellows?
* A student: Yes, we know him.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, it seems that none of you know him? Therefore it would be good for you to go to the craftsmen's market in Riyadh so that you can see the bellows, because I think there is nothing here. In any case, the bellows is like a skin, like the ghurb. The ghurb is the bucket for a camel used to raise water. This existed a year or two ago, they put "sawani" [water-wheel buckets]... yes, this is the ghurb. The point is that it is like the ghurb: it has an open end, and an end connected to a pipe that leads to the place of light, the place of the fire. He opens it like this, then closes it, then pushes it. When he pushes it, he has carried air through this pipe. We said this pipe comes to the place of the fire; the fire blazes, blazes intensely. Usually there are two, one here on the man's right and one on the left, and it is always like this, always, and the light is always blazing. The one who blows the bellows: the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Either he will burn your clothes, or you will find from him a foul smell" [[Agreed upon; recorded by al-Bukhari (2101) and Muslim (2628 / 146), from Abu Musa; the wording is al-Bukhari's.]]. When will he burn your clothes? When sparks fly from it onto you, or you find a foul smell. Therefore a person should choose the best of companions, because the good companion is all good, and the bad companion is all evil. So choose good companions for yourself. If you are deceived by someone and then sit with them time after time, and it becomes clear that they neither help you in obedience nor prevent you from disobedience, then seek someone better than them. A person sometimes associates with friends, and is deceived by them, for example, and then they benefit him not but harm him. Therefore a person's gatherings should be filled with beneficial research and with questions that open the mind, not with a person's main preoccupation in gatherings being "So-and-so said, and so-and-so said, where did so-and-so go, where did so-and-so come, so-and-so erred in this, so-and-so was right in that, so-and-so has knowledge, so-and-so has no knowledge, so-and-so is tall and so-and-so is short, so-and-so is rich and so-and-so is poor." This is not correct. This is a waste of time, and perhaps it involves backbiting, which becomes harm. "No people sit in a gathering in which they do not mention Allah except that it will be a regret for them on the Day of Resurrection" [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra (10170), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]], because they have missed the good.
* A student: We have mentioned: ﴿and record us among the witnesses﴾: everyone who bears witness to the messengers with the truth [is included]. Does this include some disbelievers who bore witness to some prophets with the truth, such as Abu Talib, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: If his testimony had been true, he would have followed him.
* The student: Yes, but he testified to him with the truth?
* The Shaykh: His testimony was not beneficial.
* A student: May Allah be good to you, Shaykh. You distinguished between the messenger and the prophet: that the messenger is one to whom revelation is sent and who is commanded to convey it, and the prophet is one to whom revelation is sent but who is not commanded to convey it. [There is] his saying (ﷺ) in Sahih Muslim: "There is no prophet except that it is a duty upon him to explain to his community the best of what he explains to them, and to warn them against evil" [[Recorded by Muslim (1844 / 46), from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]]. So this shows that the prophet likewise explains to his community what the messenger explains to them. Does this not show that there is no difference between the prophet and the messenger?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not show that, because if we say that this [explanation] was by the command of Allah, then it is?
* Students: A messenger.
* The Shaykh: Then it is a messenger. And if we say he explained voluntarily, without being obliged to do so, but out of love for good, then it is a prophet. Although the one meant in this hadith you mentioned is the prophet who is the messenger. This is why Allah often mentions the prophets without the messengers and the messengers without the prophets: ﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra' 55], and in another verse: ﴿Those messengers – We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah 253].
* A student: The signification of "prophet" for prophethood, is it by correspondence or by inclusion?
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: The signification of "prophet" for prophethood, is it by correspondence or by inclusion?
* The Shaykh: Correspondence.
* The student: Which one exactly?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this "exactly" is subsidiary.
* A student: May Allah be good to you. We said, in explaining Allah's words ﴿al-Hawariyyun﴾, that it comes from "hawr," which is intense whiteness, and the disciples' hearts are white and pure, not defiled by sins. Shaykh, the verse that is coming: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that will come to us. These who schemed are other than the disciples.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 54–55 (part 1 of 5):

Student: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers (54). When Allah said: "O 'Isa, indeed I will take you in death and raise you to Me and purify you from those who disbelieve, and I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that wherein you used to differ (55). As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers (56). As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full. And Allah does not love wrongdoers (57). That which We recite to you of the verses and the wise Reminder (58).﴾ [Al 'Imran 54–58].

The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers﴾. ﴿They schemed﴾: the pronoun refers to those who disbelieved in 'Isa. Makr (scheming) is to reach the avenging of one's opponent by means that are unexpected, that is, by hidden means: one takes revenge on one's opponent and adversary by hidden means. It resembles deception (khida'), for a person reaches the avenging of his opponent from a direction he does not perceive, by hidden means. His saying: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ means that Allah the Glorified and Exalted schemed against them when they schemed against 'Isa. ﴿And Allah is the best of schemers﴾ means: the most powerful of them in scheming, the most intense, and the most knowing of the means that surround His enemies.

If someone asks: what shows us that the pronoun in His saying ﴿they schemed﴾ refers to those who disbelieved in 'Isa? The answer to this is easy, because His saying ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ cannot proceed from a people who said: ﴿We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran 52], and who said: ﴿Our Lord, we believe in what You have sent down and we follow the Messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran 53]. This is impossible. Rather, it proceeds only from a people who disbelieved, and that is His saying: ﴿But when 'Isa perceived disbelief from them﴾ [Al 'Imran 52].

If it is said: what is this scheming that they schemed? The answer is that they schemed against 'Isa when they conspired to kill him, and Allah saved him from them, and He schemed against them by making his likeness fall upon a man, either from among them, from those who came to kill him, or from among the companions of 'Isa. Allah cast his likeness upon one of them and he was killed. The point is that these people conspired to kill and came to 'Isa, peace be upon him, and entered upon him without letting him know that they intended to kill him, so that he would not seek help from anyone or defend himself, and similar things. But Allah the Mighty and Majestic cast his likeness upon one of them, or upon one of his disciples, the Hawariyyun. There are two opinions of the exegetes on this. Some said: Allah cast his likeness upon one of them, who was their leader. Allah made the likeness of 'Isa fall upon this man, so when they wanted to kill him he said: "I am your companion." They said: "You are lying; you are not our companion, rather you are 'Isa." So they killed him and crucified him. Is this scheming or not? It is a great scheme, greater than their scheme, because this man who came claiming to lead these people to kill 'Isa became the one killed. This opinion is stronger in that it contains a great scheme against these people. As for the second opinion, they say: when 'Isa, peace be upon him, perceived that they had entered upon him to kill him, he said to one of his companions: "Who will agree to have my likeness cast upon him, and I guarantee him Paradise?" One of them volunteered for this, and Allah cast his likeness upon him. It was also said: rather, Allah cast his likeness upon all who were with 'Isa, so that when these people entered, each one would say: "Which of you is 'Isa? Which of you is 'Isa? Which of you is 'Isa?" They did not recognize him. These are two principal opinions. The first opinion: upon whom was the likeness cast?

Students: The leader.

The Shaykh: Yes, upon the leader of the people who came to kill him, and he was killed. The second opinion is that it was cast upon a man of 'Isa's companions. Then, was the likeness cast upon all of them so that it became confused for those who entered? Or was it cast upon one of them? On this too there are two opinions. The matter has no explicit text from the infallible Prophet, peace be upon him, and Allah knows best. But His saying the Exalted: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾ [An-Nisa' 157] may support the last opinion, that every one of those with 'Isa came to resemble 'Isa, so it became confused for them who 'Isa was. The point is that this is their scheme: they came to 'Isa, peace be upon him, to kill him in a manner that he would not perceive. As for Allah's scheme against them, it is that He cast the likeness either upon one of them or upon one of 'Isa's followers, so they killed him, and they thought they had killed 'Isa, and they began to announce: "We killed 'Isa, the son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah," and "they crucified him," while they did not kill him and did not crucify him.

In the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ there is, among the attributes of Allah, the affirmation of scheming to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. The discussion of this: first, is scheming in its true sense? Or is it an expression for requiting a scheme, so that the requital of a scheme is called a scheme by way of verbal correspondence and not semantic correspondence? It is like His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ [Al-Baqarah 194]. The one who takes retribution for himself is not called a transgressor, but it resembles it in wording, by verbal correspondence and not semantic correspondence. Or is it a true scheme, because Allah's treatment of them is a scheme, since the one killed was one of them according to one opinion, or the matter was confused for them according to the second opinion? The correct view in this is that Allah the Exalted is described by what He described Himself with, and we do not know Allah better than He knows Himself. He is more knowing of Himself, more truthful in speech, and better in discourse. But He must be exempted from every deficiency. Is scheming among the attributes of deficiency absolutely, meaning that there is no praise in it at all? Or is it a deficiency in some circumstances and not in others? The second is the truth: scheming in its proper place is praiseworthy and an attribute of perfection, while scheming out of its proper place is an attribute of deficiency, because scheming out of its proper place is treachery, and treachery is a blameworthy attribute. For this reason Allah did not describe Himself with it, nor in the correspondence that follows: ﴿And if they intend treachery against you, then they have already betrayed Allah before﴾ [Al-Anfal 71]?

Students: ﴿So He gave you power over them﴾.

The Shaykh: ﴿So He gave you power over them﴾ [Al-Anfal 71], and He did not say: "so He betrayed them," because treachery is a blameworthy attribute absolutely. In contrast, ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾, where Allah answered their scheme with a scheme and did not answer their treachery with treachery. So it follows that we must describe Allah with what He described Himself with of scheming in the circumstance in which Allah described Himself with scheming, and that is in response to the scheming of His enemies. So we say: Allah schemes against whom?

Students: They scheme against Him.

The Shaykh: They scheme against Him, against His messengers, and against His signs. But as for describing Allah with scheming absolutely, so that we say: "Allah is a schemer" without qualification, this is not permissible. Why? Because of the possibility of deficiency, since scheming, as we said, is not perfection in every circumstance nor deficiency in every circumstance. When it is stated absolutely, it becomes capable of being a deficiency. When it is restricted to the circumstance in which it is perfection, it does not admit of being a deficiency. So we say: scheming is attributed to Allah not absolutely, but in the circumstance in which Allah described Himself with it. For this reason it came in the hadith: "War is deception"[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3029) and Muslim (1740/18) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. Everyone knows that deception in war is perfection or deficiency?

Students: Perfection.

The Shaykh: Perfection. And it is reported of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that when 'Amr ibn Wudd came out to him to duel, and you know what a duel is? When the two lines meet, the combatants ask for a duel: who will come out against so-and-so? A duel is a cause of conquest or defeat, because when two men duel and one of them prevails, whose spirits are strengthened?

Students: His companions'.

The Shaykh: His companions', and the spirits of the others are weakened. When he came out to duel 'Amr ibn Wudd, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, came out to him and cried out to him, saying: "I did not come out to duel two men." So 'Amr ibn Wudd thought that someone from his people had followed him, so he turned to look whether anyone had reached him. When he turned, 'Ali struck him with the sword until his head rang. Is this a deception or not?

Students: A deception.

The Shaykh: Praiseworthy or not praiseworthy?

Students: Praiseworthy.

The Shaykh: Praiseworthy, because he came to kill him. He came to kill 'Ali, so he rid himself of him by this deception. This is counted as a virtue of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and an attribute of perfection. Then we say: scheming in its proper place is praise and perfection. Now, He says: ﴿And Allah is the best of schemers﴾. This is a fixed, absolute attribute; it does not need a qualifier, because it is described with perfection. What is the perfection? ﴿the best﴾. ﴿And Allah is the best of schemers﴾: meaning that no one schemes except that Allah's scheming is above it and better than it. Is scheming among the essential attributes or the active attributes?

Students: The active.

The Shaykh: The active, because it relates to His will, and every attribute that has a cause is related to His will, since every attribute of Allah that has a cause is related to His will, because the one who determines the cause is Allah; when He determines the cause, He has willed it, and what follows from it of attributes follows.

﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers (54). When Allah said: "O 'Isa, indeed I will take you in death﴾. It is possible that (idh) is connected to ﴿Allah schemed﴾, meaning: and Allah schemed when Allah said: "O 'Isa, indeed I will take you in death, and raise you to Me, and purify you from those who disbelieve." It is also possible that it is connected to an omitted element whose estimate is: "Mention, O Muhammad, extolling the virtue of 'Isa, when Allah said: 'O 'Isa, indeed I will take you in death and raise you to Me and purify you from those who disbelieve.'" ﴿When Allah said: "O 'Isa, indeed I will take you in death"﴾. Did He say it with an audible speech or an inaudible one?

Students: Audible.

The Shaykh: With audible speech, which 'Isa heard. He spoke with audible speech because He was addressing him: ﴿O 'Isa, indeed I will take you in death﴾. He says: ﴿indeed I will take you in death﴾. So what is the meaning of this death? In it the scholars have three opinions. The first opinion: "I will receive you," meaning: "I will take you," derived from the expression "tawaffa al-da'in dayna-hu," meaning he received his debt. 'Isa was taken by Allah to Himself in heaven, and raised until he descends at the end of time. The second opinion: ﴿mutawaffika﴾ is death of sleep, meaning "I will make you sleep," because the sleeper is one who is taken in death. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. And He said: ﴿And it is He who takes you in death by night, and knows what you have committed by day; then He resurrects you therein﴾ [Al-An'am 60]. The third opinion: it is an actual death; Allah caused him to die a real death, and will bring him back to life at the end of time and he will descend to the world. The correct view is that it is death of sleep, and that when Allah the Mighty and Majestic wished to raise him to heaven, He made him sleep to make the passage from earth to heaven easy for him, because passing from earth to heaven is not an easy matter, due to the length and distance of the journey, and the terrors seen between heaven and earth and within the heavens as well. So Allah made him sleep and then raised him while asleep until he reached heaven. However, this opinion does not contradict the first opinion, which means "I will receive you," because their end is one. As for the third opinion, that it is death in the sense of dying, it is a weak view, weakened by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾ [An-Nisa' 159], "before his death," meaning 'Isa's death, and this indicates that he has not died. Also, Allah the Exalted has not raised anyone after death so that he remains as in the descent of 'Isa, peace be upon him, at the end of time. And also, the application of "death" (tawaffi) to sleep is frequent in the Qur'an; it is not a strange meaning such that we would say it cannot be applied to it. Rather, it is a meaning with much frequency in the Qur'an.

He says: ﴿I will take you in death and raise you to Me﴾. ﴿raising you to Me﴾: ﴿raising you﴾ is in construct with the pronoun "ka" just as ﴿taking you in death﴾ is in construct with the pronoun "ka." So how do you parse the "ka" in both? Is it in a genitive position or an accusative position?

Some students: An accusative position.

Other students: A genitive position.

The Shaykh: Is it not the direct object?

Student: Yes.

The Shaykh: "Mutawaffa" and "marfu'"? So is it in an accusative position or a genitive position?

Students: In a genitive position.

The Shaykh: It is in a genitive position, because the action of the noun on it is stronger than the action of the meaning. That is, the action of the noun, which is the word, is stronger than the action of the meaning. It is well known that the noun is always construed with its agent and construed with its object. Then He said: ﴿and raise you to Me﴾. ﴿to Me﴾: to what place? To heaven, because raising is from a lower place, so the meaning of ﴿raising you to Me﴾ is: in heaven. So Allah the Glorified and Exalted raised him to heaven, to Allah. ﴿And purify you from those who disbelieve﴾: purify you from them. The purification here is spiritual, not physical, because those who disbelieved did not smear 'Isa with physical filth, but they smeared him with spiritual filth. They said he was a liar, that he was the son of adultery, God forbid, and that his mother was an adulteress, and they accused him of many things. So Allah purified him from them, by what He sent down of his innocence in his time and after his time. His saying: ﴿purifying you from those who disbelieve﴾: disbelieved in whom? They disbelieved in 'Isa, because the Hawariyyun believed in him as has already been mentioned. ﴿And I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection﴾. This too is among what Allah said to him: ﴿and making those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve﴾. ﴿Making﴾ here is construed with the agent or the object?

Student: The agent.

Students: The object.

The Shaykh: The object?

Students: Yes indeed.

The Shaykh: The object. ﴿Above﴾ is in an accusative position; it is an adverbial complement connected to an omitted element, functioning as the second object, because ﴿jA'il﴾ is an active participle from (ja'ala), and (ja'ala) takes two objects. Thus ﴿above﴾ is an adverbial complement connected to an omitted element as the second object: ﴿above those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection﴾. ﴿Those who follow you﴾: those who follow your law. ﴿Above those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection﴾: above the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection. This verse, the Christians boast with it and say: "We have the ascendancy until the Day of Resurrection, not until Muhammad was sent, but until the Day of Resurrection." We say: Yes, Allah the Mighty has spoken the truth. Indeed those who follow 'Isa have victory over the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection. But who is it that follows 'Isa? Are they those who rejected his good news and denied the one who gave good news of him?

Student: No.

The Shaykh: Not at all. You have not followed 'Isa. By Allah, if 'Isa were to come out he would fight you until you return to Islam. For this reason, at the end of time, nothing will be accepted but Islam. He will not accept the jizya, he will break the cross and kill the pig. At the end of time he will not accept even the jizya that used to be accepted before his descent, due to his intense aversion to what the Christians and Jews are upon. Now we permit the Jews and Christians the jizya; we say: remain upon your religion, but give the jizya willingly while you are humbled. But when 'Isa descends he will not accept this; he will say: "Submit or death," because of his aversion to what they are upon; he does not want to permit them even this. The point is that we say: those who followed 'Isa are those who believed in Muhammad, peace be upon him, after the mission of Muhammad. As for before the mission of Muhammad, yes, there is no doubt that the followers of 'Isa were Muslims and were upon the truth before they distorted and altered.

If they say: how do you answer His saying: ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾? We say: Yes, believe in Muhammad and you will have victory until the Day of Resurrection. If someone says: could it not be that by "those who followed him" is meant those who ascribed themselves to him, and they will have ascendancy over the disbelievers, not over the Muslims? For example, the Christians prevail over the Jews, and the Christians prevail over the idolaters, and similar things. And excluded from this is whom?

Students: The Muslims.

The Shaykh: The Muslims? And would God Most High have promised Jesus that those who ascribe themselves to him would be above those who disbelieve in him? So what is the answer? The answer is: this is not possible. No, it is not possible; what is possible is remote and unattainable, because these people did not follow Jesus. Have you not heard that God says on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿And when God says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two deities besides God'?" He will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen. I did not say to them except what You commanded me: 'Worship God, my Lord and your Lord.'"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 116–117]. Do the Christians say this? Never. So they did not follow him. Even if it may appear to some people to say that the Christians prevail over other disbelievers by this verse, we say: No. Because God says: ﴿those who follow you﴾, and the Christians now have not followed him. Furthermore, if the verse were interpreted in this way, reality would contradict it. The Crusader nation has not prevailed over the Communist nation; rather, it fears it. Where is the superiority? There is no superiority. Now all the states of Western Europe, with their navies and their Atlantic alliance, have been unable to be above Communism and its alliance, the Warsaw Pact. They have been unable; each one of them now fears the other. It may have happened one day that Europe feared Communism more than it fears it today. The conclusion is that the verse cannot be applied to the Christians existing today under any circumstances.

Then He said: ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾. "Then" here means afterwards: on the Day of Resurrection, to Me is your return. The Day of Resurrection is the day on which people stand before the Lord of the worlds to be recompensed for their deeds. The Day of Resurrection is named for three reasons. The first reason: people stand therein before God, the Lord of the worlds, as God Most High said: ﴿The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 6].
