As for the other, it is as though Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in showing affection toward these people and declaring their merit, said: ﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾, and did not attribute the giving to Himself, so as to grant them some measure of thanks for their deeds. The difference between addressing a person by expressing your action toward him with the first-person pronoun and expressing it with the third-person pronoun is that direct address is more intense than speaking about someone in his absence. Consider His words: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know?﴾ [ʿAbasa 1–3]. He said ﴿He frowned﴾ and did not say "you frowned," and He said ﴿And what would make you know?﴾ and did not say "and what would make him know" or "and what would make Him know." So this, and Allah knows best, is the wisdom behind expressing punishment with the verb attributed to the first-person pronoun, unlike the expression for reward. This is confirmed by His words in sūrat al-Raḥmān: ﴿Is the reward for good anything but good?﴾ [al-Raḥmān 60]. He made their action a good deed for which they are thanked and to which good is returned, even though all goodness is from Allah, since enabling a servant to do righteous deeds is one of Allah's kindnesses to him. But this is from the perfection of Allah's mercy, His reward and His recompense. And He, the Exalted, said in sūrat al-Insān: ﴿Indeed, this was for you a reward, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insān 22]. Now, their effort being appreciated: who enabled them to strive? Allah. Yet He says ﴿and your effort has been appreciated﴾. So the change of style in the two verses yields two benefits: a verbal one and a semantic one. The verbal one is the shift (*iltifāt*), which causes attention to be drawn. The semantic one is the display of authority, majesty, and might in the matter of punishment, and the display of favor and kindness toward those who act righteously in the matter of reward.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿That is what We recite to you of the signs and the wise reminder﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 58]. From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke the Qurʾān, saying ﴿That is what We recite to you﴾. Recitation is truly Allah's, and it was conveyed by Jibrīl to the Messenger ﷺ. It is possible that the recitation is by Jibrīl, but since Jibrīl is Allah's messenger, his action is attributed to Allah. This is like His words: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyāmah 16–18]. It is well known that the one who recites it is Jibrīl.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the Noble Qurʾān is a sign, indeed signs. As Allah said: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 49]. They are great signs, and its signs are many. Each verse contains several signs. But these signs are understood only by one whose heart Allah has opened to faith, knowledge, and the conviction that this Qurʾān is the speech of Allah and that in it are clear signs. As for one over whom such verses pass without his heart being moved by them, and who does not reflect upon these signs, he will not benefit from the signs in the Qurʾān. You must believe that in it are signs, and strive to extract these signs through reflection. When a person reflects upon the Qurʾān, he finds in it great signs that people cannot count.

* Another benefit of this verse: the Qurʾān is a reminder. But is it a reminder by which one draws near to Allah, or a reminder by which a person is reminded? We have mentioned that the meaning includes both. It is a reminder by which one draws near to Allah, because whoever recites it has ten good deeds for every letter. And it is a reminder by which a person is reminded. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is present﴾ [Qāf 37]. It was said: it is also a reminder by which Allah raised the status of those who held fast to it, as He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44], and as in His words: ﴿And We raised for you your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharḥ 4], meaning: We elevated your standing. Accordingly, the word *dhikr* (reminder) has how many meanings? Three: a reminder by which one draws near to Allah through its recitation; a reminder by which a person is reminded; and a reminder that means honor for whoever holds fast to it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the Noble Qurʾān is described with this great attribute, which is wisdom: ﴿and the wise reminder﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 58]. *Al-Ḥakīm* here means both "the one who judges" and "the one who makes firm," because the Qurʾān judges between people, as in His words: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 59], that is, to His Book. So it is a judge and also made firm, perfected, free of contradiction, disorder, or inconsistency.

* Another benefit of the verse: there is no ruling indicated by the Qurʾān except that it is in its fitting place. From where is this derived? From *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise), because the wise is one who places a thing in its proper places. So every ruling that the Qurʾān decrees is in its proper place. Reason does not say, "Would that it had not ruled thus." Never. Whether the ruling is affirmative or negative.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the excellence of the Messenger ﷺ in the words ﴿We recite it to you﴾. He was singled out for the recitation to him, because he ﷺ is the noblest of those who receive the Qurʾān and the most upright of people in acting upon it. So it is as though he is the one specifically addressed by the recitation: ﴿We recite it to you﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like the example of Adam﴾. It has already passed with us that these verses were revealed when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were Christians. Their coming was in the ninth year after the Hijrah, because that year many delegations came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and for this reason it is called the Year of Delegations. This is one of the reasons that prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) from performing Hajj in the ninth year, even though Makkah had already been conquered. ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like the example of Adam﴾ means: his matter. The matter of Jesus with Allah is like the matter of Adam, not different from it. Just as we all agree that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created Adam without a father or a mother, even the Christians believe this, what is the matter with the Christians who say: "How did Allah create Jesus without a father?" He is only His son, we seek refuge in Allah. So they said: he is the Son of Allah, a part of Him. They did not say that Adam is the son of Allah, even though if anyone were to claim sonship for any human being, Adam would be the most entitled to it. Sonship belongs to Allah; Adam would have been the most entitled, because he has neither mother nor father, whereas Jesus has a mother, and the mother is one of the two parents. So if we say: it is impossible for someone to exist from a mother without a father, then let us say: nor can anyone exist without a mother and a father. You, O Christians, have acknowledged that Adam is not a son of Allah, so it follows that you must acknowledge that Jesus is not a son of Allah, because the example of Jesus is like the example of Adam. ﴿He created him from dust﴾: "created him" means: He began his creation from dust, and the pronoun of the object in (khalaqahu) refers to Adam, because he is the one created from dust. ﴿He created him﴾, i.e., He created Adam from dust. ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. We have said: He began his creation, then He said: "Be." This command is for the completion of the creation. We said this so that no one would say: how can the word "Be" come after the creation, since the rational order requires that "Be" come before the creation, "Be" and then "he was." So we say: the meaning of ﴿He created him﴾ is: He began his creation from dust, then He said to him: "Be a human," and he was a human. ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. Is this saying "Be" a decreed (qadari) or a legislative (shar'i) saying? It is a decreed saying, and what is decreed is never delayed from it, because it is an absolute command. This differs from the legislative saying, for among people there are those who are arrogant toward it. Allah says: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ [al-An'am 72], and one says: "No, I will not establish the prayer." But the cosmic (kawni) saying has no repelling. ﴿"Be," and he was﴾, and He did not say "so he became," in reporting the state; that is, when He said "Be," he immediately began to come into being until it was complete.

In this verse: the establishment of proof with the same argument the opponent uses. He established the proof against the Christians with the same thing they argued with. He said: if you say that Jesus is the son of Allah because he was created without a father, then say that Adam is the son of Allah; otherwise you are contradicting yourselves.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in that He created Adam without a mother or father, and created Jesus from a mother without a father. There are also two other categories: Allah created one from a father without a mother, and created others from both a father and a mother. Who was created from a father without a mother? Eve (Hawwa'), and all the rest of mankind from both a mother and a father.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of analogy (qiyas). From where is it derived? ﴿like the example of Adam﴾. Every example presented in the Qur'an is evidence for the validity of analogy, because it attaches the thing compared to the thing it is compared with. That is, you attached the one being compared to what? To the one it is compared with.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of speech for the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿Then He said to him﴾.
Also among its benefits: that the speech of Allah is with an audible voice and with letters in sequence, by His saying: ﴿He said to him, "Be"﴾. This saying is heard, and it has letters in order, does it not? The kaf comes before the nun.

Also among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of the attribute of creation for Allah, ﴿He created him﴾. Is creation a essential (dhati) or an active (fi'li) attribute?
* The students: Active.
* The Shaykh: Active, one of the active attributes. But it has already passed with us that the category of active attributes is, what? Essential; because Allah has always been and will always be Doer (fa''al).

Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on sūrah 3, verses 56–59 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers﴾ [56]. ﴿But as for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full. And Allah does not love wrongdoers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 56–57].

From the benefits of these two verses: first, the affirmation of punishment for the disbelievers, as in His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾.

* Another benefit: the punishment in this world may not suffice in place of the punishment in the Hereafter for the disbelievers. Or we say: the punishment in this world does not substitute for the punishment in the Hereafter for the disbelievers, as in His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾. For this reason, the disbelievers are punished in this world: they are defeated, taken captive, their women and children are enslaved, and their wealth is seized as spoils. This is a great punishment, and yet they are not spared from the punishment of the Fire.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān. ﴿Indeed, the likeness of ʿĪsā before Allah is like the likeness of Ādam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [59]. ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾ [60]. ﴿Whoever argues with you about it after knowledge has come to you, say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us invoke earnestly and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars"﴾ [61]. ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative, and there is no deity except Allah; and indeed, Allah is the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [62]. ﴿And if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 59–63].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of ʿĪsā before Allah is like the likeness of Ādam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers﴾.

Several benefits are derived from this noble verse. Among them: the affirmation of recompense, as in His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them﴾.

Another: recompense is of the same kind as the deed. The worse the deed, the more severe the recompense. For this reason He said: ﴿I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾.

Another: the punishment of the disbelievers occurs both in this world and in the Hereafter. As for the punishment of this world, it comes through capture, killing, earthquakes, floods, and the like, as Allah said: ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands﴾ [al-Tawba 14]. And what is this by? By killing and capture. As for punishment through earthquakes and the like, it is like His words: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky will bring a clear smoke, covering the people. This is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhān 10–11]. This is a punishment from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while the first is a punishment at the hands of the believers.

From the benefits of this noble verse: the disbelievers have no helper against the punishment of Allah. No one can prevent them, as in His words: ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾. As for the Hereafter, this is clear, because intercession will not benefit them, as He said: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 28]. As for this world, it is likewise: when these disbelievers are punished at the hands of the believers, their fighting men are killed, their women and children are taken captive, and their wealth and lands are seized as spoils. They have no helper in this.

If someone says: Does the imam not have a choice regarding captives among four matters: killing, ransom for wealth or for a Muslim captive, enslavement, or release? The first three present no difficulty. The difficulty lies in the last, which is release, and this is not a punishment. The answer to this is: the imam may not choose any of these four except where he sees a benefit for the Muslims in it. So the choice here is a choice of benefit, not a choice of whim and preference. When there is benefit for the Muslims, it must also be a punishment for the disbelievers, because everything that benefits the Muslims contains a punishment for the disbelievers. Accordingly, they have no helper, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

Then Allah said: ﴿But as for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full﴾. From this verse is derived the eloquence of the Qurʾān and its wisdom: its eloquence lies in presenting meanings in opposition, because presenting opposing meanings stirs a person's energy, as the mind moves from one meaning to its opposite, and so grows more active and eager. As for its perfection of eloquence, when meanings are varied through opposition, the wording becomes more beautiful. This is known among the scholars of rhetoric as the science of what? The science of *badīʿ* (rhetorical embellishment). It also contains the training of the soul, because when the soul hears the punishment of the disbelievers, it fears and is dismayed, and perhaps despair overtakes it. When the reward of the believers comes, it hopes and longs, so its journey toward Allah becomes between fear and hope.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the full giving of reward is tied to two attributes: faith and righteous deeds. Faith alone is not enough; there must be a righteous deed that nourishes this faith and attests to its soundness. Mere creed is not sufficient. Moreover, when creed is sound, it necessitates righteous deeds, as the Messenger ﷺ said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhārī (52) and Muslim (107/1599) from the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr.]]

* Another benefit of the noble verse: a deed benefits only if it is righteous, and a righteous deed is one that combines two attributes: sincerity to Allah and conformity to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. That is, it is what is sincere and correct, as al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ, may Allah have mercy on him, said.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: Allah's favor upon His servants, in that He made this recompense like wages whose payment is obligatory, as in His words: ﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾. Note, and consider the difference between the two expressions: there He said ﴿I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾, and here He said ﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation of love for Allah, as in His words: ﴿And Allah does not love wrongdoers﴾. If someone says: How do you prove the affirmation of love by the negation of love, since He said: ﴿does not love wrongdoers﴾? The answer: the negation of love from wrongdoers indicates its affirmation for others. Had it been negated from all, there would be no benefit in specifying it for wrongdoers. For this reason, al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, used as evidence for the believers' seeing Allah the words of Allah concerning the wicked: ﴿No! Indeed, on that day they will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn 15]. He said in explaining the inference: He veiled His enemies from seeing Him in anger only because the believers' seeing Him in pleasure is established. This is clear.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the evil of wrongdoing, its evil upon a person, and that it is a cause for the absence of Allah's love for him. When Allah's love for a servant is absent, he has been ruined.

* Another benefit: wrongdoing is one of the major sins, because a threat is attached to it, namely the absence of Allah's love, Glorified and Exalted. However, it appears that this is not absolute. Rather, wrongdoing may be a major sin and may be a minor sin, because all sins are wrongdoing, and some sins are major while others are minor.

* Another benefit of the verse together with the preceding one: variety in style, namely the shift from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun: ﴿I will punish them﴾ and here He said ﴿He will give them﴾. Is there a difference in meaning? The answer: yes, there is a difference in meaning. As for the wording, the shift from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun is evident. But we want the difference in meaning. The difference in meaning is that punishment, being a penalty, requires authority, domination, and might. So the more fitting expression was what? *Uʿadhdhibu* (I will punish), which indicates the strength of authority. As for the other, it is as though Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in showing affection toward these people and declaring their merit, said: ﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾, and did not attribute the giving to Himself, so as to grant them some measure of thanks for their deeds. The difference between addressing a person by expressing your action toward him with the first-person pronoun and expressing it with the third-person pronoun is that direct address is more intense than speaking about someone in his absence. Consider His words: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know?﴾ [ʿAbasa 1–3]. He said ﴿He frowned﴾ and did not say "you frowned," and He said ﴿And what would make you know?﴾ and did not say "and what would make him know" or "and what would make Him know." So this, and Allah knows best, is the wisdom behind expressing punishment with the verb attributed to the first-person pronoun, unlike the expression for reward. This is confirmed by His words in sūrat al-Raḥmān: ﴿Is the reward for good anything but good?﴾ [al-Raḥmān 60]. He made their action a good deed for which they are thanked and to which good is returned, even though all goodness is from Allah, since enabling a servant to do righteous deeds is one of Allah's kindnesses to him. But this is from the perfection of Allah's mercy, His reward and His recompense. And He, the Exalted, said in sūrat al-Insān: ﴿Indeed, this was for you a reward, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insān 22]. Now, their effort being appreciated: who enabled them to strive? Allah. Yet He says ﴿and your effort has been appreciated﴾. So the change of style in the two verses yields two benefits: a verbal one and a semantic one. The verbal one is the shift (*iltifāt*), which causes attention to be drawn. The semantic one is the display of authority, majesty, and might in the matter of punishment, and the display of favor and kindness toward those who act righteously in the matter of reward.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿That is what We recite to you of the signs and the wise reminder﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 58]. From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke the Qurʾān, saying ﴿That is what We recite to you﴾. Recitation is truly Allah's, and it was conveyed by Jibrīl to the Messenger ﷺ. It is possible that the recitation is by Jibrīl, but since Jibrīl is Allah's messenger, his action is attributed to Allah. This is like His words: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyāmah 16–18]. It is well known that the one who recites it is Jibrīl.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the Noble Qurʾān is a sign, indeed signs. As Allah said: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 49]. They are great signs, and its signs are many. Each verse contains several signs. But these signs are understood only by one whose heart Allah has opened to faith, knowledge, and the conviction that this Qurʾān is the speech of Allah and that in it are clear signs. As for one over whom such verses pass without his heart being moved by them, and who does not reflect upon these signs, he will not benefit from the signs in the Qurʾān. You must believe that in it are signs, and strive to extract these signs through reflection. When a person reflects upon the Qurʾān, he finds in it great signs that people cannot count.

* Another benefit of this verse: the Qurʾān is a reminder. But is it a reminder by which one draws near to Allah, or a reminder by which a person is reminded? We have mentioned that the meaning includes both. It is a reminder by which one draws near to Allah, because whoever recites it has ten good deeds for every letter. And it is a reminder by which a person is reminded. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is present﴾ [Qāf 37]. It was said: it is also a reminder by which Allah raised the status of those who held fast to it, as He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44], and as in His words: ﴿And We raised for you your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharḥ 4], meaning: We elevated your standing. Accordingly, the word *dhikr* (reminder) has how many meanings? Three: a reminder by which one draws near to Allah through its recitation; a reminder by which a person is reminded; and a reminder that means honor for whoever holds fast to it.

From *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise), because the wise is one who places a thing in its proper places. So every ruling that the Qurʾān decrees is in its proper place. Reason does not say, "Would that it had not ruled thus." Never. Whether the ruling is affirmative or negative.

So it is as though he is the one specifically addressed by the recitation: ﴿We recite it to you﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like the example of Adam﴾. It has already passed with us that these verses were revealed when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were Christians. As for this world, it is likewise: when these disbelievers are punished at the hands of the believers, their fighting men are killed, their women and children are taken captive, and their wealth and lands are seized as spoils. They have no helper in this.

If someone says: Does the imam not have a choice regarding captives among four matters: killing, ransom for wealth or for a Muslim captive, enslavement, or release? The first three present no difficulty. The difficulty lies in the last, which is release, and this is not a punishment. The answer to this is: the imam may not choose any of these four except where he sees a benefit for the Muslims in it. So the choice here is a choice of benefit, not a choice of whim and preference. When there is benefit for the Muslims, it must also be a punishment for the disbelievers, because everything that benefits the Muslims contains a punishment for the disbelievers. Accordingly, they have no helper, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

Then Allah said: ﴿But as for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full﴾. From this verse is derived the eloquence of the Qurʾān and its wisdom: its eloquence lies in presenting meanings in opposition, because presenting opposing meanings stirs a person's energy, as the mind moves from one meaning to its opposite, and so grows more active and eager. As for its perfection of eloquence, when meanings are varied through opposition, the wording becomes more beautiful. This is known among the scholars of rhetoric as the science of what? The science of *badīʿ* (rhetorical embellishment). It also contains the training of the soul, because when the soul hears the punishment of the disbelievers, it fears and is dismayed, and perhaps despair overtakes it. When the reward of the believers comes, it hopes and longs, so its journey toward Allah becomes between fear and hope.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the full giving of reward is tied to two attributes: faith and righteous deeds. Faith alone is not enough; there must be a righteous deed that nourishes this faith and attests to its soundness. Mere creed is not sufficient. Moreover, when creed is sound, it necessitates righteous deeds, as the Messenger ﷺ said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhārī (52) and Muslim (107/1599) from the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr.]]

* Another benefit of the noble verse: a deed benefits only if it is righteous, and a righteous deed is one that combines two attributes: sincerity to Allah and conformity to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. That is, it is what is sincere and correct, as al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ, may Allah have mercy on him, said.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: Allah's favor upon His servants, in that He made this recompense like wages whose payment is obligatory, as in His words: ﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾. Note, and consider the difference between the two expressions: there He said ﴿I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾, and here He said ﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation of love for Allah, as in His words: ﴿And Allah does not love wrongdoers﴾. If someone says: How do you prove the affirmation of love by the negation of love, since He said: ﴿does not love wrongdoers﴾? The answer: the negation of love from wrongdoers indicates its affirmation for others. Had it been negated from all, there would be no benefit in specifying it for wrongdoers. For this reason, al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, used as evidence for the believers' seeing Allah the words of Allah concerning the wicked: ﴿No! Indeed, on that day they will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn 15]. He said in explaining the inference: He veiled His enemies from seeing Him in anger only because the believers' seeing Him in pleasure is established. This is clear.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the evil of wrongdoing, its evil upon a person, and that it is a cause for the absence of Allah's love for him. When Allah's love for a servant is absent, he has been ruined.

* Another benefit: wrongdoing is one of the major sins, because a threat is attached to it, namely the absence of Allah's love, Glorified and Exalted. However, it appears that this is not absolute. Rather, wrongdoing may be a major sin and may be a minor sin, because all sins are wrongdoing, and some sins are major while others are minor.

* Another benefit of the verse together with the preceding one: variety in style, namely the shift from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun: ﴿I will punish them﴾ and here He said ﴿He will give them﴾. Is there a difference in meaning? The answer: yes, there is a difference in meaning. As for the wording, the shift from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun is evident. But we want the difference in meaning. The difference in meaning is that punishment, being a penalty, requires authority, domination, and might. So the more fitting expression was what? *Uʿadhdhibu* (I will punish), which indicates the strength of authority. As for the other, it is as though Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in showing affection toward these people and declaring their merit, said: ﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾, and did not attribute the giving to Himself, so as to grant them some measure of thanks for their deeds. The difference between addressing a person by expressing your action toward him with the first-person pronoun and expressing it with the third-person pronoun is that direct address is more intense than speaking about someone in his absence. Consider His words: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know?﴾ [ʿAbasa 1–3]. He said ﴿He frowned﴾ and did not say "you frowned," and He said ﴿And what would make you know?﴾ and did not say "and what would make him know" or "and what would make Him know." So this, and Allah knows best, is the wisdom behind expressing punishment with the verb attributed to the first-person pronoun, unlike the expression for reward. This is confirmed by His words in sūrat al-Raḥmān: ﴿Is the reward for good anything but good?﴾ [al-Raḥmān 60]. He made their action a good deed for which they are thanked and to which good is returned, even though all goodness is from Allah, since enabling a servant to do righteous deeds is one of Allah's kindnesses to him. But this is from the perfection of Allah's mercy, His reward and His recompense. And He, the Exalted, said in sūrat al-Insān: ﴿Indeed, this was for you a reward, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insān 22]. Now, their effort being appreciated: who enabled them to strive? Allah. Yet He says ﴿and your effort has been appreciated﴾. So the change of style in the two verses yields two benefits: a verbal one and a semantic one. The verbal one is the shift (*iltifāt*), which causes attention to be drawn. The semantic one is the display of authority, majesty, and might in the matter of punishment, and the display of favor and kindness toward those who act righteously in the matter of reward.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿That is what We recite to you of the signs and the wise reminder﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 58]. From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke the Qurʾān, saying ﴿That is what We recite to you﴾. Recitation is truly Allah's, and it was conveyed by Jibrīl to the Messenger ﷺ. It is possible that the recitation is by Jibrīl, but since Jibrīl is Allah's messenger, his action is attributed to Allah. This is like His words: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyāmah 16–18]. It is well known that the one who recites it is Jibrīl.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the Noble Qurʾān is a sign, indeed signs. As Allah said: ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 49]. They are great signs, and its signs are many. Each verse contains several signs. But these signs are understood only by one whose heart Allah has opened to faith, knowledge, and the conviction that this Qurʾān is the speech of Allah and that in it are clear signs. As for one over whom such verses pass without his heart being moved by them, and who does not reflect upon these signs, he will not benefit from the signs in the Qurʾān. You must believe that in it are signs, and strive to extract these signs through reflection. When a person reflects upon the Qurʾān, he finds in it great signs that people cannot count.

* Another benefit of this verse: the Qurʾān is a reminder. But is it a reminder by which one draws near to Allah, or a reminder by which a person is reminded? We have mentioned that the meaning includes both. It is a reminder by which one draws near to Allah, because whoever recites it has ten good deeds for every letter. And it is a reminder by which a person is reminded. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is present﴾ [Qāf 37]. It was said: it is also a reminder by which Allah raised the status of those who held fast to it, as He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44], and as in His words: ﴿And We raised for you your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharḥ 4], meaning: We elevated your standing. Accordingly, the word *dhikr* (reminder) has how many meanings? Three: a reminder by which one draws near to Allah through its recitation; a reminder by which a person is reminded; and a reminder that means honor for whoever holds fast to it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the Noble Qurʾān is described with this great attribute, which is wisdom: ﴿and the wise reminder﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 58]. *Al-Ḥakīm* here means both "the one who judges" and "the one who makes firm," because the Qurʾān judges between people, as in His words: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 59], that is, to His Book. So it is a judge and also made firm, perfected, free of contradiction, disorder, or inconsistency.

* Another benefit of the verse: there is no ruling indicated by the Qurʾān except that it is in its fitting place. From where is this derived? From *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise), because the wise is one who places a thing in its proper places. So every ruling that the Qurʾān decrees is in its proper place. Reason does not say, "Would that it had not ruled thus." Never. Whether the ruling is affirmative or negative.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the excellence of the Messenger ﷺ in the words ﴿We recite it to you﴾. He was singled out for the recitation to him, because he ﷺ is the noblest of those who receive the Qurʾān and the most upright of people in acting upon it. So it is as though he is the one specifically addressed by the recitation: ﴿We recite it to you﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like the example of Adam﴾. It has already passed with us that these verses were revealed when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were Christians. Their coming was in the ninth year after the Hijrah, because that year many delegations came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and for this reason it is called the Year of Delegations. This is one of the reasons that prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) from performing Hajj in the ninth year, even though Makkah had already been conquered. ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like the example of Adam﴾ means: his matter. The matter of Jesus with Allah is like the matter of Adam, not different from it. Just as we all agree that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created Adam without a father or a mother, even the Christians believe this, what is the matter with the Christians who say: "How did Allah create Jesus without a father?" He is only His son, we seek refuge in Allah. So they said: he is the Son of Allah, a part of Him. They did not say that Adam is the son of Allah, even though if anyone were to claim sonship for any human being, Adam would be the most entitled to it. Sonship belongs to Allah; Adam would have been the most entitled, because he has neither mother nor father, whereas Jesus has a mother, and the mother is one of the two parents. So if we say: it is impossible for someone to exist from a mother without a father, then let us say: nor can anyone exist without a mother and a father. You, O Christians, have acknowledged that Adam is not a son of Allah, so it follows that you must acknowledge that Jesus is not a son of Allah, because the example of Jesus is like the example of Adam. ﴿He created him from dust﴾: "created him" means: He began his creation from dust, and the pronoun of the object in (khalaqahu) refers to Adam, because he is the one created from dust. ﴿He created him﴾, i.e., He created Adam from dust. ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. We have said: He began his creation, then He said: "Be." This command is for the completion of the creation. We said this so that no one would say: how can the word "Be" come after the creation, since the rational order requires that "Be" come before the creation, "Be" and then "he was." So we say: the meaning of ﴿He created him﴾ is: He began his creation from dust, then He said to him: "Be a human," and he was a human. ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. Is this saying "Be" a decreed (qadari) or a legislative (shar'i) saying? It is a decreed saying, and what is decreed is never delayed from it, because it is an absolute command. This differs from the legislative saying, for among people there are those who are arrogant toward it. Allah says: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ [al-An'am 72], and one says: "No, I will not establish the prayer." But the cosmic (kawni) saying has no repelling. ﴿"Be," and he was﴾, and He did not say "so he became," in reporting the state; that is, when He said "Be," he immediately began to come into being until it was complete.

In this verse: the establishment of proof with the same argument the opponent uses. He established the proof against the Christians with the same thing they argued with. He said: if you say that Jesus is the son of Allah because he was created without a father, then say that Adam is the son of Allah; otherwise you are contradicting yourselves.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in that He created Adam without a mother or father, and created Jesus from a mother without a father. There are also two other categories: Allah created one from a father without a mother, and created others from both a father and a mother. Who was created from a father without a mother? Eve (Hawwa'), and all the rest of mankind from both a mother and a father.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of analogy (qiyas). From where is it derived? ﴿like the example of Adam﴾. Every example presented in the Qur'an is evidence for the validity of analogy, because it attaches the thing compared to the thing it is compared with. That is, you attached the one being compared to what? To the one it is compared with.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of speech for the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿Then He said to him﴾.
Also among its benefits: that the speech of Allah is with an audible voice and with letters in sequence, by His saying: ﴿He said to him, "Be"﴾. This saying is heard, and it has letters in order, does it not? The kaf comes before the nun.

Also among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of the attribute of creation for Allah, ﴿He created him﴾. Is creation a essential (dhati) or an active (fi'li) attribute?
* The students: Active.
* The Shaykh: Active, one of the active attributes. But it has already passed with us that the category of active attributes is, what? Essential; because Allah has always been and will always be Doer (fa''al).

For this reason, the disbelievers are punished in this world: they are defeated, taken captive, their women and children are enslaved, and their wealth is seized as spoils. This is a great punishment, and yet they are not spared from the punishment of the Fire.

So it is a judge and also made firm, perfected, free of contradiction, disorder, or inconsistency.

* Another benefit of the verse: there is no ruling indicated by the Qurʾān except that it is in its fitting place. From where is this derived? From *al-Ḥakīm* (the Wise), because the wise is one who places a thing in its proper places. So every ruling that the Qurʾān decrees is in its proper place. Reason does not say, "Would that it had not ruled thus." Never. Whether the ruling is affirmative or negative.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the excellence of the Messenger ﷺ in the words ﴿We recite it to you﴾. He was singled out for the recitation to him, because he ﷺ is the noblest of those who receive the Qurʾān and the most upright of people in acting upon it. So it is as though he is the one specifically addressed by the recitation: ﴿We recite it to you﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like the example of Adam﴾. It has already passed with us that these verses were revealed when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were Christians. Their coming was in the ninth year after the Hijrah, because that year many delegations came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and for this reason it is called the Year of Delegations. This is one of the reasons that prevented the Prophet (ﷺ) from performing Hajj in the ninth year, even though Makkah had already been conquered. ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like the example of Adam﴾ means: his matter. The matter of Jesus with Allah is like the matter of Adam, not different from it. Just as we all agree that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created Adam without a father or a mother, even the Christians believe this, what is the matter with the Christians who say: "How did Allah create Jesus without a father?" He is only His son, we seek refuge in Allah. So they said: he is the Son of Allah, a part of Him. They did not say that Adam is the son of Allah, even though if anyone were to claim sonship for any human being, Adam would be the most entitled to it. Sonship belongs to Allah; Adam would have been the most entitled, because he has neither mother nor father, whereas Jesus has a mother, and the mother is one of the two parents. So if we say: it is impossible for someone to exist from a mother without a father, then let us say: nor can anyone exist without a mother and a father. You, O Christians, have acknowledged that Adam is not a son of Allah, so it follows that you must acknowledge that Jesus is not a son of Allah, because the example of Jesus is like the example of Adam. ﴿He created him from dust﴾: "created him" means: He began his creation from dust, and the pronoun of the object in (khalaqahu) refers to Adam, because he is the one created from dust. ﴿He created him﴾, i.e., He created Adam from dust. ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. We have said: He began his creation, then He said: "Be." This command is for the completion of the creation. We said this so that no one would say: how can the word "Be" come after the creation, since the rational order requires that "Be" come before the creation, "Be" and then "he was." So we say: the meaning of ﴿He created him﴾ is: He began his creation from dust, then He said to him: "Be a human," and he was a human. ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. Is this saying "Be" a decreed (qadari) or a legislative (shar'i) saying? It is a decreed saying, and what is decreed is never delayed from it, because it is an absolute command. This differs from the legislative saying, for among people there are those who are arrogant toward it. Allah says: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ [al-An'am 72], and one says: "No, I will not establish the prayer." But the cosmic (kawni) saying has no repelling. ﴿"Be," and he was﴾, and He did not say "so he became," in reporting the state; that is, when He said "Be," he immediately began to come into being until it was complete.

In this verse: the establishment of proof with the same argument the opponent uses. He established the proof against the Christians with the same thing they argued with. He said: if you say that Jesus is the son of Allah because he was created without a father, then say that Adam is the son of Allah; otherwise you are contradicting yourselves.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in that He created Adam without a mother or father, and created Jesus from a mother without a father. There are also two other categories: Allah created one from a father without a mother, and created others from both a father and a mother. Who was created from a father without a mother? Eve (Hawwa'), and all the rest of mankind from both a mother and a father.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of analogy (qiyas). From where is it derived? ﴿like the example of Adam﴾. Every example presented in the Qur'an is evidence for the validity of analogy, because it attaches the thing compared to the thing it is compared with. That is, you attached the one being compared to what? To the one it is compared with.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of speech for the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿Then He said to him﴾.
Also among its benefits: that the speech of Allah is with an audible voice and with letters in sequence, by His saying: ﴿He said to him, "Be"﴾. This saying is heard, and it has letters in order, does it not? The kaf comes before the nun.

Also among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of the attribute of creation for Allah, ﴿He created him﴾. Is creation a essential (dhati) or an active (fi'li) attribute?
* The students: Active.
* The Shaykh: Active, one of the active attributes. But it has already passed with us that the category of active attributes is, what? Essential; because Allah has always been and will always be Doer (fa''al).

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt﴾. ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾. ﴿The truth﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the implied sense is: ﴿That﴾ is the truth, meaning: this which has been related to you is the truth. On this reading, the prepositional phrase ﴿from your Lord﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial (hal) modifying ﴿the truth﴾. It is also possible, though remote, that ﴿the truth﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿from your Lord﴾ is its predicate. The benefit of this construction, according to this i'rab, is that you do not seek the truth from anyone other than Allah; it is as if He says: the source of the truth is from Allah, so do not seek it from other than Him. ﴿Al-haqq﴾ (the truth) is applied both to a judgment and to a report: if it is applied to a judgment, its meaning becomes justice ('adl); if it is applied to a report, its meaning becomes truthfulness (sidq). Both justice and truthfulness are established, and for this reason both are described as ﴿haqq﴾. The root of ﴿haqq﴾ is from ﴿haqqa al-shay'u﴾ when a thing is established, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has been fulfilled against those who transgressed, that they will not believe﴾ [Yunus 33]. ﴿Haqqat﴾ means? 

* The students: It was established (thabatat).

* The Shaykh: It was established. So there are two possibilities in its i'rab. ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾: how many possibilities are there in its i'rab?

* A student: It is said that it is a subject (mubtada') and the prepositional phrase ﴿from your Lord﴾ is the predicate; and it is said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: that is the truth.

* The Shaykh: Its subject is omitted and its predicate is... 

* The student: A subject and its predicate is omitted.

* The Shaykh: A subject whose predicate is omitted.

* A student: A predicate of an omitted subject.

* The Shaykh: A predicate of an omitted subject, correct.

* The student: That is the truth.

* The Shaykh: Yes. Good. ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾: ﴿from your Lord﴾ here attributes lordship to the Prophet ﷺ so that it is a special lordship; for lordship, as we have often noted, is general and special. The general lordship encompasses all creation: believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked, human and animal, living and inanimate. The special lordship is that which is specific to the believers and entails a more particular nurturing than the general nurturing. ﴿From your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt﴾: the particle (lā) here is a prohibitive, and for this reason the verb after it is in the jussive mood. Is the other verse like it: ﴿So you must not be of those who doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah 147]? But there is a difficulty, because the other verse is not in the jussive: ﴿فَلَا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الْمُمْتَرِينَ﴾.

* A student: The verse is in the jussive.

* The Shaykh: And where is the jussive?

* The student: The jussive (...) the jussive is by deleting the nun, and it is by sukun.

* The Shaykh: And where is the deletion of the nun?

* The student: ﴿فَلَا تَكُنْ﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿فَلَا تَكُنْ﴾: what is this?

* The student: This is sukun.

* The Shaykh: This is sukun. And ﴿فَلَا تَكُونَنَّ﴾?

* The student: The nun is deleted.

* The Shaykh: The nun is deleted?

* A student: The nun is retained and vowelled because of the meeting of two sakin letters.

* The Shaykh: In ﴿لَا تَكُونَنَّ﴾?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Wrong.

* A student: The verb here is built on fatha because it is attached to the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid).

* The Shaykh: Well said. The verb here is not inflected so as to be jussive; it is built on fatha because it is attached to what? To the emphatic nun ﴿فَلَا تَكُونَنَّ﴾, and for this reason the verb remains with all its letters.

Now, his saying: ﴿so do not be of those who doubt﴾, meaning: do not be of the doubters. This expression has troubled many people, who said: Would the Messenger ﷺ doubt? Would he doubt? The answer to this is that we say: this verse, or this expression, does not indicate that the Messenger ﷺ doubted, nor even that it was possible for him to do so. Rather it intends an allusion (ta'ridh) against the doubters and their blame. If you say to a righteous man, "Do not be of the wicked," does that mean the man is wicked? No, but its meaning is an allusion against the wicked, that they have a character from which every sensible person should flee. Likewise, ﴿لَا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الْمُمْتَرِينَ﴾ does not mean that the Messenger could be or is among them; rather the meaning is an allusion against the doubting doubters. Among them, in this matter, are the Christians, for the Christians believe that Jesus is the son of God; so they doubt the report of Allah and are uncertain about it. Yet there is nothing in the Torah, the Gospel, the Qur'an or other revealed books that says Jesus is the son of God, nor anything that indicates, apparently or by probability, that Jesus is the son of God. Despite this, these Christians have doubted and began to spread their corrupt belief that Jesus is the son of God. So then, ﴿لَا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الْمُمْتَرِينَ﴾: Allah forbids him to be among the doubters, not because he is one of them nor because he could be, but as an allusion against these doubters, a censure of them. A parallel: as I told you, if you say to an upright person, "Do not be among the wicked," he will say, "Am I wicked? May God guide you!" I say: I did not say you are wicked, but I am alluding to the blame of those wicked people.

Some scholars, as a solution to this apparent difficulty, said: the address is to the Messenger ﷺ but the intended meaning is his community (ummah). But this view is very weak, because the address is explicitly to the Messenger ﷺ, and likewise the discourse is with the Messenger: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 147]. How can we say the intended meaning is "the truth is from your Lord, so do not be, O community of Muhammad, of the doubters"? This is what this view entails, and it is remote from the Qur'anic style. The meaning I have mentioned is correct: the Messenger ﷺ did not doubt and will never doubt, but this is by way of allusion, as if he says: persist in the certainty you have, and how ugly is the state of these doubters!

* A student: Shaykh, ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam﴾: does this mean in all of his message?

* The Shaykh: No, only in creation; that is, the matter became confused for them when he was created without a father, so they said: he is the son of God.

* A student: ﴿the truth﴾: are we not parsing it as the subject (fa'il) of an omitted verb, meaning: the truth has come to you from your Lord?

* The Shaykh: If we say it is an omitted verb, what follows is the omission of three things, or not?

* The student: A subject of an omitted verb.

* The Shaykh: If we say a subject of an omitted verb, then what follows is the omission of three things. What are they? The verb, the subject and the object, or is the subject present?

* The students: Present.

* The Shaykh: Then the omission is of two things: the verb and the object. If we say it is the predicate of an omitted subject, then one thing is omitted, and also the thing most often omitted, which is the noun; for omitting the noun is generally more frequent than omitting the verb.

* A student: May Allah reward you with good, Shaykh. People find a matter confusing and say... sometimes they are scrupulous about it. For example, the Christians are among the people of the Fire. If asked "why?", he says: first, why was the jizyah imposed on them? They are not like other disbelievers. Second, one hears on some broadcasts that they commit adultery... Christianity says...?

* The Shaykh: This should not be a source of confusion, given the many clear verses: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein eternally. They are the worst of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah 6]. The Most High says in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered prophet who believes in Allah and His words, and follow him that you may be guided﴾ [al-A'raf 158]. And it is authentically related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no one from this community hears of me, be he Jew or Christian, and then does not follow what I was sent with – or he said: does not believe in what I was sent with – except that he will be among the companions of the Fire." [Related by Muslim (240/153) from Abu Hurayrah.]

* A student: What is the wisdom, Shaykh, in imposing the jizyah?

* The Shaykh: To humiliate them. And perhaps, if they live among us, they will return to the truth, because their books declare that Muhammad ﷺ is upon the truth. Although the preferred view is that the jizyah is taken from them and from others; it is taken from every person, because the aim is for Islam to be the highest.

* A student: Why can it not be said that the verse ﴿so do not be of those who doubt﴾ runs in the same course as the hadith of 'A'ishah when she said: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon your religion"?

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is a difference between supplication and report. Supplication: every person who has faith is fearful; the one who knows Allah best is the most fearful of Him, and a person fears. But Allah's report about His Messenger, that it is permissible that he be among the doubters, or that he is now among the doubters, is remote.

* The student: To indicate (...).

* The Shaykh: No, this is remote.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, we said regarding His saying ﴿He created him from dust﴾: that is, He began his creation from dust, then said "Be" and he is. In the origination, Allah the Glorified and Most High is able to bring about his origination with "Be" and it is. Likewise for the beginning and creation. Why did He choose the origination to be by "Be and it is"?

* The Shaykh: Has this not passed over us? All of Allah's creation: He says that Allah is able to say "Be" and it is before creating him from dust and then making him. All created things: Allah is able to create them by the word "Be", yet He did not do so, because the creatures of Allah require wisdom and gradualness, and some things need others. For this reason He did not create the heavens and the earth by "Be"; He created them in six days, while He was able to create them by the word "Be".

* A student: Shaykh, we have derived from His saying ﴿He said to him: Be, and he is﴾ that Allah's word is heard, in letters arranged in order. Now, was the language Arabic, so that we may derive this inference?

* The Shaykh: That is, what Allah speaks when He wills creation, we do not know whether it is in the Arabic language or not.

* A student: Then how did we derive from the letters?

* The Shaykh: The word "Be" (كن) is two letters, one before the second; this is the order.

* A student: Shaykh? In His saying ﴿so do not be of those who doubt﴾, what is derived is that the command, if the command is ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt﴾, meaning the condition is omitted in all of this: if the truth is from your Lord, then do not be of the doubters.

* The Shaykh: The brother says that the fa' is a connective for the answer of an estimated condition, is that right?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: We say: there is no need for this, because one should understand the rule that we do not resort to estimation except when necessity requires it. As for when the sentence is sound without estimation, this is what is required; for if you say the sentence cannot stand without an estimate, meaning the sentence is now deficient, and we cannot describe a sentence as deficient except in necessity. When we see that the meaning does not stand without estimation, then yes. But here it stands, and we make the fa' here a marker of consequence: that is, because it is from your Lord, do not be of the doubters.

* * *
* A student: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he is. (59) The truth is from your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt. (60) Whoever argues with you about it after knowledge has come to you, say: Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves, then let us invoke earnestly and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars. (61) Indeed, this is the true narrative, and there is no deity except Allah, and indeed Allah is the Exalted in Might, the Wise. (62) But if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters﴾ [Al 'Imran 59–63].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be of those who doubt﴾. Among the benefits of this verse: Allah the Most High does not issue anything but truth, ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾.

* And among its benefits: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ through attributing lordship to him, because this lordship is special, and special lordship conveys a more particular meaning than general lordship.

* And among its benefits: the prohibition of doubt concerning what Allah has reported, from His saying: ﴿so do not be of those who doubt﴾.

* And among its benefits: that the doubters are many, from His saying: ﴿of those who doubt﴾. Although it may be intended as a genus, which is satisfied by one, the apparent meaning is the first, and there is no doubt that the doubters among the children of Adam are many, for of the descendants of Adam, nine hundred and ninety-nine out of every thousand are all from the people of the Fire.

* And among its benefits: the permissibility of allusion, or of addressing with allusion; for His saying: ﴿so do not be of those who doubt﴾ does not mean that the Messenger could be among them; rather it is an allusion against those people, that they have a bad character, so do not be among them, even though he is not among them, neither in reality nor in the future.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever argues with you concerning it﴾. ﴿Hājjaka﴾ means: disputed with you. The dispute is called muḥājjah (argument, contention) because each of the two disputants presents his proof in order to defeat the other and overcome him with argument. From this is the hadith: "Ādam and Mūsā disputed (taḥājjā)" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6614) and Muslim (14/2652) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], meaning each of them sought to overcome the other in argument. And which of them prevailed in the argument? Ādam. Yes. So ﴿ḥājjaka﴾ means: disputed with you. The dispute is called muḥājjah because each of the disputants brings forward a proof in order to overcome the other.

And His saying: ﴿Whoever argues with you﴾, (man) here is conditional, and the response of the condition is ﴿say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons"...﴾. His saying: ﴿whoever argues with you concerning it﴾, the pronoun refers to ʿĪsā (Jesus), and the intended argument concerning ʿĪsā is not about his essence, because it is known that ʿĪsā is a human being, but about his affair and his matter. His saying: ﴿Whoever argues with you concerning it﴾: who could possibly argue with the Prophet ﷺ concerning ʿĪsā? They are the Christians, and this verse and what precedes it were all revealed concerning the delegation of Christians from Najrān. ﴿Whoever argues with you concerning it after the knowledge has come to you﴾, meaning: after you have known his matter, his affair, and been certain of it, whoever argues with you about it, call him to mubāhalah (mutual imprecation). In His saying: ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾, He used (min), which indicates that the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to mubāhalah after he had been given time to reflect upon the knowledge, because ﴿min baʿdi﴾ indicates that there is an interval between the knowledge that came to him and the argument that took place. This is unlike if He had said: "whoever argues with you concerning it after what has come to you," which conveys sequence but does not indicate a lengthy delay or distance. And it is known that a person, whenever he reflects upon what he knows, increases in what? He increases in knowledge and certainty. His saying: ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾: through which path? Through the path of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for Allah, the Exalted, revealed to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ concerning the affair of ʿĪsā knowledge that was not with anyone else. ﴿So say: "Come"﴾: We have said that ﴿qul﴾ is the response of the condition, and ﴿taʿālaw﴾ is an imperative verb built on the deletion of the nūn, with the wāw as its subject. There is a difficulty here, because ﴿taʿālaw﴾ is plural, while ﴿man ḥājjaka﴾ is singular. So how is it valid for a plural to refer back to a singular? The answer: relative nouns and conditional nouns that are shared, meaning those that can apply to the singular and to other than the singular, may have a pronoun referring to them according to the wording, or according to the meaning. If the reference is according to the wording, it is singular; if according to the meaning, it is plural. There is no difference whether this permissible usage occurs in one statement or in two statements. For example, ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [At-Ṭalāq 11]: what was observed in this? The students: the wording. The Shaykh: ﴿He will admit him﴾, ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ [At-Ṭalāq 11]. The students: the meaning. The Shaykh: the meaning, ﴿Allah has certainly provided well for him﴾ [At-Ṭalāq 11]. The students: the wording. The Shaykh: the wording. One verse in which the wording was observed, then the meaning, then the wording. Is that correct? If the wording were observed in all these clauses it would be said: "...He will admit (him) to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding (therein) forever, Allah has provided well for (him)." And if the meaning were observed it would be said: "...He will admit (them) to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding (therein) forever, Allah has provided well for (them)."

And His saying: ﴿taʿālaw﴾: is it a noun acting as an imperative verb, or an imperative verb? We say: it is an imperative verb, because the imperative noun does not accept the markers, meaning pronouns do not attach to it. The imperative noun does not take attached pronouns. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who say to their brothers, "Come (halumma) to us"﴾ [Al-Aḥzāb 18]. Why did He not say "halummū"? Because it is an imperative noun, and imperative nouns do not take attached pronouns. Therefore you say to a group: ṣah, meaning "be silent," and you do not say ṣahū. If pronouns attach to it, it becomes an imperative verb. Therefore we say: ﴿taʿālaw﴾ is an imperative verb, or an imperative noun? An imperative verb. Good. ﴿taʿālaw﴾ means: come forward, but come with elevation and rising, as if the one calling is calling them so that they rise to him and he speaks to them what he wishes.

And His saying: ﴿So say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons"﴾: (nadʿu) — how is it "nadʿu" and where is the wāw? It is deleted, with the wāw dropped by way of jazm, because it is an answer?
The students: the request.
The Shaykh: the response to a request.
A student: and that is the command.
The Shaykh: the response to a request, which is the command. It is known that when the response to a request lacks the fāʾ, jazm must be applied to it. ﴿So say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, and our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves"﴾. Why did He say "nadʿu" and not "adʿu"? Yes, He did not say that because when they come with him they become a group. ﴿Let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves.﴾ As you see, this verse is in the plural form: ﴿our sons﴾, while the Messenger is one, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿your sons﴾ are a group, fine. ﴿our women﴾: the Messenger is one and did not say "my women". ﴿your women﴾ is a group, clear. ﴿our selves and your selves﴾: the Messenger is one, or a number of selves? One. So what is intended by this? The exegetes differed concerning this. Some exegetes said: by His saying ﴿let us call our sons and your sons﴾ is meant, by "our sons," al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn; by ﴿our women﴾ is meant Fāṭimah, the daughter of the Messenger ﷺ; by ﴿our selves﴾ is meant ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. So they are four. Is that right?
The students: Yes.
The Shaykh: ﴿our sons﴾: al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn; ﴿our women﴾: Fāṭimah; ﴿our selves﴾: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. As for that delegation, there were no women with them and no children with them; all of them were grown, sensible men, whether fourteen or two. The point is that they were men with no one else. Some scholars said: what is meant is that we, the Muslims, call our sons, that is, the sons of the Muslims: we select a group from among us who come with their sons, women, and selves, and you likewise select a group who come with their sons, women, and selves; we gather and invoke a curse. This view is undoubtedly in complete agreement with the apparent meaning of the verse, because the verse is in the plural form, and custom has it that mubāhalah, as well as boasting and other things, takes place between groups. Someone says to you: "Bring your quarter and we will bring our quarter." Muḥammad Rashīd [Riḍā] went to this view in his tafsir, and it is without doubt an interpretation that exactly matches the apparent meaning of the verse. But most exegetes choose the first view: that by "our sons" is meant al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, by "our women" Fāṭimah, and by "our selves" ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, on the basis of a hadith that was narrated concerning this. The matter does not match the apparent meaning of the verse; that is, this view does not agree with the apparent meaning of the verse. First: "sons" (abnāʾ) is plural and "our" (nā) is plural, and if we say al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, they become two. Is "ibnān" (two sons) for a plural or for a singular?
A student: For a singular.
The Shaykh: For a singular. Also "women": in Arabic it was not the case that "women" means daughters; in Arabic "women" means what? Wives. It means wives. Also, "our selves": how would the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, refer to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib by "self" and not refer to al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn by "self"? Which of them is closer? al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn. Indeed, the Messenger called al-Ḥasan his son, saying: "Indeed, this son of mine is a master" [Related by al-Bukhari (2704) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah]. Therefore the apparent meaning of the verse does not match this interpretation. Muḥammad Rashīd Riḍā claimed that interpreting it as referring to the four is an interpretation of the Rafidah (Shiʿah), and said: the verse does not apply to them. But the hadith narrated on this indicates that the interpretation has a basis, and there is no doubt that the Ahl al-Bayt (People of the House) include these four; there is no doubt about this. However, its application to the verse leaves something in the soul. In any case, the matter has ended. But what is meant by "selves," "sons," and "women"? The meaning is that they wish to gather a group with them: their sons, their women, and their selves. This is the most precious thing a person has in this world; this is the most precious: his self, his sons, his wives. They come, and the opponent likewise brings his self, his sons, and his women.

But most exegetes choose the first view, that by "our sons" is meant al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, ﴿and our women﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 61] Fāṭimah, ﴿and our selves﴾ ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, on the basis of a hadith narrated concerning this [Related by al-Tirmidhi (3205) from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn Abī Salamah].
The matter does not match the apparent meaning of the verse; that is, this view does not agree with the apparent meaning of the verse.
First: "sons" (abnāʾ) is plural and "our" (nā) is plural, and if we say al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, they become two. "Ibnān" (two sons): is it for a plural or a singular? For a singular.
Also "women": in Arabic it does not mean daughters; "women" in Arabic means wives. It means wives. Also, "our selves": how would the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, refer to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib by "self" and not refer to al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn by "self"? Which is closer? al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn. Indeed, the Messenger called al-Ḥasan his son, saying: "Indeed, this son of mine is a master" [Related by al-Bukhari (2704) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah].
Therefore the apparent meaning of the verse does not match this interpretation. Muḥammad Rashīd Riḍā claimed that interpreting it as referring to the four is an interpretation of the Rafidah, and said: the verse does not apply to them. But the hadith narrated on this indicates that it has a basis, and there is no doubt that the Ahl al-Bayt include these four; there is no doubt about this. However, its application to the verse leaves something in the soul.
In any case, the matter has ended. But what is meant by "selves," "sons," and "women"?
The meaning is that they wish to gather a group with them: their sons, their women, and their selves. This is the most precious thing a person has in this world; this is the most precious: his self, his sons, his wives. They come, and the opponent likewise brings his self, his sons, and his women.

He said: ﴿Then let us earnestly invoke﴾, meaning: we humble ourselves and exert ourselves in supplication.
Then he explained the ibtihāl (earnest invocation) by His saying: ﴿and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾. This view, that ﴿nabtahil﴾ means we humble ourselves and earnestly implore in supplication, is more correct than the view that the meaning of ﴿nabtahil﴾ is "we curse one another," because if we interpret ﴿nabtahil﴾ as "we curse one another," we gain no new meaning at His saying ﴿and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾; the second becomes a repetition of the first. But if we say ﴿nabtahil﴾ means we humble ourselves in supplication and implore, we gain an additional meaning, namely the intensity of humility and urgency.
Therefore it is said: "He implored Allah in supplication" (ibtahala ilā Allāh fī al-duʿāʾ), and the listener understands only that the meaning is: he humbled himself and pleaded in righteous supplication. It is not possible that ﴿nabtahil﴾ means an evil supplication unless it is accompanied by something that indicates it. Is it clear, O people?
You say: "This man implored Allah in supplication," meaning he prayed for good but with urgency. So the correct view is that the meaning of ﴿nabtahil﴾ is that we humble ourselves and implore in supplication.
﴿fa-najʿal laʿnata Allāh ʿalā al-kādhibīn﴾: ﴿najʿal﴾ is coordinated with ﴿nadʿu﴾, because a rule has passed us: when coordinated items are repeated, the coordination is with the first, because the coordinated item is a branch and the item coordinated upon is the origin, and the item coordinated upon is the first.
﴿laʿnata Allāh﴾: ﴿laʿnat Allāh﴾ means His expelling and distancing him from mercy.
﴿ʿalā al-kādhibīn﴾: the liars among us or among you. This is justice and fairness, because Allah knows who the liar is; so if we make Allah's curse fall upon the liars, whoever is lying will bear the curse.
But what is the matter, or what is the wisdom, in bringing the sons and wives?
The wisdom in this is that when it is mutual cursing, the curse includes everyone; the curse includes everyone. Therefore, when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, called them to mubāhalah, the delegation of Najrān declined. They said: "We will consider," then they consulted among themselves and returned to the Prophet ﷺ the next day and said: "We will not curse each other." Why? Because they said: "If we cursed and returned to our families, we would not find them" (i.e., would be destroyed). So they did not curse. They knew that the Prophet ﷺ was upon the truth and that they were upon falsehood.
And His saying: ﴿upon the liars﴾: the liar is one who speaks other than the truth. This is the liar; whoever speaks other than the truth is a liar.
In this noble verse: confirmation that what the Prophet ﷺ brought is true; the proof of this is that Allah commanded him to invoke a curse with these people.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: mubāhalah is not permissible except with knowledge, meaning that a person must have certain knowledge; if he is in doubt, it is not permissible. So he must have knowledge, by His saying: ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of seeking mubāhalah when the opponent is obstinate, by His saying: ﴿So say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons"﴾ and so on to the end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the etiquettes of mutual cursing is bringing the women and children, because that is more frightening for the one invoking, who fears that destruction will encompass all of them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the permissibility of supplicating for the curse upon whoever opposes the truth, but by description, not by person. How did we say by description? Because "the liars" is a description. As for a specific person, it is not permissible to supplicate for his curse even if he is a disbeliever; one must not curse a specific person even if he is an unbeliever, because when the Prophet ﷺ cursed Abū Jahl and others among the tyrants of Quraysh, Allah forbade him from that and said: ﴿You have no part in the affair; either He will accept their repentance or punish them, for indeed they are wrongdoers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 128] [Related by al-Bukhari (4069) from the hadith of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of mubāhalah, but the scholars stipulated two conditions for mubāhalah:
The first condition: knowledge.
The second condition: that it be concerning a serious matter.
As for matters that are not serious, a person should not expose himself to danger.
Is it derived from this noble verse that a person may plunge into the enemy in combat, exposing himself to peril? This person who knows the truth is with him, and it is permissible for him to invoke a curse; it is as if he entered into a matter that could be the cause of his destruction. Yes. Since he is upon the truth, and we permitted him to enter into this matter, which is feared to be (for one who is lying) the curse falling upon him, yes. Perhaps it may be derived, but it is a distant inference.
A student: Do we take from it, regarding anyone who has heard of a point of knowledge, that he should convey it to his family?
The Shaykh: Yes? What? We take it from the verse.
The student: That is, we call our women.
The Shaykh: He says: is it derived from the verse that one should teach his family, his sons and his wives?
The students: It is not derived.
The Shaykh: It is not derived.
A student: Seeking help.
The Shaykh: Yes, that is, we bring them ourselves, we bring them at the time of mutual cursing.
A student: Shaykh, why did they (...) not have knowledge?
The Shaykh: Yes, they came while they had no knowledge.
A student: Shaykh, is it correct what the author of the Qāmūs said, that ibtahala includes both cursing and striving in supplication together?
The Shaykh: No, the correct view is the second only.
The student: It includes striving in supplication only.
The Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
A student: Among Muslims, is mubāhalah permissible or not?
The Shaykh: It is permissible in matters that are certain. For this reason Abdullah ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, called to mubāhalah in the well-known matter of the inheritance shares [Related by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (12457) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās].
A student: If, for example, the mutual cursers, for example, the people of one household, the one upon falsehood from his family... those from the opponent's family who are upon the truth...
The Shaykh: How?
