A student: From the family of the one upon falsehood, those who are (...) the family of the opponent who is upon falsehood; from his family are those who are upon the truth, meaning they follow this one who is upon the truth. If they engaged in mubāhalah, for example, and the curse descended, would it include them?
The Shaykh: (...) If they are upon the truth and say: "By Allah, we will not come to engage in mubāhalah, because that is upon the truth," they will not come.
The student: They fear their companion.

Ibn 'Uthaymin: No, *lā yakhshawā* (they should not fear). You say *lā*. This is why, when the delegation of Najran consulted among themselves, they said: "It is not possible," some of them [saying it] to the others.

Student: If we add the word *ḥaqīqatan* (in truth) to the definition of the liar, [would it be]: "one who speaks other than the truth in reality," so that *tawriyah* (equivocation) is excluded?

Shaykh: What? No, there is no need, because *tawriyah* is also called lying, as in the hadith that Abraham told three lies.[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3358) and Muslim (2371/154) from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Student: Is it permissible to curse a specific person?

Shaykh: It may be permissible if he died in disbelief. However, it may be said that it is not permissible, because the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Do not revile the dead, for they have gone to what they have put forward."[[Related by al-Bukhari (3358) from 'A'ishah.]] Leaving it is better.

Student: May Allah be good to you. So if I name a specific disbeliever and say: "May what he deserves from Allah be upon him"?

Shaykh: "O Allah, guide him." That is shorter and more beneficial.

Student: And if he dies?

Shaykh: When he dies, he will receive what he deserves, even if you did not supplicate.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative. And there is no deity except Allah. And indeed, Allah is the Exalted in Might, the Wise. (62) And if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters. (63) Say, "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords instead of Allah." And if they turn away, then say, "Bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ [Al 'Imran 62–64]

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative.﴾
His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾. As you see, this sentence is emphasized (with *inna* and the particle *lahuwa*).

Student: The benefits?

Shaykh: Yes?

Students: The benefits?

Shaykh: What benefits?

Student: The verse of *mubāhalah* (mutual imprecation). We had left out the benefits.

Shaykh: Good, the verse of *mubāhalah*. Read them to me.

Student: First: the affirmation that what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought is true. The reason is that Allah commanded him to invoke mutual curses with these people.

Second: *mubāhalah* is not permissible except with certain knowledge. If a person is in doubt, it is not permissible for him, because of His saying: ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾.

Third: the permissibility of calling for *mubāhalah* when the opponent is obstinate, because of Allah's saying, exalted is He.

Fourth: that among the etiquettes of mutual cursing is bringing the women and children, because that is more frightening in the case of *mubāhalah*.

Fifth: the permissibility of supplicating for curse upon those who oppose the truth, but by description, not by specific person, because "the liars" is a description. As for a specific person, it is not permissible to supplicate against him with a curse, even if he is a disbeliever, because the Prophet (ﷺ) cursed Abu Jahl and others of the tyrants of Quraysh... Allah forbade him from that.[[Related by al-Bukhari (4069) from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.]]

Sixth: the permissibility of *mubāhalah*, but the scholars stipulated two conditions for its permissibility. The first condition: knowledge. The second: that it be concerning a matter of importance. As for matters that are not important, a person should not expose himself to danger.

Seventh: Can it be derived from the noble verse the permissibility of a person plunging into the enemy in the context of fighting? Because this person knows that the truth is with him, and it is permissible for him to invoke mutual curses over a matter that could be the cause of his destruction. Since he is upon the truth and we permitted him to enter this matter, because it is feared that he might be lying and the curse would then apply to him... It may be derived, but its derivation is distant.

Shaykh: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narration﴾. As you can see, this sentence is emphasized by three emphatic devices. The first is (inna), since (inna) is for emphasis. The second is the lam. The third is (huwa), since (huwa) is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), and the separating pronoun has three benefits. The first benefit is restriction (ḥaṣr), the second is emphasis (tawkīd), and the third is distinguishing between an attribute (ṣifah) and a predicate (khabar).

This becomes clear through an example. If you say: "Zayd huwa al-fāḍil (Zayd is the most excellent)," here huwa is a separating pronoun. It has these three benefits. It conveys restriction: the excellence is restricted to Zayd. It conveys emphasis: your saying "Zayd al-fāḍil" without huwa is less emphatic about his excellence than "Zayd huwa al-fāḍil." The third is separating the attribute from the predicate. If you say "Zayd al-fāḍil," the listener's mind looks forward to a predicate: "Fine, Zayd the excellent, what is his condition?" But when you say "Zayd huwa al-fāḍil," it is known that the word al-fāḍil is the predicate.

Here, if it were in other than the Qur'an and it said "hādhā al-qaṣaṣ al-ḥaqq," the speech would be sound, but what would be lost from the speech? These three emphatics.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, the referent is what Allah mentioned concerning ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, peace be upon him. You know that Allah spoke about ʿĪsā ibn Maryam in these verses at extensive and lengthy length, about him and his mother.

As for His words: ﴿it is indeed the true narration﴾: al-qaṣaṣ is the verbal noun of qaṣṣa, yaquṣṣu, qaṣṣan and qaṣaṣan. Here it may be a verbal noun in the sense of the verb, and it may be a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, meaning: this is indeed the narrated matter that is true. Whether we say this or that, the meaning is one: this is indeed the true narration.

Al-ḥaqq here is an attribute of al-qaṣaṣ. If ḥaqq is said in contrast to a ruling (ḥukm), it means justice (ʿadl). If it is said in contrast to a report (khabar), it means truthfulness (ṣidq). This is due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'ām 115]. So if it is said to you: "The judge ruled on such-and-such a matter for so-and-so," and you say: "This is a true ruling (ḥukm ḥaqq)," the meaning is justice. And if it is said to you: "So-and-so informed us of such-and-such," and you say: "This is true (ḥaqq)," meaning truthful, then: if ḥaqq is in contrast to a ruling, it means justice, and if it is in contrast to a report, it means truthfulness. Here, is it in the sense of a report? That is, is it in contrast to a report or to a ruling? To a report, because qaṣaṣ is a report: ﴿Thus do We relate to you [O Muhammad] some news of what has passed﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 99].

﴿Indeed, this is the true narration﴾ means the truthfulness that does not contradict reality but rather corresponds to it completely. So what the Christians said about ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, insofar as it departs from Allah's report about him, is a lie and falsehood.

﴿Indeed, this is the true narration﴾. Then the Exalted said: ﴿And there is no deity except Allah﴾. As you see, this sentence also contains restriction and emphasis. As for restriction, its method is negation and affirmation: the negation is in His words ﴿mā (no)﴾, and the affirmation is in His words ﴿illā (except)﴾. As for emphasis, it is in His words ﴿min ilāh (any deity)﴾, since min is a preposition that is grammatically superfluous (ḥarf jarr zāʾid), but it adds to the meaning. It is grammatically superfluous, but it adds to the meaning. What does it add to the meaning? It adds emphasis to the meaning.

For this reason we say: the superfluous particles in the noble Qur'an are superfluous in a double sense: superfluous grammatically and superfluous in meaning. That is, they convey a meaning additional to what would be conveyed if they were not present.

As for His words ﴿mā min ilāhin illā Allāh (there is no deity except Allah)﴾: ilāh means maʾlūh (one who is worshipped). The maʾlūh is the one worshipped out of love and exaltation, and this is truly applicable only to Allah the Exalted.

The word ilāh here is on the pattern fiʿāl, but it has the meaning of maf'ūl (passive). This word, meaning ilāh in the sense of maʾlūh, or fiʿāl in the sense of maf'ūl, is common in the Arabic language, like ghirās (plantings, in the sense of planted), bināʾ (building, in the sense of built), firāsh (bedding, in the sense of spread out), and waṭāʾ (carpet), and what is similar to that. Ghirās means maghrūs (planted), bināʾ means mabnī (built), firāsh means mafrūsh (spread out), and ilāh means maʾlūh.

So what is the meaning of maʾlūh? We said: it is the one worshipped out of love and exaltation. This is the maʾlūh.

As for His words ﴿wa mā min ilāhin illā Allāh﴾: illā is an exception particle. The sentence preceding it contains an omitted element, whose estimated form is: "wa mā min ilāhin ḥaqqin illā Allāh (there is no true deity except Allah)." Accordingly, we parse the word ﴿Allāh﴾ as a substitute (badal) for the omitted predicate, whose estimated form is: "wa mā min ilāhin ḥaqqin illā Allāh." ﴿illā Allāh﴾ means the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Exalted. So ʿĪsā is not a deity, his mother is not a deity, Jibrīl is not a deity, Mīkāʾīl is not a deity, and no one deserves this description except the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Exalted. For this reason He said: ﴿There is no deity except Allah﴾.

Is this sentence emphasized or not emphasized?
* Students: Emphasized.
* Shaykh: With what? With the superfluous min, and it contains restriction, whose method is negation and affirmation.

﴿wa mā min ilāhin illā Allāh﴾. The word ﴿Allāh﴾ is a proper name specific to the Lord, the Exalted. It is not named by it other than Him, and it is not described by it other than Him. Originally it was ilāh, but because of frequent usage they dropped the hamza and said Allāh, just as they dropped the hamza in their saying al-nās (the people), whose origin is unās. And just as they dropped it in the words khayr and sharr: "fulān khayrun min fulān" means "akhyar minhu (better than him)," but because of frequent usage they dropped the hamza. Likewise sharr: ﴿Those are worse in position﴾ [al-Mā'ida 60], its origin is ashar, but the hamza was dropped because of frequent usage.

﴿wa inna Allāha la-huwa al-ʿazīz al-ḥakīm﴾. As you can see, this sentence also is emphasized by emphatics.
* A student: Inna, the lam, and the separating pronoun.
* Shaykh: Well done. That is, with three emphatics: inna, the lam, and the separating pronoun.

﴿wa inna Allāha la-huwa al-ʿazīz al-ḥakīm﴾. It contains emphasis by three tools: inna and the lam, and the third is the separating pronoun. As we said just now, the separating pronoun conveys restriction, so it means: ﴿la-huwa al-ʿazīz al-ḥakīm﴾, that is, not other than Him. ﴿wa inna Allāha la-huwa﴾, not other than Him, ﴿al-ʿazīz al-ḥakīm﴾. Al-ʿazīz is one of the names of Allah, glorified and exalted. To Him belongs all might, ﴿So to Allah belongs all might﴾ [Fāṭir 10].

The scholars said that ʿizza (might) has three meanings: ʿizza in the sense of esteem (qadr), ʿizza in the sense of overpowering and dominance (qahr wa ghalaba), and the third, ʿizza in the sense of inaccessibility (imtināʿ).

ʿIzza in the sense of esteem: that is, He, the Exalted, is of great esteem, and none can estimate Him except Allah the Exalted. From it is the saying of the speaker: "Fulān ʿazīz ʿalayya," meaning he is of esteem to me, he has a standing with me. So Allah the Exalted is ʿazīz in the sense of: possessing a lofty, great esteem. This is the ʿizza of what? Of esteem.

ʿIzzat al-qahr (might of dominance): that is, He, the Exalted, is the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered. From it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Give it to me [to take care of]; and he overpowered me in speech"﴾ [Ṣād 23], that is, he overpowered me in argument. This is the ʿizza of overpowering. And the first poet says:
Where is the escape, when the Seeker is God, / and the cut-nosed one is the vanquished, and the one who is not the victor.

The third: ʿizzat al-imtināʿ (might of inaccessibility): that is, He is inaccessible, so that no harm can reach Him. From it is their saying: "arḍ ʿazāz (a hard land)," because of its strength and firmness. So on this basis, ʿizza has three meanings. What is the first meaning?
* A student: ʿizzat al-imtināʿ.
* Shaykh: What do you mean?
* Student: That is: "dhū" (possessor of).
* Shaykh: No, ʿizzat al-imtināʿ is not "possessor of."
* Student: The first we said was esteem (qadr).
* Shaykh: ʿIzzat qadr. And the second?
* Student: Dominance (qahr).
* Shaykh: And the third? Ḥizza of what?
* Student: Overpowering (ghalaba).
* Shaykh: Esteem and dominance?
* Student: Overpowering.
* Shaykh: No, qahr is overpowering.
* Student: Inaccessibility (imtināʿ).
* Shaykh: ʿIzzat al-imtināʿ. Well, ʿizzat al-qadr?
* Student: Like when the speaker says...
* Shaykh: No, that's not its meaning.
* Student: That Allah the Exalted is of esteem to me.
* Shaykh: Yes, of esteem to me and lofty. And from it is the saying of the speaker?
* Student: The saying of the speaker: "Fulān ʿazīz ʿalayya."
* Shaykh: Yes. The second: ʿizzat al-qahr, what is its meaning?
* Student: That is, ʿazīz.
* Shaykh: Yes, but what is its meaning?
* Student: That is, overpowering.
* Shaykh: That is, the Overpowering. And from it is His saying, the Exalted?
* Student: ﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾ [Yūsuf 21].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿He said, "Give it to me [to take care of]; and he overpowered me in speech"﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿He said, "Give it to me; and he overpowered me in speech"﴾, that is, he overpowered me. Good, the third?
* Student: Inaccessibility, that is, Allah is inaccessible to any harm reaching Him.
* Shaykh: That is, Allah is inaccessible to any harm reaching Him. And from it is their saying?
* Student: "arḍ ʿazāz."
* Shaykh: "Arḍ ʿazāz," the hard land that tools do not affect.

When the hypocrites said: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will expel therefrom the more humble﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8], Allah granted them that, and said: "Yes, the more honorable will expel the more humble." But who is the more honorable?
* The students: Allah and His Messenger.
* Shaykh: He said: ﴿But to Allah belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿wa inna Allāha la-huwa al-ʿazīz al-ḥakīm﴾.

Al-ḥakīm is derived from ḥukm (judgment, rule) and iḥkām (perfection). Every mighty one whose might is accompanied by wisdom and rule is perfected in his might, because if the mighty one dominates and has no wisdom, his domination leads him to recklessness, and his domination leads him to recklessness and lack of self-restraint. When might and wisdom combine, the one described by them is perfected.

I say: al-ḥakīm is from ḥukm and iḥkām. He, glorified and exalted, is the Judge, and there is no judge other than Him, and He is the Perfecter, that is, the one who perfects what He has judged, whether the judgment is cosmic (kawnī) or legislative (shar'ī).

The iḥkām that means perfection is placing a thing in its fitting place, such that it cannot be said that this is not fitting or not suitable, but rather it is suitable and corresponds to what the benefit requires. So al-ḥakīm is derived from ḥukm and iḥkām.

Then we say: ḥukm is of two types: cosmic judgment and legislative judgment. The cosmic judgment is what Allah has decreed by destiny (qadar), and the legislative judgment is what He has decreed by law (sharʿ). Note: the cosmic judgment is what He decreed by destiny, and the legislative is what He decreed by law.

The difference between them is clear. The legislative judgment concerns what Allah loves, in action or abstention. If He forbids something, He loves its abandonment, and if He commands something, He loves its performance. The judgment that Allah has ruled may fail to be realized; this is the legislative judgment.

The cosmic judgment concerns what He loves and what He does not love, and it cannot fail; it must happen.

The difference between them, then: the cosmic judgment must occur, while the legislative judgment may occur and may not occur. The second difference: the legislative concerns what He loves, while the cosmic concerns what He loves and what He does not love.

This is illustrated by example. If Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not approach adultery﴾ [al-Isrā' 32], this is a legislative judgment. Is it possible that those addressed by the address do not commit adultery? Or they may commit it and they may not?

They may commit it and they may not. For this reason, we say about His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isrā' 23], the decree here is legislative, because we see many people, indeed most people, have not worshipped Allah, but have worshipped others, or have not worshipped anyone. So the decree here is legislative.

Second: does Allah decree by law what He does not love? No. He decrees only what He loves. If what He loves is abandonment, it comes in the form of a prohibition, and if what He loves is action, it comes in the form of a command: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and do not invalidate your deeds﴾ [Muḥammad 33]. Obedience to Allah and His Messenger is beloved to Allah; non-invalidation of deeds, what? It is beloved to Allah. The first is a command and the second is a prohibition.

﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him﴾ [al-Nisā' 36], the same thing: "worship" is a command, "do not associate" is a prohibition. So shirk is beloved to Allah to abandon, and worship is beloved to Allah to perform, the worship of Allah.

The cosmic decree, we said, occurs concerning what Allah loves and what He does not love, and it must occur. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We conveyed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture that you will cause corruption on the earth twice and you will [surely] become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [al-Isrā' 4]. Is this decree cosmic or legislative? Cosmic. It cannot be legislative, because Allah does not love corruption or corrupters, but it is cosmic. Did it occur or did it not occur? It occurred, yes: ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came﴾ and to the end of the verses [al-Isrā' 5].

Some of them say: the second time did not occur, and Allah knows best.

In any case, the cosmic decree concerns what He loves and what He does not love, and the decreed matter must occur; no one can fail to fulfill it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when We decreed for him death, nothing indicated to them his death except a creature of the earth﴾ [Saba' 14]. Is this cosmic or legislative? This is cosmic.

Judgment is sometimes cosmic and sometimes legislative. What is the cosmic? What Allah has decreed by destiny. And the legislative is what He has decreed by law, which the messengers brought.

Both cosmic and legislative judgment are accompanied by wisdom, because Allah is the Judge, the Perfecter. So His judgment cannot be except in accordance with wisdom.

Wisdom is either in form and configuration, or in purpose, and both are also present in the law and in destiny, that is, in law and in creation. The created things, their existence in this description and form in which they are now, is in accordance with wisdom, is it not? It is in accordance. That is, if you reflect on the universals and particulars, reflect on the human being in this description, there is no doubt that it is in accordance with wisdom. Then reflect on his small and great parts, you will find them all in accordance with wisdom.

We also find the law in accordance with wisdom. If you look at the prayer, behold, it is in the utmost wisdom, a garden among the gardens of worship: standing, sitting, bowing, prostration, recitation, glorification, exaltation, supplication, a garden: ﴿therein from every pair of a delightful kind﴾ [Qāf 7].

And if you look at zakāh, it is likewise. The fast, the Hajj: all the acts of worship, you find them corresponding to wisdom in the form they take, and then the purpose. The purpose of this creation or of this law is undoubtedly a praiseworthy end for which Allah, the Exalted, is praised: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and that between them in play. We did not create them except in truth﴾ [al-Dukhān 38–39]. So the purpose of the creation of the heavens and the earth is a praiseworthy purpose, and the purpose of the law is a praiseworthy purpose. There is no welfare for the servants except through the law that Allah has prescribed for them.

Then we say: on this basis it becomes clear that the discussion of (al-ḥakīm) includes four cases: cosmic judgment with formal and purposeful wisdom, and legislative judgment with formal and purposeful wisdom. The divisions are four, all taken from His saying: ﴿wa inna Allāha la-huwa al-ʿazīz al-ḥakīm﴾.

* In this noble verse there are benefits: the affirmation that what Allah reported about ʿĪsā ibn Maryam is the truth.
* Branching from this principle: whatever contradicts it, of what the Christians have said about ʿĪsā, is a lie and falsehood that does not correspond to reality.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that it is part of the eloquence of speech that it corresponds to reality, or is suitable to the situation (muqtaḍā al-ḥāl). Part of the eloquence of speech is that it is suitable to the situation. The reason: this sentence, ﴿Indeed, this is the true narration﴾, is emphasized by three emphatics, because the situation requires this, since the propaganda of the Christians is strong, and it is not refuted except by speech that is emphasized, either by words or by circumstances, that is, either by statement or by state. Likewise, it is appropriate for every person who speaks that if the situation requires that his speech be emphasized, then eloquence, or the requirement of eloquence, is that he emphasize it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that a narrative may be true and may be false. The narrative in itself, regardless of the narrator, may be true and may be false, a lie. From where is this derived?

From the description of the narrative as true (ḥaqq), because the principle regarding an attribute is that it distinguishes the described from what is other than it. This is the principle. For this reason, if an attribute comes that does not distinguish the described from others, they call it a descriptive attribute (ṣifah kāshifah), not a restrictive one (māniʿah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 62 (part 2 of 2):

So we say: ﴿The true narrative﴾. The basic principle is that ﴿al-haqq﴾ (the true) is an attribute of what kind? Is it restrictive or descriptive? It is restrictive, meaning it excludes everything other than it. On this basis, reports in general contain both falsehood and truth in terms of being reports. We qualified this with our statement "in terms of being reports" in order to exclude the report of whom? The report of Allah and His Messenger, for it admits of falsehood in no way at all.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is that there is no god in existence except Allah. But what is meant is: there is no true god. It is necessary that this be the intended meaning. Why? Because there are gods that exist and are worshipped besides Allah, and they are called gods. And the Quraysh, when addressing the Prophet ﷺ, denied the restriction of divinity to one God. Allah says: ﴿And the disbelievers say, "This is a magician, a liar. Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a astonishing thing"﴾ [Sad 4-5]. God is greatest! What is astonishing: that the gods should be one god, or that the gods should be many?
The second. This is the astonishing thing. As for the god being one, this is the correct view, but they are stubborn.

In any case, there is no true god in the universe (we must qualify this): no true god besides whom? Besides Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for false gods, they are false gods, and even if they are called gods, they are as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not but names that you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [An-Najm 23].

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that soundness of belief brings complete comfort, because when your belief is sound and you believe that there is no god but Allah, you will not turn toward anyone other than Allah. There is no doubt that this is comfort. The focusing of one's aim and purpose is among the greatest causes of a person's peace. When aims and purposes multiply, a person becomes confused. For this reason, it is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever has been blessed in something, let him stick with it."[1]

Whatever thing has been blessed for you, and in which you feel tranquil: a car, a house, a wife, a companion, whatever it is, stick with it, for it is better than moving from one thing to another. Some people say: "By Allah, today I read Zad al-Mustaqni', and tomorrow I study al-Muntaha, then al-Iqna', then al-Muhadhdhab, then al-Mudawwana of Malik." Each day they have a different book, and time passes for them without any gain. Why? Because their aim has not been unified. Likewise the polytheists: this one worships al-Lat, and if it does not benefit him, he goes to al-'Uzza, and if al-'Uzza does not benefit him, to Manat, and if positions do not benefit him, he takes three stones and makes them an idol for the kettle, and a fourth he makes into a god he worships. If it does not benefit him, he kneads a lump of dates, makes it a god, and if that does not benefit him, he goes to the sun and the moon.

In any case, when sound belief is that a person turns to no one but Allah and worships none but Allah, he finds complete comfort. For this reason He said: ﴿There is no god but Allah﴾.

* This also refutes the Christians who said that God is the third of three, because He said: ﴿There is no god but Allah﴾. What is strange is that, in the midst of the Christians' foolishness and error, they say: "The gods are three, yet they are one." How can three be one? If you make the three into one, it becomes one-third: a god who is a third, a second god who is a third, and a third god who is a third. But if each one is independent, and then you say they are one, this is a denial of reason.

So in the noble verse ﴿There is no god but Allah﴾ there is a refutation of whom? Of the Christians who say that the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, is God.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse is the affirmation of might, indeed complete might, belonging to Allah, by His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Mighty﴾. The definite article here (al-) indicates comprehensiveness, meaning all types of might belong to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

* Also in it: the affirmation of wisdom for Allah in His saying ﴿the Wise﴾, and also the affirmation of judgment.

* From this it follows that there is no judge but Allah. Sovereign and divine rule and legislative rule belong to Allah alone. Whoever dominates people by sovereign rule and does not answer to the Lord has shared with Allah, or has made himself a partner with Allah in this rule. Whoever legislates for people laws contrary to His law has made himself a partner with Allah and has taken for himself a position he does not deserve, because the one who legislates and judges is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed Allah, He is﴾ (not anyone else) ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾.

* It also follows from this that our duty toward Allah's cosmic and legislative decrees is submission, contentment, and acceptance, and not to seek anything else, because we know they are based on what? On wisdom. They are based on wisdom. For this reason, the righteous predecessors, may Allah be pleased with them, when Allah and His Messenger decided a matter, did not have any choice regarding their affair. Indeed, when they were asked about the wisdom, they answered: "Allah said and His Messenger said." When a woman asked 'Aisha: "What is the matter with menstruating women, that they make up the fasts but do not make up the prayers?" she said: "This used to happen to us, and we were commanded to make up the fasts, and we were not commanded to make up the prayers."[2]

And the believer in truth, the worshipper in truth, is the one who is content with what he does not know the wisdom of just as he is content with what he knows the wisdom of. This is the true believer. But one who is not content with Allah's judgment unless he knows its wisdom is, in reality, not a worshipper of Allah in perfect form, but a worshipper of his own desire. If the wisdom becomes clear to him, he is content; if it is not clear, he is not content.

For this reason we see that in the obligation of stoning the jamarat, which are the pebbles at a specific place, there is, along with establishing the remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, which the Messenger ﷺ specified, what? The completeness and perfection of servitude. Because a person carrying pebbles and throwing them at a specific place as an act of worship to Allah is among the perfection of servitude. A person praying, or avoiding adultery out of fear of Allah and hope for His reward in the prayer, has an obvious wisdom. But throwing pebbles at a specific place may not have an obvious wisdom, were it not that the Messenger informed us that it is for establishing the remembrance of Allah, and that in it is the completeness of servitude.

So the main point is that whenever you believe that Allah has wisdom in His cosmic and legislative judgment, you will increase in conviction and contentment with what He has decreed. As for the cosmic decree, it will be carried out upon you whether you are pleased or not. But the matter of greatest concern is the legislative decree, which depends on your choice. As for the cosmic decree, it is not by your choice; it will befall you regardless of the matter.

* Student: Shaykh, regarding the Jews, is the refutation of them when they said: ﴿Ezra is the son of Allah﴾ [At-Tawbah 30] that they made him a second god?

* Shaykh: No, this is not an explicit statement. It is not an explicit statement of divinity, because sonship is below the rank of fatherhood. But the Christians stated this explicitly. For this reason Allah says to 'Isa son of Maryam: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 116].

* Student: Shaykh, what is the difference between our saying hay'ah (form/appearance) and surah (image)?

* Shaykh: Hay'ah may be in actions and statements, while surah may be in bodies.

* Student: Shape.

* Shaykh: The shape of a body.

* Student: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ [Al 'Imran 62] (...) with the truth (...) the will.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: We emphasize the separation.

* Shaykh: No. This is derived from the wording. Who said it is emphasis? If you say "this is true," is there emphasis in it? The sentence itself has no emphasis, but "the truth" is understood from the meaning.

* Student: May Allah be good to you, Shaykh. If the Christians are asked: "How do you say that God is the third of three and the three are one god?" they say: "We do not take these details; we simply believe."

* Shaykh: Fine. Do you believe in something that has no reality?

* Student: He says: "This is unknown; we cannot ask. We believe in what has come."

* Shaykh: But this is part of your error, that you believe three have become one single thing. This is part of your error. If he were to say they are attributes, we would say yes, it is possible that He is described by a thousand attributes. But they say they are individual essences: 'Isa, his mother, and the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, have become one. How can they become one?!

* Student: Should a person seek the wisdom in matters whose wisdom was not stated in the Shari'ah, for reassurance?

* Shaykh: In any case, seeking wisdom for guidance is not objectionable. Seeking wisdom for guidance is not objectionable. For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ informed the women that they are the majority of the people of the Fire, they said: "Why, O Messenger of Allah?" They wanted to know the wisdom. He said: "Because you curse much and you are ungrateful to your husbands."[3] So one who asks about wisdom for reassurance is undoubtedly not at fault. But one who asks about wisdom in order to say: "If I know the wisdom I will accept, otherwise I will not accept," this person has not become a believer.

* Student: We said, Shaykh: the decree is cosmic and legislative. The cosmic decree includes what Allah loves and what He does not love, while the legislative decree is only about what He loves, and does not include what He does not love. He said: ﴿And do not approach adultery﴾ [Al-Isra 32]...

* Shaykh: What is the decree now?

* Student: ﴿Do not approach adultery﴾.

* Shaykh: It is a prohibition.

* Student: But adultery is not...

* Shaykh: Yes, it is disliked. But we said: what is beloved to Allah is either an action or an abandonment. If it is an abandonment, it is forbidden; if it is an action, it is commanded.

* Student: So it is legislative, but only regarding what Allah loves?

* Shaykh: Regarding what Allah loves. But Allah may love abandonment, so He forbids us, and He may love an action, so He commands us.

* Student: Shaykh, regarding the emphases in the Qur'an: the Qur'an, one believes it even without emphases. The wisdom...

* Shaykh: What do you all say about this?

* Student: I answered him.

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: An answer to the narratives...

* Shaykh: The brother says: if we believe the Qur'an whether it is emphasized or not, what is the benefit of emphasis?

* Student: The response.

* Shaykh: The response. Not everyone believes the Qur'an. He may say: if he is not a believer, whether it is emphasized or not makes no difference. We say: this is incorrect and not valid. First, because the Qur'an follows the style of the Arabs. Second, a thing that is emphasized must be accepted by souls more, even if they are believing souls; they must be convinced more.

* Student: Shaykh, the people of Najd call 'Abd al-'Aziz "'Uzayyiz," and some call him "'Aziz."

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Students: "'Azzuz."

* Shaykh: What is the question now?

* Student: That the attribute of might, meaning in a human being.

* Shaykh: Believers have might, and the Messenger has might, and a person who names his son "'Aziz" is like the one who named his son "Hakim" in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Among the Companions there was one named Hakim, and Hakim is a companion of 'Aziz. The meaning is that the one who gives the name does not intend the meaning from which the word is derived, but merely intends the proper name only. For this reason we say there is nothing wrong with it.

* Student: Shaykh, we discussed the legislative and cosmic decrees, each of which is connected to formal wisdom and final wisdom. What is formal wisdom, and...?

* Shaykh: It means that a thing being in this form is in accordance with wisdom. For example, a person walking on his feet is in accordance with wisdom, but if he walks on his head? That is not in accordance with wisdom.

* Student: And the final purpose?

* Shaykh: The final purpose is that Allah created people for worship...

* * *

* Student: ﴿But if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters. Say, "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords instead of Allah." But if they turn away, then say, "Bear witness that we are Muslims." O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Then will you not reason? Here you are—you argued about that of which you have knowledge; so why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge? And Allah knows, while you know not﴾ [Al 'Imran 63-66].

---

[1] Narrated by Ibn Majah (2147) from Anas, as a marfu' report: "Whoever obtains something, let him stick with it." Al-Zarkashi and others attributed it to Ibn Majah with the wording "Whoever has been blessed in something," but we have not found it as a musnad report from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.

[2] Agreed upon. Al-Bukhari (321) narrated it without mention of fasting, and Muslim (335/69) narrated it with his wording, from the hadith of 'Aisha.

[3] Narrated by al-Bukhari (304) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and by Muslim (79/132) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But if they turn away, then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters.﴾

He said: "﴿But if they turn away﴾: the pronoun refers to these Christians whom the Prophet ﷺ invited to mubahala (mutual imprecation, al-mubahala), ﴿Then say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us earnestly pray and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars."﴾ [Ali 'Imran 61]. It has already been mentioned that they refrained from mubahala, because they knew that if they performed it, the punishment would seize them, since the Messenger ﷺ is upon the truth and they are upon falsehood."

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, meaning from mubahala and from following you, O Muhammad, then they are corrupters. For this reason He said: ﴿then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters﴾, and He did not say "All-Knowing of them," but rather used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun.

Using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun has several benefits:

The first benefit: censure, or the applicability of the description in this explicit noun to the one to whom the pronoun refers. That is, this description placed in the position of the pronoun applies to the referent of the pronoun; it is as if He had said: "If they turn away, then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of them," but He described them with corruption.

The second benefit: generality. For if the pronoun had come here according to the context, "then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of them," the knowledge would be restricted to whom? To them alone. But when He says ﴿of the corrupters﴾, it becomes general, covering them and others.

The third benefit: that the act which occurred from these people, about whom the explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun, is a kind of this description which was expressed in the position of the pronoun. That is, their act is corruption, namely turning away and withdrawing from the religion of Allah.

From the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to whoever turns away from the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The indication of this is His saying: ﴿then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters﴾, because the purpose of mentioning His knowledge of them is to threaten them, and that their condition is not hidden from Him, and He will punish them according to what their condition requires.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: turning away from the religion of Allah is corruption, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum 41].

Is turning away itself corruption, or is it a cause of corruption?

The answer to this is that we say: it is both corruption and a cause of corruption. The reason it is corruption is that when one turns away from the religion of Allah, something else takes its place, and it is known that the religion of Allah is righteousness and whatever else is corruption. For this reason we find that the laws established among the servants of Allah do not reform people; only what agrees with the Shari'ah reforms them, while what contradicts the Shari'ah is corruption, however intelligent and understanding of human conditions the lawmakers may be, for when they establish laws that contradict the law of Allah, it is corruption in every case.

So turning away itself is corruption, and then it is also a cause of corruption, because drought, famine, constriction of provision and trials all have as their cause sins. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they might return﴾ [al-Rum 41].

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-A'raf 96].

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah presents an example: a town which was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the favors of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 112].

So turning away from the religion of Allah is, what? Corruption and a cause of corruption.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever turns away from the religion of Allah is a corrupter, even if he claims to be a reformer; the proof is His saying: ﴿then indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters﴾.

For this reason many exegetes, regarding His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ [al-A'raf 56], said: that is, do not corrupt it by sins.

So every disobedient person is a corrupter, whether he wills or refuses, and every person obedient to Allah is a reformer, because things are made clear by their opposites. If the disobedient is a corrupter, then the obedient is a reformer. However, the obedient person may in reality be righteous in himself without reforming others, or he may be righteous in himself and reform others. If he is a worshipper who calls to Allah, he becomes righteous and reforming; if he is a worshipper who does not call to Allah, he becomes righteous but not reforming, yet his righteousness is not complete, because part of complete righteousness is calling to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 64 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you﴾.

The address in His words ﴿Say﴾ is to the Messenger ﷺ. We have already mentioned a principle: when Allah the Exalted begins a matter with ﴿Say﴾ directed to the Messenger ﷺ, it implies particular care for that matter, because he is commanded to convey this matter what? For its particular importance. Otherwise, the entire Qur'an is something the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to recite.

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾: the People of the Scripture means the Jews and the Christians. Accordingly, the word "Scripture" here is used generically, so that it encompasses what? You mentioned that the intended meaning of the People of the Scripture is the Jews and the Christians, and you said: according to this, the word "Scripture" is generic, so that it is inclusive?
* Student: The Jews and the Christians.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: The Torah and the Gospel.
* The Shaykh: The Torah and the Gospel. So ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ means O people of the Torah and the Gospel. He addressed these people as People of the Scripture, or described them thus, because there are no revealed books whose traces remain except the Torah and the Gospel, and for this reason they were called the People of the Scripture. Otherwise, there is no messenger who did not come with a book through which he called people, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Scripture and the Balance﴾ [al-Hadid 25]. However, the books that have remained and left their traces, even though some alteration has entered them, are those that are in the hands of the Jews and the Christians.

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾: who is meant by them? The Jews and the Christians.
Here, if someone said to us: "﴿People of the Scripture﴾" — explain it by its meaning and by its wording?
We say: we explain it by its wording, namely, O owners of the Scripture, O you who have been entrusted with the Scripture. This is called literal explanation (at-tafsir al-lafzi). The explanation by intended meaning (at-tafsir al-muradi) means: who is intended by it? The Jews and the Christians. So the literal explanation is that by which a word is explained without regard to who is intended by it, while the explanation by intended meaning, which is the purpose of the speech, is who the speech is directed at.

﴿Come﴾: meaning, approach. Ta'ala (come) is an imperative verb, not an interjection (ism fi'l), contrary to what some grammarians claimed that it is an interjection. The evidence that it is a verb is the attachment of the subject to it, meaning the attachment of a pronoun to it, whereas an interjection does not take a pronoun. You say: (ta'alaw) to a group, (ta'alaya) to two, (ta'alayna) to a group of females, (ta'ali) to one female. Therefore it is a verb, meaning "approach." This differs from (halumma), which is an interjection. The evidence: it does not change and no pronoun attaches to it: ﴿And those who say to their brothers, "Halumma to us"﴾ [al-Ahzab 18], and he did not say: "halumma" with a plural suffix.

﴿Come﴾: approach to us. ﴿To a word﴾, which he explains with His words: ﴿that we worship none but Allah﴾. But he describes this word before explaining it: ﴿equitable (sawa')﴾. Sawa' means just, because sawa' here is a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, meaning level, without any unfairness in it, equal between us and you, and what is equal between opposites means that it is just, with no inclination in it from these or from those; it is equitable. So sawa' is a verbal noun used in what sense? In the sense of the active participle, meaning level between us and you, that is: just, with no inclination for us nor inclination for you.

﴿Between us and you﴾: the pronoun in ﴿between us﴾ refers to the Muslims, and ﴿and you﴾ refers to the People of the Scripture.
What is this word ﴿that we worship none but Allah﴾? This word is "equitable," and all the messengers agree upon this word, from Noah to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya' 25]. Since the messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, agree upon this word, then if we call you to it, this is justice without any unfairness. The equitable word between me and you is that we worship none but Allah. Accordingly, the position of His words ﴿that we worship none but Allah﴾ is in the genitive case, as an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to what? To ﴿word﴾. It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is what? That we worship none.

His words ﴿that we worship none but Allah﴾: "worship" means humble ourselves and submit to other than Allah the Mighty and Majestic; we do not submit or humble ourselves with complete, absolute humility except to Allah alone, the Mighty and Majestic. This is because worship (ʿibadah) is intended to mean absolute, complete humiliation and submission, and it is also intended to mean what is worshipped, that is, it is used with two meanings: it is used for the act of the servant, and it is used for the object of the servant's worship. Worship is used for the act of the servant and for the object of the servant's worship. If it refers to his act, it is humility and submission; if it refers to its object, it is the acts of worship that he performs, which Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah defined as: a comprehensive term for everything that Allah loves and is pleased with.

Here, ﴿that we worship none﴾ may be taken to include both of these meanings, or it may be taken to mean the act of the servant, that is, the servant's humbling and submission.
﴿but Allah﴾ alone. We derive oneness here from what? From the restriction (hasr), because "no" (la) is a negation and "but" (illa) is an affirmation, and when speech comes in this form of negation and affirmation, it indicates restriction.

Who disagrees with this? The Christians disagree; they do not worship Allah alone. They worship whom? Jesus and his mother. Likewise the Jews said: Ezra is the son of Allah.

﴿And not associate anything with Him﴾. ﴿And not associate﴾: association (ishrak) means equating. And ﴿anything﴾ is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it generalizes to everything. This is a confirmation of monotheism. How is it a confirmation? Because the intended purpose of this negation is to affirm the perfection of its opposite. Here what is negated is association, in order to affirm the perfection of its opposite, which is monotheism; that is, that we worship Him, the Mighty and Majestic, with a worship in which there is no association. This is because worship may contain association: a person may be worshipping Allah, but the worship is mixed with association. So when you say: "Worship your Lord and do not associate anything with Him," the worship becomes free of what? Of association.

For this reason we consider the second clause, ﴿and not associate anything with Him﴾, in meaning, as an emphasis of the monotheism in His words ﴿that we worship none but Allah﴾.

His words ﴿anything﴾ include whatever it may be, whether a human, an angel, a jinn, or an inanimate object; whatever it is. We derived this generality from what? From the fact that it is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, and an indefinite noun in the context of negation is general.

Let me give you an example that clarifies this: if I say to you, "Do something," and you do one of the things and leave others, is this general? No. "Do something": "something" here is not general, because it is indefinite but in the context of affirmation. But if I say, "Do not do anything," it becomes general, meaning whatever you do, you are in violation. For this reason, among their principles of jurisprudence, an indefinite noun in the context of affirmation is for unrestricted application (al-itlaq), and an indefinite noun in the context of negation is for generality (al-'umum).

An indefinite noun in the context of affirmation is unrestricted and in the context of negation is general. Is that right? I mentioned to you a moment ago: if I say, "Do something." Let us leave "do something" and give a clearer example: "Free a slave" (a'tiq raqabah). Is this for unrestricted application? That is, whatever slave you free, the command is fulfilled. "Do not free a slave": this is general; if you free any slave, you are in violation. And if you free any slave, it suffices. That is the difference. "Buy me a garment," and you buy a garment, any garment of the clothes: clean, dirty, new, red, black, any color. "Do not buy a garment": this is general; whatever garment you bring, I say: wrong. I said: do not buy. So an indefinite noun in the context of negation is general, and an indefinite noun in the context of affirmation is unrestricted.

He said: ﴿and not take one another as lords besides Allah﴾. This is justice, meaning: you should not make us, who make lawful and unlawful, impose on you what we make lawful and unlawful, and you should not impose on us what you make lawful and unlawful; because whoever makes lawful and unlawful and is obeyed has indeed been taken as a lord, as is reported in the hadith concerning His words: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 31]. Adi ibn Hatim said: "O Messenger of Allah, we do not worship them." He said: "Did they not make lawful what Allah had made unlawful, so you make it lawful, and make unlawful what Allah had made lawful, so you make it unlawful?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is their worship." [Reported by al-Tirmidhi (3095) from the hadith of Adi ibn Hatim.] The matter is evident: obedience to others in making lawful and unlawful is association in obedience and in legislation.

So He says: ﴿that we worship none but Allah and not associate anything with Him﴾: this is with regard to worship. ﴿And not take one another as lords besides Allah﴾: this is with regard to legislation, meaning: we do not oblige you with what we say, and you do not oblige us with what you say. So, then, who is the reference?
* The students: Allah.
* The Shaykh: For this reason He said: ﴿besides Allah﴾. As for when it is by Allah's permission, then you oblige us and we oblige you. We have not said: make us lords, so that we impose what we wish on you, or we make you lords, so that you impose on us what you wish, besides Allah. But if this is by Allah's permission, His revelation and His legislation, it is obligatory upon you.

So this is the complete justice in worship and what? And in legislation. We do not oblige you, and you do not oblige us, with anything besides Allah. ﴿And not take one another as lords besides Allah﴾. This is the complete justice and fairness in argument and debate: that the word be equitable, neither wronging us nor being wronged by us.

﴿But if they turn away﴾: they refuse and do not come to this equitable word. Then declare it yourselves, so that they may bear the sin. For this reason He said: ﴿But if they turn away, then say, "Bear witness that we are Muslims"﴾, meaning: submitting completely to Allah, and we will not heed you. Thus this verse calls the Jews and the Christians to what? To monotheism, Islam, and justice: come, present yourselves, approach: ﴿a word equitable between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, and not associate anything with Him, and not take one another as lords besides Allah﴾. This is justice. ﴿But if they turn away﴾: for they do not desire good. Declare it yourselves: ﴿then say, "Bear witness"﴾. Look at the challenge: ﴿"Bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ When we make them bear witness that we are Muslims, it is a declaration that they are not Muslims, that they are not Muslims; for if they were Muslims they would submit to this equitable word between us and them. It is known that if they submitted to this word, it would necessarily oblige them to believe in the Messenger ﷺ, Muhammad; for the one who brought the correct worship is Muhammad, and the one who brought the righteous legislation is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

In this noble verse, the Messenger ﷺ is commanded to call the People of the Scripture to this equitable word, by His words: ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture﴾.

Here is a question: Did the Messenger say that? Yes, he said it, and he even wrote it to the kings. When he wrote to Chosroes, and others wrote: ﴿O People of the Scripture, come to a word equitable between us and you﴾, but he said: ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture﴾ out of perfection of his manners. When he says ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture﴾, it is as if he is saying: I have written this verse to you by the command of whom? By the command of Allah. But if he had said: "O People of the Scripture" without "Say," there would have been a possibility that he wrote it on his own.

The point is that the Messenger ﷺ said that, called them to this word, but they refused and rejected it, because they are obstinate and stubborn, except those whom Allah guided: Allah guided some of the Christians, some of the Jews, and some of the polytheists.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: condescending to the opponent in order to bind him to the truth. How is that? Because He said: ﴿equitable between us and you﴾, although the truth is with whom? There is no doubt that it is with the Messenger ﷺ. But for the sake of binding the opponent and establishing the proof against him, I condescend to him and say: let us settle on a word of justice between us and you.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to use justice in debate, even with an enemy; for the Messenger was commanded to declare this, and if this is obligatory in debate between Muslims and disbelievers, it is even more binding and emphatic in debate among Muslims themselves. For this reason we say: it is a great error that some people, when they hold an opinion, say: whatever differs from it is wrong, and they declare others in error. It may be an error from the standpoint of his belief, and we do not object to it; that is, if he says: "This view is wrong from the standpoint of my belief," we do not object, because it is known that if he chooses its opposite, then in his view it is wrong, and he is not to be censured for that. But the censure is that he declares the one who holds it to be in error. This is a subtle distinction: between my believing that this view is wrong and I do not adopt it, and between my declaring the one who holds it to be in error; for if I declare him in error, I claim infallibility for myself and fallibility for him, and this is an error, this is the error. For this reason, in debate among Muslims, as in debate between Muslims and disbelievers, it is obligatory that it be conducted with justice. It is known that the just balance in this is the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger.

But the difficulty is that not everyone understands the Book and the Sunnah as they should. Some people are purely literalists, who do not look to the objectives of the Shari'ah and its great meanings by which the creation is reformed. You find, for example, that some people want to enforce some matters that are not considered of great importance in Islam, even if a great and significant benefit is lost thereby. Among them are the disputed matters in which conflict and estrangement among Muslims become apparent, and there are many examples of this that you can understand. You find, for example, some people saying: we must enforce this, even if it is merely a Sunnah, and even if its enforcement entails the division and enmity of the Muslims and the arising of hatred among them. They do not consider that the Shari'ah in reality is founded upon harmony and the unity of hearts. It forbade selling over the sale of a Muslim because that leads to enmity and hatred; najsh (inflating a price); proposing over the proposal of one's brother. Many other things: if you reflect on them, you find that this Shari'ah aims at people becoming united, hearts being agreed, and aims being unified, and that minor matters, if discord is feared from them, are left aside. And praise be to Allah: are you blamed if you leave the lesser for the greater? You are not blamed; rather you are praised. Blame lies in doing the lesser so as to neglect the greater; this is the blame. For this reason we know with certainty that the Companions were far more knowledgeable than us, and more upright than us in their deeds, and that they were far more intensely attached than us to the Shari'ah of Islam; and yet some of them agreed with one another in matters they did not themselves hold, for the sake of the benefit, the harmony of the people, and the agreement of hearts.

It is not hidden from you that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refrained from demolishing the Ka'bah and rebuilding it upon the foundations of Ibrahim, although this was what he wished for, and he had intended it, out of fear of what? Out of fear of discord; for the Quraysh were recently converted from disbelief [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1583) and Muslim (1333/401) from the hadith of 'A'ishah]. And the Prophet ﷺ would leave what he loved for the benefit of the people. He would fast while traveling, and when it was said that the people were finding it hard, what did he do? He broke his fast after the 'Asr prayer, and he raised water while on his camel, on his thigh, and drank while the people watched [reported by Muslim (1114/90) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah; we have not located the wording "on his thigh"]. He did not say: "By Allah, I am fasting," when only a small part remained, wishing to complete it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 64 (part 2 of 3):

As for the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), during the caliphate of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), he shortened the prayer in Mina for seven or eight years of his caliphate. How long did his caliphate last? Twelve years. After most of his caliphate had passed, he saw, for some reason, that he should complete the prayer, so he completed it. When this reached those Companions who heard of it, they objected to him, saying: "How is it that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and 'Umar, and you in the early part of your caliphate, shortened the prayer, and now you complete it?" So much so that when Ibn Mas'ud heard of it, he said the words of return: «Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1084) and Muslim (695/19), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]], as if it were a great matter. Nevertheless, they prayed behind him, praying four rak'ahs while believing that this was contrary to the Sunnah. Why? For the sake of unity of the word and avoidance of division. When Ibn Mas'ud was asked: "How do you object to the action of 'Uthman and yet pray behind him four rak'ahs?" he said: «Disagreement is evil»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1960) and Abu Ya'la (5377), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]. This is jurisprudence (fiqh), by Allah, this is jurisprudence, this is the Shari'ah...
That is, there are people who are purely literalist (zahiri), who do not look at the objectives of the Shari'ah (maqasid al-shari'ah) and its great meanings, which aim at the reform of creation. You find, for example, someone who wants to enforce some matters that are not considered of great importance in Islam, even if a great and significant benefit is lost thereby. Among them are the disputed matters in which conflict and opposition appear among the Muslims, and there are many examples that you can understand. You find, for instance, some people saying: "We must enforce this matter, even if it is a Sunnah, and even if its enforcement leads to the division and enmity of the Muslims and the arising of hatred among them." They do not consider that the Shari'ah in reality is founded upon harmony and the bringing together of hearts. It prohibited selling over the sale of a Muslim, because that leads to enmity and hatred; najash (artificial bidding); proposing over the proposal of one's brother; and many other things. If you reflect on them, you will find that this Shari'ah aims at people being united, hearts being in accord, and objectives being unified, and that minor matters, if they are feared to cause strife, are to be abandoned. Praise be to Allah. Would you be blamed if you abandoned the lesser for the greater? There is no blame on you; rather, you deserve praise. Blame lies in doing the lesser so as to neglect the greater. This is the blame. For this reason we know with certainty that the Companions were far more knowledgeable in jurisprudence than us, more upright than us in their deeds, and that they loved the Shari'ah of Islam more than we do. Yet some of them would conform to one another in matters they did not themselves hold to be correct, for the sake of benefit, the harmony of the people, and the agreement of hearts.
It is not hidden from you that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refrained from demolishing the Ka'bah and rebuilding it upon the foundations of Ibrahim, even though this was what he wished for, and he had intended it. He refrained out of fear of what? Out of fear of strife, because the Quraysh were recently converted from disbelief[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1583) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, and by Muslim (133/399) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]].
The Prophet (ﷺ) would leave what he loved for the benefit of the people. He would fast during travel, and when it was said that the people had been burdened, what did he do? He broke his fast after 'Asr, and he raised the water while he was on his camel, on his thigh, and drank while the people were watching[[Narrated by Muslim (1114/90) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, and also (710) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]]. He did not say: "By Allah, I am fasting," when only a small part remained, wishing to complete it.
As for the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), during the caliphate of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), he shortened the prayer in Mina for seven or eight years of his caliphate. How long did his caliphate last? Twelve years. After most of his caliphate had passed, he saw, for some reason, that he should complete the prayer, so he completed it. When this reached those Companions who heard of it, they objected to him, saying: "How is it that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and 'Umar, and you in the early part of your caliphate, shortened the prayer, and now you complete it?" So much so that when Ibn Mas'ud heard of it, he said the words of return: «Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return»[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1084) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, narrated by Muslim (695/19) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and narrated by Abu Dawud (1960) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]], as if it were a great matter. Nevertheless, they prayed behind him, praying four rak'ahs while believing that this was contrary to the Sunnah. Why? For the sake of unity of the word and avoidance of division.
When Ibn Mas'ud was asked: "How do you object to the action of 'Uthman and yet pray behind him four rak'ahs?" he said: «Disagreement is evil»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1960) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and narrated by Abu Ya'la in his Musnad (5377) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]. This is jurisprudence, by Allah, this is jurisprudence, this is the Shari'ah. As for people dividing and quarrelling, not dealing with one another justly, and saying: "My view is the truth, your view is wrong, and you are mistaken," this is not the path of the Shari'ah. This is contrary to the Shari'ah, even if whoever holds to it claims that he is upon the Shari'ah, that he is the one who proclaims the truth, and that he is infallible. His claim is what has made him mistaken.
Whoever claims infallibility, the first slip he makes is what? His claim of infallibility, and that he is correct and others are in error.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: all the Messengers agree upon this word: "We worship none but Allah, and we associate nothing with Him." Because, as long as it is a common word between us and them, its meaning is that it is with them as it is with us. This is the reality: all the Messengers agree upon what? This word: "We worship none but Allah, and we associate nothing with Him."
Indeed, Allah says in His great Book: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 51:56]. This creation, which was created from Adam, and the jinn before Adam, were created only for this great matter: the worship of Allah. They were not created to enjoy themselves in this world, to attain desires. No, but to worship Allah. Yet when they worship Allah, their worldly affairs are also made righteous. But the son of Adam's view is deficient. The strange thing is that when religion is made righteous, the world is made righteous, but the righteousness of the world does not necessarily entail the righteousness of religion. Indeed, if the world is given more attention than religion, religion may be corrupted. As the Messenger (ﷺ) said: «By Allah, I do not fear poverty for you. Rather, I fear that the world will be opened to you, and you will compete for it as those before you competed for it, and it will destroy you as it destroyed them»[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (3158) from the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Ansari, and by Muslim (2961/6) from the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Ansari.]].
* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: that judgment belongs to Allah among people, and that no one has the right to legislate apart from Allah. This is from His saying: ﴿and that some of us should not take others as lords besides Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:64].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that judgment and worship are linked, judgment among people and worship are linked, because Allah joined them together: "[that] we worship [none but Allah]" and "[that] some of us should not take others as lords besides Allah." Because you will not worship Allah except by His legislation. So the legislator must be who? Allah, the One worshipped. As long as you worship Allah, you will not worship Him except by His Shari'ah. Therefore, the legislator is the One who is worshipped, because He laid down a path, or set a path, saying: "Follow this so that you may reach Me." Thus every path that contradicts it will not lead to Allah. This is the aspect of the mutual necessity between His saying: ﴿that we should not worship﴾ and ﴿nor should some of us take others﴾. Whoever takes a lord besides Allah and follows him in declaring lawful and unlawful has not worshipped Allah, because the worship of Allah is not realized except by conforming to the Shari'ah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever calls people to make something lawful or unlawful, but by the permission of Allah and His legislation, he is upon the truth. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿besides Allah﴾. Pay attention. He did not say only: ﴿that some of us should not take others as lords﴾, but said ﴿besides Allah﴾. So when I call you to make something lawful or unlawful, but by the permission of Allah, I say: "This is the Shari'ah of Allah," I have not called you to take me as a lord, but I have only shown you the way so that you may take the Lord, who is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Student: Shaykh, some people, when you say "it is not permissible," say: "(...) scholars (...) said such-and-such." Are you more knowledgeable than them?
* The Shaykh: These people have a resemblance to those about whom Allah says: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 43:23]. This is indeed dangerous in reality, but the layman may not be blamed for it, because he does not trust you. This point, I think, we discussed once, and we said: one who mocks the Shari'ah cannot be declared a disbeliever, or one who mocks it among those who have knowledge of it cannot be declared a disbeliever. Because we find the common people now, if a certain person says "this is the Shari'ah of Allah," they accept it and say: "This is settled." If they see this man acting upon something as worship, they follow him. But if the same statement comes from someone else, they do not accept it, they do not trust him. Indeed, some people, out of extreme obstinacy and hatred toward others, say to their children, for example: "If you act upon this, I will beat you, abandon you, and do such-and-such," but if someone other than this man said it, they would accept it.
These common people may be excused in some respects. If they say: "By Allah, our scholars did not say this," such people should be accommodated.
* Student: Students of knowledge (...).
* The Shaykh: No, students of knowledge have no right to that, and these are not students of knowledge at all. The student of knowledge who wants to attain knowledge, these people are imitators, they are imitators. They are not students of knowledge. The student of knowledge is the one who wants to reach knowledge. We say: "Come, please. You are now citing these scholars. Do you have evidence for what they said? Bring it, and we will bring the evidence we have, a common word, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said here." This is if he is a student of knowledge. But if he is a layman, then the layman should be handled gently, little by little, like scattered camels. If you make a clanging noise behind scattered camels in a tin, they become more agitated and you can never control them. But if you calm them, they come.
* Student: Some people, when some scholars slip, for example, and make mistakes, write about them in magazines and newspapers rather than in debates, on the pretext that they are clarifying the truth?
* The Shaykh: This is wrong. This is from harshness. In reality this act is harmful in three respects:
The first respect: it is harmful to the writer, because those who trust the other person see that this one is mistaken, and his standing decreases in their eyes.
There is also in it a weakening of the one who is refuted, a weakening of him. It is well known that when the standing of the scholars in the Ummah is weakened, the Ummah is lost, because the scholars are the leaders. When their standing among the common people is weakened, they are lost, and they become like camels without a shepherd, or like sheep without a shepherd.
There is also in it a weakening of the Shari'ah, because when a scholar who refutes or is refuted says something other than this issue, people doubt and say: "Perhaps this is from the error of so-and-so," yes, or "Perhaps this is from the error of so-and-so." So it causes harm in three respects.
The obligation upon scholars among themselves, when someone among the people errs, is that they should contact him and discuss with him. If the truth is with him, they follow him; if the truth is with them, he follows them. Then, even if it is supposed that he insists on what he holds, and he has a valid point, because it is a matter of ijtihad (independent judgment), I do not see that he should be refuted at all. Because matters of ijtihad, the give-and-take and the debate about them among the common people, there is no doubt that it is harmful, especially in this time. Now, among the scholars there are people, as I have heard, who call for diminishing the standing of the scholars, speaking against them in gatherings and in everything. Why? Because they have lost the leadership they desire. So they have become like the other leaders who opposed the call of the Prophet (ﷺ). When they lost the leadership they wanted, they have no way to what they want except to weaken the other side. This is on a very great danger. So I see that if an error is found in any scholar, and a person is not infallible, a person errs, and the error may not become clear to him except through discussion, he should contact him and examine the matter with him. If the truth becomes clear, it is obligatory upon the one to whom the truth has become clear to follow it. If it does not become clear, and the matter remains one open to ijtihad, then the obligation, praise be to Allah, is this... All the scholars have differed from the time of the Companions until our day. As for the give-and-take and occupation with give-and-take, this is a waste, it wastes much time.
* Student: On the program "Noor 'ala ad-Darb" on the Holy Quran Radio, the question comes in the form: "What is the view of the Shari'ah, or what is the ruling of the Shari'ah in your opinion?" and the mufti may answer wrongly or correctly, but attributes the error to the Shari'ah, depending on the question?
* The Shaykh: (...) When they say: "What is the view of the Shari'ah," I forbid them from this. I am one of those who speak on this program, and I forbid them from this. I say: Do not say "What is the view of the Shari'ah." I am not expressing the Shari'ah. I am not a Messenger who is infallible. Say: "What is your view," or "What is the view of the Shari'ah in your opinion." I see that the Shari'ah says such-and-such, and I may err or be correct, and my error is not from the Shari'ah; my error is from me.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, can it be derived from the verse that debate is better than written replies?
* The Shaykh: Yes?
* The Student: Can it be derived from the verse that verbal debate is better than replies in writing and from the pulpits?
* The Shaykh: Yes, we will see this. We have not completed the verse. In any case, debate may be, as I said, face to face, and it may be by correspondence. The methods differ, and these return...
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords instead of Allah." But if they turn away, then say, "Bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ (64) ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham while the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Then will you not reason?﴾ (65) ﴿Here you are—you argued about that of which you have [some] knowledge, so why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge? And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ (66) ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was one inclining toward truth, a Muslim [submitting to Allah]. And he was not of those who associate others with Allah.﴾ (67) ﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham among the people are those who followed him and this prophet and those who believed, and Allah is the ally of the believers.﴾ (68) [Ali 'Imran 3:62–68]
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. I think we took the benefits derived from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, come to a word"﴾? Did we take seven benefits from it?
* Student: Up to ﴿and that some of us should not take others as lords besides Allah﴾.
* Student: The first: the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to invite the People of the Scripture to this word; from His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture"﴾.
The second: condescending to the opponent in order to bind him to the truth; from His saying: ﴿a word equitable between us and you﴾.
The third: the obligation to use justice in debate, even with an enemy.
The fourth: that all the Messengers agree upon this word.
The fifth: that judgment belongs to Allah among people, and that no one has the right to follow anyone besides Allah.
The sixth: judgment among people and worship are linked, because Allah Exalted said: [that] we [not] worship and [nor] some of us [take] others.
The seventh: that whoever calls people to make something lawful or unlawful, but by the permission of Allah and His legislation, he is upon the truth, derived from His saying: ﴿besides Allah﴾.
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But if they turn away, then say, "Bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾
* Among the benefits of this verse: that if the opponent turns away after the proof has been established against him, then he is declared free of him and committed to the truth; from His saying: ﴿Bear witness that we are Muslims.﴾
