So ﴿muslimā﴾ here means a Muslim to Allah outwardly and inwardly, so it includes both faith and Islam.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾: this is an emphasis of His saying ﴿ḥanīfan﴾. That is, although this clause is conjoined by waw, in meaning it emphasizes what preceded: he was not of those who associate partners with Allah, neither hidden shirk nor manifest shirk. Rather, he fought against shirk and was patient in calling to tawḥīd until he was thrown into the fire, peace be upon him. But his reward for that was that it was said to the fire: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 69].

﴿And he was not of the polytheists (67). Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham﴾: this is the ruling among these disputants. The disputants are three: the Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims. Observe the ruling of the just Judge: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾. He placed first what should have been the predicate, and made the subject, which is the pillar of the sentence to which the predicate is attributed, the thing He said: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾, and He did not say: "Indeed, those who followed him are most worthy of him," in order to decide that the priority belongs to these and not to others.

﴿The people most worthy of Abraham﴾, among the Jews, the Christians, the polytheists, the idol-worshippers and others, are: ﴿those who followed him﴾.

Here we ask about the lām in His saying: ﴿lalladhīna﴾, and what is its i'rab?
* A student: A preposition.
* The Shaykh: A preposition? No, the lām of the preposition is pronounced with a kasra in such a case.
* A student: For emphasis.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 65–68 (part 2 of 4):

* The Shaykh: For emphasis, yes indeed, for emphasis, and "inna" also is for emphasis, so this is a sentence emphasized with two emphatics: with "inna" and with the lam.
He says: ﴿Indeed, the closest of mankind to Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe﴾. "For those who followed him" means from the Children of Israel, those who preceded the Prophet ﷺ. And there is no doubt that many believers followed him, those who believed in him during his lifetime and those who followed his way after his death. "And this Prophet" — look, Allah is greater — refers to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and it is enough honor for him that the Lord of the worlds points to him: "this Prophet." This is a great honor for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Allah points to him with this demonstrative which conveys nearness. He did not say "and that Prophet," but said "and this Prophet," indicating his nearness, because he ﷺ is the closest of people in rank to Allah, the Exalted.
﴿And this Prophet and those who believe﴾. There is a reading: ﴿an-Nabiyy'﴾ — how is that? On this reading, ﴿an-Nabiyy'﴾ is derived from an-naba' (news), so it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il and also in the sense of maf'ul, right? In the sense of fa'il, because he informs and reports; and in the sense of maf'ul, because he is informed. For this reason Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, described the Messenger: "He is the truthful, the one who is believed"[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3208) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and related by Muslim (2643/1) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]. So it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il, and fa'il in the sense of maf'il. There remains for us how fa'il can mean maf'il? Fa'il in the sense of maf'ul is common, like jarih (wounded), kasir (broken), qatil (slain). Common. But fa'il in the sense of maf'il, how is that? We say: yes, this has been reported; and what is before us now is evidence for this. It is known that the Messenger informs people, is it not so? So it has come in the Qur'an, and the Qur'an is proof. And if you want to bring a proof from the speech of the Arabs, listen to the words of the poet:
"Does the sweet-voiced one of Rayhana, the caller, keep me awake, while my companions are sleeping?"
(Amin Rayhana al-da'i al-sami') — "al-sami'" here means "al-musmi'" (one who makes to hear).
So this "sami'" is in the sense of "musmi'" in the language of the Arabs. However, in reality we do not need a citation from the Qur'an to prove that this is the language; rather, the Qur'an is cited as evidence and is not itself in need of evidence. But it is known that the more proofs there are, the more a person gains tranquility. So, on the reading ﴿an-Nabiyy'﴾, may we read it? Yes, we may, and indeed it is recommended to read it sometimes. On this reading it is from an-naba' (news). As for the reading "an-Nabiyy" without hamza, there are two views:
The first view: it is a softened form of "an-Nabi'" with hamza, softened, meaning the hamza was made into a ya' for ease. This exists in the Arabic language: for example, "a'imma" is said in Arabic as "ayimma," softening the hamza into a ya'. So "an-Nabiyy" — its origin is "an-Nabi'," but the hamza was made into a ya' for lightness. On this view, "an-Nabiyy" comes from where? From an-naba' (news).
It is said: the ya' is original, not softened, so "an-Nabiyy" is derived from an-nubuwwah, which means a raised, protruding thing. It is said: naba yanbu, meaning he rose up. So it is derived from an-nubuwwah, which is elevation, because of the elevated rank of the Prophet; for the Messengers, peace be upon them all, and the last of them Muhammad ﷺ, are the highest in rank with Allah. For this reason Allah began with them in the mention of those whom He favored: ﴿So those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets﴾ [an-Nisa' 69].
If someone says: make it from both: from an-naba' and from an-nubuwwah? What do we say to him? We say: is it possible? It is possible; because the preferred view is that if a word admits two meanings without contradiction, it is taken to both, since that is broader in meaning. But with contradiction, one looks to the preferred meaning and takes it. However, where it is possible to combine, it is obligatory to take both meanings together.
If someone says: this is the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings — do you know the homonymous word? The homonym is a word whose form is one but whose meanings are many, like 'ayn: 'ayn is said of the eye (the one in your face is an eye), and it is said of a flowing spring — what is it? 'ayn al-ma' (a spring of water), and it is said of gold: 'ayn (gold), 'ayn waraq (silver), and for this it is said: 'ayn mawrudah and 'ayn manqudah; the manqudah is gold and the mawrudah is water. And do we say 'ayn makhulah? Yes, possibly; the 'ayn makhulah is the eye which is in the face.
Some scholars say: a homonym cannot be taken in both its meanings, because each of its meanings contradicts the other. But the correct view, which most scholars hold, is that it is permissible to take it in both its meanings on condition that there is no contradiction; if they contradict, it is necessary to seek the preferred meaning.
* A student: Shaykh, the verses do not confirm that the Qur'an... (...) our saying.
* The Shaykh: We have not completed the verses in truth; perhaps we will leave these four verses all for discussion in the benefits.
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you! The second view on ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ — does it mean he was not fanatical as you are fanatical?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it means he was not on the path of the Jews and Christians.
* The student: How, that he was not fanatical?
* The Shaykh: It means he was not on your path; that is, if you are truthful that you are on the path of Abraham, or that Abraham is on your path, then follow Muhammad.
* The student: But their saying: fanatic, how...
* The Shaykh: For example, now, the one who adopts the school of a people is not attributed to them?
* The student: Certainly.
* The Shaykh: Is that so or not? So these Jews are fanatical about their religion, and the Christians are fanatical about their religion. Abraham — we do not say that he was a fanatical Jew or a fanatical Christian; Abraham, peace be upon him, was a Muslim devoted to Allah, he was not fanatical for Judaism or Christianity.
* The student: But we said: if he had come to the time of the Messenger ﷺ, he would have embraced Islam.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is known.
* The student: He was a Muslim originally; how would he embrace Islam?
* The Shaykh: This is the establishing of proof against these Jews and Christians.
* The student: Yes, he embraced Islam meaning he left his law and followed the law of Muhammad?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he leaves his law and follows Muhammad, yes.
* Student: His saying: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾ — does it not support the second view, that by your claim you are upon his religion and he was not upon yours?
* The Shaykh: He said: it may be, it may be even according to that.
* The student: So the Torah and the Gospel did not occur until after his death?
* The Shaykh: Yes, and likewise those who say: we are upon the way of Abraham; and Abraham — they say: he was fanatical, he did not depart from his religion; this is the meaning of their saying: "upon their way."
* The student: How, Abraham worshipped with them while they...?
* The Shaykh: They say: (...) their particular worship, that is, their way, that is, upon their way.
* Student: Shaykh, Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Here you are, those who argued about what you had knowledge of; but why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾ Although in both matters they have knowledge. But in the first, that is... if you could clarify?
* The Shaykh: No, in the matter of Abraham, peace be upon him, they have no knowledge; because whoever says about Abraham that he was on the path of the Jews and Christians, or on the religion of the Jews and Christians, has no knowledge of that; he is ignorant, whether he said it with compound ignorance or simple ignorance. If he knew the reality of Abraham, peace be upon him, he would know that he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim.
* The student: Could he be obstinate, Shaykh, meaning he knows that this...?
* The Shaykh: Perhaps some of them, perhaps some of them are obstinate.
* Student: May Allah reward you with good, Shaykh. You said: if Abraham, peace be upon him, were alive, he would have abandoned his religion and followed Muhammad. Is not his religion the very same religion as Muhammad's?
* The Shaykh: The methodology differs; the root of the religion of all the prophets is one; the tawhid, the foundations of religion, are one for all the prophets. But Allah says: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48], and we recited it during the lesson; but because you (...)
I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan. We continue the discussion on the end of the noble verse: ﴿And this Prophet and those who believe. And Allah is the Walī of the believers﴾. His saying: ﴿And this Prophet﴾ is conjoined to his saying: ﴿those who followed him﴾, so it is in the nominative position; rather it is marfu'; "an-Nabiyy" is a badal (apposition) of the demonstrative, and the demonstrative, as we know, is built on sukun.
He says: ﴿And those who believe﴾ — believe in whom? They believe in this Prophet, and belief in the Prophet ﷺ includes belief in all his law, and this belief also necessarily entails acceptance and what? And submission; that one accepts what the Prophet ﷺ brought and submits to him.
Then He says: ﴿And Allah is the Walī of the believers﴾ — the Walī of every believer; these and others; every believer, Allah, the Exalted, is his walī, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Walī of those who believe; He brings them out of darknesses into the light. But those who disbelieve — their protectors are the taghut; they take them out of the light into darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah 257]. This walāyah is a special walāyah which requires that He make the believer easy toward ease and keep him from hardship; and there is a general walāyah encompassing everyone: Allah, the Exalted, is the walī of everyone. For this Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect. Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am 61-62]. So Allah, the Exalted, made Him a mawla for these, though they are disbelievers, but this is by the general walāyah.
The general walāyah is the walāyah of disposal, of disposal in the universe and management; and the special walāyah is the walāyah of care for the one under protection, that Allah, the Exalted, cares for him and makes him easy toward ease and keeps him from hardship.
In these noble verses there are many benefits. ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ This is the beginning of the benefits; ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ until the end. * In this verse are the following benefits:
First: a rebuke to these, I mean the People of the Scripture, for arguing and disputing about Abraham, peace be upon him.
* And among its benefits also: the exalted status and rank of Abraham among all the groups: the Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims.
* And among its benefits: the demonstration of argument by reason; from His saying: ﴿Why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him?﴾ How then do you argue with it when the Torah and the Gospel were revealed only after him? And this is contrary to reason.
* And it follows from this benefit: that one should not neglect reason in inference, just as one should not rely on it and abandon the text. People in their use of reason are of three positions: one extreme went to excess in it, to the point of preferring it over revelation; this applies to jurists who are proponents of opinion and analogists who rely on opinion even if it contradicts the text; and in the domain of creed, all people of innovation rely on reason and claim it over revelation, although the reason they rely upon is nothing but doubts, not proofs and evidences; there is no indication in it, but they think that reason requires such-and-such and so they affirm it, and reason requires the negation of such-and-such and so they negate it, and they do not refer back to revelation in this. Among them are the Ash'aris, the Mu'tazilah, and others; everyone who negates an attribute which Allah affirmed for Himself by an argument or a rational doubt — on the more sound view, it is not a proof, it is a rational doubt — is included among those who go to excess in using reason.
And among people — the second position — are those who rejected reliance on reason altogether and said: reason has no role in establishing any ruling or any report; so they rejected analogy, like the people of the literal (Zahiriyyah), who rejected it entirely and said: it is impossible for us to refer to reason in anything.
And among people are those of the middle position, who referred to reason in what does not contradict the sharia; because when reason does not contradict the sharia, Allah, the Exalted, refers to it in many matters, such as: ﴿Do you order the people to righteousness and forget yourselves while you recite the Scripture? Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah 44], and like this verse: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him. Will you not reason?﴾ And Allah's argument for the resurrection of the dead by the revival of the earth after its death is a sensory rational argument: it is sensory because it is observed, and it is rational because by it one infers its counterpart which does not completely differ from it.
So the summary is that in this verse reason is considered an evidence, but as I said: on condition that it does not contradict the sharia; if it contradicts the sharia, then the more correct view is that we say it is not reason; the more correct view is that we say it is not reason, because sound transmitted text never contradicts clear reason.
But if one supposes that reason contradicts revelation, then either there is no real contradiction, or the revelation is not established, or the reason is not sound, polluted by doubts and desires.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that the Torah and the Gospel were sent down from Allah; from His saying: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾.
If someone says: how do you derive from this verse that the Torah and the Gospel were sent down from Allah, given that the verb here, ﴿were revealed﴾, how does the inference from this verse stand that the Torah and the Gospel are sent down from Allah, since the verb... complete it.
* A student: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾.
* A student: The verb is in the passive voice.
* The Shaykh: The verb is in the passive voice, yes? Good, what is the answer to this?
* The student: From His saying: "from Him" (min 'indih).
* The Shaykh: How did you know it?
* The student: (...) Allah says: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue﴾, because the addressee is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the speaker is Allah: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him?﴾
* Student: Shaykh, descent comes from above, and elevation only comes by His permission, blessed and exalted is He.
* The Shaykh: That is not it, no, that is not it.
* Student: We say: the Qur'an explains itself by itself; by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44].
* The Shaykh: That the Qur'an explains itself by itself is correct, and in this same surah at its beginning: ﴿And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran 3], in the same surah. So the one who sent down the Torah and the Gospel is Allah, and then we say: the verb was made passive for the knowledge of the one who sent it down, who is Allah. If it is said: how did you know that it was sent down? We say: from the same surah at its beginning: ﴿And He revealed the Torah and the Gospel, (3) from before as guidance for the people﴾ [Al 'Imran 3-4].
This is like His saying: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa' 28] — who created him? Allah; but He omitted it because it is known. But since weakness is an attribute of deficiency, the verb here was made passive, just as it was made passive in His saying: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10]; they did not attribute evil directly to Allah, He said: ﴿whether evil is intended﴾, and they attributed right guidance directly to Allah: ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them right guidance﴾.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation. Now that it is established that the sending down is from Allah, descent can only be from above.
Can we derive from this verse that the speech of Allah is connected to His will?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, how?
* The student: That the sending down of the Torah occurred after Abraham, and this is by the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 65–68 (part 3 of 4):

* The Shaykh: This is by the will of Allah, yes. There is no doubt that the Torah was sent down from Allah, but Allah wrote the Torah. For this reason some scholars said: "We cannot establish that the Torah is the speech of Allah, but Allah undoubtedly wrote it, and it was sent down from Him." As for the Gospel (Injil), it is like the Qur'an: there is nothing stating that Allah wrote it; He said "He sent it down" (anzalahu), and it is speech, so it is His speech. As for the Torah, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of every matter an admonition and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ [al-A'raf 145].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the address to the Children of Israel with the charge of foolishness, and that their conduct, just as it opposes what is transmitted (al-manqul), it also opposes what is reasoned (al-ma'qul). Whoever wishes to know the foolishness of these people should refer to the book Ighathat al-Lahfan min Masa'id al-Shaytan by Ibn al-Qayyim. He mentioned amazing things of the foolishness of the Angry Nation and the Misguided Nation. The Angry Nation are the Jews, and the Misguided Nation are the Christians. He mentioned amazing things. Even if there were nothing else, Allah the Exalted censured their intellects in this verse and in the verse: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves, while you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah 44]. So the Jews are an angry, ignorant nation, as far from right guidance as can be.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the praise of reason ('aql), and that reason does not lead its possessor except to rectitude and correctness, by His saying: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾. The meaning of 'aql here, as we mentioned in the tafsir, is the reason of right conduct (aql al-rushd), i.e., the reason of behaviour by which one attains rectitude, not the reason of comprehension (aql al-idrak) which is the basis of accountability (manat al-taklif). For these Jews and Christians have reason; the reason of comprehension, which is the basis of accountability, is established among the Jews and Christians, and were it not so, they would not have been held accountable.
Then He said: ﴿Ah, you are those who argued about what you have knowledge of, so why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of? And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the descent to the level of the opponent (al-tanazzul ma'a al-khasm). That is, suppose that argument was accepted from you concerning what you have knowledge of, yet argument concerning what you have no knowledge of is not accepted from you.
* Among its benefits: the condemnation of arguing without knowledge, by His saying: ﴿so why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾. How much this sorry, bitter reality exists in our time! Many people today argue about what they have no knowledge of, indeed by what their deficient reasons demand. One says, for example: "Why did this happen, and why did that happen? Why was this forbidden and that permitted? Why was this obligatory and that not obligatory?" and the like. They argue about what they have no knowledge of. And many of the common folk who have eloquence and expression, and eloquence is a kind of magic, many of them dispute with a student of knowledge over a matter they themselves do not know, merely for the sake of disputation and wrangling.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of a person arguing with knowledge, but on condition that his intention is good, such that by the debate he seeks to reach the truth, his aim being to reach the truth, establishing what is true and refuting what is false.
As for one who argues, even about what he has no knowledge of, while his intention is to refute the truth and establish falsehood, there is no doubt that he is blameworthy: ﴿And those who argue concerning Allah after He has been responded to, their argument is void with their Lord, and upon them is anger, and for them is a severe punishment﴾ [al-Shura 16].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of knowledge for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿And Allah knows, while you know not﴾, ﴿And Allah knows, while you know not﴾.
* Among its other benefits: that one who argues about what he has no knowledge of has no knowledge, even if he argues; by His saying: ﴿while you know not﴾. Rather, he has no reason either, because argument is a branch of knowledge; whoever argues without knowledge has no reason, just as he has no knowledge.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge in the present. ﴿Yaʿlamu﴾ (He knows) is a present-tense verb, and the default of the present tense is that it is applied to the present and the future; it may be restricted to the past, and it may be restricted to the future. It is restricted to the past when (lam) precedes it, and restricted to the future with (sa) and (sawfa), this being an example. When it stands alone, it is suitable for both present and future. Here He says ﴿yaʿlamu﴾, meaning that His knowledge, Mighty and Majestic, is continuous and permanent, while you know not ﴿and you know not﴾.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a Hanif, a Muslim﴾ and so on to the end. Among the benefits of this noble verse: the absolving of Abraham from the religion of the Jews and Christians, or from the path of the Jews and Christians. As we mentioned that the verse has two meanings, there are two opinions. Abraham, peace be upon him, did not follow the religion of the Jews, because the religion of the Jews came after him, nor the religion of the Christians, because the religion of the Christians came after him. Likewise, Abraham, peace be upon him, was not like the Christians and Jews who fanatically cling to what they are upon, rightly or wrongly; rather he was a Hanif, a Muslim, submitting to the command of Allah, acting by the command of Allah and refraining by the prohibition of Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever does not possess a quality should make clear his innocence of it, even if that quality is in its origin praiseworthy. But if he does not possess it, it is obligatory to make it clear, because Allah negated that Abraham was a Jew or a Christian, even though Judaism after the mission of Moses, and Christianity after the mission of Jesus, were truth before they were abrogated.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the praise of Abraham, by His saying: ﴿but he was a Hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾. The aspect of praise for him is that He described him with pure monotheism, which is not mixed with any kind of shirk, by His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the indication of what is well known among people, that clearing away (al-takhliyah) comes before adorning (al-tahliyah), that is, beginning with negation before affirmation, because negation is clearing away and affirmation is adorning, i.e., establishing. Here He began with negation, which is ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾, then affirmed in His saying: ﴿but he was a Hanif, a Muslim﴾.
The apparent point is that this order accords with nature, because you first clear a thing of what disfigures it, then add to it what perfects it. When you want to clean a dirty garment, what do you do? You remove the dirt first, then add what brings perfection. In the hadith of the opening supplication: "O Allah, distance between me and my sins as You distanced between the east and the west. O Allah, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of filth. O Allah, wash me of my sins"[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (744) from Abu Hurayrah, and by Muslim (598/147) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. So distancing is not to commit sins and transgressions, cleansing is that this harm be removed, and washing is that it be purified and cleaned. Is this order clear? Let me give an example to make it plain: a person has filth and wants to place it on a prayer mat. I say: "Do not place it." This is distancing, is it not? Distancing: he does not place it. Another came with it and placed it, and I said: "Remove it." This is cleansing. The third level: after removing it there may be a trace in its place; I say: "Wash it."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that monotheism requires two things: negation and affirmation. The negation is in His saying: ﴿but he was a Hanif﴾, and the affirmation is in His saying: ﴿a Muslim﴾, because the Hanif is one who inclines away from shirk and from every religion that opposes Islam, and Islam is the affirmation of submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He emphasized this by His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾. Monotheism is not complete except with affirmation and negation, and the reason is very clear: negation alone is a nullification (ta'til), and affirmation without negation does not prevent partnership, so combining them is affirmation together with negation of partnership.
Let us give an example: if you say: "There is no one standing here," this is negation. Does it contain affirmation or not? If there is someone standing now? "There is no one standing here" is nullification; that is, the attribute of standing is now nullified, no one is characterized by it.
If you say: "Zayd is standing," this is affirmation that Zayd is standing, so you have affirmed standing now for one of the people, but does this statement prevent someone other than Zayd from standing? It does not prevent it; there may be another person other than Zayd standing. Therefore, if I say, "Zayd is standing," and you say, "And 'Amr is standing," is your statement considered a rebuttal of my statement or an addition to it? An addition to it. If you say, "No one is standing except Zayd," this contains negation and affirmation, and then monotheism is achieved: who is the one uniquely standing? It is Zayd. So it becomes clear that there is no monotheism except with negation and affirmation. For this reason, here, the Exalted said about the description of Abraham: ﴿but he was a Hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Islam, when mentioned absolutely, includes faith (iman), or when mentioned alone includes faith. The reason is that Allah described Abraham with Islam, and it is so: when Islam is mentioned alone, faith is included in it, and when faith is mentioned alone, Islam is included in it. When they are mentioned together, they become distinct: Islam is the outward act and faith is in the heart.
In the hadith of Jibril, they were combined and then distinguished, and for this reason the Prophet ﷺ explained Islam by one thing and explained faith by another thing.
In His saying: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [al-Hujurat 14], they were combined and then distinguished, so the faith they claimed became other than the Islam Allah affirmed for them: ﴿but say, "We have submitted."﴾
In His saying: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers. But We found not there except one house of Muslims﴾ [al-Dhariyat 35–36], they were combined and then distinguished. The bringing out was only of the believers, but the house was a house of Muslims. How is this? Who was brought out? Lut and his family, except his wife, his wife. So those who were brought out were the sincere believers. The house includes its people who believed with sincere faith, and his wife who betrayed him; she is a Muslim but not a believer. Thus the whole house, considering the whole, is Muslim, and for this reason He said: ﴿But We found not there except one house of Muslims﴾.
As for one who claims that Islam is faith and takes evidence from the verse, he has strayed far, because of the difference between the two expressions: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers﴾, and He did not say "of the Muslims"; He said ﴿of the believers﴾, and ﴿But We found not there except one house of Muslims﴾.
So, Islam here, in the noble verse ﴿but he was a Hanif, a Muslim﴾, does it include faith or not?
* Students: It includes it.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because it was mentioned alone.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the praise of Abraham, peace be upon him, that there was in him no attribute of the polytheists. For this reason He said: "he was not of the polytheists," and did not say "he was not a polytheist." So there was in him no attribute of the polytheists at all, neither shirk nor anything else. Likewise, it is fitting for every believer not to be characterized by any attribute of the polytheists. For example, among the attributes of the polytheists is shirk, which is clear; among the attributes of the polytheists is their hatred of monotheism. Do the polytheists hate monotheism or not?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, and they deny it, and they say: ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Sad 5]. So whoever hates monotheism, even if he is not a polytheist, has among him attributes of the polytheists; indeed he may be a disbeliever.
Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham among the people are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believed; and Allah is the Protector of the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 68]. In the verse is evidence that priorities differ, that is, people vary in precedence through priority and allegiance (wilayah). By His saying ﴿the most worthy (awla) of the people﴾, and "awla" is a comparative noun, and comparison indicates a preferred party and a non-preferred party. There is no doubt that wilayah has degrees. The most worthy of the people with wilayah toward Abraham are those who followed him, meaning the people who followed him in his time, because those who followed him in his time followed him in the root of the religion and in its branches, in its great and its subtle matters. For this reason He placed those who followed him before the Prophet and those who believed, because the Prophet ﷺ and those who believed did not follow Abraham in the branches of the Shari'ah; rather ﴿To each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48]. But they followed him in the root of the religion and in submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Otherwise, there is no doubt that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is better than those who followed Abraham, without doubt; indeed, the followers of the Messenger are better than the followers of Abraham.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the honour of the Prophet ﷺ and of those who believed with him, in that they are the most worthy of the people of whom? Of Abraham, whom nations contend over, each nation saying: "I am more worthy of him."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the Jews and Christians, who claimed that they were the most worthy of the people of Abraham, and Allah refuted them.
Among its benefits: the honouring of the Prophet ﷺ by the reference to him from the Lord of the worlds, in His saying: ﴿and this Prophet﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the prophethood of the Messenger ﷺ, which is a matter beyond doubt, and everyone described with prophethood in the Qur'an is a messenger. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa 163], then He said of those prophets: ﴿messengers as bringers of good news and warners﴾ [al-Nisa 165]. So everyone described with prophethood in the Qur'an is a messenger, by the evidence of the verse of al-Nisa: ﴿messengers as bringers of good news﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's wilayah for the believers, in His saying: ﴿and Allah is the Protector of the believers﴾. This wilayah, as we said just now, is a special wilayah, requiring complete care, and whoever is more complete in faith, Allah's wilayah for him is more complete.
(Whoever is more complete in faith, Allah's wilayah for him is more complete.) This is a benefit; from where did we derive it?
From a well-known principle among the scholars, which is: a ruling attached to an attribute increases in strength with the strength of that attribute. This is a useful principle: every ruling attached to an attribute, this ruling grows stronger with the strength of the attribute to which the ruling is attached. If you say, for example: "I love the righteous," it means that whoever is more righteous is more beloved to me, because love is attached to righteousness; as righteousness increases, love increases. ﴿And Allah is the Protector of the believers﴾: wilayah is attached to faith, so whenever a person is stronger in faith, Allah's wilayah for him is more complete and more special.
* From this benefit it follows that a person should realize and perfect his faith to the extent of his ability, so as to attain Allah's wilayah, because every person in reality who is sensible seeks to have Allah as his Protector.
We say: the matter is easy. Realize your faith and Allah will be your Protector; and as your realization of faith increases, Allah's wilayah for you increases. Otherwise, all of us seek that, and we ask Allah to make us and you among His friends. We all seek this. But just realize the faith: whoever loves for Allah's sake, hates for Allah's sake, allies for Allah's sake and opposes for Allah's sake, he attains Allah's wilayah by that. This is one of the causes of wilayah: that your love, your hatred, your dislike, your enmity and your allegiance be for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, not for the worldly life.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes (al-asbab). Affirmation of causes: from where is this derived? ﴿And Allah is the Protector of the believers﴾. The aspect of this is that Allah made faith a cause for Allah's wilayah, and there is no doubt that causes are established. Causes are legal, rational and sensory. Legal causes are those Allah the Exalted made causes in the Qur'an. For example, faith is a cause for entering Paradise; this is a legal cause, is it not? The arrival of the time is a cause for the obligation of prayer; this is a legal cause. Honey is a cause for healing.

If you say, for example, "I love the righteous," the meaning is that whoever is more righteous is more beloved to me, because love is attached to righteousness. So as righteousness increases, what increases? Love increases. ﴿And Allah is the Protector of the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 68]. Protection (wilayah) is attached to faith, so the stronger a person's faith, the more complete and more special Allah's protection of him becomes.

From this benefit it follows that a person should realize and perfect his faith as much as he can, so that he may attain Allah's protection. Every person of sense in reality seeks to have Allah as his Protector. We say: the matter is easy. Realize your faith and Allah will be your Protector, and as your realization of faith increases, Allah's protection of you increases. Otherwise, all of us seek this. We ask Allah to make us and you among His protected friends. All of us seek this, but just realize your faith. Whoever loves for the sake of Allah, hates for the sake of Allah, allies for the sake of Allah, and opposes for the sake of Allah, attains Allah's protection by this. This is among the means of attaining protection: that your love, your hatred, your aversion, your enmity, and your allegiance be for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and not for the world.

* From the benefits of this noble verse is the affirmation of causes. From where is this derived? ﴿And Allah is the Protector of the believers﴾. The basis of this is that Allah made faith a cause for Allah's protection, and there is no doubt that causes are established.

Causes are legal (shar'iyyah), rational ('aqliyyah), and sensory (hissiyyah). Legal causes are those which Allah Most High made causes in the Qur'an. For example, faith is a cause for entering Paradise. Is this a legal cause or not? The arrival of the time is a cause for the obligation of prayer; this is a legal cause. Honey is a cause for healing. This is a divinely decreed matter which we know through the Law, that is, through revelation. Is rain a cause for the growth of the earth's plants? That is a sensory cause.

* Students: Legal and sensory.

* Shaykh: Yes. Allah informed us of it, but we observe it. Suppose there were no Qur'an to guide us to this; we would have witnessed it ourselves, so it is a sensory cause.

Natural medicines that are discovered through experiment are sensory causes. As for rational causes, they are very numerous. Everything that follows from something by reason is what? A rational cause. The legal, sensory, and rational causes are all effective in themselves, since Allah placed effectiveness within them.

I say this because some people went to extremes in transcendence (tanzih) and said: causes do not have effect in themselves; rather, the effect occurs at them, not through them. So they say, for example: burning is not by the fire, but burning occurs at the contact of the fire with something that can be burned. If I made the fire burn and transform a thing from what it was at first, I would have affirmed a creator alongside Allah and become a polytheist. Who turns this stick into ash?

* Students: Allah, Glorified and Exalted.

* Shaykh: He says: none can do this except Allah. If you said that the fire turned it, you would have associated others with Allah. Therefore do not say: the fire burned it; say: it burned at it. You take a stone and throw it at a glass cup, and it shatters. He says: do not say the stone shattered it. Who can separate these tightly joined parts except Allah? So if you say the stone is what broke it, you have become a polytheist. Thus affirming the effect of causes is shirk. He says: it broke at it, not by it; it broke at the stone, not by the stone. Glory be to Allah! If you place a very, very heavy stone on glass, will it break or not?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: Strike it with a small stone and it breaks. So how can you say: at it? If it were at it, then if we placed a large stone it would break, and if we struck it with a small stone it would not break.

But we say: causes are effective, but Allah placed this effect in them. It is Allah who placed this effect in them. Were it not that Allah placed this effect in them, they would not have had any effect. This is why, when Abraham was thrown into the fire, Allah said to it: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [al-Anbiya' 69]. Did it have an effect? It did not have an effect.

So we now know that Allah made causes effective in themselves, not that they create or were created by themselves. Rather, Allah placed in them this power by which the caused effect comes about. Is this clear, everyone? This is what is reasonable. We do not go to extremes in affirming causes and say that this happens without Allah, nor do we go to extremes in transcendence and say that causes have no effect and the effect merely occurs at them. Both positions are wrong.

The middle position is generally the truth, because you find extremists, each taking one side of the truth and abandoning the other side, while the middle position takes both sides and so is the middle.

* Student: We said: when faith increases, Allah's protection increases, for example... (...) He says: the Prophet (ﷺ) (...) intense repetition. As we also said, from the increase of faith is love for the sake of Allah and hatred for the sake of Allah. Then he mentioned in (...) things that a person cannot increase or decrease in, such as believing in Allah and His angels?

* Shaykh: No, no. But is the faith of people in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers equal?

* Student: But now I cannot. As for me, as a believer, I individually am a person who believes in these matters. How can I increase in them?

* Shaykh: But is your faith like the faith of the second and the third?

* Student: No, of course not.

* Shaykh: Even your faith on one day is not like your faith on another day.

* Student: But how can I increase in them? Faith in Allah.

* Shaykh: You do increase in them. Sometimes a person comes with a strength of faith as if he were seeing the matter with his own eyes, and sometimes, with heedlessness, it is not like this.

* Student: Does he mean here, Shaykh, in relation to now, that the Prophet (ﷺ) specified the matters a person believes in?

* Shaykh: Very well: that you believe in Allah and His angels, down to the end of the six pillars. Do people equal one another in faith regarding these six matters?

* Student: They are not equal.

* Shaykh: Then whenever your faith in these grows stronger, Allah's protection of you increases.

* Student: (...) love and hatred.

* Shaykh: Yes, love for the sake of Allah, because of your faith in Allah, you loved for the sake of Allah.

* Student: O Shaykh, regarding causes: when one of the sick goes to the charlatans (mush'iwidhun), we say that healing occurred at him, not by it, meaning by its cause. What is the difference between this and the first?

* Shaykh: Because Allah did not make the words of charlatans a cause. We say: either the Law, the senses, or reason must testify that this is a cause. As for simply that a charlatan comes and speaks to us, we do not accept it. For example, if someone said: I call upon this saint and I am answered. A woman says she never conceives, goes to the grave of this saint, rolls upon it, takes some dust from it, places it in her private part during intercourse, and Allah wills that she conceive. Do we say: this happened by the dust of this saint?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: Why? Because this is not a legal cause, nor a sensory cause, nor a rational cause. Therefore it must be established that this thing is a cause. That is why amulets (tama'im) are shirk. Why? Because they are not a sensory, legal, or rational cause.

* Student: There is the matter that the prophets agreed on the root of tawhid and differed on the branches of religion. Some people cite their disagreement on the branches of religion as evidence for permitting the plurality of Islamic groups, provided they do not differ. But if they differ?

* Shaykh: Indeed, yes. I agree with them on the plurality of Islamic groups if each leader of these groups says that he is a prophet!! We agree with him on this!! If he claims to be a prophet, we say: there is no harm. But as for our Prophet being one and our religion being one, we cannot accept this principle. A plurality of Islamic groups, never. These would be independent prophets. If their leaders claim to be prophets, then so be it, with all respect. But they do not claim this; they are the furthest of people from this claim.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 65–68 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ The apparent meaning is that this verse is separate from what precedes it, and that it is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He says: ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians. They were singled out with this description because they are the ones whose books remained intact and by which guidance could be sought, until the Prophet ﷺ was sent.

His saying: ﴿Why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ The interrogative here is for denunciation and reproach. We all know that ﴿لِمَ﴾ (li-ma, "why") is an interrogative attached to the preposition lam, and that the interrogative (ma) when it is preceded by a preposition loses its alif. In (lima) there is no alif. ﴿عَمَّ يَتَسَاءَلُونَ﴾ [An-Naba' 1] has no alif either, and (ʿalā mā, "on what") likewise has no alif, and (ʿalā) changed on its account, because (ʿalā) is normally written with its alif as a yā, but when it enters upon the interrogative (mā) its alif is written as what? As an alif: (ʿalāma), like the lam.

His saying: ﴿لِمَ تُحَاجُّونَ﴾ means you dispute (tukhāṣimūn). The disputing was called muḥājja (arguing) because each of the disputants presents his proof, wishing to overcome his companion. And his saying: ﴿لِمَ تُحَاجُّونَ فِي إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ means: concerning his affair, his condition, and his religion. It does not mean concerning his essence, because Abraham, peace be upon him, was a human being about whom there is agreement and no dispute. Rather, it is an argument about his affair and his condition: why do you argue about him?

And what is the manner of this argument?

The manner of this argument is according to two opinions of the scholars:

The first opinion: their claim that they are upon the creed (millah) of Abraham. They all say: "We are upon the creed of Abraham." The Jews say: "We are upon the creed of Abraham," and the Christians say: "We are upon the creed of Abraham."

The second aspect, which is the second opinion: they argue about him because the Jews say: Abraham was a Jew, upon the religion of the Jews, and the Christians say: Abraham was a Christian, upon the religion of the Christians. This aspect is the reverse of the previous one, because in the previous aspect they claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham, while in this aspect they claim that Abraham was upon their religion.

Now let us look at the context of the verse: which of these two aspects does it support? ﴿Why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him?﴾ How can you argue about him and say that Abraham was upon our religion, or say that we are upon the religion of Abraham? How is the argument? And how could Abraham be upon your religion when the Torah had not yet been revealed, O Jews? And how could Abraham be upon your religion when the Gospel had not yet been revealed, O Christians? Or you say that you are upon his religion while you follow the Gospel, and the Gospel is not the religion of Abraham; or upon his religion while you follow the Torah, and the Torah is not the religion of Abraham. Abraham had a specific law: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a method﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 48]. So how do you argue about this? You claim that Abraham was upon the Torah or upon the Gospel, or you claim that you, who hold to the Torah or who hold to the Gospel, are upon the religion of Abraham, although the Torah and the Gospel were revealed only after him. Is this reason, or is it nonsense? It is nonsense and folly. How could Abraham be upon the religion of a book that had not yet been revealed? The Torah was revealed to Moses, and the Gospel was revealed to whom? To Jesus, and they came many ages after Abraham, so how could Abraham be upon this?

For this reason He said: ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ The hamzah is for reproach, an interrogative for reproach, meaning: Will you not have minds with which you reason about what you say? This carries the utmost blame and reproach.

﴿أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ occurs often in the Qur'an, and it has passed us that the grammarians have two opinions concerning it. Who will explain them to us? There are two opinions concerning its i'rab (grammatical analysis) ﴿أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾?

* A student: The hamzah is for interrogation, entering upon the negation (lā).
* The Shaykh: Two opinions. What is the first opinion?
* The student: It carries the meaning of challenge.
* The Shaykh: No, my brother, the i'rab, not the meaning. The meaning of reproach is clear.
* The student: The hamzah is interrogative, and ﴿أَفَلَا﴾, the fā' is for warning.
* The Shaykh: Did you forget, or did it not pass over you?
* The student: It did not pass over me.
* The Shaykh: It did not pass over you? Alright.
* A student: The alif of ﴿أَفَلَا﴾ came before the fā'.
* The Shaykh: The hamzah.
* The student: The hamzah came before the fā', and its origin is: fa-alā taʿqilūn.
* The Shaykh: We say the first aspect, the first aspect.
* The student: The second aspect...
* The Shaykh: Wait, the first aspect. Do we not understand anything now?
* The student: The first aspect: the hamzah is for interrogation, and it was placed first because interrogation has priority of position (ṣadr).
* The Shaykh: Good, and the fā'?
* The student: The fā' is conjunctive.
* The Shaykh: Conjoining what?
* The student: What comes before it.
* The Shaykh: What comes before it.
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And its origin in this aspect, in this opinion?
* The student: fa-alā taʿqilūn.
* The Shaykh: fa-alā taʿqilūn. Good, this is one aspect. The second opinion?
* The student: That the hamzah is superfluous, and it is conjoined to a deleted verb, meaning: "Have you been ignorant, so you do not reason?"
* The Shaykh: And the hamzah is superfluous?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: This is the opinion of whom? It is the opinion of Walid! Good, he has solved half of it.
* A student: It entered upon a deleted sentence.
* The Shaykh: But he says the hamzah is superfluous?
* The student: No, it is not superfluous.
* The Shaykh: What is it?
* The student: It is interrogative.
* The Shaykh: Interrogative, yes, but it enters upon a deleted sentence. The estimate is what?
* The student: "Have you been ignorant, so do you not reason?" or "Have you been heedless?"
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: "Have you been heedless?"
* The Shaykh: ("Heedless") no, is it not the opposite of reason?
* The student: Madness.
* The Shaykh: Yes, or foolishness.

﴿أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ Therefore there are two aspects:
The first aspect: the hamzah is interrogative and the fā' is conjunctive, but the hamzah was placed before it because it has priority of position. In this case there is no need for an estimate, because the sentence is conjoined to the sentence before it.
The second aspect: the fā' is a conjunctive particle and the conjoined element is deleted, estimated according to what suits the context. What suits here is to estimate: "Have you been foolish?" for example, because the opposite of reason is foolishness: ﴿أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾.

And his saying: ﴿أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾: the reason meant here is the reason of right conduct (ʿaql al-rushd), not the reason of perception (ʿaql al-idrāk), because these people have the reason of perception. The difference between them is that the reason of perception is the basis of legal responsibility (manāṭ al-taklīf), and the reason of right conduct is the basis of proper action (manāṭ al-taṣarruf). That is, by the reason of right conduct a rational person conducts himself well, while by the reason of perception the obligation is directed to the intellect. For this reason it is said of an intelligent, clever man who behaves badly: "This is a madman, this is not rational," although in terms of the reason of perception he is rational, or not? He is rational. So which of the two reasons is negated here concerning these people? The reason of right conduct. That is: Will you not have a reason by which you are guided?

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Here you are, you who argued about what you have knowledge of, but why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾ First, the i'rab of this verse, because there is some difficulty in it. ﴿هَا أَنْتُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ﴾: ها is for alerting, أنتم is a detached pronoun as subject, and ﴿هَؤُلَاءِ﴾: ها is for alerting, and أولاء is a vocative. The estimate is: "Here you are, O these people, you argued about what you have knowledge of."

﴿فَلِمَ تُحَاجُّونَ فِيمَا لَيْسَ لَكُمْ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾: concerning ﴿فَلِمَ تُحَاجُّونَ﴾ we say what we said concerning ﴿لِمَ تُحَاجُّونَ﴾ as regards i'rab.

﴿هَا أَنْتُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ﴾: first, the alerting here is apt, because He is addressing a people whom He blamed for lacking reason. One who lacks reason should be addressed with what calls for alerting him, because he is heedless, his conduct is that of a madman, so he needs to be alerted. For this reason the particle ها was used.

Then: is ﴿هَؤُلَاءِ﴾ a demonstrative for the distant or the near?
* The students: Distant... near.
* The Shaykh: ﴿هَؤُلَاءِ﴾ is a demonstrative for the distant or the near? Lā ilāha illā Allāh! This needs care, brothers. If it is for the distant, it is joined with the kāf, and here it is not joined with the kāf, but says ﴿هَؤُلَاءِ﴾. Do you understand? When the demonstrative is for the distant, it is brought with the kāf. For this Ibn Mālik said:

With the kāf as a particle, without the lām or with it,
And the lām, if you place it first, is forbidden.
"Bi-dhā, wa-dhī, wa-tā, wa-tī": point to what is near,
And with it join the kāf for distance...
...in distance...
...

The witness here is: "and join the kāf with it for distance," meaning that for nearness the kāf is not joined. So if the demonstrative is for the distant, the kāf must be used, and if it is even more distant, the lām is also used.

Therefore the one pointed to is near: ﴿هَا أَنْتُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ﴾. And despite their nearness, He brought the particle ها to indicate their dullness: even though they are near and the reference to them is near, they have a great dullness and need alerting.

﴿هَا أَنْتُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ حَاجَجْتُمْ فِيمَا لَكُمْ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ means: you argued about what you have knowledge of, namely the Torah for the Jews and the Gospel for the Christians. That is, if you argued about the Torah and the Gospel, with the Jews arguing about the Torah and the Christians about the Gospel, this is argument about what you have knowledge of. Yes, but why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of, namely Abraham and what he was upon of religion?

It has been said: what is meant by ﴿حَاجَجْتُمْ فِيمَا لَكُمْ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ is: concerning Islam, the religion of Islam. That is, you argued about it and disputed, saying: "He is not upon the religion of Abraham; the religion of Abraham is the religion of the Jews and the Christians," while you know that Islam is the true religion of Allah, because the Jews and the Christians know that the religion of Muhammad ﷺ is the religion of truth. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons, but a party of them surely conceal the truth while they know﴾ [Al-Baqarah 146]. So the argument now is about what? Either about the two books, or about Islam, the religion of Islam and what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought.

﴿فَلِمَ تُحَاجُّونَ فِيمَا لَيْسَ لَكُمْ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾: and the argument whose purpose is to establish falsehood and to refute truth is blameworthy, even if it is based on knowledge; indeed, when it is based on knowledge it is even more blameworthy. So how can you argue about what you have no knowledge of, which is Abraham, peace be upon him?

﴿وَاللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾: Allah knows the matter as it is concerning the affair of Abraham, the affair of Muhammad ﷺ, and the affair of Moses and Jesus, and you do not know what Allah the Exalted knows of this and other things.

The negation of knowledge concerning them here is not a removal of sin from them, but a notice of their ignorance and foolishness, and that their conduct is the conduct of the ignorant. In the first part He said: "you do not reason," and in the second He said: ﴿لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (you do not know). Thus they combined foolishness in opinion and planning with ignorance in knowledge and conception. For this reason He said: ﴿وَاللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the condition of Abraham, a mention issuing from knowledge, not from ignorance, so He said: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾: that is, he was not upon your creed, O Jews, nor upon your creed, O Christians. Do you understand? This is according to the view of those who say that their argument about Abraham was that the Jews say: "He is ours," and the Christians say: "He is ours," so Allah negated that: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾.

According to the second opinion, that is: Abraham was not upon what you are upon of partisanship and clinging to your religion, even if it was abrogated and superseded by the religion of Islam. Rather, he was a ḥanīf and a Muslim. Had Abraham been alive, he would have followed whom? Muhammad ﷺ. He would not have been like you, remaining upon his religion as you have remained.

So the verse now allows both aspects, based on the two opinions mentioned earlier. That is: Abraham did not walk the path of the Jews by being partisan, nor walk the path of the Christians by being partisan. The meaning according to the second opinion is not that he was not a Jew, meaning upon the religion of the Jews, or upon the religion of the Christians, but that he was not upon their manner of being partisan to what they were upon, even if the truth turned out to be otherwise. ﴿But he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim﴾, peace be upon him. ﴿He was a ḥanīf﴾: that is, inclining away from polytheism, because ḥanf in origin means inclination. He was inclining away from shirk, affirming tawḥīd. For this reason He said: ﴿a Muslim﴾. So he, peace be upon him, combined complete disavowal of shirk with complete realization of Islam. For this reason He said: ﴿a Muslim﴾.

Here there is a difficulty in the i'rab in His saying: ﴿ḥanīfan muslimā﴾. How do we parse it?
* A student: That is, he was a ḥanīf; it is the predicate of kāna.
* The Shaykh: And ﴿muslimā﴾?
* The student: ﴿muslimā﴾ is the predicate of kāna.
* The Shaykh: Second. Is it permissible for the predicate to be multiple?
* The student: It is permissible.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* A student: It may be conjoined by a conjunction; the particle is not actually present, it is an estimated particle: kāna ḥanīfan wa-kāna muslimā.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* A student: Could it be a ḥāl, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: A ḥāl? From where?
* A student: An attribute of ḥanīf.
* The Shaykh: An attribute of what?
* The student: ḥanīf.
* The Shaykh: Apparently, if we all strive, if you ask each one, we will get opinions! ﴿muslimā﴾ is a second predicate, and multiplicity of predicates is permissible. ﴿And Allah was ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nisa' 100] is abundant in the Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿muslimā﴾ means a Muslim to Allah outwardly and inwardly, so Islam, which is the action of the limbs, and faith, which is the belief of the hearts and the actions of the hearts, are both included.

This is an important principle: when Islam is mentioned alone, it includes faith; and when faith is mentioned alone, it includes Islam; and when the two are mentioned together, Islam refers to the outward and faith to the inward. This is the principle of the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah, and the Book and the Sunnah indicate it. The Prophet ﷺ described faith to the delegation of 'Abd al-Qays as Islam: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer and giving the zakat [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (87) from Ibn 'Abbas, and by Muslim (17/23) from Ibn 'Abbas]. And Allah described the prayer as faith in His saying: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [Al-Baqarah 143], meaning your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al-'Imran 19], and it includes the whole religion: faith and the actions of the limbs. So ﴿muslimā﴾ here means a Muslim to Allah outwardly and inwardly, so it includes both faith and Islam.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾: this is an emphasis of His saying ﴿ḥanīfan﴾. That is, although this clause is conjoined by waw, in meaning it emphasizes what preceded: he was not of those who associate partners with Allah, neither hidden shirk nor manifest shirk. Rather, he fought against shirk and was patient in calling to tawḥīd until he was thrown into the fire, peace be upon him. But his reward for that was that it was said to the fire: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 69].

﴿And he was not of the polytheists (67). Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham﴾: this is the ruling among these disputants. The disputants are three: the Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims. Observe the ruling of the just Judge: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾. He placed first what should have been the predicate, and made the subject, which is the pillar of the sentence to which the predicate is attributed, the thing He said: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him﴾, and He did not say: "Indeed, those who followed him are most worthy of him," in order to decide that the priority belongs to these and not to others.

﴿The people most worthy of Abraham﴾, among the Jews, the Christians, the polytheists, the idol-worshippers and others, are: ﴿those who followed him﴾.

Here we ask about the lām in His saying: ﴿lalladhīna﴾, and what is its i'rab?
* A student: A preposition.
* The Shaykh: A preposition? No, the lām of the preposition is pronounced with a kasra in such a case.
* A student: For emphasis.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 65–68 (part 2 of 4):

* The Shaykh: For emphasis, yes indeed, for emphasis, and "inna" also is for emphasis, so this is a sentence emphasized with two emphatics: with "inna" and with the lam.
He says: ﴿Indeed, the closest of mankind to Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe﴾. "For those who followed him" means from the Children of Israel, those who preceded the Prophet ﷺ. And there is no doubt that many believers followed him, those who believed in him during his lifetime and those who followed his way after his death. "And this Prophet" — look, Allah is greater — refers to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and it is enough honor for him that the Lord of the worlds points to him: "this Prophet." This is a great honor for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Allah points to him with this demonstrative which conveys nearness. He did not say "and that Prophet," but said "and this Prophet," indicating his nearness, because he ﷺ is the closest of people in rank to Allah, the Exalted.
﴿And this Prophet and those who believe﴾. There is a reading: ﴿an-Nabiyy'﴾ — how is that? On this reading, ﴿an-Nabiyy'﴾ is derived from an-naba' (news), so it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il and also in the sense of maf'ul, right? In the sense of fa'il, because he informs and reports; and in the sense of maf'ul, because he is informed. For this reason Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, described the Messenger: "He is the truthful, the one who is believed"[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3208) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and related by Muslim (2643/1) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]. So it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il, and fa'il in the sense of maf'il. There remains for us how fa'il can mean maf'il? Fa'il in the sense of maf'ul is common, like jarih (wounded), kasir (broken), qatil (slain). Common. But fa'il in the sense of maf'il, how is that? We say: yes, this has been reported; and what is before us now is evidence for this. It is known that the Messenger informs people, is it not so? So it has come in the Qur'an, and the Qur'an is proof. And if you want to bring a proof from the speech of the Arabs, listen to the words of the poet:
"Does the sweet-voiced one of Rayhana, the caller, keep me awake, while my companions are sleeping?"
(Amin Rayhana al-da'i al-sami') — "al-sami'" here means "al-musmi'" (one who makes to hear).
So this "sami'" is in the sense of "musmi'" in the language of the Arabs. However, in reality we do not need a citation from the Qur'an to prove that this is the language; rather, the Qur'an is cited as evidence and is not itself in need of evidence. But it is known that the more proofs there are, the more a person gains tranquility. So, on the reading ﴿an-Nabiyy'﴾, may we read it? Yes, we may, and indeed it is recommended to read it sometimes. On this reading it is from an-naba' (news). As for the reading "an-Nabiyy" without hamza, there are two views:
The first view: it is a softened form of "an-Nabi'" with hamza, softened, meaning the hamza was made into a ya' for ease. This exists in the Arabic language: for example, "a'imma" is said in Arabic as "ayimma," softening the hamza into a ya'. So "an-Nabiyy" — its origin is "an-Nabi'," but the hamza was made into a ya' for lightness. On this view, "an-Nabiyy" comes from where? From an-naba' (news).
It is said: the ya' is original, not softened, so "an-Nabiyy" is derived from an-nubuwwah, which means a raised, protruding thing. It is said: naba yanbu, meaning he rose up. So it is derived from an-nubuwwah, which is elevation, because of the elevated rank of the Prophet; for the Messengers, peace be upon them all, and the last of them Muhammad ﷺ, are the highest in rank with Allah. For this reason Allah began with them in the mention of those whom He favored: ﴿So those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets﴾ [an-Nisa' 69].
If someone says: make it from both: from an-naba' and from an-nubuwwah? What do we say to him? We say: is it possible? It is possible; because the preferred view is that if a word admits two meanings without contradiction, it is taken to both, since that is broader in meaning. But with contradiction, one looks to the preferred meaning and takes it. However, where it is possible to combine, it is obligatory to take both meanings together.
If someone says: this is the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings — do you know the homonymous word? The homonym is a word whose form is one but whose meanings are many, like 'ayn: 'ayn is said of the eye (the one in your face is an eye), and it is said of a flowing spring — what is it? 'ayn al-ma' (a spring of water), and it is said of gold: 'ayn (gold), 'ayn waraq (silver), and for this it is said: 'ayn mawrudah and 'ayn manqudah; the manqudah is gold and the mawrudah is water. And do we say 'ayn makhulah? Yes, possibly; the 'ayn makhulah is the eye which is in the face.
Some scholars say: a homonym cannot be taken in both its meanings, because each of its meanings contradicts the other. But the correct view, which most scholars hold, is that it is permissible to take it in both its meanings on condition that there is no contradiction; if they contradict, it is necessary to seek the preferred meaning.
* A student: Shaykh, the verses do not confirm that the Qur'an... (...) our saying.
* The Shaykh: We have not completed the verses in truth; perhaps we will leave these four verses all for discussion in the benefits.
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you! The second view on ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ — does it mean he was not fanatical as you are fanatical?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it means he was not on the path of the Jews and Christians.
* The student: How, that he was not fanatical?
* The Shaykh: It means he was not on your path; that is, if you are truthful that you are on the path of Abraham, or that Abraham is on your path, then follow Muhammad.
* The student: But their saying: fanatic, how...
* The Shaykh: For example, now, the one who adopts the school of a people is not attributed to them?
* The student: Certainly.
* The Shaykh: Is that so or not? So these Jews are fanatical about their religion, and the Christians are fanatical about their religion. Abraham — we do not say that he was a fanatical Jew or a fanatical Christian; Abraham, peace be upon him, was a Muslim devoted to Allah, he was not fanatical for Judaism or Christianity.
* The student: But we said: if he had come to the time of the Messenger ﷺ, he would have embraced Islam.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is known.
* The student: He was a Muslim originally; how would he embrace Islam?
* The Shaykh: This is the establishing of proof against these Jews and Christians.
* The student: Yes, he embraced Islam meaning he left his law and followed the law of Muhammad?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he leaves his law and follows Muhammad, yes.
* Student: His saying: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾ — does it not support the second view, that by your claim you are upon his religion and he was not upon yours?
* The Shaykh: He said: it may be, it may be even according to that.
* The student: So the Torah and the Gospel did not occur until after his death?
* The Shaykh: Yes, and likewise those who say: we are upon the way of Abraham; and Abraham — they say: he was fanatical, he did not depart from his religion; this is the meaning of their saying: "upon their way."
* The student: How, Abraham worshipped with them while they...?
* The Shaykh: They say: (...) their particular worship, that is, their way, that is, upon their way.
* Student: Shaykh, Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Here you are, those who argued about what you had knowledge of; but why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾ Although in both matters they have knowledge. But in the first, that is... if you could clarify?
* The Shaykh: No, in the matter of Abraham, peace be upon him, they have no knowledge; because whoever says about Abraham that he was on the path of the Jews and Christians, or on the religion of the Jews and Christians, has no knowledge of that; he is ignorant, whether he said it with compound ignorance or simple ignorance. If he knew the reality of Abraham, peace be upon him, he would know that he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim.
* The student: Could he be obstinate, Shaykh, meaning he knows that this...?
* The Shaykh: Perhaps some of them, perhaps some of them are obstinate.
* Student: May Allah reward you with good, Shaykh. You said: if Abraham, peace be upon him, were alive, he would have abandoned his religion and followed Muhammad. Is not his religion the very same religion as Muhammad's?
* The Shaykh: The methodology differs; the root of the religion of all the prophets is one; the tawhid, the foundations of religion, are one for all the prophets. But Allah says: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48], and we recited it during the lesson; but because you (...)
I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan. We continue the discussion on the end of the noble verse: ﴿And this Prophet and those who believe. And Allah is the Walī of the believers﴾. His saying: ﴿And this Prophet﴾ is conjoined to his saying: ﴿those who followed him﴾, so it is in the nominative position; rather it is marfu'; "an-Nabiyy" is a badal (apposition) of the demonstrative, and the demonstrative, as we know, is built on sukun.
He says: ﴿And those who believe﴾ — believe in whom? They believe in this Prophet, and belief in the Prophet ﷺ includes belief in all his law, and this belief also necessarily entails acceptance and what? And submission; that one accepts what the Prophet ﷺ brought and submits to him.
Then He says: ﴿And Allah is the Walī of the believers﴾ — the Walī of every believer; these and others; every believer, Allah, the Exalted, is his walī, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Walī of those who believe; He brings them out of darknesses into the light. But those who disbelieve — their protectors are the taghut; they take them out of the light into darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah 257]. This walāyah is a special walāyah which requires that He make the believer easy toward ease and keep him from hardship; and there is a general walāyah encompassing everyone: Allah, the Exalted, is the walī of everyone. For this Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect. Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am 61-62]. So Allah, the Exalted, made Him a mawla for these, though they are disbelievers, but this is by the general walāyah.
The general walāyah is the walāyah of disposal, of disposal in the universe and management; and the special walāyah is the walāyah of care for the one under protection, that Allah, the Exalted, cares for him and makes him easy toward ease and keeps him from hardship.
In these noble verses there are many benefits. ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ This is the beginning of the benefits; ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ until the end. * In this verse are the following benefits:
First: a rebuke to these, I mean the People of the Scripture, for arguing and disputing about Abraham, peace be upon him.
* And among its benefits also: the exalted status and rank of Abraham among all the groups: the Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims.
* And among its benefits: the demonstration of argument by reason; from His saying: ﴿Why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him?﴾ How then do you argue with it when the Torah and the Gospel were revealed only after him? And this is contrary to reason.
* And it follows from this benefit: that one should not neglect reason in inference, just as one should not rely on it and abandon the text. People in their use of reason are of three positions: one extreme went to excess in it, to the point of preferring it over revelation; this applies to jurists who are proponents of opinion and analogists who rely on opinion even if it contradicts the text; and in the domain of creed, all people of innovation rely on reason and claim it over revelation, although the reason they rely upon is nothing but doubts, not proofs and evidences; there is no indication in it, but they think that reason requires such-and-such and so they affirm it, and reason requires the negation of such-and-such and so they negate it, and they do not refer back to revelation in this. Among them are the Ash'aris, the Mu'tazilah, and others; everyone who negates an attribute which Allah affirmed for Himself by an argument or a rational doubt — on the more sound view, it is not a proof, it is a rational doubt — is included among those who go to excess in using reason.
And among people — the second position — are those who rejected reliance on reason altogether and said: reason has no role in establishing any ruling or any report; so they rejected analogy, like the people of the literal (Zahiriyyah), who rejected it entirely and said: it is impossible for us to refer to reason in anything.
And among people are those of the middle position, who referred to reason in what does not contradict the sharia; because when reason does not contradict the sharia, Allah, the Exalted, refers to it in many matters, such as: ﴿Do you order the people to righteousness and forget yourselves while you recite the Scripture? Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah 44], and like this verse: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him. Will you not reason?﴾ And Allah's argument for the resurrection of the dead by the revival of the earth after its death is a sensory rational argument: it is sensory because it is observed, and it is rational because by it one infers its counterpart which does not completely differ from it.
So the summary is that in this verse reason is considered an evidence, but as I said: on condition that it does not contradict the sharia; if it contradicts the sharia, then the more correct view is that we say it is not reason; the more correct view is that we say it is not reason, because sound transmitted text never contradicts clear reason.
But if one supposes that reason contradicts revelation, then either there is no real contradiction, or the revelation is not established, or the reason is not sound, polluted by doubts and desires.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that the Torah and the Gospel were sent down from Allah; from His saying: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾.
If someone says: how do you derive from this verse that the Torah and the Gospel were sent down from Allah, given that the verb here, ﴿were revealed﴾, how does the inference from this verse stand that the Torah and the Gospel are sent down from Allah, since the verb... complete it.
* A student: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾.
* A student: The verb is in the passive voice.
* The Shaykh: The verb is in the passive voice, yes? Good, what is the answer to this?
* The student: From His saying: "from Him" (min 'indih).
* The Shaykh: How did you know it?
