That is, Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) among them and they were guided by him before they died. If this is a blessing upon them, it is also a blessing upon those after them until the Day of Resurrection. The greatest blessing Allah bestows upon a person is to rescue him from the Fire.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of punishment by the Fire, based on His saying: ﴿and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, the Exalted, is the Creator of the servant's deeds. From where is this derived?

Students: ﴿so He saved you﴾.

The Shaykh: From His saying ﴿so He saved you﴾, because Allah saved them through their deeds, and He attributed this rescue, which was based on their deeds, to Himself. And this is so. This is the position of the people of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah): that Allah, the Exalted, is the Creator of the servant and the Creator of the servant's deeds. The servant is not independent; rather, he is created in his essence, in his will, and in his deeds. ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾ [as-Saffat 96]. That is, "your deeds" according to one view, or "what you do" according to another. If the object made is created, then He is the Creator of the act, because the made object is the result of the act. So the verse indicates that Allah is the Creator of the deeds of His servants, whether ما (ma) is taken as a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah, meaning "your doing") or as a relative pronoun (mawṣulah, meaning "what you do").

**Student:** May Allah reward you well, O Shaykh. This shows the responsibility of students of knowledge and shaykhs in particular, to establish this principle: that the fundamental brotherhood is the brotherhood of religion, not brotherhood of nationalism, or of ethnic loyalty, and so on. But, unfortunately, O Shaykh, at this time, in the present circumstances, political conditions are what impose these principles now. We find today that hatred has reached its peak among the peoples of the region. You find the Kuwaiti hating the Palestinian, or the Saudi hating the Yemeni, the Yemeni hating the Sudanese, and how is this (...)?

**Shaykh:** The obligation, may Allah bless you all, is that this matter requires a long time, but we will mention some of it, God willing. The obligation is that the peoples should not attach themselves to the rulers. The rulers are people who are keen on their thrones, and they should not be followed. The peoples must follow the methodology of Allah, whether the rulers follow it or not. It is absolutely impermissible for us to follow politics, because politics makes a person a disbeliever today and makes him one of the strongest people in faith on another day, or vice versa. Moreover, I recall that when the crescent was sighted in one country, another country would rule that the month had begun based on the sighting of that country. Then when relations deteriorated, they said: "It is not possible; every country has its own sighting. If these people gave us the moon in our hands, we would not accept it." This is not permissible. I believe that the peoples must follow the methodology of Allah, whether the rulers follow it or not, and what have we to do with politics? Eventually, one day, the truth will prevail, God willing, and this racism will disappear. Among the politicians, those who have no concern other than preserving their positions, which is the case with most Arab politicians today, you find them raising matters from which they are innocent, but they only want them for propaganda. Otherwise, they are the furthest people from achieving what they say. Indeed, they may have openly declared that they do not want what they claim today. All of that is to win over the mob. Likewise, people should not follow slogans, propaganda, and emotions. They should look with the eye of reason, not with the eye of sight, because some people have sight but not insight, they have hearing but not understanding. So the obligation is that you do not look with the eye of sight, but with the eye of insight, and do not listen with the ear, but with the hearing of reason. Otherwise, politics will sweep you away without you realizing it. Every day you will have an opinion, every day you will have a leader to follow. So I believe that the peoples should be as they are: Muslims, brothers, whether they are Saudis, Yemenis, Iraqis, Levantines, Palestinians, Egyptians, Sudanese, or from any people. Even if someone comes to us from America and he is a Muslim, he is our brother, because the bond that must exist between peoples is Islam. This is the bond. As for the desires of their rulers, those are for them, not for us. They walk, and we walk in the opposite direction if they are not upon the law of Allah.

**Student:** May Allah bless you, Shaykh. The man who was brought to the Prophet ﷺ and who used to drink wine, the Prophet ﷺ said, as in the hadith: "He loves Allah and His Messenger."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6780).]] So the love of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger requires that a person stay away from these sins. So how is the reconciliation?

**Shaykh:** No, the reconciliation is simple, because love may be accompanied by a strong driving force, which a person forgets. Perhaps this man had become so accustomed to wine that he could not give it up at the very beginning. The stages of its prohibition, as is well known, are four stages: first, its permissibility; then, the hint at its prohibition; then, its prohibition at the times of prayer; and then, its absolute prohibition.

**Student:** Shaykh, what is your opinion about some young people who, at the beginning of their lives, committed some sins and were in their days of ignorance (jahiliyyah), and then after Allah bestowed Islam upon them, they sit in gatherings and recall those days in which they disobeyed Allah, so that there may be a lesson in them for themselves, and so that others may take heed?

**Shaykh:** You mean they mention them to people?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** No, no, not at all, it is not permissible.

**Student:** No, I mean they relate the story of their repentance?

**Shaykh:** No, as for their repentance, I do not know. But in any case, the sins that he mentions, he should not say them. If he wants to mention them as a story, such as: "A man used to do such and such, and used to do such and such, and Allah guided him," this is fine. But to mention them as an incident that happened to him, this is an exposure of the veil Allah has placed over him.

* * *

**Student:** ﴿And let there be among you a community who call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And those are the successful. And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear evidence had come to them. And for them there will be a great punishment.﴾ [Al-Imran 104, 105].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And let there be among you a community who call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And those are the successful.﴾

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided.﴾

- Among the benefits of this verse: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made clear to us the cosmic and legislative signs (āyāt). The reasoning for this is that "āyāt" is a plural in construct form (jam' mudāf), and a construct plural conveys generality. The clarification of His cosmic signs is evident: the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the seas, the rivers, and other things. The legislative signs are likewise evident to whomever Allah has granted knowledge of what He sent down to His messengers, may He be exalted. Furthermore, the clarification of the cosmic signs is not merely that you know this sign cannot be created or directed except by Allah alone, but that you draw evidence from the past customs (sunan) to the present customs. For example, the destruction of the earlier nations by Allah is used as evidence that the way of Allah in creation is one. So the One who destroyed the earlier nations for their sins will destroy this nation also for its sins, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are the like thereof.﴾ [Muhammad 10].

- And among the benefits of this verse: the refutation of the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah), who distorted the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah (the Prophetic way) to meanings that their apparent wording does not indicate. The reasoning for this is that if we say that the intended meaning of these verses and hadiths is contrary to their apparent meaning, without any clarification from Allah and His Messenger, do these verses become clarifying or ambiguous?

**Students:** Ambiguous.

**Shaykh:** You say this because it is what I want, or because it has become completely clear to you?

**Students:** It has become clear.

**Shaykh:** For example, if they say: the intended meaning of Allah's "istawā" (rising) over the Throne is "istawlā" (taking control of it), without any clarification from Allah and His Messenger, we say: is Allah's expression "istawā" over the Throne instead of "istawlā" a clarification or an ambiguity? It is an ambiguity. If they say: the intended meaning of "yad" (hand) is blessing and power, we say: Glory be to Allah! How would Allah express "hand" to mean blessing and power, when He intends blessing and power, without any clarification? This is nothing but ambiguity. The point is that, according to the methodology and approach of the people of innovation, and others as well, who distort words from their places without any clarification from Allah and His Messenger, the Qur'an would not be a guidance or a clarification for people. The same applies to the Sunnah, and this contradicts this verse and others.

- And among the benefits of this noble verse: the love of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the guidance of creation, because He makes things clear so that people may be guided. Therefore, He loves for His servants to be guided.

- And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of wisdom (ʿilal) in the acts of Allah. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿la'allakum﴾ (so that you may), because "la'alla" indicates causation. Wisdom is a requirement of the perfection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because were it not for wisdom, His rulings would be pointless, both the cosmic and the legislative rulings. As Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 38, 39]. Therefore, denying wisdom is a grave slander against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Those who say that Allah has no wisdom, and that His action and command are merely by will, He wills that this should be and it is, He wills to command this and He commands, He wills to forbid this and He forbids, these people have slandered Allah most gravely, because His action becomes stripped of wisdom, and if it is stripped of wisdom, it can only be foolishness, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 104–105 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾.
He said: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾. The lam in His words ﴿Let there be﴾ is the lam of command (lam al-amr), and the evidence for this is that the verb after it is in the jussive mood (jazm), ﴿let there be﴾. The lam of command puts the present-tense verb into the jussive. ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾: ﴿ummah﴾ means a group (ṭā'ifah) that calls to good. The word ummah occurs in the Noble Qur'an with several meanings: among them a group, among them a period of time, among them leadership (imamah), and among them religion (millah). Its example in the sense of a group is this verse.
Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 104]. The lam in His words ﴿Let there be﴾ is the lam of command, and what is the evidence for this?
* Students: The jussive (jazm).
* The Shaykh: The verb after it is in the jussive mood, ﴿let there be﴾, and the lam of command puts the present-tense verb into the jussive. ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾: ﴿ummah﴾ means a group, calling to good. The word ummah in the Noble Qur'an occurs with several meanings: among them a group, among them a period of time, among them leadership, and among them religion. Its example in the sense of a group is this verse, ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 104]. Its example in the sense of religion is His saying, what is it?
* Students: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion (ummah)﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Upon a religion (ummah)﴾, i.e., upon a creed (millah). Its example in the sense of leadership?
* Students: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾ [al-Nahl 120].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾. Its example in the sense of a period of time: ﴿And he remembered after a period (ummah) [of time]﴾ [Yūsuf 45], i.e., after a time.
As for His words ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾: the ﴿min﴾ in ﴿among you (minkum)﴾ may be partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), and it may be explanatory of the genus (li-bayān al-jins). On the first, the meaning is: let some of you call to good. On the second, the meaning is: let all of you be callers to good, because if we take it as explanatory of the genus, the meaning becomes that the entire ummah must be of this type, that is, the ummah must be one that calls to good. If we take it as partitive, the meaning becomes: let some of you call to good. What follows from this will come, Allah willing, in the benefits (al-fawā'id).
He said: ﴿calling to good﴾. Calling whom? The object is omitted. Is the intended meaning that they call themselves, or that they call others among relatives, or other Muslims, or other people in general?
* Students: It includes all of them.
* The Shaykh: It includes all of them. They call to good everyone to whom the call can be directed; any person to whom the call can be directed, let them call him. Do they call the jinn?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, they call the jinn. For this reason the object was omitted, for the sake of generality.
﴿Calling to good﴾: good is everything that the Sharia has brought, so it is good. It includes what is good in religion and what is good in worldly life. As for what is good in religion, its matter is clear: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 7]. As for what concerns worldly affairs, what concerns the worldly interests that do not contradict religion is among the desirable good matters. So the good here includes the good of religion and the good of this world. For example: they call to performing acts of obedience: pray, give zakat, fast, make Hajj, be dutiful to your parents, maintain your ties of kinship, give sincere advice in buying and selling, be clear, and what is similar to that, all of this is calling to good. Do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not drink wine, do not kill a soul without right, do not disobey your parents, do not sever your ties of kinship, do not cheat people: this too is calling to good, because this is a request to refrain, and a prohibition is a request to refrain, so in reality it is a call to good, since abandoning evil is good.
Second: ﴿and enjoin what is right﴾. Enjoining what is right is mentioned after calling, because calling precedes commanding. You call first, then you command second, then you change (the wrong) third. Many students are confused about this, thinking that calling to good, enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and changing wrong are one and the same thing, and they are not. Calling to good is general. When the preacher addresses the people at the Friday sermon and commands and forbids, what is he called?
* Students: A caller (dā'in).
* The Shaykh: A caller to good. When a man takes hold of you and says: "O my brother, pray, fear Allah, O my brother, do not cheat people, fear Allah," then this is what?
* Students: Forbidding wrong.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Students: Commanding.
* The Shaykh: Commanding what is right and forbidding wrong. When the ruler sees an instrument of music and breaks it, this is changing wrong, and there are degrees. But enjoining what is right and forbidding wrong: ﴿and enjoin what is right﴾, and the word ﴿they enjoin﴾ indicates that they speak with people in a manner of authority (isti'lā') and not in a manner of exaltedness (ʿulūw); that is, in the manner of "I am the one commanding," and the one who commands good is of higher rank than the one commanded.
As for His words ﴿enjoin what is right﴾: what is al-ma'ruf? Al-ma'ruf is everything the Sharia has recognized and approved of in acts of worship, whether an act or an abandonment, or an act only? An act, because He said ﴿and forbid what is wrong﴾. Therefore, since the two are combined, the meaning of al-ma'ruf becomes everything the Sharia has recognized and approved of among the commanded acts of worship. Its meaning is al-ma'ruf.
* A student: What the Sharia has recognized and approved, an act or an abandonment.
* The Shaykh: Yes. We omitted, or left at the end, the "from performing acts of obedience," because "forbid wrong" stands in contrast to the act. So what the Sharia has recognized and approved of in matters of obedience is al-ma'ruf. Enjoining monotheism is enjoining what is right, enjoining following the predecessors in creed is enjoining what is right, enjoining prayer is enjoining what is right, enjoining dutifulness to parents is enjoining what is right, and so on. This is enjoining what is right.
He said: ﴿and forbid what is wrong﴾. ﴿They forbid﴾: the nahy is a request to refrain in a manner of authority; that is, they ask people to refrain from wrong. And what is al-munkar? Al-munkar is what the Sharia has disapproved of. Whatever the Sharia has disapproved of among deeds and morals, what is it?
* Students: Wrong (munkar).
* The Shaykh: It is munkar. Fine, adultery?
* Students: Munkar.
* The Shaykh: Theft?
* Students: Munkar.
* The Shaykh: Drinking wine?
* Students: Munkar.
* The Shaykh: Killing a soul?
* Students: Munkar.
* The Shaykh: Transgression against people by taking their wealth?
* Students: Munkar.
* The Shaykh: Violating their honor. All of these are evils, and they forbid wrong.
﴿And those are the successful﴾: ﴿those﴾ refers to the community calling to good, enjoining right and forbidding wrong. ﴿Those (ulā'ika)﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿they (hum)﴾ is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl) with no place in the grammatical structure, and ﴿the successful (al-muflihūn)﴾ is the predicate of the subject.
If someone says: why do you not make ﴿they (hum)﴾ a second subject, with ﴿the successful﴾ as the predicate of the second subject, and the whole clause the predicate of the first subject? We say: we do not say that, because if we said it we would miss the benefits of the pronoun of separation. What supports that we do not make the pronoun of separation a subject is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps we shall follow the magicians if they are the victors﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 40]. ﴿They are the victors﴾: the evidence is that He did not make the pronoun of separation a subject; had He made it a subject, He would have said: "if they are the victors," so that "the victors" would be the predicate of "they." In any case, the pronoun of separation is a particle with no place in the grammatical structure, but it came in the form of a nominal pronoun, the nominal pronoun.
﴿Al-muflihūn﴾ are those who are saved from distresses and attain what is sought. Falah is salvation from what is feared or disliked, and attaining what is desired. So it contains two matters: safety and gain. Safety from what?
* Students: From distresses.
* The Shaykh: From what is feared. And gain?
* Students: What is desired.
* The Shaykh: What is desired. For this reason the word falah is considered among the most comprehensive words. So the successful one is the one who attains his goal and is saved from what he fears. This is the successful one.
In this noble verse, let us read the following, so that we can reach it.
He said: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. And those will have a great punishment﴾. Allah forbade us to be like those who combined two blameworthy attributes: division and disagreement. He ordered as a consequence the disgraceful recompense, which is His saying: ﴿And those will have a great punishment﴾.
His saying: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾, i.e., do not become like those. On this basis we parse the kaf here as a noun, to be the predicate of ﴿be﴾: "do not be like those who became divided." Ibn Malik said:
"Liken with the kaf, and with it causation is sometimes meant, and it comes as an extra for emphasis; and it is used as a noun..."
So the kaf here is a noun meaning "like," and it is the predicate of ﴿be﴾.
His saying: ﴿like those who became divided﴾ came after His saying: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good and enjoining right and forbidding wrong﴾, because if the community abandons this, division will inevitably occur. If it abandons calling to good, enjoining right, and forbidding wrong, division is inevitable, because in that state they will have no unifying word; each one acts as he likes, since he is not called to good, and souls have divergent and different inclinations. Likewise, if there is no enjoining of right and no forbidding of wrong, people will inevitably divide, because this one wants adultery, that one wants to drink wine, another wants to steal, and another wants things other than these, so division occurs. But when they are commanded to what is right, they all become upon what is right, and when they are forbidden from wrong, they all become upon abandoning wrong.
He said: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾. Like whom?
* Students: Like the Jews and the Christians.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And they did not become divided except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah 4]. So the first people we are given as an example are the People of the Book: the Jews and the Christians differed with great difference after the clear proofs had come to them, so Allah the Exalted forbade us to be like them. Do not be like them in what? We look at the attribute in which we were forbidden to resemble them, which is division and disagreement. So, after the clear proofs had come to them: if we are forbidden from that, it is a command to its opposite. If we are forbidden from division and disagreement, it is a command to unity and harmony; "unity" is the opposite of division, and "harmony" is the opposite of disagreement. It is as if Allah says: unite and be in harmony, and let there be among you neither separation nor disagreement, lest you become like whom?
* Students: The Jews and the Christians.
* The Shaykh: Like the Jews and the Christians.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those will have a great punishment﴾. And those: they differed after the clear proofs had come to them; they became divided and differed. They became divided in their bodies and did not unite, and they became factions, and they differed in their hearts and in their methods, so each faction has a specific method in which it rejoices, from which it does not move, and it considers whoever is other than it to be in error.
He said: ﴿And those will have a great punishment﴾. ﴿Those (ulā'ika)﴾: He pointed to them with the form of distance, because ﴿ulā'ika﴾ is a demonstrative for what?
* Students: For distance.
* The Shaykh: For the distant, "those." This is due to the lowliness of their rank. Due to the lowliness of their rank, that is, as if, because of the lowliness of their rank, the speaker placed them in the position of whom?
* Students: The distant one.
* The Shaykh: The one distant from him, because he disavows them and their deeds.
﴿For them is a great punishment﴾. The punishment (ʿadhāb) is the penalty, and we seek refuge in Allah, because it pains its owner and torments him. The great (ʿaẓīm) is the thing that is magnified in its quality and its quantity. Their punishment, we ask Allah for well-being, is severe and varied, or not varied?
* Students: Varied.
* The Shaykh: Varied. They are given drink from boiling water, and we seek refuge in Allah, to coldness. The point is that it is varied. Likewise, it is great in its duration: it is continuous and eternal. We ask Allah for well-being.
* In these two verses there are benefits. In the first: the obligation of calling to good. From what is it derived?
* Students: The command.
* The Shaykh: From the lam of command in ﴿Let there be﴾, and the basic principle of a command is obligation.
* Among its benefits: that this is a collective obligation (fard kifayah), based on His saying ﴿among you (minkum)﴾, and this is on the view that ﴿min﴾ is partitive. But if it is said that ﴿min﴾ is explanatory of the genus, it indicates that the whole community is obliged to be a community calling to good; that is, they do not wait for one another to see whether someone will command or not, but rather all of them are prepared for this, all of them are callers. For example: if someone is told "Get up and call to good," and he says, "By Allah, so-and-so calls to good, that suffices," this is not appropriate. Each one should call to good as much as he can, because Allah said: ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾, meaning a community that as a whole calls to good.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: noticing sincerity, from His saying ﴿calling to good﴾, not calling to themselves. Some people call to themselves, and some people call to good. The sign of one who calls to himself is that he does not want people to oppose him even if he is in error, and there is no doubt that this one is calling to whom?
* Students: To himself.
* The Shaykh: To himself. Second: one of the signs of this is that he dislikes that someone else undertake this, that is, calling to good; he wants to monopolize it over all other people. This too is calling to oneself, to turn people's faces toward himself; we ask Allah for protection and well-being. But if he wishes to undertake the matter himself in order to gain the reward, not to deprive others or to turn people toward himself, there is nothing wrong with that, because each one loves to be a caller to good.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that following good in everything is required by the Sharia.
Good is of two kinds: good in itself, and good for something else, that is, good that serves as a means to something else. For example, if you asked a person about daily news in order to bring him joy, and otherwise you would gain nothing from it, is this of the good?
* Students: No, it is good for another.
* The Shaykh: Let me ask you: is it good or not?
* Students: Yes, it is good.
* The Shaykh: Then is it for himself or for another?
* Students: For another.
* The Shaykh: For another, because I do not benefit from this and he perhaps does not benefit, but I want to bring him joy. Thereby people began asking: is it recommended for a person to talk during eating or not? We say: consider it. If a person talks in order to distract them from eating, is this good or not good?
* Students: Not good.
* The Shaykh: This is not good; let them eat. But if he talks in order to stir their appetites so that they relax, feel at ease, and eat, is this good or not good?
* Students: Good.
* A student: Good for another.
* The Shaykh: Good for another, on the condition that the eating is in the lawful measure. The lawful measure the Messenger ﷺ explained in his saying: "The son of Adam needs only a few morsels to keep his back upright. If he must exceed that, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath." [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2380) and Ibn Majah (3349), from the hadith of al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib.] But what do you say?
* The student: It depends on the soul.
* The Shaykh: In any case, my intention is that good for another varies.
If a person wanted to reach a good for a human being by means of disobedience, that is, he flatters a person through sin, saying: "so that he may be guided, perhaps he will be guided," such as beginning to backbite Zayd or 'Amr in order to draw near to this man, is this permissible?
* Students: No, it is not permissible.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. It is not possible for calling to good to be by a forbidden means at all, because a forbidden means is corrupt in itself; how can it be a means to good? But if it is of what is permissible, it becomes good for another, and if it is also good in itself, it becomes good upon good.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the obligation to enjoin good and forbid evil, as His saying states: ﴿and let them enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾. But is it a collective obligation (fard kifaya) or an individual obligation (fard 'ayn)? This depends on the disagreement over whether (min) in ﴿min﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyya) or not. Yet there is no doubt that if we see an evil, we are obligated to disapprove of it and forbid it. However, it is not obligatory on every individual to forbid a specific evil. For example: if a person backbites in our presence and we are ten people, do we say that all of us must enjoin good and forbid this? Or, if one person forbids it and that suffices, then it is enough? If one person forbids it and that achieves the purpose, it is enough. But if he forbade it and it did not stop, then the others must stand with him. This is the opposite of what some people do now, may Allah grant us well-being: when someone forbids evil, they stand against him. Such people are feared to have Allah seal their hearts, because they abandoned the one whom it is obligatory to support, and this is an extremely great danger.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: knowledge is necessary; that is, it urges seeking knowledge. How so? Because one who does not know what is good cannot call to good, one who does not know what is right cannot enjoin what is right, and one who does not know what is wrong cannot forbid it. Knowledge is therefore necessary. From this noble verse, the urging to seek knowledge is derived, because what a obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory.

Enjoining good and forbidding evil requires the following conditions:
First: knowledge of the Sharia (divine law) and knowledge of the situation; that is, knowledge of the Sharia and of the circumstances.
Knowledge of the Sharia means that I know this is something Allah has commanded, so that I may command it. But if I do not know whether it is commanded or not, it is not lawful for me to command it, because Allah says: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has not sent down authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know.﴾ Shall you complete the verse?
* Students: ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know.﴾
* The Shaykh: ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ [al-A'raf 33]. And the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all those one will be questioned.﴾ [al-Isra' 36].
Knowledge of the situation means that I know this man has abandoned what is good or committed what is wrong. But if I enjoin him to do good while I do not know whether he has done it or not, this is not permitted, because this is from (qafw) pursuing that of which I have no knowledge. Likewise, if I forbid him from an evil while I do not know whether he committed it or not, this is not permitted, because it is from (qafw) pursuing that of which I have no knowledge. An example of this: a man entered the mosque, sat down, and I did not see him from the time he entered. Should I say to him: "Stand and pray two rak'ahs," or should I ask him whether he has prayed or not? The second. Because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon to the people on Friday, and a man entered and sat down, and he said: "Have you prayed?" He said: No. He said: "Stand and pray." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (930) and Muslim (875/54), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.] He did not command him by saying "Stand and pray, why are you sitting?" until he inquired. This is enjoining good. As for forbidding evil: you find a person walking beside a woman, and you say: "O brother, fear Allah, how can you walk with a woman?" What do you say about this?
* Student: It is not valid.
* The Shaykh: This is not permitted, because it is possible that this woman is one of his mahram (unmarriageable relatives). How can you forbid something as an evil while you do not know that it is evil?! So there must be knowledge of what? Of the situation: the situation of the one commanded and the one forbidden. Just as there must be knowledge of what? Of the Sharia: that I know this is among the good that the Sharia has commanded, or among the evil that the Sharia has forbidden. These are two conditions, and God willing we will come to the rest of the conditions.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And let there be from you﴾. We said that (min) is either partitive or for genus. What is the rule for it being for genus?
* The Shaykh: Its rule is that it clarifies the genus of that thing.
* Student: But they say: (...) substitutes for the predicate (...).
* The Shaykh: No, no, it is not necessary, it is not necessary.
* Student: Shaykh, how do we understand it?
* The Shaykh: If you say, for example: "Man is from dust," this is for clarifying the genus. And it may mean "from dust," i.e., some of the dust, not all the dust. This is like it: "from you" may mean, and let some of you be, or the meaning is: let your community, this Ummah, be.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾. Why did He not say: "after the clear proofs had come to them" (feminine)? I say: what is the point of this?
* The Shaykh: Arabic grammar in this construction permits both. That is why the verse appears elsewhere as: ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. So this is permissible in the Arabic language.
* Student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh. Regarding a gathering where people are sitting, all of them shaving their beards.
* The Shaykh: Shaving what?
* Student: Shaving the beard. And one, of course, who has a beard should not enter this gathering while he wants to shave his beard and go; that is, should he advise them about the things they do?
* The Shaykh: So he will shave his beard so that they will love him?!
* Student: No, so that he can disapprove of the things they do?
* The Shaykh: He does not disapprove of them shaving their beards until he shaves his beard?! No, this does not happen, it is not permitted.
* Student: Because some people cannot enter a place with a beard, so it becomes that he himself...?
* The Shaykh: (...) he does not say it that way.
* Student: No, no, Shaykh, he does not mean that.
* The Shaykh: Can he say it this way, or does he have a beard?
* Student: He means, O Shaykh, that sitting with clean-shaven men is not permitted? 
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: He says: clean-shaven, he says how can he sit with them?
* The Shaykh: No, no. He says: he wants to forbid them from shaving the beard, but he says: I am not forbidding them until I shave my beard, so I can say: do what I have abandoned?
* Student: No, they do it. They do things, for example they listen to songs and listen to things.
* The Shaykh: No, no, it is absolutely not valid. I do not see calling to the forbidden at all, never.
* Student: Shaykh, a saying spreads among some people: "Some of us excuse one another in what we differ about, and some of us help one another in what we agree upon." Does this saying have a legal basis?
* The Shaykh: This is wrong in both sentences. As for the first sentence, "Some of us excuse one another in what we differ about," it is like the saying of some jurists: "There is no disapproval in matters of ijtihad (independent reasoning)." This phrase is known among the jurists: "There is no disapproval in matters of ijtihad." This, taken in its absolute sense, is not correct. If the truth has not become clear in a matter, such that the dissenter is not excused, then here yes, we excuse him, because he has his opinion and we have ours. But if the truth is clear, then we do not excuse those who oppose us in that. So it is incorrect in its absolute form.
As for the second, which is his saying: "some of us help one another in what we agree upon," this is also incorrect, because if we agreed upon falsehood, it would not be lawful for some of us to help others. Rather, it would be obligatory for some of us to forbid others from this falsehood. So it too is not correct in its absolute sense. But perhaps the one who said it means what is not false and does not oppose the Sharia. But in the first sentence entered people who have deviation in creed and in method, yet they say Islam encompasses them, and they say: "We must shelter under the shade of Islam, even if we differ." That is why you find them admitting into their party the sinner, the one who shaves his beard, the smoker of tobacco, the one who is careless about prayer, and the like. This is a problem. That is, this is an error, and the strict path is also an error, which demands that people be righteous in every detail and minor matter, or else they are not our brothers. This too is an error.
* Student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh. We said that calling to good happens only through the forbidden.
* The Shaykh: It does not happen through the forbidden.
* Student: That is, it does not happen through the forbidden, yes. If a person is compelled to sit with a group, for example, who smoke tobacco or listen to musical instruments, so that he can speak with them, because he cannot find them except in this...?
* The Shaykh: No, no. This one did not smoke tobacco. If he says: "By Allah, O people, peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah," and sits and says: "O so-and-so, give me a cigarette," and he gets up and smokes, and says: "Do not smoke tobacco," this is not appropriate. But if he sat to call them, he sat to call them. The Messenger (ﷺ) would go to the polytheists in their places and call them, and calling is not possible except this way. I come to call them like a physician who cuts the skin to remove what is beneath it of harm.
* Student: Is there no difficulty, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: There is no difficulty at all, if he came intending to call them, how? That is, provided it is not necessary that he can find them only in this place.
* Student: Some people, when we call them, for example, may be neglecting prayer, and when we call them, they become uncomfortable. The second time and the third time. Do we continue calling?
* The Shaykh: What kind?
* Student: Some people are neglecting prayer, for example, persisting in sin. When we call him a second or third time, he may confront us?
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: He may disagree with us; that is, do we continue calling him? Calling him to good?
* The Shaykh: That is, with repeated calling, he may become bored, for example, and wander off? Yes. In any case, ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ [al-Nahl 125]. Wisdom must be applied: sometimes a person is angry, there are external influences, and his soul cannot accept from you anything, not even ordinary speech. Sometimes he is content and relaxed, and you can give him examples until Allah guides him. That is why some people err, for example, if a person does not agree with them or they do not treat him in the appropriate manner, they push him away. They do not know: perhaps this man has external influences you are unaware of, a tight chest, and he does not like to speak with people. Such matters should not lead a person to judge someone simply because he called him once and he pushed away. There may be reasons. Be patient, look for the time when you see him at ease, and call him to the truth.
* Student: Shaykh, which is more preferable, O Shaykh: calling the disobedient in this country or calling the disbelievers abroad?
* The Shaykh: The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And warn your closest kindred, and lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 214–215]. The obligation is that you call and reform the conditions you have, and then afterward try to reform the outside. But if within there are those who carry out the calling, and you wish to go out to its outskirts, this is good and there is no obstacle.
The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And let there be from you a nation inviting to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong﴾, to the end. The lam in His saying ﴿and let there be﴾?
* Student: The lam of command.
* The Shaykh: Of command. What indicates to you that it is a lam of command?
* Student: Because it put the present-tense verb in the jussive mood.
* The Shaykh: Well done. His saying ﴿ummah﴾?
* Student: A group.
* The Shaykh: A group. We mentioned that ummah occurs in the Qur'an in several senses? This is one sense.
* Student: It comes to mean a period of time.
* The Shaykh: It comes to mean a period of time, like what?
* Student: ﴿and he remembered after a period [ummah]﴾.
* The Shaykh: Like the statement of the Exalted: ﴿and he remembered after a period﴾.
* Student: It comes to mean a leader.
* The Shaykh: It comes to mean a leader, like what?
* Student: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was an ummah﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was an ummah﴾.
* Student: It comes to mean a religion.
* The Shaykh: It means religion.
* Student: It means religion, yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon an ummah﴾.
* The Shaykh: Like His saying: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon an ummah﴾, that is, upon a creed and religion. The fourth?
* Student: So that is four. The group in this verse.
* The Shaykh: Yes, a group, a leader, a period of time, and a creed.
His saying ﴿they invite to good﴾: what is meant by good?
* Student: What is meant by good is religion; that is, they call to religion.
* The Shaykh: To religion only?
* Student: No, all good, whether the good of religion or the good of this world.
* The Shaykh: Yes. His saying ﴿and they enjoin what is right﴾: what is "what is right" (al-ma'ruf)?
* Student: What is right is everything that agrees with the Sharia and good character.
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: Everything that agrees with the Sharia.
* The Shaykh: You mentioned "it is said." You said: "it is said, what agrees?"
* Student: Everything that the Sharia brought.
* The Shaykh: (...).
* Student: What the Sharia recognized and affirmed.
* The Shaykh: What the Sharia recognized and affirmed. And wrong (munkar)?
* Student: Wrong is everything the Lawgiver disapproved of.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Everything the Sharia disapproved of, restrained from, and forbade is wrong.
His saying ﴿and those are the successful﴾: what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of (hum) here?
* Student: It is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) with no place in i'rab.
* The Shaykh: It has no place in i'rab. And what is its benefit?
* Student: Its benefit, first: to alert the listener.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Its benefit is to separate between the attribute and the predicate.
* The Shaykh: Separating between the attribute and the predicate; that is, distinguishing between the predicate and the attribute. Is this one?
* Student: Alerting the listener, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Emphasis and restriction.
* The Shaykh: Emphasis and restriction.
* Student: And restriction, and distinguishing between the attribute and the predicate.
* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you. Who are the successful?
* Student: The successful is the one who attained the good of this world and the Hereafter; he is the one who attained what was sought and was saved from (...).
* The Shaykh: The one who attained what was sought and was saved from what was feared. Well done. His saying ﴿and do not be like those who became divided﴾: what is the connection of this verse to what precedes it?
* Student: That when they abandon enjoining good and forbidding evil, they divide.
* The Shaykh: They divide?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Well done. What is the reason for that?
* Student: When He commanded them that there be from them a community enjoining good...
* The Shaykh: No, what is the reason that when they abandon enjoining good and forbidding evil, they divide?
* Student: The enjoining of good and forbidding of evil was not established, so the community differed and disagreed.
* The Shaykh: How do they differ? Over what do they differ?
* Student: They say, each one acts according to his desire.
* The Shaykh: Yes, because then each one acts according to his own desire, and they must inevitably divide.
* The Shaykh: His saying ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾: what are the clear proofs?
* Student: The clear proofs are the Torah for the Jews and the Gospel for the Christians; that is, the clear signs. The clear signs came to them, that they should enjoin and forbid, but they abandoned enjoining good and forbidding evil and divided.
* The Shaykh: The proofs came to them concerning the command, but only the command to enjoin good and forbid evil?
* Student: And calling to Allah the Exalted.
* The Shaykh: Yes. I think we have taken the benefits?
* Students: We have not completed them.
* The Shaykh: We have not completed them? Six benefits, yes, what are they?
* Student: The obligation of calling to good, that this is a collective obligation; observing sincerity, from His saying ﴿they call to good﴾; that following good in everything is required by the Sharia, and good is of two kinds; the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil.
* The Shaykh: Wait, and good is of two kinds, because it was mentioned.
* Student: Good for oneself and good for others.
* The Shaykh: Good.
* Student: The obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil; there must be urging to seek knowledge.
* The Shaykh: The sixth?
* Student: The sixth: there must be urging to seek knowledge.
* The Shaykh: No, what is it!
Students: The urging to enjoin good and forbid evil (...).
* Student: Because it is not possible to call.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not "there must be urging to seek knowledge."
The urging to seek knowledge, because the one who enjoins and forbids must necessarily be a person of knowledge. This, I mean knowledge, we now begin the conditions:

This is the knowledge of what is good or evil, and it is one of the conditions for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil (al-amr bil-ma'ruf wa'l-nahy 'an al-munkar, the duty of commanding right and prohibiting wrong). That is, a person must have knowledge before we speak about calling to goodness, since calling to goodness itself indicates encouragement toward knowledge. For how can one who does not know goodness call to it?

So the verse encourages knowledge in three matters: in calling to goodness, in enjoining good, and in forbidding evil.

Enjoining good and forbidding evil has conditions:

First: knowledge. This is derived from the fact that one cannot enjoin good or forbid evil except when he knows that it is good and that it is evil. Knowledge of what? Knowledge first that this is good and that this is evil. That is one.

Second: knowledge of the state of the doer. That is, that he has committed an evil or abandoned a good. We do not simply see a person doing something evil and rebuke him without first inquiring. Nor do we see him neglecting a duty and rebuke him without first inquiring. If we saw a person eating carrion, we should not rebuke him until we ask: why are you eating carrion? He may say that he is compelled, and in that case eating carrion is lawful for him. Likewise, if we see someone praying the obligatory prayer sitting down, we should not rebuke him for not standing until we ask; perhaps he is unable. So there must be knowledge of the state of what? Of the one being commanded and the one being forbidden, because he may be in a condition in which the command does not apply to him and he is not sinful.

Do we have evidence for this?

Student: No.

Shaykh: We have mentioned it. We said: a man entered while the Prophet ﷺ was delivering the khutbah on Friday, and he sat down. The Prophet did not rebuke him for sitting, but said to him: "Have you prayed?" He said: No. He said: "Stand and pray two rak'ahs." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (930) and Muslim (875/54), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.] This shows that one must know the state of the one commanded and the one forbidden.

Third condition: that the evil does not lead to something worse than it. Enjoining against evil aims at reducing evil. So if forbidding it would result in the one forbidden falling into a greater evil, he should not be forbidden. Suppose a person smokes tobacco. Smoking is an evil, but if we forbid him, he will go on to drink wine. Should we forbid him from this?

Students: No.

Shaykh: Why? Because we know he will move on to a greater wrong than what he is in. Among this is what is related about Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, that he passed by a group of Tatars drinking wine with a companion of his, and he said nothing to them. His companion asked him: why do we not rebuke them? He said: If we rebuked them, they would go off to plunder people's wealth and violate their sanctities, and their harm would spread. As for their drinking wine, it harms only themselves.

If someone says: Is there evidence for this condition? We say: Yes, its evidence is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge﴾ [al-An'am 108]. Here Allah forbade the Muslims from reviling the idols of the disbelievers, although these idols deserve to be reviled and reviling them is an act of worship. But because reviling them would lead to a greater corruption, Allah forbade reviling them. Yet staying silent about the reviling of the gods of the polytheists is, in ruling, an evil. Nevertheless we remain silent about this lesser evil to prevent a greater evil. So this condition is necessary.

Fourth condition: that he knows the admonition is beneficial. That is, it is probable in his view that the doer of evil or the abandoner of an obligation is acting out of ignorance, and that he is close to returning to the truth. But if he knows that the one he is addressing has knowledge of the ruling yet is defiant and arrogant, then enjoining good and forbidding evil is not obligatory in that case. For example: shaving the beard today is known by all people to be forbidden, or by most people, or by the common people and the majority, to be forbidden. Yet you pass by ten men who have shaved their beards and ten who have let their beards grow; that is, about half the people have shaved. Is it obligatory on you, every time you see someone shaving his beard in the street, to stop him and say: fear Allah, do not shave your beard? What do you say?

Student: There is hardship.

Another student: We look: if he is incapable...

Shaykh: We say: we look. Perhaps this man is one in whom good is doubted, and if you advise him he will comply. Or it may be strongly probable to you that he is a man who knows the ruling but is arrogant toward it or treats it lightly. The point is that some scholars hold that this is one of the conditions for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. They may cite as evidence the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾ [al-A'la 9]: "if the reminder benefits", meaning if it does not benefit, then do not remind. They say: if reminding, which is calling to goodness, is obligatory only when it benefits, then enjoining good and forbidding evil is all the more so, because enjoining good and forbidding evil is more severe than calling to goodness. Calling to goodness is something anyone may do with no burden on him, but enjoining is what may bring harm from the one commanded or forbidden, and this matter has some weight in the soul.

We may say, however: he must command and forbid, and this is not without benefit, even if its only benefit were that people come to know that this is good or that this is evil. For if we remain silent under the pretext that commanding or forbidding does not benefit, evils will remain as they are, and neglect of obligations will remain as it is. The young people who are growing up will come to think that this evil is what?

Students: Good.

Shaykh: Good. And that good is not good. Therefore there is room for consideration regarding this condition. Rather, we say: enjoining good and forbidding evil is obligatory whether you think it beneficial or not, but within the limits of one's capacity, because all obligations are binding only according to capacity. ﴿So fear Allah as much as you can﴾ [al-Taghabun 16]. If it is hard for a person to stop every individual he passes in the market who is committing an evil, such as shaving his beard or anything else, then he is not required to do so. He is only required to do what he is able to do, because Allah says: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj 78].

Fifth condition: that the one who enjoins good is himself doing it, and the one who forbids evil is himself refraining from it. That is, do not enjoin good while you do not do it, and do not forbid evil while you do it. Is that correct? Do not enjoin good while you do not do it, and do not forbid evil while you do it. So if this man, for example, deals in usury, and he finds a person dealing in usury, it is not obligatory on him to say to the other: O so-and-so, abandon usury, usury is forbidden and its doer is cursed. This is not obligatory on you. Why?

Students: Because he does it.

Shaykh: He said: because he does it. He himself does it. How can he forbid something he himself does? Someone sees a man walking after the adhan near the mosque, who has left the mosque, and says to him: O so-and-so, it is forbidden for you to abandon congregational prayer, it is not permissible. This one who commands has opened his door and gone to his family to drink coffee. He commanded that one to pray, but he himself did not pray. He said: this is not obligatory. If you intended to enter your house and drink coffee with your family, even if you miss the congregation, do not command this man to pray in congregation. Let him go on his way. He cited as evidence for this the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah 44]. Allah rebuked those people for enjoining righteousness while forgetting themselves, and He explained that this is contrary to reason. How can you command people and abandon yourself? This is not reasonable. You have opposed the Shari'ah and rejected reason. He also cited what is established in the Sahih from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, so that his entrails spill out, and he will go round them as the donkey goes round the millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: What is the matter with you, O so-and-so? Did you not used to enjoin us to do good and forbid us from evil? He will say: I used to enjoin you to do good but I did not do it, and I used to forbid you from evil and I did it." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3267) and Muslim (2989/51), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd.] They said: this indicates the severity of his punishment if he enjoins good and does not do it, or forbids evil and does it. So enjoining good and forbidding evil is not obligatory upon one who does not do good and does not abandon evil.

Most scholars rejected this view and said: this is contrary to good manners, but it is forbidden. That is, for him to enjoin good without doing it, and to forbid evil while doing it, is undoubtedly contrary to good manners and contrary to reason, but it is forbidden for him. So it is obligatory on him to enjoin good and forbid evil, and to begin with himself. If he is negligent in his own right, he does not have the right to be negligent in the right of others. He does not have that right. So enjoining good and forbidding evil is obligatory upon him even if he himself does not do good and does not refrain from evil. For if he abandons enjoining good and forbidding evil while he himself does not do good and does not refrain from evil, he commits two prohibited things: abandoning an obligation toward himself, for himself, and abandoning an obligation toward himself, for others. So it is obligatory on him to enjoin good and forbid evil even if he himself does not act on good and does not refrain from evil. This is the correct view. But he should rebuke himself and say: How can I command good and not do it, and forbid evil and do it?!

This is contrary to reason and transmitted text, and contrary to good manners: contrary to good manners toward Allah and contrary to good manners among the servants of Allah. For this reason, among the descriptions by which the king of Ghassan described the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was that he said: he did not command anything without being the first to do it, and he did not forbid anything without being the first to abandon it. [Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Khasa'is al-Kubra (1/22) as narrated by Wathimah in the Kitab al-Riddah.] Peace and blessings be upon him. They said: for this reason Allah said to him: ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds. No partner has He. And with that I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-An'am 162-163]. "The first of the Muslims" does not mean first in time, as if there were Muslim nations before him. Rather it means first in deed: I am the first of those who submit to Allah and yield to His command. So this is a priority of rank, not a priority of time.

It is related of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Jawzi, may Allah have mercy on him, the famous preacher and author of the book al-Tabsirah, that he had a session every Friday in which he admonished the people, and thousands would attend. So much so that not a day passed without some people dying in his session from the intensity of the admonition's impact on their souls. One day a servant came to him and said: O my master, I have a master who harms me, wearies me, burdens me beyond my capacity, and beats me for it. I ask you to urge the people to free slaves, so that Allah may guide him and he may free me. He said: Fine, there is no objection. Friday came, and the servant waited for the Shaykh to speak about freeing slaves, but he did not speak of it. The second and third Fridays came, and he did not speak of it. After several Fridays he spoke about freeing slaves, and behold, the servant's master was present, so he freed him immediately. The servant went to Ibn al-Jawzi, may Allah have mercy on him, and said: Why did you delay? He said: Because I did not have dirhams to buy a slave and free him before I commanded the people to free slaves. Subhan Allah! He says: how can I urge people to free slaves when I have not freed any? When I have the means and free someone, then I command the people or urge them to free slaves.

This is an observed matter: the one who does good is followed by people in his command, and the one who abandons evil is followed by people in his prohibition. For people see with their eyes and their insight, and they say of the one who enjoins good while not doing it: this man lies to us, he plays with our minds. If the matter were good in his view, why would he not be the first to do it? If the evil were evil in his view, why would he not be the first to abandon it? So there is no doubt that it is part of good manners that the one who commands should do what he commands, and the one who forbids should refrain from what he forbids. But to make this a condition for the obligation, and to say to one who does not do good and does not refrain from evil: enjoining good and forbidding evil is not obligatory upon you, and you are not sinful for abandoning it, this is very far from correct. For those who say that it is a condition of obligation that one must do what he commands and refrain from what he forbids, say that if he does not enjoin good and does not forbid evil in this state, then what? There is no sin upon him, because a condition of obligation is that he himself be complying. By this it becomes clear to you the weakness of this view, and that it is obligatory on him to enjoin good even if he does not do it, and to forbid evil even if he does it. But he must rebuke himself too, and his own self should be the first he commands to good and the first he forbids from evil. So the conditions are five.

Among the etiquettes of enjoining good and forbidding evil, meaning etiquette and not obligation: that he be gentle in his commanding and gentle in his forbidding, "for gentleness is a noble quality, and Allah, the Exalted, gives through it what He does not give through harshness," as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said. [Related by Muslim (2593/77), from the hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd.] And as Allah directed Musa and Harun when He sent them to Pharaoh, so they said: ﴿Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress﴾ [Ta-Ha 45]. Yes: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾ [Ta-Ha 44]. When He sent them to Pharaoh, He said: ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he may remember or fear﴾: remember in what you command him, or fear in what you forbid him. And although he was among the most arrogant people on earth, if not the most arrogant on earth, still, in every case, it is among the etiquettes that a person be gentle in his commanding and forbidding.

Also among the etiquettes is that he be persuasive in his argument, because if he commands good, the one commanded may say: What is your evidence for this? And if he forbids evil, he may say: What is your evidence for this? So he must have persuasiveness.

Let it be known that the matter of persuasion is not the matter of knowledge. Some people have knowledge but cannot persuade others; they lack strength of argument and clarity. And some people have less knowledge than him but have strength of persuasion. So you must train yourself in the strength of persuasion, even by giving examples, because giving examples brings things closer. There is now, for example, a well-known group that calls to Allah and goes out, and they have a kind of persuasion for the common people that is not found among the great scholars. That is why you see them having a tremendous impact. For they have a method of persuasion. So if a person has a method, and he commands another and says: What is your evidence? Bring the evidence! And then he gives him reasonable examples, this is undoubtedly one of the etiquettes of enjoining good and forbidding evil.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad: "A man asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to commit fornication. He asked him to permit him to commit zina. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to him: 'Would you be pleased that this be done to your mother, your sister, or your maternal relatives?' He said: No, I would not be pleased. He said: 'If you would not be pleased that this be done to your close kin...'" [Related by Ahmad (22211) and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (7679), from the hadith of Abu Umamah.] This is the meaning of the hadith: if you are not pleased, how can you be pleased to do it yourself, to whom?

Students: To the close kin of other people.

Shaykh: To the close kin of other people? This is a persuasive method. That is, as soon as a person imagines this matter, he withdraws. If you saw someone flirting with your sister, your wife, or your daughter, what would you do? Would you be pleased?

Students: No.

Shaykh: You would not be pleased. How can you be pleased for yourself to flirt with the daughters of other people? Or worse, to commit zina, may Allah protect us. These are among the methods that the one who enjoins good and forbids evil should be aware of and skilled in.

Among the etiquettes (adab) is also patience (sabr) over harm, argument and dispute, especially when disputation among people has increased, so let him be patient. Almighty God related of Luqman that he said to his son while admonishing him: ﴿O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring resolve.﴾ [Luqman 17]. Every one who commands good must be struck by some harm, and some people may find it burdensome to enjoin good and forbid evil, and even if they are not harmed, yet their call is not accepted, or their command or prohibition is not accepted, so they become upset (fa-yazil), as the common folk say, and they cease to command or forbid. This is not correct. Enjoin good, forbid evil, and be patient over what befalls you. Look at the Prophets, peace be upon them, and what harm befell them! Great harm befell them: they were slandered in their bodies, slandered in their minds, slandered in their aims; everything about them was attacked, yet they remained patient. Musa, peace be upon him, was harmed with many harms; the seal of the Prophets, Muhammad (ﷺ), was harmed; and the first of the Prophets, Nuh, was harmed, when they would mock him: ﴿Whenever a company of his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said: If you mock us, then we mock you as you mock. (38) So you will come to know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him.﴾ [Hud 38, 39]. The Prophet (ﷺ) too was harmed with a great harm from the closest people to him. Did the Quraysh do to anyone who entered the Sacred Mosque and began to pray beneath the Ka'bah and prostrated to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did they harm anyone by bringing the entrails of a slaughtered camel and placing them upon him while he was prostrating? Never. Yet they did this to the Messenger (ﷺ), and he was patient.
Did they bring filth, dung and stench and place it at the doors of people in Makkah? No, yet they did this to the Messenger (ﷺ), and he was patient. So it is obligatory for a person to be patient, and to seek reward from Allah for this patience. This patience over commanding good and forbidding evil is greater in reward than patience over the greatest calamity that can befall a person in the nearest of people to him, because this is patience over harm suffered for the sake of Allah, not patience over the decrees of Allah. This is patience over harm suffered for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so seek the reward from Allah and be patient over what befalls you.
Among the harms that befall a person is harm by speech, such as argumentative harm: for example, he says to you, "Teach yourself," when you command him to good; you command him to good and he says, "Teach yourself"; you command him to good and he says, "Go discipline your dependents," and similar things. Some people also become heated; I mean, his blood boils and he becomes extremely angry, so we say: O brother, be patient, this is a simple matter. If he says, "Teach your dependents," say: O brother, there is no harm, may Allah reward you with good, but I am teaching my dependents and I will teach you now too; take it over a long period. If this man becomes heated and pride in sin seizes him, then soften, and he will cool down, because the problem is that the hot is met with the hot. But if the hot is met with the cool, it cools and the matter becomes normal; but if hot clashes with hot, the fire ignites. Therefore I say: it is obligatory upon us to be patient, and when we see people have pulled the rope tight, we loosen it, and when we see softness, we pull it.
These, then, are three etiquettes that the one who commands good and forbids evil should adopt. If we add the fifth condition, that among the etiquettes is that he be the first to do what he commands and the first to abandon what he forbids, the etiquettes become four and the conditions of obligation four.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the virtue of calling to good and of commanding good and forbidding evil. I hope you are highly engaged in this: calling to good, commanding good and forbidding evil. The evidence for its virtue is His saying: ﴿And those are the successful.﴾ When people lose, these are the successful, the winners.
* Among the benefits of the verse that follows: the prohibition of division, due to His saying: ﴿And do not be like those who divided﴾. We have mentioned in the exegesis that what is meant by this is division of hearts, not of opinions, because division of opinions is something unavoidable, since people differ in knowledge, memorization, understanding, faith and action; and all these five matters are among the causes of people's difference, so it is impossible for people to agree in opinion, but what is obligatory is agreement of what? 
* Students: The hearts.
* The Shaykh: The hearts.
* Among its benefits: that abandoning calling to good, commanding good and forbidding evil is a cause of division, since it follows the previous verse with this verse, which indicates that abandoning calling to good, commanding good and forbidding evil is a cause of division.
* Among its benefits: that division after the truth has become clear is more ugly than division when the truth is hidden. This is taken from His saying: ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, because when clear proofs have come and the truth has become manifest, there is no justification for division; but when the truth is hidden, division may occur. The truth, praise be to Allah, in this Shari'ah is clear and evident, because it is in the Book of Allah, preserved until the Day of Resurrection.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the severe warning against those who divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them, due to the saying of the Most High: ﴿And for them is a great punishment.﴾
* Among the benefits of this verse: that punishment differs according to the difference of the crime, since when the act of these people was great, their punishment was great.
* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. Now, when you call someone or command him, that is, you call him to good and forbid him from evil, he sometimes argues against you by what the state permits, saying: "My state is among the strictest countries in applying the Shari'ah, and if this were an evil it would not have been found in these lands. So what do we answer him?"
* The Shaykh: Yes. As for the one who argues by the act of the state, we say: this is not a proof by the consensus of the Muslims. The proof is in the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and the consensus of the Muslims, and the Muslims have agreed that the act of states is not a proof. Then, if there is something the state does which he himself acknowledges to be forbidden, we say: look, the state did such and such; do you say this is forbidden or permissible? If he acknowledges it is forbidden, we say: then there is no proof in the act of the state.
* A student: O Shaykh, in this time the muftis have multiplied, and whoever mounts a mount rides into fatwa, so we find many people when you ask them about a ruling on something, or you object to them about the ruling on smoking for example, he says: "Sheikh So-and-so says it is disliked." He does not know the disliked from the forbidden, but he follows what the common folk say: "Put between you and the Fire a pious one!" O Shaykh, do you not have a proof when he says this thing?
* The Shaykh: It is true that the muftis have now multiplied, without doubt, and that one who cannot control it has mounted the beast. But our stance toward this matter is to say: this is the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and we bring what we have of evidence, because any person who gives a fatwa without knowledge must have knowledge that contradicts what he issued, so we bring the proof from the Book and the Sunnah and we argue with this.
* A student: O Shaykh, he does not argue; he says to you: "Sheikh So-and-so says it is disliked"?
* The Shaykh: We say: the Shaykh is not evidence. We say: if we tell you, "Allah and His Messenger said," and you say, "Sheikh So-and-so said," then it means you have taken this shaykh as a prophet and abandoned the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). We say: on the Day of Resurrection, will you be asked about this shaykh or about the Messenger? About the Messenger: ﴿And on the Day He calls them and says: What did you answer the messengers?﴾ [Al-Qasas 65].
* A student: May Allah be good to you, how do we interpret His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾ [Al-A'la 9]?
* The Shaykh: This verse is the one by which those who say reminding is not obligatory except when it benefits have argued. The majority said: the meaning is, remind if these people are fit for reminding, just as one says: teach him if he knows knowledge. So it is from the category of encouragement, and from the category of warning to those being reminded.
* A student: I say, O Shaykh: one who commands good but does not practise it, leading people to fall into contradiction. For example, now we see a person who declares singing forbidden, then he himself listens to music; or he declares a thing forbidden, such as the uncovering of private parts, and then does the same. So people fall into contradiction; you find them applying this in the house, and they know this ruling, but it is not firmly established in their hearts, so this leads to a greater evil than what it was.
* The Shaykh: Then what do we do? Should the evil remain evil and we not denounce it because people are doing it?
* The student: Because it leads to something greater.
* The Shaykh: In any case, if you denounce the evil while there are people doing it, or you yourself do it, make people aware that it is evil, and some people abstain from it. For example, now when I say that singing is forbidden, or shaving the beard is forbidden, and then people do it, those who are pointed to for their social rank, do people say: "By Allah, this is permissible"? Never. They argue. The falsifier argues when a scholar errs or slips; for this reason 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and other predecessors used to warn against the slip of the scholar.[[Narrated by al-Darimi (220) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] The common folk do not argue a genuine argument; that is, they think the proof is on their side except in the matter of the scholars. This is the problem.
* A student: O Shaykh, some people, whenever evil increases, good increases, and some the opposite. So do we say to the second: do not command good lest you corrupt more than you reform?
* The Shaykh: Whenever?
* The student: Evil increases.
* The Shaykh: Evil increases, good increases; have I not conceived of this? Give an example so we can see?
* The student: Alright, O Shaykh, I mean whenever, I mean whenever something comes like what I said before, O Shaykh, I mean..
* The Shaykh: If you yourself could not conceive what you are saying, how should we conceive it?!
* The student: I mean you find him, for example, angry at it, and the second, as we say: (...) the second; I mean the one who commands good takes it with ease, and the second is bashful. If the one commanding good is himself bashful about the same thing, do we say: do not call and do not command lest you corrupt more than you reform?
* The Shaykh: We say: among the etiquettes is that he be broad-hearted and that he command gently; this is among the etiquettes, but it is not among the conditions. For example, if a person knows of himself that he is a hot-tempered man who becomes angry quickly, do we say: do not command and do not forbid?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: No, we say: command and forbid.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 104–105 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾.
He said: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾. The lam in His words ﴿Let there be﴾ is the lam of command (lam al-amr), and the evidence for this is that the verb after it is in the jussive mood (jazm), ﴿let there be﴾. The lam of command puts the present-tense verb into the jussive. ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾: ﴿ummah﴾ means a group (ṭā'ifah) that calls to good. The word ummah occurs in the Noble Qur'an with several meanings: among them a group, among them a period of time, among them leadership (imamah), and among them religion (millah). Its example in the sense of a group is this verse.
Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 104]. The lam in His words ﴿Let there be﴾ is the lam of command, and what is the evidence for this?
* Students: The jussive (jazm).
* The Shaykh: The verb after it is in the jussive mood, ﴿let there be﴾, and the lam of command puts the present-tense verb into the jussive. ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾: ﴿ummah﴾ means a group, calling to good. The word ummah in the Noble Qur'an occurs with several meanings: among them a group, among them a period of time, among them leadership, and among them religion. Its example in the sense of a group is this verse, ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 104]. Its example in the sense of religion is His saying, what is it?
* Students: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion (ummah)﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Upon a religion (ummah)﴾, i.e., upon a creed (millah). Its example in the sense of leadership?
* Students: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾ [al-Nahl 120].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾. Its example in the sense of a period of time: ﴿And he remembered after a period (ummah) [of time]﴾ [Yūsuf 45], i.e., after a time.
As for His words ﴿Let there be among you a community calling to good﴾: the ﴿min﴾ in ﴿among you (minkum)﴾ may be partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), and it may be explanatory of the genus (li-bayān al-jins). On the first, the meaning is: let some of you call to good. On the second, the meaning is: let all of you be callers to good, because if we take it as explanatory of the genus, the meaning becomes that the entire ummah must be of this type, that is, the ummah must be one that calls to good. If we take it as partitive, the meaning becomes: let some of you call to good. What follows from this will come, Allah willing, in the benefits (al-fawā'id).
He said: ﴿calling to good﴾. Calling whom? The object is omitted. Is the intended meaning that they call themselves, or that they call others among relatives, or other Muslims, or other people in general?
* Students: It includes all of them.
* The Shaykh: It includes all of them. They call to good everyone to whom the call can be directed; any person to whom the call can be directed, let them call him. Do they call the jinn?
* Students: Yes.
