Because we have a principle: a ruling attached to an attribute becomes stronger or weaker according to that attribute. If the attribute is present in great measure, the person deserves from the ruling attached to it a share proportional to that great measure, and otherwise according to its measure.

* A student: His saying, "Did you disbelieve after your faith?" implies that there are disbelievers who did not believe. Does it mean the covenant is intended, "And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins..." [al-A'raf 172]?
* The Shaykh: Where are you? We have spoken about this.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah Al 'Imran, verse 106 (part 2 of 2):**

* Student: Shaykh, is the *ghurrah* (the white mark on the forehead) one of the *simā* (distinguishing marks) of Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamā'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, it is one of the *simā* of this Ummah.
* Student: One of the *simā* of this Ummah. So can it be said that the darkness that appears on the forehead's skin is evidence of the servant's righteousness and abundant knowledge?
* Shaykh: Never, never. That is not correct. There are people who prostrate a great deal and have nothing on their foreheads, and there are people who prostrate little and have this mark on their foreheads. This is not evidence. It appears that it depends on the skin of the forehead itself.
* Student: Is the reading ﴿تَبْيَضُّ﴾ with a kasrah correct?
* Shaykh: What is the vowel? 
* Student: I mean ﴿تَبْيَضُّ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿تَبْيَضُّ﴾ with a fatḥah on the yā'?
* Student: Today I read in Fath al-Qadir, in a second reading, (تِبْيَضّ).
* Shaykh: (تِبْيَضُّ) with a kasrah on the tā', you mean?
* Student: Yes, (تِبْيَضُّ).
* Shaykh: I do not think it is a *sab'iyyah* (one of the seven canonical readings), because we do not have it. This Mushaf has the seven readings written in it, and it is not present.
* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, some natural science books speak about the sciences of nature and say: "No harm befalls anything," or, for example: "Nature willed it," or "Nature wanted it."
* Shaykh: Yes, this is not permissible.
* Student: Does it count as *shirk* (polytheism)?
* Shaykh: Yes, how could it not! But if a Muslim wrote it, that Muslim would be considered one who took this word from the *Ṭabā'iʿiyyīn* (naturalists), not knowing what it means; he is ignorant.
* Student: O Shaykh, how can a child be born upon the *fiṭrah* (natural disposition) and be a believer, when he has not received or been obligated in the matters of Islam?
* Shaykh: Yes. The nature upon which Allah created mankind is faith. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth. [Adhere to] the fiṭrah (natural disposition) of Allah upon which He has created [all] people﴾ [Ar-Rum 30]. The Prophet, peace be upon him, also informed that: "Every child is born upon the fiṭrah" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1359) and Muslim (2658/22) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. This is from the blessing of Allah, so that the proof is established against a person. If you are the one who turned away from what the fiṭrah requires, or [is it that] what your fiṭrah requires is that you are a believer?
* Student: Regarding those who deny causes, if they say, citing Allah's words: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾ [Al-Anfal 17], how is one to respond to them?
* Shaykh: How to respond to them? It is clear. Because His words ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾, since their killing was a matter beyond the ordinary, He attributed it to Himself, as in His words: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw﴾ [Al-Anfal 17]. It is known that the Messenger was the one who took a handful of dust and threw it at those people, and yet it was an unusual throw, because the custom is that such a throw does not reach the eyes of all the polytheists. Since this cause, which came from a human being, was an unusual cause, Allah attributed it to Himself.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 107–109 (part 1 of 3):

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿As for those whose faces will turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 107]. The waw (و) is a conjunction particle, and (أما, amma) is a particle of detailing, as already explained in the first verse. ﴿Those whose faces will turn white﴾ are the believers. This whiteness is of two kinds: a general whiteness for every believer, and a special whiteness for this Ummah, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «A distinguishing mark that is not for anyone other than you» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (136) and Muslim (246/37), with his wording, from Abu Hurairah]. Meaning: among you. «You will be called on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (136), and Muslim (246/35) from Abu Hurairah, with the wording «Indeed my Ummah will be called on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'»]. So this Ummah will have white faces, but they will have a light that differs from that of others. Also, for this Ummah the light reaches as far as the wudu' reaches, meaning it will be on the hands and on the feet. For this reason he said: «with bright faces and white limbs». As for others, we know of nothing except that only their faces will be white. ﴿Those whose faces will turn white﴾ are the believers. ﴿Then they are in the mercy of Allah﴾: (في, fi) is for location, and (رحمة الله, rahmat Allah) here is not the mercy mentioned in His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 58], because that is an attribute of Allah. Here, ﴿in the mercy of Allah﴾ refers to a created thing of Allah, and what is meant by it is Paradise, as in the authentic hadith in which Allah said to it, that is to Paradise: «You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850), and Muslim (2846/34) from Abu Hurairah]. It is impossible that what is meant is the attribute, because an attribute cannot be a place (ظرف, zarf) for human beings. An attribute cannot be a place for human beings. And since it is impossible for it to be a place for human beings, it is impossible for the mercy here to mean the mercy which is an attribute of Allah. Rather, it is the created mercy of Allah, and it was called by the name of mercy because it came about through the mercy of Allah, by which Allah shows mercy to whomever He wills among His servants.

And His saying: ﴿Then they will abide therein forever﴾ [Al 'Imran 107]. (هم, hum) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada') and is not a pronoun of separation (ضمير فصل, damir fasl); rather it has a place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). ﴿Khalidun﴾ is the predicate of the subject. (فيها, fiha) is a prepositional phrase (جار ومجرور, jar wa majrur) attached to (خالدون, khalidun). ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾ means they will remain. The verses indicate that this abiding is everlasting, and Allah mentioned eternity (التأبيد, ta'bid) in several verses of His Book, showing that this abiding is an everlasting abode.

Then Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. (تلك, tilka) refers to what preceded of the verses which Allah mentioned. It is possible that what is meant is the whole Quran, and this is supported, that is strengthened, by the demonstrative used, since it came in the distal form (صيغة البعد, sigha al-bu'd). So the demonstrative here includes the entire Quran. His saying ﴿the verses of Allah﴾ means the signs that point to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His existence and to what it contains of His names, attributes and actions. Here, the verses meant are the legislative verses (الآيات الشرعية, al-ayat al-shar'iyyah).

His saying ﴿We recite them to you with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran 108] means: We read them to you. Is it meant that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, recites them to the Prophet (ﷺ) directly, or through Jibril?

* The students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second. It may also sometimes be the first: sometimes revelation is cast into the heart of the Prophet, peace be upon him, by casting (إلقاء, ilqa'). But the first is more common. Indeed, regarding the Quran, the second may be the one that is definite, because Allah says: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 192–194]. The apparent meaning is that the entire Quran was brought down by Jibril. On this basis, the attribution of the recitation to Allah in this verse means what? It means the recitation of Jibril, and it is attributed to Allah because he, that is Jibril, was sent with it from Him. This is like His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its explanation﴾ [al-Qiyamah 16–19]. ﴿When We have recited it﴾: the reciter is Jibril, as the hadith confirms that when the Messenger, peace be upon him, heard the recitation of Jibril, he would hasten in reciting, fearing that he would forget something, so he would rush. Then Allah said: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾. Even if many verses were revealed at one moment, you will not forget it. For this reason He said: ﴿When We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾: it will remain, and you will forget nothing of it. ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation﴾: We must make it clear to people, both its wording and its meaning.

He says: ﴿We recite them to you with truth﴾. Is the (ب, ba') in ﴿with truth﴾ for accompaniment (المصاحبة, al-musahabah), meaning that it is accompanied by truth and sent down with truth, truthful in its reports and just in its rulings? Or does the meaning that it was sent down from Allah truly, so the (ب) here is for association (الملابسة, al-mulabasah), meaning it is clothed in truth, that is, it was sent down from Allah in a true descent, free of doubt and falsehood?

* The students: It includes both meanings.
* The Shaykh: It includes both meanings together. So it is sent down from Allah truly, without doubt, and it is also sent down with truth. The principle in the science of tafsir (interpretation) is that if a verse contains two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is obligatory to take it as both meanings. If the two meanings contradict each other, a preponderant meaning is sought, and what is preponderant is what is meant.

Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. (ما, ma) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi.

* The students: It is not Hijazi.
* The Shaykh: (ما) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi. (ما) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi.
* The students: It is Tamimi.
* The Shaykh: No, it is Hijazi, because the conditions are complete. The conditions are complete. But its subject is singular, as is customary, since the subject of a nominal sentence is usually singular, and its predicate is a clause, ﴿yurid﴾ (intends), its predicate is a clause, and the order is present, and the negation was not nullified, and it was not joined by (إن, in). So the conditions are complete, and therefore it is Hijazi. Our saying "Hijazi" does not mean that only the people of the Hijaz speak it. Rather, the Arabs in general speak it, but the people of the Hijaz make it operate like (ليس, laysa), and the Banu Tamim leave it inoperative. For example, if someone addresses you and says: ما زيد موجودًا (ma Zayd mawjudan), you know he is Hijazi; and if another person addresses you and says: ما زيد موجودٌ (ma Zayd mawjudun), you know he is Tamimi. Do you know? The meaning is that if someone addressed you in the speech of the early Hijazis, but the speech of the Hijazis today is not a proof. Do you understand? Now the poet says:

"And a slender-waisted one, I said to him: Declare your lineage, and he answered: The killing of the lover is not forbidden (ما قتل المحب حرام)."

* The Shaykh: Is this Tamimi or Hijazi?
* The students: Tamimi.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because he said "ma qatlu al-muhibbi haramun". If he were Hijazi he would have said "haraman". Good.

The noble verse: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. This (ما) is undoubtedly Hijazi, the noble name is its subject, and the clause (يريد, yurid) is its predicate.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says, negating for Himself, Glorified and Exalted, that He intends injustice to the worlds. Those whose faces turned white or whose faces turned black were not wronged. Those whose faces turned white obtained this by their deeds, that is, because of them. Those whose faces turned black also obtained it by their deeds. The first did righteous deeds and were rewarded with this reward, and the others did evil deeds and were requited with this punishment, because Allah cannot possibly wrong anyone.

His saying ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾: (العالمين, al-'alamin) refers to all that is other than Allah. As in ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves﴾ [Yunus 44].

Then He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran 109]. The predicate here is placed first for a benefit, which is restriction (الحصر, al-hasr), that is specification. Because when you put first what should be delayed, that is a restriction. Whenever you put first something that should come later, that is restriction, whether it is a predicate, a direct object, or a prepositional phrase. For example: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah 5]: the direct object was placed first to indicate restriction, meaning we worship none but You and we seek help from none but You. Here: ﴿To Allah belongs what is in the heavens﴾ means not to anyone else; so the predicate was placed first for the sake of restriction. ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: (ما, ma) is a relative pronoun (اسم موصول, ism mawsul) that includes everything in the heavens, of humans, jinn, trees, rivers, seas and other things. Correct?

* A student: It is wrong, Shaykh. There are no humans in the heavens.
* The Shaykh: Because, as far as we know, there are no humans, stones or trees in the heavens, and knowledge is with Allah. Rather, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ includes all of this: what is in the heavens of angels, and what is in the earth of humans, jinn, trees, stones and everything, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. And (ما) was used to give precedence to non-rational beings, because they are the majority, so they were given precedence. This is one aspect. Another aspect: when an attribute is intended, one expresses it with (ما) instead of (من, man), even for a rational being. Pay attention: when an attribute is intended, (ما) is used in place of (من), even for a rational being. They illustrate this with His saying: ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa' 3], and He did not say "man taba", because the individual rational person was not intended; rather, the attribute, kind and quantity were intended. Marry whatever is good, whether beautiful or ugly, one or many, of women.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. I think you know that the relative clause (صلة الموصول, silat al-mawsul) may be a sentence or a semi-sentence (شبه جملة, shibh jumlah). It may be a nominal sentence, a verbal sentence, a prepositional phrase, or an adverbial phrase: four types. The nominal and verbal sentences are clear. You say: "I like the one whose character is good." What is this? Nominal. And you say in a verbal sentence: "I like the one who was brave." This is a verbal sentence. And you say with an adverb: "I like the one who is above the roof." And you say with a prepositional phrase: "I like the one who is in the mosque." In this verse, which type is it? A prepositional phrase. Good. They say: the prepositional phrase by itself is not a sentence, because it needs a governing element, so how can it be a sentence? They say: because it contains something omitted, and therefore in i'rab we say: a prepositional phrase attached to an omitted element. Estimate the omitted element as a verb in the relative clause, and estimate it as a noun in the predicate of the subject. Pay attention! In the relative clause, it is estimated as a verb, and in the predicate of the subject, as a noun. So when you say "I like the one who is with you," the estimate is: "the one who is settled with you." And when you say "Zayd is with you," the estimate is: "Zayd is settled with you." Do you understand, everyone? Why? Because the basic form of the predicate of a subject is that it is a single word, not a sentence, and the basic form of the relative clause is that it is a sentence. So we estimate it as a verb in the relative clause, and as a noun in the predicate of the subject. This is the rule.

He says: ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is the possession of Allah, in creation, bringing into being, disposing and managing. His saying: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Baqarah 210] is also a restriction, by placing the prepositional phrase before what it governs, which is ﴿are returned﴾. And His saying: ﴿all matters are returned﴾ includes every matter. (الأمور, al-umur) is the plural of (أمر, amr) meaning affair, since the word (أمر) is used to mean affair, as He said: ﴿And the affair of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud 97], meaning his affair. And (أمر) is also used to mean a command addressed in the form of requesting an act from a position of superiority. The plural of the first is (أمور, umur), and the plural of the second is (أوامر, awamir). On this basis, (الأمور, al-umur) here is the plural of (أمر) meaning affairs. All affairs return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and come back to Him, because He is the Creator who initiated them, so they must return to Him.

* In these verses there are benefits. We begin with the first verse, which is His saying: ﴿On the day when faces will turn white and faces will turn black﴾.
* Students: We have taken them.
* The Shaykh: Have we taken the benefits from it? Good. He said: ﴿As for those whose faces will turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, therein they will abide forever﴾.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the people of faith whose faces turned white will be in Paradise, by His saying: ﴿then they are in the mercy of Allah﴾.
* And from its benefits: the abiding of the people of Paradise in it, by His saying: ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾.
* And from its benefits: that this abiding is permanent, because it came in the nominal form ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾, which indicates stability and continuity.
* And from its benefits: that mercy is applied to something other than the attribute of Allah, but to His creatures, as we have explained in the tafsir that what is meant by mercy here is Paradise. As for His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 58], what is meant there is the attribute. Good. Is the mercy of Allah, which is His attribute, created or uncreated? Uncreated. All the attributes of Allah are uncreated, and the mercy of Allah which is Paradise is created.

Allah says: ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Rum 50]. When He mentioned the descent of rain and that He gives life to the earth by it, He said: ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. What is meant by mercy here?

* Students: The attribute.
* The Shaykh: The created thing which is the rain, or the attribute?
* Students: The attribute.
* The Shaykh: It may be. It is possible that what is meant by "the traces of the mercy of Allah" is the rain, and so it is created; or "the traces of the mercy of Allah" which is His attribute, and of whose effects and what arises from it is this rain. Good. ﴿And He is the One who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 28].

* Students: The created.
* The Shaykh: The created? The created, because it is what is spread. Now pay attention: mercy is of two kinds: a created kind, which is what is separate from Allah, and an uncreated kind, which is what is an attribute of Him.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is more generous than the creation, because the deeds of those whose faces turned white, if attributed to reward alone, would be nothing; yet they are granted mercy in which they will abide forever and ever. This confirms His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am 160].

Then Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you with truth﴾ to the end [Al 'Imran 108].

* From the benefits of this verse: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, because Allah attributed it to Himself, saying: ﴿the verses of Allah﴾. Whatever is attributed to Allah and is not an independent entity is one of His attributes, because the thing attributed must subsist in something. If it is an attribute, it can only be an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So if we say "the speech of Allah," this is an attribution of an attribute. If we say "this is the creation of Allah," this is not an attribution of an attribute. Why? Because the creation is an independent entity. Good. Is "the she-camel of Allah" an attribute or not an attribute? Not an attribute, because it is an independent entity. "The House of Allah"? Likewise not an attribute, because it is an independent entity. Now: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr 29]?

* Students: An entity.
* Students: A self.
* The Shaykh: An entity. ﴿of My spirit﴾: is it an attribute or not an attribute?
* Students: Not an attribute.

**Shaykh:** A different attribute, is that right? It is created. For if it were an attribute of Allah, it would not be separated from Him. Here the mercy has been separated, separated from Allah. Where did it settle? In Adam, in Adam's body. So it is not one of the attributes of Allah, because it is separate from Him. The attribution of the spirit to Allah here is therefore the attribution of a creation to its Creator. For this reason we cannot say that it is a part of the spirit of Allah which is His attribute. That is impossible, for if we said this, something of Allah would have settled in His creatures. Alright, the mercy here in the verse, ﴿then in the mercy of Allah﴾, belongs to the category of created things. If someone argued and said, "Rather it is an attribute of Allah," we would answer him that this is impossible, because an attribute of Allah cannot be a container for human beings. Here He said, ﴿then in the mercy of Allah﴾. So we derive from this that mercy attributed to Allah divides into two kinds: created and uncreated. What is separate from Allah is created, and what is not separate is an attribute of His attributes. If someone asks, "Why did Allah call it mercy?" You say: Because it is one of the effects of the mercy of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the people of Paradise will abide in it forever, because of His saying, ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾. The abiding here is everlasting, as Allah mentioned in many verses. If someone says, "If you say it is everlasting, what is your answer to His saying: ﴿As for those who are made happy, they will abide in Paradise, forever, for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills: a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud 108], for He made an exception, saying, ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾?"

* **Student:** The answer?

* **Shaykh:** Yes.

* **Student:** That the abiding is by the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, this is one aspect.

* **Student:** We say that the abiding may have been preceded by punishment for sinful believers, so this exception is made from the will.

* **Shaykh:** You mean the exception refers back to what came before?

* **Student:** To what came before.

* **Shaykh:** Yes, this is the second.

* **Student:** O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. We say that this may be from the mutashabih (ambiguous verses), or it is from the mutashabih, and Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded us to refer the mutashabih to the muhkam (clear verses), and that is their abiding in an everlasting manner.

* **Shaykh:** So then we do not oppose the verses that indicate perpetuity with this verse, because it is among the unclear ones, so it must be referred back to the clear ones. Alright, these are three.

* **Student:** The exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But what your Lord wills." It is not connected to what precedes it.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, but "what your Lord wills," and what is the result? Alright, (...) we will make it the fourth opinion and discuss the opinions now.

* **Student:** That the heavens and the earth do not remain permanent, so the exception, "except what your Lord wills," is that they increase.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, these are five.

* **Student:** This exception has been explained in this verse and in another verse, which is His saying: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad 54].

* **Shaykh:** This is among the unclear matters, and there are clear verses about it. Even the verse we have: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾ indicates that it is continuous.

* **Student:** ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and Allah has willed that the people of Paradise abide forever.

* **Shaykh:** ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and Allah has willed. I think this is the third opinion.

* **Student:** O Shaykh, as it was understood, the abiding, in people's minds, came to mean that abiding happens without the will of Allah. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought His will to make it known that this abiding is by His will, Mighty and Majestic.

* **Shaykh:** Yes indeed. In any case, the scholars have opinions on this. But the view that gives a person peace of mind, and makes this restriction, and the restriction regarding the people of the Fire, ﴿abiding therein﴾ and ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, placing it among the ambiguous matters, so that it is interpreted in light of the clear texts, gives peace. He says: Allah said, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, even though He has willed that this remain forever and ever. It is like the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ) when visiting the graves: "And we, if Allah wills, will surely join you." [[Narrated by Muslim (249/39) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] He made it conditional on will, even though joining them is certain. A person finds peace in this and no objector can object to it, as Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) objected, saying that Allah said regarding the people of the Fire: ﴿abiding therein﴾, ﴿except what your Lord wills; indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, and He said regarding the people of Paradise: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾. He said: The difference in the endings of the two verses indicates that the abiding of the people of the Fire is not everlasting, unlike the people of Paradise, because He said of the people of Paradise: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, and He said of the people of the Fire: ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾. This, in truth, shows you that a person, however much he attains in knowledge and intelligence, will not be safe from error. The difference between the two verses is clear, for the verse about happiness is grace, so He said: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾. And the verse about the Fire, which is misery, is justice, so He said: ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, and this is from His act which He intended. The meaning of ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾ is not that He will do the opposite in the future, as Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) understood. This understanding is undoubtedly incorrect. Rather, the connection of the verse's ending with His saying, ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, is that since misery is not praiseworthy, He said: this is from the act of Allah, and Allah does what He wills, although He has not wronged them.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿These are the verses of Allah; We recite them to you in truth﴾. Among the benefits of this verse is that whoever acts as a representative for another has the ruling of the one who appointed him, because Allah attributed the recitation to Himself, although the one who recites is His Messenger. This shows that the ruling on what the Messenger carries out by what he was sent with is the ruling on what the sender said.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is entirely true, with no falsehood in it. If we take this word in its generality, we say: all its rulings are true, all its reports are true, and there is no contradiction or disagreement in it. For if there were contradiction or disagreement in it, one of the two contradictories would be false, and the Qur'an contains nothing false. It is entirely true.

* Among its benefits: establishing the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), since He said: ﴿We recite them to you in truth﴾. So the one to whom these verses are recited must definitely be a Messenger of Allah, Lord of the worlds.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: establishing the will of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾. If someone says: The verse here is a negation, ﴿And Allah does not intend﴾, so how do you say it indicates an affirmation?
We say: This negation is not absolute. Rather, it is a negation of the will of a specific thing, which is injustice. So does He intend other than injustice, or not? He intends it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: injustice is possible with respect to Allah, but He does not intend it because of His perfect justice. What is the proof? He said: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the servants﴾ [Ghafir 31], and He did not say, "It is not possible that Allah intends injustice." Even if He had said, "it is not possible," this would not indicate the absence of injustice if He willed it. In that case, it would be a refutation of those who say that injustice with respect to Allah is impossible in its very essence, and they are the Jahmiyyah. They say that injustice with respect to Allah is impossible in its essence, not because it is not willed by Allah, but in its essence. According to their view, Allah's praise of Himself by negating injustice would be pointless and without benefit, because what is impossible cannot be a matter of praise, nor can one praise himself with what is impossible for him. So injustice with respect to Allah is possible rationally, but it is prohibited by the Sharia and by justice. If Allah, exalted, willed to punish the obedient, would it be possible or not? It would be possible. But because of His perfect justice, He cannot punish him, because that would be injustice. They say: It is impossible for Allah to wrong anyone ever; injustice is impossible. Why? Is it not possible that Allah punishes the obedient one who spent his whole life in obedience to Allah? They said: Yes, it is possible, but this is not injustice, because He does it in what He owns. The servant is Allah's possession, so whatever He does to him is not injustice toward him. Do you understand now? This is their view, but it is a corrupt view. For if someone said to you: Do such and such and I will reward you; do not do such and such or I will punish you. Then you did what he commanded you and what he promised reward for, and then he punished you with the most severe punishment. Is this injustice by reason or not? It is injustice, even if he owns you. If a master said to his servant, "O my servant, prepare the lunch with such and such, and bring it to me at such and such an hour," and he did what he was commanded, in the described manner and at the time he specified, and then the master took a piece of wood and began to beat him with it, what would he be? A wrongdoer. Even if he were his servant? Even if he were his servant, rationally he would be a wrongdoer. They say: It is permissible that a person spends his whole life in obedience to Allah, complying with the command of Allah, and when he dies, Allah makes him abide in the Fire, and if He does that, He is not a wrongdoer. Why? He said: Because He did it in His own dominion. We say: If the matter is so, and injustice, according to your claim, is impossible, then it is not valid to say that Allah negates injustice from Himself as praise for Himself.

* Among the benefits of this verse: if the will of injustice is negated, injustice is negated. What is the reason? Allah has no one who compels Him. If He does not intend injustice, no one can force Him to commit injustice. So negating the will of injustice is negating injustice. Consequently, there is no contradiction between this verse and His saying: ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat 46]. There is no contradiction between them, what? Because negating the will of injustice necessitates negating injustice, and negating injustice necessitates negating the will of injustice, because if He willed to be unjust, He would be unjust. So if someone said to me: How do you reconcile this verse, ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾, with His saying, ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾, what would you say? I would say: There is no contradiction, because if the will of injustice is negated, the negation of injustice follows, and if injustice is negated, the negation of His will to do it follows, because Allah is able; if He willed to be unjust, He would be unjust.

* Among the benefits of this verse: establishing negative attributes. What Allah described Himself with divides into two kinds: affirmative (thubuti) and negative (intiqa'i), or if you prefer, say: negative (salbi). The affirmative attributes are all attributes of perfection. Every attribute Allah affirmed for Himself is an attribute of perfection. The negative ones are all attributes of deficiency negated, but they include the affirmation of a perfection. In His saying, ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [Al-Baqarah 74], there is the negation of heedlessness, for what? For the perfection of His knowledge and watchfulness. ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the servants﴾, for the perfection of His justice. ﴿And fatigue did not touch Us﴾ [Qaf 38], for the perfection of His power. Is that right? ﴿And Allah was not one to be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Fatir 44], for the perfection of His power and knowledge, and so on.

* * *

* **Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [109]. ﴿You are the best nation produced for mankind; you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah. Had the People of the Scripture believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [110]. ﴿They will not harm you except for minor harm. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs; then they will not be helped﴾ [111]. ﴿Humiliation has been stamped upon them wherever they are found, except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people. They have returned with anger from Allah, and destitution has been stamped upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing﴾ [Ali 'Imran 109–112].

* **Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾. Before we begin the explanation or the tafsir, we want to point out a recitation habit some people follow. When he stops at ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, he stops only at ﴿destitution﴾, then he returns and says, ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, even though if he had connected ﴿destitution﴾ to what precedes it, he could have done so without losing his breath. Likewise, when he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾, he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets﴾ and stops, then he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾, even though if he had connected the phrase ﴿without right﴾ to what precedes it, he would not have run out of breath. This is a fashion some reciters adopt, and in reality it is an error, because repetition without reason is not appropriate. Moreover, if he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾ or ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, he separates it from what precedes it, and then he needs to repeat the verse from its beginning. So he stops at ﴿and humiliation has been stamped upon them﴾, then repeats it again. He stops at ﴿and has been stamped﴾, then repeats again, and stops the third time at what he says, and repeats again, and so on. This is not correct. I told you before that if one or two words remain, you should follow them, even if you feel some shortness of breath, so that you do not need to repeat the speech a second time.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The sentence here is declarative, and its predicate has been placed first to convey restriction: ﴿to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾.

In His saying, ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, among the benefits: first: * Among the benefits of this verse: the generality of the dominion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because of His saying, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The word "whatever" (ma) is a relative pronoun conveying generality.

* Among its benefits: the exclusivity of Allah, glorified and exalted, in that dominion; that is, Allah alone is its owner. This is derived from the placement of the predicate first, because the established rule among the rhetoricians and the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) is that placing the object before the verb conveys restriction.

* Among the benefits of this verse: establishing the heavens and the earth, which is a known matter and is not denied. But the benefit of this benefit is to show the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted, in creating these great creations, about which Allah said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know﴾ [Ghafir 57].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the return of all matters is to Allah alone, because of His saying: ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾.

* Among its benefits: whoever tries to legislate for creation something other than what Allah has legislated has associated himself with Allah, or has made himself a partner with Allah. The reason: Allah restricted the return of all matters to Himself, saying, ﴿and to Allah﴾. So whoever tries to legislate for people matters that Allah has not legislated has made himself a partner with Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the vastness of Allah, glorified and exalted, since all matters return to Him. The word "matters" (umur) is the plural of "matter" (amr), and it has the definite article (al), which conveys generality. So all matters return to Him, the minute and the great. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ [Hud 56]. All creatures, small and large, Allah, glorified and exalted, holds their forelocks. He is the one who directs and manages them, the rational and the non-rational among them.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: it establishes that "the heavens" (al-samawat) is a plural noun. Other verses show that their number is seven heavens. As for the earth, it is mentioned in the Qur'an in the singular, but God indicated its number in His saying: ﴿It is God who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. The Sunnah is also explicit on this in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever unjustly seizes a span of the earth, God will encircle his neck with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."[[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim (1610 / 137), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 107–109 (part 1 of 3):

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿As for those whose faces will turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 107]. The waw (و) is a conjunction particle, and (أما, amma) is a particle of detailing, as already explained in the first verse. ﴿Those whose faces will turn white﴾ are the believers. This whiteness is of two kinds: a general whiteness for every believer, and a special whiteness for this Ummah, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «A distinguishing mark that is not for anyone other than you» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (136) and Muslim (246/37), with his wording, from Abu Hurairah]. Meaning: among you. «You will be called on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (136), and Muslim (246/35) from Abu Hurairah, with the wording «Indeed my Ummah will be called on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'»]. So this Ummah will have white faces, but they will have a light that differs from that of others. Also, for this Ummah the light reaches as far as the wudu' reaches, meaning it will be on the hands and on the feet. For this reason he said: «with bright faces and white limbs». As for others, we know of nothing except that only their faces will be white. ﴿Those whose faces will turn white﴾ are the believers. ﴿Then they are in the mercy of Allah﴾: (في, fi) is for location, and (رحمة الله, rahmat Allah) here is not the mercy mentioned in His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 58], because that is an attribute of Allah. Here, ﴿in the mercy of Allah﴾ refers to a created thing of Allah, and what is meant by it is Paradise, as in the authentic hadith in which Allah said to it, that is to Paradise: «You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850), and Muslim (2846/34) from Abu Hurairah]. It is impossible that what is meant is the attribute, because an attribute cannot be a place (ظرف, zarf) for human beings. An attribute cannot be a place for human beings. And since it is impossible for it to be a place for human beings, it is impossible for the mercy here to mean the mercy which is an attribute of Allah. Rather, it is the created mercy of Allah, and it was called by the name of mercy because it came about through the mercy of Allah, by which Allah shows mercy to whomever He wills among His servants.

And His saying: ﴿Then they will abide therein forever﴾ [Al 'Imran 107]. (هم, hum) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada') and is not a pronoun of separation (ضمير فصل, damir fasl); rather it has a place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). ﴿Khalidun﴾ is the predicate of the subject. (فيها, fiha) is a prepositional phrase (جار ومجرور, jar wa majrur) attached to (خالدون, khalidun). ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾ means they will remain. The verses indicate that this abiding is everlasting, and Allah mentioned eternity (التأبيد, ta'bid) in several verses of His Book, showing that this abiding is an everlasting abode.

Then Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. (تلك, tilka) refers to what preceded of the verses which Allah mentioned. It is possible that what is meant is the whole Quran, and this is supported, that is strengthened, by the demonstrative used, since it came in the distal form (صيغة البعد, sigha al-bu'd). So the demonstrative here includes the entire Quran. His saying ﴿the verses of Allah﴾ means the signs that point to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His existence and to what it contains of His names, attributes and actions. Here, the verses meant are the legislative verses (الآيات الشرعية, al-ayat al-shar'iyyah).

His saying ﴿We recite them to you with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran 108] means: We read them to you. Is it meant that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, recites them to the Prophet (ﷺ) directly, or through Jibril?

* The students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second. It may also sometimes be the first: sometimes revelation is cast into the heart of the Prophet, peace be upon him, by casting (إلقاء, ilqa'). But the first is more common. Indeed, regarding the Quran, the second may be the one that is definite, because Allah says: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 192–194]. The apparent meaning is that the entire Quran was brought down by Jibril. On this basis, the attribution of the recitation to Allah in this verse means what? It means the recitation of Jibril, and it is attributed to Allah because he, that is Jibril, was sent with it from Him. This is like His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its explanation﴾ [al-Qiyamah 16–19]. ﴿When We have recited it﴾: the reciter is Jibril, as the hadith confirms that when the Messenger, peace be upon him, heard the recitation of Jibril, he would hasten in reciting, fearing that he would forget something, so he would rush. Then Allah said: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾. Even if many verses were revealed at one moment, you will not forget it. For this reason He said: ﴿When We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾: it will remain, and you will forget nothing of it. ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation﴾: We must make it clear to people, both its wording and its meaning.

He says: ﴿We recite them to you with truth﴾. Is the (ب, ba') in ﴿with truth﴾ for accompaniment (المصاحبة, al-musahabah), meaning that it is accompanied by truth and sent down with truth, truthful in its reports and just in its rulings? Or does the meaning that it was sent down from Allah truly, so the (ب) here is for association (الملابسة, al-mulabasah), meaning it is clothed in truth, that is, it was sent down from Allah in a true descent, free of doubt and falsehood?

* The students: It includes both meanings.
* The Shaykh: It includes both meanings together. So it is sent down from Allah truly, without doubt, and it is also sent down with truth. The principle in the science of tafsir (interpretation) is that if a verse contains two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is obligatory to take it as both meanings. If the two meanings contradict each other, a preponderant meaning is sought, and what is preponderant is what is meant.

Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. (ما, ma) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi.

* The students: It is not Hijazi.
* The Shaykh: (ما) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi. (ما) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi.
* The students: It is Tamimi.
* The Shaykh: No, it is Hijazi, because the conditions are complete. The conditions are complete. But its subject is singular, as is customary, since the subject of a nominal sentence is usually singular, and its predicate is a clause, ﴿yurid﴾ (intends), its predicate is a clause, and the order is present, and the negation was not nullified, and it was not joined by (إن, in). So the conditions are complete, and therefore it is Hijazi. Our saying "Hijazi" does not mean that only the people of the Hijaz speak it. Rather, the Arabs in general speak it, but the people of the Hijaz make it operate like (ليس, laysa), and the Banu Tamim leave it inoperative. For example, if someone addresses you and says: ما زيد موجودًا (ma Zayd mawjudan), you know he is Hijazi; and if another person addresses you and says: ما زيد موجودٌ (ma Zayd mawjudun), you know he is Tamimi. Do you know? The meaning is that if someone addressed you in the speech of the early Hijazis, but the speech of the Hijazis today is not a proof. Do you understand? Now the poet says:

"And a slender-waisted one, I said to him: Declare your lineage, and he answered: The killing of the lover is not forbidden (ما قتل المحب حرام)."

* The Shaykh: Is this Tamimi or Hijazi?
* The students: Tamimi.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because he said "ma qatlu al-muhibbi haramun". If he were Hijazi he would have said "haraman". Good.

The noble verse: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. This (ما) is undoubtedly Hijazi, the noble name is its subject, and the clause (يريد, yurid) is its predicate.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says, negating for Himself, Glorified and Exalted, that He intends injustice to the worlds. Those whose faces turned white or whose faces turned black were not wronged. Those whose faces turned white obtained this by their deeds, that is, because of them. Those whose faces turned black also obtained it by their deeds. The first did righteous deeds and were rewarded with this reward, and the others did evil deeds and were requited with this punishment, because Allah cannot possibly wrong anyone.

His saying ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾: (العالمين, al-'alamin) refers to all that is other than Allah. As in ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves﴾ [Yunus 44].

Then He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran 109]. The predicate here is placed first for a benefit, which is restriction (الحصر, al-hasr), that is specification. Because when you put first what should be delayed, that is a restriction. Whenever you put first something that should come later, that is restriction, whether it is a predicate, a direct object, or a prepositional phrase. For example: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah 5]: the direct object was placed first to indicate restriction, meaning we worship none but You and we seek help from none but You. Here: ﴿To Allah belongs what is in the heavens﴾ means not to anyone else; so the predicate was placed first for the sake of restriction. ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: (ما, ma) is a relative pronoun (اسم موصول, ism mawsul) that includes everything in the heavens, of humans, jinn, trees, rivers, seas and other things. Correct?

* A student: It is wrong, Shaykh. There are no humans in the heavens.
* The Shaykh: Because, as far as we know, there are no humans, stones or trees in the heavens, and knowledge is with Allah. Rather, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ includes all of this: what is in the heavens of angels, and what is in the earth of humans, jinn, trees, stones and everything, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. And (ما) was used to give precedence to non-rational beings, because they are the majority, so they were given precedence. This is one aspect. Another aspect: when an attribute is intended, one expresses it with (ما) instead of (من, man), even for a rational being. Pay attention: when an attribute is intended, (ما) is used in place of (من), even for a rational being. They illustrate this with His saying: ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa' 3], and He did not say "man taba", because the individual rational person was not intended; rather, the attribute, kind and quantity were intended. Marry whatever is good, whether beautiful or ugly, one or many, of women.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. I think you know that the relative clause (صلة الموصول, silat al-mawsul) may be a sentence or a semi-sentence (شبه جملة, shibh jumlah). It may be a nominal sentence, a verbal sentence, a prepositional phrase, or an adverbial phrase: four types. The nominal and verbal sentences are clear. You say: "I like the one whose character is good." What is this? Nominal. And you say in a verbal sentence: "I like the one who was brave." This is a verbal sentence. And you say with an adverb: "I like the one who is above the roof." And you say with a prepositional phrase: "I like the one who is in the mosque." In this verse, which type is it? A prepositional phrase. Good. They say: the prepositional phrase by itself is not a sentence, because it needs a governing element, so how can it be a sentence? They say: because it contains something omitted, and therefore in i'rab we say: a prepositional phrase attached to an omitted element. Estimate the omitted element as a verb in the relative clause, and estimate it as a noun in the predicate of the subject. Pay attention! In the relative clause, it is estimated as a verb, and in the predicate of the subject, as a noun. So when you say "I like the one who is with you," the estimate is: "the one who is settled with you." And when you say "Zayd is with you," the estimate is: "Zayd is settled with you." Do you understand, everyone? Why? Because the basic form of the predicate of a subject is that it is a single word, not a sentence, and the basic form of the relative clause is that it is a sentence. So we estimate it as a verb in the relative clause, and as a noun in the predicate of the subject. This is the rule.

He says: ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is the possession of Allah, in creation, bringing into being, disposing and managing. His saying: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Baqarah 210] is also a restriction, by placing the prepositional phrase before what it governs, which is ﴿are returned﴾. And His saying: ﴿all matters are returned﴾ includes every matter. (الأمور, al-umur) is the plural of (أمر, amr) meaning affair, since the word (أمر) is used to mean affair, as He said: ﴿And the affair of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud 97], meaning his affair. And (أمر) is also used to mean a command addressed in the form of requesting an act from a position of superiority. The plural of the first is (أمور, umur), and the plural of the second is (أوامر, awamir). On this basis, (الأمور, al-umur) here is the plural of (أمر) meaning affairs. All affairs return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and come back to Him, because He is the Creator who initiated them, so they must return to Him.

* In these verses there are benefits. We begin with the first verse, which is His saying: ﴿On the day when faces will turn white and faces will turn black﴾.
* Students: We have taken them.
* The Shaykh: Have we taken the benefits from it? Good. He said: ﴿As for those whose faces will turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, therein they will abide forever﴾.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the people of faith whose faces turned white will be in Paradise, by His saying: ﴿then they are in the mercy of Allah﴾.
* And from its benefits: the abiding of the people of Paradise in it, by His saying: ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾.
* And from its benefits: that this abiding is permanent, because it came in the nominal form ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾, which indicates stability and continuity.
* And from its benefits: that mercy is applied to something other than the attribute of Allah, but to His creatures, as we have explained in the tafsir that what is meant by mercy here is Paradise. As for His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 58], what is meant there is the attribute. Good. Is the mercy of Allah, which is His attribute, created or uncreated? Uncreated. All the attributes of Allah are uncreated, and the mercy of Allah which is Paradise is created.

Allah says: ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Rum 50]. When He mentioned the descent of rain and that He gives life to the earth by it, He said: ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. What is meant by mercy here?

* Students: The attribute.
* The Shaykh: The created thing which is the rain, or the attribute?
* Students: The attribute.
* The Shaykh: It may be. It is possible that what is meant by "the traces of the mercy of Allah" is the rain, and so it is created; or "the traces of the mercy of Allah" which is His attribute, and of whose effects and what arises from it is this rain. Good. ﴿And He is the One who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 28].

* Students: The created.
* The Shaykh: The created? The created, because it is what is spread. Now pay attention: mercy is of two kinds: a created kind, which is what is separate from Allah, and an uncreated kind, which is what is an attribute of Him.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is more generous than the creation, because the deeds of those whose faces turned white, if attributed to reward alone, would be nothing; yet they are granted mercy in which they will abide forever and ever. This confirms His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am 160].

Then Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you with truth﴾ to the end [Al 'Imran 108].

* From the benefits of this verse: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, because Allah attributed it to Himself, saying: ﴿the verses of Allah﴾. Whatever is attributed to Allah and is not an independent entity is one of His attributes, because the thing attributed must subsist in something. If it is an attribute, it can only be an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So if we say "the speech of Allah," this is an attribution of an attribute. If we say "this is the creation of Allah," this is not an attribution of an attribute. Why? Because the creation is an independent entity. Good. Is "the she-camel of Allah" an attribute or not an attribute? Not an attribute, because it is an independent entity. "The House of Allah"? Likewise not an attribute, because it is an independent entity. Now: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr 29]?

* Students: An entity.
* Students: A self.
* The Shaykh: An entity. ﴿of My spirit﴾: is it an attribute or not an attribute?
* Students: Not an attribute.

**Shaykh:** A different attribute, is that right? It is created. For if it were an attribute of Allah, it would not be separated from Him. Here the mercy has been separated, separated from Allah. Where did it settle? In Adam, in Adam's body. So it is not one of the attributes of Allah, because it is separate from Him. The attribution of the spirit to Allah here is therefore the attribution of a creation to its Creator. For this reason we cannot say that it is a part of the spirit of Allah which is His attribute. That is impossible, for if we said this, something of Allah would have settled in His creatures. Alright, the mercy here in the verse, ﴿then in the mercy of Allah﴾, belongs to the category of created things. If someone argued and said, "Rather it is an attribute of Allah," we would answer him that this is impossible, because an attribute of Allah cannot be a container for human beings. Here He said, ﴿then in the mercy of Allah﴾. So we derive from this that mercy attributed to Allah divides into two kinds: created and uncreated. What is separate from Allah is created, and what is not separate is an attribute of His attributes. If someone asks, "Why did Allah call it mercy?" You say: Because it is one of the effects of the mercy of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the people of Paradise will abide in it forever, because of His saying, ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾. The abiding here is everlasting, as Allah mentioned in many verses. If someone says, "If you say it is everlasting, what is your answer to His saying: ﴿As for those who are made happy, they will abide in Paradise, forever, for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills: a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud 108], for He made an exception, saying, ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾?"

* **Student:** The answer?

* **Shaykh:** Yes.

* **Student:** That the abiding is by the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, this is one aspect.

* **Student:** We say that the abiding may have been preceded by punishment for sinful believers, so this exception is made from the will.

* **Shaykh:** You mean the exception refers back to what came before?

* **Student:** To what came before.

* **Shaykh:** Yes, this is the second.

* **Student:** O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. We say that this may be from the mutashabih (ambiguous verses), or it is from the mutashabih, and Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded us to refer the mutashabih to the muhkam (clear verses), and that is their abiding in an everlasting manner.

* **Shaykh:** So then we do not oppose the verses that indicate perpetuity with this verse, because it is among the unclear ones, so it must be referred back to the clear ones. Alright, these are three.

* **Student:** The exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But what your Lord wills." It is not connected to what precedes it.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, but "what your Lord wills," and what is the result? Alright, (...) we will make it the fourth opinion and discuss the opinions now.

* **Student:** That the heavens and the earth do not remain permanent, so the exception, "except what your Lord wills," is that they increase.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, these are five.

* **Student:** This exception has been explained in this verse and in another verse, which is His saying: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad 54].

* **Shaykh:** This is among the unclear matters, and there are clear verses about it. Even the verse we have: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾ indicates that it is continuous.

* **Student:** ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and Allah has willed that the people of Paradise abide forever.

* **Shaykh:** ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and Allah has willed. I think this is the third opinion.

* **Student:** O Shaykh, as it was understood, the abiding, in people's minds, came to mean that abiding happens without the will of Allah. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought His will to make it known that this abiding is by His will, Mighty and Majestic.

* **Shaykh:** Yes indeed. In any case, the scholars have opinions on this. But the view that gives a person peace of mind, and makes this restriction, and the restriction regarding the people of the Fire, ﴿abiding therein﴾ and ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, placing it among the ambiguous matters, so that it is interpreted in light of the clear texts, gives peace. He says: Allah said, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, even though He has willed that this remain forever and ever. It is like the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ) when visiting the graves: "And we, if Allah wills, will surely join you." [[Narrated by Muslim (249/39) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] He made it conditional on will, even though joining them is certain. A person finds peace in this and no objector can object to it, as Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) objected, saying that Allah said regarding the people of the Fire: ﴿abiding therein﴾, ﴿except what your Lord wills; indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, and He said regarding the people of Paradise: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾. He said: The difference in the endings of the two verses indicates that the abiding of the people of the Fire is not everlasting, unlike the people of Paradise, because He said of the people of Paradise: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, and He said of the people of the Fire: ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾. This, in truth, shows you that a person, however much he attains in knowledge and intelligence, will not be safe from error. The difference between the two verses is clear, for the verse about happiness is grace, so He said: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾. And the verse about the Fire, which is misery, is justice, so He said: ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, and this is from His act which He intended. The meaning of ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾ is not that He will do the opposite in the future, as Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) understood. This understanding is undoubtedly incorrect. Rather, the connection of the verse's ending with His saying, ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, is that since misery is not praiseworthy, He said: this is from the act of Allah, and Allah does what He wills, although He has not wronged them.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿These are the verses of Allah; We recite them to you in truth﴾. Among the benefits of this verse is that whoever acts as a representative for another has the ruling of the one who appointed him, because Allah attributed the recitation to Himself, although the one who recites is His Messenger. This shows that the ruling on what the Messenger carries out by what he was sent with is the ruling on what the sender said.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is entirely true, with no falsehood in it. If we take this word in its generality, we say: all its rulings are true, all its reports are true, and there is no contradiction or disagreement in it. For if there were contradiction or disagreement in it, one of the two contradictories would be false, and the Qur'an contains nothing false. It is entirely true.

* Among its benefits: establishing the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), since He said: ﴿We recite them to you in truth﴾. So the one to whom these verses are recited must definitely be a Messenger of Allah, Lord of the worlds.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: establishing the will of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾. If someone says: The verse here is a negation, ﴿And Allah does not intend﴾, so how do you say it indicates an affirmation?
We say: This negation is not absolute. Rather, it is a negation of the will of a specific thing, which is injustice. So does He intend other than injustice, or not? He intends it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: injustice is possible with respect to Allah, but He does not intend it because of His perfect justice. What is the proof? He said: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the servants﴾ [Ghafir 31], and He did not say, "It is not possible that Allah intends injustice." Even if He had said, "it is not possible," this would not indicate the absence of injustice if He willed it. In that case, it would be a refutation of those who say that injustice with respect to Allah is impossible in its very essence, and they are the Jahmiyyah. They say that injustice with respect to Allah is impossible in its essence, not because it is not willed by Allah, but in its essence. According to their view, Allah's praise of Himself by negating injustice would be pointless and without benefit, because what is impossible cannot be a matter of praise, nor can one praise himself with what is impossible for him. So injustice with respect to Allah is possible rationally, but it is prohibited by the Sharia and by justice. If Allah, exalted, willed to punish the obedient, would it be possible or not? It would be possible. But because of His perfect justice, He cannot punish him, because that would be injustice. They say: It is impossible for Allah to wrong anyone ever; injustice is impossible. Why? Is it not possible that Allah punishes the obedient one who spent his whole life in obedience to Allah? They said: Yes, it is possible, but this is not injustice, because He does it in what He owns. The servant is Allah's possession, so whatever He does to him is not injustice toward him. Do you understand now? This is their view, but it is a corrupt view. For if someone said to you: Do such and such and I will reward you; do not do such and such or I will punish you. Then you did what he commanded you and what he promised reward for, and then he punished you with the most severe punishment. Is this injustice by reason or not? It is injustice, even if he owns you. If a master said to his servant, "O my servant, prepare the lunch with such and such, and bring it to me at such and such an hour," and he did what he was commanded, in the described manner and at the time he specified, and then the master took a piece of wood and began to beat him with it, what would he be? A wrongdoer. Even if he were his servant? Even if he were his servant, rationally he would be a wrongdoer. They say: It is permissible that a person spends his whole life in obedience to Allah, complying with the command of Allah, and when he dies, Allah makes him abide in the Fire, and if He does that, He is not a wrongdoer. Why? He said: Because He did it in His own dominion. We say: If the matter is so, and injustice, according to your claim, is impossible, then it is not valid to say that Allah negates injustice from Himself as praise for Himself.

* Among the benefits of this verse: if the will of injustice is negated, injustice is negated. What is the reason? Allah has no one who compels Him. If He does not intend injustice, no one can force Him to commit injustice. So negating the will of injustice is negating injustice. Consequently, there is no contradiction between this verse and His saying: ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat 46]. There is no contradiction between them, what? Because negating the will of injustice necessitates negating injustice, and negating injustice necessitates negating the will of injustice, because if He willed to be unjust, He would be unjust. So if someone said to me: How do you reconcile this verse, ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾, with His saying, ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾, what would you say? I would say: There is no contradiction, because if the will of injustice is negated, the negation of injustice follows, and if injustice is negated, the negation of His will to do it follows, because Allah is able; if He willed to be unjust, He would be unjust.

* Among the benefits of this verse: establishing negative attributes. What Allah described Himself with divides into two kinds: affirmative (thubuti) and negative (intiqa'i), or if you prefer, say: negative (salbi). The affirmative attributes are all attributes of perfection. Every attribute Allah affirmed for Himself is an attribute of perfection. The negative ones are all attributes of deficiency negated, but they include the affirmation of a perfection. In His saying, ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [Al-Baqarah 74], there is the negation of heedlessness, for what? For the perfection of His knowledge and watchfulness. ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the servants﴾, for the perfection of His justice. ﴿And fatigue did not touch Us﴾ [Qaf 38], for the perfection of His power. Is that right? ﴿And Allah was not one to be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Fatir 44], for the perfection of His power and knowledge, and so on.

* * *

* **Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [109]. ﴿You are the best nation produced for mankind; you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah. Had the People of the Scripture believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [110]. ﴿They will not harm you except for minor harm. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs; then they will not be helped﴾ [111]. ﴿Humiliation has been stamped upon them wherever they are found, except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people. They have returned with anger from Allah, and destitution has been stamped upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing﴾ [Ali 'Imran 109–112].

* **Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾. Before we begin the explanation or the tafsir, we want to point out a recitation habit some people follow. When he stops at ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, he stops only at ﴿destitution﴾, then he returns and says, ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, even though if he had connected ﴿destitution﴾ to what precedes it, he could have done so without losing his breath. Likewise, when he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾, he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets﴾ and stops, then he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾, even though if he had connected the phrase ﴿without right﴾ to what precedes it, he would not have run out of breath. This is a fashion some reciters adopt, and in reality it is an error, because repetition without reason is not appropriate. Moreover, if he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾ or ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, he separates it from what precedes it, and then he needs to repeat the verse from its beginning. So he stops at ﴿and humiliation has been stamped upon them﴾, then repeats it again. He stops at ﴿and has been stamped﴾, then repeats again, and stops the third time at what he says, and repeats again, and so on. This is not correct. I told you before that if one or two words remain, you should follow them, even if you feel some shortness of breath, so that you do not need to repeat the speech a second time.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The sentence here is declarative, and its predicate has been placed first to convey restriction: ﴿to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾.

In His saying, ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, among the benefits: first: * Among the benefits of this verse: the generality of the dominion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because of His saying, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The word "whatever" (ma) is a relative pronoun conveying generality.

* Among its benefits: the exclusivity of Allah, glorified and exalted, in that dominion; that is, Allah alone is its owner. This is derived from the placement of the predicate first, because the established rule among the rhetoricians and the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) is that placing the object before the verb conveys restriction.

* Among the benefits of this verse: establishing the heavens and the earth, which is a known matter and is not denied. But the benefit of this benefit is to show the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted, in creating these great creations, about which Allah said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know﴾ [Ghafir 57].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the return of all matters is to Allah alone, because of His saying: ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾.

* Among its benefits: whoever tries to legislate for creation something other than what Allah has legislated has associated himself with Allah, or has made himself a partner with Allah. The reason: Allah restricted the return of all matters to Himself, saying, ﴿and to Allah﴾. So whoever tries to legislate for people matters that Allah has not legislated has made himself a partner with Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the vastness of Allah, glorified and exalted, since all matters return to Him. The word "matters" (umur) is the plural of "matter" (amr), and it has the definite article (al), which conveys generality. So all matters return to Him, the minute and the great. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ [Hud 56]. All creatures, small and large, Allah, glorified and exalted, holds their forelocks. He is the one who directs and manages them, the rational and the non-rational among them.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: it establishes that "the heavens" (al-samawat) is a plural noun. Other verses show that their number is seven heavens. As for the earth, it is mentioned in the Qur'an in the singular, but God indicated its number in His saying: ﴿It is God who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. The Sunnah is also explicit on this in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever unjustly seizes a span of the earth, God will encircle his neck with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."[[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim (1610 / 137), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 107–109 (part 1 of 3):

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿As for those whose faces will turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 107]. The waw (و) is a conjunction particle, and (أما, amma) is a particle of detailing, as already explained in the first verse. ﴿Those whose faces will turn white﴾ are the believers. This whiteness is of two kinds: a general whiteness for every believer, and a special whiteness for this Ummah, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «A distinguishing mark that is not for anyone other than you» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (136) and Muslim (246/37), with his wording, from Abu Hurairah]. Meaning: among you. «You will be called on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (136), and Muslim (246/35) from Abu Hurairah, with the wording «Indeed my Ummah will be called on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'»]. So this Ummah will have white faces, but they will have a light that differs from that of others. Also, for this Ummah the light reaches as far as the wudu' reaches, meaning it will be on the hands and on the feet. For this reason he said: «with bright faces and white limbs». As for others, we know of nothing except that only their faces will be white. ﴿Those whose faces will turn white﴾ are the believers. ﴿Then they are in the mercy of Allah﴾: (في, fi) is for location, and (رحمة الله, rahmat Allah) here is not the mercy mentioned in His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 58], because that is an attribute of Allah.
