Here, ﴿in the mercy of Allah﴾ refers to a created thing of Allah, and what is meant by it is Paradise, as in the authentic hadith in which Allah said to it, that is to Paradise: «You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850), and Muslim (2846/34) from Abu Hurairah]. It is impossible that what is meant is the attribute, because an attribute cannot be a place (ظرف, zarf) for human beings. An attribute cannot be a place for human beings. And since it is impossible for it to be a place for human beings, it is impossible for the mercy here to mean the mercy which is an attribute of Allah. Rather, it is the created mercy of Allah, and it was called by the name of mercy because it came about through the mercy of Allah, by which Allah shows mercy to whomever He wills among His servants.

And His saying: ﴿Then they will abide therein forever﴾ [Al 'Imran 107]. (هم, hum) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada') and is not a pronoun of separation (ضمير فصل, damir fasl); rather it has a place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). ﴿Khalidun﴾ is the predicate of the subject. (فيها, fiha) is a prepositional phrase (جار ومجرور, jar wa majrur) attached to (خالدون, khalidun). ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾ means they will remain. The verses indicate that this abiding is everlasting, and Allah mentioned eternity (التأبيد, ta'bid) in several verses of His Book, showing that this abiding is an everlasting abode.

Then Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. (تلك, tilka) refers to what preceded of the verses which Allah mentioned. It is possible that what is meant is the whole Quran, and this is supported, that is strengthened, by the demonstrative used, since it came in the distal form (صيغة البعد, sigha al-bu'd). So the demonstrative here includes the entire Quran. His saying ﴿the verses of Allah﴾ means the signs that point to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His existence and to what it contains of His names, attributes and actions. Here, the verses meant are the legislative verses (الآيات الشرعية, al-ayat al-shar'iyyah).

His saying ﴿We recite them to you with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran 108] means: We read them to you. Is it meant that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, recites them to the Prophet (ﷺ) directly, or through Jibril?

* The students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second. It may also sometimes be the first: sometimes revelation is cast into the heart of the Prophet, peace be upon him, by casting (إلقاء, ilqa'). But the first is more common. Indeed, regarding the Quran, the second may be the one that is definite, because Allah says: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 192–194]. The apparent meaning is that the entire Quran was brought down by Jibril. On this basis, the attribution of the recitation to Allah in this verse means what? It means the recitation of Jibril, and it is attributed to Allah because he, that is Jibril, was sent with it from Him. This is like His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its explanation﴾ [al-Qiyamah 16–19]. ﴿When We have recited it﴾: the reciter is Jibril, as the hadith confirms that when the Messenger, peace be upon him, heard the recitation of Jibril, he would hasten in reciting, fearing that he would forget something, so he would rush. Then Allah said: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾. Even if many verses were revealed at one moment, you will not forget it. For this reason He said: ﴿When We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾: it will remain, and you will forget nothing of it. ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation﴾: We must make it clear to people, both its wording and its meaning.

He says: ﴿We recite them to you with truth﴾. Is the (ب, ba') in ﴿with truth﴾ for accompaniment (المصاحبة, al-musahabah), meaning that it is accompanied by truth and sent down with truth, truthful in its reports and just in its rulings? Or does the meaning that it was sent down from Allah truly, so the (ب) here is for association (الملابسة, al-mulabasah), meaning it is clothed in truth, that is, it was sent down from Allah in a true descent, free of doubt and falsehood?

* The students: It includes both meanings.
* The Shaykh: It includes both meanings together. So it is sent down from Allah truly, without doubt, and it is also sent down with truth. The principle in the science of tafsir (interpretation) is that if a verse contains two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is obligatory to take it as both meanings. If the two meanings contradict each other, a preponderant meaning is sought, and what is preponderant is what is meant.

Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. (ما, ma) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi.

* The students: It is not Hijazi.
* The Shaykh: (ما) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi. (ما) is a negation particle, and it is Hijazi.
* The students: It is Tamimi.
* The Shaykh: No, it is Hijazi, because the conditions are complete. The conditions are complete. But its subject is singular, as is customary, since the subject of a nominal sentence is usually singular, and its predicate is a clause, ﴿yurid﴾ (intends), its predicate is a clause, and the order is present, and the negation was not nullified, and it was not joined by (إن, in). So the conditions are complete, and therefore it is Hijazi. Our saying "Hijazi" does not mean that only the people of the Hijaz speak it. Rather, the Arabs in general speak it, but the people of the Hijaz make it operate like (ليس, laysa), and the Banu Tamim leave it inoperative. For example, if someone addresses you and says: ما زيد موجودًا (ma Zayd mawjudan), you know he is Hijazi; and if another person addresses you and says: ما زيد موجودٌ (ma Zayd mawjudun), you know he is Tamimi. Do you know? The meaning is that if someone addressed you in the speech of the early Hijazis, but the speech of the Hijazis today is not a proof. Do you understand? Now the poet says:

"And a slender-waisted one, I said to him: Declare your lineage, and he answered: The killing of the lover is not forbidden (ما قتل المحب حرام)."

* The Shaykh: Is this Tamimi or Hijazi?
* The students: Tamimi.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because he said "ma qatlu al-muhibbi haramun". If he were Hijazi he would have said "haraman". Good.

The noble verse: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran 108]. This (ما) is undoubtedly Hijazi, the noble name is its subject, and the clause (يريد, yurid) is its predicate.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says, negating for Himself, Glorified and Exalted, that He intends injustice to the worlds. Those whose faces turned white or whose faces turned black were not wronged. Those whose faces turned white obtained this by their deeds, that is, because of them. Those whose faces turned black also obtained it by their deeds. The first did righteous deeds and were rewarded with this reward, and the others did evil deeds and were requited with this punishment, because Allah cannot possibly wrong anyone.

His saying ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾: (العالمين, al-'alamin) refers to all that is other than Allah. As in ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves﴾ [Yunus 44].

Then He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran 109]. The predicate here is placed first for a benefit, which is restriction (الحصر, al-hasr), that is specification. Because when you put first what should be delayed, that is a restriction. Whenever you put first something that should come later, that is restriction, whether it is a predicate, a direct object, or a prepositional phrase. For example: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah 5]: the direct object was placed first to indicate restriction, meaning we worship none but You and we seek help from none but You. Here: ﴿To Allah belongs what is in the heavens﴾ means not to anyone else; so the predicate was placed first for the sake of restriction. ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: (ما, ma) is a relative pronoun (اسم موصول, ism mawsul) that includes everything in the heavens, of humans, jinn, trees, rivers, seas and other things. Correct?

* A student: It is wrong, Shaykh. There are no humans in the heavens.
* The Shaykh: Because, as far as we know, there are no humans, stones or trees in the heavens, and knowledge is with Allah. Rather, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ includes all of this: what is in the heavens of angels, and what is in the earth of humans, jinn, trees, stones and everything, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. And (ما) was used to give precedence to non-rational beings, because they are the majority, so they were given precedence. This is one aspect. Another aspect: when an attribute is intended, one expresses it with (ما) instead of (من, man), even for a rational being. Pay attention: when an attribute is intended, (ما) is used in place of (من), even for a rational being. They illustrate this with His saying: ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa' 3], and He did not say "man taba", because the individual rational person was not intended; rather, the attribute, kind and quantity were intended. Marry whatever is good, whether beautiful or ugly, one or many, of women.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. I think you know that the relative clause (صلة الموصول, silat al-mawsul) may be a sentence or a semi-sentence (شبه جملة, shibh jumlah). It may be a nominal sentence, a verbal sentence, a prepositional phrase, or an adverbial phrase: four types. The nominal and verbal sentences are clear. You say: "I like the one whose character is good." What is this? Nominal. And you say in a verbal sentence: "I like the one who was brave." This is a verbal sentence. And you say with an adverb: "I like the one who is above the roof." And you say with a prepositional phrase: "I like the one who is in the mosque." In this verse, which type is it? A prepositional phrase. Good. They say: the prepositional phrase by itself is not a sentence, because it needs a governing element, so how can it be a sentence? They say: because it contains something omitted, and therefore in i'rab we say: a prepositional phrase attached to an omitted element. Estimate the omitted element as a verb in the relative clause, and estimate it as a noun in the predicate of the subject. Pay attention! In the relative clause, it is estimated as a verb, and in the predicate of the subject, as a noun. So when you say "I like the one who is with you," the estimate is: "the one who is settled with you." And when you say "Zayd is with you," the estimate is: "Zayd is settled with you." Do you understand, everyone? Why? Because the basic form of the predicate of a subject is that it is a single word, not a sentence, and the basic form of the relative clause is that it is a sentence. So we estimate it as a verb in the relative clause, and as a noun in the predicate of the subject. This is the rule.

He says: ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is the possession of Allah, in creation, bringing into being, disposing and managing. His saying: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Baqarah 210] is also a restriction, by placing the prepositional phrase before what it governs, which is ﴿are returned﴾. And His saying: ﴿all matters are returned﴾ includes every matter. (الأمور, al-umur) is the plural of (أمر, amr) meaning affair, since the word (أمر) is used to mean affair, as He said: ﴿And the affair of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud 97], meaning his affair. And (أمر) is also used to mean a command addressed in the form of requesting an act from a position of superiority. The plural of the first is (أمور, umur), and the plural of the second is (أوامر, awamir). On this basis, (الأمور, al-umur) here is the plural of (أمر) meaning affairs. All affairs return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and come back to Him, because He is the Creator who initiated them, so they must return to Him.

* In these verses there are benefits. We begin with the first verse, which is His saying: ﴿On the day when faces will turn white and faces will turn black﴾.
* Students: We have taken them.
* The Shaykh: Have we taken the benefits from it? Good. He said: ﴿As for those whose faces will turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, therein they will abide forever﴾.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the people of faith whose faces turned white will be in Paradise, by His saying: ﴿then they are in the mercy of Allah﴾.
* And from its benefits: the abiding of the people of Paradise in it, by His saying: ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾.
* And from its benefits: that this abiding is permanent, because it came in the nominal form ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾, which indicates stability and continuity.
* And from its benefits: that mercy is applied to something other than the attribute of Allah, but to His creatures, as we have explained in the tafsir that what is meant by mercy here is Paradise. As for His saying: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 58], what is meant there is the attribute. Good. Is the mercy of Allah, which is His attribute, created or uncreated? Uncreated. All the attributes of Allah are uncreated, and the mercy of Allah which is Paradise is created.

Allah says: ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Rum 50]. When He mentioned the descent of rain and that He gives life to the earth by it, He said: ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. What is meant by mercy here?

* Students: The attribute.
* The Shaykh: The created thing which is the rain, or the attribute?
* Students: The attribute.
* The Shaykh: It may be. It is possible that what is meant by "the traces of the mercy of Allah" is the rain, and so it is created; or "the traces of the mercy of Allah" which is His attribute, and of whose effects and what arises from it is this rain. Good. ﴿And He is the One who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 28].

* Students: The created.
* The Shaykh: The created? The created, because it is what is spread. Now pay attention: mercy is of two kinds: a created kind, which is what is separate from Allah, and an uncreated kind, which is what is an attribute of Him.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is more generous than the creation, because the deeds of those whose faces turned white, if attributed to reward alone, would be nothing; yet they are granted mercy in which they will abide forever and ever. This confirms His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am 160].

Then Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you with truth﴾ to the end [Al 'Imran 108].

* From the benefits of this verse: that the Quran is the speech of Allah, because Allah attributed it to Himself, saying: ﴿the verses of Allah﴾. Whatever is attributed to Allah and is not an independent entity is one of His attributes, because the thing attributed must subsist in something. If it is an attribute, it can only be an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So if we say "the speech of Allah," this is an attribution of an attribute. If we say "this is the creation of Allah," this is not an attribution of an attribute. Why? Because the creation is an independent entity. Good. Is "the she-camel of Allah" an attribute or not an attribute? Not an attribute, because it is an independent entity. "The House of Allah"? Likewise not an attribute, because it is an independent entity. Now: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr 29]?

* Students: An entity.
* Students: A self.
* The Shaykh: An entity. ﴿of My spirit﴾: is it an attribute or not an attribute?
* Students: Not an attribute.

**Shaykh:** A different attribute, is that right? It is created. For if it were an attribute of Allah, it would not be separated from Him. Here the mercy has been separated, separated from Allah. Where did it settle? In Adam, in Adam's body. So it is not one of the attributes of Allah, because it is separate from Him. The attribution of the spirit to Allah here is therefore the attribution of a creation to its Creator. For this reason we cannot say that it is a part of the spirit of Allah which is His attribute. That is impossible, for if we said this, something of Allah would have settled in His creatures. Alright, the mercy here in the verse, ﴿then in the mercy of Allah﴾, belongs to the category of created things. If someone argued and said, "Rather it is an attribute of Allah," we would answer him that this is impossible, because an attribute of Allah cannot be a container for human beings. Here He said, ﴿then in the mercy of Allah﴾. So we derive from this that mercy attributed to Allah divides into two kinds: created and uncreated. What is separate from Allah is created, and what is not separate is an attribute of His attributes. If someone asks, "Why did Allah call it mercy?" You say: Because it is one of the effects of the mercy of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the people of Paradise will abide in it forever, because of His saying, ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾. The abiding here is everlasting, as Allah mentioned in many verses. If someone says, "If you say it is everlasting, what is your answer to His saying: ﴿As for those who are made happy, they will abide in Paradise, forever, for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills: a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud 108], for He made an exception, saying, ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾?"

* **Student:** The answer?

* **Shaykh:** Yes.

* **Student:** That the abiding is by the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, this is one aspect.

* **Student:** We say that the abiding may have been preceded by punishment for sinful believers, so this exception is made from the will.

* **Shaykh:** You mean the exception refers back to what came before?

* **Student:** To what came before.

* **Shaykh:** Yes, this is the second.

* **Student:** O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. We say that this may be from the mutashabih (ambiguous verses), or it is from the mutashabih, and Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded us to refer the mutashabih to the muhkam (clear verses), and that is their abiding in an everlasting manner.

* **Shaykh:** So then we do not oppose the verses that indicate perpetuity with this verse, because it is among the unclear ones, so it must be referred back to the clear ones. Alright, these are three.

* **Student:** The exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But what your Lord wills." It is not connected to what precedes it.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, but "what your Lord wills," and what is the result? Alright, (...) we will make it the fourth opinion and discuss the opinions now.

* **Student:** That the heavens and the earth do not remain permanent, so the exception, "except what your Lord wills," is that they increase.

* **Shaykh:** Alright, these are five.

* **Student:** This exception has been explained in this verse and in another verse, which is His saying: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad 54].

* **Shaykh:** This is among the unclear matters, and there are clear verses about it. Even the verse we have: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾ indicates that it is continuous.

* **Student:** ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and Allah has willed that the people of Paradise abide forever.

* **Shaykh:** ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and Allah has willed. I think this is the third opinion.

* **Student:** O Shaykh, as it was understood, the abiding, in people's minds, came to mean that abiding happens without the will of Allah. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought His will to make it known that this abiding is by His will, Mighty and Majestic.

* **Shaykh:** Yes indeed. In any case, the scholars have opinions on this. But the view that gives a person peace of mind, and makes this restriction, and the restriction regarding the people of the Fire, ﴿abiding therein﴾ and ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, placing it among the ambiguous matters, so that it is interpreted in light of the clear texts, gives peace. He says: Allah said, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, even though He has willed that this remain forever and ever. It is like the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ) when visiting the graves: "And we, if Allah wills, will surely join you." [[Narrated by Muslim (249/39) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] He made it conditional on will, even though joining them is certain. A person finds peace in this and no objector can object to it, as Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) objected, saying that Allah said regarding the people of the Fire: ﴿abiding therein﴾, ﴿except what your Lord wills; indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, and He said regarding the people of Paradise: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾. He said: The difference in the endings of the two verses indicates that the abiding of the people of the Fire is not everlasting, unlike the people of Paradise, because He said of the people of Paradise: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, and He said of the people of the Fire: ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾. This, in truth, shows you that a person, however much he attains in knowledge and intelligence, will not be safe from error. The difference between the two verses is clear, for the verse about happiness is grace, so He said: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾. And the verse about the Fire, which is misery, is justice, so He said: ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, and this is from His act which He intended. The meaning of ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾ is not that He will do the opposite in the future, as Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) understood. This understanding is undoubtedly incorrect. Rather, the connection of the verse's ending with His saying, ﴿indeed your Lord is the Effector of what He intends﴾, is that since misery is not praiseworthy, He said: this is from the act of Allah, and Allah does what He wills, although He has not wronged them.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿These are the verses of Allah; We recite them to you in truth﴾. Among the benefits of this verse is that whoever acts as a representative for another has the ruling of the one who appointed him, because Allah attributed the recitation to Himself, although the one who recites is His Messenger. This shows that the ruling on what the Messenger carries out by what he was sent with is the ruling on what the sender said.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is entirely true, with no falsehood in it. If we take this word in its generality, we say: all its rulings are true, all its reports are true, and there is no contradiction or disagreement in it. For if there were contradiction or disagreement in it, one of the two contradictories would be false, and the Qur'an contains nothing false. It is entirely true.

* Among its benefits: establishing the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), since He said: ﴿We recite them to you in truth﴾. So the one to whom these verses are recited must definitely be a Messenger of Allah, Lord of the worlds.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: establishing the will of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾. If someone says: The verse here is a negation, ﴿And Allah does not intend﴾, so how do you say it indicates an affirmation?
We say: This negation is not absolute. Rather, it is a negation of the will of a specific thing, which is injustice. So does He intend other than injustice, or not? He intends it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: injustice is possible with respect to Allah, but He does not intend it because of His perfect justice. What is the proof? He said: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the servants﴾ [Ghafir 31], and He did not say, "It is not possible that Allah intends injustice." Even if He had said, "it is not possible," this would not indicate the absence of injustice if He willed it. In that case, it would be a refutation of those who say that injustice with respect to Allah is impossible in its very essence, and they are the Jahmiyyah. They say that injustice with respect to Allah is impossible in its essence, not because it is not willed by Allah, but in its essence. According to their view, Allah's praise of Himself by negating injustice would be pointless and without benefit, because what is impossible cannot be a matter of praise, nor can one praise himself with what is impossible for him. So injustice with respect to Allah is possible rationally, but it is prohibited by the Sharia and by justice. If Allah, exalted, willed to punish the obedient, would it be possible or not? It would be possible. But because of His perfect justice, He cannot punish him, because that would be injustice. They say: It is impossible for Allah to wrong anyone ever; injustice is impossible. Why? Is it not possible that Allah punishes the obedient one who spent his whole life in obedience to Allah? They said: Yes, it is possible, but this is not injustice, because He does it in what He owns. The servant is Allah's possession, so whatever He does to him is not injustice toward him. Do you understand now? This is their view, but it is a corrupt view. For if someone said to you: Do such and such and I will reward you; do not do such and such or I will punish you. Then you did what he commanded you and what he promised reward for, and then he punished you with the most severe punishment. Is this injustice by reason or not? It is injustice, even if he owns you. If a master said to his servant, "O my servant, prepare the lunch with such and such, and bring it to me at such and such an hour," and he did what he was commanded, in the described manner and at the time he specified, and then the master took a piece of wood and began to beat him with it, what would he be? A wrongdoer. Even if he were his servant? Even if he were his servant, rationally he would be a wrongdoer. They say: It is permissible that a person spends his whole life in obedience to Allah, complying with the command of Allah, and when he dies, Allah makes him abide in the Fire, and if He does that, He is not a wrongdoer. Why? He said: Because He did it in His own dominion. We say: If the matter is so, and injustice, according to your claim, is impossible, then it is not valid to say that Allah negates injustice from Himself as praise for Himself.

* Among the benefits of this verse: if the will of injustice is negated, injustice is negated. What is the reason? Allah has no one who compels Him. If He does not intend injustice, no one can force Him to commit injustice. So negating the will of injustice is negating injustice. Consequently, there is no contradiction between this verse and His saying: ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat 46]. There is no contradiction between them, what? Because negating the will of injustice necessitates negating injustice, and negating injustice necessitates negating the will of injustice, because if He willed to be unjust, He would be unjust. So if someone said to me: How do you reconcile this verse, ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾, with His saying, ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾, what would you say? I would say: There is no contradiction, because if the will of injustice is negated, the negation of injustice follows, and if injustice is negated, the negation of His will to do it follows, because Allah is able; if He willed to be unjust, He would be unjust.

* Among the benefits of this verse: establishing negative attributes. What Allah described Himself with divides into two kinds: affirmative (thubuti) and negative (intiqa'i), or if you prefer, say: negative (salbi). The affirmative attributes are all attributes of perfection. Every attribute Allah affirmed for Himself is an attribute of perfection. The negative ones are all attributes of deficiency negated, but they include the affirmation of a perfection. In His saying, ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [Al-Baqarah 74], there is the negation of heedlessness, for what? For the perfection of His knowledge and watchfulness. ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the servants﴾, for the perfection of His justice. ﴿And fatigue did not touch Us﴾ [Qaf 38], for the perfection of His power. Is that right? ﴿And Allah was not one to be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Fatir 44], for the perfection of His power and knowledge, and so on.

* * *

* **Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [109]. ﴿You are the best nation produced for mankind; you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah. Had the People of the Scripture believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [110]. ﴿They will not harm you except for minor harm. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs; then they will not be helped﴾ [111]. ﴿Humiliation has been stamped upon them wherever they are found, except by a rope from Allah and a rope from the people. They have returned with anger from Allah, and destitution has been stamped upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing﴾ [Ali 'Imran 109–112].

* **Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾. Before we begin the explanation or the tafsir, we want to point out a recitation habit some people follow. When he stops at ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, he stops only at ﴿destitution﴾, then he returns and says, ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, even though if he had connected ﴿destitution﴾ to what precedes it, he could have done so without losing his breath. Likewise, when he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾, he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets﴾ and stops, then he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾, even though if he had connected the phrase ﴿without right﴾ to what precedes it, he would not have run out of breath. This is a fashion some reciters adopt, and in reality it is an error, because repetition without reason is not appropriate. Moreover, if he says, ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾ or ﴿and destitution has been stamped upon them﴾, he separates it from what precedes it, and then he needs to repeat the verse from its beginning. So he stops at ﴿and humiliation has been stamped upon them﴾, then repeats it again. He stops at ﴿and has been stamped﴾, then repeats again, and stops the third time at what he says, and repeats again, and so on. This is not correct. I told you before that if one or two words remain, you should follow them, even if you feel some shortness of breath, so that you do not need to repeat the speech a second time.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The sentence here is declarative, and its predicate has been placed first to convey restriction: ﴿to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾.

In His saying, ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, among the benefits: first: * Among the benefits of this verse: the generality of the dominion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because of His saying, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The word "whatever" (ma) is a relative pronoun conveying generality.

* Among its benefits: the exclusivity of Allah, glorified and exalted, in that dominion; that is, Allah alone is its owner. This is derived from the placement of the predicate first, because the established rule among the rhetoricians and the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) is that placing the object before the verb conveys restriction.

* Among the benefits of this verse: establishing the heavens and the earth, which is a known matter and is not denied. But the benefit of this benefit is to show the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted, in creating these great creations, about which Allah said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know﴾ [Ghafir 57].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the return of all matters is to Allah alone, because of His saying: ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾.

* Among its benefits: whoever tries to legislate for creation something other than what Allah has legislated has associated himself with Allah, or has made himself a partner with Allah. The reason: Allah restricted the return of all matters to Himself, saying, ﴿and to Allah﴾. So whoever tries to legislate for people matters that Allah has not legislated has made himself a partner with Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the vastness of Allah, glorified and exalted, since all matters return to Him. The word "matters" (umur) is the plural of "matter" (amr), and it has the definite article (al), which conveys generality. So all matters return to Him, the minute and the great. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ [Hud 56]. All creatures, small and large, Allah, glorified and exalted, holds their forelocks. He is the one who directs and manages them, the rational and the non-rational among them.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: it establishes that "the heavens" (al-samawat) is a plural noun. Other verses show that their number is seven heavens. As for the earth, it is mentioned in the Qur'an in the singular, but God indicated its number in His saying: ﴿It is God who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. The Sunnah is also explicit on this in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever unjustly seizes a span of the earth, God will encircle his neck with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."[[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim (1610 / 137), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]]

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾. This verse has already been explained. ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾: the address is to this Ummah. As for His words ﴿You were﴾, it has been said: in the knowledge of Allah. This is because (kāna) denotes the past, and it is known that this Ummah is the last of the nations, so it cannot be spoken of as a nation that has perished. Therefore some scholars said: the past tense here is considered with respect to the knowledge of Allah, meaning: you were in the knowledge of Allah, and Allah's knowledge precedes the existence of nations. ﴿The best nation﴾. It has also been said, and this is the correct view, that (kāna) here indicates the attribution of the predicate to the subject and the realisation of its existence in it, and it does not denote time. This is the more correct view, and there are examples of it, among them His saying: ﴿And Allah has always been Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nisa 96], and ﴿And Allah has always been Mighty and Wise﴾ [An-Nisa 158]. Do we say that (kāna) here indicates the past and that this is an attribute that has ceased to belong to Allah? No. Rather, it is stripped of time and indicates the realisation of its subject's attribution of what its predicate denotes. ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾: "nation" (ummah) means a group. We have already mentioned that the word (ummah) is used in the Qur'an with four meanings. ﴿The best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ means: Allah the Mighty and Majestic brought it forth, made it manifest, clarified it and made it appear. ﴿The best nation brought forth﴾, and He did not say "created", because this Ummah is characterised by emergence, which is becoming apparent and visible. So the best nation that appeared and became visible is this Ummah. There were other nations brought forth for mankind, which became apparent and distinct, but they did not attain the excellence that this Ummah attained.

Then Allah the Exalted clarified the aspect of this excellence in His saying: ﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah﴾. ﴿You enjoin what is right﴾: the meaning of enjoining, of what is right (ma'ruf), of forbidding and of what is wrong (munkar) has already been explained in His saying: ﴿And let there be [arising] from you a nation inviting to [all that is] good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran 104].

His saying ﴿and believe in Allah﴾ includes belief in everything Allah commanded belief in, and also includes implementing in action everything Allah commanded, and abstaining from everything Allah forbade. This is because it is among the requirements of faith in Allah that you believe in what He has informed of. Is that not so? Accordingly, all that Allah has informed of concerning the unseen is included in belief in Allah. Among the realisation of belief in Allah is that you submit to Him and accept His ruling, and this includes all of Islam and all righteous deeds. For this reason it is the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community that faith increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience. Consider how belief in Allah was placed after enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong: this is because the nature of a nation is to be dominant, prevailing, commanding and forbidding. So enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong was placed before belief in Allah, although enjoining and forbidding without belief in Allah is of no benefit. But since the nation, by its outward standing, is the sign of its strength, it is to be one that enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿and believe in Allah﴾. We always hear from many authors, may Allah have mercy on them, saying that faith is affirmation (iqrar), and some of them say that faith is confirmation (tasdiq). But this, taken in its absolute sense, is not correct according to the legal meaning of faith. Legally, faith is affirmation that entails acceptance and submission. Whoever confirms and affirms but does not accept and submit is not a believer. The evidence for this is that Abu Talib, the uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), affirmed and acknowledged the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), yet he was not a believer, because he did not accept what he brought and did not submit to it. Indeed, he says in his poems:

*And they certainly know that our son is not one who is denied among us, nor is he concerned with vain speech.*

Abu Talib says: "They certainly know", meaning the Quraysh, "that our son", meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), "is not one who is denied among us", meaning he is confirmed by us, "nor is he concerned with vain speech": he does not care for false or baseless speech. And he says:

*And I certainly know that the religion of Muhammad is among the best of the religions of mankind as a religion. Were it not for blame, or fear of disgrace, you would see me clearly accepting it.*

I seek refuge in Allah. Yet this faith did not benefit him; rather, he died upon disbelief. Thus, legally, faith is affirmation that entails acceptance and submission.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed, it would have been better for them﴾. (law) here is conditional, its condition is ﴿believed﴾ and its response is ﴿it would have been better for them﴾. When the response of (law) is affirmative, the more eloquent usage is that it is accompanied by the lam, as in this verse: ﴿If only they had believed, it would have been better for them﴾; ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it crushed debris﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 65]; ﴿And had We willed, We would have made among you angels upon the earth succeeding [you]﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 60]. Examples of this are numerous, and sometimes the lam is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it salty﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 70], where He did not say "la-ja'alnahu ujajan" (with the lam). But when its predicate is negated, the usual practice is to omit the lam. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it﴾ [Al-An'am 112], and He did not say "lama fa'aluhu". And He said: ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another﴾ [Al-Baqarah 253]. The lam accompanies it only rarely; that is, your saying: "If you had willed, you would not have done it" is rare, though it does occur. The reason it is rare is that the lam expresses emphasis, while (ma) expresses negation, and there is a kind of opposition between them, and one does not combine a thing with its opposite.

(law) also comes as a verbal particle like (an), and this is when it follows (wadda) and similar verbs, in which case it is verbal. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could turn you back﴾ [Al-Baqarah 109], meaning: they wish for your return. ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [Al-Qalam 9], meaning: your compromise. And so on. So here we say that (law) is verbal. Thus it comes as a verbal particle when it follows (wadda) and what resembles it of expressions of love. You say: "I love that you go," meaning: I love your going, and "I love that you understand," meaning: I love your understanding.

He said: ﴿it would have been better for them﴾: if they had believed, it would have been better for them. Better for them than what? Than disbelief. If they had believed, it would have been better for them than disbelief, as He said: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, then reward from Allah would have been better﴾ [Al-Baqarah 103], and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment? [It is that] you believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you﴾ [As-Saff 10-11]. So it would have been better for them than remaining in their disbelief. It may also be said: ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ meaning it would have been doubly better, as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed: "A man from the People of the Scripture who believes in his prophet and then believes in Muhammad (ﷺ), Allah will give him his reward twice." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (97) and Muslim (154/241), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]

Then He said: ﴿Among them are believers﴾. ﴿Among them﴾ means among the People of the Scripture. ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. "Among them" means among the People of the Scripture there are believers, meaning those who believed, such as al-Najashi among the Christians. And who else?

* The students: Abdullah ibn Salam.
* The Shaykh: And Abdullah ibn Salam from the Jews. These believed with a faith that settled in their hearts. ﴿But most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. "Defiantly disobedient" here means those who go out of obedience to Allah absolutely, which is disbelief, because fisq (defiance, transgression) is used to mean going out of obedience in a restricted sense, and also to mean going out of obedience in an absolute sense. Going out of obedience in a restricted sense is as the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, said: the one who commits a major sin is a fasiq, because he has gone out of obedience in a restricted way through that sin by which he became a fasiq. Going out of obedience absolutely occurs through fisq, and among its examples is His saying: ﴿And as for those who defied, their refuge is the Fire. Every time they wish to get out of it, they are returned to it﴾ [As-Sajdah 20], and the rest of the verse.

﴿But most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. There are benefits in this verse. Among them: this Ummah is the best of nations, by His saying: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾. If someone asks: how do we reconcile this excellence with what came about the Children of Israel, that Allah preferred them over the worlds, and it is known that the one preferred is better than the one over whom he is preferred? We say: we have two verses, or two texts that conflict, both in a general sense. This verse, ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾, is general and includes whom? The Children of Israel and others. And His saying about the Children of Israel: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [Al-Baqarah 47] requires general preference over this Ummah and others. So between the two texts there is now a conflicting generality. If you claim that the generality of the verse about the Children of Israel is specified by this verse's specificity, the Israelite will say to you: and I claim that the generality of this verse is specified by what? By the specificity of the Children of Israel. So I say: you are the best nation brought forth for mankind except the Children of Israel. It is said: the Prophet (ﷺ) clarified for us which of the two generalities is intended, when he said: "You will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured of them with Allah." [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3001), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (20015), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah.] So the Messenger (ﷺ) clarified that this Ummah is the best of the nations whose number it completes and with which it is concluded. This is an explicit text from the Messenger (ﷺ), so the generality of His saying ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ takes precedence over the generality of His saying ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [Al-Baqarah 47]. Then His saying ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ becomes specified by His saying about this Ummah ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾, by the explicit words of the Messenger (ﷺ). Some scholars said: the intended meaning of "the worlds" in general is specifically the worlds of their own time, do you understand? The intended meaning of "the worlds" is specifically the worlds of their time, meaning the worlds of this era, that is, the time of the Children of Israel. So it falls under the category of general wording intended in a particular sense, and was not intended in its generality from the outset. Generality intended in a particular sense is common in the Qur'an and Sunnah. Among its examples is His saying: ﴿Those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them"﴾ [Al 'Imran 173]. The word "people" in His saying ﴿to whom people said﴾ does not mean all people; rather, the speaker was one person. And His saying ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran 173] also does not mean all people, since only the Quraysh gathered against them; the common mass of mankind did not gather against the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions. So His saying ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ is general in form but intended in a particular sense. On this basis, there is no generality in the verse at all, and then this verse does not conflict with it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: this Ummah surpasses the others in excellence through a quality that the others do not have, namely that it enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong. As for those before it, this is not so. Allah the Exalted says about the Children of Israel: ﴿Cursed were those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel by the tongue of David and Jesus, the son of Mary. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing. They used not to prohibit one another from wrongdoing that they committed﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 78-79].
* Among its benefits: whenever this quality by which this Ummah was preferred is removed, namely enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, its being the best nation brought forth for mankind is removed. This is because a ruling that is given a reason exists with the existence of its cause, ceases with its cessation, strengthens with its strength, and weakens with its weakness.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the importance of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, since the consequence of excellence being attached to it indicates its importance.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whenever enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong exists in the Ummah, good exists in it, and whenever it weakens, good weakens. For this reason, when the Ummah was strong in enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong in this our land, the land was in the best of conditions; and when this Ummah weakened, or when enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong weakened, the land lost good in proportion to what it lost of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.
* A student: Shaykh, the specification of the general in the verse about the Children of Israel, since we said it is specified, what is the evidence for this specification? We derive the specification from reconciling the two generalities, and we say that specification is preferable.
* The Shaykh: If we say that the intended meaning of "the worlds" regarding the Children of Israel is the general mass of people, then there are two conflicting generalities. But the Sunnah clarified that the generality of this verse takes precedence over the generality of the Children of Israel verse. And if we say that the Children of Israel verse did not originally intend generality, but only a particular sense, the problem disappears.
* A student: The second verse, ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾, is later in time than the verse about the Children of Israel, so by what (...)?
* The Shaykh: Someone may say: then you are the best nation brought forth for mankind in this time, unlike the time of the Children of Israel.
* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, why was the People of the Book specified in His saying ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed, it would have been better for them﴾, meaning, does this not include the Magians, the Sabians and others?
* The Shaykh: This objection says: why did He say ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed, it would have been better for them﴾ when others too would have been better off had they believed? The answer is that these people claim to be People of a Book and that they are upon a religion. So it is said to them: if you want to remain on your religion for the sake of the merit and reward of the religion, then your faith is better. If you were truthful that you want excellence, then entering Islam would be a necessity for you, since you want excellence. Unlike others, who perhaps do not make this claim.
* A student: Shaykh, you said that enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is specific to this Ummah, and Allah the Exalted says in the verse: ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you those of virtue who would forbid corruption on earth?﴾ [Hud 116], which states explicitly..
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. But these are a few; they are not the whole Ummah. For this reason He said about the Children of Israel: ﴿They used not to prohibit one another from wrongdoing that they committed﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 79]. Whenever there is ﴿except a few of those We saved from among them﴾ [Hud 116], a few of those We saved are not considered anything. A few compared to the Ummah is nothing.
* A student: What is the benefit of the expression in His saying ﴿and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ with the definite article (lam), when what was expected was..
* The Shaykh: With (al).
* The student: Yes, that it be said: "and most of them are disobedient" as in many verses?
* The Shaykh: Because it is ﴿Among them are believers﴾, and He did not say "minhum mu'minun". So for the sake of correspondence between the two opposites this was preferable.
* The student: Would the benefit not be, O Shaykh, as if this attribute is restricted to them...

**Shaykh:** No, because He said ﴿most of them﴾, and disobedience (fisq) also exists among others. That is why in the verse of al-Ma'idah it says ﴿But most of them are defiant wrongdoers﴾ [5:81], without the definite article (al).

**Student:** Shaykh, we restricted the meaning of "the worlds" (al-'alamin) in the case of the Children of Israel to their own time. Someone might claim that it is likewise specific to this Ummah, meaning its own time.

**Shaykh:** Did we say this? Did we say it? Yes, we answered this: the hadith is what clarifies the matter. Otherwise, in reality, there is a contradiction between the two, unless we interpret "the worlds" in reference to the Children of Israel as meaning a specific group.

**Student:** May God be good to you. In the Qur'an, enjoining what is right (al-amr bil-ma'ruf) is always mentioned before forbidding what is wrong (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), even though warding off harms takes precedence over securing benefits. What is the ruling on this order?

**Shaykh:** It is well known. This is because "what is right" (al-ma'ruf) includes upholding the pillars of Islam: the two testimonies of faith, prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage. Without these matters, which are considered what is right, avoiding what is wrong does not benefit a person. Even if a person avoids wrongdoing, does not commit adultery, does not steal and does not drink wine, but does not pray, this will not benefit him.

**Student:** Regarding God's words ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them﴾: is there evidence in it that the People of the Book will never believe, or that only a few of them will believe?

**Shaykh:** It does not appear so, it does not appear so. That is, if they believed it would be better for them, and this does not indicate that only a few will believe.

**Student:** Then why did He say it while He knows they will not believe?

**Shaykh:** No. It is an exhortation to them to believe. They presently claim that they are upon the truth, so it is as if He said: If you claim that you are upon the truth, and that you have remained upon this seeking the pleasure of God, then if you believed it would be better for you. A sensible person who is sincere in wanting good, whenever good becomes clear in anything, follows it.

**Student:** You mentioned to us earlier that the eloquent form of the answer to "law" (if/had) is when it is accompanied by the lam (la) if it is affirmative. Now, if a verse in the Qur'an comes with the answer to "law" without the lam, can it be said that this is not eloquent?

**Shaykh:** No, no. It is less common. We did not say "eloquent," brother, we did not say "eloquent." We said "the more common."

**Students:** "The more eloquent" (al-afsah).

**Shaykh:** Yes, yes, correct: "the more eloquent," because it is more common.

**Student:** But can it not be said about the other form that it is not "the more eloquent"?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it can be said. One says "the more eloquent," because the more common usage is with the lam. So when this is the more common, it becomes more eloquent. Otherwise we would have to say that this and that are equal. The Qur'an contains the eloquent and the more eloquent, but sometimes one departs from the more eloquent to the eloquent for some reason.

\* \* \*

I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾. The expression with "kana" (was/were), which indicates the past tense. Yes indeed.

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [3:110]. The expression with "kana," which indicates the past tense?

**Yes indeed.**

**Student:** It is said that there are two opinions on it.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** It is said that it indicates past time in the past, and it is said that it does not function as a past tense verb. This is the saying of God: ﴿And God was...﴾.

**Shaykh:** That is, it does not indicate a time.

**Student:** It does not indicate a time.

**Shaykh:** Now, according to the first opinion, that it indicates a past time, how can He say ﴿you were﴾ when they are the last of the nations? What does He say? ﴿You were the best nation﴾, not "was," because it is the last nation.

**Student:** That is the second opinion.

**Shaykh:** No, the second opinion is that "kana" does not indicate time, but rather indicates the realization of its subject being characterized by its predicate.

**Student:** That is, in the knowledge of God, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** That is, in the knowledge of God. ﴿You were﴾ means: in God's foreknowledge, prior to the creation of the heavens and the earth. Now, the clause ﴿you enjoin﴾: what is its position in meaning relative to what comes before it?

**Student:** It is causal (ta'lilliyyah).

**Shaykh:** It is causal, yes.

**Student:** Because you enjoin.

**Shaykh:** Because you enjoin. Now, the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾. Is the intended meaning all of mankind, or that it was brought forth for mankind at the time of its bringing forth?

**Student:** All of mankind.

**Shaykh:** If you say this, then God's words about the Children of Israel become problematic for us: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [2:47]?

**Student:** Over the worlds who preceded them, or over their own time.

**Shaykh:** Or the worlds of their time. And according to this interpretation, what is the meaning of "the worlds"?

**Student:** They are those who were before the Children of Israel, from among the Children of Israel and those who were before them.

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed.

**Student:** A general term intended in a specific sense.

**Shaykh:** It would be a general term intended in a specific sense.

**Student:** In another verse.

**Shaykh:** Excellent. Now, God the Exalted said: ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them﴾ [3:110]. Who are the People of the Book?

**Student:** The Jews and the Christians.

**Shaykh:** ﴿It would have been better for them﴾ than what?

**Student:** Better for them than disbelief.

**Shaykh:** Better for them than disbelief? Yes, good. How can He say "better for them than disbelief," when there is no good in disbelief at all: ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them﴾?

**Student:** Better for them than disbelief.

**Shaykh:** It is well known that the elative form (ism al-tafdil) indicates that the one preferred and the one it is preferred over share in the basic meaning. So is there any good in disbelief?

**Student:** No, there is no good in it.

**Shaykh:** Then.

**Student:** The verse ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them﴾ means: better for them than disbelief.

**Shaykh:** Good. Is there no good in disbelief at all?

**Student:** That is, it has no relation to it?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** Yes, it has no relation to it.

**Shaykh:** Then how does He say ﴿better for them﴾ and make a relation in it?

**Student:** Because in their view it is good.

**Student:** This statement is made while they think they have knowledge of the Book, or that they have some part of the religion.

**Shaykh:** That is, like what He said: that they have some good?

**Student:** Yes, they have some good.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** Because the elative form may be used even when the side preferred over has nothing of that quality in it, as in God's words: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿Better in dwelling place and finer in resting place﴾ [25:24]. So the answer to this is that the elative form may be used even when the side it is compared to has none of that quality, as in God's words: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in their dwelling place﴾, even though the people of the Fire have no good in their dwelling place at all. Now, what is the rhetorical point in this?

**Student:** In what?

**Shaykh:** In His saying "better," ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them﴾?

**Student:** Yes, better than their remaining in disbelief.

**Shaykh:** Correct, but what is the rhetorical point and the meaning the verse is aiming at?

**Student:** Shaykh, since they used to claim that they had knowledge and that they had a Book, it is as if God the Exalted is saying: If you claim that you have, that you are people of a Book, then believe. It is as if He is commanding them, I mean.

**Shaykh:** That is, it is as if He is rebuking them for not believing, because if they were sincere and wanted the excellence, then belief is good. Now, ﴿Among them are the believers﴾: like whom?

**Student:** Like Abdullah ibn Salam, and like Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from among the Jews.

**Shaykh:** Abdullah ibn Salam is from where?

**Student:** From the Jews.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and the Christians?

**Student:** And from the Christians, al-Najashi.

**Shaykh:** Like al-Najashi. Good. As for His saying "the defiant ones": ﴿most of them are the defiant ones﴾, what does it mean?

**Student:** That is, the vast majority of them are sinners.

**Shaykh:** What is meant by disobedience (fisq)?

**Student:** Disbelief.

**Shaykh:** Disbelief.

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Does disobedience come with the meaning of disbelief?

**Student:** Yes, it does.

**Shaykh:** An example?

**Student:** In God's words: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the defiant ones﴾ [5:47].

**Shaykh:** And in the verse ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ [5:45].

**Student:** And in the verse ﴿the disbelievers﴾ [5:44].

**Shaykh:** Yes, so there is no evidence in it.

**Student:** Shaykh, the scholars distinguished between these.

**Shaykh:** Indeed the scholars distinguished. Is the meaning that each description applies in some circumstances, or that they are descriptions of one state, so that every disbeliever is a wrongdoer and every disbeliever is defiant?

**Student:** God's words: ﴿As for those who were defiant, their refuge is the Fire﴾ [32:20].

**Shaykh:** In contrast to what?

**Student:** In contrast to those who believed: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will have the Gardens of refuge as a lodging, for what they used to do. And as for those who were defiant, their refuge is the Fire﴾ [32:19–20].

**Shaykh:** Excellent. ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has come into effect against those who were defiant, that they will not believe﴾ [10:33].

Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse, ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾: that the more a person enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, the better he is than others, because what is conditioned on a quality strengthens with its strength and weakens with its weakness.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that workers, or the doers, differ in excellence. From where is this derived? From His words ﴿best nation﴾. This is clear. The differing of workers according to the differing of their deeds, is it not so? And the differing of deeds is established by the Book and the Sunnah: ﴿Not equal are those believers who sit [at home] other than those with a disability and those who strive in the way of God with their wealth and their lives. God has preferred those who strive with their wealth and lives over those who sit [at home] by a degree﴾ [4:95]. This is the preference of the worker according to the excellence of the work. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (the people of the Sunnah and the community), that faith increases and decreases, and that the worker's description increases in obedience and decreases according to what he has of deeds.
* Among its benefits: the condemnation of the People of the Book, in that they disbelieved in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), even though they claim they want good; and had they been sincere in wanting good, they would have believed in the Messenger (ﷺ).
* Among the benefits of this verse: that among the People of the Book there are those who are believers, and among them are those who are defiant, and they are the majority; the majority are defiant.

If someone says: Does this mean that the People of the Book existing today are believers? No. This is why He said ﴿Among them are the believers﴾, and the "al" here is the mental definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhihni), meaning: the well-known belief, which is belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). He did not say "some of them are believers." He said ﴿Among them are the believers﴾, meaning: the belief known to you, O Muslims, which is belief in whom? In the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

* Among the benefits of this verse: that most of the People of the Book are defiant, outside the religion, and this is so; and the few among them believed and still believe. Even now there are people from the People of the Book who believe in God.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance﴾ [Ali 'Imran 111]. ﴿They will not harm you﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions who hold fast to his guidance. The subject of ﴿they will harm you﴾ refers to the People of the Book; that is, the People of the Book will not harm you except with annoyance. As for His saying ﴿except for some annoyance﴾, the exegetes differed concerning it: is it an exception that is disjunct (munqati') or connected (muttasil)? Some of them said it is a connected exception, because this is the original state of exception; the original state of exception is that it be connected. According to this view, there is some ellipsis in the verse, its estimated meaning being: "they will not harm you except with the harm of annoyance; not the harm of a physical assault that severs a limb or takes wealth, but rather it is annoyance, namely that they make you hear what you dislike, by reproach, mockery and the like." This is if we say that it (the exception) is connected. There is no doubt that annoyance is a type of harm, but it is not the harm that is called by the name "harm."

The second view: the exception here is disjunct (munqati'). According to this view the meaning is: "They will not harm you, but they will annoy you, but they will annoy you." Annoyance does not necessarily entail harm. For this reason Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab 57]. So He affirmed that they annoy Allah and His Messenger, and He said: ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all﴾ [Ali 'Imran 176]. And in the sacred hadith: "O My servants, you will never reach My harm so as to harm Me" [Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr]. So harm is negated with respect to Allah, while annoyance?

* A student: It is present.

* The Shaykh: It is present; annoyance is present. Among its examples is His saying in the sacred hadith: "The son of Adam annoys Me: he curses time, while I am Time" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (4826) and Muslim (2246/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. What makes this clear is that if a man prays beside you who has eaten onion or garlic, you will be pained by its smell, but does it harm you? No, it does not harm you. This view is more correct: that the exception is disjunct. Although it is contrary to the original rule, it is more eloquent in rhetoric. This is in terms of rhetoric: "They will not harm you, but you will endure the annoyance, and annoyance is not harm." ﴿They will not harm you except for some annoyance﴾.

If someone asks: Is this verse definitive (muhkam) and general until the Day of Resurrection, or is it abrogated (mansukh) and specific to what was before abrogation? The answer: the first.

If someone asks: Your claim that the intended meaning is the first raises an objection, namely that the Jews today inflict upon us what is among the gravest harms, and it is well known that Allah's report cannot be broken. So what is the answer?

The answer is that we say: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions, and whoever is upon the like of what the Prophet ﷺ and his companions were upon, the Jews and Christians will not harm him. As for people who believe the Islamic religion to be a religion of backwardness and regression, and who replace it with other reactionary man-made laws, these will not be granted victory, and they will be harmed with annoyance in speech, in action, economically, and in every way. Otherwise, the word of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is never broken. But there are people who fight a tribal, jahili battle based on what? On divided nationalism, and on a false religion opposed to the religion of Allah. These do not deserve victory. For this reason the Jews now do their deeds against us: whoever is able to act with his body does so, and whoever is not able, they do to him the harms that they do, the global economic harms, as is known. Then the verse remains definitive, not abrogated, lasting until the Day of Resurrection. But a conditional statement depends on its condition: the negation of harm is contingent on the existence of its condition, which is that we follow the conduct of those who were promised this promise, namely the Prophet ﷺ and his companions.

Then He said: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 111]. That is: if it were supposed that fighting took place between the Muslims and the People of the Book, they would turn their backs; they would turn their backs, they could not stand firm: ﴿They will not fight you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls﴾ [al-Hashr 14]. But the address, as you know, is to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ and his companions, and whoever is upon the guidance of the Messenger ﷺ and his companions. Good. ﴿If they fight you, they will turn [their backs] to you﴾: we have a condition and a consequence; the condition is fighting, and the consequence is turning the backs. So as soon as an encounter occurs between us and them, and before the first arrow reaches them, Allah knows best, what do they do? They flee, they turn their backs. Here He says: ﴿they will turn their backs to you﴾, meaning they make their backs face you, and this is a metonymy for what? For defeat; because the one who is defeated turns his back to the one from whom he is defeated. Isn't that so?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: For this reason 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was besieged in Makkah, said, reciting or declaiming:

"We are not those whose heels bleed from wounds, / but on our feet the blood drips."

The one whose blood drips on his feet is advancing, and the one whose heels bleed is retreating.

The phrase ﴿they will turn their backs﴾: the nun has been dropped from it because it came as the answer to the condition. He said ﴿then they will not be helped﴾. ("Then," thumma, indicates a pause and delay.) The verb ﴿they will not be helped﴾ carries the nun, and this is a point of difficulty, because thumma is a conjunctive particle and ﴿they will turn their backs﴾ is conjoined to it; and a verb conjoined to a jussive is itself jussive. But we say: thumma here is not conjunctive but resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), and the estimated meaning is: "then they will not be helped." This estimate is necessary, because if it were a conjunction to his saying ﴿they will turn their backs﴾ it would have been jussive, and it would have been said: "then they will not be helped" (lā yunsarū). Then the meaning would be corrupted, the meaning would be corrupted; because if the negation of help for them applied only when they fight us, one could say that they will be helped after that. If He had said: "they will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped," the negation of help would have been restricted to when they fight us. But the matter is not so: they will never be helped, whether they fight us or not. For this reason He said: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. So it is now clear that thumma here is not conjunctive but?

* The students: Resumptive.

* The Shaykh: Resumptive, and the verb after it is in the nominative, because it is a sentence begun on its own; it was not conjoined to an accusative or a jussive. As for His saying ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, what is help? Help is protection, strength, and turning away; and the like. So the meaning of "I helped him" is that I turned his enemy away from him, supported him and strengthened him; this is the meaning of help. So these will never be helped. But someone may say: wars took place between the Muslims and the Christians, and between the Muslims and the Jews, and the Christians were given victory over the Muslims, and the Jews were given victory over the Muslims. The sentence ﴿they will not be helped﴾ is a declarative sentence, and the report of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be broken. So what is the answer? As for the first, some scholars said: this is about the Jews, and the Jews never gained victory over the Muslims at any time in history; rather, it was defeat after defeat. They were defeated in Madinah: Banu Qaynuqa', Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah; and they were defeated at Khaybar, Banu al-Nadir [again]; and no standing up for them before the Muslims occurred. On this basis we say: the verse is specific to whom? To the Jews. As for the Christians, the verse does not address them. But we answer with a more correct answer than this: we say the address is to the Muslims at the time when they represented Islam in belief, speech and action, and in that state they will be helped over the Jews, the Christians, the Magians and all the disbelievers. Have you understood?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Then it is not problematic; it does not trouble us, the domination of the Crusader Christians over the Muslims does not trouble us, nor does the Jewish dominance over the Arabs trouble us; because fighting with the Jews under the banner of Arabism is a jahili fight, a fight of one sect against another, not for religion. Rather, they may believe that they are fighting for religion; they believe that the holy land which Allah decreed for them is written for them until the Day of Resurrection. So they fight confident in Allah's promise, and Musa had said to them: ﴿O my people, enter the holy land which Allah has written for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 21]. So they say: the land is ours by the text of the word of our prophet, so we fight to reach a land which Allah has decreed for us. It is mentioned that when the defeat of the year 1967 CE occurred, when they entered Sinai and seized what they seized of the lands of the Arabs, one of the soldiers would take the dust, kiss it, then prostrate upon it and weep, because he had returned to his land that had been promised to him. So they fought for a belief; but as for a wretched, frivolous nationalism, there is no good in it.

So our answer is on two aspects. The first aspect: that this is specific to the Jews, and that the Jews have not stood up since the Messenger ﷺ expelled them from Madinah; then they were expelled afterward from Khaybar. The second view: the intended are the Jews and the Christians, but on condition that the one opposing them is fighting for Islam, so that the word of Allah may be the highest.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. As for His saying ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾, there are two readings, indeed three readings: ﴿'alayhim﴾, and the second: ﴿'alayhum﴾; these are two readings. The third: ﴿'alayhimi al-dhillah﴾, with ﴿'alayhimi﴾ substituted for ﴿'alayhim﴾. So the hā' has two readings: the ḍammah and the kasrah, or not?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the mīm has two readings: the ḍammah and the kasrah.

And His saying ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾: who decreed it? Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and He called that a "decreeing," like the stamping on coins, which remains impressed and does not disappear by rubbing the hands. Do you know the coins?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: The coins, this iron currency.

* A student: Known.

* The Shaykh: Known. When it is struck, what is struck remains on it: a name, for example, of the ruler of such-and-such state, or an indication that this is worth half a riyal, more or less. This is striking, because it is impressed and does not change. So it is as if this humiliation is stamped upon them and cannot change.

His saying ﴿al-dhillah﴾ is on the pattern fi'lah, and it differs from al-dhull, because it indicates a specific, particular humiliation. Ibn Malik said:

"Fa'lah is for a single occurrence, like jalsah (a sitting); and fi'lah is for a manner or form, like jilsah (a way of sitting)."

In any case, "dhillah" is on the pattern "fi'lah," meaning a specific humiliation, just as you say: "So-and-so sat the sitting of a lion," meaning a known sitting. What then is this humiliation? It is humiliation—and God forbid—that does not leave their hearts; because He said: ﴿it has been decreed upon them﴾, so just as the engraving on a struck coin does not transform or disappear, so this humiliation.

﴿wherever they are found﴾: in my copy it is written "ayna mā" with "ayna" alone; is it so in yours?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: The rule is that they are joined together as "aynamā," but what is in the Muṣḥaf is an old convention.

His saying ﴿wherever they are found﴾ means: wherever they are encountered. Allah said: ﴿and kill them wherever you find them﴾ [al-Baqarah 191], meaning: wherever you find them. So these Jews and Christians, who are also from the Children of Israel, have humiliation decreed upon them; wherever they are on earth, they are humbled, because Allah decreed humiliation upon them.

But He says: ﴿except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. In this case humiliation is not decreed upon them. "A rope from Allah" means the means of salvation from this humiliation, which comes from Allah, and that is Islam; for Islam is a rope from Allah by which a person protects himself, his family and his wealth. Accordingly, the "rope of Allah" here means what? Islam; because the rope is the means: that is, by means from Allah, namely that they become Muslims and humiliation departs from them. It was also said that "the rope of Allah" means the covenant, the covenant between the Muslims and these disbelievers, by which they remain under our shade and protection, because they are covenanted people, dhimmis.
