As for His saying ﴿and a rope from the people﴾, what is meant is safe-conduct: the safe-conduct granted by one man to a captive, for example. That is because when we fight a town and conquer it, we have the right to grant protection to its people, as the Prophet ﷺ said when he conquered Makkah: "Whoever enters his house is safe" [al-Bayhaqi in al-Kubra (18274) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah with the wording: "Whoever enters his dwelling is safe"]. "Whoever enters his house is safe": this is a particular protection. A general protection is that there be between us and them a covenant whereby they do not transgress against us and we do not transgress against them, and they do not defend us and we do not defend them; and this is like what exists at the present time in international agreements, such as the Charter of the United Nations and the like.

* A student: Shaykh, we said regarding it, "They will not harm you except for some annoyance," meaning, for example, harm in proportion; sometimes the Muslims, of course, annoy the Jews in every way, with weapons...

* The Shaykh: The Jews annoy them, and they do not annoy us?

* The student: No, the Jews harm the Muslims in all respects, such as this harm; they say: "We are the advanced ones in weapons and things, anything in comparison to ..." the images of women, for example; is this harm or not?

* The Shaykh: Did you hear his words?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: He says: they now annoy the Muslims and harm them by killing, wounding, plundering wealth and the like. So what is the way out of this difficulty? I think that if he were alert he would know it, but it seems he has put some sleep in his eye.

* A student: Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: We mentioned that this verse was specific to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions, and this applies only to whoever is characterized by their guidance, the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ and his companions; as for whoever follows other than that, humiliation is his.

* The Shaykh: Well said. Do you understand?

* The student: Yes, I understand, but, that is, the harm, for example...

* The Shaykh: The harm now occurring from the Jews or other disbelievers upon the Muslims is because the Muslims themselves have not fulfilled the obligation; and Allah says: ﴿They will not harm you﴾, meaning you, O Muslims, and those who are like you. That is the distinction.

* A student: Shaykh, did not the Prophet ﷺ suffer great harm at the Battle of Uhud, and at his death he died from the effect of poison from the Jewess? And also in the Battle of Banu al-Mustaliq he was afflicted in his honor and his family?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Then did the condition fail?

* The Shaykh: It is impossible; we say: was he harmed by that?

* The student: Yes, he was harmed.

* The Shaykh: By what?

* The student: The effect of the poison, which he found in his heart.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: And also his front tooth was broken at the Battle of Uhud.

* The Shaykh: Who was facing him?

* The student: The polytheists.

* The Shaykh: Yes; and this?

* The student: The Jews.

* The Shaykh: Among the Jews and Christians, the People of the Book.

* A student: Is it not general, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: No. Allah says: ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them; among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient. (110) They will not harm you except for some annoyance﴾.

* A student: The humiliation: he says, ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾, would it be like the seal upon the heart?

* The Shaykh: Like what?

* The student: Like the sealing upon the heart.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the striking means sealing upon the heart.

* The student: Humiliation?

* The Shaykh: No, this humiliation we have not explained.

* A student: May Allah reward you well. As history mentions, at the Battle of Mu'tah, those who fought the Romans, who were Christians, most of them were Companions, yet they were punished and defeated; is that so?

**Shaykh:** Correct, but the Messenger ﷺ called it a conquest (*fath*) when Khalid, may Allah be pleased with him, led them up to the mountain and they were saved. He said: "Then Khalid ibn al-Walid took the banner, and Allah granted him victory,"[[Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (1750), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ja'far, with the wording: "Then Khalid ibn al-Walid took the banner, and Allah granted him victory through it."]] so he called it a victory.

**Student:** They were harmed.

**Shaykh:** It is true that some of them were killed; there is no doubt about this. But we may say that this killing will not harm them, because they move from one abode to a higher one.

**Student:** And in other instances, in the time of 'Umar and Abu Bakr, when the armies went to face the Romans in al-Sham, some battles were lost by the Muslims?

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, if they were defeated. But the meaning of the verse indicates that they can harm us only with hurt. Even harm that occurs may be of the same rank as hurt. That is, the outcome is not always victory. This can be understood in this way.

**Student:** Shaykh, we said that the principle regarding the exception (*istithna'*) is that it should be connected (*muttasil*). Yet we always see the exegetes and others, when they interpret a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), bring in "but" (*lakin*). Is it a consistent rule that a disconnected exception is interpreted by what follows it being rendered with "but"?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** It cannot be interpreted with any particle other than "but"?

**Shaykh:** Because "but" (*lakin*) is the one used for correction (*istidrak*), and the disconnected exception is a correction.

**Student:** May Allah reward you well, Shaykh. Do the Shi'ah and the hypocrites enter among the People of the Book, the Jews and Christians, in their harm to the believers, despite their varied kinds?

**Shaykh:** In any case, the hypocrites harm the believers without doubt. But do they harm them by speech and action? If they harm them by speech and action in a manner that causes damage, then the verse is applied to other people, who can harm us only with hurt.

**Student:** Is the harm that is established or negated when the fighting is collective, or when a person fights alone?

**Shaykh:** No, the apparent meaning is collective fighting. For example, if we, the Muslims, gather upon true Islam and fight them, they will not be victorious over us.

**Student:** And if a single person fights, and (...) deception against them?

**Shaykh:** Allah has not committed Himself to that.

**Student:** ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ indicates that (...) among them, to the point that we mentioned that they may flee at the first arrow that reaches them (...) when they meet, they fight the Muslims (...) and afterwards the fighting continued with them until they were defeated (...)?

**Shaykh:** To whom is the address? ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾: who is the subject?

**Student:** The Jews.

**Shaykh:** These Jews are not Arabs.

**Student:** (...) Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** They are not Arabs.

\* \* \*

**Student:** ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found, except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people. They have earned anger from Allah, and poverty has been decreed upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾ (112) ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing [in obedience]; they recite the verses of Allah during the night and prostrate. They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous. And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it. And Allah is Knowing of the righteous.﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112–115]

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. The saying of Allah, ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾, does not specify the one who decreed it, but it is known. Who is it? Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He left it unspecified because it is known, like His saying: ﴿And mankind was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa' 28], although it is Allah who created him. However, it is among the methods of the Qur'an that Allah expresses undesirable matters in the passive voice, whereas desirable matters are expressed with the active participle, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10].

Here He says: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾. The pronoun refers to the People of the Book. But is the intended meaning the People of the Book, both Jews and Christians, or is it specific to the Jews? The scholars differ on this. Some said it is specific to the Jews, while other scholars said it is general, and the default is generality, because the pronoun ﴿upon them﴾ refers to the People of the Book mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed﴾ [Ali 'Imran 110]. So we say the pronoun refers to the People of the Book, Jews and Christians. If it is assumed that they gained honor at some time, that occurred for a reason that required it, so it is contrary to the default. Otherwise, the default is that humiliation is decreed upon them.

His saying: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾: here "humiliation" means degradation, meaning that Allah the Exalted has degraded them.

﴿Wherever they are found﴾: "wherever" (*ayna*) is an adverb of place, and it also indicates generality of places. Its generality is emphasized by the added *ma*, ﴿wherever they are found﴾. And ﴿found﴾ (*thuqifu*) means "encountered." That is, in whatever place they are encountered, humiliation is decreed upon them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾. The "rope" is the means (*sabab*), and the means is called a rope because it leads to the goal, just as a rope leads to the goal, as when a person lowers his bucket into a well, for example, and reaches the goal through it.

What is the rope from Allah? Some of the scholars said: the rope from Allah is Islam, because Islam contains honor, dominance and victory. They are humiliated unless they embrace Islam, unless they embrace Islam. So the rope from Allah means Islam. When they embrace Islam, humiliation is lifted from them. It was also said: the rope from Allah means the *dhimmah* (protected covenant), that is, that they be among the *ahl al-dhimmah* (protected people), because Islam protects the *dhimmis* and defends them. For this reason, it is obligatory upon us regarding the *dhimmis* among us to protect them from anyone who transgresses against them in property, blood or honor, because they are under our care, and they pay us the *jizyah* (poll tax) as long as they do not break the covenant. If they break the covenant, they return to the status of combatants and are killed for the violation of their pact. So the rope from Allah has two views among the people:

One view: it is Islam. The second view: it is the *dhimmah*.

As for His saying: ﴿and a rope from the people﴾, its apparent meaning is generality: that is, by means of a cause from the people, meaning that people defend them, raise their morale, and strengthen them. But what is the rope from the people? It was said: it is the covenant and the safe-conduct (*amān*). The covenant is like what takes place between the Muslims and the disbelievers, when a covenant occurs between them that no one will transgress against another and that a truce remains, as happened at the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The safe-conduct is that a man from the polytheists, or from the Jews and Christians, enters under the protection of one of the Muslims who grants it to him. The difference between the covenant and the safe-conduct is that the safe-conduct is valid from every individual Muslim, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We have granted protection to whomever you have granted protection, O Umm Hani'";[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (357) and Muslim (336/82), from the hadith of Umm Hani'.]] whereas the covenant is only made by those who bind and loose, that is, by the Imam, the commander of the army, or what is similar to that. The difference between the covenant, the safe-conduct and the *dhimmah* is that the *dhimmah* establishes rights for the *ahl al-dhimmah* that are obligatory upon the Muslims, by which they defend them. For this reason they take a compensation for that: the Muslims take from them the *jizyah* in exchange. So the rope from the people is the covenant and the safe-conduct. It is possible that the covenant from the people is more general than that, meaning that it may refer to covenant, safe-conduct, support and strengthening, as happened to the Jews now from the Christians, from the Americans and others. The Jews are humble, and Allah has decreed upon them humiliation and abasement, but the Christian nations now support and strengthen them, not out of love for them, but because they are against the Muslims, because they are against the Muslims. So the rope from the people here means what is more general than covenant and safe-conduct. And it is known that when a word is suitable for generality, the preferable course is to leave it, what? On its generality, to leave it on its generality. So the meaning of ﴿a rope from the people﴾ is: with support and protection from them, such as covenant, safe-conduct, assistance, guardianship and what resembles them.

He says: ﴿They have earned anger from Allah.﴾ ﴿Earned﴾ (*ba'u*) means "returned." From it is His saying: ﴿And those who had already settled the abode and the faith﴾ [al-Hashr 9], meaning they had dwelt in it. So this root, *ba*, *alif*, *hamza*, indicates returning and settling. The meaning is that they returned with anger from Allah, that is, accompanied by anger. Anger is an emotional attribute (*sifah infi'aliyyah*), an emotional attribute and not an active one. The difference between the emotional and the active is that the active is by a person's choice and through outward limbs, such as striking, for example, whereas the emotional occurs without a person's choice, and it is among the inner powers. So anger is an emotional attribute and not an active one. For this reason it comes to a person without his choice: someone provokes him and he becomes angry, his face turns red, his veins swell, his hair stands on end, and he may kill those in front of him, may divorce his wives, and may even commit suicide, we ask Allah for well-being. So anger is an emotional attribute, and as the Prophet ﷺ said, it is "a live coal that Satan throws into the heart of the son of Adam,"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2191) and Ahmad in his Musnad (11587), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri with the wording: "Anger is a live coal kindled in the heart of the son of Adam."]] so he boils over and becomes angry. This is regarding the anger of a human being. As for the anger of Allah, it is one of His attributes whose modality we cannot know, but it is undoubtedly an attribute established for Allah. He becomes angry, is pleased, is displeased, dislikes and loves. All these attributes are affirmed for Allah in the manner that befits Him.

His saying: ﴿with anger from Allah﴾: the particle "from" (*min*) here indicates origin, that is, with anger issuing from Allah. This statement is among what supports the view that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾ is who? The Jews, that the intended people are the Jews, because they are the ones upon whom anger has come. We said that "from" (*min*) indicates origin, that is, anger issuing from Him. Someone may say that it is more general than that the anger issues from Allah, rather it is anger from Allah's decree, and on this view "from" indicates causation, and the intended anger is the anger of Allah and the anger of others. This is the secret behind His saying: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked anger﴾ [al-Fatihah 7], and He did not say "not of those with whom You are angry," because these are those upon whom anger has come from Allah and from the friends of Allah. ﴿And they have earned anger from Allah.﴾

﴿And poverty has been decreed upon them.﴾ Who is the one who decreed it?

**Student:** Allah, Glorified is He.

**Shaykh:** Allah. And poverty (*maskanah*) is destitution. Poverty is destitution. They are humble, having no courage, poor, having no wealth. But we must know that wealth is not an abundance of possessions; wealth is the wealth of the soul and heart. Poverty has been decreed upon these people. They are always in poverty, even if a person among them acquires millions upon millions, they are still in poverty. For this reason, even now, we find that the Jews are the people most greedy for wealth, that they cannot spend a fils except that they hope to acquire a dirham, and they do not spend a dirham except that they hope to acquire a dinar. Such is their condition. Consequently they have become among the wealthiest of the world, if we do not say they are the wealthiest of the world. But they are the wealthiest of the world in abundance of possessions, not in heart and soul. So they are the most destitute of people. ﴿And poverty has been decreed upon them.﴾

﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah.﴾ ﴿That﴾ refers to what preceded: the decreeing of humiliation, anger and poverty. The pronoun referred to here is singular masculine, even though these are three things, because the reference returns to them as something mentioned, so the implied reference is: that which was mentioned. ﴿Because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah.﴾ The particle "because" (*bi-anna*): what does "that because they" mean?

**Student:** The particle *ba'* is a preposition.

**Shaykh:** What does it mean?

**Student:** A particle...

**Shaykh:** It is causative. The *ba'* is causative, meaning: that is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah. "They used to disbelieve" (*kanu yakfuruna*): the word "used to" (*kana*) indicates the attribution of its subject to its predicate, and ﴿yakfuruna﴾ is a present-tense verb, indicating the continuation of disbelief on their part. And so it is: they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah even though they were clear and manifest. To the point that they said to their Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf 138], even though he had told them that Allah is one God. So they disbelieve in the signs of Allah, and among their disbelief is that they disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ, even though they knew him as they know their own sons, and no knowledge is more certain than a person's knowledge of his son; yet they disbelieved in him, upon him be prayers and peace.

His saying: ﴿they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾. "Signs" (*ayat*) is the plural of *ayah*, which means a sign, a mark upon a thing, such that when it exists, the thing exists, because it is its sign. As if I said to you, for example: the sign of the sunrise is that you see its light on the top of the mountain. Here, whenever you see the light on the top of the mountain, the sun has risen.

The signs of Allah are divided, according to the scholars, into two categories: cosmic signs and legislative signs, and all of them are signs pointing to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for the cosmic signs, they are the creatures: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals and others. Every creature of Allah is one of His signs, glorified and exalted is He:

*And in everything there is a sign for Him / indicating that He is One.*

As for the legislative signs, they are what the books have brought, that is, those which Allah sent down upon the messengers. Or, if you wish, say: what the messengers have brought, so as to include the books and the Sunnah. The meaning of something being a sign is that no one other than Allah can bring about that thing or produce it, because if it were possible for someone else to produce it, it would not be a sign. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it. And if the fly should snatch away from them something, they could not recover it from it﴾ [al-Hajj 73]. This is a challenge with which of the signs? With the cosmic signs. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, challenged these people with the smallest of His cosmic signs: the fly. They cannot create it, even if they gather together for it. As for the legislative signs, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce its like, even if they were to each other assistants﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. For this reason it is a sign: no one can ever bring the like of the Qur'an, neither in the truthfulness of its reports, the benefit of its narratives, the justice of its rulings, the eloquence of its speech, nor in other respects. Even if there were nothing in it except that, if you recite it morning and evening, you would never tire of it, whereas other speech, if you read it many times, you would tire of it and leave it. As for the Qur'an, glory be to Allah, you never tire of it. We recite al-Fatihah how many times a day? At least seventeen times a day, we recite al-Fatihah at least seventeen times in one day, and yet you recite it in the second rak'ah as if you had not recited it in the first rak'ah, out of your tenderness toward it and your love for it. This is undoubtedly one of the signs of Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 111–112 (part 4 of 4):

* Among the benefits of this verse: God struck upon these People of the Book the humiliation (maskanah), and it has already been mentioned that what is meant by it is humiliation of the heart; for they may be people of abundant wealth, yet they remain in stinginess, miserliness and pursuit of wealth.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of causation (ithbat al-'illah), meaning that the actions of God, glorified and exalted be He, are causal, that is, joined with wisdom. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿That is because they﴾. The Jabriyyah (determinists) have denied the wisdom of God and the causality of His actions. Their doubt in this matter is that they say: causation (al-'illah) is a purpose (gharad), a purpose that the agent wills, and God, glorified and exalted be He, is exempt from purposes. Among their common sayings they say: God is exempt from purposes (aghrad), accidents (a'rad) and parts (ab'ad), three things: exempt from purposes, accidents, and parts. "Purposes" means wisdom. For this reason they deny all causes, both legislative causes (al-asbab al-shar'iyyah) and natural causes (al-asbab al-kawniyyah). "Accidents" means the attributes of action, such as coming, laughing and the like, and "parts" means the attributes of information, such as the two hands, the face, the two eyes and the like.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the actions of God, mighty and majestic, and His punishments must have wisdom behind them; for this wrath with which they returned and the striking of humiliation and abasement, God has made clear their wisdom, which is that they used to kill, that is, kill the prophets of God unjustly, disbelieve in the signs of God, and disobey God.

* Among its benefits also: disbelief in the signs of God is a cause of punishments, because of His saying: ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾. Several verses of the Qur'an indicate this, such as His saying: ﴿And God struck a parable: a town that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it disbelieved in the blessings of God, so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 112].

* Among its benefits: the transgression (utuww) of the Children of Israel in disbelief, the killing of the prophets, disobedience and aggression, because of His saying: ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾, to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the killing of the prophets necessitates punishment, because God mentioned several causes for this punishment, among them the killing of the prophets.

* Among them: the killing of the prophets cannot be rightful, because of His saying: ﴿without right﴾, and the explanation of this has already been given during the tafsir.

* Among them also: the permissibility of multiple causes for a single effect (ta'addud al-'ilal li-ma'lul wahid), the permissibility of multiple causes for a single effect. This is agreed upon, because the punishments mentioned are several punishments, while the cause is one but multiple in type: the cause is one, except that it is multiple in kind. It is also permissible that a single cause may give rise to multiple effects, such as a person doing one action from which several things follow.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Children of Israel had aggression against the right of God and against the right of the prophets and others; because of His saying: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. These attributes and the punishments that result from them must be taken as a lesson. This is the important practical benefit: that we should not read them as an event that occurred and a historical story; we must read them in order to take a lesson, because of the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].

Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance﴾ [Ali 'Imran 111]. ﴿They will not harm you﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions who hold fast to his guidance. The subject of ﴿they will harm you﴾ refers to the People of the Book; that is, the People of the Book will not harm you except with annoyance. As for His saying ﴿except for some annoyance﴾, the exegetes differed concerning it: is it an exception that is disjunct (munqati') or connected (muttasil)? Some of them said it is a connected exception, because this is the original state of exception; the original state of exception is that it be connected. According to this view, there is some ellipsis in the verse, its estimated meaning being: "they will not harm you except with the harm of annoyance; not the harm of a physical assault that severs a limb or takes wealth, but rather it is annoyance, namely that they make you hear what you dislike, by reproach, mockery and the like." This is if we say that it (the exception) is connected. There is no doubt that annoyance is a type of harm, but it is not the harm that is called by the name "harm."

The second view: the exception here is disjunct (munqati'). According to this view the meaning is: "They will not harm you, but they will annoy you, but they will annoy you." Annoyance does not necessarily entail harm. For this reason Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab 57]. So He affirmed that they annoy Allah and His Messenger, and He said: ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all﴾ [Ali 'Imran 176]. And in the sacred hadith: "O My servants, you will never reach My harm so as to harm Me" [Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr]. So harm is negated with respect to Allah, while annoyance?

* A student: It is present.

* The Shaykh: It is present; annoyance is present. Among its examples is His saying in the sacred hadith: "The son of Adam annoys Me: he curses time, while I am Time" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (4826) and Muslim (2246/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. What makes this clear is that if a man prays beside you who has eaten onion or garlic, you will be pained by its smell, but does it harm you? No, it does not harm you. This view is more correct: that the exception is disjunct. Although it is contrary to the original rule, it is more eloquent in rhetoric. This is in terms of rhetoric: "They will not harm you, but you will endure the annoyance, and annoyance is not harm." ﴿They will not harm you except for some annoyance﴾.

If someone asks: Is this verse definitive (muhkam) and general until the Day of Resurrection, or is it abrogated (mansukh) and specific to what was before abrogation? The answer: the first.

If someone asks: Your claim that the intended meaning is the first raises an objection, namely that the Jews today inflict upon us what is among the gravest harms, and it is well known that Allah's report cannot be broken. So what is the answer?

The answer is that we say: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions, and whoever is upon the like of what the Prophet ﷺ and his companions were upon, the Jews and Christians will not harm him. As for people who believe the Islamic religion to be a religion of backwardness and regression, and who replace it with other reactionary man-made laws, these will not be granted victory, and they will be harmed with annoyance in speech, in action, economically, and in every way. Otherwise, the word of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is never broken. But there are people who fight a tribal, jahili battle based on what? On divided nationalism, and on a false religion opposed to the religion of Allah. These do not deserve victory. For this reason the Jews now do their deeds against us: whoever is able to act with his body does so, and whoever is not able, they do to him the harms that they do, the global economic harms, as is known. Then the verse remains definitive, not abrogated, lasting until the Day of Resurrection. But a conditional statement depends on its condition: the negation of harm is contingent on the existence of its condition, which is that we follow the conduct of those who were promised this promise, namely the Prophet ﷺ and his companions.

Then He said: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 111]. That is: if it were supposed that fighting took place between the Muslims and the People of the Book, they would turn their backs; they would turn their backs, they could not stand firm: ﴿They will not fight you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls﴾ [al-Hashr 14]. But the address, as you know, is to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ and his companions, and whoever is upon the guidance of the Messenger ﷺ and his companions. Good. ﴿If they fight you, they will turn [their backs] to you﴾: we have a condition and a consequence; the condition is fighting, and the consequence is turning the backs. So as soon as an encounter occurs between us and them, and before the first arrow reaches them, Allah knows best, what do they do? They flee, they turn their backs. Here He says: ﴿they will turn their backs to you﴾, meaning they make their backs face you, and this is a metonymy for what? For defeat; because the one who is defeated turns his back to the one from whom he is defeated. Isn't that so?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: For this reason 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was besieged in Makkah, said, reciting or declaiming:

"We are not those whose heels bleed from wounds, / but on our feet the blood drips."

The one whose blood drips on his feet is advancing, and the one whose heels bleed is retreating.

The phrase ﴿they will turn their backs﴾: the nun has been dropped from it because it came as the answer to the condition. He said ﴿then they will not be helped﴾. ("Then," thumma, indicates a pause and delay.) The verb ﴿they will not be helped﴾ carries the nun, and this is a point of difficulty, because thumma is a conjunctive particle and ﴿they will turn their backs﴾ is conjoined to it; and a verb conjoined to a jussive is itself jussive. But we say: thumma here is not conjunctive but resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), and the estimated meaning is: "then they will not be helped." This estimate is necessary, because if it were a conjunction to his saying ﴿they will turn their backs﴾ it would have been jussive, and it would have been said: "then they will not be helped" (lā yunsarū). Then the meaning would be corrupted, the meaning would be corrupted; because if the negation of help for them applied only when they fight us, one could say that they will be helped after that. If He had said: "they will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped," the negation of help would have been restricted to when they fight us. But the matter is not so: they will never be helped, whether they fight us or not. For this reason He said: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. So it is now clear that thumma here is not conjunctive but?

* The students: Resumptive.

* The Shaykh: Resumptive, and the verb after it is in the nominative, because it is a sentence begun on its own; it was not conjoined to an accusative or a jussive. As for His saying ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, what is help? Help is protection, strength, and turning away; and the like. So the meaning of "I helped him" is that I turned his enemy away from him, supported him and strengthened him; this is the meaning of help. So these will never be helped. But someone may say: wars took place between the Muslims and the Christians, and between the Muslims and the Jews, and the Christians were given victory over the Muslims, and the Jews were given victory over the Muslims. The sentence ﴿they will not be helped﴾ is a declarative sentence, and the report of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be broken. So what is the answer? As for the first, some scholars said: this is about the Jews, and the Jews never gained victory over the Muslims at any time in history; rather, it was defeat after defeat. They were defeated in Madinah: Banu Qaynuqa', Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah; and they were defeated at Khaybar, Banu al-Nadir [again]; and no standing up for them before the Muslims occurred. On this basis we say: the verse is specific to whom? To the Jews. As for the Christians, the verse does not address them. But we answer with a more correct answer than this: we say the address is to the Muslims at the time when they represented Islam in belief, speech and action, and in that state they will be helped over the Jews, the Christians, the Magians and all the disbelievers. Have you understood?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Then it is not problematic; it does not trouble us, the domination of the Crusader Christians over the Muslims does not trouble us, nor does the Jewish dominance over the Arabs trouble us; because fighting with the Jews under the banner of Arabism is a jahili fight, a fight of one sect against another, not for religion. Rather, they may believe that they are fighting for religion; they believe that the holy land which Allah decreed for them is written for them until the Day of Resurrection. So they fight confident in Allah's promise, and Musa had said to them: ﴿O my people, enter the holy land which Allah has written for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 21]. So they say: the land is ours by the text of the word of our prophet, so we fight to reach a land which Allah has decreed for us. It is mentioned that when the defeat of the year 1967 CE occurred, when they entered Sinai and seized what they seized of the lands of the Arabs, one of the soldiers would take the dust, kiss it, then prostrate upon it and weep, because he had returned to his land that had been promised to him. So they fought for a belief; but as for a wretched, frivolous nationalism, there is no good in it.

So our answer is on two aspects. The first aspect: that this is specific to the Jews, and that the Jews have not stood up since the Messenger ﷺ expelled them from Madinah; then they were expelled afterward from Khaybar. The second view: the intended are the Jews and the Christians, but on condition that the one opposing them is fighting for Islam, so that the word of Allah may be the highest.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. As for His saying ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾, there are two readings, indeed three readings: ﴿'alayhim﴾, and the second: ﴿'alayhum﴾; these are two readings. The third: ﴿'alayhimi al-dhillah﴾, with ﴿'alayhimi﴾ substituted for ﴿'alayhim﴾. So the hā' has two readings: the ḍammah and the kasrah, or not?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the mīm has two readings: the ḍammah and the kasrah.

And His saying ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾: who decreed it? Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and He called that a "decreeing," like the stamping on coins, which remains impressed and does not disappear by rubbing the hands. Do you know the coins?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: The coins, this iron currency.

* A student: Known.

* The Shaykh: Known. When it is struck, what is struck remains on it: a name, for example, of the ruler of such-and-such state, or an indication that this is worth half a riyal, more or less. This is striking, because it is impressed and does not change. So it is as if this humiliation is stamped upon them and cannot change.

His saying ﴿al-dhillah﴾ is on the pattern fi'lah, and it differs from al-dhull, because it indicates a specific, particular humiliation. Ibn Malik said:

"Fa'lah is for a single occurrence, like jalsah (a sitting); and fi'lah is for a manner or form, like jilsah (a way of sitting)."

In any case, "dhillah" is on the pattern "fi'lah," meaning a specific humiliation, just as you say: "So-and-so sat the sitting of a lion," meaning a known sitting. What then is this humiliation? It is humiliation—and God forbid—that does not leave their hearts; because He said: ﴿it has been decreed upon them﴾, so just as the engraving on a struck coin does not transform or disappear, so this humiliation.

﴿wherever they are found﴾: in my copy it is written "ayna mā" with "ayna" alone; is it so in yours?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: The rule is that they are joined together as "aynamā," but what is in the Muṣḥaf is an old convention.

His saying ﴿wherever they are found﴾ means: wherever they are encountered. Allah said: ﴿and kill them wherever you find them﴾ [al-Baqarah 191], meaning: wherever you find them. So these Jews and Christians, who are also from the Children of Israel, have humiliation decreed upon them; wherever they are on earth, they are humbled, because Allah decreed humiliation upon them.

But He says: ﴿except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. In this case humiliation is not decreed upon them. "A rope from Allah" means the means of salvation from this humiliation, which comes from Allah, and that is Islam; for Islam is a rope from Allah by which a person protects himself, his family and his wealth. Accordingly, the "rope of Allah" here means what? Islam; because the rope is the means: that is, by means from Allah, namely that they become Muslims and humiliation departs from them. It was also said that "the rope of Allah" means the covenant, the covenant between the Muslims and these disbelievers, by which they remain under our shade and protection, because they are covenanted people, dhimmis.

As for His saying ﴿and a rope from the people﴾, what is meant is safe-conduct: the safe-conduct granted by one man to a captive, for example. That is because when we fight a town and conquer it, we have the right to grant protection to its people, as the Prophet ﷺ said when he conquered Makkah: "Whoever enters his house is safe" [al-Bayhaqi in al-Kubra (18274) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah with the wording: "Whoever enters his dwelling is safe"]. "Whoever enters his house is safe": this is a particular protection. A general protection is that there be between us and them a covenant whereby they do not transgress against us and we do not transgress against them, and they do not defend us and we do not defend them; and this is like what exists at the present time in international agreements, such as the Charter of the United Nations and the like.

* A student: Shaykh, we said regarding it, "They will not harm you except for some annoyance," meaning, for example, harm in proportion; sometimes the Muslims, of course, annoy the Jews in every way, with weapons...

* The Shaykh: The Jews annoy them, and they do not annoy us?

* The student: No, the Jews harm the Muslims in all respects, such as this harm; they say: "We are the advanced ones in weapons and things, anything in comparison to ..." the images of women, for example; is this harm or not?

* The Shaykh: Did you hear his words?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: He says: they now annoy the Muslims and harm them by killing, wounding, plundering wealth and the like. So what is the way out of this difficulty? I think that if he were alert he would know it, but it seems he has put some sleep in his eye.

* A student: Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: We mentioned that this verse was specific to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions, and this applies only to whoever is characterized by their guidance, the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ and his companions; as for whoever follows other than that, humiliation is his.

* The Shaykh: Well said. Do you understand?

* The student: Yes, I understand, but, that is, the harm, for example...

* The Shaykh: The harm now occurring from the Jews or other disbelievers upon the Muslims is because the Muslims themselves have not fulfilled the obligation; and Allah says: ﴿They will not harm you﴾, meaning you, O Muslims, and those who are like you. That is the distinction.

* A student: Shaykh, did not the Prophet ﷺ suffer great harm at the Battle of Uhud, and at his death he died from the effect of poison from the Jewess? And also in the Battle of Banu al-Mustaliq he was afflicted in his honor and his family?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Then did the condition fail?

* The Shaykh: It is impossible; we say: was he harmed by that?

* The student: Yes, he was harmed.

* The Shaykh: By what?

* The student: The effect of the poison, which he found in his heart.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: And also his front tooth was broken at the Battle of Uhud.

* The Shaykh: Who was facing him?

* The student: The polytheists.

* The Shaykh: Yes; and this?

* The student: The Jews.

* The Shaykh: Among the Jews and Christians, the People of the Book.

* A student: Is it not general, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: No. Allah says: ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them; among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient. (110) They will not harm you except for some annoyance﴾.

* A student: The humiliation: he says, ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾, would it be like the seal upon the heart?

* The Shaykh: Like what?

* The student: Like the sealing upon the heart.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the striking means sealing upon the heart.

* The student: Humiliation?

* The Shaykh: No, this humiliation we have not explained.

* A student: May Allah reward you well. As history mentions, at the Battle of Mu'tah, those who fought the Romans, who were Christians, most of them were Companions, yet they were punished and defeated; is that so?

**Shaykh:** Correct, but the Messenger ﷺ called it a conquest (*fath*) when Khalid, may Allah be pleased with him, led them up to the mountain and they were saved. He said: "Then Khalid ibn al-Walid took the banner, and Allah granted him victory,"[[Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (1750), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ja'far, with the wording: "Then Khalid ibn al-Walid took the banner, and Allah granted him victory through it."]] so he called it a victory.

**Student:** They were harmed.

**Shaykh:** It is true that some of them were killed; there is no doubt about this. But we may say that this killing will not harm them, because they move from one abode to a higher one.

**Student:** And in other instances, in the time of 'Umar and Abu Bakr, when the armies went to face the Romans in al-Sham, some battles were lost by the Muslims?

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, if they were defeated. But the meaning of the verse indicates that they can harm us only with hurt. Even harm that occurs may be of the same rank as hurt. That is, the outcome is not always victory. This can be understood in this way.

**Student:** Shaykh, we said that the principle regarding the exception (*istithna'*) is that it should be connected (*muttasil*). Yet we always see the exegetes and others, when they interpret a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), bring in "but" (*lakin*). Is it a consistent rule that a disconnected exception is interpreted by what follows it being rendered with "but"?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** It cannot be interpreted with any particle other than "but"?

**Shaykh:** Because "but" (*lakin*) is the one used for correction (*istidrak*), and the disconnected exception is a correction.

**Student:** May Allah reward you well, Shaykh. Do the Shi'ah and the hypocrites enter among the People of the Book, the Jews and Christians, in their harm to the believers, despite their varied kinds?

**Shaykh:** In any case, the hypocrites harm the believers without doubt. But do they harm them by speech and action? If they harm them by speech and action in a manner that causes damage, then the verse is applied to other people, who can harm us only with hurt.

**Student:** Is the harm that is established or negated when the fighting is collective, or when a person fights alone?

**Shaykh:** No, the apparent meaning is collective fighting. For example, if we, the Muslims, gather upon true Islam and fight them, they will not be victorious over us.

**Student:** And if a single person fights, and (...) deception against them?

**Shaykh:** Allah has not committed Himself to that.

**Student:** ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ indicates that (...) among them, to the point that we mentioned that they may flee at the first arrow that reaches them (...) when they meet, they fight the Muslims (...) and afterwards the fighting continued with them until they were defeated (...)?

**Shaykh:** To whom is the address? ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾: who is the subject?

**Student:** The Jews.

**Shaykh:** These Jews are not Arabs.

**Student:** (...) Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** They are not Arabs.

**Student:** ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found, except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people. They have earned anger from Allah, and poverty has been decreed upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾ (112) ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing [in obedience]; they recite the verses of Allah during the night and prostrate. They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous. And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it. And Allah is Knowing of the righteous.﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112–115]

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Ali 'Imran 112]. The saying of Allah, ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾, does not specify the one who decreed it, but it is known. Who is it? Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He left it unspecified because it is known, like His saying: ﴿And mankind was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa' 28], although it is Allah who created him. However, it is among the methods of the Qur'an that Allah expresses undesirable matters in the passive voice, whereas desirable matters are expressed with the active participle, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10].

Here He says: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾. The pronoun refers to the People of the Book. But is the intended meaning the People of the Book, both Jews and Christians, or is it specific to the Jews? The scholars differ on this. Some said it is specific to the Jews, while other scholars said it is general, and the default is generality, because the pronoun ﴿upon them﴾ refers to the People of the Book mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed﴾ [Ali 'Imran 110]. So we say the pronoun refers to the People of the Book, Jews and Christians. If it is assumed that they gained honor at some time, that occurred for a reason that required it, so it is contrary to the default. Otherwise, the default is that humiliation is decreed upon them.

His saying: ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾: here "humiliation" means degradation, meaning that Allah the Exalted has degraded them.

﴿Wherever they are found﴾: "wherever" (*ayna*) is an adverb of place, and it also indicates generality of places. Its generality is emphasized by the added *ma*, ﴿wherever they are found﴾. And ﴿found﴾ (*thuqifu*) means "encountered." That is, in whatever place they are encountered, humiliation is decreed upon them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿except with a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾. The "rope" is the means (*sabab*), and the means is called a rope because it leads to the goal, just as a rope leads to the goal, as when a person lowers his bucket into a well, for example, and reaches the goal through it.

What is the rope from Allah? Some of the scholars said: the rope from Allah is Islam, because Islam contains honor, dominance and victory. They are humiliated unless they embrace Islam, unless they embrace Islam. So the rope from Allah means Islam. When they embrace Islam, humiliation is lifted from them. It was also said: the rope from Allah means the *dhimmah* (protected covenant), that is, that they be among the *ahl al-dhimmah* (protected people), because Islam protects the *dhimmis* and defends them. For this reason, it is obligatory upon us regarding the *dhimmis* among us to protect them from anyone who transgresses against them in property, blood or honor, because they are under our care, and they pay us the *jizyah* (poll tax) as long as they do not break the covenant. If they break the covenant, they return to the status of combatants and are killed for the violation of their pact. So the rope from Allah has two views among the people:

One view: it is Islam. The second view: it is the *dhimmah*.

As for His saying: ﴿and a rope from the people﴾, its apparent meaning is generality: that is, by means of a cause from the people, meaning that people defend them, raise their morale, and strengthen them. But what is the rope from the people? It was said: it is the covenant and the safe-conduct (*amān*). The covenant is like what takes place between the Muslims and the disbelievers, when a covenant occurs between them that no one will transgress against another and that a truce remains, as happened at the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The safe-conduct is that a man from the polytheists, or from the Jews and Christians, enters under the protection of one of the Muslims who grants it to him. The difference between the covenant and the safe-conduct is that the safe-conduct is valid from every individual Muslim, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We have granted protection to whomever you have granted protection, O Umm Hani'";[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (357) and Muslim (336/82), from the hadith of Umm Hani'.]] whereas the covenant is only made by those who bind and loose, that is, by the Imam, the commander of the army, or what is similar to that. The difference between the covenant, the safe-conduct and the *dhimmah* is that the *dhimmah* establishes rights for the *ahl al-dhimmah* that are obligatory upon the Muslims, by which they defend them. For this reason they take a compensation for that: the Muslims take from them the *jizyah* in exchange. So the rope from the people is the covenant and the safe-conduct. It is possible that the covenant from the people is more general than that, meaning that it may refer to covenant, safe-conduct, support and strengthening, as happened to the Jews now from the Christians, from the Americans and others. The Jews are humble, and Allah has decreed upon them humiliation and abasement, but the Christian nations now support and strengthen them, not out of love for them, but because they are against the Muslims, because they are against the Muslims. So the rope from the people here means what is more general than covenant and safe-conduct. And it is known that when a word is suitable for generality, the preferable course is to leave it, what? On its generality, to leave it on its generality. So the meaning of ﴿a rope from the people﴾ is: with support and protection from them, such as covenant, safe-conduct, assistance, guardianship and what resembles them.

He says: ﴿They have earned anger from Allah.﴾ ﴿Earned﴾ (*ba'u*) means "returned." From it is His saying: ﴿And those who had already settled the abode and the faith﴾ [al-Hashr 9], meaning they had dwelt in it. So this root, *ba*, *alif*, *hamza*, indicates returning and settling. The meaning is that they returned with anger from Allah, that is, accompanied by anger. Anger is an emotional attribute (*sifah infi'aliyyah*), an emotional attribute and not an active one. The difference between the emotional and the active is that the active is by a person's choice and through outward limbs, such as striking, for example, whereas the emotional occurs without a person's choice, and it is among the inner powers. So anger is an emotional attribute and not an active one. For this reason it comes to a person without his choice: someone provokes him and he becomes angry, his face turns red, his veins swell, his hair stands on end, and he may kill those in front of him, may divorce his wives, and may even commit suicide, we ask Allah for well-being. So anger is an emotional attribute, and as the Prophet ﷺ said, it is "a live coal that Satan throws into the heart of the son of Adam,"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2191) and Ahmad in his Musnad (11587), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri with the wording: "Anger is a live coal kindled in the heart of the son of Adam."]] so he boils over and becomes angry. This is regarding the anger of a human being. As for the anger of Allah, it is one of His attributes whose modality we cannot know, but it is undoubtedly an attribute established for Allah. He becomes angry, is pleased, is displeased, dislikes and loves. All these attributes are affirmed for Allah in the manner that befits Him.

His saying: ﴿with anger from Allah﴾: the particle "from" (*min*) here indicates origin, that is, with anger issuing from Allah. This statement is among what supports the view that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them﴾ is who? The Jews, that the intended people are the Jews, because they are the ones upon whom anger has come. We said that "from" (*min*) indicates origin, that is, anger issuing from Him. Someone may say that it is more general than that the anger issues from Allah, rather it is anger from Allah's decree, and on this view "from" indicates causation, and the intended anger is the anger of Allah and the anger of others. This is the secret behind His saying: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked anger﴾ [al-Fatihah 7], and He did not say "not of those with whom You are angry," because these are those upon whom anger has come from Allah and from the friends of Allah. ﴿And they have earned anger from Allah.﴾

﴿And poverty has been decreed upon them.﴾ Who is the one who decreed it?

**Student:** Allah, Glorified is He.

**Shaykh:** Allah. And poverty (*maskanah*) is destitution. Poverty is destitution. They are humble, having no courage, poor, having no wealth. But we must know that wealth is not an abundance of possessions; wealth is the wealth of the soul and heart. Poverty has been decreed upon these people. They are always in poverty, even if a person among them acquires millions upon millions, they are still in poverty. For this reason, even now, we find that the Jews are the people most greedy for wealth, that they cannot spend a fils except that they hope to acquire a dirham, and they do not spend a dirham except that they hope to acquire a dinar. Such is their condition. Consequently they have become among the wealthiest of the world, if we do not say they are the wealthiest of the world. But they are the wealthiest of the world in abundance of possessions, not in heart and soul. So they are the most destitute of people. ﴿And poverty has been decreed upon them.﴾

﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah.﴾ ﴿That﴾ refers to what preceded: the decreeing of humiliation, anger and poverty. The pronoun referred to here is singular masculine, even though these are three things, because the reference returns to them as something mentioned, so the implied reference is: that which was mentioned. ﴿Because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah.﴾ The particle "because" (*bi-anna*): what does "that because they" mean?

**Student:** The particle *ba'* is a preposition.

**Shaykh:** What does it mean?

**Student:** A particle...

**Shaykh:** It is causative. The *ba'* is causative, meaning: that is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah. "They used to disbelieve" (*kanu yakfuruna*): the word "used to" (*kana*) indicates the attribution of its subject to its predicate, and ﴿yakfuruna﴾ is a present-tense verb, indicating the continuation of disbelief on their part. And so it is: they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah even though they were clear and manifest. To the point that they said to their Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf 138], even though he had told them that Allah is one God. So they disbelieve in the signs of Allah, and among their disbelief is that they disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ, even though they knew him as they know their own sons, and no knowledge is more certain than a person's knowledge of his son; yet they disbelieved in him, upon him be prayers and peace.

His saying: ﴿they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾. "Signs" (*ayat*) is the plural of *ayah*, which means a sign, a mark upon a thing, such that when it exists, the thing exists, because it is its sign. As if I said to you, for example: the sign of the sunrise is that you see its light on the top of the mountain. Here, whenever you see the light on the top of the mountain, the sun has risen.

The signs of Allah are divided, according to the scholars, into two categories: cosmic signs and legislative signs, and all of them are signs pointing to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for the cosmic signs, they are the creatures: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals and others. Every creature of Allah is one of His signs, glorified and exalted is He:

*And in everything there is a sign for Him / indicating that He is One.*

As for the legislative signs, they are what the books have brought, that is, those which Allah sent down upon the messengers. Or, if you wish, say: what the messengers have brought, so as to include the books and the Sunnah. The meaning of something being a sign is that no one other than Allah can bring about that thing or produce it, because if it were possible for someone else to produce it, it would not be a sign. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it. And if the fly should snatch away from them something, they could not recover it from it﴾ [al-Hajj 73]. This is a challenge with which of the signs? With the cosmic signs. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, challenged these people with the smallest of His cosmic signs: the fly. They cannot create it, even if they gather together for it. As for the legislative signs, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce its like, even if they were to each other assistants﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. For this reason it is a sign: no one can ever bring the like of the Qur'an, neither in the truthfulness of its reports, the benefit of its narratives, the justice of its rulings, the eloquence of its speech, nor in other respects. Even if there were nothing in it except that, if you recite it morning and evening, you would never tire of it, whereas other speech, if you read it many times, you would tire of it and leave it. As for the Qur'an, glory be to Allah, you never tire of it. We recite al-Fatihah how many times a day? At least seventeen times a day, we recite al-Fatihah at least seventeen times in one day, and yet you recite it in the second rak'ah as if you had not recited it in the first rak'ah, out of your tenderness toward it and your love for it. This is undoubtedly one of the signs of Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 111–112 (part 4 of 4):

* Among the benefits of this verse: God struck upon these People of the Book the humiliation (maskanah), and it has already been mentioned that what is meant by it is humiliation of the heart; for they may be people of abundant wealth, yet they remain in stinginess, miserliness and pursuit of wealth.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of causation (ithbat al-'illah), meaning that the actions of God, glorified and exalted be He, are causal, that is, joined with wisdom. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿That is because they﴾. The Jabriyyah (determinists) have denied the wisdom of God and the causality of His actions. Their doubt in this matter is that they say: causation (al-'illah) is a purpose (gharad), a purpose that the agent wills, and God, glorified and exalted be He, is exempt from purposes. Among their common sayings they say: God is exempt from purposes (aghrad), accidents (a'rad) and parts (ab'ad), three things: exempt from purposes, accidents, and parts. "Purposes" means wisdom. For this reason they deny all causes, both legislative causes (al-asbab al-shar'iyyah) and natural causes (al-asbab al-kawniyyah). "Accidents" means the attributes of action, such as coming, laughing and the like, and "parts" means the attributes of information, such as the two hands, the face, the two eyes and the like.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the actions of God, mighty and majestic, and His punishments must have wisdom behind them; for this wrath with which they returned and the striking of humiliation and abasement, God has made clear their wisdom, which is that they used to kill, that is, kill the prophets of God unjustly, disbelieve in the signs of God, and disobey God.

* Among its benefits also: disbelief in the signs of God is a cause of punishments, because of His saying: ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾. Several verses of the Qur'an indicate this, such as His saying: ﴿And God struck a parable: a town that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it disbelieved in the blessings of God, so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 112].

* Among its benefits: the transgression (utuww) of the Children of Israel in disbelief, the killing of the prophets, disobedience and aggression, because of His saying: ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾, to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the killing of the prophets necessitates punishment, because God mentioned several causes for this punishment, among them the killing of the prophets.

* Among them: the killing of the prophets cannot be rightful, because of His saying: ﴿without right﴾, and the explanation of this has already been given during the tafsir.

* Among them also: the permissibility of multiple causes for a single effect (ta'addud al-'ilal li-ma'lul wahid), the permissibility of multiple causes for a single effect. This is agreed upon, because the punishments mentioned are several punishments, while the cause is one but multiple in type: the cause is one, except that it is multiple in kind. It is also permissible that a single cause may give rise to multiple effects, such as a person doing one action from which several things follow.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Children of Israel had aggression against the right of God and against the right of the prophets and others; because of His saying: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. These attributes and the punishments that result from them must be taken as a lesson. This is the important practical benefit: that we should not read them as an event that occurred and a historical story; we must read them in order to take a lesson, because of the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 113–114 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ [Al 'Imran 113]. The pronoun in ﴿They﴾ refers to the People of the Book, and ﴿alike﴾ (sawa') means equal in these attributes. Rather, among them is ﴿a community standing [upright], reciting the verses of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 113], to the end of the verse, and among them is a deviant community that does not stand upright by the command of Allah. ﴿They are not all alike﴾ means: they are not equal in disobedience, conditions and attributes. Then He clarified this by saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community standing [upright]﴾ [Al 'Imran 113].

One of the benefits of this noble verse is that the Children of Israel have transgression against the right of Allah and against the rights of the prophets and others, as shown by His saying: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾ [Al 'Imran 112].

These attributes, and the punishments that result from them, require that we take a lesson from them, and this is the important practical benefit: that we do not read them as a mere event or a historical story. We must read them in order to learn a lesson, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Certainly in their stories is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ [Al 'Imran 113]. ﴿They﴾ refers to the People of the Book, and ﴿alike﴾ (sawa') means equal, i.e., they are not equal in these attributes. Rather, among them is ﴿a community standing [upright], reciting the verses of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 113], to the end, and among them is a deviant community that does not stand upright by the command of Allah. ﴿They are not all alike﴾ means: they are not equal in disobedience, conditions and attributes.

Then He clarified this by saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community standing [upright]﴾.

His saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book﴾ refers to the Jews and the Christians, as has passed us many times. The noun is made explicit here in place of the pronoun, either because of the long separation between the explicit noun to which the pronouns refer, or because the sentence is resumed (isti'naf), since ﴿Among the People of the Book﴾ is a new sentence. ﴿Ummah﴾ means a group, ﴿standing﴾ means steadfast and upright in obedience to the command of Allah. The standing here means steadfastness and uprightness in obedience to the command of Allah, not the standing that is the opposite of sitting, since the Muslim is standing upright in the command of Allah whether he is standing, sitting or lying down.

﴿They recite the verses of Allah in the watches of the night﴾: the word ﴿standing﴾ is an adjective; the clause ﴿they recite the verses of Allah﴾ is another adjective, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (hal). There is a grammatical rule: when an indefinite noun is described, the second description may be either a circumstantial clause or an adjective. This rule holds whether the second description is a clause or a single word. So if you say: (A noble man came to me riding) it is correct, because it is a description; and if you say: (A noble man came to me riding) with the active participle, it is also correct. In this noble verse, ﴿ummah﴾ is indefinite and ﴿standing﴾ is its adjective; ﴿they recite﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, in which case the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and it may be an adjective.

﴿They recite the verses of Allah﴾: recitation (tilawah) is sometimes meant as following (ittiba'), and sometimes meant as reading (qira'ah). If the context fits both meanings, it is understood as both; if it is specific to one of them, it is specific to it. When you say: (He recited to me a verse from the Quran), the meaning is reading; and when you say: (This man recites the verses of Allah, sincerely and in worship), this may mean reading and may mean following. When it is open to both meanings, and they do not contradict each other, it is understood as both.

So His saying: ﴿They recite the verses of Allah﴾ includes reciting the words and reciting by acting upon the verses of Allah.

His saying: ﴿in the watches of the night﴾: ﴿ānā'﴾ means times, and from it comes the word nawʾ (rising of a star), referring to the time of a star's rising or to the star itself. So ﴿ānā'﴾ means times, ﴿in the watches of the night﴾ meaning the times and hours of the night.

﴿And they prostrate﴾: this clause, ﴿and they prostrate﴾, allows two possibilities: that it is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), or that it is a circumstantial clause from the waw in His saying ﴿they recite﴾, meaning they recite the verses of Allah while they are prostrating. He described them with reciting the verses of Allah, which is the best of remembrance, and with prostration, which is the best of states, because prostration is better than standing and better than bowing, since the one prostrating is closest to his Lord. But recitation of the verses is the best of the remembrances, and for this reason the standing was specified for it. So His saying ﴿they recite the verses of Allah﴾ mentions the highest attribute of speech, and ﴿and they prostrate﴾ mentions the highest attribute of action, which is prostration.

﴿They believe in Allah﴾: the clause is a resumed sentence explaining the condition of these people, and it may be an adjective of ﴿ummah﴾ or a circumstantial clause.

﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. Belief in Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, encompasses four things:
- Belief in His existence.
- Belief in His lordship.
- Belief in His divinity.
- Belief in His names and attributes.

These are all necessary. Whoever denies the existence of Allah has not believed in Him; whoever believes in Him but denies His unity in lordship has not believed in Him; whoever believes in Him and His lordship but denies that He alone is to be worshipped has not believed in Him; whoever believes in all of that but denies some of His attributes has not believed in Him. So there is no belief in Allah except with these four matters.

As for belief in the Last Day: the Last Day refers first to the Day of Resurrection. It is called the last day because there is no day after it, since it is the final end of creation, and in it there is no night and no day; it is all one day, with no sun, no moon and no stars, each in its place, either in Paradise or in the Fire. It is the last thing in which the servants will be.

It is known that the servants have four abodes: the first is in the wombs of their mothers, the second is in this world, the third is in the barzakh, and the fourth is in the Last Day, which is the final one, and for this it is called the Last Day. The Last Day includes in belief in it everything the Prophet ﷺ informed us of that will occur after death. Everything he informed of that occurs after death: so the questioning of the dead in his grave falls within belief in the Last Day, and the punishment or bliss of the grave falls within belief in the Last Day. The reason is that whoever dies, his resurrection has already begun, so what he finds in his grave is like what he finds after being raised, all of it is from the unseen matters, all of it is in the abode of recompense. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Included in belief in the Last Day is everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will occur after death."

Belief in it means that you believe in everything that came in the Book and the Sunnah concerning what occurs after death, in summary and in detail. But know that in books of admonition (wa'z) there are weak hadiths, indeed fabricated ones, concerning the conditions of the grave and the conditions of the Resurrection, which the reader should guard against. There is no better course than returning to the authentic books on this subject, so that we do not mislead people. Some preachers choose such hadiths for the sake of encouragement or warning, but the truth is that this is not a good method, because filling people's minds with weak or fabricated hadiths is an error, even if they contain encouragement or warning. What is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ is sufficient. People will take everything mentioned as authentic, saying: "What is said from the pulpit is correct."

It is obligatory upon the one who compiles on encouragement and warning to mention only what is a proof, from the sahih or the hasan; as for the weak, there is no need to mention it, because we are free of it, free of this weak material that was not established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As for His saying: ﴿and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾: this has been mentioned in this surah twice. Is it mentioned twice, or once?
* Students: Twice.
* Other students: Three times.
* The Shaykh: This is the third. I say: it has preceded (sabaq), I do not say: it has been mentioned (dhukira). It has preceded with its mention twice: enjoining right and forbidding wrong. And we mentioned at the beginning, when it passed us, its conditions and etiquettes.

﴿and they hasten in good works﴾: meaning that together with being believers and being reformers, they are also hastening in good works, i.e., they race toward good works as people race for spoils.

His saying: ﴿they hasten in (fi) good works﴾, and He did not say ﴿to (ila) good works﴾, although (sara'a) takes (ila), as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran 133]. The reason is that what is meant here is their hastening toward them and within performing them. Pay attention: the meaning is hastening toward them; when they reach them, they do not stop hastening; they hasten within them. This is the reason, and Allah knows best, why it was said ﴿they hasten in good works﴾ and not ﴿toward them﴾.

His saying: ﴿in good works﴾: (al-khayrat) is the plural of khayr or khayrah, and it is everything from which the servant benefits or which benefits others. Prayer is good, teaching people the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ is good, calling to Allah is good, and enjoining right and forbidding wrong is also good. Everything that brings one closer to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is good, and hastening in it is hastening toward it, and hastening in it is during the performance of the act.

He said: ﴿And those are among the righteous﴾. ﴿Those﴾ refers to this standing community from the People of the Book.

The scholars said: the righteous one is the one who upholds the right of Allah and the rights of the servants, and its opposite is the corrupt. Righteousness revolves around two things: knowledge and action, and its opposite is ignorance, disbelief and rebellion. Whoever is ignorant is not righteous, meaning not righteous in the sense of the highest level of righteousness; otherwise he has righteousness in proportion to his knowledge. Whoever does not act is not righteous, and he lacks righteousness in proportion to what he lacks of action.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾: (ma) is a conditional particle, and the clause ﴿they will not be denied it﴾ is the answer to the condition.

In this verse there are two readings: ﴿And whatever you do of good, you will not be denied it﴾ with the taa', and the second: ﴿And whatever they do of good, they will not be denied it﴾ with the yaa'. On the second reading with the yaa', there is no iltifat in the verse, since it follows the third-person pronoun as in the verse before it. On the reading with the taa', ﴿whatever you do﴾, there is an iltifat from the third person to the second person, and also the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ and to this community.

His saying: ﴿whatever you do of good﴾: the (min) here is explicative (bayaniyyah), because it comes after the conditional noun, and the conditional noun is an ambiguous noun that needs clarification; for this reason, whenever (min) comes after a conditional noun, it is explicative.

His saying: ﴿of good (khayr)﴾: we have already said that what is meant by good is everything that brings one closer to Allah.

His saying: ﴿they will not be denied it (fa-lan yukfaru-hu)﴾: meaning they will not be deprived of its reward. Kufr (disbelief) originally means covering, and from it comes al-kufra, and what is al-kufra? 
* Student: It is the spathe of the date palm.
* The Shaykh: It is the sheath of the spathe. The sheath of the date-palm spathe is called kufra; this kufra covers. For this reason they said that kufr originally means covering, because a person covers Allah's blessing upon him and does not show it. Blessing requires gratitude, so if it is not thanked, this is kufr.

So ﴿they will not be denied it﴾ means they will not be deprived of its reward, because if they were deprived of its reward, their doing of this good would be hidden and would have no visible effect.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious﴾: He will reward them for their God-consciousness. God-consciousness (taqwa) has many benefits, and I think we once held a competition about it.

Specifying knowledge with the God-conscious is to encourage God-consciousness and to warn against opposing it and failing to uphold it; otherwise Allah knows everything.

Let us take the benefits of this verse:
* One of the benefits of this verse: the People of the Book are not all alike; among them is a misguided community and among them is a community standing by the command of Allah, and this is explicit in the verse: ﴿They are not all alike, of the People of the Book﴾.
* Among its benefits: the demonstration of the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He gives everyone his due right.
