When the blame was mentioned, the blame of the People of the Book in the previous verses, understanding might turn to think that all the People of the Book have this description: that they disbelieve in the verses of Allah, kill the prophets without right, disobey Allah and transgress against His right and the rights of His servants. So Allah said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾, meaning that among them are those who are not like that.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the People of the Book is a community (ummah), and ummah implies a gathering and a large number upon the praiseworthy and desired attribute. They mentioned that about twenty men from the Jews embraced Islam, and a large number from the Christians as well, and for this He expressed it with His saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community﴾.

Some scholars held that what is meant by the ummah here is the Muslim ummah, but this is very far-fetched, because ﴿ummah﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿of the People of the Book﴾; and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not express this community as the People of the Book. Rather He said: ﴿He named you Muslims before and in this﴾ [Al-Hajj 78]. Just as He did not express the People of the Book as believers. Every verse in which there is ﴿O you who believe﴾ is addressed to the believers in Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and every verse in which there is ﴿O People of the Book﴾ means by them the Children of Israel to whom Moses and Jesus were sent.

* One of the benefits of this verse: praise for standing in obedience to Allah and steadfastness upon it. From where is this benefit taken from the verse?
* Student: ﴿And those are among the righteous﴾.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿A standing community﴾, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: ﴿A standing community﴾ is the basis of their praise.
* One of the benefits of the verse: praise for those who recite the Book of Allah, by reading and by acting. From where do we take it?
* Student: From the saying of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community standing, reciting the verses of Allah﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They recite the verses of Allah﴾. From where did you know that reciting the Book, by reading and by acting, is praiseworthy, and that its doer is to be praised?
* Student: In Surat al-Baqarah.
* The Shaykh: No, we want from these verses.
* Student: The praise by what He described them with, which is: ﴿whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾.
* The Shaykh: Because this is the opposite of those who had the first attributes; for when He mentioned the first attributes, He said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾, then He mentioned the distinction.
* One of the benefits of the verse: the virtue of prostration?
* Student: ﴿In the watches of the night, and they prostrate﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And they prostrate﴾.
* One of the benefits of this verse: also praise for those who believe in Allah and the Last Day. From where do you take it?
* Student: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. If Allah praises a person for an attribute, is he to be blamed if he does not have it?
* Student: If this is absent, praise for him is absent.
* The Shaykh: Meaning praise is absent from him; and he may deserve blame, or may not?
* Student: He deserves blame if (...) is absent.
* The Shaykh: Meaning belief in the Last Day, there is no doubt that if it is absent, he is blamed because he is a disbeliever. But in other matters, if we praised a person for performing the Duha prayer, would that mean that if he did not pray it, he is blamed?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: So we take a rule: the absence of praise does not necessarily entail the establishment of blame.

From this a jurisprudential benefit also follows: that leaving a recommended act does not necessarily mean falling into a disliked act. If a man prayed and did not raise his hands at the takbir of the opening, do we say that this is disliked? No.

This is a useful rule: abandoning a sunnah does not necessarily mean that a person falls into what is disliked, but his reward is reduced, without doubt; yet he is not blamed, nor is it said that he has fallen into what is disliked or into something forbidden.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: praise for enjoining right and forbidding wrong?
* Student: From the verse: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾.
* The Shaykh: If someone said: why did Allah mention belief in Allah and the Last Day between the mention of reciting the verses and the mention of enjoining right and forbidding wrong? Look, He began with reciting the verses of Allah and prostration, then doubled with belief in Allah and the Last Day, and then mentioned enjoining right and forbidding wrong; so why did He place belief, which is the foundation, between the recitation of the Book and enjoining right and forbidding wrong?
* Student: Because the recitation of the verses reminds of the Last Day and establishes belief in it.

**Shaykh:** This means that faith in something is not possible except after knowledge of it, is that right? So when they recite God's verses, they know about the Last Day and then believe in it.

**Student:** Also, because it [the recitation] is a motivation, since they hope for the reward of this deed on the Last Day.

**Shaykh:** You mean that it is the goal?

**Student:** Yes.

**Student:** Do you say: the explicit mention of the recitation?

**Shaykh:** Is it possible to mention the recitation explicitly by delaying it, after he says: "They believe in God and the Last Day and recite the Book of God"?

**Student:** Placing it first and mentioning it explicitly, Shaykh.

**Another student:** Could we say: it is the general (*'amm*) being coordinated with the specific (*khass*)?

**Shaykh:** No, recitation is a deed.

In any case, what appears to me is that faith in something is not possible except after knowledge of it, and we do not know about the Last Day except after the recitation of the Book of God. But the prostration was placed before belief in the Last Day because it is linked to the recitation.

**Student:** (...) that the verses may be recited by one who believes in them and by one who does not believe in them. Some disbelievers were found to recite the verses, and the praise is not complete until they believe in them?

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, this is good. But when the context is one of praise, the intended meaning of "those who recite" becomes those who recite it with belief in it.

**From the benefits of this verse:** Praise for those who hasten to good deeds.

**Student:** ﴿And they hasten to good deeds﴾.

**Shaykh:** From His saying ﴿And they hasten to good deeds﴾.

If someone says: How can we reconcile this verse, which contains praise for hastening to good, with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When you hear the iqamah, walk to the prayer, with tranquility and dignity upon you, and do not hasten"?[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (636), and Muslim (602 / 151), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

**Student:** I say, our Shaykh: hastening to good deeds (...) with tranquility and dignity.

**Shaykh:** You mean that the meaning of "good deeds" is what the Shariah has commanded, is that right? And hurrying to the prayer is not from good, because the Prophet ﷺ forbade it. So the answer is that we say: hastening to good deeds is hastening to conform to the Shariah, is that right?

**Student:** The second interpretation: hastening in establishing the prayer itself.

**Shaykh:** In what?

**Student:** The second explanation: intending the prayer itself and hastening to it by perfecting it.

**Shaykh:** No, this is included in the general meaning, and there is no problem with it. But how did he forbid hastening to it?

**Student:** How?

**Shaykh:** I say: for example, perfecting the prayer is without doubt from hastening to good deeds and is included in the general meaning. But our question concerns the prohibition of hastening to it. So it is said: the intended meaning of hastening to good deeds is hastening to adhere to the Shariah and to act upon it.

**Student:** One who goes to the prayer calmly and with tranquility has a greater good than one who goes to it quickly, becomes preoccupied, and so becomes distracted.

**Shaykh:** Fine, this is possible. It means that the good deeds are those that agree with the Shariah, so hastening to them is to adhere to them.

**From the benefits of this verse:** Praise of these people for righteousness, by His saying ﴿And they are among the righteous﴾. Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to adhere to, or to perform, these deeds for which God praised these people from the People of the Book and commended them.

If someone asks: Is righteousness something acquired or something innate? Because if you say it is innate, how can a person make himself righteous? And if you say it is acquired, then that is possible?

The answer: The original state is that it is innate, ﴿the nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾ [Ar-Rum 30]. But ultimately, in its outcome and end, it becomes acquired. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "His parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1358), and Muslim (2658 / 22), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Righteousness has causes, among them what God mentioned here: reciting the verses of God, frequent prayer, belief in God and the Last Day and its realization, and enjoining good and forbidding evil.

For this reason many people today complain that they find in their hearts something of corruption. How do they fix it?

We say: Fix it by what God mentioned of these states of the People of the Book, for this is among the causes of righteousness. Therefore He said: ﴿And they are among the righteous﴾.

Keeping good company is among the causes of righteousness. Does the verse contain anything that indicates it?

Yes, because if they are enjoining good and forbidding evil, they cannot keep company with anyone from the people of evil and wrongdoing. So in the verse there is an indication of keeping company with the good, and there is no doubt that keeping good company is among the causes of righteousness.

For this reason it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he likened the righteous companion to what? To the bearer of musk.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5543), and Muslim (2628 / 146), from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] And it is related from him ﷺ that he said: "A man follows the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look at whom he befriends."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4833), al-Tirmidhi (2378), and Ahmad (8028), and the wording is Ahmad's.]]

The poet took up this meaning and said:
Do not ask about the man, but ask about his companion, For every companion follows the one he accompanies.

**Student:** Shaykh, the rule: "Failing to do a recommended act does not necessarily mean falling into what is disliked" is it a legal (fiqh) rule or a principle of jurisprudence (usul)?

**Shaykh:** This is closer (...) to fiqh.

**Student:** Were these People of the Book at the time of the Prophet ﷺ, or before the Prophet ﷺ was sent? God, glory be to Him..?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it includes those who believed in the Messenger after his mission, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others, and it includes those who were upright in the past.

**Student:** Shaykh, is it permissible for a person to go to the prayer running, for example, or rushing?

**Shaykh:** The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not hasten." He said: "When you hear the iqamah, walk to the prayer, with tranquility upon you,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (636), and Muslim (602 / 151), from Abu Hurayrah.]] then he said to Abu Bakrah, when he hurried and bowed before reaching the row: "May God increase your eagerness, but do not return to it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (783), from Abu Bakrah.]]

**Student:** Is the virtue of night prayer not derived from it?

**Shaykh:** What is derived from it is the virtue of night prayer and the recitation of the Qur'an at night.

**Student:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is a community standing (upright)...﴾: "community" (ummah) is an indefinite subject modified by an indefinite word. How is it permissible for it to be a subject?

**Shaykh:** It is permissible to begin with an indefinite noun when it conveys meaning, and when it is placed after (the predicate) it conveys meaning. If you say: "In the house there is a man," it conveys meaning; and if you say: "A noble man is in the house," it also conveys meaning. So when it is qualified or postponed, it conveys meaning.

**Student:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, while they prostrate﴾: Does this not indicate that recitation means reading, and not action, because it is specified with the night, meaning that action happens by night and by day?

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed, this favors that it is recitation as reading. But even at night a person needs his deed to conform to the Shariah. If he innovates in night prayer, it will not benefit him.

**Student:** Some books, Shaykh, mention that there is no harm in mentioning weak hadiths regarding the virtues of deeds. What is your opinion?

**Shaykh:** Some scholars permitted mentioning a weak hadith concerning the virtues of deeds, but with three conditions:
The first: that the basis of the deed be established.
The second: that the weakness not be severe.
The third: that one does not believe that the Prophet ﷺ said it.
An example of that: if someone mentions a weak hadith about the virtue of congregational prayer, the basis of the deed is established, but on condition that he does not believe the Messenger ﷺ said it, and on condition that the weakness is not severe. The common people, if you recite the hadith to them, will immediately believe that the Messenger ﷺ said it...

Some scholars tried to specify the food that Israel (Jacob) forbade upon himself. What is your opinion on this?

**Student:** The correct position is to leave it as the Qur'an came, meaning we do not specify it.

**Shaykh:** We do not specify it, because if specifying it had a benefit..

**Student:** God would have specified it.

**Shaykh:** God would have specified it. Is there a parallel to this, of something that some scholars tried to specify while it is left vague in the Qur'an?

**Student:** Yes, in: ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, to see which of them would take charge of Mary﴾ [Ali 'Imran 44]. What are the "pens" here?

**Shaykh:** No, there is no problem in specifying them.

**Student:** But some scholars said: they are arrows or..

**Shaykh:** Yes, they differed only regarding its meaning.

**Student:** The names of the People of the Cave.

**Shaykh:** Yes, the names of the People of the Cave and the color of their dog.

﴿...the House﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97]: is there a second reading of it?

**Student:** ﴿And for God, upon mankind, is the pilgrimage (ḥajj) to the House﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿ḥajju al-bayt﴾ with a fatha on the ḥā'. What does this verse indicate?

**Student:** It indicates that God, glory be to Him, obligated mankind to perform the pilgrimage to the House.

**Shaykh:** That God obligated mankind to perform the pilgrimage to the House. Is "mankind" to be taken in its generality?

**Student:** No, only the believers to whom the address is directed. This is a general term intended in a specific sense: ﴿And for God, upon mankind, is the pilgrimage (ḥijj) to the House﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97], meaning..

**Shaykh:** So then the disbeliever is not held accountable for abandoning the pilgrimage?

**Student:** No, all of mankind, but the primary intended audience is the believers. As for the disbeliever, he is held accountable for abandoning the branches of the Shariah, but the primary intention is the believers.

**Student:** Mankind in general, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** General. Even the incapable?

**Student:** The incapable no, ﴿for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97].

**Shaykh:** So this is not general in its scope; it is restricted by His saying: ﴿for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾.

What is the benefit of His mentioning the general first and then saying ﴿for whoever is able﴾? That is, why did He not say at the beginning of the statement: "For God, upon the one who is able, is the pilgrimage to the House"?

**Student:** To encourage the pilgrimage, that the pilgrimage is obligatory upon all people, to encourage it, and to show its importance. Then after that He said: some people (...).

**Shaykh:** That is, to show the importance of the pilgrimage, and then to show God's mercy by stipulating ability.

If someone says: All obligations require ability, so why did He restrict it here?

**Student:** We say: it is restricted because the pilgrimage is generally accompanied by hardship.

**Shaykh:** Yes, well said: it is generally more hardship than other acts.

* * *

**It is derived from them:** A warning against obeying the People of the Book. From where is it taken?

**Student:** His saying: ﴿They will turn you back after your belief﴾.

**Shaykh:** His saying: ﴿They will turn you back after your belief﴾, meaning God informed us of this so that we would be wary of them.

**Student:** That we not obey them.

**Shaykh:** That we not obey them, and that we be wary of them, because they are extremely eager to turn us back into disbelievers after our belief.

His saying: ﴿Be mindful of God with the mindfulness due to Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran 102]. Is this verse, on its apparent meaning, muhkam (definitive) or mansukh (abrogated)?

**Student:** The scholars differed on this. Some scholars said it is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He, in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286]. The correct view is that it is muhkam.

**Shaykh:** That it is muhkam, not abrogated.

**Student:** That is: be mindful of God to the extent you are able.

**Shaykh:** To the extent you are able.

If the scholars differ about a verse or a hadith, whether it is abrogated or not abrogated, who has the original presumption in his favor?

**Student:** The original presumption is that we reconcile the narrations.

**Shaykh:** No, who has the presumption in his favor? The one who says it is abrogated, or the one who says it is not abrogated?

**Student:** In this verse?

**Shaykh:** No, it is a general disagreement. That is, if the scholars differ about a verse or a hadith, whether it is abrogated or not abrogated, who has the presumption in his favor?

**Student:** The presumption is non-abrogation.

**Shaykh:** The presumption is with the one who says non-abrogation, correct. So since the scholars differed about this verse, whether it is abrogated or not, the original presumption is that it is not abrogated and remains muhkam.

If someone says: His saying: ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [Ali 'Imran 102]: what is the meaning of the verse?

**Student:** That is: begin from now on obeying God, glory be to Him.

**Shaykh:** That is: persist in Islam until when?

**Student:** Until you die.

**Shaykh:** Until you die. Persist in Islam until you die. Well said.

The clause: ﴿while you are Muslims﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rab)? Its place in the grammatical structure?

**Student:** The waw follows what precedes it.

**Shaykh:** No, we do not want you to analyze the waw; we want the clause: what is its place in the grammatical structure?

**Student:** "You" (antum).

**Shaykh:** What is the place in grammar of this clause in ﴿except while you are Muslims﴾?

**Student:** An exception.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed, it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause...

In two places, where are they?

**Student:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of God﴾ first, and the second place is ﴿and do not be divided﴾.

**Shaykh:** No, because holding firmly to the rope of God all together is a command to hold firmly to it.

**Student:** First ﴿and do not be divided﴾, second: ﴿so He joined your hearts﴾.

**Shaykh:** The prohibition of division explicitly.

**Student:** ﴿And do not be divided﴾.

**Shaykh:** That is one. The second?

**Student:** This verse, Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** No, with all the verses you have recited?

**Student:** ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾: what do we derive from this?

**Student:** From this we derive the prohibition of division.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and that division...?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** That is, its matter is great and momentous.

And when division is forbidden, it necessarily follows that its opposite is commanded, which is unity and togetherness.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hold firmly to the rope of God﴾: what is meant by the rope of God?

**Student:** It is the path that leads to Him.

**Shaykh:** And what is it?

**Student:** It is Islam.

**Shaykh:** Good. Why was it called a rope?

**Student:** Because it was legislated from God, glory be to Him.

**Shaykh:** No, why was "the rope of God" called a rope?

**Student:** Because it leads to God, mighty and majestic is He.

**Shaykh:** It leads to a goal. And it was attributed to God?

**Student:** Because He is the one who legislated it, glory be to Him.

**Shaykh:** And because it leads?

**Student:** To Him.

**Shaykh:** To Him.

His saying: ﴿And let there be among you a community﴾: is "min" here partitive (lit-tab'īḍ) or for origin and specification of the kind (li-ibtidā' wa bayān al-jins)?

**Student:** Partitive.

**Shaykh:** Partitive? What follows from the difference between the two opinions, since there are two opinions among the scholars? What follows from their disagreement? ﴿And let there be among you a community﴾: if we say "min" is partitive, or we say it is to specify the kind, or for origin?

**Student:** If it is partitive, that is: a group of you, from some of you.

**Shaykh:** That is, some of you, so calling to good and enjoining good and forbidding evil is a collective obligation (fard kifāyah).

And if we say it is for origin or to specify the kind?

**Student:** It is an obligation upon everyone.

**Shaykh:** It becomes an obligation upon everyone. That is: "and let you all be a community," let you all together be a community calling to good.

The well-known position among the people of knowledge is the first, that "min" is partitive, and that calling, enjoining good, and forbidding evil are collective obligations.

His saying: ﴿They will not harm you except for some annoyance﴾: is the exception here disconnected (munqaṭi') or connected (muttaṣil)?

**Student:** There is disagreement. It was said: the exception is connected, and the meaning is: "They will not harm you except with the harm of annoyance." And it was said: the exception is disconnected, and the meaning is: "They will not harm you, but they will annoy you." We preferred the latter, because harm is other than annoyance.

**Shaykh:** Yes, what is the evidence that annoyance is other than harm?

**Student:** The evidence is the saying of God, mighty and majestic, in the hadith qudsi: "The son of Adam annoys Me: he insults time, while I am time."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4826), and Muslim (2246 / 2), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

**Shaykh:** Yes.

- Student: He said in the Hadith Qudsi (a hadith in which the wording is attributed to Allah, the Exalted): "O My servants, you will never reach My harm so as to harm Me." [[Recorded by Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] So He negated harm and affirmed hurt.
- Shaykh: Yes. And what is the reality?
- Student: The reality bears witness to this.
- Shaykh: It bears witness to it. A person may be hurt by a foul smell without being harmed.

* * *

- Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing (in obedience), reciting the verses of Allah during the hours of the night while they prostrate. They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous. And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it. And Allah is Knowing of the righteous. Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them against Allah at all. And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally. The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind containing frost which strikes the crop of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ [Ali 'Imran 113–117].
- Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing (in obedience), reciting the verses of Allah during the hours of the night while they prostrate.﴾ To whom does the pronoun refer in His saying ﴿They are not all alike﴾?
- Student: To the People of the Scripture.
- Shaykh: And what is the meaning of ﴿سَوَاءً﴾ (sawaan, "alike")?
- Student: It means they are not equal.
- Shaykh: They are not equal.

His saying ﴿مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ أُمَّةٌ قَائِمَةٌ﴾ (among the People of the Scripture is a community standing): who is meant here? Are they those who embraced Islam, or those who, during the time of their prophethood, were characterized by these qualities?

- Student: It includes both; it includes all of them.
- Shaykh: That is, it includes those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who were upon the truth during the time of their messengers' mission.

His saying Exalted is He: ﴿يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ﴾ (they hasten to good deeds), and He did not say ﴿إِلَى الْخَيْرَاتِ﴾ (hasten toward the good deeds). What is the difference?

- Student: ﴿يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ﴾ means they hasten into these good deeds, so when they reach them, they continue in them.
- Shaykh: They continue in them. And if He had said ﴿إِلَى﴾ (to)?
- Student: With ﴿إِلَى﴾ (to), when they reach the good deeds they would stop there and not continue.
- Shaykh: That is, ﴿إِلَى﴾ does not indicate their continuing in hastening after reaching them.

What is the difference between this and His saying Exalted is He: ﴿وَسَارِعُوا إِلَى مَغْفِرَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord)? He said ﴿سَارِعُوا إِلَى مَغْفِرَةٍ﴾ and did not say ﴿فِي مَغْفِرَةٍ﴾ (in forgiveness)?

- Student: Because forgiveness is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, whereas with good deeds, if they were the means of entering it, then it would not be (...); forgiveness is from Allah.
- Shaykh: Yes.
- Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. It cannot be that it is a container for them, that they hasten in (...) the righteous deeds.
- Shaykh: It is an end, not a deed. In any case, the two answers are close. The difference between them is clear, because forgiveness is the goal of the deed and the fruit of the deed, unlike the deed itself, which is the vessel for a person's striving.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 113–114 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ [Al 'Imran 113]. The pronoun in ﴿They﴾ refers to the People of the Book, and ﴿alike﴾ (sawa') means equal in these attributes. Rather, among them is ﴿a community standing [upright], reciting the verses of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 113], to the end of the verse, and among them is a deviant community that does not stand upright by the command of Allah. ﴿They are not all alike﴾ means: they are not equal in disobedience, conditions and attributes. Then He clarified this by saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community standing [upright]﴾ [Al 'Imran 113].

One of the benefits of this noble verse is that the Children of Israel have transgression against the right of Allah and against the rights of the prophets and others, as shown by His saying: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾ [Al 'Imran 112].

These attributes, and the punishments that result from them, require that we take a lesson from them, and this is the important practical benefit: that we do not read them as a mere event or a historical story. We must read them in order to learn a lesson, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Certainly in their stories is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ [Al 'Imran 113]. ﴿They﴾ refers to the People of the Book, and ﴿alike﴾ (sawa') means equal, i.e., they are not equal in these attributes. Rather, among them is ﴿a community standing [upright], reciting the verses of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 113], to the end, and among them is a deviant community that does not stand upright by the command of Allah. ﴿They are not all alike﴾ means: they are not equal in disobedience, conditions and attributes.

Then He clarified this by saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community standing [upright]﴾.

His saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book﴾ refers to the Jews and the Christians, as has passed us many times. The noun is made explicit here in place of the pronoun, either because of the long separation between the explicit noun to which the pronouns refer, or because the sentence is resumed (isti'naf), since ﴿Among the People of the Book﴾ is a new sentence. ﴿Ummah﴾ means a group, ﴿standing﴾ means steadfast and upright in obedience to the command of Allah. The standing here means steadfastness and uprightness in obedience to the command of Allah, not the standing that is the opposite of sitting, since the Muslim is standing upright in the command of Allah whether he is standing, sitting or lying down.

﴿They recite the verses of Allah in the watches of the night﴾: the word ﴿standing﴾ is an adjective; the clause ﴿they recite the verses of Allah﴾ is another adjective, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (hal). There is a grammatical rule: when an indefinite noun is described, the second description may be either a circumstantial clause or an adjective. This rule holds whether the second description is a clause or a single word. So if you say: (A noble man came to me riding) it is correct, because it is a description; and if you say: (A noble man came to me riding) with the active participle, it is also correct. In this noble verse, ﴿ummah﴾ is indefinite and ﴿standing﴾ is its adjective; ﴿they recite﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, in which case the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and it may be an adjective.

﴿They recite the verses of Allah﴾: recitation (tilawah) is sometimes meant as following (ittiba'), and sometimes meant as reading (qira'ah). If the context fits both meanings, it is understood as both; if it is specific to one of them, it is specific to it. When you say: (He recited to me a verse from the Quran), the meaning is reading; and when you say: (This man recites the verses of Allah, sincerely and in worship), this may mean reading and may mean following. When it is open to both meanings, and they do not contradict each other, it is understood as both.

So His saying: ﴿They recite the verses of Allah﴾ includes reciting the words and reciting by acting upon the verses of Allah.

His saying: ﴿in the watches of the night﴾: ﴿ānā'﴾ means times, and from it comes the word nawʾ (rising of a star), referring to the time of a star's rising or to the star itself. So ﴿ānā'﴾ means times, ﴿in the watches of the night﴾ meaning the times and hours of the night.

﴿And they prostrate﴾: this clause, ﴿and they prostrate﴾, allows two possibilities: that it is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), or that it is a circumstantial clause from the waw in His saying ﴿they recite﴾, meaning they recite the verses of Allah while they are prostrating. He described them with reciting the verses of Allah, which is the best of remembrance, and with prostration, which is the best of states, because prostration is better than standing and better than bowing, since the one prostrating is closest to his Lord. But recitation of the verses is the best of the remembrances, and for this reason the standing was specified for it. So His saying ﴿they recite the verses of Allah﴾ mentions the highest attribute of speech, and ﴿and they prostrate﴾ mentions the highest attribute of action, which is prostration.

﴿They believe in Allah﴾: the clause is a resumed sentence explaining the condition of these people, and it may be an adjective of ﴿ummah﴾ or a circumstantial clause.

﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. Belief in Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, encompasses four things:
- Belief in His existence.
- Belief in His lordship.
- Belief in His divinity.
- Belief in His names and attributes.

These are all necessary. Whoever denies the existence of Allah has not believed in Him; whoever believes in Him but denies His unity in lordship has not believed in Him; whoever believes in Him and His lordship but denies that He alone is to be worshipped has not believed in Him; whoever believes in all of that but denies some of His attributes has not believed in Him. So there is no belief in Allah except with these four matters.

As for belief in the Last Day: the Last Day refers first to the Day of Resurrection. It is called the last day because there is no day after it, since it is the final end of creation, and in it there is no night and no day; it is all one day, with no sun, no moon and no stars, each in its place, either in Paradise or in the Fire. It is the last thing in which the servants will be.

It is known that the servants have four abodes: the first is in the wombs of their mothers, the second is in this world, the third is in the barzakh, and the fourth is in the Last Day, which is the final one, and for this it is called the Last Day. The Last Day includes in belief in it everything the Prophet ﷺ informed us of that will occur after death. Everything he informed of that occurs after death: so the questioning of the dead in his grave falls within belief in the Last Day, and the punishment or bliss of the grave falls within belief in the Last Day. The reason is that whoever dies, his resurrection has already begun, so what he finds in his grave is like what he finds after being raised, all of it is from the unseen matters, all of it is in the abode of recompense. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Included in belief in the Last Day is everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will occur after death."

Belief in it means that you believe in everything that came in the Book and the Sunnah concerning what occurs after death, in summary and in detail. But know that in books of admonition (wa'z) there are weak hadiths, indeed fabricated ones, concerning the conditions of the grave and the conditions of the Resurrection, which the reader should guard against. There is no better course than returning to the authentic books on this subject, so that we do not mislead people. Some preachers choose such hadiths for the sake of encouragement or warning, but the truth is that this is not a good method, because filling people's minds with weak or fabricated hadiths is an error, even if they contain encouragement or warning. What is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ is sufficient. People will take everything mentioned as authentic, saying: "What is said from the pulpit is correct."

It is obligatory upon the one who compiles on encouragement and warning to mention only what is a proof, from the sahih or the hasan; as for the weak, there is no need to mention it, because we are free of it, free of this weak material that was not established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As for His saying: ﴿and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾: this has been mentioned in this surah twice. Is it mentioned twice, or once?
* Students: Twice.
* Other students: Three times.
* The Shaykh: This is the third. I say: it has preceded (sabaq), I do not say: it has been mentioned (dhukira). It has preceded with its mention twice: enjoining right and forbidding wrong. And we mentioned at the beginning, when it passed us, its conditions and etiquettes.

﴿and they hasten in good works﴾: meaning that together with being believers and being reformers, they are also hastening in good works, i.e., they race toward good works as people race for spoils.

His saying: ﴿they hasten in (fi) good works﴾, and He did not say ﴿to (ila) good works﴾, although (sara'a) takes (ila), as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran 133]. The reason is that what is meant here is their hastening toward them and within performing them. Pay attention: the meaning is hastening toward them; when they reach them, they do not stop hastening; they hasten within them. This is the reason, and Allah knows best, why it was said ﴿they hasten in good works﴾ and not ﴿toward them﴾.

His saying: ﴿in good works﴾: (al-khayrat) is the plural of khayr or khayrah, and it is everything from which the servant benefits or which benefits others. Prayer is good, teaching people the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ is good, calling to Allah is good, and enjoining right and forbidding wrong is also good. Everything that brings one closer to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is good, and hastening in it is hastening toward it, and hastening in it is during the performance of the act.

He said: ﴿And those are among the righteous﴾. ﴿Those﴾ refers to this standing community from the People of the Book.

The scholars said: the righteous one is the one who upholds the right of Allah and the rights of the servants, and its opposite is the corrupt. Righteousness revolves around two things: knowledge and action, and its opposite is ignorance, disbelief and rebellion. Whoever is ignorant is not righteous, meaning not righteous in the sense of the highest level of righteousness; otherwise he has righteousness in proportion to his knowledge. Whoever does not act is not righteous, and he lacks righteousness in proportion to what he lacks of action.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾: (ma) is a conditional particle, and the clause ﴿they will not be denied it﴾ is the answer to the condition.

In this verse there are two readings: ﴿And whatever you do of good, you will not be denied it﴾ with the taa', and the second: ﴿And whatever they do of good, they will not be denied it﴾ with the yaa'. On the second reading with the yaa', there is no iltifat in the verse, since it follows the third-person pronoun as in the verse before it. On the reading with the taa', ﴿whatever you do﴾, there is an iltifat from the third person to the second person, and also the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ and to this community.

His saying: ﴿whatever you do of good﴾: the (min) here is explicative (bayaniyyah), because it comes after the conditional noun, and the conditional noun is an ambiguous noun that needs clarification; for this reason, whenever (min) comes after a conditional noun, it is explicative.

His saying: ﴿of good (khayr)﴾: we have already said that what is meant by good is everything that brings one closer to Allah.

His saying: ﴿they will not be denied it (fa-lan yukfaru-hu)﴾: meaning they will not be deprived of its reward. Kufr (disbelief) originally means covering, and from it comes al-kufra, and what is al-kufra? 
* Student: It is the spathe of the date palm.
* The Shaykh: It is the sheath of the spathe. The sheath of the date-palm spathe is called kufra; this kufra covers. For this reason they said that kufr originally means covering, because a person covers Allah's blessing upon him and does not show it. Blessing requires gratitude, so if it is not thanked, this is kufr.

So ﴿they will not be denied it﴾ means they will not be deprived of its reward, because if they were deprived of its reward, their doing of this good would be hidden and would have no visible effect.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the God-conscious﴾: He will reward them for their God-consciousness. God-consciousness (taqwa) has many benefits, and I think we once held a competition about it.

Specifying knowledge with the God-conscious is to encourage God-consciousness and to warn against opposing it and failing to uphold it; otherwise Allah knows everything.

Let us take the benefits of this verse:
* One of the benefits of this verse: the People of the Book are not all alike; among them is a misguided community and among them is a community standing by the command of Allah, and this is explicit in the verse: ﴿They are not all alike, of the People of the Book﴾.
* Among its benefits: the demonstration of the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He gives everyone his due right. When the blame was mentioned, the blame of the People of the Book in the previous verses, understanding might turn to think that all the People of the Book have this description: that they disbelieve in the verses of Allah, kill the prophets without right, disobey Allah and transgress against His right and the rights of His servants. So Allah said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾, meaning that among them are those who are not like that.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the People of the Book is a community (ummah), and ummah implies a gathering and a large number upon the praiseworthy and desired attribute. They mentioned that about twenty men from the Jews embraced Islam, and a large number from the Christians as well, and for this He expressed it with His saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community﴾.

Some scholars held that what is meant by the ummah here is the Muslim ummah, but this is very far-fetched, because ﴿ummah﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿of the People of the Book﴾; and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not express this community as the People of the Book. Rather He said: ﴿He named you Muslims before and in this﴾ [Al-Hajj 78]. Just as He did not express the People of the Book as believers. Every verse in which there is ﴿O you who believe﴾ is addressed to the believers in Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and every verse in which there is ﴿O People of the Book﴾ means by them the Children of Israel to whom Moses and Jesus were sent.

* One of the benefits of this verse: praise for standing in obedience to Allah and steadfastness upon it. From where is this benefit taken from the verse?
* Student: ﴿And those are among the righteous﴾.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿A standing community﴾, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: ﴿A standing community﴾ is the basis of their praise.
* One of the benefits of the verse: praise for those who recite the Book of Allah, by reading and by acting. From where do we take it?
* Student: From the saying of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community standing, reciting the verses of Allah﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They recite the verses of Allah﴾. From where did you know that reciting the Book, by reading and by acting, is praiseworthy, and that its doer is to be praised?
* Student: In Surat al-Baqarah.
* The Shaykh: No, we want from these verses.
* Student: The praise by what He described them with, which is: ﴿whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾.
* The Shaykh: Because this is the opposite of those who had the first attributes; for when He mentioned the first attributes, He said: ﴿They are not all alike﴾, then He mentioned the distinction.
* One of the benefits of the verse: the virtue of prostration?
* Student: ﴿In the watches of the night, and they prostrate﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And they prostrate﴾.
* One of the benefits of this verse: also praise for those who believe in Allah and the Last Day. From where do you take it?
* Student: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. If Allah praises a person for an attribute, is he to be blamed if he does not have it?
* Student: If this is absent, praise for him is absent.
* The Shaykh: Meaning praise is absent from him; and he may deserve blame, or may not?
* Student: He deserves blame if (...) is absent.
* The Shaykh: Meaning belief in the Last Day, there is no doubt that if it is absent, he is blamed because he is a disbeliever. But in other matters, if we praised a person for performing the Duha prayer, would that mean that if he did not pray it, he is blamed?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: So we take a rule: the absence of praise does not necessarily entail the establishment of blame.

From this a jurisprudential benefit also follows: that leaving a recommended act does not necessarily mean falling into a disliked act. If a man prayed and did not raise his hands at the takbir of the opening, do we say that this is disliked? No.

This is a useful rule: abandoning a sunnah does not necessarily mean that a person falls into what is disliked, but his reward is reduced, without doubt; yet he is not blamed, nor is it said that he has fallen into what is disliked or into something forbidden.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: praise for enjoining right and forbidding wrong?
* Student: From the verse: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾.
* The Shaykh: If someone said: why did Allah mention belief in Allah and the Last Day between the mention of reciting the verses and the mention of enjoining right and forbidding wrong? Look, He began with reciting the verses of Allah and prostration, then doubled with belief in Allah and the Last Day, and then mentioned enjoining right and forbidding wrong; so why did He place belief, which is the foundation, between the recitation of the Book and enjoining right and forbidding wrong?
* Student: Because the recitation of the verses reminds of the Last Day and establishes belief in it.

**Shaykh:** This means that faith in something is not possible except after knowledge of it, is that right? So when they recite God's verses, they know about the Last Day and then believe in it.

**Student:** Also, because it [the recitation] is a motivation, since they hope for the reward of this deed on the Last Day.

**Shaykh:** You mean that it is the goal?

**Student:** Yes.

**Student:** Do you say: the explicit mention of the recitation?

**Shaykh:** Is it possible to mention the recitation explicitly by delaying it, after he says: "They believe in God and the Last Day and recite the Book of God"?

**Student:** Placing it first and mentioning it explicitly, Shaykh.

**Another student:** Could we say: it is the general (*'amm*) being coordinated with the specific (*khass*)?

**Shaykh:** No, recitation is a deed.

In any case, what appears to me is that faith in something is not possible except after knowledge of it, and we do not know about the Last Day except after the recitation of the Book of God. But the prostration was placed before belief in the Last Day because it is linked to the recitation.

**Student:** (...) that the verses may be recited by one who believes in them and by one who does not believe in them. Some disbelievers were found to recite the verses, and the praise is not complete until they believe in them?

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, this is good. But when the context is one of praise, the intended meaning of "those who recite" becomes those who recite it with belief in it.

**From the benefits of this verse:** Praise for those who hasten to good deeds.

**Student:** ﴿And they hasten to good deeds﴾.

**Shaykh:** From His saying ﴿And they hasten to good deeds﴾.

If someone says: How can we reconcile this verse, which contains praise for hastening to good, with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When you hear the iqamah, walk to the prayer, with tranquility and dignity upon you, and do not hasten"?[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (636), and Muslim (602 / 151), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

**Student:** I say, our Shaykh: hastening to good deeds (...) with tranquility and dignity.

**Shaykh:** You mean that the meaning of "good deeds" is what the Shariah has commanded, is that right? And hurrying to the prayer is not from good, because the Prophet ﷺ forbade it. So the answer is that we say: hastening to good deeds is hastening to conform to the Shariah, is that right?

**Student:** The second interpretation: hastening in establishing the prayer itself.

**Shaykh:** In what?

**Student:** The second explanation: intending the prayer itself and hastening to it by perfecting it.

**Shaykh:** No, this is included in the general meaning, and there is no problem with it. But how did he forbid hastening to it?

**Student:** How?

**Shaykh:** I say: for example, perfecting the prayer is without doubt from hastening to good deeds and is included in the general meaning. But our question concerns the prohibition of hastening to it. So it is said: the intended meaning of hastening to good deeds is hastening to adhere to the Shariah and to act upon it.

**Student:** One who goes to the prayer calmly and with tranquility has a greater good than one who goes to it quickly, becomes preoccupied, and so becomes distracted.

**Shaykh:** Fine, this is possible. It means that the good deeds are those that agree with the Shariah, so hastening to them is to adhere to them.

**From the benefits of this verse:** Praise of these people for righteousness, by His saying ﴿And they are among the righteous﴾. Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to adhere to, or to perform, these deeds for which God praised these people from the People of the Book and commended them.

If someone asks: Is righteousness something acquired or something innate? Because if you say it is innate, how can a person make himself righteous? And if you say it is acquired, then that is possible?

The answer: The original state is that it is innate, ﴿the nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾ [Ar-Rum 30]. But ultimately, in its outcome and end, it becomes acquired. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "His parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1358), and Muslim (2658 / 22), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Righteousness has causes, among them what God mentioned here: reciting the verses of God, frequent prayer, belief in God and the Last Day and its realization, and enjoining good and forbidding evil.

For this reason many people today complain that they find in their hearts something of corruption. How do they fix it?

We say: Fix it by what God mentioned of these states of the People of the Book, for this is among the causes of righteousness. Therefore He said: ﴿And they are among the righteous﴾.

Keeping good company is among the causes of righteousness. Does the verse contain anything that indicates it?

Yes, because if they are enjoining good and forbidding evil, they cannot keep company with anyone from the people of evil and wrongdoing. So in the verse there is an indication of keeping company with the good, and there is no doubt that keeping good company is among the causes of righteousness.

For this reason it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he likened the righteous companion to what? To the bearer of musk.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5543), and Muslim (2628 / 146), from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] And it is related from him ﷺ that he said: "A man follows the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look at whom he befriends."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4833), al-Tirmidhi (2378), and Ahmad (8028), and the wording is Ahmad's.]]

The poet took up this meaning and said:
Do not ask about the man, but ask about his companion, For every companion follows the one he accompanies.

**Student:** Shaykh, the rule: "Failing to do a recommended act does not necessarily mean falling into what is disliked" is it a legal (fiqh) rule or a principle of jurisprudence (usul)?

**Shaykh:** This is closer (...) to fiqh.

**Student:** Were these People of the Book at the time of the Prophet ﷺ, or before the Prophet ﷺ was sent? God, glory be to Him..?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it includes those who believed in the Messenger after his mission, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others, and it includes those who were upright in the past.

**Student:** Shaykh, is it permissible for a person to go to the prayer running, for example, or rushing?

**Shaykh:** The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not hasten." He said: "When you hear the iqamah, walk to the prayer, with tranquility upon you,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (636), and Muslim (602 / 151), from Abu Hurayrah.]] then he said to Abu Bakrah, when he hurried and bowed before reaching the row: "May God increase your eagerness, but do not return to it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (783), from Abu Bakrah.]]

**Student:** Is the virtue of night prayer not derived from it?

**Shaykh:** What is derived from it is the virtue of night prayer and the recitation of the Qur'an at night.

**Student:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is a community standing (upright)...﴾: "community" (ummah) is an indefinite subject modified by an indefinite word. How is it permissible for it to be a subject?

**Shaykh:** It is permissible to begin with an indefinite noun when it conveys meaning, and when it is placed after (the predicate) it conveys meaning. If you say: "In the house there is a man," it conveys meaning; and if you say: "A noble man is in the house," it also conveys meaning. So when it is qualified or postponed, it conveys meaning.

**Student:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, while they prostrate﴾: Does this not indicate that recitation means reading, and not action, because it is specified with the night, meaning that action happens by night and by day?

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed, this favors that it is recitation as reading. But even at night a person needs his deed to conform to the Shariah. If he innovates in night prayer, it will not benefit him.

**Student:** Some books, Shaykh, mention that there is no harm in mentioning weak hadiths regarding the virtues of deeds. What is your opinion?

**Shaykh:** Some scholars permitted mentioning a weak hadith concerning the virtues of deeds, but with three conditions:
The first: that the basis of the deed be established.
The second: that the weakness not be severe.
The third: that one does not believe that the Prophet ﷺ said it.
An example of that: if someone mentions a weak hadith about the virtue of congregational prayer, the basis of the deed is established, but on condition that he does not believe the Messenger ﷺ said it, and on condition that the weakness is not severe. The common people, if you recite the hadith to them, will immediately believe that the Messenger ﷺ said it...

Some scholars tried to specify the food that Israel (Jacob) forbade upon himself. What is your opinion on this?

**Student:** The correct position is to leave it as the Qur'an came, meaning we do not specify it.

**Shaykh:** We do not specify it, because if specifying it had a benefit..

**Student:** God would have specified it.

**Shaykh:** God would have specified it. Is there a parallel to this, of something that some scholars tried to specify while it is left vague in the Qur'an?

**Student:** Yes, in: ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, to see which of them would take charge of Mary﴾ [Ali 'Imran 44]. What are the "pens" here?

**Shaykh:** No, there is no problem in specifying them.

**Student:** But some scholars said: they are arrows or..

**Shaykh:** Yes, they differed only regarding its meaning.

**Student:** The names of the People of the Cave.

**Shaykh:** Yes, the names of the People of the Cave and the color of their dog.

﴿...the House﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97]: is there a second reading of it?

**Student:** ﴿And for God, upon mankind, is the pilgrimage (ḥajj) to the House﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿ḥajju al-bayt﴾ with a fatha on the ḥā'. What does this verse indicate?

**Student:** It indicates that God, glory be to Him, obligated mankind to perform the pilgrimage to the House.

**Shaykh:** That God obligated mankind to perform the pilgrimage to the House. Is "mankind" to be taken in its generality?

**Student:** No, only the believers to whom the address is directed. This is a general term intended in a specific sense: ﴿And for God, upon mankind, is the pilgrimage (ḥijj) to the House﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97], meaning..

**Shaykh:** So then the disbeliever is not held accountable for abandoning the pilgrimage?

**Student:** No, all of mankind, but the primary intended audience is the believers. As for the disbeliever, he is held accountable for abandoning the branches of the Shariah, but the primary intention is the believers.

**Student:** Mankind in general, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** General. Even the incapable?

**Student:** The incapable no, ﴿for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97].

**Shaykh:** So this is not general in its scope; it is restricted by His saying: ﴿for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾.

What is the benefit of His mentioning the general first and then saying ﴿for whoever is able﴾? That is, why did He not say at the beginning of the statement: "For God, upon the one who is able, is the pilgrimage to the House"?

**Student:** To encourage the pilgrimage, that the pilgrimage is obligatory upon all people, to encourage it, and to show its importance. Then after that He said: some people (...).

**Shaykh:** That is, to show the importance of the pilgrimage, and then to show God's mercy by stipulating ability.

If someone says: All obligations require ability, so why did He restrict it here?

**Student:** We say: it is restricted because the pilgrimage is generally accompanied by hardship.

**Shaykh:** Yes, well said: it is generally more hardship than other acts.

* * *

**It is derived from them:** A warning against obeying the People of the Book. From where is it taken?

**Student:** His saying: ﴿They will turn you back after your belief﴾.

**Shaykh:** His saying: ﴿They will turn you back after your belief﴾, meaning God informed us of this so that we would be wary of them.

**Student:** That we not obey them.

**Shaykh:** That we not obey them, and that we be wary of them, because they are extremely eager to turn us back into disbelievers after our belief.

His saying: ﴿Be mindful of God with the mindfulness due to Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran 102]. Is this verse, on its apparent meaning, muhkam (definitive) or mansukh (abrogated)?

**Student:** The scholars differed on this. Some scholars said it is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He, in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286]. The correct view is that it is muhkam.

**Shaykh:** That it is muhkam, not abrogated.

**Student:** That is: be mindful of God to the extent you are able.

**Shaykh:** To the extent you are able.

If the scholars differ about a verse or a hadith, whether it is abrogated or not abrogated, who has the original presumption in his favor?

**Student:** The original presumption is that we reconcile the narrations.

**Shaykh:** No, who has the presumption in his favor? The one who says it is abrogated, or the one who says it is not abrogated?

**Student:** In this verse?

**Shaykh:** No, it is a general disagreement. That is, if the scholars differ about a verse or a hadith, whether it is abrogated or not abrogated, who has the presumption in his favor?

**Student:** The presumption is non-abrogation.

**Shaykh:** The presumption is with the one who says non-abrogation, correct. So since the scholars differed about this verse, whether it is abrogated or not, the original presumption is that it is not abrogated and remains muhkam.

If someone says: His saying: ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [Ali 'Imran 102]: what is the meaning of the verse?

**Student:** That is: begin from now on obeying God, glory be to Him.

**Shaykh:** That is: persist in Islam until when?

**Student:** Until you die.

**Shaykh:** Until you die. Persist in Islam until you die. Well said.

The clause: ﴿while you are Muslims﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rab)? Its place in the grammatical structure?

**Student:** The waw follows what precedes it.

**Shaykh:** No, we do not want you to analyze the waw; we want the clause: what is its place in the grammatical structure?

**Student:** "You" (antum).

**Shaykh:** What is the place in grammar of this clause in ﴿except while you are Muslims﴾?

**Student:** An exception.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed, it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause...

In two places, where are they?

**Student:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of God﴾ first, and the second place is ﴿and do not be divided﴾.

**Shaykh:** No, because holding firmly to the rope of God all together is a command to hold firmly to it.

**Student:** First ﴿and do not be divided﴾, second: ﴿so He joined your hearts﴾.

**Shaykh:** The prohibition of division explicitly.

**Student:** ﴿And do not be divided﴾.

**Shaykh:** That is one. The second?

**Student:** This verse, Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** No, with all the verses you have recited?

**Student:** ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾: what do we derive from this?

**Student:** From this we derive the prohibition of division.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and that division...?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** That is, its matter is great and momentous.

And when division is forbidden, it necessarily follows that its opposite is commanded, which is unity and togetherness.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hold firmly to the rope of God﴾: what is meant by the rope of God?

**Student:** It is the path that leads to Him.

**Shaykh:** And what is it?

**Student:** It is Islam.

**Shaykh:** Good. Why was it called a rope?

**Student:** Because it was legislated from God, glory be to Him.

**Shaykh:** No, why was "the rope of God" called a rope?

**Student:** Because it leads to God, mighty and majestic is He.

**Shaykh:** It leads to a goal. And it was attributed to God?

**Student:** Because He is the one who legislated it, glory be to Him.

**Shaykh:** And because it leads?

**Student:** To Him.

**Shaykh:** To Him.

His saying: ﴿And let there be among you a community﴾: is "min" here partitive (lit-tab'īḍ) or for origin and specification of the kind (li-ibtidā' wa bayān al-jins)?

**Student:** Partitive.

**Shaykh:** Partitive? What follows from the difference between the two opinions, since there are two opinions among the scholars? What follows from their disagreement? ﴿And let there be among you a community﴾: if we say "min" is partitive, or we say it is to specify the kind, or for origin?

**Student:** If it is partitive, that is: a group of you, from some of you.

**Shaykh:** That is, some of you, so calling to good and enjoining good and forbidding evil is a collective obligation (fard kifāyah).

And if we say it is for origin or to specify the kind?

**Student:** It is an obligation upon everyone.

**Shaykh:** It becomes an obligation upon everyone. That is: "and let you all be a community," let you all together be a community calling to good.

The well-known position among the people of knowledge is the first, that "min" is partitive, and that calling, enjoining good, and forbidding evil are collective obligations.

His saying: ﴿They will not harm you except for some annoyance﴾: is the exception here disconnected (munqaṭi') or connected (muttaṣil)?

**Student:** There is disagreement. It was said: the exception is connected, and the meaning is: "They will not harm you except with the harm of annoyance." And it was said: the exception is disconnected, and the meaning is: "They will not harm you, but they will annoy you." We preferred the latter, because harm is other than annoyance.

**Shaykh:** Yes, what is the evidence that annoyance is other than harm?

**Student:** The evidence is the saying of God, mighty and majestic, in the hadith qudsi: "The son of Adam annoys Me: he insults time, while I am time."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4826), and Muslim (2246 / 2), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

**Shaykh:** Yes.

- Student: He said in the Hadith Qudsi (a hadith in which the wording is attributed to Allah, the Exalted): "O My servants, you will never reach My harm so as to harm Me." [[Recorded by Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]] So He negated harm and affirmed hurt.
- Shaykh: Yes. And what is the reality?
- Student: The reality bears witness to this.
- Shaykh: It bears witness to it. A person may be hurt by a foul smell without being harmed.

* * *

- Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing (in obedience), reciting the verses of Allah during the hours of the night while they prostrate. They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous. And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it. And Allah is Knowing of the righteous. Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them against Allah at all. And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally. The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind containing frost which strikes the crop of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ [Ali 'Imran 113–117].
- Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing (in obedience), reciting the verses of Allah during the hours of the night while they prostrate.﴾ To whom does the pronoun refer in His saying ﴿They are not all alike﴾?
- Student: To the People of the Scripture.
- Shaykh: And what is the meaning of ﴿سَوَاءً﴾ (sawaan, "alike")?
- Student: It means they are not equal.
- Shaykh: They are not equal.

His saying ﴿مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ أُمَّةٌ قَائِمَةٌ﴾ (among the People of the Scripture is a community standing): who is meant here? Are they those who embraced Islam, or those who, during the time of their prophethood, were characterized by these qualities?

- Student: It includes both; it includes all of them.
- Shaykh: That is, it includes those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who were upon the truth during the time of their messengers' mission.

His saying Exalted is He: ﴿يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ﴾ (they hasten to good deeds), and He did not say ﴿إِلَى الْخَيْرَاتِ﴾ (hasten toward the good deeds). What is the difference?

- Student: ﴿يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ﴾ means they hasten into these good deeds, so when they reach them, they continue in them.
- Shaykh: They continue in them. And if He had said ﴿إِلَى﴾ (to)?
- Student: With ﴿إِلَى﴾ (to), when they reach the good deeds they would stop there and not continue.
- Shaykh: That is, ﴿إِلَى﴾ does not indicate their continuing in hastening after reaching them.

What is the difference between this and His saying Exalted is He: ﴿وَسَارِعُوا إِلَى مَغْفِرَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord)? He said ﴿سَارِعُوا إِلَى مَغْفِرَةٍ﴾ and did not say ﴿فِي مَغْفِرَةٍ﴾ (in forgiveness)?

- Student: Because forgiveness is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, whereas with good deeds, if they were the means of entering it, then it would not be (...); forgiveness is from Allah.
- Shaykh: Yes.
- Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. It cannot be that it is a container for them, that they hasten in (...) the righteous deeds.
- Shaykh: It is an end, not a deed. In any case, the two answers are close. The difference between them is clear, because forgiveness is the goal of the deed and the fruit of the deed, unlike the deed itself, which is the vessel for a person's striving.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 115:

His words: ﴿And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them﴾. There are two readings here. What are they?

Student: ﴿And whatever good they do﴾ and ﴿And whatever good you do﴾.

* The Shaykh: Complete the verse: ﴿And whatever good they do﴾.

* The student: ﴿So it will not be denied them﴾.

* The Shaykh: Or?

* The student: ﴿And whatever good you do, so it will not be denied you﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿So it will not be denied you﴾. What is the difference between the two readings?

* The student: The first reading, ﴿whatever good they do﴾, cannot be a shift (iltifat), because it is in the third person (ghayb).

* The Shaykh: But to whom does the pronoun refer in this reading?

* The student: To the People of the Book.

* The Shaykh: To the People of the Book.

* The student: To the People of the Book. ﴿And whatever good you do﴾ with the letter ta, is the nation of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and it contains an iltifat, because the pronoun is in the second person (khitab).

* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of his words: ﴿So it will not be denied them﴾?

* Student: It will not be diminished or reduced in their reward for it.

* The Shaykh: That is, it will not be withheld from them?

* The student: Yes indeed (...).

* The Shaykh: His exalted words: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the God-fearing﴾. Is Allah's knowledge specific to the God-fearing, or comprehensive?

* Student: Comprehensive.

* The Shaykh: But why did He restrict it to the God-fearing?

* The student: I say: for added care for them.

* The Shaykh: Care for them, or what?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: What do you all say?

* Student: Encouragement to piety (taqwa).

* The Shaykh: Yes, encouragement to piety, and care for them, that He will not waste the reward of their piety.

* Student: Shaykh, ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the God-fearing﴾ means it would be a response to the Jews, who thought they were the God-fearing and were upon the truth. He said: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the God-fearing﴾, meaning a rebuttal to them. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the God-fearing﴾?

* The Shaykh: This is according to the reading with the ya, yes, it can have this meaning too.

* From the benefits of this verse: His exalted words: ﴿And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them﴾. Among its benefits: whoever does good is rewarded for it, because the negation here means full affirmation, that is, they will be given their reward in full, without any deficiency.

* Among its benefits: the perfection of Allah's justice, the Mighty and Majestic; for the doer, if he does a deed, is rewarded for it, and if he were held to account for the blessings Allah has given him, he would perish. Rather, he is rewarded, and Allah's blessings upon him are merely a bounty from Allah.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, from His words: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the God-fearing﴾.

* Among its benefits: praise of the people of taqwa (God-consciousness). Taqwa is mentioned in the Noble Qur'an in varied and numerous ways: as a command, as praise of its people, and as an explanation of its fruits: ﴿O you who believe, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you﴾ [al-Anfal 29].

* Among its benefits: the establishment of reward for doing good, whether little or much, from His words: ﴿of good﴾, and it is in the context of a conditional, so it is general.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 116–117 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all.﴾ [Al 'Imran 116]. His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ includes everyone who disbelieves in Allah, whether a Jew, a Christian, a communist, a materialist (dahri), or a Muslim who apostatises. The essential point is that whoever disbelieves in Allah, this is his ruling.

The scholars have mentioned that disbelief (kufr) is of two kinds: disbelief that expels one from the religion (millah), and disbelief that does not expel one from the religion. To this belongs the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding the words of Allah, ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]: he said, «It is a disbelief short of disbelief» [[Tafsir 'Abd al-Razzaq (717), and al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak (3258).]].

Among the examples of this type, meaning the disbelief that does not expel one from the religion, is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Insulting a Muslim is depravity (fusuq), and fighting him is disbelief» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (48) and Muslim (64 / 116), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]. The fighting of a Muslim is not disbelief in the sense of expelling one from the religion; rather, it is disbelief short of disbelief, because no one proceeds to kill a Muslim except a disbeliever. So when a Muslim proceeds to kill his Muslim brother, he has committed one of the characteristics of disbelief.

The proof that fighting a Muslim is not disbelief that expels from the religion is the saying of Allah: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah﴾ [al-Hujurat 9], up to His saying: ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your two brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat 10].

From this is His saying ﷺ: «Two things among people are disbelief in them: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead» [[Narrated by Muslim (67 / 121), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. There are other examples. The essential point is that this is a lesser disbelief that does not take one out of Islam.

As for the greater disbelief, it is the disbelief that takes one out of Islam, such as the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding therein eternally. They are the worst of creatures﴾ [al-Bayyinah 6].

Here Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾. Is what is meant by it the lesser disbelief, by which a person is not expelled from the religion, or the greater?

The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that what is meant is the greater, because of His saying: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ [Al 'Imran 116]. The companions of the Fire are none other than the disbelievers in the greater sense, because the companion of a thing is the one who is constantly attached to it, and whoever disbelieves with the lesser disbelief will not be constantly attached to the Fire; rather, he must eventually leave it.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all﴾ means: they will not repel from them anything of the punishment of Allah if Allah intends harm for them. Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah intends for a people misfortune, there is no repelling it﴾ [al-Ra'd 11]. At that point we say: His saying ﴿will not avail﴾ means will not prevent and will not repel; they are powerless to prevent what Allah wills and to lift it.

His saying: ﴿their wealth, nor their children, against Allah at all﴾: wealth is mentioned because a person ransoms himself with wealth in times of distress. If someone seized a person and wished to imprison him, kill him, or violate his honour, and the person said to him, "Leave me, I will give you whatever you want of money, take whatever you wish of my wealth," then wealth would avail him in that situation. As for children, how do they avail a person? Because children defend their fathers and mothers, and they are the most zealous of people in defending them. Children are the most zealous in defending their fathers and mothers. A person cannot allow his enemy to assault his mother or father while he is alive. Therefore He said: ﴿nor their children﴾, because children are the ones who defend their fathers and mothers.

﴿against Allah at all﴾: (shay'an) is an indefinite noun in a context of negation. Where is the negation? ﴿will not avail﴾.

The jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun) said: An indefinite noun in a context of negation conveys generality, i.e., whatever thing it may be, whether that thing is great or small.

He said: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾. So in this world their wealth and their children do not avail them anything, and in the Hereafter likewise: they are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein eternally.

The Fire is well known; it is that hot substance. But the heat of the Fire in the Hereafter is not like the heat of the fire in this world. It has been given precedence over the heat of the fire of this world by sixty-nine parts, may Allah grant us safety. So if you now estimate the greatest of the fires in this world in heat, the Fire of Hell is more intense than it, meaning it exceeds it by sixty-nine parts. So if we take the base and the addition together, it becomes seventy: its heat is seventy times the heat of the fire of this world.

His saying: ﴿companions of the Fire﴾ means its inhabitants who are constantly attached to it, and ﴿they will abide therein eternally﴾ means they will remain.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said, explaining that their wealth does not avail them anything and does not benefit them: ﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like the example of a wind containing frost which strikes the crops of a people who wronged themselves and destroys them﴾. This is a parable or a figurative comparison (tashbih tamthili). The rhetoricians say that comparison is of two kinds: a single comparison (tashbih ifradi), such as when you say: "So-and-so is like the sea," "So-and-so is like a lion"; and a figurative comparison (tashbih tamthili), meaning that a state is compared to a state, where the thing compared is composed of several elements and the thing compared to is likewise composed of several elements. This is called by the rhetoricians a figurative comparison, and the former a single comparison.

﴿like the example of a wind containing frost which strikes the crops of a people who wronged themselves﴾. The image now: a severe wind with great coldness, and with it a crackling sound from its intensity. ﴿Strikes the crops of a people who wronged﴾: so the comparison is composed of a severe, cold wind striking the crops of a people, meaning the striker and the struck. ﴿The crops of a people﴾ means their produce. ﴿Who wronged themselves﴾ means they deserved that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, punish them with this wind. ﴿And destroys it﴾: so when a violent, cold, strong wind blows as retribution upon the children of Adam, it will surely destroy this crop.

The point of resemblance is clear: they were given great power over their wealth, but they did not benefit from this power; it became as dust, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to averted from the way of Allah. They will spend it, and then it will be a regret for them; then they will be overcome﴾ [al-Anfal 36]. This is the state of the disbelievers: when they spend their wealth, they will not benefit from it at all. ﴿Like the example of a wind containing frost which strikes the crops of a people who wronged themselves and destroys them﴾.
