As for His saying ﴿or wrong themselves⟩, someone may say: how can it be conceived that a person wrongs himself? A person repels wrong from himself, so how does he wrong himself?!

The answer to this is that we say: whoever opposes the command of Allah by committing a forbidden act or abandoning an obligatory duty has wronged himself. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has certainly wronged himself⟩ [at-Talaq 1]. Why? Because the self is a trust (amanah) in your hands, and it is obligatory upon you to safeguard it, and Allah has enjoined you regarding it, saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves⟩ [an-Nisa' 29].

And He said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them, four are sacred. That is the correct religion, so do not wrong yourselves therein⟩ [at-Tawba 36]. Thus Allah forbade the killing of the self and the wronging of the self, because it is a trust in your hands.

Incidentally, the scholars said: Allah is more merciful to you than your father, your child, and yourself. What is the evidence? As for His being more merciful to you than your father, Allah said: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children⟩ [an-Nisa' 11]. So He enjoined fathers and mothers concerning whom? Concerning the children. Therefore He is more merciful to them than their fathers and mothers. As for the reverse, that He is more merciful to you than your children, He said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man regarding his parents⟩ [al-'Ankabut 8]. As for His being more merciful to you than yourself, it is because Allah said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves⟩ [an-Nisa' 29] and ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands⟩ [al-Baqara 195]. So we say: the reason a person is one who wrongs himself is that his self is a trust in his hands. If he neglects this trust by plunging himself into what Allah has forbidden him, or lags behind what Allah has made obligatory upon him, then he has wronged his self. The wronging of the self is in reality also a wronging of the rights of others, because wronging the self is either in a right related to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or in a right related to the creature. If it is in the right of Allah, you are a wrongdoer toward Allah; if it is in the right of the creature, you are a wrongdoer toward the creature. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The delay of the wealthy in paying a debt is an injustice" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2287) and Muslim (1564/33) from Abu Hurayra]. From this we know that whoever wrongs himself has wronged three parties: he has wronged himself, he has wronged the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and he has wronged the creature, because all of these relate to the commands and prohibitions of Allah.

﴿They remembered Allah⟩. With what do they remember Allah? With the tongue, with the limbs, with the heart, or with all of them?
* Students: With all of them.
* The Shaykh: With all of them. They remember Allah with all of them. As for remembering Allah with the heart: when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, they remember the greatness of Allah and what He has prepared for the disobedient of punishment, and they also remember the mercy of Allah and what He has prepared for the obedient of reward. Pay attention, brothers: this is remembrance with the heart. If they remember Allah in the first sense, remembering His greatness, they fear His punishment and remain upright in His religion out of flight from His punishment. If they remember Allah in the second sense, remembering His mercy and reward, they remain upright in His Sharia seeking to attain to Him. So the first remembrance is from the aspect of fleeing, and the second is from the aspect of seeking. Worship driven by seeking, or the worshipper driven by seeking, is higher in state than the worshipper driven by fleeing. They said: because the seeker is sincere both in the absence of the sought and in its presence, while the fleer is sincere in the presence of the feared, but in its absence he is not concerned. This may be derived from the saying of the Messenger ﷺ: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), the wording is his, and Muslim (9/5) from Abu Hurayra]. So remembrance with the heart occurs in two ways. The first is: remembrance of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His punishment, so one remains upright in His Sharia out of fleeing from His punishment. The second is: remembrance of the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, His grace, His favor, and His great reward, so one remains upright in His Sharia out of seeking His reward and hoping for it.

Remembrance of Allah by the tongue may refer to a specific remembrance, such as "There is no god but Allah," as is reported that the Devil said: "I destroyed the children of Adam through sins, and they destroyed me through 'There is no god but Allah' and seeking forgiveness" [Narrated by Abu Ya'la (136) and al-Tabarani in ad-Du'a' (1780) from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq]. Remembrance of Allah is undoubtedly among the causes of the forgiveness of sins. So they remember Allah with their tongues, saying "There is no god but Allah," and they utter the word of sincerity; when a person says it sincerely, Allah forgives him. Likewise, remembrance of Allah with the tongue through seeking forgiveness: "O Allah, forgive me," or "I seek Allah's forgiveness," or what is similar to that. When they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, they remember Allah by seeking forgiveness: "O Allah, forgive me," or "I ask Allah's forgiveness," or the like.

Remembrance by action is that they do what expiates these sins and transgressions, and among that is charity (sadaqa). The Prophet ﷺ said: "Charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire" [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (614) from Ka'b ibn 'Ujra]. Likewise prayer: when a person performs wudu' and completes it well, then prays two rak'at without letting his mind wander in them, Allah forgives him what preceded of his sins. Thus remembrance encompasses...
* A student: Remembrance encompasses, first, remembering Allah with the tongue; first, remembrance of the heart, which has two kinds.
* The Shaykh: With the heart. And the second?
* The student: With the tongue.
* The Shaykh: And the third?
* The student: With the limbs.
* The Shaykh: And remembrance with the heart has two aspects.

﴿They remembered Allah and sought forgiveness for their sins⟩. The "fa" (fa') here indicates sequence and immediacy: meaning, when they remember Allah, they seek forgiveness for their sins, that is, they ask Allah, glorified and exalted, to forgive their sins. It has been mentioned to us many times that forgiveness (maghfira) means covering the sin and overlooking it. As for His saying ﴿for their sins⟩: the sins (dhunub) are acts of disobedience and sinful transgressions, so they ask Allah, Exalted, to forgive them these acts of disobedience and transgressions. When a person seeks forgiveness from his Lord with a sincere intention and with dependence upon Him, Allah, Exalted, forgives him. For this reason He said: ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?⟩. Here "man" (man) is an interrogative particle, not a conditional particle. The evidence that it is an interrogative and not a conditional is that the verb after it is marfu' (nominative): ﴿and who forgives⟩. Then the particle of affirmation came after it, which is "illa" (except). Based on this, we say: "man" is an interrogative with the meaning of negation, and what shows it has the meaning of negation is the affirmation that follows it: ﴿except Allah⟩.

If someone says: what is the benefit of expressing negation in the form of a question? Why was the verse not "and none forgives sins except Allah," as in the hadith of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, which the Prophet ﷺ taught him, where he said: "O Allah, I have wronged myself greatly, and none forgives sins except You"?

The point we want is His saying: "and none forgives sins," and this verse came in His saying: ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?⟩. We say: because negation in the form of a question is more emphatic than bare negation. Why? Because when negation comes in the form of a question, it becomes imbued with a challenge, as if the questioner were saying: bring me so-and-so; bring me someone who forgives sins except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus the question here indicates negation imbued with challenge.

﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?⟩: "except Allah" is in the nominative case (marfu') even though it comes after "illa", because the statement is unrestricted (mufarragh). What is meant by unrestricted? The unrestricted exception is one in which the excepted-from element (mustathna minhu) is not mentioned. That is the unrestricted exception. Is that clear? If you say: "None stood except Zayd," the exception here is unrestricted, why? Because the excepted-from element is not mentioned. If you say: "No one stood except Zayd," this is not unrestricted, because the excepted-from element was mentioned. If you say: "I did not see except Zayd," it is unrestricted, why? Because the excepted-from element is not mentioned. If you say: "I did not see anyone except Zayd," this is not unrestricted. Here: ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?⟩.
* Students: Unrestricted.
* The Shaykh: Unrestricted? How? If he said... "the sins that exist"? They are not the excepted-from element; the sins exist, but here the sins are the object of the action, and the one who forgives is the one from whom the action proceeds.

﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?⟩ means no one forgives sins except Allah. Even if all creation sought forgiveness from you for your sin, it would not benefit you. For example, if you went to everyone in the mosque and said: "I seek your forgiveness for the sin I committed." Would their forgiveness be of any use? Suppose a man committed a forbidden offense in the mosque that harmed the worshippers, and came and said: "O worshippers, I ask your forgiveness for what I did." Could they forgive him?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What relates to them, they may forgive him for what relates to them. But the root of the sin, they cannot forgive him, because Allah says: ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?⟩.

He said: ﴿And they did not persist in what they had done while they knew⟩ [Ali 'Imran 135]. His saying ﴿and they did not persist⟩ is conjoined to His saying ﴿they remembered Allah and sought forgiveness for their sins⟩, upon His saying ﴿and sought forgiveness for their sins⟩.
﴿And they did not persist⟩ is conjoined to His saying ﴿and sought forgiveness⟩.
﴿And they did not persist in what they had done⟩: ﴿yusirru⟩ means they continue upon what they did and remain upon it, because one who seeks forgiveness cannot persist. How can you say, "O Allah, forgive me," while you are persisting in your disobedience? That is mockery and derision. For this reason He said: ﴿And they did not persist in what they had done⟩. What they had done: from the indecency and the wronging of the self. ﴿And they knew⟩. His saying ﴿and they knew⟩ may be a resumptive clause: it means that they know the gravity of sins and the greatness of the One they disobeyed, and therefore they do not persist in what they did. It may also be that the waw is circumstantial (hal): meaning, and they did not persist in what they did while knowing that persistence in sin does not bring forgiveness, or while knowing that this is a sin; so if a sin occurs from them and they persist in it, they do not know it is a sin. As long as the verse can bear these three possibilities, we say, according to the principle: that it is to be understood as all of them. Whatever meaning the verse can bear without contradiction among the meanings, it must be understood as all of them. If the meanings contradict or conflict, then one seeks the preponderant meaning (murajjih), because it is impossible to take the speech as both a thing and its opposite; then we seek the preponderance. This is the principle.

This verse contains benefits. * Among its benefits: the one who is God-conscious (muttaqi) is not immune from committing an indecency or wronging himself, because Allah did not say, "They do not commit indecencies or wrong themselves," but said: ﴿And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves⟩. Thus committing an indecency does not nullify piety if a person seeks forgiveness and repents. There has come in a hadith from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "Every son of Adam is a sinner, and the best of sinners are those who repent often" [al-Tirmidhi (2499) and Ibn Majah (4251), wording his, from Anas ibn Malik]. It is also authentically reported that he, peace be upon him, said: "If you did not sin, Allah would take you away and bring a people who sin, then seek Allah's forgiveness, and He forgives them" [Muslim (2749/11) from Abu Hurayra].

So the matter is not that a person never commits disobedience; every person must disobey. The matter is that when he commits disobedience, he returns to Allah.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: sins are divided into two kinds: indecencies and what is below them, by His saying ﴿And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves⟩, and "or" here is for classification. It is agreed among the scholars that sins are divided into minor sins and major sins. But what is the criterion for major and minor sins?

Some scholars say that the major sins are enumerable, so they enumerate them, saying: the first major sin, the second major sin, the tenth major sin, until they reach what their knowledge has attained of major sins. Others say that the major sins are bounded (mahdudah), not enumerated, and "bounded" means defined by a description rather than by a number. They said, for example: whatever has a prescribed punishment (hadd) in this world is a major sin, such as adultery, theft, and slander. Whatever has a curse attached to it is a major sin, such as: "Allah curses whoever shelters an innovator" [Muslim (1978/43) from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib], "Allah curses the one who gives bribes and the one who takes them" [al-Tirmidhi (1336) and Ahmad (9023), wording his, from Abu Hurayra], and what is similar to these. Whatever has anger attached to it is a major sin, like...?
* Students: ﴿And Allah became angry with him and cursed him⟩.

Shaykh: Like His saying, Exalted is He, concerning the killer: ﴿And Allah is angry with him﴾ [an-Nisa 93]. It entails a threat in the Hereafter, or a text stating that whoever does such-and-such will be in the Fire, or something similar, such as: "Whatever is below the ankles is in the Fire"[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (5787) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Some scholars said, and I saw it in the words of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: every sin for which a specific punishment is prescribed, whether a specific punishment in this world or in the Hereafter, is a major sin (kabira), and whatever prohibition came without mention of a punishment is a minor sin (saghira). So he said, for example: deceit is among the major sins, because the Lawgiver assigned it a specific punishment: "Whoever deceives is not of us"[[Recorded by Muslim (102) and al-Tirmidhi (1315), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Harming one's neighbour is a major sin, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him not harm his neighbour"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5185) and Muslim (47 / 75), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

What Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, defined includes a great many sins. But there is no doubt that his statement does not mean that these major sins are all at one level. Rather, even among the major sins there are greater and lesser ones, as in the sound hadith: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2654) and Muslim (87 / 143), from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]]. Accordingly we say: sins are divided into minor sins and major sins, as derived from this verse. Then the major sins vary in rank according to the corruptions and sins that follow from them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a person is entrusted with (responsible for) himself.

* Student: Shaving the beard (...)?
* Shaykh: Persisting in it makes it a major sin.
* Student: No..
* Shaykh: No, once only, it is not..
* Student: Imitating the Jews and the Christians.
* Shaykh: Complete the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the example. قام (qāma): a past-tense verb built on...
* Student: قام is a past-tense verb built on the fatha.
* Shaykh: And زيد (Zayd)?
* Student: زيد: a predicate (khabar).
* Shaykh: What is Zayd doing now when you say قام زيد? What is he doing? He is standing, so he is the doer (fa'il), a subject in the nominative case. What is the sign of its nominative case?
* Student: The fatha.
* Shaykh: Does the nominative come with a fatha?!
* Student: قام زيد, with the damma, built (mabni)...
* Shaykh: The sign of its nominative case is a visible damma at its end.
If you say قام زيدًا, is it correct?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: Why? Because he is the doer, and the doer must be in the nominative case. Good.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿Those – their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; and excellent is the reward of the workers. (136) Routes have already passed before you, so travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers. (137) This is a clarification for mankind and a guidance and instruction for the righteous. (138) So do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are believers. (139) If a wound has touched you, a wound has already touched the people like it. And these days We alternate among the people so that Allah may give knowledge of those who believe and take from among you martyrs – and Allah does not love the wrongdoers. (140)﴾ [Al 'Imran 136–140].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Those – their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; and excellent is the reward of the workers.﴾
The ones referred to are those of the earlier mentioned righteous, who are characterized by the attributes you heard before, among them that ﴿when they commit an immoral act or wrong themselves, they remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾. We have mentioned the explanation of this verse and what can be derived from it, or some of what can be derived from it. Among that: * among its benefits is the quick awareness of these people when committing sins, as in His saying: ﴿when they commit an immoral act or wrong themselves, they remember Allah﴾, so they hasten to repentance. Hastening to repentance is one of the attributes of the righteous. Is it obligatory?
The answer: Yes, hastening to repentance is obligatory, because repentance is not accepted once the appointed time (death) arrives, and a person does not know when his appointed time will come. Therefore, a person must repent from his sins immediately, without delay.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: sins are divided into two types: immoral acts (fawahish) and what is less than them.
* Among the benefits of this verse: remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a cause of repentance and returning to Allah, as in His saying: ﴿they remembered Allah﴾. We have already explained the aspects of this remembrance. What are they?
* Student: Remembrance by the heart, remembrance by the tongue, and remembrance by action.
* Shaykh: By the limbs? Yes.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: they hasten to repentance. And it has already been mentioned: the seeking of forgiveness by these righteous people for their sins, as in His saying: ﴿and sought forgiveness for their sins﴾. From this is derived, or follows from this benefit: the incapacity of those people who say, "Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," and do not seek forgiveness from Allah. Some sinners, when you forbid them from a sin, say, "Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," yet they themselves do not seek forgiveness. If these noble people seek forgiveness from their Lord, and if Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to seek forgiveness, then what of those below him? Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Ghafir 55] ﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah; indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa 106].
* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: no one can forgive sins except Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?﴾
It follows from this: you should not rely on anyone for the forgiveness of sins or for seeking forgiveness; rather your direction should be towards whom? Towards Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among its benefits: these noble righteous people do not persist in what they did of immoral acts or wronging themselves while they know.
* Among its benefits: if a man sins and seeks forgiveness, then sins and seeks forgiveness, then sins and seeks forgiveness, he will be forgiven even if the sin is repeated from him. This is because Allah said here: ﴿and they did not persist in what they did﴾, and He did not say: "and they did not repeat what they did." They did not persist in it while knowing. If a person, whenever he sins, seeks forgiveness, he will be forgiven, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins"﴾ [az-Zumar 53]. However, his seeking forgiveness must not be with his tongue while his heart is set on returning (to sin). If it is so, this seeking of forgiveness benefits him not. Rather, his seeking of forgiveness must be genuinely with his heart and tongue. A person is a human being, and his self may overpower him in the future so that he commits the disobedience even though he has sought forgiveness for it. So we say: however much you do, and however often the sin recurs from you, as long as you keep seeking forgiveness, Allah, Exalted is He, will forgive you.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a rebuke of the one who persists in sin while knowing of it, as in His saying: ﴿and they did not persist in what they did while they knew﴾. For this reason the scholars said: persisting in a minor sin makes it a major sin, because his persistence in it indicates his indifference towards the One he disobeyed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 136 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those—their reward is forgiveness﴾. "Those" (ulā'ika) here contains a demonstrative and an address. The demonstrative is taken from the word (ulā'), and the address is the kaf in (ulā'ika). We must know, from the standpoint of the Arabic language, that the demonstrative noun agrees with the thing pointed to, but the kaf of address agrees with whom? With the one addressed. Then, if it agrees with the one addressed, does it remain singular, fixed and built on fatha? Or does it agree with the one addressed in masculine and feminine, dual and plural, singular? Or is it fatha for the masculine in all cases, even if plural or dual, and kasra for the feminine in all cases, even if plural or dual?

On this there are three dialects of the Arabs:

The first: that it is always fixed with fatha, on the grounds that the addressee is treated as a generic noun. So when you say (dhalika), addressing two people, the meaning is that you address them by the generic category of males, or by the generic category of person.

The second: that it is fatha for the masculine in all cases and kasra for the feminine in all cases. And what is meant by "in all cases"? In the dual, the plural and the singular.

The third, which is the most eloquent: that it agrees with the one addressed in every case. If he is a single masculine addressee, it is with fatha, singular. If it is dual, it takes the dual form. If it is a group of males, it takes the mim attached to it; a group of females takes the nun attached to it.

﴿She said: "That is the one about whom you blamed me"﴾ [Yusuf 32], because she is addressing a group of women. ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾ [Yusuf 37], addressing two. ﴿That is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 54], addressing a group of males. This is the most eloquent usage. Here He says: ﴿Those—their reward is forgiveness﴾. "Those": the address is to whom? To one person; that is, "those, O addressee." So the address is to one, and the demonstrative refers to a plural; that is, "those, the God-fearing, O addressee." ﴿Their reward﴾, i.e., their reward and recompense for their deeds. ﴿Forgiveness from their Lord﴾, by which deliverance from the Fire is attained. ﴿And gardens﴾, by which the attainment of what is sought is achieved in the gardens of bliss. ﴿Forgiveness from their Lord﴾, i.e., pardon and overlooking of sins and concealment from the creation. ﴿And gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: "gardens" is plural, because Paradise has many levels and varied dwellings, in which people differ according to their deeds. The Prophet ﷺ informed us that the people of Paradise see the upper chambers as you see the bright star that is far off in the horizon. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, those are the dwellings of the Prophets, which no one else can attain." He said: "Yes, by the One in whose hand is my soul, [they are for] men who believed in Allah and affirmed the Messengers."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3256) and Muslim (2831/11) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] O Allah, make us among them. These dwellings are where people differ; the people of Paradise see them as we see the bright, shining star that is far off in the horizon, not directly overhead but distant. They are levels, and therefore they are in the plural. The highest of them is al-Firdaws, because above it is the Throne of Allah, Majestic is His majesty; it is the center of Paradise and its highest part, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth.

﴿And gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Allah described them as gardens because in them are kinds of bliss that do not occur to the mind, so it is an abode which a human being cannot fully grasp in its reality and essence, for it is greater than our imagination can encompass. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah 17]. And Allah the Exalted said in the Hadith Qudsi: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3244) and Muslim (2824/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

As for His saying: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, the scholars said: "beneath" means beneath its palaces and trees, not beneath its ground; for if it were beneath the ground, they would be at the bottom of a pit. Rather, they walk on the surface of the land of Paradise, but they are beneath the palaces and trees. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾. It has been reported in a hadith that these rivers flow without a trench and without digging. On this Ibn al-Qayyim said in his Nuniyyah:

Its rivers flow without a trench,
Glory be to the One who holds them back from overflowing.

They flow over the ground without there being a trench for them, meaning channels or pits; yet they flow wherever a person wishes, wherever he wishes.

As for His saying: ﴿the rivers﴾, it is the plural of (nahr). Allah has explained in Surah Muhammad that they are four kinds: ﴿In it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muhammad 15]. Rivers of water unaltered: that is, it does not become stagnant, unlike the water of this world, which becomes stagnant, meaning changed; for when it is left and delayed it changes, but the water of Paradise does not change. ﴿And rivers of milk whose taste does not change﴾ [Muhammad 15], unlike the milk of this world, which changes and spoils when it stays beyond its time. ﴿And rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers﴾ [Muhammad 15]: delicious, and in it there is no harm (ghawl), nor are they made drunk by it (la yunzifun), it does not cause headache nor steal the minds, and it is at its utmost in delight. The fourth: ﴿And rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muhammad 15]: rivers of honey, not the honey of bees, half or more of which is wax, but honey that has been purified.

﴿Abiding therein﴾: that is, remaining in them for a long duration. Other verses have come indicating that this abiding is everlasting, and the scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah have agreed that Paradise, with its bliss, is everlasting.

﴿And excellent is the reward of the workers﴾. The sentence here is an expression of praise and commendation. Commendation of what? Of this great reward. And ﴿the reward of the workers﴾ means their recompense. He made it a "reward" (ajr), the bounty and beneficence of the Possessor of grace, so that a person may be assured of obtaining it when he presents his deed in exchange. Otherwise, the favor belongs to whom? The favor belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, first and last. But He bestows upon us—and praise be to Allah—the deed, then He bestows upon us a second time the recompense, and He says: ﴿Is the reward for good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman 60], as if we were doers of good independently and from the outset. So when we do good, our recompense is that He does good to us, though it is by Allah that He did good to us first and last.

Similarly He says: ﴿And your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insan 22], and ﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward, and your effort has been appreciated﴾. Glory be to Allah! He bestows upon us the effort, grants us success in it and helps us in it, then He thanks us for it. This is the utmost of grace and beneficence from Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: those who work for this great reward. As for His saying ﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾, we say in its grammatical analysis: (ajr) is the subject (fa'il), and the specified object (al-makhsus) is omitted, its estimate being: "Excellent is the reward of the workers, it is [or it is] Paradise," as the poet said:

Excellent is the reward of the God-fearing: Paradise,
In it are hopes, desires, and bounty.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the explanation of the reward of the God-fearing, and that it is a reward a person cannot grasp by imagining it, for it is greater than what can be imagined.

And in it: that their reward includes the attainment of what is sought and the averting of what is disliked. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿forgiveness﴾ and gardens. By forgiveness is averted what is disliked, and by Paradise is attained what is sought.

* And from the benefits of this verse: that the forgiveness of Allah the Mighty and Majestic toward a person is among the greatest of rewards, so do not be surprised that you should frequently ask for forgiveness. When the Surah of Victory (al-Nasr) was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ used to frequently say in his bowing and prostration: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; O Allah, forgive me."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (817) and Muslim (848/217) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]

* And from its benefits: the description of the state of the gardens which the God-fearing were promised, and what His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ depicts of great bliss.

* And from its benefits: that the people of Paradise abide therein forever, by His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾, and the texts have shown that this abiding is everlasting.

* And from its benefits: the greatness of this reward, for when the Great praises something, it indicates its greatness, and Allah the Exalted is the greatest of things, and He has praised this bliss.

* And from its benefits: the explanation of the grace of Allah the Mighty and Majestic toward His servants, in that He made this recompense a reward in the position of a binding reward which the servant must attain. If a questioner says: "How do you reconcile this verse with His ﷺ saying: 'No one will enter Paradise by his deed'?" They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5673) and Muslim (2816/75), the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] He said: "No one enters Paradise by his deed." The apparent meaning of the verse before us is that this Paradise prepared for them is a reward for them, a recompense for what they did of deeds. The answer to this is to say: the statement of the Messenger ﷺ "No one will enter Paradise by his deed" means: by way of exchange, that is, that the reward is equivalent to the deed and is a substitute for it. But as for it being a cause among causes, while Allah by His grace has made it in the position of a recompense, this is established. Our deeds are a cause; and if they were weighed against the blessings of Allah, they would be nothing. If you gathered the blessings of Allah upon you and compared them with your deed, the deed would be very slight and would not even be attributed to anything. If a person were afflicted with distress in his soul, he would spend everything he owns to remove that trial. Likewise the urine, the feces, hearing, sight, and other blessings: many blessings which deeds cannot match. Some poets have said:

If my thanks is a blessing from Allah upon me,
For which, as a blessing like it, thanks is due to Him,
How then can thanks be fulfilled except by His grace,
Even if the days lengthen and life continues?

Is this correct? We say: if you are granted success in giving thanks and you thank Allah, that is itself a blessing, because Allah said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba' 13], and how many are those who deny the blessing of Allah. Then, if you thank Allah, we say: it is a blessing which in turn requires another thanks; if you are granted success in thanking for the thanks, that is a third blessing requiring thanks, and so on. Therefore he said:

How then can thanks be fulfilled except by His grace,
Even if the days lengthen and life continues?

* Student: O Shaykh, regarding His saying ﴿and they do not persist﴾: sometimes a person repents and resolves never to return, and after a while his soul tempts him to return. Is the repentance annulled in this case?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not annulled.
* Student: He persisted in returning?
* The Shaykh: He did not persist. The one who persists is the one who remains upon sin as though it were not a sin. But the person who repents, then his soul overcomes him in the future and he commits the sin, this is not a persister. For this reason it was reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "A man committed a sin and asked Allah for forgiveness; then he sinned again and asked for forgiveness; then he sinned again and asked for forgiveness. Allah the Exalted said: 'My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sin and takes account for it. I have forgiven My servant, so let him do what he wishes.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7507) and Muslim (2758/29) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] So the fact that a person, whenever he sins, seeks forgiveness, and whenever he seeks forgiveness returns and sins, does not nullify his first repentance.
* Student: We mentioned regarding ﴿And excellent is the reward of the workers﴾ that this is an expression of praise; how can it be a predicate for Paradise (...)? What is intended?
* The Shaykh: How can it be a predicate?
* Student: I mean, it is an expressive (insha'i) sentence (...) and a predicate.
* The Shaykh: Well done. Since its form is the form of a declarative statement, it is valid for it to be the predicate of the subject. Its form is the form of a predicate: we say (ni'ma) is a past-tense verb, and (ajr) is its subject; but what is intended by it is the expression of praise, like (bi'sa).
* Student: O Shaykh, this verse does not support the hadith: "None of you enters Paradise by his deed," for Allah the Exalted began the verse with forgiveness: ﴿Their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens﴾, so the first is that He admits them to Paradise by His forgiveness, then He recompenses them for these deeds by raising them in levels.
* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning of the verse is that Paradise is the reward, because it mentions only gardens beneath which rivers flow.
* Student: We said that the verse, for example, refers to what they did while knowing.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And they do not persist in what they did while they know﴾.
* Student: That is, the ignorant person has no sin.
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: The ignorant person commits a sin while ignorant of it; that is, our Lord does not record the sin against him.
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, correct.
* Student: And we have taken the principle, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: We have taken the principle that the ignorant person is not held accountable for his sin, and it is correct.
* Student: May Allah reward you well. In the Qur'an Allah praised those who seek forgiveness and do not persist in sins, and those who abandon them entirely.
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: He praises them for seeking forgiveness and not persisting in them, not for abandoning them entirely. The Prophet ﷺ says: "The son of Adam has been decreed his share of adultery; he will inevitably encounter it,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6612) and Muslim (2657/21), the wording from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] so is there evidence that major preliminaries (al-muqaddimat al-kabirah) are something a person must necessarily do?
* The Shaykh: It is not so in every case; its meaning is that a person, as a human being, will do this, while by his ability he can lower his gaze. But the children of Adam must err: "Every son of Adam is an erring one, and the best of the erring are those who repent,"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2499) and Ibn Majah (4251), the wording of the latter, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] "If you did not sin, Allah would take you away and bring a people who sin, then seek forgiveness from Allah, and He would forgive them."[[Narrated by Muslim (2749/11) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* Student: The one who persists in a minor sin: we said that persistence in a minor sin is among the major sins, although those who persist in minor sins differ greatly; some of them make light of the sacred prohibitions of Allah, and some believe it is not a forbidden matter. How can they be equal?
* The Shaykh: No, they are not equal, may Allah bless you. Even the major sins are not equal. When we say "major," it means they are among the major sins, but the major sins differ. No deed is without difference; if you consider the good deeds, you find them differing. Disbelief itself differs, does it not? The major sins differ: the greatest of the major sins, the middling major sins, and the lowest of the minor sins. The minor sins also differ: looking at a woman with desire, for example a non-related woman, is a minor sin, and touching her is a minor sin, and which is greater? Touching is greater.
* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you: one who committed sins, repented from some of them but did not repent from others, will Allah accept his repentance, knowing that he repented from some minor sins and left the major one?
* The Shaykh: I think this has passed over us.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on the surah 3, verse 136 (part 2 of 2):

It has already been mentioned that the scholars differed regarding the person who repents from one sin while persisting in another: is his repentance from the first sin accepted or not? We mentioned that there is a difference of opinion on this. Some said: it is not accepted. Others said: it is accepted absolutely. And others said: if the sin he persists in is of the same kind as the sin he repented from, his repentance is not accepted; but if it is of a different kind, it is accepted. For example, if a person repents from cheating people in sales, but he cheats them in renting (ijarah), this is one kind of sin, even though the object of the cheating differs. In sum, there are three opinions among the scholars. The correct view is that it is accepted: if a person repents from a sin, even if he persists in a similar sin or one of the same kind, his repentance from that sin is accepted. However, he does not deserve the absolute description in the praise of those who repent (at-tawwabin), meaning that he does not fall under the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222]. Rather, it is said: this is a restricted (muqayyadah) repentance.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 137 onward:**

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿Ways (sunan) have passed away before you, so travel through the earth and see what was the end of those who denied.﴾ (3:137) ﴿This is a clarification for mankind, and guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾ (3:138) ﴿Do not weaken or grieve, for you will be superior if you are believers.﴾ (3:139) ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched the other people. We alternate these days among people so that Allah may know those who believe, and take martyrs from among you. Allah does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ (3:140) ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers.﴾ (3:141) [Al 'Imran 137–141].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Ways have passed away before you, so travel through the earth and see what was the end of those who denied.﴾ The phrase ﴿qad khalat﴾ ("have passed away") is a sentence emphasized by (qad). When *qad* precedes a past-tense verb, it indicates certainty. When it precedes a present-tense verb, it indicates lessening or occasionality, though it may also indicate certainty depending on context. So the saying "qad yajud al-bakhil" ("the miser sometimes gives") expresses lessening. Allah's saying ﴿qad ya'lamu Allahu al-mu'awwiqina minkum﴾ ("Allah certainly knows those among you who hinder others," 33:18) expresses certainty. When *qad* precedes the past tense, it indicates certainty, as in the words of the one who calls to prayer: "qad qamati al-salah" ("the prayer has indeed been established").

﴿Khalat﴾ means "passed away." ﴿Sunan﴾ is the plural of (sunnah), which means a way or practice. What is meant here is Allah's way (sunan) toward those who deny, that He seizes them and destroys them, as He said: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar things.﴾ (47:10). He said ﴿Allah destroyed them﴾, meaning He annihilated them and wiped them out, and ﴿for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾ meaning similar fates for the disbelievers of this nation. Therefore, ﴿sunan﴾ is the plural of (sunnah), meaning a way, and what is meant is Allah's path toward those who denied the messengers, whose end is ruin and destruction.

As for His saying ﴿fa-siru fi al-ardi﴾ ("so travel through the earth"), the (fa) here indicates sequence and is conjunctive, linking one sentence to another. (Siru) is an imperative verb from *sayr*, which means walking. What is meant here is the journey of the hearts and the journey of the feet. The journey of the heart is through reflection: a person reflects on the earlier nations who preceded him in time, and likewise on the nations that preceded him in place. As He said: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ (37:137–138). A person travels with his heart and travels with his feet. His journey with his heart is to reflect on the end of those who passed away in time and the end of those who passed away in place. For example, the dwellings of Thamud exist now. Does a person reflect on them in terms of time or place? He reflects on them in terms of both place and time, and he considers what their end was. The journey on foot may be more impactful than the journey of the heart, because a person may reach through it the certainty of knowledge and direct observation with the eye. The journey of the heart is more general and comprehensive, because through it a person reaches what he cannot reach by walking forward. Is that not so?

As for His saying ﴿siru fi al-ardi﴾, the (fi) here indicates location, but according to the exegetes here it means (ʿala), that is, "travel on the earth," because travel within the interior of the earth is neither possible nor beneficial. Travel only benefits on the surface of the earth. His saying ﴿siru fi al-ardi﴾ means the land of those who came before, so the (al) here is the definite article of prior reference, referring to what is understood from His saying ﴿Ways have passed away before you﴾. That is: travel through their land and see what their end was.

As for His saying ﴿fa-unzuru kayfa kana ʿaqibatu al-mukadhdhibin﴾ ("so see what was the end of those who denied"), should you look with the eye of sight, or with the eye of insight, or with both? With both together. If one reaches the places of these nations, then looking is with the eye of sight and the eye of insight. If one does not reach them but reflects in his heart, then looking is with the eye of insight, because sight cannot reach them, and he is only looking within his heart.

﴿Fa-unzuru kayfa kana ʿaqibatu al-mukadhdhibin﴾: (unzuru) is an imperative verb, and it governs a direct object, but it has been suspended from acting on it (ʿallaqa), because it is followed by an interrogative clause. When an interrogative clause follows a transitive verb, it suspends the verb's action. Suspended here means prevented. Accordingly, the clause ﴿kayfa kana ʿaqibatu al-mukadhdhibin﴾ is in the accusative position as the object of (unzuru).

As for the detailed grammatical analysis (iʿrab) of ﴿kayfa kana ʿaqibatu al-mukadhdhibin﴾: (kayfa) is an interrogative noun, indeclinable, in the accusative position as the predicate of (kana) placed first. Is its placement here obligatory or permissible? It is obligatory, because the interrogative has priority at the start of the sentence. When an interrogative functions as a predicate, it must be placed first. So here (kayfa) is an interrogative noun, indeclinable with a fatha vowel, in the accusative position as the predicate of (kana). (ʿAqibatu) is its subject. As for (al-mukadhdhibin), it is known to be a genitive complement (mudaf ilayh).

﴿ʿAqibatu al-mukadhdhibin﴾ means the outcome of their affair. The ʿaqibah of a thing is what follows it and what it leads to. Here, "those who deny" refers to those who denied Allah and His messengers. So what was their end? Their end was ruin and destruction, and their punishment was according to their sins, as Allah said: ﴿So each We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those seized by the blast, and among them those We caused the earth to swallow, and among them those We drowned﴾ (29:40). Those upon whom Allah sent a storm of pebbles, like the people of Lut: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a storm of pebbles, except the family of Lut; We saved them before dawn﴾ (54:34). And among them were those seized by the blast, like the people of Salih.

﴿Fa-minhum man arsalna ʿalayhi hasiban wa-minhum man akhadhat-hu al-sayhah wa-minhum man khasafna bihi al-ard wa-minhum man aghraqna wa-ma kana Allahu liyazlimahum wa-lakin kanu anfusahum yazlimun﴾ (29:40). Those upon whom Allah sent a storm of pebbles, like the people of Lut: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a storm of pebbles, except the family of Lut; We saved them before dawn﴾ (54:34). ﴿And among them were those seized by the blast﴾, like the people of Salih, Thamud. ﴿And among them those We caused the earth to swallow﴾, like Qarun. ﴿And among them those We drowned﴾, like Pharaoh and the people of Noah. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, drowned them according to what wisdom requires. Minds are often unable to know the proportion between the punishment and the deed. Be precise in your estimation: I say that minds are often incapable of knowing the proportion between the punishment and the deed. And I say "often," because sometimes they do recognize the proportion. For example, we know the reason for the destruction of 'Ad by wind: they used to say ﴿Who is stronger than us in strength?﴾ (41:15). So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, wanted to show them that He destroys them by something among the most subtle things, which is wind, air. Air is subtle, yet Allah destroyed with it this nation that boasted of its strength.

Regarding the family of Pharaoh: Pharaoh took pride in the rivers flowing beneath him and said to his people: ﴿O my people, is not the dominion of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Will you not then see? Or am I better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾ (43:51–52). So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, destroyed him by the same kind of thing he had boasted of, which is water. As for the rest, I cannot determine the proportion between the deed and the punishment precisely. However, Allah's saying ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ indicates that the punishment is proportionate to the deed. Among well-known sayings among people is: "As you judge, so you will be judged" (kama tadin tudan).

* Among the great benefits of this verse: Allah, glory be to Him, destroyed nations before this nation, as shown by His saying ﴿sunan﴾ (3:137). Is "sunan" a plural of abundance or a plural of paucity?

* The students: Abundance.

* The Shaykh: Or paucity? Is "sunan" paucity or abundance?

* The students: Abundance.

* The Shaykh: Abundance. Paucity. Both are possible; neither this nor that. The division is now fourfold. I will read you a verse by Ibn Malik, and pay attention. Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

*Af'ilah, af'ul, then fi'lah,*
*then af'al are the plurals of paucity.*

What is "sunan"?

* The students: Abundance.

* The Shaykh: It is a plural of abundance, unanimously agreed. The meaning is that the plural of paucity is restricted to these four patterns only: af'ilah, af'ul, fi'lah, and af'al.

* Among the benefits of this verse: it consoles this nation in one respect and warns it in another respect. It consoles it by showing that Allah, glory be to Him, punished those before it. His punishment of it at Uhud is one of Allah's ways (sunan), because there is no doubt that what happened at Uhud was a punishment: ﴿Until, when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He showed you what you love﴾ (3:152). It also warns in another respect about a more severe punishment, because the earlier nations were annihilated and utterly destroyed, every last one of them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of analogical reasoning (qiyas, reasoning from a known case to a similar unknown case). How? Because what is meant by His saying ﴿fa-siru fi al-ardi﴾ is contemplation and taking lessons, and that what is present should be compared with what has passed and preceded.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the command to travel through the earth. But is this absolute, or only for the sake of taking lessons? Let us consider: ﴿So travel through the earth and see﴾. Therefore, traveling through the earth for a purpose that is not legally sanctioned is blameworthy, as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, and other scholars have said. Traveling through the earth without a legitimate purpose involves exhausting oneself, exposing oneself to ruin, wasting wealth, and wasting time. If it is for a legitimate purpose, then it follows that purpose. Accordingly, travel through the earth is divided into categories: one for forbidden purposes, which is undoubtedly prohibited; another for permissible and desirable purposes, which is undoubtedly recommended; and a third for mere sightseeing and recreation. The last one is examined: its basic ruling is permissibility, but if it leads a person to something forbidden, it becomes forbidden, and if it leads him to something legitimate, it becomes legitimate. An example of the first, traveling for a forbidden purpose, is what some affluent people do, who tour lands of disbelief and immorality in order to obtain their desires, which they cannot obtain in their own countries. There is no doubt that this is forbidden, because travel for this purpose is forbidden, this purpose itself is forbidden, and wasting wealth on it is forbidden. It is compounded wrongdoing, "darkness upon darkness," and we seek refuge in Allah.

The second is that which is legitimate, such as traveling through the earth to seek obligatory provision, like a person who has no means to sustain himself and his family and travels to obtain such provision. Likewise, traveling through the earth to seek knowledge. The early scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, would travel for a month in search of a single issue. They would journey extensively through the earth for one question. Travel in that time was not like travel in our time; it involved hardship and great dangers. As for travel that is neither for this nor for that, such as some people's trips for relaxation and recreation during holidays, festivals, and the like, we say that in principle there is nothing wrong with it. But it may lead to good, and then it becomes good, such as when such travel involves maintaining family ties, dutifulness to parents, or similar things, in which case it becomes a recommended matter.

Is traveling to the lands of those who were destroyed among the recommended matters? We say: yes, if the purpose is to take admonition. But if the purpose is to gawk at the strength of those people and similar things, then it is not permissible. When the Prophet ﷺ passed by the dwellings of Thamud on his way to Tabuk, he passed quickly, covering his head, fearful, peace and blessings be upon him, and he said: "Do not enter upon these people except while weeping; if you are not weeping, do not enter them." (Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.) This contradicts what some people do whose hearts have died; they go to the dwellings of Thamud in order to view their monuments, remains, and power. There is no doubt that this is forbidden, because the Messenger ﷺ forbade it. He said: "Do not enter upon these people unless you are weeping; if you are not weeping, do not enter upon them."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the end of one who denies Allah and His messengers is dreadful, as shown by His saying ﴿so see what was the end of those who denied﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 138–139 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is a clear statement for mankind, and a guidance and an admonition for those who are mindful of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran 138]. Does this "this" refer to the Qur'an, or to what was mentioned in His words: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ up to the end [Al 'Imran 133]?

On this there are two opinions among the exegetes (mufassirun). Some said: it refers to the Qur'an, because this usage is frequent in the Book of Allah, such as His words, blessed and exalted: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya' 50], and similar verses in which the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an itself. So "this" – that is, the Qur'an – is a clear statement for mankind.

Others said: it refers to the nearest thing mentioned, because both the demonstrative and the pronoun refer to the nearest antecedent. But the preferable view is the first: that it refers to the whole Qur'an, and this verse is part of it. If we make "this" refer to the whole Qur'an, then what was mentioned in His words ﴿And hasten to forgiveness﴾ up to the end is included within it.

As for His words ﴿a clear statement (bayan) for mankind﴾: bayan is a verbal noun (masdar), or rather an ism al-masdar (a noun of the verbal action), from bayyana, yubayyinu, whose masdar is tabyin, just as baddala, yubaddilu has tabdil, and as kallama, yukallimu has taklim, while bayan is an ism al-masdar, and ism al-masdar is a kalam. When we say that "this is a bayan" and treat it as an ism al-masdar, then he has expressed the one described as "clear statement" by the noun of the action which is bayan. This is of the category of hyperbole (mubalaghah), where the described thing itself is made to be the attribute. Pay attention: when we express the described thing by the attribute, this is of the category of hyperbole, as if we have negated its being described by it, until we make it the very attribute itself. This is why they say: the saying of the speaker "so-and-so is justice (adl)" is more emphatic than their saying "so-and-so possesses justice (dhu adl)", as if he made the described thing itself the attribute. So the Qur'an does not contain clarity; rather, it is itself the clarity.

"A clear statement for mankind": who is mankind? All of mankind. Everyone who recites the Qur'an has what it indicates made clear to him. But does everyone to whom this becomes clear become guided? No. This is why He said: ﴿and a guidance and an admonition for those who are mindful of Allah﴾. Guidance (huda) here means a sign by which the mindful one is led to conclusions; admonition (mawizah) means compliance (imtithal), because admonition is the softening of hearts by mentioning what is feared or mentioning what is desired. So it is guidance, meaning indication, and admonition, meaning compliance.

Allah described the Qur'an with three attributes: a general attribute, and two specific ones. The general attribute is that it is a clear statement for mankind; the two specific ones are guidance and admonition, for none are guided by it except the mindful, and none are admonished by it except the mindful. As for those who are not like that, it is a blindness upon them – we seek refuge with Allah – a blindness upon them, and they do not increase in admonition by it. Rather Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to their filth upon their filth﴾, meaning filth added to their impurity, ﴿and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah 125]. Glory be to Allah! One speech has this divergent effect: for a people it is guidance and admonition, and upon another people it is blindness and filth. This is because hearts are like lands. Among lands there is good land which accepts water, grows pasture, and from which people benefit. Among them is hard ground which does not drink water but holds water, so people benefit from it. And among them is salty, barren flat land which drinks water but does not grow anything, so water only increases its harm; for when it is dry, it is possible to walk on it, but when it is wet it is not possible to walk on it, for it becomes slippery and treacherous, and yet people do not benefit from it, neither by water it retains nor by plants it produces. Likewise is the Qur'an. In relation to people, some benefit from it and increase in guidance and piety, and some do not benefit from it but increase only in blindness and misguidance, because whenever they deny a verse, their sin and punishment increase.

﴿And do not be weak, nor grieve, and you will be superior, if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 139]. The (la) here is a prohibitive particle (nahiyah), and the verb after it is in the jussive mood by dropping the nun: (tahinu), whose original is (tahinuna); the nun was dropped because of the jussive. ﴿And do not be weak﴾: the address is to this community, headed by our Prophet ﷺ and his companions. Wahn means weakness, meaning: do not become weak, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not be weak in pursuing the enemy﴾ [al-Nisa' 104], do not become weak and cowardly. ﴿Nor grieve﴾ over what has befallen you. ﴿And you will be superior﴾. So Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned their state of advancing and their state of retreating. In their state of advancing He forbade them from weakness, and this gives them strength and boldness. In their state of retreating He forbade them from grief, and this gives them the disposition to turn away from what lies behind them and not to look back at it. It is well known that grief occurs over what is distressing, and grieving over what has passed does not benefit a person; rather it weakens resolve, disturbs peace, and gains nothing. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ forbade them from what hinders them in the state of advancing and from what hinders them in the state of retreating. How so? I say: ﴿Do not be weak﴾ – this is what hinders in the state of advancing and boldness, so he forbade them from weakness, meaning: advance, do not be cowardly, do not hold back. ﴿Do not grieve﴾ over what would cause them to halt in the state of retreating, because when a person grieves over what has passed, he remains anxious and cannot act well. So He forbade them from this and that.

Then He said: ﴿and you will be superior﴾. The exegetes have differed over whether the waw here is a circumstantial waw (hal) or a resumptive waw (isti'nafiyyah). What do you think? If we say it is a circumstantial waw, then this prohibition is restricted to the community as long as it is superior; meaning, if it is brought low, then it may be weak and may grieve, because it is weak and cannot advance, nor can it console itself over what has passed, for with what would it console itself? Do you know what follows if we make it circumstantial? If we make the waw resumptive, so that the meaning is "do not be weak and do not grieve; you are the superior," then in it there is encouragement for the community not to become weak and not to grieve, because they are the superior, so that even if they are struck by what they are struck with, in accordance with what Allah's wisdom requires by the alternation of days among people, the final outcome is theirs. On this basis, this second view is closer to the correct, although the first view is also possible.

His words ﴿and you will be superior﴾ present a difficulty from the standpoint of grammatical inflection (i'rab). For it is known that the waw of the masculine plural is preceded by a damma, so one says: muslimun, and one does not say: muslimaun. Here He said: ﴿and you will be superior﴾ and did not say: wa antum al-a'lunu?

* A student: The waw which is preceded by a damma was dropped, because its original form is a'lawun, and after it the waw was dropped; then the first waw was changed into an alif, and the alif was dropped because of the meeting of two sukun, and the lam is fatha, which indicates the dropped waw. Therefore it becomes a'lawn.

* The Shaykh: Did you hear? He says that (al-a'lawn) originally was (al-a'la). The alif was dropped because of the meeting of two sukun, so the alif is sakin and the waw is sakin. When the alif is dropped because of the meeting of two sukun, the vowel that precedes it must remain as it is, and what is the vowel before it? A fatha. For if you made it a damma, it would not be clear that there is a dropped alif; if you made the lam a damma (al-a'lun), it would not be clear that there is a dropped alif. So the fatha must remain, to indicate the dropped alif because of the meeting of two sukun. So the difficulty is removed. Is that correct? ﴿and you will be superior﴾.

* A student: The words of the Exalted: ﴿So travel through the earth﴾. Some people derive from this verse the gathering of the traces of earlier peoples, and they spend money on relics and travel (...)?

* The Shaykh: He says that the words of the Exalted ﴿So travel through the earth﴾ are used as evidence by some who are infatuated with collecting relics, who take an ancient piece that is not worth a qirsh for many dirhams. Does this fall under it? The answer is: no, it does not fall under it. Even those who collect relics do not intend by them consideration (i'tibar) and that the end of those who were of that condition is destruction and ruin; rather they are things their souls incline toward, just as we have heard and hear often that some people collect (...) or postage stamps, to the extent that one buys a stamp worth five qurush for perhaps fifty riyals.

* The student: Millions of pounds sterling, if the stamp differs from... the complete one, I mean, sixty million pounds sterling, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: There is no power nor strength except with Allah! Well, in any case, what we see is that if there is a legitimate benefit in it, then there is no harm; otherwise, leaving it is better.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, what is the difference between tourism (siyahah) and travel (sayr)?

* The Shaykh: There is no difference between them.

* The student: Tourism is travel?

* The Shaykh: Yes, tourism on the earth means travelling in it.

* The student: So there is no restriction to four months if it is the same thing?

* The Shaykh: No, no, as I say: travel in the earth for four months.

* The student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, one who travels in the earth for a legitimate purpose, such as treatment for example, but his companion is doing something forbidden, is he prevented from travelling?

* The Shaykh: If he cannot travel for treatment except by committing this forbidden act, then it becomes forbidden, because treatment by means of what is forbidden is forbidden. Treatment by means of what is forbidden is forbidden, because committing a forbidden act is a certain harm, while recovery from illness is an expected benefit that is not certain. Were it not so, we would say: whoever needs to eat pork for treatment may eat it, although it is not permitted. This is the difference between the permissibility of eating pork out of hunger and eating pork for seeking a cure: the second is forbidden and the first is permitted, because eating meat in hunger certainly benefits, for it removes hunger and sustains a person's life, but treating by the forbidden may succeed or may not succeed. So he commits a certain corruption for the sake of an anticipated benefit that is imagined; and if you wish, say it is also a preponderant benefit, but the preponderant is not like the certain. This is why it has come in the hadith: "Indeed Allah has not placed your cure in what He has forbidden to you" [Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq (17097) and Ibn Abi Shaybah (23839), from the saying of Ibn Mas'ud], and this is true. But suppose some medicines contain some pork, yet it has no effect on taste or smell; is it permissible or not?

* A student: It is permissible.

* The Shaykh: It is permissible?

* A student: Does one know that these medicines contain pork? It is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: Yes, one knows, one knows, but it is a small part that has no effect. Is it absolutely not permissible in any circumstances?

* A student: It is permissible.

* A student: This medicine is not eaten; it is used as valves for the heart; it is only placed, not eaten.

* The Shaykh: Yes, you mean the impure substance.

* The student: This is what we know regarding pork: it is used for treatment only, meaning tissue for a valve, which is merely placed, not eaten. That is, there is no medicine into which food is placed.

* The Shaykh: I gave it as an example. Let us suppose a medicine contains alcohol. Leave aside pork; this alcohol shows neither its effect nor its taste. Is it permissible? We say: yes, and we take as evidence for this the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed water is pure; nothing makes it impure except what changes its taste, colour, or smell" [Narrated by Abu Dawud (66) and al-Tirmidhi (66), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri without the final sentence containing the exception; the exception was narrated by Ibn Majah (521) from the hadith of Abu Umamah al-Bahili]. Although this exception is weak, the scholars agree upon its ruling: that water is pure and is not made impure except by what alters its smell. If water is not made impure and it is permissible for you to perform ablution with it and drink it, then so too is other than it. But using pork meat or pork fat in a manner that does not reach the body, meaning one does not eat it, is it permissible? We say: yes, it is permissible. So if it were stipulated that a person be prescribed to anoint himself with pork fat, and he anointed with it, but when he wishes to pray he washes it off, then that is permissible. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, stated this explicitly in his Fatawa, and it is correct, because it does no harm, like greasing ships with impure fat and what resembles it.

* * *

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you precedents, so travel through the earth﴾. What is meant by "precedents" (sunan) here?

* A student: Sunan means what Allah has established... the Messenger ﷺ.

* The Shaykh: Sunan means, for example, voluntary prayer and voluntary fasting.

* A student: The earlier nations.

* The Shaykh: The earlier nations; meaning sunan is applied to nations. That is one opinion. The second opinion?

* Students: The ways.

* The Shaykh: The ways. That is, the ways of Allah, mighty and majestic, passed on those who denied the messengers.

His words: ﴿travel through the earth﴾: is what is meant the travel of the feet or the travel of the heart?

* A student: Both.

* The Shaykh: Yes, both: the travel of the heart and the travel of the feet. Well, is it derived from this verse that a person should read history?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, because reading history is in reality travel through the earth. Now, His words ﴿travel through the earth﴾: (fi) here means what?

* A student: It means (ala, upon).

* The Shaykh: It means (ala, upon), or is (fi) used for location?

* The student: For location, but the exegetes agreed that it means (ala), because it is not possible to travel inside the earth.

* The Shaykh: So it is originally for location, and it comes for other than location according to context.

What do you say about his ﷺ words: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat which she confined"? [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3318) and Muslim (2242/151), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar.]

* The student: For the sake of.

* The Shaykh: For causation?

* A student: Yes.

* A student: It differs according to context.

* The Shaykh: Correct.

His words, exalted: ﴿Then see how was the end of those who denied﴾. Where is the object of (see)?

* A student: The clause (how was).

* The Shaykh: The clause (how), and where is the predicate of (was)?

* The student: The predicate of (was) is placed before it.

* The Shaykh: Where is it?

* The student: (How).

* The Shaykh: (How) is placed first. Is this fronting obligatory or permissible here?

* The student: Obligatory.

* The Shaykh: Obligatory. Why?

* The student: Because (how) is an interrogative particle, and interrogative particles hold the front position.

* The Shaykh: Yes, correct: the predicate of (how) is fronted obligatorily, because it is an interrogative, and interrogation has the front of the sentence.

His words, exalted: ﴿This is a clear statement for mankind﴾. (This) – what does the demonstrative refer to?

* A student: The Qur'an.

* The Shaykh: The Qur'an. Is there another opinion?

* A student: There is another opinion that what preceded is the statement, and the first opinion is that it is the Qur'an in general.

* The Shaykh: The Qur'an in general. Which of them is preferable?

* The student: The nearer, the Qur'an.

* The Shaykh: It is preferable to say: the Qur'an, because it is more general; whenever something is more general, it is preferable, because it is more comprehensive. Well, why did He distinguish with His words: ﴿a clear statement for mankind, and a guidance and an admonition for those who are mindful of Allah﴾?

* A student: Because clarity is a general attribute, so it is for the believer and for the non-believer. But whomever Allah guides, for him it is guidance and admonition, and whomever He does not guide, for him it is clarity.

* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning it is a clarification for all, but none are guided by it and admonished by it except the mindful.

Here He stated "clear statement" without restriction: ﴿This is a clear statement for mankind﴾. If we say it is the Qur'an, in what is there clarity? Is it in every matter, or only in matters of worship?

* A student: In all things: in narratives, in rulings, and in creed.

* The Shaykh: In everything. Do you have evidence from the Qur'an that it is general in everything?

* The student: Yes.

* A student: The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 89].

* The Shaykh: The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ – clear.

Well, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is a clear statement for mankind, and a guidance and an admonition for those who are mindful of Allah﴾.

* Benefitting from this noble verse: that the Qur'an is a clear statement for mankind in every matter. It is general in terms of clarification and general in terms of the one to whom clarification is made. We take the generality of the recipients from His words ﴿for mankind﴾, and the comprehensiveness of the clarification from the omission of the object of the verb, and omission of the object indicates generality: this is a clear statement for mankind in everything. This is supported by the verse we mentioned earlier, His words: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the Qur'an is suitable for guidance for both believer and disbeliever, as in His words ﴿for mankind﴾, which includes both believer and disbeliever.

* Among its benefits also: it is a guidance only for the God-fearing (al-muttaqin), meaning that only the God-fearing benefit from it, due to His saying: ﴿and a guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾.

* And among its benefits also: whoever is not admonished by the Qur'an should suspect himself. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿for the God-fearing﴾. So if you are not admonished by the Qur'an, then suspect yourself, for there is a trial within you. Likewise, whoever is not restrained by his prayer from indecency and wrongdoing should suspect himself, for his prayer is deficient. This is because the One who informed us that prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His report is true and corresponds to reality. So if a person knows from the reality of his own self that his prayer does not restrain him from indecency and wrongdoing, then he should suspect himself, because Allah's report cannot be doubted. For this reason, one of the early generation (al-salaf) said: "Whoever is not restrained by his prayer from indecency and wrongdoing, his prayer only increases him in distance from Allah."[[Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur in his Tafsir (1705), and Abu Dawud in al-Zuhd (134), from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] We ask Allah for well-being, and we ask Allah to help us.
Here, if you are not admonished by the Qur'an, then suspect yourself of not being God-fearing, because the God-fearing person must be admonished by the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of taqwa (God-consciousness), and that it is a cause of being guided and of being admonished by the Qur'an.

* Among its benefits: the more a person increases in taqwa, the more guidance and admonition he gains. Why? Because a ruling attached to a description grows stronger with its strength and weakens with its weakness. So since guidance and admonition are attached to taqwa, they must increase and grow stronger with taqwa, and weaken and decrease with its absence. Is it clear?

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve, for you will be the superior ones if you are believers.﴾

* In this verse: a prohibition to the believers from weakness (al-wahn). ﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve, for you will be the superior ones.﴾ A human being is in reality between two times: a past time and a future time. If good has escaped him or evil has befallen him in the past, his state is grief; he grieves over what has passed. In the future, if he becomes weak and cowardly, he loses good in proportion to his weakness and cowardice. For this reason He said: ﴿do not weaken﴾, meaning from acting in the future, ﴿nor grieve﴾ over what befell you in the past. So do not grieve over what befell you in the past, because you are the superior ones, and whoever is superior, the outcome will be his. Whatever is in the future, do not be weak in it nor be cowardly in it, for the outcome belongs to you, since you are the superior ones.

His saying: ﴿do not weaken, nor grieve, for you will be the superior ones﴾: we have mentioned that this sentence may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah), meaning: while you are the superior ones, because the superior one does not befit weakness or grief. We have also mentioned that it may be a new independent statement (isti'nāfiyyah) in which Allah affirms the supremacy of the believers. When their supremacy is established, their state requires what? That they should not weaken and should not grieve. The two meanings are interrelated, for whoever believes that he is the superior one will not be cowardly nor grieve, and whoever's state is superiority will likewise not weaken nor grieve.

His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾: this is a condition for superiority. That is: you are the superior ones while being believers. Faith, as you know, is more specific than Islam, because Islam can be found in the hypocrite and in the one whose faith is weak, whereas faith exists only in one whose faith is complete, the true believer. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed."﴾ See, the desert Bedouins say "We have believed." ﴿Say, "You have not believed, but say, 'We have submitted,'"﴾ Why? He said: ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [Al-Hujurat 14]. Until now faith has not entered the heart. You have Islam, but you do not have faith yet, though faith is near to you, because His saying "lamma" (not yet) is a negation particle that indicates the nearness of what is negated. That is, faith will soon enter your hearts, but not yet.

So we say: this nation is the superior one on a condition, what is it? The condition of faith. As for if it does not have faith, it has no covenant with Allah for victory, because the binding covenant between Allah and His servants regarding victory is that victory is reciprocal: ﴿O you who believe, if you support Allah, He will support you and make firm your feet﴾ [Muhammad 7], and ﴿Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Mighty﴾ [Al-Hajj 40]. But if there is no support of Allah the Mighty and Majestic from us, then Allah's support may be withheld; that is, it is not guaranteed.

Alright, then you are the superior ones if you are believers. The signs of faith are many, among them: that a person does not fear anyone among the creation in implementing the command of Allah.
