This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl 97]. So we say: it is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) to affirm love for Allah, that Allah loves and that He is loved.
Did some people deny the love of Allah?
Yes, some people denied the love of Allah, but it was not a denial of rejection, rather a denial by interpretation. They said: the intended meaning of love is will, or reward. So the meaning of "He loves" is that He wills to reward them, or it means He rewards them, and the meaning of "He loves them" is that He rewards them. These are the Ash'ariyyah and those who were more extreme in negation (ta'til). The Ash'ariyyah say: It is forbidden for you to say that Allah loves. Forbidden for you. Then Allah says: He loves? They say: The meaning of "He loves" is: He wills to reward them, or its meaning is He rewards them. Such things have passed us many times, and we have explained the invalidity of their doctrine, and that what they adopted is distortion (tahrif) of the Book of Allah, not interpretation of it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: warning against wrongdoing. Its manner: through His saying ﴿Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ [Al 'Imran 57], and every person flees from every act that leads to Allah not loving him as one flees from a lion. So in this there is a warning against wrongdoing.
Wrongdoing has types: either against Allah, or against the human being. Wrongdoing against the human being is either in wealth, or in life, or in honor, with various kinds. But every wrongdoing, Allah does not love it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the love of Allah may be partial, meaning that He loves this more than that, and dislikes this more than that. Its manner: when a ruling is attached to an attribute, it increases with its increase and strengthens with its strength, and decreases with its decrease and weakens with its weakness. So if the absence of love is because of wrongdoing, then the more a person is a wrongdoer, the further he is from the love of Allah, mighty and majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 141–142 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah mentioned another benefit. How many is it? ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran 141].
* Students: The fourth.
* Shaykh: The fourth. He said: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾. *(Yumahhisa)* means *(yunaqqi)*, that is, to purify. Is the intended meaning that He purifies them from others, so that the sincere believer of pure faith becomes distinguished? Or that He purifies them from sins through the wound that befell them? Or both? Both, because we have a principle that has already preceded: when a word can carry two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is interpreted as having both meanings together.
So He purifies them: He purifies them from sins through the wound that befell them, and He also purifies them in the sense of selection, meaning that through this the elite of the believers become distinguished from those whose faith contains some doubt or disbelief. This is an obvious matter, and it is what Allah pointed to in His saying: ﴿And that Allah may make known those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran 140].
So among the wisdom in what befell the Muslims of the wound is that Allah purifies whom? Those who believe. He purifies them from sins through this calamity, and He purifies them by making clear the sincere, the elite of the chosen ones.
The fifth: He said: ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran 141]. Destroy the disbelievers. Glory be to Allah! If He grants them victory, will that be a cause of their destruction? Yes, it will be a cause of their destruction, because when they win they become arrogant, feel superior, become puffed up in themselves, and think they will always have dominance. Then they repeat the attempt a second time by fighting the Muslims, and thus it becomes their destruction. This is the meaning of the verse. Some scholars said: *"yamhaqu al-kafirin"* means He destroys them by what they inflicted upon the Muslims of the wound, so *al-mahq* is taken to mean punishment and destruction in the Hereafter. But the first meaning is more appropriate: that He destroys them with a perceptible destruction, because when they win this time, they try to repeat the attempt a second time; for what? For the sake of, what? For the sake of another victory, and thus it becomes their destruction and their annihilation.
And His saying: ﴿al-kafirin﴾ is derived from *kufr* (disbelief). The root meaning of *kufr* in the language is covering, and from it comes *al-kufra*, meaning the sheath of the date-palm spathe, because it covers what is within it.
So Allah mentioned in these two verses the touch of the wound: how many benefits? Five benefits.
Then He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾ [Al 'Imran 142]. *(Am)* here is *munqati'ah* (disjunctive), so it means *(bal)* (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah, that is: Rather, did you think you would enter Paradise? Their saying *(munqati'ah)* is to distinguish it from *muttasilah* (connective). What is the difference between them, between the connective and the disjunctive? Let the brother answer. Yes, what is the difference between disjunctive *(am)* and connective *(am)*?
* Student: The connective is coordinating.
* Shaykh: And this one is coordinating.
* Student: (...) the second sentence..
* Shaykh: And this one is coordinating.
* Student: That is, everything connected to it (...) is the beginning of a new statement.
* Another student: The connective is where the occurrence of one of the two matters is certain. Some of them mention it in the connective, like saying "this or that." Some of them mention it after the interrogative, actually or verbally, and it is followed by the hamzah, one of the two matters. These are its conditions.
* Another student: The difference between them is in one respect: first, this disjunctive is in the sense of *(bal)* and the hamzah, while the connective is in the sense of *(aw)* (or). The second..
* Shaykh: Yes, the disjunctive is in the sense of *(bal)* and the hamzah, and that one is in the sense of *(aw)*.
* Student: The connective is accompanied by the *mu'addil* (the counterpart).
* Shaykh: The connective *(am)* is accompanied by the counterpart, and the disjunctive *(am)* has no counterpart.
This is the meaning of what the brother (Hidayatullah) said. The difference becomes clear through an example. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 6]. What do we say about this?
* Students: Connective.
* Shaykh: Connective, because a counterpart is mentioned in it, and because it is in the sense of *(aw)*. Alright, ﴿Do their intellects command them to this, or are they a transgressing people?﴾ [al-Tur 32]?
* Student: Disjunctive.
* Shaykh: Pay attention: ﴿Do their intellects command them to this, or are they a transgressing people?﴾.
* Students: Disjunctive.
* Other students: In the sense of *(bal)*.
* Shaykh: In the sense of *(bal)*. Yes, because the matter of their intellects (i.e., their minds) commanding this is not a counterpart to their being transgressors. Rather, He said: Do their intellects command them to this or not? The answer: They were not commanded, but they are a transgressing people.
Alright, here: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾, is it connective or disjunctive?
* Students: Disjunctive.
* Shaykh: Disjunctive, because no counterpart is mentioned, and because it is in the sense of *(bal)* and the hamzah.
﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾, that is: Did you suppose that you would enter Paradise? The interrogative here is for rebuke, meaning: Do you think you will enter Paradise without being tested? For this reason He said: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove, and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran 142]. ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾. Paradise is the abode of the righteous and the everlasting home, may Allah make us and you among its people. ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾: *lamma* here is a jussive particle, and the proof of its jussive effect is that the verb after it is jussive. Let us ask the brother: is the verb after it jussive?
* Student: ﴿wa-lamma ya'lami﴾, yes, it is jussive.
* Shaykh: Jussive. The verb ﴿yaʿlami Allāh﴾ is kasra. How do you say it is jussive?
* Student: Kasra because of the meeting of two sukun.
* Shaykh: That is, it was vocalized with a kasra.
* Student: Because of the meeting of two sukun.
* Shaykh: And its origin?
* Student: Its origin: *wa-lamma ya'lam*.
* Shaykh: *Wa-lamma ya'lam*. But since what follows it is sukun, it took kasra, because of the principle that Ibn Malik indicated in his Al-Kafiyah:
If two sukun meet, vocalize the first with kasra,
and if it is a soft letter, its deletion is due.
His saying: ﴿lamma ya'lami﴾: *(lamma)*, we said, is jussive, as proven by the fact that the verb after it is jussive, but it was vocalized with kasra because of the meeting of two sukun.
Can *(lamma)* come in a non-jussive sense? We want to recall what has passed. Can *(lamma)* come in a non-jussive sense?
* Student: Extra (zaʼida).
* Shaykh: Extra?
* Student: *(lamma)* comes as a conditional, and *lamma* (extra) (...).
* Student: It appears so, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: It comes as what?
* Student: It comes as non-jussive.
* Shaykh: But it comes for what meaning?
* Student: That is, the meaning for which it comes..
* Shaykh: It comes as jussive; we have finished with it. And it comes as?
* Student: And I memorized an example.. It comes as conditional.
* Shaykh: It comes as conditional. Like what?
* Student: *Lamma qama Zaydun qama 'Amrun* (When Zayd stood, 'Amr stood).
* Shaykh: ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling Him, they almost became a crowd around him﴾ [al-Jinn 19]. That is one.
* Student: It comes as temporal.
* Shaykh: Temporal, meaning what?
* Student: Meaning *(hina)* (when).
* Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: ﴿So when We decreed death for him, nothing showed them his death﴾ [Saba' 14].
* Shaykh: That one is conditional.
* Student: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿So their gods that they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came﴾ [Hud 101].
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿So their gods that they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came﴾, that is, when the command of your Lord came. That is three.
* Student: In the sense of exceptive *(illa)*.
* Shaykh: In the sense of exceptive *(illa)*.
* Student: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq 4].
* Shaykh: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾, that is: except that over it is a guardian. Four meanings.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding His saying: ﴿and that He may take martyrs from among you﴾. Can we not take from this a general principle: that Allah does not take all people as martyrs, but takes only those who have the qualities of faith and piety? Are these the ones He takes as martyrs?
* Shaykh: This allows for it if we say *(min)* is partitive. But if we say it is explanatory, then it is not determined.
* Student: That is, He may take martyrs from others too..
* Shaykh: Rationally it is permissible, but it did not happen, because many Muslims died without martyrdom.
* Student: Especially in jihad?
* Shaykh: Yes, even in jihad, many Muslims did not attain martyrdom.
* Student: So we do not take it as a general principle?
* Shaykh: No, we do not take it as a general principle, because since *(min)* may be explanatory, we do not affirm that it is partitive.
* Student: The principle, Shaykh, regarding deriving the attributes of Allah from the implicit meaning (mafhum) of some verses, like: ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ [Al 'Imran 140] (...), because this may be indicated by other texts. But there are verses that are not indicated by other texts: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾ [Luqman 18] (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, He loves whoever is free of that.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾ [Luqman 18]. Regarding one who is not self-deluded and not boastful, do we say that Allah loves him?
* Shaykh: Yes, He loves whoever is free of these two qualities.
* Student: Is it possible that he has other qualities?
* Shaykh: Yes, he may have another quality that makes Him dislike him, and another quality that makes Him love him. But the negation of love from the self-deluded boaster indicates the affirmation of love for others, or for its opposite, which is better.
* Student: But, Shaykh, can the opposite also be among the attributes?
* Shaykh: Yes, but he has attributes that make Him hate him. However, as we said: hatred and love can be partial. Allah may love a person in one respect and hate him in another respect. There is no prohibition.
* Student: Shaykh, some people, when a calamity befalls them, cite this verse: ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾ [Al 'Imran 140]. Is citing something like this (...)?
* Shaykh: What do you all say? Is it correct?
* Students: Correct.
* Shaykh: Yes, correct.
* Student: May Allah be good to you, can it be derived from this that if fighting occurs, for example, between two groups, the victorious one is always the one Allah loves?
* Shaykh: Yes, because Allah the Exalted may test the other with this affliction as a trial. But it is never permissible to think that Allah the Exalted causes falsehood to prevail over truth in an independent alternation.
* Student: May Allah bless you. If there are two football teams and one team defeats the other, and one of them cites: ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾, is this mockery of the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?
* Shaykh: What do you say? He says: one team won a football match against another team, and the next day it was reversed. Do we say: we cite the verse ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible. The victory of the first by the command and decree of Allah, and the victory of the others also by the command and decree of Allah.
* * *
I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran 141].
This is the fourth wisdom of the alternation of days among people, and of what happened to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions at Uhud. The fourth: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾.
* From this noble verse it is derived that Allah the Exalted may test the believer in order to purify him. We have mentioned that purification is of two kinds:
The first kind: the distinguishing of whose faith is sincere, who is patient under adversity, from whose faith is shaky and does not endure.
The second kind: that these calamities contain purification for the believers through the expiation of sins.
* Among its benefits, the fifth benefit: the destruction of the disbelievers. From this is derived a benefit: that blessing may be a cause of retribution, for the victory of the disbelievers leads to their joy and insolence, and when they become insolent, they are destroyed.
* Among its benefits: that the end of the disbeliever is destruction, because of His saying: ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-An'am 21] and ﴿Indeed, Allah does not reform the work of corruptors﴾ [Yunus 81], and similar examples are numerous.
* Among them: that Allah the Exalted has perfect management over His servants, because of His saying: ﴿purifies [yumahhisa]﴾ and ﴿destroys [yamhaq]﴾, for this act contained good for the believers and evil for the disbelievers.
Then the Exalted said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾. *(Am)* here is disjunctive, in the sense of *(bal)* and the interrogative hamzah, and the interrogative here is for rebuke, meaning: Do you think you will enter Paradise while what was mentioned has not occurred? His saying: ﴿hasibtum﴾ means you supposed, so *al-hisban* here means *al-zann* (supposition): ﴿that you would enter Paradise﴾, and it is the abode of the righteous which Allah the Exalted prepared for them, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Every believer in it must strive for it and hope to enter it.
His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾: the *wa* here is circumstantial, meaning: while the state is that Allah has not known those of you who strove.
*(Lamma)* comes in four senses in the Arabic language, which we mentioned previously, and here it is a particle of negation and jussive. It is distinguished from *(lam)* in that what follows it is expected to occur, as in His saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8], meaning: they have not tasted it, but it is near. Here He said: ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾, meaning: Allah has not known, but their being known is near.
His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those who strove﴾, meaning they exerted their effort in raising His word through fighting in His cause. The knowledge here is not like the eternal knowledge. The knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of two kinds: eternal, preceding, which does not entail reward or punishment; and knowledge of what has occurred after its occurrence, and this is what entails reward and punishment. Some scholars call it *"ʻilm zuhur"* (knowledge of manifestation), meaning He knows it openly after it was not. So the knowledge meant here is what? The knowledge of a thing after its existence and occurrence, because that is the knowledge that entails reward and punishment.
His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾, we said: those who exerted their effort and capacity in raising His word. ﴿and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾: *(ya'lama)* is conjoined to the previous *(ya'lami)*, and for this reason it came jussive, but it was vocalized with kasra because of the meeting of two sukun. ﴿the patient﴾, that is, those who endure what befalls them. Do you have it with a fatha? I thought it was with a kasra: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and [He has not yet known]﴾, is it only vocalized in your copy? No, with a fatha. Yes, ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾. There was a reading with kasra. With jazm in your copy?
* Student: His saying: ﴿and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾. The common reading is with a fatha on the *mim*, and it has two explanations, the more famous of which:
* Shaykh: After this one, after this, and the second?
* Student: This one is "they wished".
* Shaykh: No (...). He said: the common reading. The opposite of the common reading?
* Student: The common reading has a fatha on the *mim*, and it has two explanations:
The more famous of them is that the verb is in the accusative, and the accusative is by an implied *(an)* after the *wa* that indicates joining, so it is like your saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk," meaning do not combine them. This is the view of the Basrans. Or by the *wa* of change (*wa al-sarf*), which is the view of the Kufans, meaning that this verb should have been inflected like what precedes it.
The second: that the fatha is for the meeting of two sukun, and the verb is jussive, so when another sukun came after it, the final letter had to be moved, and the fatha was preferable because it is lighter, and the assimilation is to the vowel of the *lam*, as in the reading: ﴿and [He has not yet known] Allah﴾ with a fatha on the *mim*. The first is the preferred explanation. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur and others read it with a kasra on the *mim*, conjoined to *(ya'lam)* which is jussive by *(lamma)*. Abd al-Warith, from Ibn 'Amr and Ibn al-'Ala', read: ﴿wa-ya'lamu﴾ with a *damma*, meaning in the nominative.

**The Shaykh:** But the reading is not one of the seven canonical readings. The other two readings are not among the seven either. So ﴿وَيَعْلَمَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ with a fatḥah (on the mīm of يَعْلَمَ, the reading "and [that] He may know the patient"). Here there are three possible i'rab (grammatical analyses). The first: the wāw is the wāw of accompaniment (wāw al-ma'iyyah), as in the common saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk." Let us pause at this example to see how the meaning changes with the vowelling. You say: "Do not eat fish and drink(a) milk" (with fatḥah on the final letter), and it has one meaning. You say: "Do not eat fish and drink(i) milk" (with kasrah), and it has a different meaning from the first. You say: "Do not eat fish and drink(u) milk" (with ḍammah), and it has a meaning different from both the first and the second. So what is the meaning of the first case?

**Student:** The wāw of accompaniment.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, but what does "Do not eat fish and drink(a) milk" mean?

**The Student:** It means fish together with milk.

**The Shaykh:** That is, do not combine them. If you eat fish alone and drink milk alone, there is no harm. So fish and milk are both permissible, but the prohibited thing is combining them.

Now with ḍammah: "Do not eat fish and drink(u) milk"?

**The Student:** It contains a prohibition on eating fish and permission to drink milk.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, and it permits drinking milk. With jazm (the jussive)?

**The Student:** With jazm, it means: do not eat fish and do not drink milk.

**The Shaykh:** That is?

**The Student:** That is, each one of them is...

**The Shaykh:** Each one is forbidden, whether together or separately.

﴿وَلَمَّا يَعْلَمِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا مِنْكُمْ وَيَعْلَمَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ means: while Allah knows the patient. Patience in this context includes its three kinds. This is because jihad involves patience in obeying Allah, patience in refraining from the disobedience of Allah, and patience over painful decrees. Is that not so? So there is patience in obeying Allah, because a person must restrain himself and hold himself back. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:216]. So a person must restrain himself and hold himself back until he goes out to fight. There is patience in refraining from disobeying Allah, namely not fleeing when the two lines meet. This requires patience and endurance, because a person's patience before entering the battle may be manageable, but after entering it, when he sees the swords in front of his face, he may flee. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless it is a tactical withdrawal or to join another company, he has certainly incurred anger from Allah﴾ [al-Anfal 8:16]. And there is patience over the painful decrees of Allah, because jihad is never free of wounds, fatigue, hardship and difficulty. So in it are all three kinds of patience: ﴿and [that] He may know the patient﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: wishful thinking is the capital of the bankrupt. That is, when a person wishes for something without taking the means to it, this is a loss, like the capital of a bankrupt who will gain nothing. This is based on His saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾, to the end of the verse [Āl ʿImrān 3:142].

* Among its benefits: Paradise cannot be attained by wishing. As some of the early generations (al-salaf, the pious predecessors) said, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (may Allah have mercy on him): "Faith is not by wishful thinking nor by adornment (i.e., wishful thinking of the heart, nor adornment of outward appearance), but faith is what settles in the heart and is confirmed by deeds."[[Narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah (30866) from the hadith of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.]]

* Among its benefits: Paradise is both precious and cheap. It is precious because its price is high, since it involves giving up one's self in obedience to Allah and striving to raise His word. It is cheap because this matter is very easy for the one whom Allah makes it easy for. For this reason you find the one who is granted success hastening to be among those whose names are registered for jihad, so that he goes out and strives in the way of Allah.

* Among its benefits: Allah the Exalted tests the servant with that which shows whether he is patient or impatient, based on His saying: ﴿and [while] Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and known the patient﴾.

* Among its benefits: the recompense of Allah, whether it is punishment or reward, must be preceded by a test that the servant undergoes, based on His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾. So there must first be a test, in order to see.

* Among them: the eternal knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not itself entail reward or punishment. Rather, reward and punishment follow from the knowledge of Allah that is joined with the action, which is knowledge of a thing after its existence.

* Among its benefits: jihad is a means of entering Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾. There is no difference between jihad with weapons and jihad with knowledge; both are jihad. Indeed, the Islamic ummah may need jihad of knowledge more than jihad of weapons, and sometimes the reverse, and sometimes the two are equal. But both must exist in the Islamic ummah. There must be scholars, there must be students of knowledge, and there must be armed men who fight the disbelievers with weapons, because the obligation of jihad does not cease until the Day of Resurrection; it must remain established.

* Among the benefits of this verse: patience is also a means of entering Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿and [that] He may know the patient﴾. Know that the recompense is according to the measure of the deed. Since the reward for jihad is Paradise, and the reward for patience is likewise Paradise, this shows the great rank of both in the religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among its benefits: patience is a high station, but it requires something to be patient over. This is because patience over what agrees with one's nature is not patience. For this reason, one does not call a person who stands under a shower pouring cold water on him on a hot day "patient." Why? Because this agrees with his nature. Patience necessarily requires something that the person endures which does not agree with his nature.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 141–142 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah mentioned another benefit. How many is it? ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran 141].
* Students: The fourth.
* Shaykh: The fourth. He said: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾. *(Yumahhisa)* means *(yunaqqi)*, that is, to purify. Is the intended meaning that He purifies them from others, so that the sincere believer of pure faith becomes distinguished? Or that He purifies them from sins through the wound that befell them? Or both? Both, because we have a principle that has already preceded: when a word can carry two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is interpreted as having both meanings together.
So He purifies them: He purifies them from sins through the wound that befell them, and He also purifies them in the sense of selection, meaning that through this the elite of the believers become distinguished from those whose faith contains some doubt or disbelief. This is an obvious matter, and it is what Allah pointed to in His saying: ﴿And that Allah may make known those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran 140].
So among the wisdom in what befell the Muslims of the wound is that Allah purifies whom? Those who believe. He purifies them from sins through this calamity, and He purifies them by making clear the sincere, the elite of the chosen ones.
The fifth: He said: ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran 141]. Destroy the disbelievers. Glory be to Allah! If He grants them victory, will that be a cause of their destruction? Yes, it will be a cause of their destruction, because when they win they become arrogant, feel superior, become puffed up in themselves, and think they will always have dominance. Then they repeat the attempt a second time by fighting the Muslims, and thus it becomes their destruction. This is the meaning of the verse. Some scholars said: *"yamhaqu al-kafirin"* means He destroys them by what they inflicted upon the Muslims of the wound, so *al-mahq* is taken to mean punishment and destruction in the Hereafter. But the first meaning is more appropriate: that He destroys them with a perceptible destruction, because when they win this time, they try to repeat the attempt a second time; for what? For the sake of, what? For the sake of another victory, and thus it becomes their destruction and their annihilation.
And His saying: ﴿al-kafirin﴾ is derived from *kufr* (disbelief). The root meaning of *kufr* in the language is covering, and from it comes *al-kufra*, meaning the sheath of the date-palm spathe, because it covers what is within it.
So Allah mentioned in these two verses the touch of the wound: how many benefits? Five benefits.
Then He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾ [Al 'Imran 142]. *(Am)* here is *munqati'ah* (disjunctive), so it means *(bal)* (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah, that is: Rather, did you think you would enter Paradise? Their saying *(munqati'ah)* is to distinguish it from *muttasilah* (connective). What is the difference between them, between the connective and the disjunctive? Let the brother answer. Yes, what is the difference between disjunctive *(am)* and connective *(am)*?
* Student: The connective is coordinating.
* Shaykh: And this one is coordinating.
* Student: (...) the second sentence..
* Shaykh: And this one is coordinating.
* Student: That is, everything connected to it (...) is the beginning of a new statement.
* Another student: The connective is where the occurrence of one of the two matters is certain. Some of them mention it in the connective, like saying "this or that." Some of them mention it after the interrogative, actually or verbally, and it is followed by the hamzah, one of the two matters. These are its conditions.
* Another student: The difference between them is in one respect: first, this disjunctive is in the sense of *(bal)* and the hamzah, while the connective is in the sense of *(aw)* (or). The second..
* Shaykh: Yes, the disjunctive is in the sense of *(bal)* and the hamzah, and that one is in the sense of *(aw)*.
* Student: The connective is accompanied by the *mu'addil* (the counterpart).
* Shaykh: The connective *(am)* is accompanied by the counterpart, and the disjunctive *(am)* has no counterpart.
This is the meaning of what the brother (Hidayatullah) said. The difference becomes clear through an example. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 6]. What do we say about this?
* Students: Connective.
* Shaykh: Connective, because a counterpart is mentioned in it, and because it is in the sense of *(aw)*. Alright, ﴿Do their intellects command them to this, or are they a transgressing people?﴾ [al-Tur 32]?
* Student: Disjunctive.
* Shaykh: Pay attention: ﴿Do their intellects command them to this, or are they a transgressing people?﴾.
* Students: Disjunctive.
* Other students: In the sense of *(bal)*.
* Shaykh: In the sense of *(bal)*. Yes, because the matter of their intellects (i.e., their minds) commanding this is not a counterpart to their being transgressors. Rather, He said: Do their intellects command them to this or not? The answer: They were not commanded, but they are a transgressing people.
Alright, here: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾, is it connective or disjunctive?
* Students: Disjunctive.
* Shaykh: Disjunctive, because no counterpart is mentioned, and because it is in the sense of *(bal)* and the hamzah.
﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾, that is: Did you suppose that you would enter Paradise? The interrogative here is for rebuke, meaning: Do you think you will enter Paradise without being tested? For this reason He said: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove, and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran 142]. ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾. Paradise is the abode of the righteous and the everlasting home, may Allah make us and you among its people. ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾: *lamma* here is a jussive particle, and the proof of its jussive effect is that the verb after it is jussive. Let us ask the brother: is the verb after it jussive?
* Student: ﴿wa-lamma ya'lami﴾, yes, it is jussive.
* Shaykh: Jussive. The verb ﴿yaʿlami Allāh﴾ is kasra. How do you say it is jussive?
* Student: Kasra because of the meeting of two sukun.
* Shaykh: That is, it was vocalized with a kasra.
* Student: Because of the meeting of two sukun.
* Shaykh: And its origin?
* Student: Its origin: *wa-lamma ya'lam*.
* Shaykh: *Wa-lamma ya'lam*. But since what follows it is sukun, it took kasra, because of the principle that Ibn Malik indicated in his Al-Kafiyah:
If two sukun meet, vocalize the first with kasra,
and if it is a soft letter, its deletion is due.
His saying: ﴿lamma ya'lami﴾: *(lamma)*, we said, is jussive, as proven by the fact that the verb after it is jussive, but it was vocalized with kasra because of the meeting of two sukun.
Can *(lamma)* come in a non-jussive sense? We want to recall what has passed. Can *(lamma)* come in a non-jussive sense?
* Student: Extra (zaʼida).
* Shaykh: Extra?
* Student: *(lamma)* comes as a conditional, and *lamma* (extra) (...).
* Student: It appears so, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: It comes as what?
* Student: It comes as non-jussive.
* Shaykh: But it comes for what meaning?
* Student: That is, the meaning for which it comes..
* Shaykh: It comes as jussive; we have finished with it. And it comes as?
* Student: And I memorized an example.. It comes as conditional.
* Shaykh: It comes as conditional. Like what?
* Student: *Lamma qama Zaydun qama 'Amrun* (When Zayd stood, 'Amr stood).
* Shaykh: ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling Him, they almost became a crowd around him﴾ [al-Jinn 19]. That is one.
* Student: It comes as temporal.
* Shaykh: Temporal, meaning what?
* Student: Meaning *(hina)* (when).
* Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: ﴿So when We decreed death for him, nothing showed them his death﴾ [Saba' 14].
* Shaykh: That one is conditional.
* Student: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿So their gods that they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came﴾ [Hud 101].
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿So their gods that they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came﴾, that is, when the command of your Lord came. That is three.
* Student: In the sense of exceptive *(illa)*.
* Shaykh: In the sense of exceptive *(illa)*.
* Student: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq 4].
* Shaykh: ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian﴾, that is: except that over it is a guardian. Four meanings.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding His saying: ﴿and that He may take martyrs from among you﴾. Can we not take from this a general principle: that Allah does not take all people as martyrs, but takes only those who have the qualities of faith and piety? Are these the ones He takes as martyrs?
* Shaykh: This allows for it if we say *(min)* is partitive. But if we say it is explanatory, then it is not determined.
* Student: That is, He may take martyrs from others too..
* Shaykh: Rationally it is permissible, but it did not happen, because many Muslims died without martyrdom.
* Student: Especially in jihad?
* Shaykh: Yes, even in jihad, many Muslims did not attain martyrdom.
* Student: So we do not take it as a general principle?
* Shaykh: No, we do not take it as a general principle, because since *(min)* may be explanatory, we do not affirm that it is partitive.
* Student: The principle, Shaykh, regarding deriving the attributes of Allah from the implicit meaning (mafhum) of some verses, like: ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ [Al 'Imran 140] (...), because this may be indicated by other texts. But there are verses that are not indicated by other texts: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾ [Luqman 18] (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, He loves whoever is free of that.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾ [Luqman 18]. Regarding one who is not self-deluded and not boastful, do we say that Allah loves him?
* Shaykh: Yes, He loves whoever is free of these two qualities.
* Student: Is it possible that he has other qualities?
* Shaykh: Yes, he may have another quality that makes Him dislike him, and another quality that makes Him love him. But the negation of love from the self-deluded boaster indicates the affirmation of love for others, or for its opposite, which is better.
* Student: But, Shaykh, can the opposite also be among the attributes?
* Shaykh: Yes, but he has attributes that make Him hate him. However, as we said: hatred and love can be partial. Allah may love a person in one respect and hate him in another respect. There is no prohibition.
* Student: Shaykh, some people, when a calamity befalls them, cite this verse: ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾ [Al 'Imran 140]. Is citing something like this (...)?
* Shaykh: What do you all say? Is it correct?
* Students: Correct.
* Shaykh: Yes, correct.
* Student: May Allah be good to you, can it be derived from this that if fighting occurs, for example, between two groups, the victorious one is always the one Allah loves?
* Shaykh: Yes, because Allah the Exalted may test the other with this affliction as a trial. But it is never permissible to think that Allah the Exalted causes falsehood to prevail over truth in an independent alternation.
* Student: May Allah bless you. If there are two football teams and one team defeats the other, and one of them cites: ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾, is this mockery of the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?
* Shaykh: What do you say? He says: one team won a football match against another team, and the next day it was reversed. Do we say: we cite the verse ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible. The victory of the first by the command and decree of Allah, and the victory of the others also by the command and decree of Allah.
* * *
I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran 141].
This is the fourth wisdom of the alternation of days among people, and of what happened to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions at Uhud. The fourth: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾.
* From this noble verse it is derived that Allah the Exalted may test the believer in order to purify him. We have mentioned that purification is of two kinds:
The first kind: the distinguishing of whose faith is sincere, who is patient under adversity, from whose faith is shaky and does not endure.
The second kind: that these calamities contain purification for the believers through the expiation of sins.
* Among its benefits, the fifth benefit: the destruction of the disbelievers. From this is derived a benefit: that blessing may be a cause of retribution, for the victory of the disbelievers leads to their joy and insolence, and when they become insolent, they are destroyed.
* Among its benefits: that the end of the disbeliever is destruction, because of His saying: ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-An'am 21] and ﴿Indeed, Allah does not reform the work of corruptors﴾ [Yunus 81], and similar examples are numerous.
* Among them: that Allah the Exalted has perfect management over His servants, because of His saying: ﴿purifies [yumahhisa]﴾ and ﴿destroys [yamhaq]﴾, for this act contained good for the believers and evil for the disbelievers.
Then the Exalted said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾. *(Am)* here is disjunctive, in the sense of *(bal)* and the interrogative hamzah, and the interrogative here is for rebuke, meaning: Do you think you will enter Paradise while what was mentioned has not occurred? His saying: ﴿hasibtum﴾ means you supposed, so *al-hisban* here means *al-zann* (supposition): ﴿that you would enter Paradise﴾, and it is the abode of the righteous which Allah the Exalted prepared for them, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Every believer in it must strive for it and hope to enter it.
His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾: the *wa* here is circumstantial, meaning: while the state is that Allah has not known those of you who strove.
*(Lamma)* comes in four senses in the Arabic language, which we mentioned previously, and here it is a particle of negation and jussive. It is distinguished from *(lam)* in that what follows it is expected to occur, as in His saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8], meaning: they have not tasted it, but it is near. Here He said: ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾, meaning: Allah has not known, but their being known is near.
His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those who strove﴾, meaning they exerted their effort in raising His word through fighting in His cause. The knowledge here is not like the eternal knowledge. The knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of two kinds: eternal, preceding, which does not entail reward or punishment; and knowledge of what has occurred after its occurrence, and this is what entails reward and punishment. Some scholars call it *"ʻilm zuhur"* (knowledge of manifestation), meaning He knows it openly after it was not. So the knowledge meant here is what? The knowledge of a thing after its existence and occurrence, because that is the knowledge that entails reward and punishment.
His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾, we said: those who exerted their effort and capacity in raising His word. ﴿and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾: *(ya'lama)* is conjoined to the previous *(ya'lami)*, and for this reason it came jussive, but it was vocalized with kasra because of the meeting of two sukun. ﴿the patient﴾, that is, those who endure what befalls them. Do you have it with a fatha? I thought it was with a kasra: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and [He has not yet known]﴾, is it only vocalized in your copy? No, with a fatha. Yes, ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾. There was a reading with kasra. With jazm in your copy?
* Student: His saying: ﴿and [He has not yet known] the patient﴾. The common reading is with a fatha on the *mim*, and it has two explanations, the more famous of which:
* Shaykh: After this one, after this, and the second?
* Student: This one is "they wished".
* Shaykh: No (...). He said: the common reading. The opposite of the common reading?
* Student: The common reading has a fatha on the *mim*, and it has two explanations:
The more famous of them is that the verb is in the accusative, and the accusative is by an implied *(an)* after the *wa* that indicates joining, so it is like your saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk," meaning do not combine them. This is the view of the Basrans. Or by the *wa* of change (*wa al-sarf*), which is the view of the Kufans, meaning that this verb should have been inflected like what precedes it.
The second: that the fatha is for the meeting of two sukun, and the verb is jussive, so when another sukun came after it, the final letter had to be moved, and the fatha was preferable because it is lighter, and the assimilation is to the vowel of the *lam*, as in the reading: ﴿and [He has not yet known] Allah﴾ with a fatha on the *mim*. The first is the preferred explanation. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur and others read it with a kasra on the *mim*, conjoined to *(ya'lam)* which is jussive by *(lamma)*. Abd al-Warith, from Ibn 'Amr and Ibn al-'Ala', read: ﴿wa-ya'lamu﴾ with a *damma*, meaning in the nominative.

**The Shaykh:** But the reading is not one of the seven canonical readings. The other two readings are not among the seven either. So ﴿وَيَعْلَمَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ with a fatḥah (on the mīm of يَعْلَمَ, the reading "and [that] He may know the patient"). Here there are three possible i'rab (grammatical analyses). The first: the wāw is the wāw of accompaniment (wāw al-ma'iyyah), as in the common saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk." Let us pause at this example to see how the meaning changes with the vowelling. You say: "Do not eat fish and drink(a) milk" (with fatḥah on the final letter), and it has one meaning. You say: "Do not eat fish and drink(i) milk" (with kasrah), and it has a different meaning from the first. You say: "Do not eat fish and drink(u) milk" (with ḍammah), and it has a meaning different from both the first and the second. So what is the meaning of the first case?

**Student:** The wāw of accompaniment.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, but what does "Do not eat fish and drink(a) milk" mean?

**The Student:** It means fish together with milk.

**The Shaykh:** That is, do not combine them. If you eat fish alone and drink milk alone, there is no harm. So fish and milk are both permissible, but the prohibited thing is combining them.

Now with ḍammah: "Do not eat fish and drink(u) milk"?

**The Student:** It contains a prohibition on eating fish and permission to drink milk.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, and it permits drinking milk. With jazm (the jussive)?

**The Student:** With jazm, it means: do not eat fish and do not drink milk.

**The Shaykh:** That is?

**The Student:** That is, each one of them is...

**The Shaykh:** Each one is forbidden, whether together or separately.

﴿وَلَمَّا يَعْلَمِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا مِنْكُمْ وَيَعْلَمَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ means: while Allah knows the patient. Patience in this context includes its three kinds. This is because jihad involves patience in obeying Allah, patience in refraining from the disobedience of Allah, and patience over painful decrees. Is that not so? So there is patience in obeying Allah, because a person must restrain himself and hold himself back. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:216]. So a person must restrain himself and hold himself back until he goes out to fight. There is patience in refraining from disobeying Allah, namely not fleeing when the two lines meet. This requires patience and endurance, because a person's patience before entering the battle may be manageable, but after entering it, when he sees the swords in front of his face, he may flee. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless it is a tactical withdrawal or to join another company, he has certainly incurred anger from Allah﴾ [al-Anfal 8:16]. And there is patience over the painful decrees of Allah, because jihad is never free of wounds, fatigue, hardship and difficulty. So in it are all three kinds of patience: ﴿and [that] He may know the patient﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: wishful thinking is the capital of the bankrupt. That is, when a person wishes for something without taking the means to it, this is a loss, like the capital of a bankrupt who will gain nothing. This is based on His saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾, to the end of the verse [Āl ʿImrān 3:142].

* Among its benefits: Paradise cannot be attained by wishing. As some of the early generations (al-salaf, the pious predecessors) said, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (may Allah have mercy on him): "Faith is not by wishful thinking nor by adornment (i.e., wishful thinking of the heart, nor adornment of outward appearance), but faith is what settles in the heart and is confirmed by deeds."[[Narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah (30866) from the hadith of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.]]

* Among its benefits: Paradise is both precious and cheap. It is precious because its price is high, since it involves giving up one's self in obedience to Allah and striving to raise His word. It is cheap because this matter is very easy for the one whom Allah makes it easy for. For this reason you find the one who is granted success hastening to be among those whose names are registered for jihad, so that he goes out and strives in the way of Allah.

* Among its benefits: Allah the Exalted tests the servant with that which shows whether he is patient or impatient, based on His saying: ﴿and [while] Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and known the patient﴾.

* Among its benefits: the recompense of Allah, whether it is punishment or reward, must be preceded by a test that the servant undergoes, based on His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾. So there must first be a test, in order to see.

* Among them: the eternal knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not itself entail reward or punishment. Rather, reward and punishment follow from the knowledge of Allah that is joined with the action, which is knowledge of a thing after its existence.

* Among its benefits: jihad is a means of entering Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾. There is no difference between jihad with weapons and jihad with knowledge; both are jihad. Indeed, the Islamic ummah may need jihad of knowledge more than jihad of weapons, and sometimes the reverse, and sometimes the two are equal. But both must exist in the Islamic ummah. There must be scholars, there must be students of knowledge, and there must be armed men who fight the disbelievers with weapons, because the obligation of jihad does not cease until the Day of Resurrection; it must remain established.

* Among the benefits of this verse: patience is also a means of entering Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿and [that] He may know the patient﴾. Know that the recompense is according to the measure of the deed. Since the reward for jihad is Paradise, and the reward for patience is likewise Paradise, this shows the great rank of both in the religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among its benefits: patience is a high station, but it requires something to be patient over. This is because patience over what agrees with one's nature is not patience. For this reason, one does not call a person who stands under a shower pouring cold water on him on a hot day "patient." Why? Because this agrees with his nature. Patience necessarily requires something that the person endures which does not agree with his nature.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 143:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you had certainly been wishing for death before you encountered it. So now you have seen it, while you were looking on.﴾ [Al 'Imran 143]

﴿And you had certainly⁠﴾: Allah emphasized this sentence to establish the proof against them. ﴿Certainly you had⁠﴾ — the sentence here is emphasized with three emphatics: the implied oath, the lam that falls in its answer, and (qad). "You had" refers to the past, ﴿wishing for death before you encountered it⁠﴾. They were wishing for death, not death on the bed, but death in the cause of Allah. This is because, as many people know, many of the Companions stayed away from Badr. The expedition of Badr was not undertaken for fighting but to seize the caravan. For this reason, no more than three hundred and some men from all of Madinah went out, intending the caravan. But Allah brought them together with their enemy without appointment, so some of the Muslims were martyred, about thirteen men. Those who had not reached this expedition wished that they had gone out in it, especially the young among them.

For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ consulted them at the Battle of Uhud, asking: "Should he go out to the enemy or remain in Madinah?" They all said: "No, let us go out," especially those who had stayed away from Badr. What were they wishing by that? Martyrdom, as their brothers were martyred at Badr. They were wishing for death, saying: "Would that we had gone out! Would that we had been killed at Badr!" They wish for death. Wishing (tamanni) is that a person seeks, in his heart, something that is difficult to attain. This is wishing: that a person wishes in his heart for something difficult to obtain, whether it is difficult and then obtained, or difficult and never obtained. For this reason, wishing falls upon impossible things, like the words of the poet:

"Would that youth might return one day, and I would inform it of what old age has done."
Can it return? It is impossible for it to return. It can also be about something that is hard but rare. So they were wishing for death in their souls, wishing that they had been with the people of Badr, that they had been martyred and killed in the cause of Allah.

﴿before you encountered it, so now you have seen it⁠﴾: meaning, what you wished for has come to you; what you are wishing for has happened to you. ﴿while you were looking on⁠﴾: meaning you saw it while you were at the utmost of perception. Consider His words ﴿while you were looking on⁠﴾: is it emphatic or newly informative?

Most exegetes hold that it is emphatic, saying: because whoever sees has looked. But in reality it is informative, because a person may see without truly grasping what he sees; he may see a thing while heedless of it. But if he sees it while looking at it fully, concentrated, this is a specific looking, more specific than general looking. We take it to be so because the basic principle in speech is informing (ta'sis), since emphasis (tawkid) is a kind of addition; emphasis is a kind of addition that contains only the confirmation of what has passed, and may not be needed. But informing is the basic principle.

So Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿you had been wishing for death before⁠﴾ and establishes the testimony with emphasis: ﴿certainly you had been wishing for death⁠﴾, ﴿so now you have seen it while you were looking on⁠﴾. So why does this cowardice occur from you? Yes, and for this reason He said: ﴿so now you have seen it⁠﴾, meaning death; yes, you have seen it, meaning death. They saw those who were martyred at the Battle of Uhud; they saw them with their own eyes.

Some exegetes went to the view that the meaning is that they saw its causes, which is fighting, because whoever was not killed did not see death. But this interpretation is open to question, because a person sees death in himself and in others. ﴿So now you have seen it⁠﴾ means among yourselves ﴿while you were looking on⁠﴾.

In this verse there is a grammatical problem: the phrase ﴿you had been wishing⁠﴾, whose form is that of the past but which is expressed in the form of the present. There is a difficulty, because tamanna is past.

* Student: The taa was dropped.

* Shaykh: Which one?

* Student: The taa of the present tense: "wa-laqad kuntum tatamannawna al-mawt."

* Shaykh: Excellent, its original form is: tatamannawna al-mawt.

We want you to bring us another example in the Qur'an?

* Student: Many. When two taas come together, one of them is deleted (...) for heaviness.

* Shaykh: I want one, one example in the Qur'an that attests to this?

* Student: ﴿tadhakkarun⁠﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿la'allakum⁠﴾.

* Student: Yes, indeed: ﴿la'allakum tadhakkarun⁠﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿la'allakum tadhakkarun⁠﴾ is correct, meaning: tatadhakkarun. ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire blazing⁠﴾ [al-Layl 14], meaning: tatalaззā, and it is abundant, as the brother said.

* Benefits of this verse:

* First: Establishing the proof against those who were wishing for death, and having seen it, cowardice still occurred from them; by His words: ﴿And you had certainly been wishing for death before you encountered it. So now you have seen it⁠﴾, meaning: here you now have seen it, so what is your position?

* And in it: a person should not wish for something disliked, because if he wishes for it and it happens, he may recoil and not be patient. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not wish to meet the enemy, and ask Allah for well-being. But when you meet them, be patient, for Paradise is under the shade of the swords." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3024) and Muslim (1742/20) from 'Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, and the wording is his.] Likewise, a person may feel within himself that he is able to endure something, but he is unable to bear it. They mention that Sahnun, the student of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, was among the worshippers, and one day he said a statement meaning: "O Lord, I am patient, so however You will, test me." Look at the poor, needy son of Adam; that is, "I will be patient with every trial, so test me, O Lord." He was afflicted with difficulty in urination; he could not urinate except with severe hardship. They said: He would go around the schools of the children, the schools where the young children were, and say: "Pray for your liar uncle, pray for your liar uncle." He went to the children because they are closer to being answered, due to the purity and soundness of their hearts, and they have no sins. (He called himself) "the liar" because he had said: "I am patient, so however You will, test me," and he did not endure. Likewise, a person should ask Allah for well-being, but if he is tested, let him be patient.

* Another benefit of this verse: there is no harm in rebuking a person who challenged and claimed a lofty position for himself, if one finds that he has shrunk back in that position. For example, if a man claims that he is steadfast and resolute and the like, but when calamities strike him he becomes a coward, faint-hearted, unable to bear it, then he is reminded of it. I think one of the poets used to say in his poetry:

"The horses, the night, and the desert know me, and the sword, the spear, the paper, and the pen."
Courage and knowledge, writing everything. An expedition took place and this poet was present in it; he wanted to flee and turn his back, and those around him had memorized this line of his poetry, so they said: "What is wrong with you, so-and-so, when you say:"

"The horses, the night, and the desert know me, and the sword, the spear, the paper, and the pen."
He reproached himself and returned. I think, if I have not forgotten, that he was killed.

So a person, before being struck by trial, may feel in himself that he is strong and will be patient, but he is unable. If you remind someone of something he used to boast about, saying: "I do this, I say this, I am patient," this is not objectionable. But is this praiseworthy if the matter is harmful, or should one look to the public interest? One looks to the public interest. The poor man may be boasting about what is nothing to boast of; if he falls into it and wants to back away, then if you incite him, he falls into harm. So the matter is referred to the public interest.

* Another benefit of this verse: the permissibility of emphasis according to the view of one who holds that His words ﴿you have certainly seen it while you were looking on⁠﴾ contain emphasis, i.e., the permissibility of emphasizing a wording when there is need for it, and that this is what eloquence requires; indeed, it may even be required, as in this verse. So this verse, according to the view that His words ﴿while you were looking on⁠﴾ are emphatic and bring no new meaning, but according to the preferred view which we favored, that they bring a new meaning, we do not derive this benefit from this verse, but we derive it from another verse, such as: ﴿And what can make you know what is the Day of Recompense? Then, what can make you know what is the Day of Recompense?⁠﴾ [al-Infitar 17-18], ﴿No! You are going to know. Then, no! You are going to know⁠﴾ [al-Takathur 3-4], ﴿Woe to you, and woe! Then woe to you, and woe!⁠﴾ [al-Qiyamah 34-35]. There are many such emphases for importance in the Qur'an.

* Student: O Shaykh, in the verse: ﴿And you had certainly been wishing for death⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran 143], "The Messenger ﷺ forbade wishing for death" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5671), Muslim (2680/10) from Anas ibn Malik], so how do we reconcile the two?

* Shaykh: Yes, this incident is a question that needs to be pointed out. They were wishing for death; we mentioned in the exegesis they were wishing for what?

* Students: Martyrdom.

* Shaykh: Martyrdom, death in the cause of Allah, not death in absolute terms. But it is derived from it that it is permissible for a person to wish for martyrdom; it is permissible for a person to wish for martyrdom while he is in that state. Indeed, if it were said that this is legislated, it would not be far-fetched. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Allah, grant me martyrdom in Your way and death in the city of Your Messenger" [related by al-Bukhari (1890) from 'Umar]. So people would say: how is this supplication, and how is it answered? Madinah is an Islamic city, but Allah answered his supplication: he was killed unjustly while praying. He was not killed because he was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab; he was killed because he was upholding the command of Allah, implementing the law of Allah. He was killed by a Magian hostile to the Muslims, a warmonger against them, so he was killed in the city of the Messenger ﷺ and died there.

So wishing for death is permissible, but some later scholars mentioned that it is not permissible to wish for martyrdom, saying: because your wishing for martyrdom entails that the enemies overcome the Muslims. So reflect on this statement: is it true or false?

And here He says: ﴿Muhammad is but a Messenger; the Messengers have passed away before him﴾ [Al 'Imran 144]. Muhammad, that is, Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib al-Qurashi al-Hashimi, the Seal of the Prophets. ﴿Muhammad is but a Messenger; the Messengers have passed away before him﴾. This is the point of benefit. As for his being a Messenger, that is a known matter. But the point of benefit is His saying: ﴿the Messengers have passed away before him﴾, as a preparation for what follows, which is His saying: ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ [Al 'Imran 144]. The meaning is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a Messenger, and the Messengers passed away before him. Some of them died, and some of them were killed, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and they killed the Prophets without right﴾ [Al-Baqarah 61]. If that is so, did their peoples abandon their religions when their prophets died or were killed?

The answer: No, they did not abandon the religions. That is because nations worship Allah and follow the Messengers, and the Messengers' message is not cut off by their death. Rather, their message remains as long as the message remains, until a message comes that abrogates it (naskh, abrogation). As for the message of the Prophet ﷺ, there is no abrogating message for it, because it is the last of the messages.

This verse was revealed when Satan cried out on the day of Uhud. Satan shouted that Muhammad had been killed. When he said this, it weakened the resolve of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, for two reasons:

First: because the death of the Prophet ﷺ is a great calamity that saddens the heart and weakens the soul.

Second: because Muhammad ﷺ was their leader, and when a leader dies, it will undoubtedly have an effect on those who are guided by his leadership.

When the news spread that Muhammad ﷺ had been killed, what happened to the Muslims happened. Grief upon grief befell them, and some of them experienced some weakness. But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rebuked them, saying: ﴿Muhammad is but a Messenger; the Messengers have passed away before him﴾. If that is so, did the Messengers who came before and died or were killed see their peoples apostatize after them? No. Rather, the messages remained and the followers remained.

Here He said: ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾. The hamzah here is the interrogative of rebuke (al-istifham al-tawbikhi). That is, "Will you turn back on your heels if he dies or is killed?" This does not befit you, nor is it proper for you. Rather, as long as his Sharia remains, following him remains, and it does not befit any believer to turn back on his heels when the Messenger ﷺ dies.

His saying ﴿So if he dies﴾ contains the interrogative hamzah, and after it the conjunctive fa'. It has already passed us that a structure like this—

* Shaykh: Yes, but a structure like this is permissible in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). I say: a structure like this, what is permissible in terms of i'rab?
Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is permissible to parse it in two ways. The first way?

* Shaykh: Is the hamzah now before the fa' in ﴿أَفَإِنْ مَاتَ﴾?
* Student: Or it comes after the fa'.
* Shaykh: Is that not clear?
* Student: That it be conjunctive (ʿatifah).
* Shaykh: Is the hamzah of interrogation in its place, and the fa' after it, or the conjunctive particle after it?

* Shaykh: The conjunctive particle after it. This is the case if we keep the hamzah in its place, unchanged; so the conjunctive particle after it is what?

* Shaykh: It is conjunctive to what?

* Shaykh: A deleted thing. And what is the estimate of this deleted thing?

* Shaykh: Whatever suits the context. That is one way. The second way?

* Shaykh: Yes. But is this its original place or not, in this second way?

* Shaykh: The place of the hamzah is after the conjunctive particle, but it was moved forward for the sake of the front position (al-sadr). And based on this way?

* Shaykh: The conjunctive particle is conjunctive to what came before, meaning to the thing previously mentioned.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back?﴾ [Al 'Imran 144]. This is a conditional sentence. ﴿If he dies﴾ is the conditional verb (fi'l al-shart), and ﴿will you turn back on your heels?﴾ is the response of the condition (jawab al-shart). But the locus of rebuke is in reality the response of the condition, because He rebukes them for turning back on the supposition that he dies or is killed. That is: "Will you turn back on your heels if he dies or is killed? It does not befit you."

His saying ﴿If he dies﴾ means by other than human action, ﴿or is killed﴾ by human action.

His saying ﴿you turned back on your heels﴾ means you went backward. The plural a'qab is of 'aqib, which is the heel (al-'urquub). One who turns back on his heels is walking without guidance, like one who walks face-down, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is one who walks face-down more guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ [Al-Mulk 22]. Turning back on the heels is more severe and more eloquent, because in turning back on the heel a person walks in a manner other than the usual posture. It is also possible that the intended meaning of turning back on the heel is that he falls on his back and cannot advance or stand straight.

His saying ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all﴾ [Al 'Imran 144]. Here He said ﴿whoever turns back﴾, so He shifted the sentence to a general form, rather than saying "And if you turn back on your heels, you will not harm Allah at all," so that the ruling would be general and comprehensive. So His saying ﴿whoever turns back﴾: this "man" is conditional, encompassing every person who turns back on his heels. The verb after it is in the jussive mood (majzum). (...) As for the response of the condition, it is what?
* Student: ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿will not harm Allah at all﴾. It is known that the response of the condition is in the jussive mood, but here it is in the accusative.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿will not harm﴾. It is known that the response of the condition occurs in the jussive mood?
* Student: (lan) is a particle of the accusative, which precedes the imperfect verb, with the estimate (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. We say: because (lan) entered upon it, the response of the condition became a sentence. And why was it accompanied by the fa'?
Why was it joined with the fa' in: ﴿so He will not harm Allah﴾?
* Student: For the sake of conjunction.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: It was preceded by (lan).
* Shaykh: Because it was introduced by it; the response of the condition was introduced by (lan). Recite the rule verse for this?
* Student:
A nominal sentence, and imperative, and with an inert word, and with mā, and with qad, and with lan, and with the sīn and the sawf.
* Shaykh: ﴿will not harm Allah at all﴾: "shay'an" is an indefinite in a negative context, so it is general. That is, whoever turns back on his heels and apostatizes from faith will not harm Allah, because Allah, glorified and exalted, does not benefit from the obedience of the obedient, nor is He harmed by the disobedience of the disobedient. For this reason He said: ﴿whoever turns back on his heels﴾, so he returns after having been a Muslim, ﴿will not harm Allah at all﴾. Rather, in reality, he harms only himself.

﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ [Al 'Imran 144]. The sīn is for the near future (al-tanfīs), and it transforms the imperfect verb from being suitable for the present and future (...) to being for the future. Sawf is similar to it, except that sawf indicates a delay, while the sīn indicates immediacy.

﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾: that is, He will recompense them. The grateful (al-shakirin) are those who have performed the thanks of Allah's blessing. It has already passed us that gratitude (shukr) is the performance of obedience toward the Bestower with the heart, tongue, and limbs. So acknowledging with the heart that blessings are from Allah is gratitude; praising Allah for them with the tongue is gratitude; and carrying out obedience appropriate to that blessing is gratitude. Thus the gratitude for knowledge, for example, is acting upon it and spreading it; the gratitude for wealth is spending it in obedience to Allah; the gratitude for physical strength is using the body in obedience to Allah, and so on.

Know that between shukr and hamd (praise) there is a partial overlap in both generality and specificity, meaning that each is more general than the other in some respect. In that praise may be for the perfection of the one praised and for his bestowing favors, praise is more general than gratitude. And in that praise is with the tongue, it is more specific than gratitude. Gratitude, in that it relates to the heart, tongue, and limbs, is more general than praise, and in that it is in return for a blessing, it is more specific than praise. A poet says:

The blessings have benefited you from me in three: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden inner heart.

By this explanation we know that there is no synonymy between praise and gratitude; rather they are distinct. They agree when one praises Allah, the Exalted, for His blessing, as when one eats or drinks and says "Praise be to Allah." This is considered both gratitude and praise. They differ when one praises Allah for His perfection; here this is not from the category of gratitude. And when one thanks Allah with his limbs, this is not from the category of praise.

He said: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ [Al 'Imran 144]. With what will He reward them? Allah, glorified and exalted, clarified this general statement in His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Al-An'am 160]. ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ is this reward. And it is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that "Allah multiplies the good deed up to ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times"[[Reported by Muslim (1151/164) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

* We take the benefits:
* In this verse: the clarification that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a human being to whom death befalls, as it befalls all the Messengers; by His saying: ﴿Muhammad is but a Messenger; the Messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed﴾ and so on [Al 'Imran: 144].
* And also in it: that the Prophet ﷺ is not a lord to be invoked, nor a god to be worshipped; by His saying: ﴿but a Messenger; the Messengers have passed away before him﴾.
* Among its benefits: that it is appropriate to present evidence by mentioning similar cases, so that a person is convinced by what he hears; by His saying: ﴿the Messengers have passed away before him﴾. For whoever hears this is convinced, and says: since the earlier Messengers died or were killed, this is a consolation for him.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation that Muhammad ﷺ is the Seal of the Messengers; by His saying: ﴿the Messengers have passed away before him﴾, where the definite article here is for generality. He did not say "Messengers have passed away before him," but said "the Messengers." If all the Messengers have passed away before him, it follows that he is their last.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the permissibility of the Messenger's death and killing, peace and blessings be upon him; by His saying: ﴿So if he dies or is killed﴾.

If someone says: this is problematic, because Allah said about the martyrs: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran 169], and ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾ [Al-Baqarah 154]. If this is the case for the martyrs, how can the Messenger ﷺ be dead when he is better than the martyrs?

The answer to that: we say that life is of two kinds: worldly physical life, which is the life of this world, and barzakhi life (life in the intermediate state), which is not like the life of this world. It is this which is established for whom? For the martyrs. And the Prophets are better than the martyrs, in that Allah has forbidden the earth to consume their bodies, whereas the earth may consume the bodies of the martyrs. So the bodies of the Prophets remain, and their barzakhi life is more complete than the life of the martyrs without doubt.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the refutation of one who imagines or claims that the Messenger ﷺ is alive in his grave; by His saying: ﴿So if he dies or is killed﴾. And we know by necessity from the mass-transmitted report (al-naql al-mutawatir) that the Prophet ﷺ was not killed, is that not so? He was not killed by sword or spear; he died on his bed. But it is established from him ﷺ that he said: "The morsel of Khaybar has continued to afflict me, and this is the time of the severing of the aorta from me"[[Reported by al-Bazzar (8007) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

Al-abhar: a vein in the instep (al-ibhām); if it is severed, a person dies. This indicates that his eating of the poisoned sheep in Khaybar had an effect on his death. For this reason some of the Successors (tabi'un), and I think it was al-Zuhri, said: "The Prophet ﷺ was a martyr, because the Jews killed him"[[Reported by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (1684) from the hadith of al-Zuhri.]]. But Allah, the Exalted, prolonged his life until it was delayed. And this is not far-fetched, this is not far-fetched, because the morsel of Khaybar, as was established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Its effect has remained in my palate"[[Reported by Muslim (2190/45) from the hadith of Anas.]]: the trace of poison remained in his palate. The poison was severe, and for this reason some of the Companions died. One of the Companions who ate with him died, but the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, did not swallow the meat he had eaten.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that apostasy from Islam is turning back on one's heels, and the effect of turning back on one's heels is not hidden from us. ﴿You turned back on your heels﴾, and so it is; for one who is upon Islam walks upon proof and light, walks upon a straight path.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the refutation of the atheists who say that Islam is reactionary and a return to the past. We say to them: you are the reactionaries; you are the ones who turned back on your heels. As for one who holds fast to Islam, he is the progressive, because Islam urges progress toward every virtue: ﴿Hasten to forgiveness﴾ [Al 'Imran 133], ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾ [Al-Baqarah 148], ﴿Race to forgiveness﴾ [Al-Hadid 21]. All these verses indicate that Islam commands progress. But it is not progress toward disbelief, of which Allah said about its leader: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire﴾ [Hud 98]. Rather, it is progress toward a Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous. The point is that this verse contains a refutation of whom? Of the atheists who claim that adherence to Islam is reactionary. We say to them: adherence to Islam is progress, and lagging behind Islam is reaction.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is free of need of the obedience of the obedient; by His saying: ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the negation of harm from Allah, and that nothing can harm Him. But if someone says: Has not Allah said in His Book: ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [Al-Ahzab 57]? And in the sacred hadith: "The son of Adam hurts Me; he reviles time"[[Agreed upon: reported by al-Bukhari (4826) and Muslim (2246/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], thus affirming harm to Allah?

The answer: harm does not necessarily entail damage. Allah may be hurt without being harmed. Let me give you an example: if a person sat beside you having eaten onions or smoked tobacco, would you not be hurt by its smell?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. But are you harmed? You are not harmed. When you see something disagreeable, you are hurt but not harmed. Therefore, it does not follow from Allah, the Exalted, being (...) that He is harmed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the encouragement to gratitude; by His saying: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾. Its aspect: the reward is attributed to Allah, which indicates its greatness, because the reward from the Great is great. For this reason a good deed is multiplied ten times, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of using a general statement in speech when it has been explained in detail in another place, based on His saying: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾. This verse is mujmal (general, unspecified), for Allah the Exalted did not clarify how this reward will be. However, it has been clarified in other texts, and the Sharia (sacred law) explains one part of it by another, qualifies one part by another, and specifies one part by another. Whatever you find general in one place, you find clarified in another place, and this is among the perfections of the Sharia.
