For when something comes to you in general terms, your soul yearns to know the clarification of that generality, so you strive, search, compare the evidences, and connect them to one another until the matter becomes clear to you, and so that you are familiar with all the texts at all times.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: even if all of creation were to apostatize, Allah the Exalted would not be harmed by that, based on His saying: ﴿they will not harm Allah at all﴾. This is general, encompassing any harm whatsoever, whether it comes from an individual or from a group.
* Student: (...) barzakhi life (...). They may raise an objection to us, saying: the barzakh life is shared by all the dead, whether a martyr or not?
* Shaykh: No, not at all. The non-martyr does not live this life.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this is not that life. For in the barzakh, the most that has been reported is that his soul is returned to him for the sake of answering the two angels only. But those (martyrs) are living permanently until they are resurrected.
* Student: We said: we cite His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾ [Aal 'Imran 144], as evidence that he is the Seal of the Prophets (...) the messengers, and the verse in which it is stated: ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was but a messenger; messengers had passed away before him, and his mother was a truthful woman﴾ [al-Ma'idah 75]?
* Shaykh: ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was but a messenger; messengers had passed away before him, and his mother was a truthful woman﴾ — yes, this is correct. It indicates generality, and therefore there is no messenger between Muhammad and Jesus. So if the first verse is general concerning Jesus, this verse specifies it, meaning: messengers have passed away before him, except Muhammad.
* Student: (...) The Prophet ﷺ has absolute sovereignty in this world over all people. So, O Shaykh, can we say that so-and-so is the master of the martyrs (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, according to the opinion of al-Zuhri.
* Student: We said: does this statement contradict the hadith that (...) is the master of the martyrs?
* Shaykh: No, it does not contradict. That is, the master of the martyrs is from among the followers (tabi'un) who followed the messengers. I say: the master of the martyrs is from among those who followed the messengers, meaning from among the nations; as for the Messenger, he is unique.
* Student: We said: the abhar (the artery in the thumb) — if it is severed, a person dies. If a thief steals and his hand is cut off, does he not die?
* Shaykh: Fine, if his hand is cut off, the stump must be cauterized. For this reason they said: there must be boiling oil present; from the moment his hand is cut, it is dipped in this oil so that the bleeding stops. If it were left, he would bleed out and die.
* Student: But the intent is, if it is cut, even if, for example, the blood is stopped?
* Shaykh: No, if it is stopped, he does not die, that is known.
* Student: (...) Thanking Allah instead of praising Allah?
* Shaykh: Correct, there is nothing wrong with it.
* Student: (...) It is not said that "al-hamd" is better (...)?
* Shaykh: You asked: is it permissible to say "ash-shukr lillah" or not? We say: there is no harm.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Better what?
* Student: "Al-hamdu lillah" (...).
* Shaykh: It depends on the situation. I say: it depends on the situation. The hadith: "Indeed, Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a morsel and praises Him for it" [[Narrated by Muslim (2734/88) from the hadith of Anas.]], and here it is praise, and it is also thanks at the same time.

**Student:** Verse 145 through 147 of Surah Al ʿImran:

﴿It is not for any soul to die except by Allah's permission, at an appointed time. Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him from it. We will reward the grateful.﴾ [145] ﴿How many a prophet has fought, and with him many devoted followers. They did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they grow feeble or submit. Allah loves the steadfast.﴾ [146] ﴿Their only words were: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs, make our feet firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people."﴾ [147]

**The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿It is not for any soul to die except by Allah's permission﴾. ﴿Mā kāna li-nafsin an tamūt﴾ means that it is absolutely impossible for any soul among souls to die except by Allah's permission. Whatever people try to cause someone's death without Allah's permission, they will never be able to do so. When ﴿mā kāna﴾ occurs, it denotes something that is impossible, either legally (sharʿan) or by divine decree (qadaran). So in this verse, ﴿mā kāna li-nafsin an tamūt illā bi-idhni Allāh﴾ means that it is not decreed for any soul to die except by Allah's permission.

His saying ﴿li-nafsin﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it covers every soul, whether human or non-human. No soul can die except by Allah's permission.

His saying ﴿an tamūt﴾: death is the separation from life. It occurs by the complete separation of the soul from the body. The soul is connected to the body in a complete connection, and it separates from it in a partial separation and in a complete separation. When a person is awake, the connection is complete. When he is asleep, it is a partial separation. When a person dies, it is a complete separation. However, this does not prevent the soul from returning to him in his grave in a manner not the same as in this world, because the life of the barzakh (the intermediate state) differs from the life of this world. The person in his grave has his soul returned to him, and he sits, is addressed, speaks, and understands. But this life is not like the life of this world, because if it were the life of this world, he would perish immediately, since he is buried under the earth above him, and perhaps he would be drowned in water or burned by fire.

His saying ﴿illā bi-idhni Allāh﴾: the word ﴿idhn﴾ (permission) here is meant as the cosmic permission (al-idhn al-kawnī), because the permission of Allah is divided into two types: cosmic permission and legislative permission.

Legislative permission is what Allah has decreed in the Law and permitted in the Law. It falls under His will, so it may or may not occur. For example, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shūrā 21]. The permission here is legislative, not cosmic, because Allah has permitted it cosmically but has not permitted it legislatively. Likewise His saying: ﴿Say: "Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?"﴾ [Yūnus 59]. Here the permission is legislative. But in verses such as this one, ﴿illā bi-idhni Allāh﴾, it is cosmic permission, meaning that a person cannot die unless Allah has cosmically permitted it.

His saying ﴿illā bi-idhni Allāh﴾ means by His decree and His destiny.

﴿kitāban muʾajjalan﴾: ﴿kitāban﴾ is an absolute object (maṣdar muʾakkid) emphasizing the sentence before it. That is, death is written as an appointed writing, determined by a known limit, which it neither exceeds nor falls short of. This writing is recorded in several books. It is written on the Night of Decree that he will die on such-and-such day, at such-and-such hour, in such-and-such month. This is a yearly recording. It is also written when the person is in his mother's womb, when the angel is sent to him and commanded to write his provision, his term, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or happy. It is also written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) fifty thousand years before the creation of the heavens and the earth. These records do not change: ﴿an appointed writing﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 145], neither increasing nor decreasing.

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it﴾: ﴿man﴾ is a conditional particle, ﴿yurid﴾ is the conditional clause, and ﴿nu'tihi﴾ is the response of the condition. In both the conditional clause and its response, there is elision. In the conditional clause the elision is in the middle of the word, and in the response it is at the end of the word. ﴿Yurid﴾ originally was ﴿yurīd﴾, and the yāʾ was dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. ﴿Nu'tihi﴾ originally was ﴿nu'tīhi﴾, and the yāʾ was dropped because of the jussive (al-jāzim), since a defective verb (al-fiʿl al-muʿtall) is jussive by dropping its weak letter.

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world﴾ means: whoever desires the reward in this world from this world, Allah the Exalted will give him from it. ﴿Nu'tihi﴾ means: We will give him. ﴿Minhā﴾ means: from it, not that We give him all of this world. A person may desire a great deal of this world but not obtain it, rather he is given a portion of it. ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it﴾: for example, whoever desires mansions, great wealth, wives, fine vehicles, and the like, Allah gives him from it, because whoever desires this must strive for it. Is that not so? If he must strive for it, then generally, complete striving brings about the attainment of what is sought. This is why He said: ﴿We will give him from it﴾, and Allah decrees the causes for obtaining what he desires from this world.

His saying ﴿nu'tihi minhā﴾ clearly indicates that Allah does not give him all of this world but gives him from it. This may refer to what he desires, meaning that Allah does not give him everything he wants. It may also refer to the world in general, so that Allah gives him everything he desires. In either case, this verse is restricted by the verse in Surat al-Isrāʾ: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We will﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 18]. Here "the immediate" means this world. He did not say "what he desires," but said ﴿mā nashāʾ﴾ (what We will). This is confirmed by reality, for many people desire this world and strive for it with their hands, feet, tongues, eyes, and noses, but do not attain it. Is that not so? Because Allah restricted this generality here by His saying in Surat al-Isrāʾ: ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will﴾, not what he wills. Thus the one hastened and the one to whom it is hastened are restricted by ﴿what We will, for whom We will﴾. So this unrestricted statement is restricted by that.

﴿Whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him from it﴾: ﴿We will give him from it﴾, and We do not give him the whole Hereafter, because the Hereafter has degrees in which people differ, and it is impossible for a person to be given all the degrees of people. Rather, he is given from the Hereafter. This is why He said ﴿nu'tihi minhā﴾. However, it differs from the gift of this world, as Allah says: ﴿Rather, you prefer the worldly life, but the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-Aʿlā 16–17]. The gift of the Hereafter is not like the gift of this world but is greater. This is why He said in the verse of al-Isrāʾ: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it while he is a believer, those are the ones whose striving is appreciated﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 19]. Here He said: ﴿We will reward the grateful﴾. This indicates that whoever desires the Hereafter is among the grateful, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will reward the grateful by His vast bounty. Whoever brings a good deed will be given ten good deeds up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples. Now, a person purifies himself in his house and performs wuḍūʾ thoroughly, so his sins are expiated with the last drop of water. When he recites the tashahhud, the eight gates of Paradise are opened for him, and he enters by whichever he wishes. When he leaves his house after this purification, intending the mosque, with nothing bringing him out except prayer, he does not take a single step without Allah raising him a degree and removing a sin for him. This is also great reward. Every step has two benefits: the first is the raising of degrees, and the second is the removal of sin. There is great reward for a small deed. When he enters the mosque and prays, the angels continue to send blessings upon him as long as he remains in his place of prayer, saying: "O Allah, bless him; O Allah, forgive him; O Allah, have mercy on him." These are supplications from angels whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has subjected to this service. So you see that whoever desires the Hereafter is among the grateful, and ﴿Allah will reward the grateful﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 144], rewarding them for their gratitude with multiples far beyond their deeds.

**Some benefits of this noble verse:**

* That the appointed terms of souls are fixed, as indicated by ﴿kitāban muʾajjalan﴾.

* Second: the consolation of the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), when it was said to them that Muhammad had been killed, and grief befell them. Allah told them that Muhammad could not be killed before his appointed time: ﴿It is not for any soul to die except by Allah's permission, at an appointed time﴾. If Allah has ended his term, he will end; and if his term has not ended, he will remain until the appointed time. So why do you despair? Why do you despair when it is said that Muhammad has died or been killed? This is something appointed by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and by His permission. What is appointed by Allah and by His permission, a person must submit to it, be patient with it, and be content with it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation that everything, even death, is created by Allah. This is indicated by ﴿illā bi-idhni Allāh﴾, and whatever proceeds from permission is created. This is supported by His saying: ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk 2].

* Among the benefits of the verse: a person cannot advance or delay beyond the term Allah has decreed for him. This is indicated by ﴿kitāban muʾajjalan﴾, and several verses support it, including: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [al-Naḥl 61], and: ﴿And Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 11].

If someone says: This is problematic in light of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever wishes to have his provision expanded and his lifespan extended, let him join the ties of kinship" [agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (2067) and Muslim (2557/20), from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik]. This indicates that if a person joins the ties of kinship, his lifespan is increased.

The answer to this is: this, meaning the extension of the term, is like the expansion of provision. The hadith says: "that his provision be expanded for him and his lifespan extended," and provision is written, is it not? It is written. The Messenger explained that provision is expanded and increased when a person joins the ties of kinship, so likewise the term is extended when a person joins the ties of kinship, and there is no difference. This is like our saying: "Whoever wishes to have a child, let him marry." Is this correct or not? It is correct. The hadith "Whoever loves that his provision be expanded and his lifespan extended" can only be an explanation of the cause of long life. It does not mean that a person has two lifespans, one when he severs ties of kinship and another when he maintains them, because what is known to Allah and written by Him is one lifespan, one lifespan connected with a cause. What is the cause? Maintaining the ties of kinship. So when a person joins the ties of kinship, we know that he has one extended lifespan, connected with a cause. Similarly, we may say: when a hungry person eats, he is saved from death. Is this correct? A person on the very last breath of life is brought food, eats, and lives. Do we say he had two lifespans? Yet if we had delayed in feeding him by just one minute, he would have died. We do not say he has two lifespans; we say he has one lifespan, but the cause of averting death from him, which was caused by hunger, is this food. The cause is this food. So there is no problem in this matter. If a person reflects on it, he finds that the cause of increased lifespan, which is maintaining kinship, is like the other causes the Law encourages. Likewise, we say: whoever desires Paradise should do righteous deeds while believing in Allah. Do we say that a person has two states, one of disbelief and one of belief? Or do we say that Allah has decreed by His prior decree that he will be a believer among the people of Paradise? Is the second answer or the first? The second. Likewise, the one who joins the ties of kinship: we say that from the beginning he had only one lifespan, established upon a cause, which is maintaining kinship. Thus the meaning of the hadith is to encourage people to maintain the ties of kinship, which is a cause of long life.

* Among the benefits of this verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (a sect who deny human choice), because of His saying ﴿man yurid﴾, where He affirmed for the human being a will. The Jabriyyah say that the human being has no will, and that he acts without choice or intention. But all the textual and rational evidences refute their view.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: people have different paths and every way is different, as indicated by ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world﴾ and ﴿Whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter﴾. And so it is.

* Among them: reporting that something occurs, or that something happens, does not indicate that it is permissible. His saying ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him from it﴾ does not indicate that it is permissible for a person to desire the world by his deeds. It does not indicate that. It is only a report about something that has occurred. Permissibility and prohibition are taken from another proof in the Law. From this it becomes clear that the error of one who says that a woman does not need a mahram for travel is manifest, because the Messenger reported that a woman (al-ẓaʿīnah) would travel from Ṣanʿāʾ to ʿAdan fearing none but Allah and not fearing for herself [al-Bukhārī (3595), from the hadith of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, with the wording: "You will surely see the caravan (al-ẓaʿīnah) setting out from al-Ḥīrah until it circles the Kaʿbah, fearing no one but Allah"]. This is a report about what? About reality, and it is not a legislative approval of it. Did the Messenger (ﷺ) not say: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you"? They said: "The Jews and the Christians?" He said: "Who else?" [agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (2456) and Muslim (2669/6), from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī]. Yes, he said that. Does this mean it is permissible for us to follow the ways of the Jews and Christians because the Messenger reported that we would follow them? Certainly not. Reporting that something occurs does not indicate its legal permissibility; its permissibility or impermissibility is taken from other evidences.

* Among the benefits of this verse: a person may intend by his deed to be praised by people, and from his deed he gets nothing except what he obtains of this world, and we seek Allah's protection. For example, a person prays so that it may be said, "He is diligent in worship"; recites so that it may be said, "He is a reciter"; gives charity so that it may be said, "He is generous"; fights so that it may be said, "He is brave," and the like. Whoever intends with his righteous deed these worldly matters (for all of these are worldly matters) has no share in the Hereafter, no share at all: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth, and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We will give him from it, but he has no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shūrā 20].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: preference for desiring the Hereafter over this world, because of His saying ﴿We will reward the grateful﴾. This indicates that whoever desires the Hereafter is among the grateful whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rewards.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of reward for deeds. This reward for deeds falls between two matters: between justice and bounty. The third matter, injustice, is impossible with respect to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Those who pay workers for their work divide their payment into three categories. Does Adam explain them to us?

* **Student:** Justice, bounty, and injustice.

* **The Shaykh:** Yes: justice, bounty, and injustice. Those who pay workers. This is why we now find that workers with their sponsors: some sponsors wrong them, some give them their full rights, and some give more. As for Allah's reward, Glorified and Exalted is He, injustice is impossible for Him, impossible not out of inability but because of the perfection of His justice, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿We will reward the grateful﴾.

Among the benefits of the verse also: encouragement to be grateful (shukr), because the statement that Allah rewards the grateful is meant to convey what? Encouragement to gratitude. The scholars said that gratitude relates to the heart, the tongue and the limbs. With the heart: a person feels within himself that this blessing is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and not from his own power and strength; that is, not from the person's own might and strength, but by the grace of Allah. With the tongue: he thanks Allah, meaning he speaks of the blessing of Allah, both by the tongue of state (lisan al-hal) and by the tongue of speech (lisan al-maqal). The tongue of speech is that he says: "Praise be to Allah who has preferred me over many of His creation with a [clear] preference." "Praise be to Allah who gave me a child." "Praise be to Allah who gave me wealth." "Praise be to Allah who made a house easy for me," and the like. The tongue of state is that the effect of the blessing appears upon the servant, for Allah loves that when He bestows a blessing upon His servant, the effect of His blessing be seen upon him. Based on this, if Allah gives a person wealth and he goes out among people in worn-out clothes, or in coarse woolen garments, or the like, would he be considered grateful?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: No. Is this not asceticism (zuhd)?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: It is not asceticism. Whoever sees him says: "This is a poor man; Allah has not blessed him with anything." So this appearance indicates what? That Allah has not bestowed blessings upon this person.

Good. As for the third, which is action: a person performs obedience to Allah. If Allah blesses him with wealth, he gives charity from it; with knowledge, he spreads it; with standing (jah), he intercedes for people and advocates on their behalf, and the like. This is gratitude in action. Based on this, the poet speaks on gratitude relating to the heart, the tongue and the limbs. Have we recited a verse to you before?

* A student: He says:
"The blessings from me have benefited you in three ways: my hand, my tongue, and my hidden, veiled heart."

* The Shaykh: Well done.

"The blessings from me have benefited you in three ways: my hand, my tongue, and my hidden, veiled heart."

And Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned that Allah made it easy for him (Ibn al-Qayyim) to [meet] Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and he stated that he cannot repay him with what? With his hand nor his tongue. This has passed us in the Nuniyyah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 146 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, glorified and exalted be He, said: ﴿And how many a prophet fought, along with him many devoted men (rabbiyyun) ...﴾ [Al 'Imran 146] to the end of the verse.

First: The recitations of this verse are as follows. ﴿Wa ka-ayyin﴾ is one reading. The second is ﴿wa ka'ayyin min nabiyyin﴾, where the second word (nabi) has two readings: ﴿nabiyy﴾ and ﴿nabi'﴾ with a hamza. The third is ﴿qatala﴾, which has two readings: ﴿qutila﴾ and ﴿qatala﴾. What we have in the Mushaf is ﴿qatala ma'ahu ribbiyyun﴾.

﴿Ka-ayyin﴾: the correct view is that it is a simple word (kalimah ghayr murakkabah), meaning not compound. The term "simple" (basitah), as the grammarians use it, means non-compound: when they say this is a simple word, they mean it is not composed of two words. The correct view, then, is that ﴿ka-ayyin﴾ is a simple, non-compound word. Some have said that it is compounded of the kaf (the kaf of comparison) and ay (the interrogative "ay"), but the correct view is otherwise. The correct view is that it is a simple word which the Arabs pronounced in this form, just as they pronounced "kam" (how many). The meaning of ﴿ka-ayyin min nabiyy﴾ is: "how many a prophet." It is therefore for multiplication (al-takthir). It is built on a sukun: ﴿ka-ayyin﴾ or ﴿ka'ina﴾ in the two dialects, it is built on the sukun of the nun. As for its place in i'rab, it is a subject (mubtada'), and the sentence after it is its predicate (khabar).

And His saying ﴿min nabiyy﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur) serving as the specifier (tamyiz) of ﴿ka-ayyin﴾, the specifier of "ka-ay," because "ka-ay" is one of the ambiguous words (al-alfaz al-mubhamah). ﴿Ka-ayyin﴾ is among the ambiguous words, and ambiguous words require a specifier. For example, number words for things are ambiguous: "I have twenty" — twenty what? It is ambiguous and requires a specifier: twenty men, twenty books, twenty houses, twenty cars, and the like. ﴿Ka-ayyin﴾ is among the ambiguous words that require a specifier, and its specifier comes after it in the genitive governed by min: ﴿ka-ayyin min nabiyy﴾.

And His saying ﴿qatala ma'ahu﴾ means: many of the prophets. This is the meaning of ﴿ka-ayyin min nabiyy﴾: many of the prophets. This is the meaning of the word.

As for His saying ﴿qatala ma'ahu ribbiyyun katheer﴾, the word ﴿qatala﴾ or ﴿qutila﴾ has been disputed by the exegetes. Some stopped at it and read: ﴿wa ka-ayyin min nabiyyin qutila﴾ or ﴿ka-ayyin min nabiyyin qatala﴾, then began anew with: ﴿ma'ahu ribbiyyun katheer﴾. The clause ﴿ma'ahu ribbiyyun﴾ is then a nominal sentence consisting of subject and predicate: ﴿ribbiyyun﴾ is the subject and ﴿ma'ahu﴾ is the fronted predicate. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿qutila﴾ or ﴿qatala﴾, meaning: he was killed while with him were many devoted men, or he fought.

It has also been said that His saying ﴿wa ka-ayyin min nabiyy﴾ is an independent clause on which one stops, and then begins anew: ﴿qutila ma'ahu ribbiyyun katheer﴾, meaning: how many a prophet was found, was sent, was raised up, was supported with signs, and was followed by people, and was killed, and with him in companionship were many devoted men. According to this view, ﴿ribbiyyun﴾ is what? It is a deputy subject (na'ib fa'il) according to the reading ﴿qutila﴾, and a subject (fa'il) according to the reading ﴿qatala﴾. Then, is the prophet here killed or unharmed under this second interpretation?

* Students: Unharmed.

* The Shaykh: He would be unharmed. As for the first view, he would be killed.

* A student: May Allah bless you, O Shaykh. Historians mention that three men ruled the world, among them Dhul-Qarnayn and others. We have said that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, gives His servants only a little, or some... ?

* The Shaykh: He does not give them the whole world.

* The student: And this statement?

* The Shaykh: This is correct, because Dhul-Qarnayn did not rule the whole world. But it is said that he is among those who ruled the world according to what people knew at that time. He did not reach America; he did not cross the Atlantic Ocean.

* A student: Shaykh, has anyone interpreted the increase in lifespan other than this interpretation?

* The Shaykh: Yes. Some, thinking that the intended meaning is not the extension of the term, said: the intended meaning is the blessing of life, meaning that blessing is placed in his life, or his term is lengthened, that is, his remembrance after his death lasts long, and a person who is remembered after death is as if he were alive. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is he who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people...?﴾ [al-An'am 122]. Al-Mutanabbi says:

"The remembrance of a man is his second life, and his need..." ... (the verse is incomplete).

So the meaning would be that he is remembered after his death with good. These are three opinions: either the intended meaning is that he is remembered after his death with good, or the intended meaning is blessing in his life, and the correct view is that it is an actual increase in his lifespan, and that what is written with Allah, known to Him, is that this man will maintain his ties of kinship and his life will be extended.

* A student: Shaykh, Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that it is said to the angel: two terms are written for him with the angel; if he keeps ties of kinship, it is the second, the greater; and if not, the lesser. Is there evidence for this?

* The Shaykh: There is no evidence for it, there is no evidence, except that someone includes it in His saying, Exalted be He: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd 39]. But even if this were established, it would apply to everything, even to the expansion of provision, and even to marriage, and even to wealth, and even to Paradise also.

* The student: It is said to the angel: write for him two terms, meaning?

* The Shaykh: Meaning that if this is correct, if it is correct, we do not deny anything that admits of this and that. The angel would have been told that, but this needs evidence.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. If a person has everything written for him according to what he does, the believer, when he enters Paradise, it is said to him: "This is your seat in Paradise, and this is your seat in the Fire had you disobeyed Allah." So, is there for each person a specific seat in Paradise and a specific seat in the Fire according to his deeds, or...?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is known, and he is reminded of this so that he may know the value of Allah's blessing upon him. It is said: "This is your seat," meaning had you been a disbeliever, and "this is your seat" when you were a believer, and it has come to him. It is like if you said to someone you honored: "This is your standing, or this is your place, had you not been of this noble character."

* A student: But Shaykh, Allah knows what he will do; do we say the same as with the lifespan?

* The Shaykh: Yes, Allah knows, but the person does not know. So it is said: "This is your seat had you disobeyed Allah," so that he may rejoice and know the excellence of Allah's blessing upon him.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. (...) three possibilities: "his term is postponed" [agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2067), Muslim (2557/20), and Ibn Hibban (438), the wording is his, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik], and you mentioned an earlier principle: if a verse admits of several meanings with no contradiction between them, we take it in all of them. Three, that is, we apply all the meanings?

* The Shaykh: No, but here it does not admit of the other two meanings, it does not admit them. But a person may be recompensed with blessing, that blessing is placed in his life as a reward for his deed, and this is even outside of kinship ties. And a person may be remembered after his death, as we now see among the people of knowledge who are remembered after their deaths.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the first meaning is the apparent one, (...).

* A student: May Allah be good to you. Does "ka-ay" come with the meaning of "kam"?

* The Shaykh: "Kam."

* The student: So it is an explanation of it?

* The Shaykh: It is for multiplication.

* The student: Is the explanation here not in the sense of "kam"?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is valid.

* The student: We explained it with the meaning of "many."

* The Shaykh: Yes, and "kam" means "many": ﴿And how many a town We destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf 4].

* A student: May Allah pardon you. Does this verse include that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, destroyed some nations, as He did to the Children of Israel, and then brought them back to life after their death?

* The Shaykh: Like whom?

* The student: Like the Children of Israel who said...

* The Shaykh: Like whom? The Children of Israel (...) from Jacob until the Day of Resurrection.

* The student: Those who said to Moses: "Show us Allah openly," so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking?

* The Shaykh: Good, yes, these were brought back to life because Moses called upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, asking Allah, Glorified and Exalted, to revive them (...) from his people: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me﴾ [al-A'raf 155].

* The student: But was a book written for them (...)?

* The Shaykh: Death and then life was written for them from the beginning, but this life was not by their action or their deed; rather, it was because of the supplication of Moses, peace be upon him, and Allah answered him.

* A student: But might it conflict with a hadith ...?

* The Shaykh: No, it does not conflict, because this is written with Allah in this way. This state that occurred is written with Allah in this way. They were made to die as a punishment for their deed when they said: "Show us Allah openly," while they were hearing the speech of Allah, and they said: "We will not believe you until we see Allah openly." This was not up to them, so they were punished with death, they were struck down. Then Moses, peace be upon him, supplicated his Lord and He revived them.

* A student: Is there not in the hadith of the father of Jabir, who said that Allah spoke to him directly, that He said: "Indeed I have decreed that they will not return to it" [al-Tirmidhi (3010), Ibn Majah (190), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah]? Does it not conflict with it?

* The Shaykh: It does not conflict, may Allah bless you, it does not conflict.

* The student: How, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: The reason for this, as I told you, is that these were brought back to life not so that they might be given luxury, but to avert the harm that would fall upon Moses. Bring also, bring the whole verse that refers to it, all of which came for a reason: ﴿Those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death﴾ [al-Baqarah 243]. Allah caused them to die so that they would know that there is no escape from Allah except to Him. And the one who passed by a town, Allah honored him by causing him to die and then raising him up: a specific case.

* * *

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah, a decree with a specified term﴾. What is the intended meaning of this verse?

* A student: The intended meaning (...) that it is impossible in the utmost sense...

* The Shaykh: No, that is not its meaning. I mean, what is its purpose?

* A student: It is consolation for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when it was rumoured that the Prophet ﷺ had been killed, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said that he would not die until his term had ended.

* The Shaykh: You have done well, may Allah bless you.

The saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿except by the permission of Allah﴾. What is meant by permission here?

* A student: Universal permission (idhn kawni), Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: Universal permission. From what you understand, permission is divided into universal and non-universal. What is the second?

* The student: Legislative permission (idhn shar'i).

* The Shaykh: Legislative permission. What is the difference between them?

* The student: Universal permission must necessarily occur.

* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning that what Allah has permitted in the universal sense must necessarily occur, unlike...?

* The student: Legislative permission.

* The Shaykh: This is one difference. Is there another difference?

* A student: Universal permission may be beloved to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and may not be beloved.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: As for legislative permission, it is beloved to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* The Shaykh: So Allah does not permit except what He loves. Good.

* A student: That universal and legislative permission combine with respect to the obedient and...

* The Shaykh: No, this is not important, this is a relation. Good. Can you bring an example of legislative permission?

* A student: ﴿Have they partners who have legislated for them in religion what Allah did not permit?﴾ [al-Shura 21].

* The Shaykh: Yes, but that is in negation.

* The student: ﴿Or have they partners who have legislated for them in religion what Allah did not permit?﴾

* The Shaykh: That is in negation. And in affirmation?

* A student: In affirmation: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people﴾ [al-Tawbah 3].

* The Shaykh: No.

* The student: (...) legislative permission.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what you mentioned is the negation of legislative permission, and we want the affirmation of legislative permission.

* A student: The saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent against Allah?﴾ [Yunus 59].

* The Shaykh: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent against Allah?﴾ Well done. Universal permission is like?

* A student: The saying of the brother of Joseph: ﴿I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾ [Yusuf 80].

* The Shaykh: No, that is the universal decree; we want universal permission.

* A student: ﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾, this is universal permission, correct.

The saying: ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it﴾. Is this verse absolute or restricted?

* A student: Restricted.

* The Shaykh: Restricted by what?

* The student: Restricted by the will of Allah. One is not given the whole world even if he seeks it; he is given what Allah wills, by His saying: ﴿We will give him of it﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the apparent meaning of the verse is that whoever desires the reward of this world, Allah must give him of it, because the response of the condition occurs when the condition's act is found.

* The student: He is given of it, not all of it.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* A student: Restricted by not taking all the reward of this world, but only part of it.

* The Shaykh: This is known from the wording ﴿We will give him of it﴾. But is he given of it even if only a part, when he desires the reward of this world, or may he be deprived of all of it?

* The student: He is given of it (...).

* A student: It is restricted by the verse of al-Isra'.

* The Shaykh: And what is it?

* The student: ﴿Whoever desires the present life and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾ [Hud 15].

* The Shaykh: That is not (...).

* A student: The saying of Allah, Exalted, in Surat al-Isra': ﴿Whoever desires the hasty life, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We will﴾ [al-Isra' 18].

* The Shaykh: Well done. ﴿Whoever desires the hasty life, We hasten for him therein what We will﴾, not what he himself wills; ﴿for whom We will﴾. Well done. Now, the saying: ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾, was the verse concluded with it as a hint?

* A student: A hint that whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter is among the grateful.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and he will be given more than he desired, because Allah said: ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾. Well done.

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And how many a prophet fought﴾; we mentioned that there are two readings of ﴿qatala﴾.

* A student: ﴿Qatala﴾ and ﴿qutila﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Qatala﴾ and ﴿qutila﴾. Well done.

* The Shaykh: The saying: ﴿qatala﴾ or ﴿qutila﴾, and the difference between them is clear.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful: ﴿And how many a prophet fought﴾, meaning: fought his enemies and was not killed. And how many a prophet was killed though he did not fight. So His saying ﴿qutila﴾ means whether in fighting or not in fighting, and His saying ﴿qatala﴾ means whether he was killed or not killed. That is: how many were the prophets who fought, and how many were the prophets, on the second reading, who were killed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 146 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿maʿahu ribbiyyūn﴾. "Maʿa" (with) is a circumstantial noun of place (ẓarf) functioning as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and "ribbiyyūn" is a postponed subject (mubtada' muakhkhar), on the basis that the pronoun in "qātala" or "quti'a" refers to the Prophet. ﴿wa-ka-ayyin min nabiyyin﴾ — "qutila" or "qātala." However, there is another possibility: that "ribbiyyūn" is the subject (fā'il) of "qātala," or the deputy subject (nā'ib al-fā'il) according to the reading "quti'a." On this basis the grammatical analysis differs: "maʿa" becomes a circumstantial noun of place linked to "qātala" or to "quti'a," and "ribbiyyūn" is the subject according to the reading "qātala," and the deputy subject according to the reading "quti'a." On this estimation, the fighting or the killing falls upon the ribbiyyūn and not upon whom? Upon the Prophet. The ruling differs with regard to the Companions: if "qātala" or "quti'a" has a pronoun referring to "nabiyy," it becomes a consolation for the Companions, a consolation that the prophets were killed and fought before Muhammad. On the second possibility, that "ribbiyyūn" is the subject or deputy subject, there is an indication that the trial of fighting or killing was not specific to the Companions, but rather it preceded among the earlier nations. Thus the meaning of the verse includes some rebuke and blame for the Companions who despaired at what befell them at Uhud. For this reason He said: ﴿fa-mā wahanū li-mā aṣābahum fī sabīl Allāh wa-mā ḍaʿufū﴾ to the end. Is it clear, O brothers, now? This is with regard to the structure of the sentence.

As for the individual words: His saying ﴿min nabiyyin﴾: what is meant by "nabī" is one to whom a law (sharʿ) was revealed but who was not commanded to convey it. However, the word "nabī" in the Qur'an is never used except to mean "rasūl" (messenger), because the prophet who was not charged with a message is not mentioned in the Qur'an by the term "nabī." There is no occurrence of the word "nabī" in the Qur'an except that it is meant as "rasūl." ﴿Innā awḥaynā ilayka kamā awḥaynā ilā Nūḥin wa-l-nabiyyīna min baʿdihi wa-awḥaynā ilā Ibrāhīm﴾ [al-Nisā' 163] to the end. Nuh, it is well known, is among the messengers, indeed he is among the steadfast messengers (ulū al-ʿazm). On this basis, what is the rule?

* Student: That a nabī is one to whom a law was revealed but who was not commanded to convey it.

* Shaykh: This is the rule, but the scholars disagree with you.

* Student: The rule is that whatever is mentioned of a nabī in the Qur'an is considered a rasūl.

* Shaykh: In any case, according to the scholars, a nabī is one to whom a law was revealed but who was not commanded to convey it, and a rasūl is one to whom a law was revealed and who was commanded to convey it. For this reason the rasūl is called rasūl from risālah (message). But every nabī mentioned in the Qur'an is a rasūl.

Some people were confused and said: How can a law be revealed to someone who is not commanded to convey it? In reality, however, this is not a problem, because it can be answered that the law was revealed to him so that he would worship by it, and this is a form of reminder for him if he was a prophet after messengers, and a form of clarification for him if he was a prophet not preceded by messengers. An example of the second is Adam, for Adam was a prophet and was not preceded by messengers. An example of the first is those prophets of the Children of Israel who had no followers and were not commanded to convey, so God's informing them is a favor upon them by mentioning the earlier law and reviving it, even though they were not obligated to convey it to the people. With this the confusion is removed, and it is possible that God informs someone and does not command him or obligate him to convey.

And His saying: ﴿qātala maʿahu ribbiyyūn﴾. "Qātala" or "quti'a": al-muqātalah (fighting) is a form of mufāʿalah that requires mutual repelling by killing from both sides, and it is more general than killing. For this reason fighting may be permissible while killing is not. Take those who do not give the call to prayer (adhān): if we found a village that did not give the adhān, for example, it is obligatory to fight them, but it is not permissible to kill them. That is, if we are able to seize a specific person, we do not kill him, but we fight them until they give the adhān, for example. If we found a village that does not perform the ʿĪd prayer, it is obligatory upon us to fight them until they perform the ʿĪd prayer, but it is not permissible to kill them. So killing is more specific than fighting, in the sense that fighting may be permitted for a people while killing them is not. Among this, according to the opinion of some scholars, is the man who wants to pass between you and your sutrah, and you repel him but he refuses. The Prophet ﷺ said: «If he refuses, let him fight him» [agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (509), and Muslim (505/258), from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī], but it is not permissible for him to kill him. The difference is clear, for if we said that it is permissible for him to kill him, it would be permissible for this worshipper to strike that one who wanted to pass in a place that causes death, and he would fall dead. But this is not permissible; rather he fights him with a fight of defense, and when he is repelled he desists from him.

And His saying: ﴿ribbiyyūn kathīr﴾. Some of them said: "ribbiyyūn" is a relative adjective (nisbah) to "rabb," but the rāʾ was vowelled with kasra because it changed in the relative form, and many a vowel changes in the relative form. For example, "Banū Umayyah": do we say "al-Umawiyyīn" or "al-Amawiyyīn"? "al-Amawiyyīn." So the letter changes when the relative form exists. The word "ribbiyyūn" originally is "rabbiyyūn" from "al-Rabb" or from "al-tarbiyyah," and its rāʾ is fatḥah, but when it became a relative it was given kasra. On this basis, "ribbiyyūn" are those who worshipped the Lord and so attained from Him, glory be to Him and exalted, a special upbringing (tarbiyyah). A parallel to this is the saying of the scholars: "This is a rabbānī scholar," a relative to what? To "al-Rabb" and "al-tarbiyyah." It was also said that it is attributed to "ribbah" with kasra, meaning relative to "ribbah," which is a group, so the meaning is: with him are many groups. ﴿ribbiyyūn kathīr﴾, that is, many groups. In any case, God Almighty makes clear that many of the prophets fought or were killed, and with them were many ribbiyyūn, or many of the prophets were fought alongside by ribbiyyūn, or were killed alongside by ribbiyyūn.

And His saying: ﴿kathīr﴾ is an attribute of "ribbiyyūn," and it does not imply the majority. It does not imply the majority. That is, for example, if we have a hundred and fifty of them survived, we say: these are many; if twenty of them survived, we say: this is many; if sixty survived, we say: this is many; but for what is below fifty we do not say "more" (akthar), we say "more" only for what exceeds half. The point is that ﴿kathīr﴾ here means many groups who fought or were killed.

﴿fa-mā wahanū li-mā aṣābahum fī sabīl Allāh﴾: that is, they did not become cowardly because of what afflicted them in the way of God; rather, what afflicted them in the way of God increased them only in courage and boldness, because they have in faith what drives them to what befalls them in the way of God. Just as it is in human nature that when a person is attacked he becomes protective, he is protected or he becomes heated and increases in boldness, so likewise these people did not become cowardly because of what befell them in the way of God.

And His saying: ﴿fī sabīl Allāh﴾ means: in His path and His law, because they believe that whatever befalls them is for good. When the finger of the Prophet ﷺ bled in one of the military campaigns, he said:
«Are you anything but a finger that bled, and in the way of God you have suffered what you have suffered» [agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (2802), and Muslim (1796/112), from the hadith of Jundub ibn Sufyān].
﴿wa-mā ḍaʿufū﴾: that is, their resolve did not weaken, so that even if many of them were killed, their resolve does not weaken, unlike one who has cowardice, whose resolve weakens when someone from his people is killed.

﴿wa-mā istakānū﴾: from al-istikānah, which is humiliation; that is, they did not submit in humiliation to their enemy, even though many of them were killed, but they remained in dignity. For the one who knows that whoever of his people is killed is in the way of God does not worry, since he believes that if he himself were killed he would be killed in the way of God, so he does not abase himself before the enemies of God.

﴿wa-mā istakānū wa-llāhu yuḥibbu al-ṣābirīn﴾: God loves the patient, those who are patient in everything in which patience is obligatory. And they say that patience is of three kinds.

* Student: Patience in obedience to God, patience in refraining from disobedience to God, and patience in God's painful decrees.

* Shaykh: Yes, that is it. Patience in obedience to God: a person restrains himself upon obedience and is not bored with it nor abandons it. Patience in refraining from disobedience to God: a person restrains himself from sin so that he does not commit it. Patience upon God's painful decrees: he does not rage at the painful things God decrees for him.

* Benefits of this noble verse:

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: God Almighty has a special care for this nation, in that He consoles them with what happened to the earlier nations; by His saying: ﴿wa-ka-ayyin min nabiyyin qutil﴾ according to the reading of pausing.

* And among its benefits: that jihad is prescribed in other than this nation; by His saying: ﴿qātala﴾, and fighting by the prophets and their followers is only in the context of jihad, and so it is.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of those who preceded and who deserve praise; for this reason He said: ﴿fa-mā wahanū﴾ to the end.

* And among its benefits: that one of the methods of encouraging a thing and inciting toward it is to mention to a person a predecessor whom he may emulate and take courage to follow; by His saying: ﴿fa-mā wahanū li-mā aṣābahum fī sabīl Allāh﴾ to the end.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of the lowness of rank of those who abase themselves before the enemies of God. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿wa-mā istakānū﴾, for the believer must be lofty like a mighty mountain before the enemies of God, to the point that it is permissible for a person to show pride and to trail his garment in the face of enemies, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «Indeed it is a walk that God hates except in this situation» [recorded by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr (6508), from the hadith of Khālid ibn Abī Dujānah]. Some scholars even said: it is permissible for the Islamic army to dye its head and beard black in front of the enemies in order to terrify them, because they think those facing them are young men. In any case, whether or not we adopt this view, a person should not abase himself before his enemy, but rather show dignity to him by word and by deed, because humiliating the disbelievers is beloved to God. Blessed and exalted is God, describing the Prophet ﷺ and his companions: ﴿Muḥammadun rasūlu Llāh, wa-lladhīna maʿahu ashiddāʾu ʿalā al-kuffār, ruḥamāʾu baynahum, tarāhum rukkaʿan sujjadan yabtaghūna faḍlan mina Llāh wa-riḍwānan, sīmāhum fī wujūhihim min athari al-sujūd, dhālika mathaluhum fī al-Tawrāh, wa-mathaluhum fī al-Injīl, ka-zarʿin akhraja shaṭʾahu fa-āzarahu fa-istaghlaẓa fa-istawā ʿalā sūqihi yuʿjibu al-zurrāʿa li-yaghīẓa bihimu al-kuffār﴾ [al-Fath 29]. And God the Exalted said: ﴿wa-lā yaṭaʾūna maw.ṭiʾan yaghīẓu al-kuffāra wa-lā yanāluna min ʿaduwwin naylan illā kutiba lahum bihi ʿamalun ṣāliḥ﴾ [al-Tawbah 120]. So everything with which you enrage the disbelievers is a means of drawing near to God; everything by which the disbelievers are harmed, whether by injury or killing or otherwise, is a act of worship that brings you closer to God, the Mighty and Majestic, except when there is a covenant between us and them, in which case the obligation is to fulfil the covenant; by God's saying: ﴿fa-mā istaqāmū lakum fa-staqīmū lahum, inna Llāha yuḥibbu al-muttaqīn﴾ [al-Tawbah 7].

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of love for God; by His saying: ﴿wa-llāhu yuḥibbu al-ṣābirīn﴾. Love is one of the attributes of God Almighty connected with His will, so it is among the attributes of action (ṣifāt fiʿliyyah), because it is connected with will. The reason it is connected with will is that it is tied to a cause, and every attribute tied or linked to a cause is among the attributes of action. On the basis of this useful rule we say: what about good pleasure (riḍā)?

* Students: It is among the attributes of action.

* Shaykh: Action-based, why?

* Students: Because it is tied to a cause.

* Shaykh: Yes, tied to a cause. Joy, laughter, and so on: every attribute linked to or tied to a cause is among the attributes of action. Is God loved? Yes, He is loved, and there is nothing more delightful to a person than the love of God, that he loves God the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason, when you stand to pray with a clear heart, far from the world and turned toward God, you will find in this prayer love for God and a great delight that makes you forget the whole world, because you find nothing more delightful than the love of God, glory be to Him and exalted. And it has passed us many times, and there is no need to repeat, that the people of ta'ṭīl (denial of attributes) deny the reality of love and say: what is meant by love is what? Reward, or the intention to reward; that is, a created thing separate from God, which is the reward, or the will. So the meaning of ﴿yuḥibbu al-ṣābirīn﴾ according to their view is: He rewards them, or He wants to reward them.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the exhortation to patience; by His saying: ﴿wa-llāhu yuḥibbu al-ṣābirīn﴾, for we know of no benefit more exalted and greater than urging patience in such an expression.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿wa-mā kāna qawlahum illā an qālū rabbanā ighfir lanā dhunūbanā wa-isrāfanā fī amrinā﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 147].

* Student: Is the reading of "ribbiyyūn" the second reading?

* Shaykh: Yes, it is not a reading; we said that it is derived from "al-Rabb" or from "al-Ribbah" only. As for the reading, there is only one reading in it, but "qātala" is the one that has two readings.

* Student: Does it not come from (...) rabb, rabbānīyūn?

* Shaykh: No, it did not come, it did not come.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 147:**

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And their words were no more than that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾ to the end of the verse. So we ask: why has the subject of (kāna) (the subject of *kāna*, the noun following it) become accusative?

* Student: Because its action has been nullified, so *kāna* has no effect.

* Shaykh: So when its action is nullified, its subject is put in the accusative! Does that require, when its action is nullified, that it be put in the nominative as a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence)? Because the original state is that it is nominative?

* Student: This is not its subject, this is its predicate.

* Shaykh: ﴿And their words were﴾.

* Student: This is *tāmmah* (complete, not requiring a predicate).

* Shaykh: And if it is *tāmmah*, its subject must be in the accusative!

* Student: No, Shaykh, here it is *nāqisah* (incomplete, requiring a predicate).

* Shaykh: *Nāqisah*. Fine. If it is *nāqisah*, then it puts the *mubtada'* in the nominative and the predicate in the accusative.

* Student: Allah knows best.

* Shaykh: Allah knows best. May Allah reward you with good.

* Student: The predicate of *kāna* is fronted here, this is (*qawlahum*).

* Shaykh: The predicate of *kāna* is fronted?

* Student: Yes, indeed.

* Shaykh: Where is its subject?

* Student: The verbal noun clause ﴿that they said﴾.

* Shaykh: (*an*) and what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun? Yes, then: ﴿And their words were no more than their saying, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾. Is that clear? Is it permissible for the predicate of *kāna* to be placed before its subject?

* Student: It is permissible.

* Shaykh: It is permissible for the predicate of *kāna* to be placed before its subject. Do you have evidence for that?

* Student: Yes, His saying: ﴿And their words were﴾.

* Shaykh: I said: do you have evidence? That means what we have before us is the original, and we want evidence for it?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: The saying of Ibn Mālik:

 ................. ∗∗∗ ......*ka-kāna sayyidan ʿUmar*

* Shaykh: This is not evidence, because the grammarians' own statements are not cited as proof.

* Student: (...) But the original, Shaykh, (...).

* Shaykh: (...) if we get evidence from the speech of the Arabs, or from the Qur'an, or from a Prophet.

* Student: His saying: ﴿was with His servants Knowing﴾ [al-Isrā' 30]. *bi-ʿibādihi* is a prepositional phrase functioning as the predicate, and *khabīran*...

* Shaykh: No, *khabīr* is not the predicate, that does not work.

* Student: (...) Their origin is the subject and predicate, and in a subject-predicate sentence it is permissible to front the predicate before the subject.

* Shaykh: But that is not evidence.

* Student: His saying: ﴿And the answer of his people was no more than that they said﴾ [al-A'rāf 82].

* Shaykh: ﴿no more than that they said﴾ is enough. Fine, here the noun was placed before the predicate.

* Student: ﴿And it was an incumbent duty upon Us to help the believers﴾ [al-Rūm 47].

* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿And it was an incumbent duty upon Us to help the believers﴾, this is in the Qur'an. In the Arabic language:

 ................. ∗∗∗ *fa-laysa sawāan ʿālimun wa-jahūlu*

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, we mentioned that the reason for the kasra in *Ribbiyyūn* is the relative adjective (*nisba*).

* Shaykh: It changed through the *nisba*.

* Student: Yes, may Allah be good to you. Does not the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, contradict this: ﴿But be ribbāniyyīn (devoted to the Lord) by what you have been teaching of the Book and by what you have been studying﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 79]? Here (...) its meaning (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, but it is different. ﴿But be ribbāniyyīn﴾ here means scholars who are devoted to the Lord. As for this one, the intended meaning is fighters, related to *tarbiyah* (upbringing/nurturing).

* Student: But are scholars who are devoted to the Lord not also related to *tarbiyah*, like the fighters?

* Shaykh: And also to the Lord, and to the Lord. But the intended meaning is not the fighters.

* Student: But does this have an effect?

* Shaykh: Perhaps it has an effect. Or what you mentioned is undoubtedly an objection to this.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you all. Regarding those who permitted the army's fighters to dye their beards black, is this not *istiḥsān* (juristic preference) against a clear text that did not permit it (...)?

* Shaykh: What do you say about this? He says: those who permitted dyeing gray hair black in fighting the enemy, is this not *istiḥsān* in opposition to the text?

* Student: We have a text (...).

* Shaykh: What is it?

* Student: "Verily this is a gait that Allah dislikes." [Narrated by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr (6508), from the hadith of Khālid ibn Abī Dujānah.]

* Shaykh: The strutting? Yes.

* Student: This is a text.

* Shaykh: Which one?

* Student: The Messenger's saying: "This is a gait." This is a text.

* Shaykh: Yes, that is fine. Strutting is permitted in war, but dyeing gray hair black?

* Student: (...) the reason, Shaykh.

* Student: It is apparent, Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, that the presumption of continuity (*istiṣḥāb*) is indeed in opposition to the text, so this view is not valid, because the Prophet ﷺ forbade changing gray hair to black.

* Shaykh: Yes, the closer view to me is this: that it is *istiḥsān* against the text. How many a shaykh was stronger in might than a young man. Yes indeed.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding ﴿And how many a Prophet fought, and with him many devoted company﴾ (...)?

* Shaykh: This is prevented by the verse.

* Student: I mean (...).

* Shaykh: Yes (...). We say: since the verse has a possibility of meaning, where is the proof that no Prophet was commanded to fight and was killed? He may be killed while commanded to fight.

* Student: Pardon us, Shaykh. There are Prophets who were not commanded to convey the message, and why is this one stated as they were commanded to convey (...). I have a problem. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 110], and the Messenger ﷺ said (...) the nation is to convey.

* Shaykh: What is the question?

* Student: The question is that this nation, the nation of Muhammad ﷺ (...), were they commanded to convey (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, because the scholars of this nation are the heirs of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 40], and He did not say "the Seal of the Messengers," as an indication that there is no Prophet in this nation.

* * *

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And their words were no more than that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the excellence of the deeds of these *ribbiyyūn* who fought alongside the Prophets and were killed, and that they did not weaken, nor were they feeble, nor did they submit, which is an excellent action, He mentioned the excellence of their speech, saying: ﴿And their words were no more than that they said﴾. This sentence conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*), meaning that their words at these calamities were restricted to asking Allah for forgiveness, forgiveness of their sins and excesses, and asking Him for steadfastness. That is because what befell them befell them only because of sins, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Why, when a calamity struck you, though you had struck (the enemy with) twice as much, did you say, "From where is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 165]. So the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned the excellence of their actions, He mentioned the excellence of their words.

His saying: ﴿And their words were no more than that they said﴾, grammatically, the grammarians say: *qawl* is the predicate of *kāna* placed first, and *an* and what follows it in ﴿that they said﴾ is its subject placed last. On this basis, it is from the category of fronting the predicate of *kāna*. The predicate of *kāna* may be permissibly fronted, obligatorily fronted, or prohibited from fronting, depending on the context. If the predicate has precedence in the sentence, such as an interrogative noun or a conditional noun, it must be fronted, as you say: "Where was Zayd?" If the subject contains a pronoun referring to the predicate, it may also be obligatory to front it. The original rule is permissibility of fronting and postponing; this is the original rule. But sometimes fronting is obligatory and sometimes it is postponed. So here, did he front it permissibly or obligatorily?

* Students: Permissibly.

* Shaykh: In any case, according to the recitation it is obligatory, because it is not permissible to change the words of Allah. But if it were in other than the Qur'an, it would be permissible. ﴿And their words were﴾, meaning at the time of the killing, ﴿no more than that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾. ﴿no more than that they said﴾: the pronoun refers to those among them who remained and were not killed, because those who were killed cannot say this. ﴿"Our Lord, forgive us"﴾, ﴿"Our Lord"﴾ means "O our Lord." It is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been deleted, for lightness and for seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah. So the deletion of the particle of calling here has two reasons. The first: lightness. The second: what? Seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah. ﴿no more than that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾. ﴿"Our Lord"﴾: they called upon Allah, exalted is He, in supplication by the name of Lordship, because Lordship is the aspect in which there is governance. And answering supplication belongs to the category of Lordship or of Divinity? It belongs to Lordship. You seek means through the name of Allah that suits what they ask for, which is the answering of supplication. ﴿no more than that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾. ﴿"Forgive"﴾ means: cover and overlook, because it is derived from *maghfar*, which is the helmet a fighter protects his head with from arrows, and in it there is covering and protection. For this reason, if Allah, glorified is He, exposed the sinner's concealment, the forgiveness would not be complete, and if He punished him for it and kept it hidden from people, the forgiveness would not be complete either. But if He covers him and pardons him, then the forgiveness becomes complete. ﴿"Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾. The root *dhunūb* is used with several meanings, among them a share, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged is a share like the share of their companions﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 59], meaning a portion. From it comes *dhanūb al-māʾ*, the bucket of water, because it is a determined quantity of water. And *dhanb* is used for sin, because it is the share of the doer. ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 7-8]. So this root, *dh-n-b*, revolves around this meaning.

﴿"our sins and our excesses in our affair"﴾. *Isrāf* is exceeding the limit, and exceeding the limit is either in excess or in deficiency. As for exceeding the limit in excess, it is obvious. As for deficiency, it is because what is required of the responsible person is that he not transgress the bounds of Allah, nor come near them either. So if a person commits what is forbidden, he is a *musrif* (one who exceeds), because he has overstepped the limit of servanthood, since the requirement of servanthood is that he avoid what Allah has forbidden. And if he neglects an obligation, he is also one who exceeds in what servanthood requires, because the requirement of servanthood is that he fulfill the obligations. So a person may exceed in obligations, in prohibitions, and in permissible matters as well, as if he exceeds in spending on himself and his family; he is then within *isrāf*.

His saying: ﴿"and our excesses in our affair"﴾: the word *amr* here means matter, that is, in our affairs. It is singular and in construct, so it encompasses all matters.

﴿"and make firm our feet"﴾. Make our feet firm when? At the meeting with enemies, at the arrival of doubts, and at the onset of desires. A person needs Allah to make him firm in the places of fighting, for if Allah did not make him firm, he would flee. He needs Allah to make him firm against doubts, for if Allah did not make him firm, he would swerve. He needs Allah to make him firm against desires, for if Allah did not make him firm, he would perish. Many people slip when doubts arise. You find someone with certainty, but when even a slight doubt comes to him, he is affected, because he was not made firm. Many people also have knowledge and certainty and no doubt, but desire overcomes them and they are not made firm. So the making firm of feet is in every place where one may slip. This includes, as I said, making feet firm in fighting, which is the context of the verses, making feet firm against doubts, and making feet firm against desires.

﴿"and help us against the disbelieving people"﴾. ﴿"help us"﴾ means: grant us victory, which is dominance. ﴿"against the disbelieving people"﴾ means those who disbelieve in Allah. This includes that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, help you against yourself, because if Allah does not help you against your soul, it will command you to evil: ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent commander of evil﴾ [Yūsuf 53]. ﴿And man carried it. Indeed, he was a wrongdoer and ignorant﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 72]. So if Allah does not help you against it, it destroys you. And if Allah helps you against it and gives the victory to the soul at peace, you are saved from it. Victory against the disbelieving people also includes victory against Satan, for Satan is a disbeliever. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Except Iblīs. He refused and was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah 34]. It also includes victory against disbelieving humans, at the time of fighting them, for if Allah does not help a person against them, he has no helper, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If Allah should aid you, no one can overcome you; but if He should forsake you, who is there that can aid you after Him?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 160].

* Among the benefits of this verse: that these *ribbiyyūn* who fought with the Prophet had perfected both their actions and their words. Their actions: they did not submit, did not weaken, did not waver. ﴿So they did not weaken for what afflicted them in the way of Allah, nor did they become weak, nor did they submit﴾. Their words: they turned to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, asking forgiveness for their sins and their excesses in their affair, because they knew that what befell them was only because of sins.

* And among the benefits of this verse: a person should supplicate Allah, exalted is He, with this supplication, especially when meeting the disbelievers, so that he may be victorious over them: ﴿"Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾

* And among the benefits of this verse: that a person is in need of Allah's forgiveness, as shown by His saying: ﴿"Our Lord, forgive us"﴾. Had he been independent of it, he would not have asked for it. But he is in need of it to the utmost degree. Indeed, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he told his companions that "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds alone," they said: "Not even you?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (5673) and Muslim (2816/72), from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.]

* And among its benefits also: that a person is never free of excess against himself. He is never free of excess, either in exaggeration or in deficiency. The reason is that their asking Allah to forgive them the excess indicates its existence. If you reflect on yourself, you will find that you are never free of excess.

* And among the benefits of this verse: that a person is in need of Allah making his feet firm, as shown by His saying: ﴿"and make firm our feet"﴾. We have mentioned that this covers three situations: when facing enemies, at doubts, and at desires.

* And among its benefits also: that if Allah does not help you against your enemy, you will not be victorious, as shown by His saying: ﴿"and help us against the disbelieving people"﴾. If you say: does this contradict the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to take what we are able of, or to prepare for the enemies what we are able of in strength? The answer: No. Because when you ask Allah for something, what is required of you is that you strive to attain and bring it about. For this reason, if you ask Allah for Paradise, what is required of you is to work for it, not to say, "O Allah, I ask You for Paradise," and then abandon action. Likewise, when we ask Allah to help us against the disbelieving people, we must take the means we are able to, whether these means are moral or material.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 148 (part 1 of 2):**

Then Allah, may He be exalted, said, explaining what follows from their good condition and their words: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran 148]. What does ﴿atahum﴾ mean?

* Student: He gave them.
* Shaykh: And *atahum*?
* Student: He came to them.
* Shaykh: He came to them. *Ata* (أتى) without the long vowel means "came," and *ataa* (آتى) with the long vowel means "gave." Here the second meaning is intended: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world﴾. ﴿Atahum﴾ means "Allah gave them." *Ataa* takes two objects, and they are not originally a subject and predicate, because it belongs to the category of *kasa* (clothed) and *a'ta* (gave). In ﴿atahumu Allahu thawaba al-dunya﴾, the first object is the *ha'* in *atahum*, and the second is *thawab* (reward). ﴿Thawaba al-dunya﴾ means its recompense, namely victory over their enemies and booty for those for whom booty is lawful. It is well known that booty is not lawful except for this Ummah, but what is meant is victory over the enemies, honor, and dominance over them.

﴿And the good reward of the Hereafter﴾: He did not say "the reward of the Hereafter" but said "its goodness," because the reward of the Hereafter is good: a good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundred times, and up to many multiples. It is not merely a reward in kind. If it were only a reward equal to the deed, a good deed would be repaid with what? With its equivalent. But it is a good and bountiful reward, and for this reason He said ﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾. This is one aspect. The second aspect is that He did not describe the reward of this world as good, because this world, however it may be, is a house of hardship, toil, and turbidity. Its pure part cannot be free of turbidity. For this reason He did not say "the good reward of this world," since in reality it has no goodness. Although it is good, its goodness is relative. Otherwise there is undoubtedly goodness in it: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ [al-Baqarah 201]. But it is a relative matter. Even those blessed with favors sometimes encounter what disturbs that favor.

He says: ﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, meaning on the Day of Resurrection, through elevation in ranks in the Gardens of Bliss and deliverance from the depths of the Hellfire.

﴿And Allah loves the doers of good﴾: meaning they are doers of good, so Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, loved them. Among the requirements of His love for them is this reward, which they receive in this world and in the Hereafter. As for His saying ﴿loves﴾, love is one of Allah's real attributes. He, may He be mighty and majestic, truly loves. His love does not mean reward or recompense, as some of the people of distortion (*ahl al-tahrif*, those who distort the attributes) have said. They deny some attributes, and love is one of those they deny. They say that Allah does not love and is not loved. Their justification is that love can only exist between what? Between two similar things: a creature and a creature. But we say to them: this is false. Love may exist between two distant things. Among the sayings of the Messenger (ﷺ) is: "Uhud is a mountain that loves us, and we love it" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1889) and Muslim (1365/462), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik]. It is inanimate. Among tangible, perceptible things, a person loves his furniture, his belongings, his mounts, his cars, and his houses. He loves them with an apparent, tangible, perceptible love, though they are not of his kind but of another kind. Indeed they are even lower than him, because they are his possessions. So this justification by which they negated the attribute of love for Allah is a false justification.

As for His saying ﴿loves the doers of good﴾: are the doers of good (*muhsinin*) those who do good in worship of Allah, or those who do good to the servants of Allah?

* Students: It includes both.
* Shaykh: Yes, it includes both: those who do good in the worship of Allah and those who do good to the servants of Allah. As for those who do good in worship of Allah, the Messenger (ﷺ) explained how goodness is achieved. When Jibril asked him about *ihsan* (excellence), he said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, [know that] He sees you" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah]. That means you worship Allah seeking Him with complete certainty. If you do not reach this level, then at least the second level: that you worship Allah out of fleeing (from His punishment), worshipping Him as though He sees you, so you flee from His punishment in order to perform His obedience. Thus the Messenger (ﷺ) indicates that *ihsan* is of two kinds: *ihsan* through seeking, and *ihsan* through fleeing. The first is that you worship Allah as though you see Him, so you seek Him and desire to reach Him. The second is that you know He sees you, so you fear Him, hold Him in awe, and magnify Him. The first is more complete than the second. This is the preferred view regarding the meaning of the hadith. Some say it is a single level, and that the meaning is: if you do not see Him, He sees you, which is close to the first meaning. The two sentences are close to being synonymous (*taradif*), but the correct view is what we said first.

Since He loves the doers of good, many things follow from Allah's love, some in this world and some in the Hereafter. Among what occurs in this world is that when Allah loves a person, He guides his deeds, steps, words, and actions, as in the authentic hadith: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him. My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely protect him" [al-Bukhari (6502), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah]. This is among the benefits of Allah's love.

* Among the benefits of Allah's love, may He be mighty and majestic, is making it easy to perform obedience and to abandon disobedience. A person who loves something seeks to reach it. If he loves wealth, he seeks to reach wealth through buying, selling, renting, and other means. If he loves a person, he seeks to reach him through companionship and friendship. Whatever a person loves, he seeks to reach it. So when Allah loves the servant, the servant loves Him, and seeks to reach Him.
