* Among its benefits also: when opinions converge with good intention, the general tendency is that Allah grants them success in what is correct. When opinions converge with good intention, Allah grants them success in what is correct.
* Among its benefits: a person may see benefit in a matter and miss the harm that follows from it, especially if he has a desire (hawa). Desire, as it is said, blinds and deafens. Sometimes a person has a desire, so he sees the benefit in something and does not see its harm. When consultation takes place, the benefits become distinguished from the harms.
* Among the benefits of consultation: when the community is unified in its opinion, people have no objection. It is well known that those who are consulted are people of trustworthiness, people who bind and loosen (ahl al-hall wal-aqd), and people of knowledge. If the ruler is confused by a legal (shar'i) issue, whom does he consult? The scholars of the Sharia. If he is confused by a political issue, he consults political scholars. If he is confused by a social issue, he consults sociology scholars. If he is confused by a geological issue, he consults geology scholars. A medical issue, he consults medical scholars. This does not mean that he makes them permanent advisers. Sometimes they may, in certain situations, be more ignorant than donkeys. No, he appoints advisers for each situation according to what suits it, because a condition of consultation is that the adviser must have an opinion, a sound opinion, and trustworthiness.

It is well known that if you consulted a scholar of the Sharia, one of the best scholars, about a medical matter, what would he say? He could not say anything.

It is said that a man came to a person who claimed to be a physician and said to him: I need an operation, an operation for a hernia. Do you know what a hernia is? A hernia is in the abdomen, meaning the abdomen splits and the intestines come out. This pseudo-physician said to him: I know how to cut open the abdomen, but I do not know how to sew it up. He said to him: My brother, this wolf knows how to cut open the abdomen but does not know how to sew it.

I say: Some people may enter into matters they do not know, and this is a mistake. It is obligatory for a person to know himself. If he is asked about something outside his specialty, he should say: this is not for me.

For example, if someone comes to consult a legal scholar about a medical matter, that is not appropriate. But if he comes to consult a geology scholar about a social matter, is that appropriate?

* Students: It is not appropriate.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because it is not within his specialty. So consultation is for each person according to his field, according to what suits him, because the adviser is trusted.
* Also among the benefits of consultation: if the imam or ruler errs, the error is not attributed to him. To whom is it attributed? To the advisers. That is why some say about consultation: consultation is a cover for your fault. If you err, they say: this is from the advisers. If you are correct, they praise me and them together.

Are there other benefits?

* Student: It is obedience to Allah and His Messenger.
* The Shaykh: Well said. It is obedience to Allah and His Messenger, because Allah commanded it.
* Student: Shaykh, there is in it the obligation of consultation, due to His saying: ﴿and consult them﴾.
* The Shaykh: No, no. Leave aside its ruling; we are now talking about its benefits.
* Student: That it may be more conducive to the scholars giving sincere advice to the leaders, because when they know that their advice will be taken and acted upon.
* The Shaykh: Did we say this? We mentioned it.
* Student: Shaykh, training the community to bear responsibility.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it. May Allah reward you with good.
* Student: (...) The enemies of Islam, when they see the Muslims have gathered upon one opinion.
* The Shaykh: Well said. Angering the enemies of Islam. When they see the Muslims gathering upon one opinion and uniting upon it, there is no doubt that this angers them.
* Student: Unity of word, unity of word and gathering of the community.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned its meaning.
* Student: (...) the thoughts of the advisers.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it.
* Student: Achieving harmony and cohesion among the believers.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it, or something close to it.
* Student: The greatness of the matter consulted about and the attention given to its concerns.
* The Shaykh: This is not among the benefits of consultation. This is the subject of consultation: that it is for great matters...
* Student: That it is a means of bringing about affection and love between rulers and subjects.
* The Shaykh: That is, it is a means of bringing about affection and love, or causing familiarity.
* Student: One.
* The Shaykh: It is a difference of expression, my brother. This is a difference of expression.
* Student: A connection between the leader and the soldiers.
* The Shaykh: (...) It is a difference of expression, everyone.
* Student: Allah's support for them, because the hand of Allah is with the group.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it.
* Student: The one who consults may benefit from the advisers in matters he does not know.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned its meaning approximately.
* Student: That it is among the attributes of the believers, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿and their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾ [al-Shura 38].
* The Shaykh: Alright, this is fine, that this is among the attributes of the believers.
* Student: Ending disagreement.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned its meaning. Harmony (al-i'tilaf) is the ending of disagreement.
* Student: Multiplicity of alternatives (...).
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it, because each one brings an opinion, and they agree on one. Apparently you have run out of points, and all that is left is repetition.
* Student: Showing (...) a person in thinking; he is not correct every time.
* The Shaykh: Did we not mention this?
* Students: We mentioned it.
* The Shaykh: Apparently we mentioned it at the very beginning: that a person knows his own worth, so he consults. Apparently we should stop here. This is the last one.
* Student: Strengthening the resolve of the one who consults.
* The Shaykh: Let us see this. Does it fit what was said before? Strengthening the resolve of the one who consults: when he sees that these people have agreed with him, for example, his resolve is strengthened, so this is more conducive to being certain of the ruling and not hesitating. Perhaps if he issued it on his own, he might hesitate or fear that someone would object. So when there is the gathering of consultation, he becomes determined. Who says: we mentioned it?
* Student: We mentioned it: strengthening the resolve.
* The Shaykh: Strengthening what?
* Student: With respect to the community.
* The Shaykh: And the ruler is not from the community?
* Student: The tolerance (samaha) of the Sharia and Islam.
* The Shaykh: How?
* Student: It leads to the unity of the community.
* The Shaykh: That is: the perfection of the Islamic Sharia? What do you all think? Is that correct? Perfection comes through perfection.

Alright, the question now: is consultation obligatory or not?

We mentioned a little while ago: it is either obligatory or recommended. In great matters it must be done. Or, when the difficulty is great, it must be done here, especially when it concerns the right of others.

As for when that is not the case, then no. This is why Allah, Mighty and Majestic, even mentioned the weaning of a child: ﴿And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 233]. So important matters that concern others are subject to consultation.

But does this mean that the Prophet, peace be upon him, formed a consultative council to which he referred? No. He consulted them when the reason for consultation existed, not that a council be formed to which he would refer. This is because if a council were formed to which he referred, that council might remain permanently even as the circumstances of its members change and better people come along.

So when we say: if a ruler is struck by a calamity, then he consults whomever he sees as fit for consultation, the ruler continues to have new men to consult, and this consultative council does not remain with its head raised, with all matters referred to it. There is no doubt that this is the way of the Prophet, peace be upon him. However, the ruler may have particular companions whom he consults on matters, such as Abu Bakr and Umar. The Prophet ﷺ always referred to their opinions and consulted them, seeing in their opinion soundness and right guidance, but not in everything. He did not refer to them in everything. Sometimes he consulted the rest of the Companions in general.

The second question: His saying: ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾. If a decision comes from the advisers, is it binding, or is it merely revealing an opinion?

It reveals an opinion and is not binding. Because if it were binding, the ruling would be in the hands of a group, and the ruling is in the hands of one person. But the one consulting must follow what he sees as most beneficial, and he may not defend his own opinion merely because it is his. Rather, it is obligatory upon him, for the right of Allah and for the right of those whom Allah has placed under his authority, to follow what is most beneficial, even if they oppose him. If the most beneficial thing is in their opinion, he must follow it. But it is not binding, not binding in the sense that we do not say these people have authority over the ruler. No, the ruler has the authority. That is why here He said: ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾, and did not say: when they advise you, then take it. ﴿When you have decided﴾, and he may decide upon what they advised or decide upon something else.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is obligatory for a person to rely upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while taking the means, due to His saying: ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the Prophet ﷺ experienced what human beings experience of hesitation in matters. The indication is first in His saying: ﴿consult them﴾, and second in His saying: ﴿So when you have decided﴾, for resolve may be preceded by hesitation, as is the reality.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: when a person has decided upon a matter, he should not hesitate, because hesitation confuses a person and throws him into anxiety. That is why the poet said:

If you are a person of opinion, then be a person of resolve,
For the corruption of opinion is that you hesitate.

Many people see benefit in something and decide upon it, then hesitate, so they become wavering, sometimes this, sometimes that.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, reported a very beneficial statement, which is his saying: "Whoever is blessed in something, let him persist in it." [Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (1184) from the hadith of Anas, raised to the Prophet, with the wording: "Whoever is provided (ruzika) in something, let him persist in it."] It is a wondrous statement; if it were weighed against gold, it would outweigh it: "Whoever is blessed in something, let him persist in it." Meaning: if a person does a deed and sees in it blessing and fruit, let him persist in it.

Let us give an example of this with the situation of the seeker of knowledge. For example, a seeker of knowledge began a book, studying or reviewing it, and found good in it. He found that he benefits and is helped by it. What do we say to him? Persist in this. Do not say: by Allah, this is a short, insignificant book (...).

A student (...) and sees blessing in it and benefits from it, then says: this is not enough, I want to read al-Insaf; this is not enough, I want to read al-Mughni; this is not enough, I want to read al-Majmu'; Dawr al-Funun by Ibn Aqil; this is not suitable for him. If Allah has blessed you in something, then stick to it, so that your time is not wasted.

Here is another matter that comes to my mind and may come to yours: for example, a person wants to read a question in the Fatawa of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah. He looks at the index so he can find it, then notices a second question and goes (...), wasting his time, goes (...), the original thing he intended to go to, perhaps he returns later, then another question comes up and he says: let us look at it, and then his time is wasted.

This is why it was part of the wisdom of the Messenger, peace be upon him, to begin with the thing he intended. "When 'Attab ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, invited him to pray in a place in his house that he had taken as a prayer place, the Prophet, peace be upon him, went out to him with some of his Companions. When he entered the house, he said: O Messenger of Allah, I have prepared food for you. He said: 'Show me the place where you want me to pray.'" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (425) from the hadith of 'Attab ibn Malik in similar wording.] before the food. Why? Because he came for this purpose.

Begin with the purpose for which you came. This is a matter a person should keep in mind in his conduct in knowledge, and also in worldly affairs. For example, some merchants deal in al-bazz. Do you know al-bazz? Cloth. Then he hears that someone bought land, sold it, and profited from it, so he says: that is it, we are finished, let us go to land. Then he hears that someone made profit from cars, and says: we are finished. Then his affairs are wasted. No. If he has found blessing in his first trade, he should continue in it and not accustom himself to transitions that have no benefit. We take this from His saying: ﴿When you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾: if you are a person of resolve, rely upon your resolve.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of love for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that Allah loves. Is the love of Allah real? Yes, it is real.

Because the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah) have a principle: everything Allah has described Himself with is real (haqiqah). Everything Allah has described Himself with is real. But their position is free of tamthil (likening Allah to His creation) and takyif (specifying how His attributes are).

Now, what about tahrif (distortion) and ta'til (denial of attributes)? It suffices to say that it is real. That is, if we say it is real, it means it is free of tahrif and ta'til. As for tamthil and takyif, they also disavow takyif and tamthil. They do not liken Allah's attributes to the attributes of His creation, nor do they specify how they are. So what is the love of Allah? Or what is love in general?

The love (المحبة) is love itself; it cannot be defined more clearly than by its own word, because, as we said earlier, what is that? Psychological states cannot be defined except by their own words, never otherwise. If someone said to you, "What is the meaning of hatred (al-bughd)?" you would say, "Aversion (al-karahiyah)." "And what is the meaning of aversion?" "Hatred (al-bughd)." "And what is the meaning of...?" These can only be defined by their effects.

* From the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of love for Allah, that is, the attribute of love.

The scholars of the qiblah who affiliate themselves with Islam have differed regarding it in three opinions:

The first opinion: negating its reality from Allah and from the created beings. They say: Allah neither loves nor is loved, we seek refuge in Allah. He neither loves nor is loved. Their reasoning is that love only exists between two things of the same kind, and the difference between the Creator and the created is well known.

A second opinion: they say that Allah is loved but does not love.

The third opinion: Allah loves and is loved. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:54]. In the Noble Qur'an there are many attributes to which Allah attached love: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ [at-Tawbah 9:4], ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222], and many other examples.

We hold that love is a real attribute established for Allah, and that among its effects are what? Reward, good pleasure, and other things that follow from it.

Those who deny it say: the intended meaning of Allah's love is reward. So they say, for example, regarding ﴿Allah loves those who rely upon Him﴾ [Aal 'Imran 3:159], that it means: He rewards those who rely upon Him. This is an error.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of tawakkul (reliance upon Allah). Its basis is that Allah attached love to it, and this indicates its excellence and encouragement toward it.

If someone says: Is tawakkul exclusive to Allah?

The answer: As for the tawakkul of worship, in which a person relies upon his Lord and entrusts the matter to Him, this is exclusive to Allah.

As for the tawakkul of delegation, meaning that a person appoints another to act on his behalf in some matter, this is permissible.

The difference between the two is clear. The first: relying upon Allah cuts a person's ties to everything other than Allah, even to himself; he entrusts the matter to Allah with complete entrustment. But in delegation, he regards the agent as being above the one who delegates, isn't that so? If I appoint a person to buy something for me, am I relying on him or not relying on him? I am relying on him. But is my reliance on him like my reliance on Allah? Never; because my reliance on Allah is entrusting to Allah with absolute entrustment, and I believe that He is sufficient for me. But this man, my reliance on him is as a deputy acting for me, not as one prostrate before him having entrusted the matter to him; he is my deputy. Can I dismiss him or not? I can dismiss him. I can rebuke him if he opposes my wishes, isn't that so? I can hold him accountable if he causes me harm. This is unlike reliance upon Allah.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, we mentioned that the ruler consults the scholars of the Shari'ah in matters of the Shari'ah, the scholars of politics in politics, the doctors in medicine, and likewise.

I say: may Allah be good to you, the separation of medicine, geology and the like from the science of the Shari'ah is clear and there is no problem with it. But how is politics separated from the Shari'ah? Although, may Allah be good to you, the Shari'ah came with politics and Shari'ah together, especially in this age in which they can never be separated. This is while we see today that political affairs are entrusted to people in whom there is what there is. So how, may Allah be good to you, can we make this distinction when...?

* The Shaykh: I tell you: the Shari'ah is politics. Do you know what politics means? Its origin is from (sāsa yasūsu), and the sā'is (tender/handler) is the one who manages animals, like the elephant handler, the gazelle handler, the sheep handler. The entire Shari'ah is politics. But there are matters hidden from the scholars of the Shari'ah, which they do not know, and which are political matters of the Shari'ah, but they do not know them. For example, if the ruler wants to appoint, for instance, an authorized representative, what is called an ambassador in some country, he must ask the people of politics: Can we appoint so-and-so or so-and-so or so-and-so in this country, or the like? This is what the scholars of the Shari'ah do not know. But his establishing relations between himself and this state, for example, or his concluding a treaty between himself and this state, these are Shari'ah matters, these are Shari'ah matters that return to the scholars of the Shari'ah.

* Student: O Shaykh, in the Consultative Council (majlis al-shura) when you mentioned that it is not, in the sense of being correct, but some countries have a consultative council and issue decisions that bind the people, so what should the people do?

* The Shaykh: By Allah, I do not see this as conforming to the shura that Allah commanded. The shura that Allah commanded, and that the Prophet ﷺ actually practiced, is that the ruler is the ruler, but when difficult matters befall him he consults concerning them. You know that the consultative council may include people who are not qualified for that, and you know that the consultative council is also by election, and how many consciences are bought through elections. A wealthy man comes who has how many millions...

* Student: Billions.

* The Shaykh: A billion, and he passes by these villages, each person gives him ten riyals, and they vote for him by the thousands.

* Student: Not just riyals, O Shaykh, he promises them?

* The Shaykh: Or he promises them and wishes them well, and Satan promises them nothing but delusion.

* Student: He sins, O Shaykh, this citizen who follows the decision sins.

* The Shaykh: How? It is known that whoever buys people's consciences with coins... and the common people are insects; place bait for them and they agree with you in what you want, except what Allah wills.

* Student: May Allah be good to you, regarding the ruler's consultation of the doctors and the geologists, why is it not (...) with the scholars of the Shari'ah?

* The Shaykh: By Allah, my brother, if they give the doctors pills for use, and you know that pills are most of the medicines in the English language, and you put them for example in the refrigerator with other pills, then if you come tomorrow you will not recognize the pills. Who knows these matters except the doctors? For example, if we assume that a country wants to supply us with medicines, does he come to the scholars of the Shari'ah and say: "What do you say, O so-and-so, about these medicines?" Or does he go to the doctors?

* Student: O Shaykh, but I mean after the doctors say (...), is this opinion presented to the scholars of the Shari'ah?

* The Shaykh: No, no, it is by no means necessary, it is not necessary at all. But in the Shari'ah rulings, for example, is it permissible for a woman to be a doctor for men or a man a doctor for women? This is a Shari'ah question, it is not a medical one.

* Student: O Shaykh (...), are they not guardians of affairs?

* The Shaykh: Guardians of affairs in what relates to their own affairs and specializations. No. As for me, if I am among the scholars, I have no involvement in medicine at all.

* Student: May Allah be good to you, what is the ruling on shura for individuals?

* The Shaykh: Individuals, this returns to you. Perhaps there is a matter that is difficult for you, but you do not want to reveal it to people. But if you consult, fine. And here, the istikhara: does one precede consultation or does consultation precede istikhara?

* Student: There is a difference of opinion.

* Another student: Consultation.

* Another student: Istikhara.

* The Shaykh: There are two opinions. Some say: seek Allah's guidance (istakhir Allah), and if after the istikhara you see an inclination toward something, do not consult anyone, because you have entrusted the matter to Allah, and Allah has guided you to that thing, so do not ask anyone, do not consult anyone. Others say: if you have sought Allah's guidance and the matter has not become clear to you, then consult, and the advice given by someone will be what Allah has chosen for you through istikhara.

* Student: Shaykh, does it not show that consultation precedes istikhara, the saying of Allah: ﴿And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Aal 'Imran 3:159]?

* The Shaykh: No, there is no istikhara in this. My intention by istikhara is the one the Messenger ﷺ commanded: when a person resolves upon a matter and it is unclear to him, he prays two units of prayer.

* Student: But here it shows that a person does not forget tawakkul.

* The Shaykh: No, it is not an istikhara matter we ask about. Is the prayer of istikhara before or after? As for example if he consults about some matter, whether or not he has prayed istikhara, here when he resolves, he relies upon Allah.

* Student: O Shaykh, is it a condition for the adviser to be just (ʿadl)?

* The Shaykh: What do you say about this question? Is it a condition for the adviser to be just? I do not think anyone consults someone who is not just, because he is not trustworthy.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: He does not consult him, because he fears him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 157–159 (part 1 of 5):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or you die﴾. Is it written like this with you? ﴿Or you die﴾?
* The students: ﴿Or you die (mutum)﴾.
* The Shaykh: There are two readings: ﴿Or you die (mutum)﴾ and ﴿Or you die (mitum)﴾ with a kasra. ﴿Surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾ and ﴿better than what you amass﴾ are two readings. So in this verse there are two words that have two readings. The first, he said: ﴿mitum﴾ is derived from mata, yamatu. And if it is derived from mata, yamutu, how do we say it? ﴿mutum﴾ with a damma on the mim. Or from mata, yamatu?
* The students: ﴿mitum﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿mitum﴾ from mata, yamatu. That is, all of it is Arabic. You say: (mata al-rajul, yamatu al-rajul), (mata al-rajul, yamutu al-rajul), (mata) like (yakhafu). Its origin is: mawita, yamwatu. This is its origin, like khafa, yakhafu, its origin being: khawifa, yakhwafu. So it is of the pattern: fariha, yafrahu. Khawifa, yakhwafu. It is said of it: khawifa, yakhwafu. We say of it: ﴿mitum﴾, as you say: ﴿khiftum﴾.
The second: ﴿better than what they amass﴾ and ﴿better than what you amass﴾. Is there an iltifat (shift) in the verse?
* A student: Yes, the second reading.
* The Shaykh: Which is the ya and which is the ta?
* The student: The ya.
* The Shaykh: The ya has an iltifat, and on the ta reading there is none, because the whole verse is in the second person.
Also in the verse, from the standpoint of Arabic grammar: ﴿And if you are killed...﴾ ... ﴿or you die, surely forgiveness from Allah﴾. An oath and a condition have come together in the sentence. Which is prior?
* A student: The oath, O Shaykh, ﴿And if (wa-la-in)﴾.
* The Shaykh: Which is prior?
* The student: The waw, the waw of the oath.
* The Shaykh: And when the oath comes first, which of them has its answer omitted: the condition or the oath?
* The student: The oath.
* The Shaykh: The oath?
* A student: The answer of the later one, the condition.
* The Shaykh: The answer of the later one. The condition or the oath? Ibn Malik said:
"Omit, when a condition and an oath come together, the answer of whichever is later, and that is obligatory."
("Omit when a condition and an oath come together") meaning when the condition and the oath are together in the sentence, omit ("the answer of whichever is later, and that is obligatory").
Here, what is prior? The oath. So the one whose answer is omitted is the condition, and that is the case here. In the verse, the answer given is ﴿surely forgiveness﴾, the answer of an oath. ﴿Surely forgiveness﴾ is the answer of the oath, so the lam here falls in the answer of the oath, and the lam in ﴿la-in﴾ is the lam that prepares for the oath, and the answer of the condition is omitted.
If someone says: how can it be omitted when it is a pillar of the sentence? We say: because there is something that stands in its place, namely the answer of the oath.
Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if you are killed﴾, addressed to the believers. ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah﴾, that is, in jihad in His way. It may be more general than that, meaning: you are killed in the way of Allah in jihad, or you are killed in the way of Allah in enjoining good and forbidding evil, or you are killed in the way of Allah in calling to Him, or you are killed in the way of Allah in making the truth clear. All of this falls under the way of Allah. Jihad is jihad against the disbelievers, enjoining good and forbidding evil, calling to Allah, making the truth clear, because what unites them is that this person was killed while defending what? The religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So whoever is killed in the way of Allah, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾, better than the world and whatever is in it.
As for His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿or you die﴾, do we say that the meaning is: or you die in the way of Allah, so that it refers to one who dies in jihad, or you die absolutely?
The second is apparent, because if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had intended the first, He would have said: "And if you are killed or die in the way of Allah." Since He placed ﴿mitum﴾ after the restriction, it is known that it is not intended in the second clause.
For this reason the scholars say: if a qualifier or condition follows several clauses, it returns to all of them; if it comes in the middle of clauses, it belongs to what precedes it. What is the rule? Every restriction, whether by a condition, a qualifier, an exception or otherwise, every restriction, if it follows several clauses, that is, comes at their end, it refers to all of them, and if it comes in the middle, it refers only to what precedes it and not what follows, unless evidence indicates otherwise.
On this we apply the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not bring four witnesses, lash them with eighty lashes, and never accept their testimony, and those are the defiantly disobedient (4). Except those who repent after that and make amends, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nur 4, 5]. This verse contains a restriction by exception that follows three clauses. Does it return to all three? We say: as for the first, it does not return to it by consensus; as for the third, it returns to it by consensus; as for the middle, there is disagreement.
﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not bring four witnesses﴾ is the first clause. ﴿Lash them with eighty lashes﴾ is the second. ﴿And never accept their testimony﴾ is the third clause. ﴿And those are the defiantly disobedient (4). Except those who repent after that and make amends, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is the exception. The exception does not return to the first by agreement, so if the slanderer repents, the right of the one slandered does not lapse; he is still lashed eighty lashes even if he repents. And if the slanderer repents, the attribute of defiant disobedience is removed from him by agreement. And if the slanderer repents, is his testimony accepted or not?
On this there is disagreement. Some of them said: it is accepted, and some said: it is not accepted.
He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or you die, surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾. Forgiveness contains deliverance from what is disliked, and mercy contains the attainment of what is sought.
As for His saying: ﴿better than what they amass﴾, that is, than what they amass of the entire world. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they amass﴾ [Yunus 58].
* A student: Regarding imitation (tashabbuh): if a thing is well known among the Muslims, that is, a group of Muslims does it and it is not specific to the disbelievers, but a person does it not because the Muslims do it but because the disbelievers do it, that is, he imitates them in the form... in eating, for example. He does not eat it because Muslims eat it but because the people of Europe eat it, or is it otherwise?
* The Shaykh: No, but apparently it is not considered imitation.
* The student: Or clothing, some garments?
* The Shaykh: This is something that does not pertain to the person himself: eating, tools and the like. If someone says: I slaughter with knives of the disbelievers, but there is no veneration of them in my heart, there is no harm. As for the saying of the Messenger ﷺ: "As for the claw, it is the blade of the Abyssinians," the reason is not that it is the blade of the Abyssinians, but that lengthening the nail is an action of the Abyssinians, so that they can slaughter with it. The Abyssinians grow their nails until they are like knives, and instead of carrying a knife in his pocket, he says: the knife is ready on the finger. Because if people habitually did this, they would depart from the natural disposition, which is trimming what?
* The students: The nails.
* The Shaykh: Trimming the nails, yes.
* A student: In some countries most scholars wear garments resembling those of bishops and monks, so is this imitation of them?
* The Shaykh: Apparently it is imitation, as long as when a person sees them he says: these are bishops, so it is imitation. Although the matter may be said to be that the precedence in this clothing belongs to the Muslims.
* The student: Why do they not wear the clothing of the people of the land?
* The Shaykh: But do you not think that this clothing preceded the Muslims, that it is specific to the scholars?
* The student: No, O Shaykh, the bishops came first.
* The Shaykh: They came first? This is a problem; this is not resembling the Christians.
* The student: But, O Shaykh, they do not know and do not intend?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but it is well known; whoever knows the clothing of bishops says: this is a bishop.
* The student: They imitate the scholars before them, and do not know that they are imitating?
* The Shaykh: We have said: imitation does not require intention.
* A student: I say, may Allah be good to you, O Shaykh: some women have certain haircuts that the disbelievers do, but they did not intend imitation, rather it is a custom?
* The Shaykh: Not at all. As long as this has not spread among the Muslims and become part of their clothing or their appearance, it is forbidden imitation.
* The student: They did not intend?
* The Shaykh: Even if they did not intend, because whoever intends imitation, as I told you, this is dangerous, since he would not intend imitation except with veneration and love for them in his heart.
* A student: O Shaykh, did you make forgiveness and mercy conditional on the mere dying?
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or you die﴾.
* The Shaykh: The meaning is that whoever dies, and in any case we have reached the end of it, but the meaning of "whoever dies" is that forgiveness will not escape him. Then when he dies he moves to something better than what he was in. That is, those who die in the way of Allah move to what is better, and for this reason they wish to return to the world, not to live in it but to be killed again in the way of Allah. Likewise death, and Allah is the One sought for help. We have repeated to you many times: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾ [ad-Duha 4], ﴿But you prefer the worldly life (16), while the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ [al-A'la 16, 17]. Do you think that the believer, when he dies, regrets dying because of the loss of something beloved to him? No, it is for the sake of deeds; he wishes to remain so that his deeds may increase, not to enjoy the world, because he moves to a better abode. As long as, may Allah make me and you among them, as long as his grave is widened as far as his sight reaches and there comes to him the bliss and spirit of Paradise, and this has no parallel in this world.
* A student: Regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And if you are killed﴾ ... ﴿or you die, surely forgiveness from Allah﴾, we want clarification of the oath particle and the sworn matter?
* The Shaykh: (Wallahi la-in) this is the particle of the oath: (wallahi la-in).
* A student: ﴿And they said﴾ is for the past, and ﴿when they struck﴾ is for the future; is there no difficulty?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but in any case there is some difficulty. What is the difficulty that could arise? ﴿And they said﴾ ... ﴿when they struck﴾. Some scholars said: here (idha) is not intended for the future; the indication of the future has been removed from it, and what is intended is merely a time adverb, and it resembles the saying: "And they said, when they struck upon the earth, and they said to their brothers when they struck upon the earth or were raiders." They said: the meaning may be stripped from a word, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah was ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa 96]. Is the meaning: He was in eternity, then now He is not Forgiving and Merciful? No, the indication of time was removed. Likewise "idha" here had the indication of the future removed, and what is intended is merely time alone.
* * *
* A student: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were lenient toward them. And if you had been rude and harsh of heart, they would have disbanded from around you. So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him (159)﴾ [Ali 'Imran 159].
* The Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. This person asks about those who annotate the copies of the Qur'an in the mosque?
Whoever wants to annotate the readings may buy a copy and annotate it; that is fine. That copy has the readings annotated on it. But in the mosque it is not permitted, because perhaps common people who do not know will take it, and this emboldens people toward incorrect annotations. So be careful: it is prohibited. Annotating the mosque's copies is forbidden. Do you understand, everyone? Because first, they are not ours that we should annotate them, and second, people who read them do not know, the common folk, and I fear this.
I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or you die, surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾.
﴿And if you are killed﴾: this expression occurs often in the Qur'an, where an oath and a condition come together. The oath is derived from the lam in ﴿la-in﴾, because this lam here prepares for the oath. As for the condition, it is with (in). When a condition and an oath come together, the answer of the later one is omitted, and the stated answer belongs to the earlier one, because it precedes. Ibn Malik said in the Alfiyya:
"Omit, when a condition and an oath come together, the answer of whichever is later, and that is obligatory."
In this verse: ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or you die, surely forgiveness﴾, the answer ﴿surely forgiveness﴾ is the answer of the oath, since it is joined with the lam.
In this verse, in His saying ﴿or you die (mitum)﴾, there are two readings: a reading with a kasra on the mim and a reading with a damma on the mim. As for the damma, it is from mata, yamutu. Here is a rule that will benefit you: when a past verb is attached to a pronoun of the nominative, it follows the present form. For example, if the present has a damma on the ayn, this too has a damma: qama, yaqumu, you say: qumtu; ba'a, yabi'u: bi'tu; khafa: khiftu. Why? Because its origin is khawifa, yakhwafu, with a kasra, so you say: khiftu. Mata, yamatu: mittu; mata, yamutu: mutu. So ﴿mutum﴾ is from mata, yamutu, and ﴿mitum﴾ is from mata, yamatu. These are two readings.
Also in His saying ﴿better than what they amass﴾ there are two readings: ﴿yajma'un﴾ with the ya and ﴿tajma'un﴾ with the ta. This is what was said about the readings and about the grammar.
Allah the Exalted says, explaining and consoling His believing servants: that if they leave their homes and are killed or die, what they turn toward is better than what they leave behind. This is connected to what precedes it: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾, and so on to the end. That is, he says: if you die or are killed, this is not regret; it is good. ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah﴾, that is, in jihad in the way of Allah, and the meaning may be more general than jihad in the way of Allah with weapons, to include jihad in the way of Allah through calling to Allah the Mighty and Majestic and through knowledge. Whoever is killed for being a caller (to Allah) is killed in the way of Allah, because he is like the fighter with his weapon.
His saying ﴿or you die﴾ means without being killed in the way of Allah. ﴿Surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾, from the entire world. ﴿Forgiveness﴾ for whom? For you: ﴿from Allah, and mercy﴾ for you as well.
The difference between forgiveness and mercy: forgiveness involves the removal of what is disliked, and mercy involves the attainment of what is sought; that is, what you seek will be attained for you and you will be saved from what you fear. Forgiveness is the covering of sin and overlooking it, and mercy is an attribute of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, which entails kindness to the one shown mercy and bestowing favor upon him.
In His saying ﴿surely forgiveness from Allah﴾, the attribution of forgiveness to Allah indicates the greatness of this forgiveness, because a thing becomes great according to the greatness of the one who gives it. For example, if you say: the king gave me a gift, and if you say: the pauper gave me a gift, who is the pauper? The poor man. What do people imagine when you say: the king gave me a gift? That it is large. The pauper gave me a gift? That it is twenty-five halalas, little. So a thing becomes great according to what? What it is attributed to. Therefore He said: ﴿forgiveness from Allah﴾, that is, its beginning is from Him; He is the One who initiates it, the Mighty and Majestic, and bestows it as a favor.
﴿And mercy﴾, that is, from Him, ﴿is better than what they amass﴾ or ﴿better than what you amass﴾, of the entire world.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: whoever among the believers is killed in the way of Allah or dies has moved to something better than the entire world; by His saying: ﴿better than what they amass﴾.

Among its benefits: Allah's favor upon His servants in consoling them over matters they dislike losing. A person is concerned about losing this world, since everyone loves to remain in it. When consolation comes from Allah and it is said, "If you die or are killed, you will move on to something better," a person is consoled by this and says, "Praise be to Allah that when I pass on to the Hereafter, I pass on to something better than this world."

Among the benefits of this noble verse: combining forgiveness and mercy so that a person's happiness is complete, for through forgiveness the disliked is removed, and through mercy the desired is attained.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of making a comparison between two things that are completely far apart, for when you compare what is in this world with the Hereafter, it is nothing. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than this world and everything in it." [Reported by al-Bukhari (2892) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi (may Allah be pleased with him).] And clearer than this is the Most High's saying: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?﴾ [An-Naml 59].

Then Allah the Most High said: ﴿And if you die or are killed, to Allah you will be gathered.﴾ Regarding ﴿if you die﴾, from the standpoint of i'rab (grammatical analysis), we say what we said about the verse before it: a Qur'anic oath and a conditional clause have come together, so the response of the conditional has been omitted. And regarding ﴿mittum﴾, there are two readings, as in the previous verse: with a kasra on the mim, as from mata–yamatu (to die), and with a damma on the mim, as from mata–yamutu.

He, Mighty and Majestic, says: If you die or are killed, your return is to Allah, however long or short the days you spend. When the return is to Allah, a person will remain reassured, for whoever has his return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not fear injustice or diminution. Indeed, if he is a believer, he will rejoice. How so? Because of Allah's saying: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him, and give good tidings to the believers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 223]. When the Prophet (ﷺ) told 'Aishah: "Whoever loves meeting Allah, Allah loves meeting him, and whoever dislikes meeting Allah, Allah dislikes meeting him." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, all of us dislike death" (and meeting Allah occurs through death). He said: "It is not as you think. Rather, when the believer's appointed time approaches and he is given good news of Paradise, he yearns for his Lord and loves meeting Allah. And the disbeliever, when his appointed time approaches—may Allah protect us—is given news of the Fire, so he dislikes meeting Allah, and Allah dislikes meeting him." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (6507) and Muslim (2683/14), from the hadith of Ubadah ibn al-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him).]

* In this verse: the return is to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, however long a person's life is extended, and in whatever manner he dies, whether by killing or otherwise. The return is to Allah.
* Among its benefits: increased consolation for the believers, for when the believer knows that his return is to Allah, he will be reassured, will rejoice, and his chest will be expanded by this.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of meeting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿to Allah you will be gathered.﴾
* Among its benefits also: the affirmation of the gathering (hashr) on the Day of Resurrection, for people will rise from their graves and be gathered to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to be recompensed.

Then He, Most High, said: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them.﴾

First, the i'rab: the fa' is conjunctive (ʿātifah), the ba' is a preposition, and ﴿mā﴾ is extra (zā'idah), but it is extra in wording only, not in meaning; it conveys an added meaning. Some scholars disliked saying that it is extra, or saying about a particle in the Qur'an that it is superfluous, saying that the Qur'an contains no superfluity. Rather, we say that by calling it extra we mean from the standpoint of i'rab, not from the standpoint of meaning.

As for His saying ﴿fabima rahmatin﴾: if we consider ﴿mā﴾ extra, then ﴿rahmatin﴾ is in the genitive, governed by the ba'. This is common in the Qur'an, including His saying: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant﴾ [An-Nisa' 155], meaning: because of their breaking their covenant. And among its examples is His saying: ﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 40], meaning: "in a little while."

As for His saying ﴿fabima rahmatin mina Allahi linta lahum﴾, the prepositional phrase is connected to the verb in ﴿linta﴾.

As for His saying ﴿walaw kunta﴾: here ﴿law﴾ is conditional, the conditional verb is ﴿kunta﴾, and its response is ﴿lanfaḍḍū min ḥawlika﴾ ("they would have dispersed from around you"). The rest has no difficulty.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, addresses His Prophet (ﷺ), explaining His blessing upon him and upon his community. He says: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them.﴾ That is: because of Allah's mercy toward you and toward your community, you were gentle toward them. ﴿You were lenient with them﴾: you were gentle; gentle in your speech, gentle in your sitting, gentle in your dealings, in all your circumstances. The Messenger (ﷺ) was among the easiest of people in disposition and the most generous in hospitality, and Allah said about him, and sufficient is His word: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character.﴾ [Al-Qalam 4].

His saying ﴿by mercy from Allah﴾ attributes the mercy to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because He is the one who bestows it, and because attributing it to Him indicates its greatness and that it is a great mercy. His saying ﴿linta lahum﴾: the pronoun refers to the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and also to those who came after them, for the legislation that occurred in the time of the Companions is legislation for them and for the community until the Day of Resurrection.

That it was a mercy for him is clear; that it was a mercy for them is also clear, so that they would become attached to him and feel at ease with him, and so that dealing with them would be made easy. For this reason, "the Prophet (ﷺ) never had to choose between two things without choosing the easier of them, as long as it was not sinful." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (6786) and Muslim (2327/78), from the hadith of 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), with the wording: The Prophet (ﷺ) was never given a choice between two matters without choosing the easier of them, so long as he would not sin.]

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if you had been harsh, hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you.﴾ This is coordinated with His saying ﴿you were lenient with them﴾. Leniency is opposed by harshness, and harshness may be in bearing, in speech, or in the heart. He said: ﴿And if you had been harsh (faẓẓ)﴾: faẓẓ is one who is coarse and severe in speech; you find him rough, caring for no one, turning his cheek away from people, not concerned with anyone, rough in his very name. Also in His saying, you find him violent and severe, not soft; ghilẓ (hard-heartedness) is in the heart: you find his heart harsh, not merciful, and not placing people in their proper stations, not considering the circumstances surrounding a person's actions. Sometimes there are circumstances accompanying a person's act for which he is excused, yet you find the hard-hearted, may Allah protect us, treating people all the same, not considering their conditions nor their circumstances, as they say; rather, you find him hard-hearted, harsh, not soft.

Among the clearest indications of this is what some people display in dealing with children. You find them harsh with children, wanting a child to have the manners of an adult. This is without doubt a grave error, and it is from hardness of heart. "When al-Aqra' ibn Habis saw the Prophet (ﷺ) kissing al-Hasan or al-Husayn, he said: 'You kiss your children?!' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'I have ten children and I have never kissed any of them.' He said: 'Can I do anything if Allah has removed mercy from your heart?'" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5997) and Muslim (2318/65), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: al-Aqra' ibn Habis saw the Prophet (ﷺ) kissing al-Hasan, and said: "I have ten children and have never kissed one of them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy."] So a person should be merciful and gentle of heart.

Allah the Most High said: ﴿And if you had been harsh (faẓẓ)﴾. What did we say about faẓẓ? The one who is coarse and severely harsh in speech.

Ghaliẓ al-qalb (hard-hearted): the one whose heart is hard and does not soften for any reason whatsoever.

He says: ﴿they would have dispersed from around you﴾: "dispersed" (infaḍḍū) means scattered and gone away. From it is His saying: ﴿And when they saw a trade or a diversion, they dispersed toward it﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah 11], meaning they scattered toward it and went out.

As for His saying ﴿lanfaḍḍū min ḥawlika﴾, He did not say "min-ka" (from you); because "min ḥawlika" (from around you) is more emphatic than "minka." That is, they would disperse and move away until they would not come near even a place close to you. ﴿Dispersed from around you﴾ means they would keep away even from the vicinity of your place.

He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So pardon them﴾. This is a branch (tafrī') from His saying ﴿by mercy from Allah you were lenient with them﴾. ﴿So pardon them﴾ if they fall short regarding your right. Pardon (al-'afw) is tolerance and not holding someone to account. ﴿And ask forgiveness for them﴾ regarding the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, if they fall short in it.

The Companions might fall short regarding the right of the Messenger (ﷺ), and they might fall short regarding the right of Allah. As for the right of the Messenger, He said: ﴿pardon them﴾. How often did harsh bedouins or others say offensive things to the Messenger (ﷺ), yet he would be patient, bear it, and pardon them. To the extent that "a man from the Ansar said to him, when he judged in a dispute between him and al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, a man from the Ansar said: 'Was it because he is the son of your paternal aunt, O Messenger of Allah?'" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2359) and Muslim (2357/129), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them both).] This is a monstrous accusation. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam's mother was Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, the paternal aunt of the Messenger (ﷺ). So this Ansari man said—may Allah pardon him—: "Was it because he is the son of your paternal aunt, O Messenger of Allah?"

"And a man said to him while he was distributing spoils: 'This is a distribution by which the face of Allah was not sought.' And he said to him: 'Be just.'" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3138) and Muslim (1063/142), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him).] All these words, the Prophet (ﷺ) would endure with patience, seeking reward from Allah, and pardon. Even at times he would receive from his wives what arises from jealousy among women, and he would pardon them.

He said: ﴿And ask forgiveness for them﴾, meaning for what they erred in regarding the right of Allah; that is, ask Allah to forgive them, as He said: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin, and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad 19].

﴿And consult them in the matter﴾: the pronoun in ﴿shāwirhum﴾ refers to your companions; that is, consult your companions in the matter. Consultation (mushawarah) is seeking opinion, whereby a matter is presented to the one consulted so that his opinion is sought and his view on it is considered. And "the one consulted is trusted" (al-mustashār mu'tamanun), so he must discharge the trust in the manner that he sees as best for the one who consults him.

As for His saying, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿in the matter﴾: the word "al-amr" here is first intended as the singular of "umūr" (affairs), not the singular of "awāmir" (commands), because commands are not something one consults about; one commands with them, they are legislated. Rather, ﴿fi al-amr﴾ means "in the affair." It is singular with the definite article. So is this article for generality, meaning consult him in every matter, or is it a general expression intended in a specific sense, meaning consult him in matters that are shared or whose aspect is unclear to you, or what?

The second, without doubt. The second, without doubt, because it is not possible that Allah would command His Prophet to consult them about everything. Rather, he consults them about shared public matters, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And their affair is by consultation among them﴾ [Ash-Shura 38]. Their affair that unites them all is by consultation among them. As for specific matters, consultation is sought when the matter becomes unclear, "as the Prophet (ﷺ) did when he consulted 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Usamah ibn Zayd about the affair of 'Aishah, when the incident of the slander (al-ifk) occurred." [Reported by al-Bukhari (2637) from the hadith of 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her).] When the talk about it increased and the rumor spread, the Prophet (ﷺ) consulted Usamah ibn Zayd and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib about her affair, and other specific matters that may be unclear to the Messenger (ﷺ), about which he consults.

So: ﴿shāwirhum﴾ means seek their opinion; ﴿fi al-amr﴾ means in the shared matter, or in a specific matter—what? When the matter is unclear to you. This is because consultation has benefits, which we will mention, God willing, in the benefits.

﴿Then when you have resolved, rely upon Allah﴾: "when you have resolved" means you have determined upon the action. After the consultation, or before it?

Apparently after the consultation, because the fa' indicates that what follows is a branch of what precedes it: that is, when you have resolved after seeking counsel and seeking opinion, then do not rely on their advice; rely on whom? On Allah: ﴿then rely upon Allah﴾. Here he is commanded both to take the means and to rely upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The means are the consultation, and reliance upon Allah is trusting in Him.

So what is tawakkul (trust in Allah)? The meaning of tawakkul is relying upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: relying upon Allah to bring benefit and avert harm, with confidence in Allah, and the soul's sense that a person is in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He, Most High, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him﴾. When He commanded tawakkul, He explained the great fruit of this tawakkul, and it has many fruits, of which this is the one Allah mentioned: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him.﴾ Upon whom? Upon Him: indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him.

* In this verse there are many benefits.
* First: the demonstration of the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, toward His Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. By what?
* Student: ﴿So by mercy from Allah﴾.
* Shaykh: By what is the mercy? I am not asking, "Where is the evidence?"
* Student: (...) (ﷺ) toward his Companions.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is the object of the mercy. But by what was this mercy?
* Student: This mercy was that when the Companions disobeyed the Messenger's (ﷺ) command in the battle of Uhud, Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded him to be gentle with them.
* Shaykh: No, this is a report that he was gentle; it is not a command.
* Student: Allah's direction to His Messenger, so that he would be kind to his Companions.
* Another student: The Messenger's being gentle toward them.
* Shaykh: Correct. The mercy is in making the Messenger (ﷺ) gentle toward them; by making him gentle toward them. This is mercy toward him and toward them.
* Among its benefits: whoever has leadership over his people should be gentle, so that he becomes deserving of Allah's mercy, the Mighty and Majestic. The evidence for this is clear: the Messenger was the leader of his people, indeed the leader of the whole community, and Allah made him gentle toward them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: gentleness is far better than harshness and severity. Because Allah made it part of mercy. However, when the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, mentioned what a judge should adopt as conduct, they said: he should be gentle without weakness, for some people are gentle and their gentleness makes them weak; they are not firm. This is a deficiency in gentleness. Rather, he should be gentle together with firmness and strength in their proper places, for strength in its place is wisdom. So gentleness that loses wisdom is blameworthy, and gentleness combined with wisdom is praiseworthy.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an explanation of the harms of harshness and hard-heartedness, and that among its greatest harms is people's aversion from a person who is harsh, coarse, and hard-hearted. This is from His saying to His Messenger: ﴿And if you had been harsh, hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you.﴾ Even though they hope from being close to the Messenger (ﷺ) for what they hope for, how much more so when a person from whom what is hoped for from the Messenger cannot be hoped? If a person is harsh and hard-hearted, it is evident that it is not enough for them to disperse from around him; they may even pelt him with stones. The Companions hoped for good from the Messenger by being close to him; so if it were assumed he was harsh and hard-hearted, they would disperse from around him. Then anyone other than him would be even more so.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that a person should use with people everything that draws them to him. The reason: Allah made—?
* Student: He made with them the means that lead to hearts.
* Shaykh: Yes, He made harshness and hard-heartedness a cause of repulsion, by way of blame, not by way of praise. So a person should use in dealing with people everything that brings them closer to him, on condition that he does not neglect any of the obligations.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 157–159 (part 3 of 5):

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: a person may be excused for keeping away from people of goodness if they are harsh and hard-hearted, because of the Exalted's words: ﴿they would have dispersed from around you﴾. And who is meant by "them"? The Companions. And what is meant by "dispersed from him" is the Messenger. So if the Companions would not be blamed for dispersing from the Messenger had he been harsh and hard-hearted, then how much more so for someone far below him. Therefore, if a person is harsh and rough and people do not gather around him, he has only himself to blame. And we see now that a person may be a disbeliever, yet if he treats people with gentleness, kindness, cheerfulness and generosity, they may prefer him over a Muslim who is harsh and hard-hearted.
* Among the lessons of the noble verse: it is recommended for a person to forgo his right in dealing with his brothers, because of His words: ﴿so pardon them﴾. But this verse is restricted to when the pardon is a reform. It is qualified by His words: ﴿And whoever pardons and reforms, his reward is with Allah﴾ [Ash-Shura 40]. As for when pardoning brings greater corruption and transgression, this is a benefit that contains a greater harm. For example, if the wrongdoer is known for evil and corruption, is it better for us to pardon him or to hold him accountable for his wrong?
It is better to hold him accountable for the wrong. For this reason, in car accidents, a person should not hasten to pardon the one who caused the accident, but should consider: if he is one of the reckless men who, if we pardon him today, will cause another accident tomorrow, then here it is better not to pardon. But if we know the man is extremely careful about the safety of lives and property, and this was a matter decreed, and we know he will take the utmost care in the future, then pardoning is better in this case. So pardon is restricted by what? By reform: ﴿So whoever pardons and reforms﴾.
And is pardon obligatory?
It is not obligatory, because Allah says: ﴿And whoever retaliates after being wronged, those—there is no path [of blame] against them﴾ [Ash-Shura 41]. Whoever defends himself after being wronged, there is no blame upon him. But it is better to pardon when pardoning brings reform.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: neglecting the right of the Prophet ﷺ may be a sin, because when Allah commanded His Prophet to pardon what concerned his personal right, He said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾, and that is so, for the Messenger ﷺ is not like others, since he has rights: the right of Islam and the right of prophethood, and because he is the greatest of people in rights over us. So transgression against him is more severe than against others and earns sin. For this reason He said: ﴿pardon them and ask forgiveness for them﴾. For anyone other than the Messenger ﷺ, if a person pardons his personal right, the matter ends. But when the matter concerning the Messenger ﷺ is connected with the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾. Therefore, if someone insults an individual among people, he does not become a disbeliever; but if he insults the Prophet ﷺ, he disbelieves, because of the greatness of his right.
* Among the lessons of the noble verse: the command to consult, consulting the Muslims in their affairs, regarding matters that concern affairs.
We stop here at ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾.
* Student: (...) Between His words ﴿And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted﴾, does it mean that this is a cause for dispersing from around the Messenger, and between the awe the Messenger ﷺ had, such that the Companions revered him, and would be in awe of him, and would hesitate to speak to him about some matters?
* Shaykh: This awe is something that falls into the heart, but the one who is revered has nothing of this in himself. For this reason, among his qualities is that whoever sees him at first sight is awed by him, and whoever mixes with him loves him. So he ﷺ is revered out of majesty and magnification, not because he himself is harsh and hard-hearted.
* Student: May Allah be good to you. I say: sometimes in pardoning, a person is compelled, O Shaykh, to overlook—I say—the question of whether pardon will bring reform or not. For example, if the wrongdoer is poor. So if, for instance, in a car accident or the like, a person is compelled to overlook whether pardon will bring reform, because this person is poor? For example, if one says: I will hold him responsible until he learns discipline and reforms and does not transgress against people; his limit is something very difficult, you find him poor and owning nothing...
* Shaykh: In any case, it is not a contradiction. The matter is in his hands. If he sees that pursuing the matter will cause him harm, he pardons later.
* Student: The words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, to Allah you will be gathered﴾, is the lam for emphasis?
* Shaykh: The lam falls in the answer of the oath, because what is omitted is the answer of the condition.
* Student: The pardon intended in the verse here, ﴿so pardon them﴾, since Allah (...) commanded (...) absolute pardon?
* Shaykh: Did we not mention that whoever defends himself, there is no path against him?
* Student: So does that mean it is obligatory in the verse?
* Shaykh: No, it is not obligatory.
* Student: In His words ﴿so pardon them﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, it is not obligatory.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What diverts it is, as we said, the second verse: ﴿And whoever pardons and reforms, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers (40). And whoever retaliates after being wronged, those—there is no path [of blame] against them﴾ [Ash-Shura 40, 41].
* Student: First: what is the meaning of the interpretation (...)? Second: what is the meaning of the consequence (tafrī') in His words ﴿so pardon them﴾? A consequence (...)?
* Shaykh: Tafrī' means that because you are gentle, pardon them.
* Student: Among some people, they consult, for example, one of the judges in his house or one of the scholars about an act that requires a legal penalty (hadd). Does the confession of this person require the judge, for example, to impose the penalty upon him?
* Shaykh: No, it is not appropriate.
* Student: The reason?
* Shaykh: The reason is that it is not a court session. He came to consult him, saying: I have committed a sin, what should I do? He says: Repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness.
* Student: Regarding death and killing in the second verse, is it different from the death and killing in the first verse?
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Are the death and killing in the second verse different from the first?
* Shaykh: In the second it is more general, because he did not restrict it to the cause of Allah.
* Student: The address in both contexts, are the two addresses to the believers and others?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible. Although, as we said to you, the apparent meaning is that the address is to the believers, and that when they are gathered to Allah, Allah is their Protector, as He said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ [Al-Baqarah 223].
* Student: Are the callers to innovation—is wisdom in calling them with gentleness or with harshness?
* Shaykh: If it is possible to call them with gentleness, that is better. But if they persist and are arrogant with arrogance, then we deal with them according to what they deserve. However, the matter is not in our hands. For example, if someone says: I want to beat this innovator, or stone him, or lock him in his house, we say: this is not up to you.
Although, as we said to you, the apparent meaning of the address to the believers is that they are gathered to Allah, Allah is their Protector, as He said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ [Al-Baqarah 223].
* Student: May Allah reward you well, O Shaykh. The callers to innovation, is wisdom in calling them with gentleness or with harshness?
* Shaykh: If it is possible to call them with gentleness, that is better. But if they persist and are arrogant with arrogance, then we deal with them according to what they deserve. However, the matter is not in our hands. For example, if someone says: I want to beat this innovator, or stone him, or lock him in his house. We say: this is not up to you.
* Student: Is harshness and severity, like pardon, restricted by benefit?
* Shaykh: No, regarding believers, no; it is general. But toward disbelievers, harshness is better: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾ [At-Tawbah 73].
* Student: Harshness and severity are not restricted by benefit with respect to believers at all?
* Shaykh: They are not restricted.
* Student: Even if he commits a sin, for example?
* Shaykh: Yes, even if he commits it. But when he commits a sin, if a legal penalty must be carried out upon him, for example, you should intend by that his reform, not intend revenge against him.
* Student: O Shaykh, if a person has a close friend who was harsh and he cut off from him, does the saying of the Messenger ﷺ not apply: «It is not lawful for a Muslim to boycott his brother for more than three [days]»?[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6237) from the hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.]]
* Shaykh: Yes, he is sinful.
* Student: (...) that a person may be excused for keeping away from people of goodness if they are (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but do you know what boycotting (hajr) is? Hajr means that you pass by him and do not greet him. But if you keep away from him and do not go near him, this is not boycotting; otherwise the necessary implication would be that we go around people's houses now, going around them (...).
* Student: Regarding this innovator, do we have the right to expose his innovation by his person?
* Shaykh: It is known.
* Student: By his person?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, if the situation calls for it. If we know this man draws people to himself, we must mention him by name. How else can we turn people away from him except by this?
* Student: O Shaykh, you told us that among the benefits is the permissibility of preferring between two things that have between them a (...), although this verse is facts.
"Did you not see that the sword diminishes in its worth / when it is said that the sword is more effective than the staff?"
Does this line mean something wrong?
* Shaykh: No, its meaning is not wrong, but you say: is this good or such-and-such?
As for this, this is correct: when you say "the sword is more effective than the staff," it does not occur to people that the sword and the staff are equal, because this is a self-evident statement (taḥṣīl ḥāṣil). The one who does not know the sword thinks they are equal.
* Student: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so pardon them﴾ [Al 'Imran 159]. We said that it concerns the right of the Prophet ﷺ. Can it be taken from it, O Shaykh, that whoever insults the Prophet (...)?
* Shaykh: No, we said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾ [Al 'Imran 159]. As for anyone other than the Messenger, we say: pardon him, and we need not seek forgiveness for him. But insulting the Messenger ﷺ involves two rights: his personal right and the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Student: Can it be taken from this verse that he must be killed, because the Messenger cannot pardon him?
* Shaykh: This is the correct view: the correct position is that one who insults the Messenger ﷺ, his repentance is accepted yet he is killed, and one who insults Allah, his repentance is accepted and he is not killed.
* Student: Can it be taken from this verse, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: That is... a bit far-fetched.
* Student: The difference between (mittum) and (qutiltum)?
* Shaykh: Killing is by a human's action, and death is more general. But when killing and death are mentioned together, the meaning is: death is without a killer, and killing is by a human's action.
* Student: A disbeliever who insults the Messenger ﷺ?
* Shaykh: If he insults the Messenger and then embraces Islam, he is killed.
* Student: Even if he does not embrace Islam?
* Shaykh: Even if he does not embrace Islam. Even if he does not embrace Islam, even if he insults Allah, he is killed. For this reason the scholars said: if a dhimmi with whom we have a covenant insults Allah, his covenant is broken and his blood and property become lawful.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: No, but the matter is not in our hands; yet it is obligatory upon the rulers to kill him.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them. And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you. So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely [upon Him] (159). If Allah helps you, no one can overcome you; and if He forsakes you, then who is there that can help you after Him? And upon Allah let the believers rely (160). And it is not for a prophet to defraud. And whoever defrauds will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul will be payed in full what it has earned, and they will not be wronged﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159–161].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. The Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿And if you are killed in the cause of Allah or die, forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they accumulate﴾ [Al 'Imran 157]. This verse contains an oath and a condition. So what has been found as its answer: the answer of the oath or the answer of the condition in the verse?
* Student: The answer of the condition.
* Shaykh: Think, brother.
* Student: The answer of the oath.
* Shaykh: What informed you that it is the answer of the oath?
* Student: The words of the versifier.
* Shaykh: No, not the versifier's words; the versifier was not present in our lesson. No, what informed you just now from the verse?
* Student: (...) ﴿khayr﴾, O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: ﴿khayr﴾ is the answer.
* Student: No, ﴿aw mittum la-maghfiratun﴾, ﴿la-maghfiratun﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿la-maghfiratun﴾. What informed you that this is the answer of the oath and not the answer of the condition?
* Student: (...) the rule, O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: No, you said: this applies to it, and there is a sign that it is the answer of the oath, not the answer of the condition.
* Student: The lam.
* Shaykh: The lam. And if it were the answer of the condition, it would have had the fa'; because when the answer of the condition is a nominal sentence, it is joined with fa', while the answer of the oath with lam. Clear?
Who can recite for us Ibn Malik's verse on this rule?
* Student: "And omit, when condition and oath come together..."
* Shaykh: No, brother; because "aw qasam" (or oath) means each one stands on its own, but "wa-qasam" (and oath), the joining of this and that, the meaning clearly differs.
* Student:
"And omit, when condition and oath come together, / the answer of whichever is placed later; it is obligatory."
* Shaykh: Perfect, correct. Now, in the first verse Allah, the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And if you are killed in the cause of Allah﴾, and in the second He says: ﴿And if you die or are killed﴾ [Al 'Imran 158]. What is the reason?
* Student: Two readings.
* Shaykh: No, no, I do not mean the kasra and damma on the mim. I mean: he placed killing first in the first and dying first in the second?
* Student: The second, O Shaykh, is more general than the first.
* Shaykh: The second is more general; it includes whoever dies in the cause of Allah or otherwise. And the second [i.e., the first verse] is about whoever is killed in the cause of Allah. So he placed killing in the cause of Allah first, because killing in the cause of Allah is more common than dying: the fighters die by killing more than by natural death, is that not so? Unlike the second.
In His words: ﴿Indeed, to Allah you will be gathered﴾, some students raised a difficulty: ﴿Indeed, to Allah you will be gathered﴾, what is its meaning, and what is the answer?
* Student: Restriction of ﴿to Allah﴾, meaning: your return is to Allah.
* Shaykh: But without this, what is the construction of the verse, what is the implied sense?
* Student: Meaning: you will be gathered to Allah.
* Shaykh: Yes, you will be gathered to Allah, but He placed the prepositional phrase first to convey restriction.
His words: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them﴾. Brother, the (bā')?
* Student: The bā' is a preposition.
* Shaykh: And (mā)?
* Student: And (mā) is grammatically superfluous.
* Shaykh: Grammatically superfluous; what is its meaning-function?
* Student: Its function is emphasis.
* Shaykh: Emphasis, well done.
The governing element, the (bā'): does it govern (mā) or what follows it?
* Student: What follows it.
* Shaykh: What follows it?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Perfect, correct.
Where is the complement of ﴿fa-bimā raḥmatin﴾?
* Student: ﴿Linta lahum﴾.
* Shaykh: The verb ﴿Linta﴾, and the address is to whom?
* Student: To the Messenger ﷺ.
* Shaykh: To the Messenger. Allah says: ﴿So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them﴾. Pardon them with respect to what?
* Student: With respect to the Prophet ﷺ.
* Shaykh: With respect to the Prophet; the whole address is to the Messenger in this and that.
* Student: ﴿So pardon them﴾ concerns your right, ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾ concerns the right of Allah.
* Shaykh: Well said. Can it not include: ﴿ask forgiveness for them﴾ concerning the right of Allah and your right as well?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: It includes it; because harming the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is disobedience to Allah, distinct from harming other people. Harming other people is a pure right of the person, which lapses if he forgives.
His words: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾. What is meant by "the matter"?
* Student: The meaning is one of the affairs; what is intended is the general matter that concerns the Muslims, or a particular matter that presents a difficulty to the Prophet ﷺ.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verses 157–159 (part 4 of 5):**

* The Shaykh: Can you give us an example of a particular matter on which the Messenger, peace be upon him, sought counsel?
* Student: Yes, in the incident of the slander (al-ifk), the Prophet ﷺ consulted Usama ibn Zayd and Ali ibn Abi Talib about what the people were saying.
* The Shaykh: Concerning 'Aisha. Good. Are there other instances of consultation in which he consulted his Companions?
* Student: Did the Prophet, peace be upon him, consult only particular individuals?
* The Shaykh: In general.
* Student: In general. He consulted them about digging the trench (al-khandaq), when some of the Companions suggested digging the trench.
* The Shaykh: Who?
* Student: The Companion Salman al-Farisi suggested it.
* The Shaykh: Salman al-Farisi. Also in the matter of the trench, the Messenger consulted about whether to give the confederates (al-ahzab) some of the dates of Madinah so that they would withdraw. But the two Sa'ds, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn Ubadah, opposed that; they said: it is not possible. In any case, there are many examples.
