* Student: There is another instance of consultation as well.
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: The day of al-Hudaybiyyah.
* The Shaykh: There are many examples. As for His saying: ﴿And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾. What is the benefit of this sentence?
* Student: His saying, O Shaykh, ﴿when you have decided﴾ means: after consultation, then rely upon Allah. That is: after taking the means, then rely upon Allah.
* The Shaykh: That is, do not depend on their counsel and think that their counsel will bring victory.

I think we are still on the benefits.

* Student: We have stopped at the command to consult.
* The Shaykh: The benefits of consultation. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter﴾. What benefits did we mention from: ﴿So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them﴾?
* Student: (...)
* Student: There are three or four benefits in it.
* The Shaykh: What are they?
* Student: A person pardons his right in dealing with his brothers, due to His saying: ﴿So pardon them﴾.
* The second: Neglecting the right of the Prophet ﷺ may be a sin, because when Allah commanded His Prophet to pardon his personal right, He said: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾.
* The third: The command to consult in his affairs.
* The Shaykh: It may be a sin related to the right of Allah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the command to consult, due to His saying: ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾. This command may be obligatory or recommended, depending on the matter consulted about and the difficulty that arises in it. So in great matters with great difficulty, consultation is obligatory, while in minor matters or matters with slight difficulty, consultation is recommended.

So the command here, ﴿consult them﴾, is shared between obligation and recommendation, according to what the situation requires. The wisdom behind the command to consult becomes clear through the benefits of consultation. There are benefits of consultation that we will enumerate, and you as well. I will answer, and you answer too.

* Among its benefits: the ruler or guardian of affairs does not act arbitrarily according to his own opinion. This is a very important benefit.
* Among its benefits: accustoming the community to look into its affairs, so that they train and practice this matter.
* Among its benefits: humility. Humility toward whom? Toward those he consults. There is no doubt that whoever consults is humble.
* Among its benefits: energizing the community, as it sees that he refers to them for their opinion, so they become active and work for what benefits the general public. This is in contrast to when the ruler acts arbitrarily in his opinion; even if his opinion is correct, people's souls may recoil from it, so they say, for example: he did not refer to us, he did not consult us in this great matter, and similar things.
* Among its benefits also: when opinions converge with good intention, the general tendency is that Allah grants them success in what is correct. When opinions converge with good intention, Allah grants them success in what is correct.
* Among its benefits: a person may see benefit in a matter and miss the harm that follows from it, especially if he has a desire (hawa). Desire, as it is said, blinds and deafens. Sometimes a person has a desire, so he sees the benefit in something and does not see its harm. When consultation takes place, the benefits become distinguished from the harms.
* Among the benefits of consultation: when the community is unified in its opinion, people have no objection. It is well known that those who are consulted are people of trustworthiness, people who bind and loosen (ahl al-hall wal-aqd), and people of knowledge. If the ruler is confused by a legal (shar'i) issue, whom does he consult? The scholars of the Sharia. If he is confused by a political issue, he consults political scholars. If he is confused by a social issue, he consults sociology scholars. If he is confused by a geological issue, he consults geology scholars. A medical issue, he consults medical scholars. This does not mean that he makes them permanent advisers. Sometimes they may, in certain situations, be more ignorant than donkeys. No, he appoints advisers for each situation according to what suits it, because a condition of consultation is that the adviser must have an opinion, a sound opinion, and trustworthiness.

It is well known that if you consulted a scholar of the Sharia, one of the best scholars, about a medical matter, what would he say? He could not say anything.

It is said that a man came to a person who claimed to be a physician and said to him: I need an operation, an operation for a hernia. Do you know what a hernia is? A hernia is in the abdomen, meaning the abdomen splits and the intestines come out. This pseudo-physician said to him: I know how to cut open the abdomen, but I do not know how to sew it up. He said to him: My brother, this wolf knows how to cut open the abdomen but does not know how to sew it.

I say: Some people may enter into matters they do not know, and this is a mistake. It is obligatory for a person to know himself. If he is asked about something outside his specialty, he should say: this is not for me.

For example, if someone comes to consult a legal scholar about a medical matter, that is not appropriate. But if he comes to consult a geology scholar about a social matter, is that appropriate?

* Students: It is not appropriate.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because it is not within his specialty. So consultation is for each person according to his field, according to what suits him, because the adviser is trusted.
* Also among the benefits of consultation: if the imam or ruler errs, the error is not attributed to him. To whom is it attributed? To the advisers. That is why some say about consultation: consultation is a cover for your fault. If you err, they say: this is from the advisers. If you are correct, they praise me and them together.

Are there other benefits?

* Student: It is obedience to Allah and His Messenger.
* The Shaykh: Well said. It is obedience to Allah and His Messenger, because Allah commanded it.
* Student: Shaykh, there is in it the obligation of consultation, due to His saying: ﴿and consult them﴾.
* The Shaykh: No, no. Leave aside its ruling; we are now talking about its benefits.
* Student: That it may be more conducive to the scholars giving sincere advice to the leaders, because when they know that their advice will be taken and acted upon.
* The Shaykh: Did we say this? We mentioned it.
* Student: Shaykh, training the community to bear responsibility.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it. May Allah reward you with good.

* The Shaykh: Well said. Angering the enemies of Islam. When they see the Muslims gathering upon one opinion and uniting upon it, there is no doubt that this angers them.
* Student: Unity of word, unity of word and gathering of the community.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned its meaning.
* Student: (...) the thoughts of the advisers.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it.

* The Shaykh: We mentioned it, or something close to it.
* Student: The greatness of the matter consulted about and the attention given to its concerns.
* The Shaykh: This is not among the benefits of consultation. This is the subject of consultation: that it is for great matters...
* Student: That it is a means of bringing about affection and love between rulers and subjects.
* The Shaykh: That is, it is a means of bringing about affection and love, or causing familiarity.
* Student: One.
* The Shaykh: It is a difference of expression, my brother. This is a difference of expression.
* Student: A connection between the leader and the soldiers.
* The Shaykh: (...) It is a difference of expression, everyone.
* Student: Allah's support for them, because the hand of Allah is with the group.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it.

* The Shaykh: We mentioned its meaning approximately.
* Student: That it is among the attributes of the believers, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿and their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾ [al-Shura 38].
* The Shaykh: Alright, this is fine, that this is among the attributes of the believers.
* Student: Ending disagreement.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned its meaning. Harmony (al-i'tilaf) is the ending of disagreement.
* Student: Multiplicity of alternatives (...).
* The Shaykh: We mentioned it, because each one brings an opinion, and they agree on one. Apparently you have run out of points, and all that is left is repetition.
* Student: Showing (...) a person in thinking; he is not correct every time.
* The Shaykh: Did we not mention this?
* Students: We mentioned it.
* The Shaykh: Apparently we mentioned it at the very beginning: that a person knows his own worth, so he consults. Apparently we should stop here. This is the last one.
* Student: Strengthening the resolve of the one who consults.
* The Shaykh: Let us see this. Does it fit what was said before? Strengthening the resolve of the one who consults: when he sees that these people have agreed with him, for example, his resolve is strengthened, so this is more conducive to being certain of the ruling and not hesitating. Perhaps if he issued it on his own, he might hesitate or fear that someone would object. So when there is the gathering of consultation, he becomes determined. Who says: we mentioned it?
* Student: We mentioned it: strengthening the resolve.
* The Shaykh: Strengthening what?
* Student: With respect to the community.
* The Shaykh: And the ruler is not from the community?
* Student: The tolerance (samaha) of the Sharia and Islam.
* The Shaykh: How?
* Student: It leads to the unity of the community.
* The Shaykh: That is: the perfection of the Islamic Sharia? What do you all think? Is that correct? Perfection comes through perfection.

Alright, the question now: is consultation obligatory or not?

We mentioned a little while ago: it is either obligatory or recommended. In great matters it must be done. Or, when the difficulty is great, it must be done here, especially when it concerns the right of others.

As for when that is not the case, then no. This is why Allah, Mighty and Majestic, even mentioned the weaning of a child: ﴿And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 233]. So important matters that concern others are subject to consultation.

But does this mean that the Prophet, peace be upon him, formed a consultative council to which he referred? No. He consulted them when the reason for consultation existed, not that a council be formed to which he would refer. This is because if a council were formed to which he referred, that council might remain permanently even as the circumstances of its members change and better people come along.

So when we say: if a ruler is struck by a calamity, then he consults whomever he sees as fit for consultation, the ruler continues to have new men to consult, and this consultative council does not remain with its head raised, with all matters referred to it. There is no doubt that this is the way of the Prophet, peace be upon him. However, the ruler may have particular companions whom he consults on matters, such as Abu Bakr and Umar. The Prophet ﷺ always referred to their opinions and consulted them, seeing in their opinion soundness and right guidance, but not in everything. He did not refer to them in everything. Sometimes he consulted the rest of the Companions in general.

The second question: His saying: ﴿and consult them in the matter﴾. If a decision comes from the advisers, is it binding, or is it merely revealing an opinion?

It reveals an opinion and is not binding. Because if it were binding, the ruling would be in the hands of a group, and the ruling is in the hands of one person. But the one consulting must follow what he sees as most beneficial, and he may not defend his own opinion merely because it is his. Rather, it is obligatory upon him, for the right of Allah and for the right of those whom Allah has placed under his authority, to follow what is most beneficial, even if they oppose him. If the most beneficial thing is in their opinion, he must follow it. But it is not binding, not binding in the sense that we do not say these people have authority over the ruler. No, the ruler has the authority. That is why here He said: ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾, and did not say: when they advise you, then take it. ﴿When you have decided﴾, and he may decide upon what they advised or decide upon something else.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is obligatory for a person to rely upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while taking the means, due to His saying: ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the Prophet ﷺ experienced what human beings experience of hesitation in matters. The indication is first in His saying: ﴿consult them﴾, and second in His saying: ﴿So when you have decided﴾, for resolve may be preceded by hesitation, as is the reality.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: when a person has decided upon a matter, he should not hesitate, because hesitation confuses a person and throws him into anxiety. That is why the poet said:

If you are a person of opinion, then be a person of resolve,
For the corruption of opinion is that you hesitate.

Many people see benefit in something and decide upon it, then hesitate, so they become wavering, sometimes this, sometimes that.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, reported a very beneficial statement, which is his saying: "Whoever is blessed in something, let him persist in it." [Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (1184) from the hadith of Anas, raised to the Prophet, with the wording: "Whoever is provided (ruzika) in something, let him persist in it."] It is a wondrous statement; if it were weighed against gold, it would outweigh it: "Whoever is blessed in something, let him persist in it." Meaning: if a person does a deed and sees in it blessing and fruit, let him persist in it.

Let us give an example of this with the situation of the seeker of knowledge. For example, a seeker of knowledge began a book, studying or reviewing it, and found good in it. He found that he benefits and is helped by it. What do we say to him? Persist in this. Do not say: by Allah, this is a short, insignificant book (...).

A student (...) and sees blessing in it and benefits from it, then says: this is not enough, I want to read al-Insaf; this is not enough, I want to read al-Mughni; this is not enough, I want to read al-Majmu'; Dawr al-Funun by Ibn Aqil; this is not suitable for him. If Allah has blessed you in something, then stick to it, so that your time is not wasted.

Here is another matter that comes to my mind and may come to yours: for example, a person wants to read a question in the Fatawa of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah. He looks at the index so he can find it, then notices a second question and goes (...), wasting his time, goes (...), the original thing he intended to go to, perhaps he returns later, then another question comes up and he says: let us look at it, and then his time is wasted.

This is why it was part of the wisdom of the Messenger, peace be upon him, to begin with the thing he intended. "When 'Attab ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, invited him to pray in a place in his house that he had taken as a prayer place, the Prophet, peace be upon him, went out to him with some of his Companions. When he entered the house, he said: O Messenger of Allah, I have prepared food for you. He said: 'Show me the place where you want me to pray.'" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (425) from the hadith of 'Attab ibn Malik in similar wording.] before the food. Why? Because he came for this purpose.

Begin with the purpose for which you came. This is a matter a person should keep in mind in his conduct in knowledge, and also in worldly affairs. For example, some merchants deal in al-bazz. Do you know al-bazz? Cloth. Then he hears that someone bought land, sold it, and profited from it, so he says: that is it, we are finished, let us go to land. Then he hears that someone made profit from cars, and says: we are finished. Then his affairs are wasted. No. If he has found blessing in his first trade, he should continue in it and not accustom himself to transitions that have no benefit. We take this from His saying: ﴿When you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾: if you are a person of resolve, rely upon your resolve.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of love for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that Allah loves. Is the love of Allah real? Yes, it is real.

Because the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah) have a principle: everything Allah has described Himself with is real (haqiqah). Everything Allah has described Himself with is real. But their position is free of tamthil (likening Allah to His creation) and takyif (specifying how His attributes are).

Now, what about tahrif (distortion) and ta'til (denial of attributes)? It suffices to say that it is real. That is, if we say it is real, it means it is free of tahrif and ta'til. As for tamthil and takyif, they also disavow takyif and tamthil. They do not liken Allah's attributes to the attributes of His creation, nor do they specify how they are. So what is the love of Allah? Or what is love in general?

The love (المحبة) is love itself; it cannot be defined more clearly than by its own word, because, as we said earlier, what is that? Psychological states cannot be defined except by their own words, never otherwise. If someone said to you, "What is the meaning of hatred (al-bughd)?" you would say, "Aversion (al-karahiyah)." "And what is the meaning of aversion?" "Hatred (al-bughd)." "And what is the meaning of...?" These can only be defined by their effects.

* From the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of love for Allah, that is, the attribute of love.

The scholars of the qiblah who affiliate themselves with Islam have differed regarding it in three opinions:

The first opinion: negating its reality from Allah and from the created beings. They say: Allah neither loves nor is loved, we seek refuge in Allah. He neither loves nor is loved. Their reasoning is that love only exists between two things of the same kind, and the difference between the Creator and the created is well known.

A second opinion: they say that Allah is loved but does not love.

The third opinion: Allah loves and is loved. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:54]. In the Noble Qur'an there are many attributes to which Allah attached love: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ [at-Tawbah 9:4], ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222], and many other examples.

We hold that love is a real attribute established for Allah, and that among its effects are what? Reward, good pleasure, and other things that follow from it.

Those who deny it say: the intended meaning of Allah's love is reward. So they say, for example, regarding ﴿Allah loves those who rely upon Him﴾ [Aal 'Imran 3:159], that it means: He rewards those who rely upon Him. This is an error.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of tawakkul (reliance upon Allah). Its basis is that Allah attached love to it, and this indicates its excellence and encouragement toward it.

If someone says: Is tawakkul exclusive to Allah?

The answer: As for the tawakkul of worship, in which a person relies upon his Lord and entrusts the matter to Him, this is exclusive to Allah.

As for the tawakkul of delegation, meaning that a person appoints another to act on his behalf in some matter, this is permissible.

The difference between the two is clear. The first: relying upon Allah cuts a person's ties to everything other than Allah, even to himself; he entrusts the matter to Allah with complete entrustment. But in delegation, he regards the agent as being above the one who delegates, isn't that so? If I appoint a person to buy something for me, am I relying on him or not relying on him? I am relying on him. But is my reliance on him like my reliance on Allah? Never; because my reliance on Allah is entrusting to Allah with absolute entrustment, and I believe that He is sufficient for me. But this man, my reliance on him is as a deputy acting for me, not as one prostrate before him having entrusted the matter to him; he is my deputy. Can I dismiss him or not? I can dismiss him. I can rebuke him if he opposes my wishes, isn't that so? I can hold him accountable if he causes me harm. This is unlike reliance upon Allah.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, we mentioned that the ruler consults the scholars of the Shari'ah in matters of the Shari'ah, the scholars of politics in politics, the doctors in medicine, and likewise.

I say: may Allah be good to you, the separation of medicine, geology and the like from the science of the Shari'ah is clear and there is no problem with it. But how is politics separated from the Shari'ah? Although, may Allah be good to you, the Shari'ah came with politics and Shari'ah together, especially in this age in which they can never be separated. This is while we see today that political affairs are entrusted to people in whom there is what there is. So how, may Allah be good to you, can we make this distinction when...?

* The Shaykh: I tell you: the Shari'ah is politics. Do you know what politics means? Its origin is from (sāsa yasūsu), and the sā'is (tender/handler) is the one who manages animals, like the elephant handler, the gazelle handler, the sheep handler. The entire Shari'ah is politics. But there are matters hidden from the scholars of the Shari'ah, which they do not know, and which are political matters of the Shari'ah, but they do not know them. For example, if the ruler wants to appoint, for instance, an authorized representative, what is called an ambassador in some country, he must ask the people of politics: Can we appoint so-and-so or so-and-so or so-and-so in this country, or the like? This is what the scholars of the Shari'ah do not know. But his establishing relations between himself and this state, for example, or his concluding a treaty between himself and this state, these are Shari'ah matters, these are Shari'ah matters that return to the scholars of the Shari'ah.

* Student: O Shaykh, in the Consultative Council (majlis al-shura) when you mentioned that it is not, in the sense of being correct, but some countries have a consultative council and issue decisions that bind the people, so what should the people do?

* The Shaykh: By Allah, I do not see this as conforming to the shura that Allah commanded. The shura that Allah commanded, and that the Prophet ﷺ actually practiced, is that the ruler is the ruler, but when difficult matters befall him he consults concerning them. You know that the consultative council may include people who are not qualified for that, and you know that the consultative council is also by election, and how many consciences are bought through elections. A wealthy man comes who has how many millions...

* Student: Billions.

* The Shaykh: A billion, and he passes by these villages, each person gives him ten riyals, and they vote for him by the thousands.

* Student: Not just riyals, O Shaykh, he promises them?

* The Shaykh: Or he promises them and wishes them well, and Satan promises them nothing but delusion.

* Student: He sins, O Shaykh, this citizen who follows the decision sins.

* The Shaykh: How? It is known that whoever buys people's consciences with coins... and the common people are insects; place bait for them and they agree with you in what you want, except what Allah wills.

* Student: May Allah be good to you, regarding the ruler's consultation of the doctors and the geologists, why is it not (...) with the scholars of the Shari'ah?

* The Shaykh: By Allah, my brother, if they give the doctors pills for use, and you know that pills are most of the medicines in the English language, and you put them for example in the refrigerator with other pills, then if you come tomorrow you will not recognize the pills. Who knows these matters except the doctors? For example, if we assume that a country wants to supply us with medicines, does he come to the scholars of the Shari'ah and say: "What do you say, O so-and-so, about these medicines?" Or does he go to the doctors?

* Student: O Shaykh, but I mean after the doctors say (...), is this opinion presented to the scholars of the Shari'ah?

* The Shaykh: No, no, it is by no means necessary, it is not necessary at all. But in the Shari'ah rulings, for example, is it permissible for a woman to be a doctor for men or a man a doctor for women? This is a Shari'ah question, it is not a medical one.

* Student: O Shaykh (...), are they not guardians of affairs?

* The Shaykh: Guardians of affairs in what relates to their own affairs and specializations. No. As for me, if I am among the scholars, I have no involvement in medicine at all.

* Student: May Allah be good to you, what is the ruling on shura for individuals?

* The Shaykh: Individuals, this returns to you. Perhaps there is a matter that is difficult for you, but you do not want to reveal it to people. But if you consult, fine. And here, the istikhara: does one precede consultation or does consultation precede istikhara?

* Student: There is a difference of opinion.

* Another student: Consultation.

* Another student: Istikhara.

* The Shaykh: There are two opinions. Some say: seek Allah's guidance (istakhir Allah), and if after the istikhara you see an inclination toward something, do not consult anyone, because you have entrusted the matter to Allah, and Allah has guided you to that thing, so do not ask anyone, do not consult anyone. Others say: if you have sought Allah's guidance and the matter has not become clear to you, then consult, and the advice given by someone will be what Allah has chosen for you through istikhara.

* Student: Shaykh, does it not show that consultation precedes istikhara, the saying of Allah: ﴿And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Aal 'Imran 3:159]?

* The Shaykh: No, there is no istikhara in this. My intention by istikhara is the one the Messenger ﷺ commanded: when a person resolves upon a matter and it is unclear to him, he prays two units of prayer.

* Student: But here it shows that a person does not forget tawakkul.

* The Shaykh: No, it is not an istikhara matter we ask about. Is the prayer of istikhara before or after? As for example if he consults about some matter, whether or not he has prayed istikhara, here when he resolves, he relies upon Allah.

* Student: O Shaykh, is it a condition for the adviser to be just (ʿadl)?

* The Shaykh: What do you say about this question? Is it a condition for the adviser to be just? I do not think anyone consults someone who is not just, because he is not trustworthy.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: He does not consult him, because he fears him.

Student: "If God helps you, none can overcome you, and if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? In God let the believers put their trust. (160) It is not for a Prophet to deceive; and whoever deceives will bring what he deceived upon the Day of Resurrection, then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, and they will not be wronged. (161) Is one who follows the pleasure of God like one who has earned wrath from God, and his refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination." [Surah Al 'Imran 160–162].

Shaykh: Repeat, because the answer to the conditional must be linked to what precedes it.

Student: "And whoever deceives will bring what he deceived upon the Day of Resurrection, then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, and they will not be wronged. (161) Is one who follows the pleasure of God like one who has earned wrath from God, and his refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination." [Ali 'Imran 160–162].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: "If Allah helps you, none can overcome you."

This sentence is a conditional sentence. Its verb of condition is in the present jussive form: "in yansurkum" (if He helps you). Its answer of condition is a nominal sentence introduced by "la" (no). Why was the fa' (then) attached to it?

Student: (La al-nafiya, the negating "la").

Shaykh: The negation. Good. Is it introduced by "la" or by the negation?

Student: By "la al-nafiya."

Another student: (...).

Shaykh: "Fa la ghaliba lakum," my brother. Where is the "lan"? "Fa la ghaliba lakum" is introduced by what?

Student: By "la al-nafiya."

Shaykh: By "la al-nafiya." When "la al-nafiya" is at the head of the answer of condition, is the answer linked with the fa' optionally or obligatorily?

Student: Obligatorily.

Shaykh: Obligatorily. Do you have evidence from the words of the scholars?

Student: There is a verse, but...

Shaykh: What is the verse?

Student:
"Nominal, imperative, and with an inflected (jamid) word, and with ma, qad, la, and with the tanfis."

Shaykh: "And with ma, qad" — where is "la"?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: The answer to "ma"... and this... The fact is that "la ghaliba lakum" is a nominal sentence. Do you understand? "Fa la ghaliba lakum." Also, "wa in yakhdhulkum fa man dha alladhi yansurukum min ba'dihi" — this sentence is also a conditional sentence whose verb of condition is a present verb, and whose answer of condition is an interrogative sentence linked with the fa' obligatorily or optionally?

Student: Obligatorily.

Shaykh: Obligatorily, why?

Student: Because (...).

Shaykh: Complete (...) the verse: "wa in yakhdhulkum fa man dha alladhi"? Because the sentence is nominal, correct?

And his saying: "fa man dha alladhi yansurukum min ba'dihi" contains: "man," "dha," and "alladhi." Is "dha" after "man" a relative noun or nullified?

Student: Nullified.

Shaykh: Why?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Because a relative noun came after it. The "dha" after "man" is a relative noun only on condition that no relative noun comes after it; if a relative noun comes after it, it is necessarily nullified. Some grammarians said: it is not necessarily nullified, and the second relative noun is an emphasis of the first relative noun, as one would say: "fa man alladhi alladhi yansurukum min ba'dihi?" This is what relates to the verse in terms of grammar.

As for His saying, exalted is He: "And upon Allah let the believers put their trust," what was said about its like has already preceded.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says in this verse: "If Allah helps you, none can overcome you." That is: if God decrees your victory, no one will overcome you. I said "if God decrees your victory" because if the intended meaning were actual victory, the saying "none can overcome you" would have no benefit, since the victory has already occurred. On this basis the meaning is: "in yansurkum," i.e., if He decrees your victory. This is similar to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Know that what has struck you would never have missed you." Some scholars said: "what struck you" means what was decreed to strike you, because what has actually struck you has already happened, so his saying "would never have missed you" would not be correct. But the correct view is that the hadith is on its apparent meaning: what struck you would never have missed you; that is, the matter cannot occur contrary to what happened. So what struck you would never have missed you at all, and there is no need for regret.

Here He says: "If Allah helps you, none can overcome you." The "la" here is "la li-l-jins" (the la denoting absolute negation of the genus), and the la denoting absolute negation is explicit in generality, because a negation may be general explicitly and may be general apparently.

The difference between the explicit and the apparent is that the explicit does not admit specification, while the apparent admits that it may be general but intended particular. The people of knowledge in grammar said: the negating "la" is explicit in generality. Just as the redundant "min," when it comes after a negation, makes the negation explicit in generality, as if you said: "ma fi al-dar min rajul" (there is no man in the house). This is explicit in generality, like your saying: "la rajul fi al-dar."

The summary: His saying "fa la ghaliba lakum" is general; that is, no one can overcome you, whatever their strength and whatever their number. Allah said that so that we attach victory to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and not to anything else.

He said: "And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?" What is the meaning of "yakhdhulkum"? It is opposite to "yansurkum," the counterpart of victory; forsaking is the opposite of victory. This is one of the rules that help you in interpreting the Qur'an: that a word's meaning may become clear through its paired opposite. A word's meaning may be made clear by what is juxtaposed with it of its opposite.

If someone asked you: what is the meaning of His saying: "fa-infiru thubat aw infiru jami'an" (An-Nisa 71)? What is the meaning of "thubat"?

Students: Individually.

Shaykh: Individually? Did you check the dictionary? No. From where did you know that it means individually? You paired it with His saying: "or go forth all together."

"In yakhdhulkum": that is, if He decrees for you forsaking, which is the absence of victory, "fa man dha alladhi yansurukum min ba'dihi." It is also possible to derive the meaning of forsaking from His saying: "fa man dha alladhi yansurukum min ba'dihi." The "man" is interrogative in meaning of negation, but it came, I mean the negation, in the form of interrogation, because it is imbued with the meaning of what? The meaning of challenge; as if Allah were saying: We challenge you: if Allah wills to forsake you, may anyone help you after Him, even if all the powers of the earth combined to support you, while Allah has not supported you, you will not be able to be victorious: "And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?" The answer?

Students: No one.

Shaykh: No one.

"And upon Allah let the believers put their trust." "Upon Allah" is a prepositional phrase fronted before its governor, which is "yatawakkal," and fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction; that is: upon Allah and not other than Him, let them put their trust.

The fa' here, the grammarians said, is redundant to beautify the expression, and it cannot be conjunctive, because the waw in His saying "wa 'ala Allah" suffices for it; therefore if one said "wa 'ala Allah li-yatawakkal" it would be correct.

So it is redundant to beautify the expression, and the reason it beautifies the expression is apparent: if you said "wa 'ala Allah li-yatawakkal al-mu'minun," there would be no eloquence in it, but when you say "fa-li-yatawakkal" it becomes more eloquent.

His saying "fa-li-yatawakkal" means: let him rely. But trust in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is not like trust in a human being; trust in Allah involves humility, submission, lowliness, entrusting, and complete reliance upon Allah, unlike when a person relies upon a deputy whom he has appointed, for he undoubtedly depends on him in what he has delegated to him, but he does not feel in his heart that he is completely entrusting and turning in repentance to Allah and submitting to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. So trust in Allah is an act of worship. For this reason He said "wa 'ala Allah," meaning Him alone: "fa-li-yatawakkal al-mu'minun," the believers in whom? The believers in Him. Faith in Allah, when stated without qualification, includes all that must be believed in from the six pillars which the Messenger (ﷺ) explained when he said to Jibril: "Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree, its good and its evil."

Among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying "If Allah helps you, none can overcome you."

Among its benefits: the obligation of attaching the heart to Allah alone in seeking victory, from His saying "If Allah helps you, none can overcome you." So from whom do we seek victory, based on this rule? From Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: that if Allah decrees the forsaking of anyone, there is no helper for him, from His saying "And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?"

Among its benefits: that if a person believes in this, he must necessarily take the means of victory, the means by which victory is achieved. Correct?

If you believe that victory is in the hand of Allah, and that if Allah forsakes you no one can help you, will you then take the means of victory that Allah has ordained victory upon, or not? Yes, undoubtedly. So what are the means of victory? The means of victory are numerous, and they are five:

First: sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: "Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth, as He granted it to those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and that He will surely change their state after their fear into security: they worship Me, not associating anything with Me" (An-Nur 55). Sincerity to Allah in worship.

Second: establishing prayer, giving zakat, enjoining good and forbidding evil. Allah said: "Allah will surely help those who help Him; indeed Allah is Strong and Mighty. Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil; and to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters" (Al-Hajj 40–41). These are not (...), but these four are means; add them to the first and they become five.

Reflect on His saying: "Indeed Allah is Strong and Mighty" and it will become clear to you that this victory is certain, because if Allah is Strong and Mighty, then everyone before Him is weak and humbled. Then reflect again on His saying: "and to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters," and it will become clear to you that apparent material powers, however great they are, their outcome is in whose hand? In the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He is the One who gives the outcome to whomever He wills: "and the outcome is for the God-fearing" (Al-A'raf 128). For this reason some foolish people said: "Subhan Allah! If we establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin good and forbid evil, we will overcome America and Russia?" We say: Yes, O fool, the outcome is for whom? For the God-fearing: "and to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters." It is not for Russia, nor America, nor England, nor France; to Allah alone belongs the outcome of matters. If you want to know this from a historical perspective, look at what happened to the Islamic nation in its earliest era: the great superpowers of its time were brought down, the Byzantine state, the Persian state, and the Coptic state in Egypt, and the Muslims emerged and ruled the eastern and western parts of the earth. This is the historical perspective. From the practical perspective, one earthquake, in a moment, from the Lord of the Throne destroys everything, and no one can prevent that earthquake. I think two years ago there was an earthquake and volcanoes erupted, the solid, deaf and dumb mountains melted onto people and burned them, by the command of whom? By the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

So we say: from weakness of faith is that a person looks at the matter in front of him, the material matter, and does not look to the power and might of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

So: whether He helps you or forsakes you, we must take the path of what? The means of victory, and if we take the means of victory with faith and certainty, it will be realized for us.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the warning, the warning against doing the causes of forsaking; from His saying: "And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?" Among the causes of forsaking is allying with the disbelievers, supporting them and backing them, for this is one of the causes of forsaking. Rely upon whom? Upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah said: "And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?"

Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of trusting in Allah alone. From where is this derived? From His saying: "And upon Allah let the believers put their trust." Good. Specifying Him alone with trust is derived from fronting the complement before its governor, because fronting what should be delayed, pay attention to this rule, fronting what should be delayed conveys what?

Students: It conveys restriction.

Shaykh: It conveys restriction. This is a rule even between the subject and predicate: if you say "lillahi mulk al-samawati wa al-ard" (Ash-Shura 49), it means to Him and not to other than Him.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: that trust is one of the requirements of faith, because He linked the ruling to a quality, which is faith. This indicates that whenever faith strengthens, trust in Allah strengthens, and whenever faith weakens, trust in Allah weakens.

If someone says: Does trust in Allah, or specifying Allah alone with trust, contradict taking the means?

The answer: No. Rather, taking the means is part of trust in Allah, because when you trust in Allah, among the requirements of trusting in Him is that you do what He commanded you to do.

So if someone said: "I will sleep in winter under the stars and on snow, with no mattress beneath me and no covering above me," why? Because of the cold? "I am trusting in Allah." Is this correct? Never, this is not correct.

If someone said: "I will enter the fire trusting in Allah?" We say: this is not correct, except if it happens as a challenge, in which case it could be a sign from the signs of Allah, Allah helping that doer for the victory of His religion, and what happened to him of entering the fire would be a karamah (miraculous gift).

It is mentioned that Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, when he debated the chief of the Bataihiyya, who came to debate him on issues of the fundamentals of religion, the chief of the Bataihiyya said to him: "I am more correct than you, because I can enter the fire and nothing from it will touch me. Can you enter the fire and nothing from it touch you?"

Shaykh al-Islam said: "Yes, I can, on the condition that you and I go down into this river and wash ourselves thoroughly, then we enter the fire." Why (...)? Because the man had smeared his body with something that counters fire, and wanted to deceive people into thinking he entered the fire and escaped from it, while this man was incapable. But Ibn Taymiyya, praise be to Allah, had been given by Allah intelligence, shrewdness and insight. He said: "There is no objection; let us all enter the fire, but on condition that we wash in this river first." What happened? The man was defeated, and said: "No, there is no such thing."

In any case, I say: taking the means does not contradict trust. And there are evidences for this:

First: we know with certainty that our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) is the master of those who trust in Allah, is that not so? And yet he protects himself from heat, protects himself from cold, eats to ward off hunger, drinks to ward off thirst, is that not so? In battles he wore armor to protect himself from arrows, and at the Battle of Uhud he wore two coats of armor.

In the Battle of the Trench, when the confederates surrounded Madinah, what did he do? He dug the trench on the advice of Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, and he did not say: "Whoever trusts in Allah, if they can come, let them come, and if they cannot come, let them not come." No, he took the means.

The incidents in this regard are many, showing that taking the means does not contradict trust. But we must observe an essential condition: that the means be legislated means or natural means, not imaginary means. Legislated means, meaning it has been established by the Sharia that they are a means; or natural means, meaning it has been established by experience that they are a means, because what is established by experience was not indicated by the Sharia, but experience indicated it, and this is a natural cause. As for an imaginary cause, such as hanging unlawful amulets and the like, and tiyarah (superstitious omen-taking) is also an imaginary cause, so relying on it is not permissible. So the means are?

Student: Three.

Student: Natural, legislated; the third I do not recall.

* The Shaykh: What?
* A student: The imaginary causes.
* The Shaykh: The imaginary causes. There are legislated causes (asbab shar'iyyah), natural causes (asbab kawniyyah), and imaginary causes (asbab wahmiyyah). Therefore, taking means does not contradict reliance on Allah (tawakkul, trust in Allah). Rather, it is part of perfecting tawakkul. Is that clear, everyone?

If someone says: legislated causes do not contradict tawakkul, without any doubt. For this reason, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek refuge with the protective surahs (al-mu'awwidhat), and he said: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi) at night, there will not cease to be a guardian from Allah over him, and no devil will come near him until morning."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2311) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] This is one of the legislated causes. And he said about al-Fatihah: it is what?
* The student: He said about al-Fatihah that it is a cure (shafiyah).
* The Shaykh: And what else? It is a ruqyah (protective incantation): "And what would make you know that it is a ruqyah?"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2276) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim) on Surah 3, verse 161 (part 1 of 2):**

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿It is not for a prophet to defraud. And whoever defrauds will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection.﴾

First: The readings (qira'at, variant recitations):

He says: ﴿It is not for a prophet (linabiyyin)﴾ has a reading: ﴿linabiy'in﴾ (with a hamza).

﴿an yaghulla﴾ has a reading: ﴿an yughalla﴾.

What is the difference between the two readings in ﴿linabiyyin﴾ and ﴿linabiy'in﴾?

As for ﴿linabiy'in﴾, it is on the pattern fa'il from al-naba' (news/information) with a hamza. Does it mean fa'il (active) or maf'ul (passive), or both?

* Students: It includes both.

* The Shaykh: It includes both. So ﴿nabiy'﴾ is fa'il in meaning, because he informs (munabbi'), and fa'il in meaning maf'ul, because he is informed (munabba'). The Messenger (ﷺ) is both munabba' and munabbi'. On the reading ﴿linabiyyin﴾ with the yā', it is said that it is a softened form (musahhal) and that its origin is (linabi'). The hamza was softened into a yā'. It is also said that it is derived from al-nubuwwah, which means elevation (irtifa'), so that (linabiyyin) would originally be (linabiyyun)... but due to a morphological reason the wāw became a yā'. What is the rule or standard for turning the wāw into a yā' in this way?

They say: when a wāw and a yā' come together in one word and the first of them is sakin (vowelless), the wāw is changed into a yā'. So if we say (linabiyyun), the wāw and yā' have come together in one word and the first of them is sakin, so the wāw is changed into a yā' and it becomes (linabiyyin). Can we say, on this reading, that it is derived from both: from al-naba' and from al-nubuwwah?

It is possible, based on what preceded: when a word in the Qur'an can carry two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is taken to carry both, because the meanings of the Qur'an are broad.

As for ﴿an yaghulla﴾, it has a reading ﴿an yughalla﴾. The difference between them is clear: ﴿an yaghulla﴾ is in the active voice, and ﴿an yughalla﴾ is in the passive voice.

On the reading ﴿an yaghulla﴾, the meaning is that Allah negated that the Prophet would defraud. The defrauding (ghulul) of a prophet may carry two meanings: defrauding of wealth and defrauding of knowledge. Defrauding of knowledge is concealing it, and defrauding of wealth is hiding it and taking it. All of this is negated of the Prophet by the Sharia, and we do not know of it occurring by divine decree (qadar). It is not possible for it to occur by decree, as far as we know. The Prophet cannot conceal what Allah has revealed to him, nor can he steal from the wealth of the Muslims.

As for the reading ﴿an yughalla﴾, its meaning is that the Prophet is defrauded by someone else. That is, it was not for a prophet to be defrauded, by the Sharia and by decree?

It may happen by decree. A prophet may be defrauded by decree, as this occurred in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Then He said: ﴿And whoever defrauds will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ In terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), we are still at the beginning of the tafsir.

Grammatical analysis: ﴿And whoever defrauds will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ The difficulty lies in ﴿yati bima ghalla﴾.

* The student: The difficulty is with (ya'ti) here. The yā' has been dropped, Shaykh, because it is jussive (majzum) as the response of the conditional.

* The Shaykh: Jussive as the response of the conditional. Why is it vowelled with a kasra, when the response of the conditional should be jussive?

* The student: About (...), Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: How?

* The student: As compensation for dropping the yā', the yā' was given a kasra.

* The Shaykh: The tā' is kasra anyway, even if the yā' were present. If you say (ya'tī).

* The student: Then that's settled, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: What do you mean, settled?

* The student: I mean that the verb takes a kasra at its end when the yā' is dropped, like the jussive takes a kasra at its end.

* The Shaykh: In grammatical analysis (i'rab)?

* The student: Yes, in i'rab.

* The Shaykh: Do not say it is jussive by i'rab.

* A student: In pronunciation (lafzan), not in i'rab.

* The Shaykh: In pronunciation, not in i'rab. That is: the kasra before the yā' remains as evidence of the dropped yā'. So it comes out jussive in this form: the response of the conditional is jussive by the dropping of the yā', and the kasra before it is evidence of it.

﴿bima ghalla yawma al-qiyamah﴾. What is the grammatical analysis of ﴿yawma al-qiyamah﴾? Is (yawm) the object of (ghalla)?

* A student: The direct object.

* The Shaykh: Governed by what?

* A student: Governed by the verb (ghalla).

* The Shaykh: By the verb (ghalla). That is: he brings what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection?

* A student: It is in the accusative of time (zaraf).

* The Shaykh: It is an adverbial object of time (maf'ul fihi), and being in the accusative of time means the same thing, but governed by what?

* The student: By (ya'ti).

* The Shaykh: By (ya'ti)? Which of them is more correct, everyone?

* Students: The last one.

* The Shaykh: The last one, because the Day of Resurrection has no defrauding in it.

As for His words: ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned.﴾ Apparently there is no difficulty in grammar here.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿It is not for a prophet to defraud﴾. When ﴿ma kana﴾ appears in the Qur'an, its meaning is a definite negation, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal 33], and like His saying: ﴿Allah would not leave the believers as they are﴾ [Al 'Imran 179], and ﴿We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15]. The examples of this are many. It means that this is definitely negated and cannot be.

﴿It is not for a prophet to defraud﴾: on this reading, Allah is saying that the prophets, peace be upon them, cannot defraud. All the prophets? Yes, because nabiy is indefinite in the context of the negation (ma), and an indefinite noun in a negative context gives generality.

So Allah, exalted is He, negates that a prophet defrauds by the Sharia, correct? And by decree as well, since we do not know that Allah, glorified and exalted, has decreed for a prophet to defraud himself, and that is far-fetched.

On the reading ﴿an yughalla﴾, Allah negates by the Sharia that the prophet be defrauded. That is, it would be by the Sharia that the prophet be defrauded? Because if the prophet earns wealth, his wealth belongs to all the Muslims. And if it belongs to all the Muslims, it is not permitted for anyone to defraud any of it, because if he defrauded any of it, this would concern all the Muslims. This wealth belongs to all the Muslims, so if you take from it, you have betrayed all the Muslims, especially those who share in this booty.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Whoever defrauds will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ ﴿Whoever defrauds﴾ here is general. He did not say, "whoever among the prophets defrauds," supposing that one would defraud. He said ﴿whoever defrauds﴾, that is, among the followers of the prophets: ﴿will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection﴾, bringing it on the Day of Resurrection carrying it before the people in that great station which all creation witnesses, as Allah said: ﴿By the promised Day, and the witness and the witnessed﴾ [al-Buruj 2–3].

And His saying: ﴿will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Will he bring the very thing he defrauded, or will he bring the punishment that results from it?

We say: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that he will bring the very thing he defrauded. If it was a sheep that bleats, or a camel that roars, he will bring whatever he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection.

If he defrauded garments? He will bring them on the Day of Resurrection. But will he bring them wearing them? No. He will bring them carrying them, while he is naked.

The camel that he defrauded and then rode, will he bring it on the Day of Resurrection riding it? No. The camel rides him, may Allah protect us, and he brings it carrying it, as a punishment for him.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. What is the purpose of it?

* A student: Attaching the heart to Allah.

* The Shaykh: Yes, that they attach their hearts to Allah and rely upon Him, and seek victory only from Him. It also strengthens their hearts against their enemies, because if Allah is their helper, then their enemies, however many they are, will never overcome them.

What is the lām in His saying: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾?

* A student: "And upon Allah"?

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿fal-yatawakkali﴾. The lām?

* A student: ﴿fal-yatawakkal﴾? This lām is the lām of command.

* The Shaykh: The lām of command. What does it signify to restrict reliance (tawakkul) to the believers? He did not say, "let people rely." 

* A student: The believers are the ones who rely upon Allah (...). His heart may be attached to Allah while he relies upon Allah.

* The Shaykh: He is the one who relies upon Allah, and this indicates that reliance is part of faith and one of its signs.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿It is not for a prophet to defraud﴾: how many readings are there in it?

* A student: ﴿nabiyyin﴾ has two readings: ﴿nabiyyin﴾ and ﴿nabiy'in﴾. And ﴿yaghulla﴾ has two readings: ﴿yaghulla﴾ and ﴿yughalla﴾.

* The Shaykh: Well done. Now: ﴿nabiyyin﴾ with the yā', derived from what?

* A student: From prophethood (nubuwwah).

* The Shaykh: From nubuwwah, which is elevation, due to the elevated rank of the prophet. And it was said?

* A student: From nabi'.

* The Shaykh: From (nabi') so it is derived from al-naba'. (Nabi') in the sense of fa'il or maf'ul?

* A student: Nabi'? 

* The Shaykh: Yes?

* The student: Maf'ul.

* The Shaykh: Nabi' in the sense of maf'ul, or in the sense of fa'il?

* A student: I don't know it precisely.

* The Shaykh: You don't know it. Is it fa'il in meaning, or maf'ul in meaning?

* A student: Fa'il in meaning.

* The Shaykh: Fa'il in meaning, meaning what?

* A student: That is: he informs (yunabbi'u).

* The Shaykh: He informs.

* A student: Fa'il and maf'ul in meaning.

* The Shaykh: Fa'il and maf'ul in meaning, both of them?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Fa'il in meaning, we understand that he is munabbi' (one who informs). Maf'ul in meaning?

* A student: Munabba' (one who is informed).

* The Shaykh: Munabba'. Does fa'il come in the sense of maf'il? Fa'il in the sense of fa'il is common. Fa'il in the sense of maf'il?

* A student: Sami' (hearing).

* The Shaykh: Sami' in the sense of sami' (hearing): ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39].

* A student: And in the sense of musmi' (one who makes to hear).

* The Shaykh: Yes. Where is the evidence? Do you have a line of poetry?

* The student: 

أَمِنْ رَيْحَانَةَ الدَّاعِي السَّمِيعُ ∗∗∗ ..................

* The Shaykh:

أَمِنْ رَيْحَانَةَ الدَّاعِي السَّمِيعُ ∗∗∗ يُؤَرِّقُنِي وَأَصْحَابِي هُجُوعُ

Translation: "Is it from Rayhana, the one who calls and makes to hear, that I am kept awake, while my companions sleep?"

This is three (points of evidence). I'll allow the one who took it before. This is the first time you hear it, so go on.

* A student:

أَمِنْ رَيْحَانَةَ الدَّاعِي السَّمِيعُ ∗∗∗ يُؤَرِّقُــنِي وَأَصْــــــــابِيهُجُـــــــــوعُ

* The Shaykh: Perfect. In any case, fa'il can mean mufil (causative) and fa'il can mean maf'al, and fa'il in the sense of maf'al is common.

﴿yughallu﴾ and ﴿yaghullu﴾ are two readings. What is the meaning of the word on the two readings?

* A student: ﴿yughallu﴾ is passive: it is done to him; that is, he is defrauded by someone else. And ﴿yaghullu﴾ is, that is, the active subject.

* The Shaykh: He acts, he defrauds. I think we discussed it? The defrauding of the Prophet means ﴿an yughalla﴾ in what sense?

* A student: ﴿yughalla﴾ means the verb is passive, that he is defrauded?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: He is attacked by the disbelievers and polytheists.

* The Shaykh: No, that is not correct.

* A student: It may have two meanings, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: And they are?

* The student: The first: that he is defrauded in wealth...

* The Shaykh: Meaning?

* The student: Meaning there is defrauding in wealth.

* The Shaykh: Meaning he is defrauded from the booty he seized. That is one.

* The student: And the second: from knowledge.

* The Shaykh: What?

* The student: Knowledge.

* The Shaykh: Knowledge?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: What does that mean?

* The student: It means he conceals knowledge.

* The Shaykh: This is if it is: ﴿yaghulla﴾, the second meaning on the second reading. ﴿yaghulla﴾ means: he conceals something of what Allah has given him.

* A student: ﴿yughalla﴾ means that if he acquires something, someone defrauds it.

* The Shaykh: We are finished with that.

* The student: No, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: ﴿yughalla﴾.

* The student: Yes, ﴿yughalla﴾.

* The Shaykh: But ﴿an yaghulla﴾.

* The student: ﴿an yaghulla﴾, what does it mean?

* The Shaykh: Yes. We have learned something of its meaning, but is there another meaning?

* The student: It is impossible for the Prophet by decree.

* The Shaykh: That is, it is also impossible that he defraud himself? Good. The defrauding of the Prophet would be in concealing knowledge, and also in concealing something of the booty. All of this is impossible.

* The Shaykh: His saying: ﴿And whoever defrauds will bring what he defrauded on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al 'Imran 161]. In ﴿yati﴾ there is a difficulty in the apparent wording. What is the difficulty?

* A student: It is a jussive verb, Shaykh. It is said that it is moved with a kasra, so how can it be jussive?

* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.

* The student: And the sign of jussive is normally sukun, but in this verb the sign of jussive is the dropping of the weak letter, which is the yā'.

* The Shaykh: Well done. We say: it is jussive by dropping the weak letter, which is the yā', and the kasra before it is evidence of it. ﴿yawma al-qiyamah﴾ is governed by ghalla or by what?

* A student: By ﴿yati﴾.

* The Shaykh: By ﴿yati﴾, and it cannot be governed by ghalla?

* The student: No.

* The Shaykh: Why?

* The student: Because it means (ya'ti), that is, the defrauding would be on the Day of Resurrection.

* The Shaykh: And is there defrauding on the Day of Resurrection?

* The student: There is no defrauding in it.

* The Shaykh: There is no defrauding in it. In it there is recompense and punishment.

* A student: We said: the meaning of (...) the author mentioned (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, al-Jalalayn?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Its meaning is reliance upon a thing, which only comes after trust in it. The meaning is the same, and he explained it by its necessary consequence.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾ [Al 'Imran 161]. Then: that is, after people are resurrected on the Day of Resurrection and every person comes with what he defrauded, ﴿every soul will be paid in full﴾. ﴿tuwaffa﴾ is from tawfiyah (full payment). It is said: he paid his right in full, that is, he gave it to him in full.

His saying ﴿every soul will be paid in full for what it earned﴾ includes even the messengers. It includes the messengers and those to whom they were sent: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf 6]. Each is given what he earned.

His saying ﴿every soul will be paid in full for what it earned﴾ may mean, by generality here, those who were responsible (mukallaf), because one who is not responsible is not punished, since the pen is lifted from him. But it may be said that it includes even one who is not responsible, because full payment does not necessarily entail punishment. His due may be paid in reward, and it is known that one who is not responsible is rewarded. He is recorded for good and nothing is recorded against him.

His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), a circumstantial clause relating to ﴿every soul﴾, because ﴿every soul﴾ carries generality. ﴿And they﴾, that is, the souls, ﴿will not be wronged﴾, that is, they will not have good deeds reduced nor have evil deeds increased. This is because wronging (zulm), in its origin, is reduction, as Allah said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾ [al-Kahf 33], that is, it did not reduce. Wronging includes two things: the first is increase in evil deeds, and the second is reduction of good deeds. Both are impossible with respect to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He said: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat 46], ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ [al-Kahf 49]. Wronging was negated of Him because of the perfection of His justice, not because of incapacity to wrong. He is able to wrong, Mighty and Majestic, but because of the perfection of His justice He does not wrong.

We have a principle in creed: all attributes that Allah negated of Himself are not intended as mere negation, but to affirm the perfection of their opposite. For example, wronging: what is its opposite?

* The students: Justice.

* The Shaykh: Justice. So when Allah negates wronging of Himself, what is meant is that because of the perfection of His justice He does not wrong. We say this because pure negation is never found in the attributes of Allah, since pure negation is pure non-existence. It is only a negation in name, and negation affirms nothing, and pure non-existence is nothing, let alone being a perfection. Did you understand this, everyone? So whenever you see something that Allah negated of Himself, know that the intention is not only the negation of that thing, but the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite. ﴿And no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38], that is, from weariness. What is intended?

* Students: The affirmation of perfect strength.

* The Shaykh: The affirmation of perfect strength. That is, no fatigue touched Us because of Our perfect strength, and so on.

The scholars said: negation may be due to incapacity to do a thing, and it may be due to the thing's not being capable of it, whether through incapacity or non-capability. So if you say: our wall does not wrong?

* Students: Because it is not capable of it.

* The Shaykh: That is because the wall is not capable of wronging or justice, correct? And if we say of a weak man, whom people beat and who does not speak, who would, if someone struck him, say, "May Allah reward you with good," and who cannot defend himself: do we say that this man does not wrong?

* Students: That is incapacity and laziness.

* The Shaykh: Is this blame or praise?

* Students: This is blame.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 161 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: This is a dispraise. That is why the poet, dispraising a tribe, says:
"A tribe that does not betray a covenant, and does not wrong people even to the weight of a mustard seed."
The one who recites this verse says: "Masha'Allah, these people are good! They do not betray a covenant, meaning they fulfil their pledge; and they do not wrong people to the weight of a mustard seed." But the meaning is that they are incapable: they cannot betray covenants because they fear being punished, and they do not wrong people because they are unable to wrong people. Is that clear? Among the same kind is the poet's saying:
"But my people, though they are many in number, are not in anything of evil, and they keep far from it."
Meaning: they keep far from evil even when it is trivial.
"They repay the wrong of the wrongdoers with forgiveness, and the evil of the evildoers with kindness."
This is fine speech. The one who hears it says: "How good these people are!" Why? Because they repay the wrong of wrongdoers with forgiveness: if someone wrongs them, they say, "May God forgive us and you; you are forgiving." And if someone harms them, they go and send him gifts, repaying harm with kindness. When the listener hears this verse he thinks they are at the peak of lofty character, but it is the opposite. That is why he says:
"Would that I had among them a people who, when they ride out, launch raids as horsemen and as riders on foot."
"Would that I had among them" means: would that I had instead of them.
So now we have understood that the first statement is praise or dispraise?
* The students: Dispraise.
* The Shaykh: The first statement is a dispraise. As for the attributes of Allah, the Exalted: when you find negation in them, it is praise. When you find the negation of injustice, it is for the perfection of justice; when you find the negation of weariness, it is for the perfection of power; when you find the negation of inability: ﴿And He was not wearied by their creation﴾ [al-Ahqaf 33], it is also for the perfection of power; when you find the negation of heedlessness: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [Al 'Imran 99], it is for the perfection of knowledge and watchfulness; and so on.
Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; and if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ [Al 'Imran 160]. We have taken its benefits.
He says: ﴿It is not for a prophet to betray﴾.
* From this noble verse is derived: that it is not permissible for the Prophets, peace be upon them, to conceal what Allah has revealed to them; due to His saying: ﴿that he should betray﴾, ﴿It is not for a prophet that he should betray﴾.
* And from this it is derived: that it is not permissible for the followers of the Prophet to commit ghulul (embezzlement from war booty): ﴿It is not for a prophet that he should betray﴾. So then his followers?
* Students: They do not embezzle.
* The Shaykh: It is not for them to embezzle. That is why ghulul is among the major sins. Even the scholars say, and the Sunnah has also come with it, that the one who embezzles has his baggage burned, except the Mushaf and what has a soul, and weapons.[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (2713) and al-Tirmidhi (1461) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Whoever you find has embezzled in the cause of Allah, burn his belongings." Salih said: I entered upon Maslamah and with him was Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, and he found a man who had embezzled, so Salim narrated this hadith, and he ordered it, and his belongings were burned, and in his belongings a Mushaf was found, and Salim said: Sell this and give its price in charity.]] Burning the baggage is for the purpose of making an example of him. Otherwise someone might say: Why do you burn his baggage? Why not leave it in the public treasury, so that the Muslims benefit from it? But we say: burning it is better than putting it in the public treasury. Why? For the sake of making an example of him, so that it deters him and others from returning to embezzlement.
* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: that Prophets do not embezzle, legally or by decree?
* A student: Legally.
* The Shaykh: Legally. And that it is not permitted for anyone to embezzle from the spoils that he has gained through war.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed; due to His saying: ﴿And whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Is this by way of punishment or by way of honour? By way of punishment. By this we know the weakness of the view of some of the early scholars who said: the one who embezzles a Mushaf will bring it on the Day of Resurrection. This is an error, because he will bring it on the Day of Resurrection as a punishment, not as a reward; and perhaps he will bring it on the Day of Resurrection not in the form in which he embezzled it in this world.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of resurrection, due to His saying: ﴿he will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾.
* And among its benefits: the affirmation of the power of Allah, the Exalted, and that He, glory be to Him, is able to bring a person what he embezzled, even though it has perished and vanished, and if it was food that has been eaten. But Allah, glory be to Him, is over all things capable: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya Sin 82].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the recompense of every soul for what it has earned; due to His saying: ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾, with neither increase nor decrease. Some scholars have used this verse to argue that gifting the reward of acts of worship is of no benefit, because it is not part of the earnings of the one to whom it is gifted. An example: a man prays two rak'ahs intending them for so-and-so. Some scholars say: it is derived from this verse that this is of no benefit, and that its reward will either be lost or belong to the doer. That is because the one who gifts acts of worship has no reward except for the kindness to another; as for the reward of the specific act which is prescribed for it, if it is said that gifting acts of worship is valid, then it goes to whom? To the one to whom it is gifted. And if we say it is not valid, then it is wasted, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Actions are only by intentions."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Accordingly they say: what the Sunnah has brought of acts done on behalf of others is excepted from this generality, such as His saying ﷺ: "Whoever dies owing fasts, his guardian fasts on his behalf."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1952) and Muslim (1147/153), from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.]] Likewise in Hajj, and likewise in charity; all of this the Sunnah has brought.
But Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, holds the generality, meaning that he holds that if a person does a deed intending it for a specific person who is deserving of reward, then ... and who is deserving of reward?
* Students: The Muslim.
* The Shaykh: The Muslim. The reward reaches him. He cites the generality of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155), the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.]] In truth, if you reflect on the evidences, you will find that some of them stand in a relation of general and specific in part with the other evidences: some are general in that a soul benefits only from what it has earned, and some are general in that a person has what he intended. The rule when two general texts conflict, one of which is more general than the other in part, is that a preponderating factor must be sought. Note this rule. Do you understand this meaning or not?
* A student: Repeat it, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: I say: when two general texts conflict, each more general than the other in some respect, a preponderating factor must be sought, because it is impossible to prefer the generality of one over the other. So here we ask: does the generality of his saying "Actions are only by intentions" have a preponderating factor? We say: yes. It is reported that charity counts for the dead, that Hajj counts for the dead, and that fasting counts for the dead. Therefore the generality of His saying: ﴿what it earned﴾ has been specified by this, according to the Sunnah. And when a general text is specified, its indication of generality is weakened, to the point that some scholars said: when a general text is specified, its indication of generality is dropped, because its specification shows that it is not meant to be general. But the correct view is that when a general text is specified?
* Students: It remains...
* The Shaykh: It remains general in what it was not specified for. So the correct view on this question is that we prefer the generality of his saying: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155), the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.]] But on condition that the one for whom the act is intended is a Muslim deserving of it. That is why, if a person gives charity on behalf of his father who has died and who did not pray, the charity is not valid for his father.
Does our statement, that according to the preponderant view all acts of worship may validly be gifted to one who is deserving of that act, include the Prophet ﷺ?
Meaning: if a person wants to gift the Messenger ﷺ an act of worship, whether a prayer or something else, does he say: "O Allah, the reward of this prayer I am about to pray is for the Messenger"; or "these dirhams I give in charity, their reward is for the Messenger"?
We say: some scholars did this, but the pious predecessors (salaf) did not do it. The Companions did not gift the Messenger ﷺ any acts of worship, and neither did the Successors and their successors. It is mentioned that this matter first occurred in the fourth century, after the preferred generations; that is because the preferred generations had deeper knowledge than those after them. The people of the first generations say: when we do any righteous deed, the Prophet ﷺ receives a reward like ours. And if that is so, there is no need for me to say: "O Allah, make its reward for the Messenger"; because the Prophet ﷺ already deserves the reward. I gain nothing from saying "O Allah, make its reward for the Messenger," or "I intend its reward for the Messenger," except that I deprive myself of the reward. As for the Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, every good deed we do is recorded for him in its like.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that Allah is free from injustice; due to His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾.
* Branching from this, based on the rule we mentioned concerning the attributes: the affirmation of the perfection of His justice, glory be to Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 162 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who returns with anger from Allah?﴾ The hamzah here is the interrogative particle (hamzat al-istifham), and it is followed by a conjunction particle. We have mentioned previously that when the interrogative hamzah comes followed by a conjunction particle, the grammarians have two opinions on this matter.

The first opinion: the hamzah enters upon a suppressed sentence that suits the context, and the fa' is conjunctive to that sentence.

The second opinion: the hamzah enters upon the sentence as it exists, nothing has been omitted, but it has been moved forward from its place, because the interrogative has precedence (sadr al-kalam). The fa' in such cases as ﴿afa-man ittaba'a﴾ originally stood before the hamzah, and the estimate is: (fa-amman ittaba'a). But since the interrogative has precedence, it was placed before the conjunction particle. We said that this is easier. Its ease lies in that it does not require the burdensome estimation of an omitted element, for it is sometimes difficult for you to estimate the omitted element, and perhaps you estimate one element while another estimates something else. So we rely on the view that the hamzah is interrogative and that the fa' is conjunctive to what precedes it.

﴿Afa-man ittaba'a ridwana Allah ka-man ba'a﴾: Is "man" here an interrogative noun or a relative pronoun?
* Student: A relative pronoun.
* The Shaykh: The estimate is (a-fa-alladhi ittaba'a); so it is a relative pronoun, because we do not make the interrogative particle enter upon an interrogative noun or upon an interrogative sentence. ﴿Afa-man ittaba'a ridwana Allah﴾, i.e., follows it, i.e., follows what pleases Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; so whoever does what pleases Allah. ﴿Ka-man ba'a bi-sakhatin min Allah﴾: meaning, like the one who ba'a, i.e., returned, ﴿ba'a﴾ meaning "returned," i.e., like one who returned with anger from Allah, the opposite of ridwan.
Who is it that is exposed to ridwan, and who is exposed to sakhat? The obedient person is exposed to ridwan, and the disobedient to sakhat.

﴿Ka-man ba'a bi-sakhatin min Allah wa-ma'wahu Jahannam﴾: the waw may be for resumption (isti'naf), and its meaning would be informing about the destination of this one who returned with anger from Allah; and it may be conjunctive to the relative clause, which is: ﴿ba'a﴾, i.e., like one who returned and whose abode is Hell.
﴿Wa-ma'wahu Jahannam﴾: ma'wahu, i.e., his place of return, where he takes refuge, a dwelling from which there is no departure afterward. ﴿Jahannam﴾ is one of the names of the Fire; may Allah protect us and you from it. It was named by this name derived from al-juhmah. Al-juhmah includes the sense of blackness and obscurity, because Jahannam is black, deep, and of great depth. It was also said that Jahannam is a word that has been arabicized (mu'arrab), from (kahannam), and kahannam originally means the fire, the name of the Fire; that is, it is said: "fire kahannam." I do not know, is this a Pakistani language or...?
* Student: Persian.
