What is the basis of the inference?
* Student: Faith decreases and increases.
* Shaykh: What is the indication from the verse?
* Student: ﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith.﴾
* Shaykh: Whenever a person draws nearer to faith, his faith increases, and whenever he moves away from it...?
* Students: It decreases.
* Shaykh: It decreases. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), that faith increases and decreases. But does it increase through outward action, or does it also increase in inward action?
* Student: In both.
* Shaykh: Yes, it increases in this and in that. As for outward action, we find some people who abundantly perform righteous deeds, so their faith increases. As for the inward, a person's faith also increases inwardly according to the clear proofs he has. Ibrahim said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ He said: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, but so that my heart may be assured.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:260]. A person perceives by his own senses that when a trustworthy person informs him of a report, then another trustworthy person informs him of the same report, then another trustworthy person, then another, he feels within himself that whenever the informants increase, what?
* Students: His faith increases.
* Shaykh: His faith increases. This is something observed, and there is no difficulty in it.
* It is also derived from the noble verse that disbelief is the opposite of faith, from His saying: ﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith.﴾ But can faith and disbelief be combined in the heart of one man?
We say: As for absolute faith and absolute disbelief, they cannot be combined. As for incomplete faith, or disbelief that falls short of disbelief (kufr dun al-kufr), they can be combined according to the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah: a person may have qualities of faith and qualities of disbelief, so he is loved for what faith he has and disliked for what disbelief he has.
* Another benefit of the noble verse is that a person should be cautious in judgment and should not issue judgments absolutely, but should qualify them. This is from His saying: ﴿They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith.﴾ This is what is called the custom of diplomats: caution. The phrase ﴿that day﴾ is a qualification excluding what came before and what will come after, since perhaps previously they were nearer to faith, and perhaps in the future Allah will also change their state so that faith is nearer. So when you pass judgment on a person, you should qualify it, because an absolute judgment may hold the one judged to that judgment absolutely. Suppose you want to vouch for someone and say he is upright; if you grant him the attribute of uprightness in an absolute sense, he may later commit wrongdoing and that testimony remains with him. But praise be to Allah, people now guard against this by mentioning the date, because when the date is mentioned and you vouched for him at that date, you are not blamed in the future if his state changes, since you only vouched for him at that time. His state may change and he may become a wrongdoer afterward, and you are not responsible for that.
Then He said: ﴿Those who said of their brothers while they sat behind, "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say, "Then avert from yourselves death, if you are truthful."﴾ This also contains benefits.
* Students: (...).

Shaykh: Then it will be in the future, God willing.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Those who said of their brethren while they sat back﴾. Here ﴿those who﴾ (alladhina) is either a substitute (badal) for the earlier ﴿those who﴾ in His words ﴿and so that He might make known those who were hypocrites﴾, or a qualifier (sifah). Its being a qualifier is preferable, indeed it is the definite reading. This is because the substitute is the intended object of the ruling, the intended object of the ruling. Pay attention to the difference. The substitute is the intended object of the ruling, not the word it replaces. If you say, "Honour Zayd, 'Amr," then 'Amr is a substitute for Zayd. Who is being honoured?

Students: 'Amr.

Shaykh: 'Amr. If you say, "Eat the loaf, its third," then

Students: The third.

Shaykh: The third. For this reason, if he ate half, he would have eaten a sixth without right. If he says, "You told me, 'Eat the loaf'?" you reply, "But I substituted and said, 'its third.'" The sixth you have now eaten in excess counts as eating without right, so you are sinful, and the owner of the loaf may demand from you the value of the sixth. In any case, the substitute is the intended object of the ruling, as Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Alfiyya:

"The follower that is intended by the ruling without intermediary
is what is named the substitute."

Based on this, the second ﴿those who﴾ must be what?

Students: A qualifier.

Shaykh: A qualifier of the first ﴿those who﴾. The relative pronoun can be a qualifier, because with its relative clause it carries the meaning of a derived noun.

﴿Those who said of their brethren while they sat back﴾. His words ﴿of their brethren﴾ mean their brethren outwardly. This is the correct view. Some of them said: of their brethren by lineage. The first meaning is more correct, because they did not address only their brethren by lineage, but addressed everyone who was martyred at the Battle of Uhud. Not every martyr was a brother of one of the hypocrites. So what is meant by "their brethren"?

Students: Outwardly.

Shaykh: That is, outwardly. Because the hypocrites, alongside the believers, appeared to be believers. For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ was asked permission to kill them, he said: "People should not say that Muhammad kills his companions." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari, no. 3518, and Muslim, no. 2584/63, from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him.] So they are, outwardly, what?

Student: Brethren.

Shaykh: Brethren and companions. Therefore we say: ﴿of their brethren﴾, the correct meaning being: their brethren outwardly, because they show Islam and conceal disbelief.

As for His words ﴿while they sat back﴾, sat back from what?

Students: From fighting.

Shaykh: From fighting. Allah, glorified and exalted, calls those who stayed behind from fighting "those who sit back," as He says: ﴿Not equal are those who sit back among the believers, other than those with a disability, and those who strive in the cause of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 95]. He called those who stayed behind from fighting "those who sit back." And He says: ﴿It was said, "Sit back with those who sit back"﴾ [At-Tawbah 46], and ﴿And had they wanted to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation, but Allah disliked their being sent forth, so He discouraged them, and it was said, "Sit back with those who sit back"﴾ [At-Tawbah 46].

So ﴿they sat back﴾ means from fighting. The clause in His words ﴿and they sat back﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), with the implied (qad), meaning: "and they had indeed sat back." This is preferable to making the clause conjoined to the relative clause, i.e. ﴿said﴾ and ﴿sat back﴾, because their saying it while sitting back is more severe. They combined two things: evil in speech and evil in action. What did they say? ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.﴾ Obeyed us in what? In not going out, because the hypocrites had advised not going out. But the Prophet ﷺ and the sincere believers insisted on going out. On the way, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and those with him withdrew with a third of the army, and they stayed behind, may Allah protect us. For this reason He says: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾.

And in one reading: ﴿mā qutthilū﴾ (they were not slain, with doubled tā'), for emphasis, because among those who were martyred mutilation occurred, such as with Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him. He was mutilated, to the point that Hind bint ʿUtbah took his liver and chewed it, but she could not digest it; she did not swallow it. [Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad, no. 4414, from Ibn Mas'ud.] So we say: ﴿qutthilū﴾ is based on this killing being exaggerated because of the mutilation involved. As for ﴿qutilū﴾, its meaning is clear.

﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say﴾, i.e., O Muhammad, to these people: ﴿Then avert from yourselves death, if you are truthful.﴾ Idra'ū means: push away. That is, did you escape death by staying behind?

The answer: No. "If you are truthful, then avert death from yourselves when death comes to you." They cannot do this. They cannot push death away from themselves.

His words ﴿if you are truthful﴾ are a form of challenge. That is: if you are truthful that whoever stays behind does not die, then push death away from yourselves. The answer is no.

﴿Say: then avert from yourselves death﴾, i.e., push it away, ﴿if you are truthful﴾. The answer: they are unable to do that. In concluding this challenge with ﴿idra'ū﴾ and His words ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is an affirmation of their lie in their saying ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾. That is, if they had stayed behind, death would still have come to them. And Allah knows best.

Student: Shaykh, the divorce of one who is obsessive-compulsive, which does not take effect if he intended to divorce (...)?

Shaykh: No. If he intended to go to the court and divorce.

Student: To ease his mind?

Shaykh: No, it is not a divorce.

Student: But he divorced, Shaykh, intending divorce?

Shaykh: Not at all. He intended it under compulsion. He intended divorce in order to flee from divorce.

Student: But he did not divorce (...).

Shaykh: How did he not divorce (...)? That is, if you asked this obsessive person now: Did you divorce by choice?

Student: He doubted the divorce, so he divorced to ease his mind.

Shaykh: No, he does not ease his mind. His mind is eased by the principle that the default is no divorce.

Student: And the second divorce is not counted?

Shaykh: Not at all, it is not counted.

Student: Shaykh, when we say "the traits of disbelief," what is meant by "the traits of disbelief" (...)?

Shaykh: The traits of disbelief means the things that cause disbelief. For example, the Messenger's, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Two things among people are disbelief in them: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead." [Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih, no. 67/121, from Abu Hurayrah.] These are two traits.

Student: Attributes.

Shaykh: Attributes or actions.

Student: So if, for example, one abandons prayer, do we say about him..

Shaykh: No, abandoning prayer is major disbelief that expels one from the religion, because there are evidences for it.

Student: Minor?

Shaykh: It is not minor.

Student: Or an attribute.

Shaykh: No, it is major disbelief, because there are evidences from the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

Student: ﴿Those who said of their brethren﴾: is "brethren" here brethren by lineage, or brethren (...)? The hypocrites outwardly show Islam. What is meant by "their brethren"..

Shaykh: We said that some scholars said: brethren by lineage. The correct view is that they are brethren outwardly.

Student: Why can it not be understood also as their brethren in hypocrisy?

Shaykh: None of the hypocrites was killed. All those martyred at Uhud were sincere believers.

Student: May Allah reward you well, Shaykh. The benefit is that the hypocrites are eager to conceal their hypocrisy (...) when Islam is dominant (...) their hypocrisy, but when Islam is weak they show hypocrisy.

Shaykh: They show disbelief, yes, that is correct.

Student: May Allah reward you well. Is it correct to say that the sinner, while in his sin, is closer to disbelief than to faith?

Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt about it, because all sins are traits of disbelief. Every sin is disbelief, just as all acts of obedience are faith. But we do not describe every sin as disbelief except with evidence.

Student: Those who hold the intermediate position (al-manzilah) cite this verse as evidence.

Shaykh: With what?

Student: The one who commits a major sin is in an intermediate position between two positions. They say: Allah (...).

Shaykh: But they expel him from faith. Do not think he is in a position between two positions, meaning between the position of perfection and the position of deficiency. If this were their meaning, it would be correct. But they expel him from faith entirely.

Student: (...) the intermediate position between the two positions.

Shaykh: And in the Hereafter he is in the Fire. But we say: the intermediate position you mean, we do not agree with you on it. But if they said he is in an intermediate position between the two positions, between the position of perfection and the position of deficiency, we would say: correct.

Student: The obsessive person, we said his divorce does not take effect. But if he has a discharge and deliberately causes the discharge, we say his ablution (...)?

Shaykh: Known, there is no doubt about it, because discharge is an act, and the one who has discharge, even if he is compelled to produce discharge and does, his ablution is nullified, because (...) is a cause. As for divorce, it is entrusted to a person's choice: ﴿When you marry﴾ [Al-Ahzab 49], then you divorce. As for discharge, it is a cause on which ablution is ordained.

Student: We said that a person did not intend (...), he hung it and it does not take effect.

Shaykh: He did not intend the meaning.

Student: He did not intend the meaning (...) it does not take effect. Then, if he possesses this thing and it is not attached (...) the right of another, (...) the right of another, the penalty for slander, because divorce (...) possesses (...) slander?

Shaykh: No. Aggression against another, even if he is ignorant, aggression against another is not excused, neither by ignorance, nor forgetfulness, nor compulsion. Even if a person compels another to strike someone, the compeller is held accountable.

Student: (...) he intends by his saying.

Shaykh: The meaning is the speech that concerns the person himself. But if someone insults a person and says, "I did not intend it, I meant to praise him," ..

Student: Does even divorce concern another?

Shaykh: Yes, but the default is in the husband's hand. It is true that it concerns the woman's right, but if the woman says, "I do not want divorce," and he divorces her, he has that right; it is in his hand.

Student: We said that disobedience is among the traits of disbelief, and Allah, glorified and exalted, distinguished between disobedience, wickedness, and disbelief in His words: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you faith and made it pleasing in your hearts, and He has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance, and disobedience﴾ [Al-Hujurat 7], and He distinguished between them. Does disobedience not become one of the traits of disbelief in this verse?

Shaykh: There are words which, when mentioned together with others, have a meaning, and when mentioned alone have a meaning. For example, faith and Islam: when both are mentioned together, Islam has a meaning and faith has a meaning; if one of them is mentioned alone, they have the same meaning. So when he says "disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience," or "wickedness and transgression," or "sin and oppression," they differ. But when mentioned without qualification, this has the meaning of that.

Student: Do we say that sins are wickedness, sins are wickedness?

Shaykh: Yes, sins are wickedness, but it is a trait of disbelief, not expulsive disbelief. For this reason we qualified it; we told you. But we do not describe a sin as disbelief except when the Law describes it as such. But it is one of the traits of disbelief; a person follows his desire in it.

Student: How can we reconcile the statement that a person is held accountable for speech with the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "A person utters a word without giving it thought, and it throws him into the Fire"? [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari, no. 6478, and Muslim, no. 2988/50, from Abu Hurayrah.] How do we reconcile?

Shaykh: We reconcile them by saying the one who utters the word does so deliberately, but he does not care about it; he does not give it thought. So he is deliberate, and for this reason it throws him into the Fire for seventy autumns, or further than the distance between the heaven and the earth. So there is a difference between one who deliberately does not give it thought, and one who did not intend it.

Student: (...) "Can a believer be a coward?" He said: "No." Then he was asked: "Can he be a liar?" To all of them he said: "Yes," and about the liar he said: "No." [Narrated by Malik in al-Muwatta, no. 2832, from Safwan ibn Sulaym.] Is this to be understood as a permanent state or as individual acts?

Shaykh: No, even individual acts. Lying is among the traits of the hypocrites. So if a person lies once, a trait of hypocrisy is present in him. But even if he is a liar at all times, he is not a disbeliever in an absolute sense, meaning in the sense that expels one from the religion.

Student: But does the name of faith not get removed from him to become hypocrisy, since the Prophet ﷺ negated faith from him?

Shaykh: What is removed from him is the perfection of faith. The position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community is that what is mentioned with a negation of faith, and does not necessarily imply faith, means the negation of perfection.

Student: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat 10], and here He says: ﴿Those who said of their brethren﴾. The hypocrites said to their brethren. Does this mean it is correct to say the hypocrite is a brother of the believer?

Shaykh: Outwardly. As for the believers, they are brothers outwardly and inwardly.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Even outwardly he becomes a brother. Two people come and pray side by side: one prays while he does not believe in Allah, but among the people, and the second prays believing in Allah, sincere to Him. Outwardly they are brothers; they are all in one row and behind one imam.

Student: (...) absolute disbelief or traits of disbelief?

Shaykh: No, the hypocrites, the apparent meaning is absolute disbelief.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No. Perhaps some hypocrites did not disbelieve in an absolute sense and are closer to disbelief, and some of them are absolute disbelievers from the outset, not close to faith.

Student: (...) some exegetes (...) disbelief (...).

Shaykh: This goes against the apparent meaning, or does it have a correct meaning? It is correct, but it goes against the apparent meaning.

Student: May Allah reward you well. His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And to ʿĀd, their brother Hūd﴾ [Al-A'raf 65]. Is it like the issue we have in this verse, Shaykh?

Shaykh: How?

Student: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And to ʿĀd, their brother Hūd﴾. Does it mean outward brotherhood, Shaykh?

Shaykh: And what do you say?

Students: By lineage.

Shaykh: By lineage. For this reason, look at the people of the Thicket in Surat ash-Shuʿara. He said: ﴿The companions of the Thicket denied the messengers. When Shuʿayb said to them﴾ [Ash-Shuʿara 176–177]. Since they were not from his people, He said: ﴿When Shuʿayb said to them﴾. But the people of Madyan, what did He say about them? ﴿And to Madyan, their brother Shuʿayb﴾ [Al-A'raf 85].

Student: The context, Shaykh, requires distinguishing between believers and hypocrites.

Shaykh: How?

Student: This context requires distinguishing between believers and hypocrites, why, I mean. I am not objecting to Allah's words ﴿of their brethren﴾, but if one objects (...) how do we say, although at the end of (...) to the end of the verses, does the context (...).

Shaykh: The context is that they claim to be brothers, and that they are one hand, and they pray with the people and give charity. So they say: we are sincere to you, we are your brothers.

Student: Shaykh, the one who is compelled to do something and chooses to be killed, would he be a martyr?

Shaykh: Would he be what?

Student: Would he be a martyr?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 168 (part 2 of 2):**

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for (169). Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve (170). They rejoice in a favor from Allah and a bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers (171). Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after injury had befallen them. For those among them who did good and feared Allah is a great reward (172). Those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them," but it increased them in faith and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" (173). So they returned with a favor from Allah and a bounty, not touched by any harm, and they followed the pleasure of Allah, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty (174).﴾ [Aal 'Imran 169–174].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. The Almighty said: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead..﴾
The Almighty, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Those who said of their brothers while they sat [at home], "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed."﴾ Where is the object of the speech in His words: ﴿Those who said of their brothers﴾?

* Student: His words: ﴿If they had obeyed us﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿If they had obeyed us﴾ is the object of the speech. And what is the grammatical position of His words: ﴿while they sat﴾?

* Student: It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), the meaning of the sentence being: "while they had [already] sat."

* The Shaykh: Excellent. Is it not permissible for it to be coordinated (ma'ṭūfah) with ﴿they said﴾?

* Student: As a relative clause complement (ṣilat al-mawṣūl).

* The Shaykh: Coordinated with ﴿they said﴾, which is the relative clause complement.
The Almighty said: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.﴾ What is the type of (law) here?

* Student: This is an expression of hope (tarajjī).

* The Shaykh: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.﴾

* Student: It is an expression of regret.

* The Shaykh: But what is it? I mean its grammatical analysis (i'rāb), not its meaning.

* Student: It is "prevention of something because of the prevention of something else" (imtinā' li-imtinā').

* The Shaykh: Its grammatical analysis?

* Student: It is conditional.

* The Shaykh: Conditional, its analysis is conditional. The verb of the condition?

* Student: ﴿They obeyed us﴾.

* The Shaykh: And its response?

* Student: The response: ﴿they would not have been killed﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿They would not have been killed.﴾
(Law) comes with several meanings, among them that it is conditional. What are the others?

* Student: You mean its grammatical analysis, Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.

* Student: A conditional particle that is not jussive.

* The Shaykh: I understand that. Does it come for other than the condition?

* Student: Verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah).

* The Shaykh: Verbal-noun like what?

* Student: The words of Allah, glorified and exalted: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam 9].

* The Shaykh: ﴿They wish that you would compromise﴾, meaning they wish that you compromise.
The Almighty's words: ﴿If you are truthful﴾, what is this clause?

* Student: ﴿If you are truthful﴾?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. What is the clause?

* Student: A nominal clause.

* The Shaykh: Nominal?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: How is it nominal when it begins with a verb?

* Student: "In" is a particle of nasb (accusative governing).

* The Shaykh: The clause in ﴿If you are truthful﴾?

* Student: Yes indeed, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: What is it?

* Student: It is conditional, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: Conditional. Where is the verb of the condition?

* Student: The verb of the condition: ﴿you were﴾.

* The Shaykh: Where is the response?

* Student: The response is disputed. Some said: a construction like this has no response. Others said: the response is omitted, its estimate being: "If you are truthful, then ward off death from yourselves."

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, that is correct. There are two opinions on it. Some say the response is omitted, and some say it does not need a response, because it is known from what precedes. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him.

* Among the lessons of this verse: the condemnation of those who combined the ugliness of action with the ugliness of speech. It is derived from His words: ﴿they said﴾ and ﴿they sat﴾. The ugliness of the action is from their being...?

* The students: They sat.

* The Shaykh: And the ugliness of speech is from their saying: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.﴾

* Among its lessons: that these people, despite the ugliness of their words and their causing regret among their people, objected to the divine decree (qadar), by their saying: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed.﴾

* Also among its lessons: an indication that such a statement when the decree has come to pass is not permissible, because it was brought in the context of blame, and that is so. For this reason the Prophet, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, said: "If something befalls you, do not say: 'If only I had done such and such, it would have been such and such.'" [Reported by Muslim (2664 / 34) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] As for if a person says it as a statement of fact, not as an objection to the decree and not as regret over what has occurred, there is no harm in it. Among it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Had I known at the beginning of my affair what I came to know at its end, I would not have brought the offering, and I would have released myself with you." [Reported by al-Bukhari (7229) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.] This is not from the category of wishing (tamannī), as some scholars held, that (law) here is used to express the wish for good. Rather, we say: it is a statement of fact, and this occurs often. You may say to a person: "If you had visited me yesterday, I would have honored you," and similar things, meaning by it a statement of fact.

On this basis we say: the use of (law) occurs in several ways:

* The first way: that it is an objection to the decree. This is not permissible, and it is a dispute with the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, over His judgment and decree.

* The second case: that it is a cause of regret and sorrow. This too is not permissible, because the Prophet ﷺ forbade it, saying: "If something befalls you, do not say: 'If only I had done such and such, it would have been such and such.'"

* The third: that it is a report about what has actually happened. This is not objectionable, because it does not compel a person to regret, and there is in it no dispute with the decree of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It occurs often in people's speech.

* Among the lessons of this verse: the challenge to those who said these words, to ward off death from themselves, by His words: ﴿Say: "Then ward off from yourselves death."﴾

* Among its lessons: that it is impossible to ward off death, because what is posed as a challenge cannot occur. For if it were possible to occur, there would be no benefit in the challenge. From here we know that the saying of the Almighty: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass. You will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman 33] cannot be taken to mean that people now reach the depths of space and the planets, and the depths of the planets, as some claimed when people reached the moon and landed on it. They said: "This is something the Quran indicates, because Allah said: ﴿You will not pass except with authority﴾, and authority is knowledge. These people were given knowledge until they reached what they reached, so the Quran bears witness to it!"

But in reality this is a distortion of the Quran. The Quran in these verses is for a challenge, as evidenced by the Almighty's saying: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman 26], ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him. Every day He is in a matter﴾ [al-Rahman 29], ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass﴾, ﴿There will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and molten brass﴾ [al-Rahman 35], ﴿And when the sky splits open and becomes red like rose-colored leather﴾ [al-Rahman 37]. All this indicates that the intended meaning is when? The challenge, and it will be on the Day of Resurrection, not in this world. For this reason we say: even if these people passed beyond the regions of the earth, they would not pass beyond the regions of the heavens, and the verse contains the challenge in both respects.

The essential point is that one should not (...) the texts of the Quran in order to say that they indicate what has happened or what is happening. Rather, we say: what has happened or is happening, when proofs establish its truth, does not need to be forced into the indication of the Quran. We say: this is something that has occurred and that all people witness, so it is true. If we forced everything of the sciences that occurs in the present time into the Quran, we would be burdening the Quran with what it cannot bear.

Let it be known that the interpretation of the Quran is an expression of Allah's will by these words, or an expression of what Allah intends. Whoever interprets it contrary to what appears of His intention is lying against Allah and fabricating against Him. The matter is not light. That is, I have permitted myself to interpret the speech of one of the people, and lying about Allah is not like lying about people. But I do not permit myself to say about the Book of Allah what we do not know Allah intended. The interpreter bears witness on behalf of Allah that Allah intended such-and-such. So let him beware, let him beware of this matter.

* Among the lessons of the noble verse: the Prophet, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, was given a specific charge to convey something of the Quran or to dispute with someone among the people, by His words: ﴿Say: "Then ward off."﴾ That is, you should dispute with them and challenge them, so say: "Ward off death from yourselves, if you are truthful."

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: dealing with people according to what appears of their state, by His words: ﴿those who said of their brothers while they sat﴾. For we have already said that the correct understanding of "brothers" here is brotherhood in outward appearance, not brotherhood by lineage, because not everyone who was killed at Uhud had kinship with these hypocrites.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 169–171 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And do not think that those who were killed in the cause of Allah are dead.﴾ There are two readings for it: ﴿qutTilū﴾ and ﴿qutilū﴾, and likewise ﴿taḥsabanna﴾ and ﴿taḥsibanna﴾; both are among the seven canonical readings.

The address in ﴿And do not think﴾ is either directed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone to whom address can be directed. If it is to everyone to whom address can be directed, then the Prophet (ﷺ) and others are included in it. If it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), then others are included by way of following him, so the primary intended addressee of this address is the Prophet (ﷺ), and others are included secondarily. As for when we say that it—that is, the address—is directed to everyone to whom address can be directed, it is general, meaning: "And do not think, O addressee," according to the second view, or "And do not think, O Prophet," according to the first view. The word ḥusbān (thinking) here means ẓann (supposition), meaning: do not suppose that those who were killed in the cause of Allah are dead.

And His saying ﴿were killed in the cause of Allah﴾ includes the one whom the enemy killed and the one who was killed while being a means of harm to the enemy, as when an arrow rebounds onto its shooter and kills him; he is considered killed in the cause of Allah.

And His saying ﴿in the cause of Allah﴾ was explained by the Messenger (peace be upon him) to mean one who fights so that the word of Allah is supreme. This was when he was asked about a man who fights for bravery, fights for zeal, and fights for show—and in another wording: fights so that his position may be seen—"which of these is in the cause of Allah?" So he (ﷺ) said a comprehensive and restrictive statement, saying: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the cause of Allah."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (123) and Muslim (1904 / 150) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]]. What was the Messenger (ﷺ) asked about?
* Student: About fighting in the cause of Allah.
* Shaykh: What was asked—the questions addressed to him?
* Student: A man fights for bravery, fights for zeal, and fights so that his position is seen; which of these is in the cause of Allah? So he said a comprehensive statement: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the cause of Allah."
* Shaykh: Yes. So who are intended by "those who were killed in the cause of Allah"? They are those who, what? Fought so that the word of Allah is supreme, not for bravery, nor zeal, nor show. Bravery means that a person is driven by his courage to fight, because the brave person loves fighting, just as the fisherman in the sea loves fishing even if he catches only a little, and likewise the bird hunter in the air loves hunting even if he catches only a little. The brave man loves to fight. So if a man fights for the sake of bravery, moved by his courage to fight, this is not in the cause of Allah. Zeal, whether national or tribal, is not in the cause of Allah. Whoever fights only to defend the homeland, his fighting is equal to the fighting of the disbeliever, since even disbelievers fight to defend their countries. But whoever fights to defend his country because it is an Islamic country, to protect Islam by this fighting, he is in the cause of Allah. Therefore, when we direct soldiers to fight in defense of the homeland, we must say: "Note that you are defending your homeland as an Islamic homeland, not merely as a nation."

The third, showing off: one who fights only for show, so that it is seen that he is a man who fights in the cause of Allah, this is not in the cause of Allah, even if there are other intentions. One who fights only out of obedience to his commander is not in the cause of Allah. That is, the Messenger (peace be upon him) was asked about three things and did not answer each one individually; rather he answered with a comprehensive and restrictive statement, so that it includes other intentions besides these three, since other intentions may come beyond these three, and so they are either excluded or included by the hadith: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the cause of Allah."
Who are those who were killed in the cause of Allah? Are they the people of Badr or the people of Uhud, or is it general?
It is general, but the first to be included are the martyrs of Badr and Uhud, without doubt.

And His saying ﴿And do not think that those who were killed in the cause of Allah are dead﴾: "in the cause of Allah" — sabil Allah means His path, and it is sometimes attributed to the believers. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers—We will give him what he has taken and drive him into Hell﴾ [An-Nisa 115]. So it is attributed to Allah in two respects: in respect that He is its establisher, He who legislated this path, and in respect that it leads to Him; and it is attributed to the believers in one respect, which is that they are the ones who traversed it.
Here, what is attributed to Allah is in the respect that Allah the Exalted is the one who legislated this religion, and that this religion leads to Him.

﴿Dead﴾ (amwātan) is the second object of ḥasiba, because ḥasiba takes two objects whose origins are a subject and predicate, unlike kasā and aʿṭā, which take two objects whose origins are not a subject and predicate.

He says: ﴿dead, but rather alive﴾. Here He said: ﴿dead, but rather alive﴾, and it is well known that when someone is killed, he dies. So how is that?!
The meaning: do not think that they died and ended. No, they died but they transferred to another life, better than the one they left. So the meaning is: do not think of them as dead, meaning that they died and ended. It is not so. Rather they are alive: they died the death of this world, but they are alive with another life, distinguished from the life of this world, and it is better and superior.

And His saying ﴿but rather alive with their Lord﴾: ﴿with﴾ (ʿinda) indicates nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that is so. The spirits of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that roam in Paradise wherever they wish, then they ascend to lamps suspended beneath the Throne. This is a special nearness, in which they are distinguished by closeness to Allah, glorified and exalted.

His saying ﴿but rather alive﴾ means: rather they are alive, and what is meant is the life of their spirits. As for their bodies, they have died without doubt, but their spirits are alive with a barzakh life. For this reason He said ﴿with their Lord﴾, and it is not the absolute life which is the life of this world, because if it were the life of this world they would not have been killed in the cause of Allah; they would have remained, and it would not be valid for them to be buried. They have left this world and been buried, yet they are alive with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with a life unlike the life of this world.

And His saying ﴿they are provided for﴾ means they are given, because provision (rizq) in the language means giving. From it is His saying: ﴿And when the division is present to the relatives and the orphans and the needy, provide for them﴾ [An-Nisa 8]. "Provide for them" means give to them. So they are given; given from what?
They are given from the provision of Allah in Paradise wherever they wish. But this giving is incomplete compared to the more perfect giving which will be after resurrection; because the giving here, before the Resurrection, is a giving to the body and a giving to the spirit, and both are incomplete relative to what comes after. It is a giving to the body because in the grave it is widened as far as the eye can see, and a door to Paradise is opened for him, and its breeze and bliss come to him, but he does not enjoy it with complete enjoyment. Likewise the spirits do not enjoy complete enjoyment while in Paradise. Complete enjoyment will be after resurrection, when spirits meet bodies in a meeting after which there is no separation, because when spirits meet in resurrection there is no parting; they remain forever and ever, and then the perfect bliss is attained.

Then He said: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾. Joy (farah) is the opposite of sorrow, and is close in meaning to gladness. The meaning is that they are glad with what Allah has given them of His bounty. As you observe, it is now in the accusative: ﴿rejoicing﴾ — in what capacity? It is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), in the accusative as a circumstance. But is it a circumstance of the hidden pronoun in ﴿alive﴾: "but rather alive while they are rejoicing"; or a circumstance of the adverbial phrase: ﴿with their Lord﴾, meaning from the complement of the adverb; or a circumstance of the deputy subject in ﴿they are provided for﴾?
All of this is permissible, and the meaning does not differ greatly.

And His saying ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given﴾ means in what He has given them, ﴿of His bounty﴾. He did not specify it, rather He mentioned it in summary, because it is mentioned in detail in other verses after entering Paradise on the Day of Resurrection; here it is a summary.
﴿in what Allah has given them﴾: ātāhum means gave them, whereas atāhum (with a different vowelling) means came to them.
He says: ﴿what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾. Fadl (bounty) in the language means increase, and what is meant by bounty here is what Allah has bestowed upon them of bliss that had never occurred to their minds.

He said: ﴿and they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them﴾. The waw here is a conjunction. Is it joined to ﴿rejoicing﴾ by coordinating a verb with a noun, or joined to ﴿they are provided for﴾?
We say: it may be either, and the meaning does not differ greatly; the meaning does not differ greatly.
His saying ﴿yastabshirūn﴾ means: some of them give glad tidings to others about what will be mentioned. So the meaning of (istabshara) is: he gave glad tidings to others, or: (istabshara) means glad tidings came to him through the action of another.
And His saying ﴿in those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾ means in their brothers who have not yet joined them, and have not yet been killed in the cause of Allah.

﴿That there is no fear﴾: here (anna) is a verbal particle, but it has been assimilated with (lā), ﴿allā khawfun﴾. The last rule in writing is to write (anna), but the older rule is not to write it, and here it was not written: ﴿allā khawfun﴾, but the original word is (anna lā).
Regarding (anna) here they say: it is a substitute for His saying ﴿those who have not yet joined them﴾, as if He said: they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that there is no fear for them. What type of substitution is this? A substitution of inclusion; because fear is not a part of the person. Substitution of inclusion: they rejoice that there is no fear upon them ﴿concerning what lies ahead of them﴾ and ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over what has passed of their affairs; because the principle is that fear is for the future, and grief is for the past.

﴿That there is no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve (170). They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty﴾: the sentence is a resumptive sentence showing a joy whose cause is different from the first cause. The first: its cause is that they await brothers of theirs who have not yet joined them. The second cause of joy: what Allah has bestowed upon them of blessing and bounty. Here He said ﴿they rejoice﴾, and a little earlier He said ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them﴾. There is no contradiction between them: they rejoice in what has taken place, and they rejoice in what will take place. They are rejoicing in what Allah has given them, content with it, glad with it, and despite that they rejoice in an additional bounty, and for this He said ﴿with a blessing from Allah and bounty﴾. Among that is that they hope to look upon the Face of Allah, and that they have been given good news that their state is eternity without death, and they also rejoice in what Allah, glorified and exalted, promised them in this world, and they continue to mention it; because in Paradise is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

He said: ﴿And that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾. In it there are two readings: ﴿wa-inna Allāha﴾ and ﴿wa-anna Allāha﴾ with a fatha. On the reading with fatḥa, it is joined to? ﴿niʿmatin﴾, meaning "and that Allah..." and on the reading with kasra, it is a resumptive statement from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, not from their speech; meaning they rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and Allah the Exalted has rewarded them for their deeds: ﴿And indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾, meaning He does not leave it unrewarded and in vain, but He must certainly reward them for it.

The sentence, as you see, is emphasized by (inna), and what else? The lām? By (inna), the lām and the oath?
* Student: There is no lām, there is no oath.
* Shaykh: There is no lām, and the oath? There is no oath. So it is emphasized by what? By (inna) only.
﴿And indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾.
* These verses contain benefits:
* The first benefit: the virtue of those who are killed in the cause of Allah, because they are alive with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among its benefits also: encouragement to jihad so that a person may attain martyrdom.
But here is an issue: is it legislated for a person to wage jihad in order to be killed in the cause of Allah, or the one who fights so that the word of Allah is supreme?
The second. For this reason, when a person goes out to jihad in the cause of Allah, he should intend that he fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, not merely to be killed in the cause of Allah; because being in the cause of Allah is a consequence of fighting so that the word of Allah is supreme. Some scholars even say: if he fights only so that he may be killed, then he fought in order to die; but the true fighting is to fight so that the word of Allah is supreme, and if he is killed, he is in the cause of Allah.
Some scholars say: there is no harm in intending by jihad that he be killed in the cause of Allah, because it will not be attained for him to be killed in the cause of Allah unless he fights so that the word of Allah is supreme.
But even if this is said, the first intention and the first rank is that he goes out to fight so that the word of Allah is supreme, and then he wishes for martyrdom on the basis of this.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is valid to negate a thing with respect to a certain aspect, not absolutely; because of His saying: ﴿And do not think that those who were killed in the cause of Allah are dead﴾, for the negation of their being dead here is meant as what? The death in which there is annihilation without benefit and without reward.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of the martyrs in being with Allah; because of His saying: ﴿but rather alive with their Lord﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the refutation of the argument of those who say that the Messenger (ﷺ) is alive in his grave and is provided for, and say that the station of prophethood is higher than the station of martyrdom. There is no doubt about this: the station of prophethood is higher than the station of martyrdom. But their saying that he is alive in his grave and provided for: if they mean that it is a barzakh life, then this is true; and if they mean that it is a worldly life, then this is undoubtedly a lie, because if it were a worldly life he would not have been washed, nor shrouded, nor prayed over, nor buried, and the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, would have buried the Prophet (ﷺ) alive; they would have buried him while alive.
It is not objected to this that his spirit is returned to him so that he returns the greeting to whoever greets him; because the return of the spirit into the body in the grave is not like its return in the life of this world; rather it is a special return. For this reason the dead person in his grave does not need food, drink, or air, even if his spirit is returned to him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the martyrs are provided for while they are dead; because of His saying: ﴿but rather alive with their Lord, they are provided for﴾. But does this provision need what people need in this world? In the sense of needing to relieve themselves, front or back? No; because this is an otherworldly provision, and otherworldly provision does not need that. Even the people of Paradise remain in it forever and ever and do not need this; rather food and drink come out as sweat, but it is not like the sweat of this world either: a foul, malodorous sweat; rather it is more fragrant than musk—O Allah, make us among them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿with their Lord they are provided for﴾.
* Student: The hadith in the Musnad[[Related by Ahmad in al-Musnad (15780) from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik.]] from Ubayy ibn Ka'b or Ka'b ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The soul of the believer is a bird that hangs in Paradise until Allah returns it to Him." What is the difference between the believer now and the martyr?
* Shaykh: Some scholars hold that what is meant by the believer here is the believing mujahid who was killed in the cause of Allah, and others hold that it is general, and this is the correct view. The difference is that the soul of the believer in Paradise is a bird that hangs there, meaning it eats from it; but the spirits of the martyrs are in the crops of the insides of green birds that take shelter in lamps suspended. Just as their bodies were torn apart in this world, Allah the Exalted replaced them with other bodies, namely these green birds, so the spirits of the martyrs are distinguished from the rest of the believers by this, and this is the closer view.
* Student: Do you mean, O Shaykh, that all the spirits in Paradise become...?

**Shaykh:** This is the closer view: the souls of the believers are in Paradise. But Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said: some souls may be detained for a reason, such as debt, which may prevent the soul from entering Paradise. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked whether martyrdom expiates sins, and he said: "It expiates everything." Then Jibril came to him and said: "Except debt." So he said: "Except debt." [Narrated by Muslim (1885/117) from Abu Qatada.] This shows that the reward of the one who fights in the cause of Allah may be withheld if he has debt. So there may be obstacles, but the basic principle is that the souls of the believers are in Paradise. This is the basic principle.

**Student:** We said that Allah's words ﴿فَرِحِينَ﴾ (*fariḥīn*, "rejoicing") may be a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause, "state") of ﴿أَحْيَاءٌ﴾ (*aḥyā'*, "alive").

**Shaykh:** No, it is a *ḥāl* of the pronoun.

**Student:** Doesn't that contradict the meaning, Shaykh? That they are alive while in the state of rejoicing?

**Shaykh:** Yes. They are alive, and joy is among them.

**Student:** Continuously? That is, constant joy?

**Shaykh:** Yes, there is no doubt about it: constant joy, and they have no sorrow.

**Student:** When 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh wanted to go out to fight in the way of Allah, he wanted Paradise, but his sons prevented him. So he complained to the Messenger, and the Messenger ﷺ permitted him... (ﷺ). Does this mean a struggle in which the word of Allah is supreme?

**Shaykh:** It is known that he did not go out except for this.

**Student:** He wanted Paradise.

**Shaykh:** He wanted Paradise on the basis that he went out so that the word of Allah would be supreme. For this reason, when a person goes out so that the word of Allah is supreme, this is what he attains: he attains Paradise.

**Student:** Has it been reported that the body of a martyr does not decay or turn to dust in the grave?

**Shaykh:** No, this has not been established for martyrs. But they have witnessed events indicating that the earth does not consume them. What is certain, however, is that the earth does not consume the prophets: "Allah has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets." [Narrated by al-Nasa'i in al-Sughra (1374) from Aws ibn Aws.]

**Student:** We worship Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, according to what is with Him. You say: a person fights to attain martyrdom, this is... (...) or he recites Ayat al-Kursi (...), it protects him from Satan (...)?

**Shaykh:** As for reciting Ayat al-Kursi so that it protects you, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, indicated this. When Abu Hurayrah came and informed the Prophet ﷺ of what Satan had said, he said: "He told you the truth, though he is a liar." And he said: "Whoever recites it at night, there will remain with him a guardian from Allah, and Satan will not come near him until morning." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (2311) from Abu Hurayrah.] So if a person recites it for this purpose, this purpose is attained for him. But he will be lacking compared to the one who recites it for worship and for attaining the purpose. The second is more complete.

**Student:** ﴿وَيَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾ (*wa-yastabshirūn*, "and they rejoice") the first is in conjunction with ﴿فَرِحِينَ﴾. Alright, is ﴿فَرِحِينَ﴾ in the accusative?

**Shaykh:** Because it is a noun. The sense of the sentence is: "rejoicing and joyful." If ﴿يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾ were a noun, it would be: "و مستبشرين" (*wa-mustabshirīn*, "and joyful").

**Student:** Alright, does the retention of the *nūn* here indicate the nominative case ﴿وَيَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾?

**Shaykh:** Yes, because it is a verb, not a noun, and the subject is the *wāw*. This *wāw* is not a sign of i'rab (grammatical inflection). Here the *wāw* is a pronoun.

**Student:** The verbal noun (*ta'wīl al-maṣdar*) in ﴿أَنْ يَغُلَّ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 161].

**Shaykh:** Jussive by what?

**Student:** Jussive by the deletion of the weak letter?

**Shaykh:** Why is it jussive?

**Shaykh:** Where is the condition?

**Student:** ﴿أَنْ﴾. This is the conditional particle and its verb.

**Shaykh:** This is the conditional particle and its verb: ﴿أَنْ يَغُلَّ﴾!

**Student:** ﴿وَمَنْ يَغْلُلْ﴾ (*wa-man yaghlul*, "and whoever embezzles").

**Shaykh:** ﴿وَمَنْ يَغْلُلْ﴾, good, well done.

﴿لَقَدْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 164]. Why was this a favor?

**Student:** Because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, brought people out through him from darkness into light, from ignorance.

**Shaykh:** What?

He said: ﴿رَسُولًا مِنْ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (*rasūlan min anfusihim*, "a messenger from among themselves"), and in Surat al-Jumu'ah: ﴿رَسُولًا مِنْهُمْ﴾ (*rasūlan minhum*, "a messenger from among them") [al-Jumu'ah 2]. What is the difference?

**Student:** ﴿مِنْ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ means from among them.

Among its examples is Allah's saying: ﴿لَوْلَا إِذْ سَمِعْتُمُوهُ ظَنَّ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتُ بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ خَيْرًا﴾ ["Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of their own kind?" al-Nur 12].

**Student:** Conditional?

**Shaykh:** Conditional! How conditional? The meaning does not work if it is conditional.

**Student:** (*mā*) in the sense of *alladhī* (relative pronoun, "that which").

**Shaykh:** Relative.

**Student:** (...).

**Student:** Because it is a nominal sentence.

**Shaykh:** No, my brother.

**Student:** The cosmic permission.

**Shaykh:** Cosmic. Do you know that permission is divided into two types: cosmic and legislative? Can you give examples?

**Student:** To the universe.

Concerning His saying ﴿مَا قُتِلُوا﴾ (*mā quti'lū*, "they would not have been killed"), are there two readings?
