Here it is good to mention the types of *tawassul*. *Tawassul* is divided into two kinds: prohibited and permissible.

The prohibited is what the Sharia has not sanctioned, and the permissible is what the Sharia has sanctioned. This is the governing rule. Whatever types of *tawassul* the Sharia has not sanctioned are prohibited, such as seeking a means through the high standing (*jāh*) of the Messenger (ﷺ). This occurs often among some people who say: "I seek a means to You through the standing of Your Prophet." Here, the *tawassul* is not legislated, so it is prohibited. This is because *tawassul* means making something a means, and something being a means is not established except by evidence from the Sharia. The standing of the Prophet (ﷺ) is not a cause for the acceptance of our supplication, because his standing, peace and blessings be upon him, is something whose virtue belongs to him alone. As for us, we have no connection to it.

So what is the governing rule for the prohibited? It is what the Sharia has not sanctioned. The reason it is prohibited is that whoever seeks a means through something has made it a cause, and a cause's validity depends on an indication from the Sharia.

As for the permissible, it is what the Sharia has brought. It has several kinds, among them:

First, seeking a means through the names of Allah. This is done by saying: "O Allah, I ask You by Your Beautiful Names." Its evidence is the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, in the supplication of distress and grief: "I ask You by every name that is Yours, which You named Yourself with, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept hidden in the knowledge of the unseen with You, that You make the Great Qur'an the spring of my heart" (recorded by Ahmad, 4318), and so on to the end. So this is a *tawassul* by what?

* **Students:** By the names of Allah.
* **Shaykh:** By the names of Allah: "by every name that is Yours."

Second, seeking a means through the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Among this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, keep me alive if You know life to be good for me" (recorded by al-Nasa'i, 1305, 1306, from the hadith of 'Ammar ibn Yasir). So his saying, "by Your knowledge of the unseen," is a *tawassul* to Allah by what?

By His attribute.

And among this is: "O Allah, by Your mercy I seek help" (recorded by al-Tirmidhi, 3524, from the hadith of Anas, but with the wording: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting, by Your mercy I seek help"). This is not seeking help *from* mercy, but seeking help from Allah by His attribute, which is mercy, for the Merciful one gives aid.

Third, seeking a means to Allah through His actions. An action, although it is among the attributes, is an attribute that is not eternal and everlasting. Among this is our saying in the tashahhud: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy and Glorious" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari, 3370, and Muslim, 406/66, from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah). So his saying, "as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim," the meaning of this is a *tawassul* to Allah. That is, "just as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim, so send blessings upon Muhammad." If we say this, the particle *al-kaf* ("as") is causal (*lil-ta'līl*). With this explanation, the difficulty that some scholars raised is removed. They said: "It is well known that Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to Ibrahim."

The rule is that the thing compared is below the rank of the thing it is compared to. Here he said: "Send blessings upon Muhammad as You sent blessings," and if we say that the particle *al-kaf* is not for comparison but for causation, and that this is a case of *tawassul*, meaning that we are not asking You for something strange, we are asking You for something You have done before, then what is the difficulty here? It is removed, and there remains no difficulty in it.

* **Student:** (...)?
* **Shaykh:** No. Seeking a means to Allah by His names, seeking a means to Allah by His attributes, seeking a means to Allah by His actions.

Fourth, seeking a means to Allah, exalted is He, through faith: faith in Him and in His messengers. Among this is this verse: "Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, 'Believe in your Lord,' so we believed. Our Lord, so forgive us" (Al 'Imran 193). They made their faith a means of asking for forgiveness: "Our Lord, so forgive us our sins" (Al 'Imran 193).

Fifth, seeking a means to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through righteous deeds. This is not through faith itself but through righteous deeds. Among this is the story of the three companions of the cave, when a rock closed over them, sealing the mouth of the cave, and they could not move it. They said: "Seek a means to Allah through your best deeds." So one of them sought a means through his complete kindness to his parents, the second through his complete chastity, and the third through his complete trustworthiness, and Allah relieved them (agreed upon; al-Bukhari, 2272, and Muslim, 2743/99, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar). Is it clear, brothers?

If someone says: "Seeking a means through this and what came before it is problematic, because someone may say: Is this not presumption upon Allah, and self-admiration and pride in the deed? It is as if he says: O Lord, I did such and such, and I did such and such, so forgive me, for example."

The answer is: No. Rather, this is from the aspect of humility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is from the aspect of humbling oneself before Him, and that I, O Lord, have humbled myself to You, and I know that You are the refuge, so I worshipped You and believed in You, and I ask You to forgive me, for example.

Sixth, seeking a means to Allah by mentioning the condition of the one supplicating. This is seeking a means to Allah by mentioning one's state, so that you mention your condition and say: "O Allah, I have wronged myself, so forgive me." The first was a *tawassul* through a righteous deed, whereas here it is the opposite, through one's condition. Among this is the saying of Musa: "My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me" (Al-Qasas 24). He mentioned nothing but this. This is a *tawassul* to Allah by what? By mentioning one's condition. Because when a person mentions his state, and that he is in need of Allah, this compels him to turn to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is one of the causes of the answering of supplication.

Seventh, seeking a means to Allah, exalted is He, through the supplication of a righteous man. Among this is the saying of 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan to the Prophet (ﷺ), when he said: "Indeed, among my nation seventy thousand will enter Paradise without reckoning and without punishment." He said: "Supplicate to Allah that He makes me one of them." He said: "You are among them" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari, 5752, and Muslim, 220/374, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas). Among this is the saying of a Bedouin: "O Messenger of Allah, wealth has perished and the roads have been cut off, so supplicate to Allah that He gives us relief." So he supplicated (agreed upon; al-Bukhari, 1013, and Muslim, 897/8, from the hadith of Anas). Among this is the saying of 'Umar to al-'Abbas: "Stand and supplicate to Allah." So he said: "O Allah, we seek a means to You through our Prophet, and You gave us rain, and we seek a means to You through the paternal uncle of our Prophet" (recorded by al-Bukhari, 1010, from the hadith of Anas).

The student should note, regarding this seventh type, what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed out: when you ask someone to supplicate for you, you intend by this the benefit of the one supplicating and his reward, because the one who supplicates is rewarded when he supplicates for his brother. He said this to guard against the case where the seeker wants only to benefit himself. He said: "This is the reprehensible request, that you say: 'Supplicate to Allah for me,' intending only the benefit of yourself. No, say: 'Supplicate to Allah for me,' and you intend that he also benefits from his supplication for you, because he is rewarded for his kindness to you, and because when he supplicates for you in your absence, the angel says: 'Amin, and for you the same,' or: 'And for you the like of it.'" This is when you want to ask a specific person to supplicate for you personally. But if you ask him to supplicate for the Muslims in general, this is not the reprehensible request, even if you do not consider his benefit. The parallel is that if you asked a man for a dirham for yourself, or said: "Give me a dirham for so-and-so the poor man," the first would be the reprehensible request, and the second would be a kindness to both the giver and the one given to, because you benefit the giver in the Hereafter and benefit the recipient in this world.

These, then, are seven types of *tawassul*, all of which the Sunnah has brought, and they are permissible, because each is in reality a cause among the causes. The word *wasīlah* (means) is in origin similar to *wasīlah* (a connection), and the letters *sīn* and *ṣād* alternate often, as in the saying: "Guide us to the straight path" (*ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*) and "guide us to the straight path" (*ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*) (Al-Fatihah 6). Both are recognized Sab'ī recitations.

So from this verse, "Our Lord, so forgive us," we take the permissibility of seeking a means through what? Through faith. And we digressed into mentioning the categories of *tawassul*.

Is the polytheism of the polytheists with their gods a form of prohibited *tawassul*, or what?

* **Student:** Something else.
* **Shaykh:** Something else. Yes, it is not *tawassul* but worship, because they say: "We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to Allah" (Az-Zumar 3). They intend worship. They call upon these idols, bow to them, prostrate to them, make vows to them, and slaughter for them. So it is not from the aspect of *tawassul* but from the aspect of intention and purpose, that these idols are worshipped.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: every person is in need of the forgiveness of sins, based on their saying: "So forgive us our sins" (Al 'Imran 193). So do not be deceived by the abundance of acts of obedience. The more a person's acts of obedience increase, the more he should fear for himself that these acts may be rejected and his deeds go to waste.

* From the benefits of this verse: the distinction among sins, that some are sins (*dhunūb*) and some are misdeeds (*sayyi'āt*). This is like our saying that they are divided into major and minor sins, and that major and minor sins differ in their essence and differ among themselves. Major sins include greater and lesser ones, and minor sins include some that approach major sins and some that are below that.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of asking for death in the manner of people of goodness, based on their saying: "And cause us to die with the righteous" (Al 'Imran 193). We mentioned in the previous lesson that this is not a supplication for a hastened death, but a supplication for death in a desired state, namely that one dies in the condition in which the righteous died. We mentioned parallels to this. Who recalls them?

* **Student:** The saying of Maryam: "Would that I had died before this and become a thing forgotten and out of mind" (Maryam 23).
* **Shaykh:** The saying of Maryam: "Would that I had died before this and become a thing forgotten." The meaning is: "Would that I had died before the calamity."
* **Student:** And the saying of Yusuf: "Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous" (Yusuf 101).
* **Shaykh:** Excellent.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the praise of the people of righteousness and goodness, based on His saying: "And cause us to die with the righteous" (Al 'Imran 193).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 189–193 (part 1 of 5):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

His saying: ﴿To Allah﴾: the prepositional phrase is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), ﴿dominion﴾ is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and ﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾ is a resumptive independent clause (jumla isti'nafiyya).

His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾: the dominion of the heavens means dominion over the substances (mulk al-a'yan) and dominion of disposal (mulk al-tasarruf). He is the Owner of their substances and the Owner of the disposal of them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have therein any share [in creation], nor is there for Him from among them any supporter. And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba' 22–23]. ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight﴾ means by way of independent possession; ﴿nor do they have therein any share﴾ means by way of partnership; ﴿nor is there for Him﴾ means for Allah; ﴿from among them﴾ means from among these deities you invoke; ﴿any supporter﴾ means any helper; ﴿and intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ means no one intercedes with Allah except with His permission.

They say: this verse cut off the connections of the polytheists who worship idols and images, because He says: Do these idols have independent dominion in the heavens and the earth? Did they share with Allah? Did they help Him? Does their intercession benefit except with His permission? No. Every answer is negative, and accordingly they do not benefit them; the worship of these idols does not benefit them.

The point is that His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾ includes what? The substances and the disposal. So Allah the Exalted is the Owner of substances and the Owner of disposal. His saying: ﴿the heavens﴾ means the seven, and ﴿the earth﴾ is generic, so it includes the seven earths.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ Capability (qudra) is the ability to act without incapacity (ajz); the ability to act without weakness is called power (quwwa). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is He who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength﴾ [al-Rum 54], so He contrasted weakness with strength. And He said: ﴿And never could anything in the heavens or on the earth cause Him incapacity; indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44], so He contrasted capability with what?
* Student: With incapacity.
* The Shaykh: ﴿to cause Him incapacity﴾, with incapacity. So the opposite of capability is incapacity, and the opposite of strength is weakness.

His saying: ﴿over all things competent﴾ is general over everything. There is no existent thing except that Allah is able to annihilate it, no non-existent thing except that Allah is able to bring it into existence, and no existent thing except that Allah is able to change it and transform it from one state to another. So He is competent over all things, and He is capable of His acts, is He not? Yes, He is capable of His acts; He does what He wills. And is He capable of His own essence?
* Student: That is not relevant.
* The Shaykh: They say: if one supposes that the essence of Allah, mighty and majestic, could be annihilated, for example, far be it, this is not something capability relates to at all, because it is impossible. For this reason al-Saffarini, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his creed:

Life, speech, sight, hearing, will, knowledge, and power are His,
With a power that relates to the possible ...................

Nevertheless, we say: it is good manners to say that Allah is over all things competent and remain silent, because the verses that came with this are general. Do not say that Allah is not able to do the impossible, because the impossible in itself is not related to action. For example: can stillness and motion be combined? No, because if it moves it is not still, and if it is still it is not moving.

So Allah, glorified and exalted, is able to make the still moving and the moving still, but you want it to be still and moving at the same moment: this is impossible. Still means not moving, moving means not still.

If someone asks: can Allah make the moving still? Yes, He turns the moving into the still. Or make the still moving? Yes, but making motion and stillness at the same moment is impossible in itself, because as long as there is motion, that means what? It equals the absence of stillness; stillness equals the absence of motion. The moment it moves, stillness is negated from it; the moment it becomes still, motion is negated from it.

But as I told you: it is good manners to say that Allah is over all things competent, and there is no need to elaborate. We simply recognize within ourselves that the impossible is not possible, by its name: impossible.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, would it not be correct, for example, if it were said that the (al) in (al-Kitab) is generic, meaning revealed scriptures generally, including the Qur'an, and that the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿they threw it behind their backs﴾ is an explanation of some general expressions, and among them are the Jews and the Christians, since this is more general?
* The Shaykh: It is more general, without doubt. But even if we assume that the verbal generality does not include this nation in His saying: ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾, the meaning-based generality includes it. Otherwise the apparent sense of the wording is that the intended are the People of the Book, as He said at the beginning: ﴿and you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture﴾. But we say: although it does not include this nation verbally, it includes it in meaning.
* Student: In the saying of Allah the Exalted in the long hadith in Sahih Muslim: «Indeed I am over what I will competent» at the end of the hadith, and the last one to enter Paradise (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. When it is tied to a specific act, it is correct to restrict capability by will, because this man was surprised that he would enter Paradise after what had happened to him, so he said: «Indeed I am over what I will competent»[[Recorded by Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]. It is like His saying: ﴿and He is, when He wills, over their gathering competent﴾ [al-Shura 29], meaning if He wills to gather them, He is competent over them, and He is competent whether He wills or does not will. But when it is tied to a specific act, it is correct to restrict it by will.

A similar example in a human: you say, "I am competent over what I will." If someone asks, "Can you do such and such?" and he says, "Yes, what I want I am capable of," the meaning is not that he is only capable of what he wills; he is capable of what he wills and what he does not will. But because it relates to a specific act, it is correct to restrict it by will. It is as if he says: if I will this thing, then I am capable of it.
* Student: Many people of knowledge, or whoever has knowledge, when you ask him, "Why do you not (...) your knowledge and advise the people," he says: I have no knowledge (...). Is one threatened for the sake of Allah?
* The Shaykh: Yes, one is warned for the sake of Allah. It is said: you must spread it, and people need knowledge... Sometimes the circumstance calls for the need for knowledge, such as when an innovation spreads among people generally, and then you must clarify. And sometimes a person asks you a specific question, and you must clarify as well. This is why we say: a question by the tongue of speech and a question by the tongue of circumstance. A question by the tongue of speech is when a person comes to you and says, "What do you say about such and such?" This is a question by the tongue of speech; you must clarify the truth for him, unless you know that he is a follower of desires and only wants to take what you have without acting on it. In that case Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'ida 42], because they do not come to the Messenger seeking truth, but they want what he has: if it agrees with their desires they take it, and otherwise they leave it. As for the tongue of circumstance, it is when a forbidden act or innovation or the like spreads among people, so you clarify it to the people, because the circumstance calls for clarification.
* Student: ﴿Wretched is what they sell﴾ [Al 'Imran 187]. I say: is the (ma) in ﴿بِئْسَ مَا يَشْتَرُونَ﴾ negative, or... is it relative (mawsula) or...?
* The Shaykh: Descriptive (mawsufa)?
* The Student: Or verbal-source (masdariyya)?
* The Shaykh: It is permissible. No, it cannot be masdariyya; it is either relative (mawsula) or descriptive (mawsufa).
* The Student: If it were descriptive (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, restrictive.
* The Student: Restrictive by what?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, by the description (yashtarun).
* Student: May Allah reward you with good. Regarding the one who clarifies, we say: he clarifies in private and public gatherings and in writing, as much as he can. But if the man restricts himself to one type of them, for example he sits with certain persons and teaches them private lessons, is it said that this is discrimination?
* The Shaykh: Is it said? Yes, because it may be in the interest that you do not teach everything you know. It may be in the interest that you focus on jurisprudence, on monotheism, on exegesis, but you are prepared and ready to convey knowledge by any means.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you with good. Regarding the generality in His saying: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran 187], is it a general term that is specified at the time of the Prophet ﷺ? Because many of the People of the Book did not conceal.
* The Shaykh: How did they not conceal? Right now?
* The Student: No, since Musa and Isa, peace be upon them, were sent; there were rabbis and scholars among them who acted upon the Scripture.
* The Shaykh: This is considered rare, like 'Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good, and he was one of their rabbis. But this is considered rare; the consideration is the generality.
* Student: ﴿لَتُبَيِّنُنَّهُ﴾ — does the pronoun refer to the knowledge or to the Scripture?
* The Shaykh: Or to the covenant. The Scripture: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, [saying], "You must make it clear"﴾, meaning the Scripture.
* The Student: The Scripture?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: May Allah reward you with good. Regarding the generality in His saying: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran 187], is it a general term specified at the time of the Prophet ﷺ, because many did not conceal?
* The Shaykh: How did they not conceal?
* The Student: Many of the People of the Book.
* The Shaykh: Right now?
* The Student: No, since Musa and Isa, peace be upon them, were sent; there were rabbis and scholars among them who acted upon the Scripture.
* The Shaykh: This is considered rare; that is why, like 'Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good, and he was one of their rabbis. But this is considered rare; the consideration is the generality.
* Student: ﴿لَتُبَيِّنُنَّهُ﴾ — does the pronoun refer to the knowledge or to the Scripture?
* The Shaykh: Or to the covenant, the Scripture: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, [saying] "You must make it clear"﴾, meaning the Scripture.
* The Student: The Scripture?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding (190). Who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], "Our Lord, You did not create this aimlessly; exalted are You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire (191). Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced; and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers (192). Our Lord, indeed we have heard a caller calling to faith, 'Believe in your Lord,' so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds and cause us to die with the righteous (193). Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not fail in promise (194)﴾ [Al 'Imran 190–194].
* The Shaykh: Well done. I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding (190)﴾. His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾: it is not hidden that this sentence is emphasized. By what?
* Student: By the emphasis particle.
* The Shaykh: And what is the emphasis particle?
* Student: The emphasis particle (inna).
* The Shaykh: (inna).
And in it there is a difference in the order of the two parts, I mean the two parts of the subject and predicate. What is this difference?
* Student: Fronting of the predicate.
* The Shaykh: Fronting of the predicate: ﴿in the creation of the heavens﴾ is the predicate.
And is there in it another emphasis besides (inna)?
* Student: The lam in ﴿لَآيَاتٍ﴾.
* The Shaykh: The lam in ﴿لَآيَاتٍ﴾, yes.
Allah the Mighty and Majestic, emphasizing the content of this declarative sentence, says: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. ﴿Creation﴾ (khalq) is: innovation without a prior pattern; that is, bringing a thing into existence without a prior pattern is called khalq.
And in the creation of the heavens and the earth there are signs in several respects:
The first aspect: in terms of their greatness and vastness.
The second aspect: what is in them of beauty, splendor, and loveliness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk 5]. Whoever looks into what the scholars have depicted of these great signs will see the majesty of Allah the Mighty and Majestic in this creation.
Likewise, in the creation of the heavens in terms of their perfection and their lack of fissures. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So return your vision; do you see any flaw? (3) Then return your vision twice; your vision will return to you humbled while it is fatigued﴾ [al-Mulk 3–4].
In the creation of the heavens by what Allah placed in them of material: many materials of diverse kinds, forms, and benefits, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And in the earth are neighboring plots﴾ [al-Ra'd 4], meaning adjacent to one another, yet between them is a difference that none knows but Allah.
Also in them: the great benefits for creation. The sun has great good, and so does the moon, and trees and others; all of them contain great bounties, among the signs of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. You see palm trees on one land watered with one water, and Allah favors some over others in size, color, taste, and storage, though they are one kind but differ.
The signs in this are numerous. If a person sat reflecting, contemplating, and writing down everything that comes to his mind, he would gather many signs in this. We are commanded to reflect: ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves? Allah did not create the heavens and the earth ...﴾ [al-Rum 8]. We are commanded to reflect on the signs in the heavens and the earth, so that we may use them as evidence for the perfect power of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and for the great wisdoms and mercy in that.
His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾: this Qur'anic expression generally mentions the heavens in the plural and the earth in the singular. The Qur'an did not explicitly state the number of the earths, unlike the heavens, for which the number is explicitly stated as seven heavens, as Allah said: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ [al-Talaq 12], and He said: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Great Throne?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 86]. As for the earths, they were indicated as seven in His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾, meaning in number, not in manner or in essence. The Sunnah is also explicit on this in the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: «Whoever usurps a span of the earth, Allah will encircle him with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim (1610/137), the wording is his with the addition "unjustly", from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr.]].
His saying: ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾ also: in this there are signs, the alternation of night and day. That is, in what respect of alternation is meant? The answer: it is meant that they alternate in various ways.

First, from the standpoint that night is darkness and day is light, and this is among the signs of Allah. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "Have you considered? If Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then listen?" (71) Say: "Have you considered? If Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you a night in which you rest? Will you not then see?" (72) And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful." (73)﴾ [Al-Qasas 71–73]. This is a sign of Allah. ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ [Al-Isra 12].

Likewise, their alternation in length and shortness: sometimes the night lengthens, sometimes the day lengthens, and sometimes they are equal, and no one is able to do this; it is among the signs of Allah.

Even if all the people of the earth gathered to make part of the night enter the day, they could not do it, nor the reverse; this is among the signs of Allah.

Included in this is the alternation of night and day in heat and cold: sometimes one is hot and the other cold, and sometimes they are equal.

Also among this is their alternation in ease and hardship: sometimes days pass over you in ease, and sometimes days pass over you in hardship.

And among these signs is their alternation in honour and humiliation, and in victory and abandonment: at times certain peoples are given victory, and those same peoples are forsaken at another time, and so on.

So the night and the day contain signs in their alternation, in their very nature, and in what happens within them. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾ [Ali 'Imran 140]. If a person reflects, he will find more than what we have mentioned of the alternation of night and day.

As for His saying: ﴿Surely in them are signs for people of understanding﴾: "signs" (āyāt) is plural, because they are varied and numerous. But none understands them or takes them as signs except the people of understanding (ulū al-albāb). For this reason He said: ﴿signs for people of understanding﴾, meaning for the people of reason. Reason is called lubb (ʿaql, "reason") because it is the pure essence of a person, just as the lubb is the pure kernel of a seed, for example. A person is by his reason, not by his thinking. Reason is not intelligence, as many people may think; reason is soundness in conduct. The more sound a person's judgement and conduct, the more rational he is. Being more intelligent does not necessarily make one more rational. No, that cannot be, for some of the intelligent are the furthest of people from reason.

For this reason we may say of the arrogant leaders of disbelief, who are full of cleverness, that they are not rational, even if they are intelligent. Allah said to the Children of Israel: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves, while you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾ [Al-Baqara 44], although they had reason. The people of understanding are those who recognise in these four things the great signs: the creation of the heavens, the creation of the earth, the alternation of night, and the alternation of day.

Then Allah the Exalted described the qualities of these people, saying: ﴿who remember Allah﴾. This is an explanatory description; we may take it as explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān), and we may also take it as a clarifying description of their state. ﴿who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾, meaning: they remember Allah in every state.

﴿Standing (qiyāman)﴾, which is the highest state of the body, ﴿and sitting (quʿūdan)﴾, which is a level between standing and lying down, and the third: ﴿on their sides﴾. With what do they remember Allah? They remember Allah, glorified and exalted, by reflecting on these creatures; whenever they see something, they take it as evidence of the perfection of Allah's wisdom, power, and knowledge. This is remembrance. They remember Allah with their tongues: by tahlil, tasbih, takbir, reciting the Qur'an, and other things. They remember Allah with their limbs: by standing, sitting, bowing, and prostrating in prayer, by circumambulating the House, by standing at Muzdalifa, by standing at ʿArafa, by standing at Mina, and by stoning the pillars. Every act of worship performed for Allah the Exalted that is an action, what is it? It is remembrance of Allah, because you intend by it the Face of Allah, and by that you are remembering Him.

As for His saying: ﴿and on their sides﴾: they remember Allah on their sides with their hearts and their limbs, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to ʿImran ibn Husayn: "Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on your side."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (1117) from the hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn.]]

﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. ﴿They reflect﴾: tafakkur is the exercise of thought, meaning exercising the brain, as they say. They reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: For what purpose were they created? How were they created? How was the sky raised? How was the earth spread out? And so on. The point is that they engage their thoughts, then they reflect on whether these heavens and earth created themselves or were created. Through this reflection they conclude that the heavens and earth were created, because through reflection they perceive what others do not perceive.

As for His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾: this sentence is the content of an omitted statement. That is, they say: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain." That is, after they reflect on the creation of the heavens and earth, this blessed result arises for them: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾.

The word ﴿mā khalaqta﴾ here is negative, and ﴿bāṭilan﴾ (in vain) is a necessary circumstantial clause (ḥāl lāzima): if it were omitted the sentence would be corrupted. Accordingly it is necessary. The rule for a necessary circumstantial clause is that if it is omitted the sentence is corrupted. If ﴿bāṭilan﴾ were omitted, the wording would be: "Our Lord, You did not create this," while in fact He did create it. Many a circumstantial clause, whether a sentence or a single word in the accusative, becomes indispensable in the speech; this is called a necessary circumstantial clause.

As for His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾: meaning "O our Lord," so it is a vocative in the accusative, with the omitted vocative particle yā. ﴿Subḥānaka﴾ (Glory be to You): subḥān is a verbal noun in the accusative functioning as an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq), and its governing verb is omitted. The implied meaning is: "We glorify You with Your proper glorification," that is, we declare You far above what is unfitting for You. The root meaning of tasbīḥ is declaring transcendence and distancing from evil. From it comes the saying "Sabaḥa fulān," meaning he went far away, and "yasbaḥu" meaning he swims in water.

As for His saying: ﴿Subḥānaka﴾, it means: "Exaltation to You, that You would create these heavens and earth in vain." Allah has explained in another verse that whoever thinks Allah created something in vain has adopted the assumption of whom? The assumption of the disbelievers. What is the evidence? ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27]. For this reason He said: ﴿So protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ The fa' here is a conjunction indicating that the second sentence follows from the first.

And (qi): is an imperative verb formed of a single letter, because it is what? It is a defective verb whose initial letter is a weak letter (ḥarf ʿilla). A triliteral defective verb whose first radical is a weak letter, in the imperative or the jussive, is reduced to a single letter. So you say: (qi): derived from (waqā), (ʿi): from (waʿā), (di): from diyya (blood-money) from (waddā). It has many examples, which al-Khuḍarī (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned in his gloss on Ibn ʿAqil's commentary on the Alfiyya. This gloss, I mean al-Khuḍarī's gloss on Ibn ʿAqil's commentary, is among the best glosses written on the commentaries of Ibn Malik's Alfiyya, because he is later and gathered the opinions of those before him, and he has a good verification of some matters he clarifies. So I direct everyone who wants to read Ibn Malik's Alfiyya and Ibn ʿAqil's commentary to it, for this gloss is beneficial. He mentioned several examples of the triliteral verb beginning with a weak letter and ending with a weak letter, in which, I mean, what is deleted? Both weak letters.

The grammarians say: what begins with a weak letter is a mithāl (regular), what has a weak letter in the middle is ajwaf (hollow), and what ends with a weak letter is nāqiṣ (defective) or maqṣūr. Is that correct? Yes.

﴿Fa-qinā ʿadhāba al-nār﴾: (qinā) is derived from al-wiqāya (protection), meaning: "Protect us from the punishment of the Fire," by whatever You will: either by not entering it, meaning that we never enter it at all, or by bringing us out of it through intercession, because the believer who is a sinner deserves entry into the Fire for his sin, then afterwards is brought out of it, and Allah may pardon him, due to His saying: ﴿Surely Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [Al-Nisa 48].

Let us mention the benefits of these two verses:

* Among the benefits of the first verse: the encouragement to reflect upon the creation of the heavens.
* Student: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Ali 'Imran 189].
* Shaykh: Did we explain it?
* Student: We did not take the benefits.
* Shaykh: The benefits, the verse before these two.
* Among the benefits of His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: that the dominion of the heavens and the earth is exclusively Allah's, the glorified and exalted. Its basis is the fronting of the predicate, and the rule is that when something that should be delayed is placed first, that indicates restriction.
* Among its benefits: absolute dominion belongs to Allah alone, for He put the predicate first in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs dominion﴾. Our specifying the dominion as absolute removes the apparent contradiction between His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾, where dominion is restricted to Him alone, and His saying: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 6], and His saying: ﴿or what you possess the keys of, or your friend﴾ [Al-Nur 61]. The explanation is that dominion attributed to a creature is restricted dominion, not absolute dominion. The proof: if such a creature-owner wanted to dispose of his property contrary to what the Sharia has brought, he would be prevented from doing so and would not truly own it, whereas Allah, majestic and exalted, possesses a general and comprehensive dominion by which He is independent of anything else.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that it is not permissible for a person to dispose of his property except within the permission of the Lawgiver, because the fact that dominion belongs to Allah shows that our disposal of it is only by way of agency, restricted to what we have been permitted. For this reason, if you appoint someone as agent to sell a house, he does not have the right to rent it out, because he was appointed only to sell, and the owner who owns the house did not permit him to rent it, only to sell. So with respect to what our right hands possess, we do not own it with absolute ownership by which we dispose of it however we wish; rather our ownership of it is restricted ownership.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that what is common to all creation is not owned by anyone. Whatever Allah brought forth and is not the making of a human being is not owned by anyone, except one who has acquired it according to the texts of the Sharia. The explanation: Allah made the heavens and the earth His dominion. Since they belong to Him, you do not own any part of His earth except in the manner He has permitted.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of Allah's power, glorified and exalted, by His saying: ﴿and Allah is over all things capable﴾. When you recite this verse and apply it to what some people of falsehood raise as doubts about the Sharia, you will find rest. For example, some atheists who do not believe in the Last Day say: "How can a human being return to being a human after he was what? Dust." Our answer to this is easy: we say that this is from the power of Allah: ﴿and Allah is over all things capable﴾.
* Among its benefits: whoever believes in this, that is, that Allah is capable of all things, will have despair removed from him. How so? A person may be afflicted with an illness, for example, and despair of recovering after treatment. It is said to him: "Do not despair; Allah is capable of all things. And if Allah wills that the illness remain with you, it may be good for you, because you gain what? Reward from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through it: ‘No harm, nor fatigue, nor sorrow, nor hurt befalls a believer, not even a thorn that pricks him, but that Allah expiates some of his sins by it.’"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5641, 5642) and Muslim (2573/52) in similar wording, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]] That is, of his sins. So do not despair if an illness afflicts you whose removal is not expected, for example; do not despair, for Allah is capable of all things.
* Among its benefits: that what Allah has told about Himself, of matters which reason finds improbable, is true, because Allah is capable of all things. Is that clear, brothers? For example, if someone says: "How can He descend to the lowest heaven while He is upon the Throne?" we say to him: "Allah is capable of all things, and you have no right to oppose what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reported about his Lord in mutawatir hadiths by mere imagination."

Then He said: ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, to the end of the verse.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the encouragement to contemplate the creation of the heavens and the earth, because Allah mentioned that there are signs in them, and signs are indicators. The more the signs become clear, the stronger faith becomes.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: looking at the creation of the heavens and the earth in the aspects we mentioned in the commentary: in terms of their essences, their benefits, and the good and interests in them, so that no one goes on to claim that they were created in vain.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: an indication of the alternation of night and day, from ease to hardship and vice versa, from war to peace, from honour to humiliation, from poverty to wealth, and vice versa in these matters.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of people of understanding, because Allah made this alternation a sign for whom? For those of intellect. As for one who has no intellect, he does not benefit from these signs nor takes lessons from them; they pass by him as if they were natural phenomena with no connection to Allah's action. This, and we seek refuge in Allah, is from the sealing of hearts and blinding of sight, because this cosmos ordered in this wonderful system could never have come about except from a wise Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and it could never have come about from an agent in a manner of folly, never.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, manifested His signs to His creatures, although mere faith that Allah the Exalted is living and existing is sufficient. But the more the evidences and signs multiply, the more certain a matter becomes. The evidence for this is that Abraham said to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said: 'Do you not believe?' He said: 'Yes, but that my heart may be at rest.'﴾ [Al-Baqara 260]. A person may be a believer and have no difficulty with the matter, but he needs someone to reassure him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of intellect, and is it the intellect of rational discernment (ʿaql al-rushd) or the intellect of legal accountability (ʿaql al-taklīf)? It is the intellect of rational discernment, due to His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿surely in them are signs for people of understanding﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the more rational a person is, the more he knows Allah and His signs, due to His saying: ﴿surely in them are signs for people of understanding﴾. A ruling attached to a description holds with its existence and lapses with its absence. So if the people of intellect are those who benefit from these creatures and use them as evidence for the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, and for His attributes of perfection, then whoever has an animal-like intellect does not benefit from these signs, because he is not among the people of understanding.

If someone says: "Intellects are a gift from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, a gift. How then is a person blamed for lacking them or praised for having them?"

The answer: intellect, meaning the intellect of rational discernment, is of two kinds: instinctive intellect and acquired or earned intellect. Instinctive intellect does not require contemplation and reflection, whereas acquired intellect requires contemplation, consideration, and reflection, because the more a person reflects, the more his faith, certainty, and rational discernment increase.

Is it derived from the noble verse that the people of intellect are praised? Yes, because Allah made these signs beneficial to whom? To them, to the people of understanding. On this basis, you should devote your efforts to reflection grounded in reason, so that you have both instinctive intellect and acquired intellect.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾, to the end.

Student: Shaykh, the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and Allah is over all things capable﴾: some scholars restrict the power here to what is related to the possible. Is this possibility rational possibility or factual possibility?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 3, Verses 189–193 (Part 3 of 5)**

* The Shaykh: No. The rational (ʿaqlī) and the actual (wāqiʿī) differ. Something may be impossible to occur in fact because of existing obstacles, yet still be possible in the intellect (ʿaql).
* A student: The grammarians define the ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a state of the subject or object) as a supplementary element that ... (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. What is meant by the fuḍla (supplementary element) is that which the essential components (arkān) of the sentence can do without.
* The student: Each sentence according to its own type?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
* * *
* A student: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers. (192) Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous. (193) Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed You do not break the promise.﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 192–194].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, are signs for those of understanding.﴾ Where is the predicate (khabar) of "inna" in His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾?
* A student: ﴿signs﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿signs﴾. How can it be its predicate when it is in the kasra (genitive ending)?
* The student: ﴿signs﴾ is in the accusative after "inna", and its sign of accusative is the kasra, because it is a sound feminine plural.
* The Shaykh: Is that correct?
* A student: It is a postponed subject (mubtada' muakhkhar).
* The Shaykh: Glory be to Allah! ﴿Indeed, in the creation﴾ is a postponed subject in the accusative!
* Students: It is the subject of "inna" (ism inna).
* The Shaykh: How is it a postponed predicate?
* Students: It is the subject of "inna".
* The Shaykh: The subject of "inna", I am asking about the subject of "inna", where is it? He answered, so he answered.
* Students: It is the predicate of "inna".
* The Shaykh: How?
* Students: By the predicate, the predicate of "inna".
* The Shaykh: In any case, he answered correctly: ﴿signs﴾ is the subject of "inna".

His saying: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing and sitting﴾, what is the i'rab (grammatical position) of ﴿those who﴾?
* A student: ﴿those who﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān).
* The Shaykh: And it cannot be a descriptive adjective (ṣifa)?
* The student: It can be a descriptive adjective.
* The Shaykh: It can be a descriptive adjective.

His saying: ﴿standing﴾ is in the accusative because of what? In the accusative because of what?
* A student: Because of the waw (conjunction).
* The Shaykh: No, ﴿standing﴾ has no waw at all.
* A student: Because it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).
* The Shaykh: From what?
* The student: ﴿standing﴾, meaning: a state in which they are standing.
* The Shaykh: Where is the owner of the state (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl)? The ḥāl needs an owner.
* The student: ﴿they remember﴾, they.
* The Shaykh: Where is the owner of the state?
* The student: ﴿those who remember Allah﴾, meaning: they remember Allah, from ﴿those who﴾.
* The Shaykh: From ﴿those who﴾?
* A student: From the plural waw in ﴿they remember﴾.
* The Shaykh: From the plural waw in ﴿they remember﴾, correct.

His saying: ﴿and they reflect upon the creation of the heavens﴾, what is the i'rab position of the clause?
* A student: It is conjoined (maʿṭūfa).
* The Shaykh: Conjoined to what?
* The student: To ﴿they remember﴾.
* The Shaykh: What is its i'rab position?
* A student: If we say that ﴿those who﴾ is an adjective of ﴿creation﴾, we say it is in the genitive.
* The Shaykh: How is it in the genitive?
* The student: Meaning: what is conjoined to the genitive is genitive.
* The Shaykh: Where is the genitive? Did you not say it is conjoined to ﴿they remember﴾?
* The student: ﴿those who﴾, yes, yes. ﴿they remember﴾ is a ḥāl, so it is in the state position.
* The Shaykh: A ḥāl clause, accusative as a ḥāl.
* A student: It has no i'rab position; it is a relative clause (ṣilat al-mawṣūl).
* The Shaykh: Yes, this has no i'rab position, because it is conjoined to the relative clause, and the relative clause has no i'rab position.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾, what is its i'rab position?
* A student: It is in the accusative as the object of a saying (maqūl al-qawl).
* The Shaykh: The object of a deleted saying; they say: "Our Lord."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿for those of understanding (190). Those who remember Allah standing and sitting﴾.

* From the noble verse it is derived: that the remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is among the requirements and implications of reason, by His saying: ﴿for those of understanding (190). Those who remember Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: the virtue of persistent remembrance, remembering Allah the Mighty and Majestic in every state, by His saying: ﴿those who remember Allah standing and sitting﴾. The one who most fully fulfilled this right was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to remember Allah in all his times."[[Narrated by Muslim (373/117) from ʿĀʾisha.]]
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of remembering Allah for one in a state of janāba (major ritual impurity), meaning it is permissible for the one in janāba to remember Allah, because he is included in the generality of: ﴿they remember Allah standing and sitting and on their sides﴾.
* Among its benefits: that remembering Allah while a person is lying on his side is not considered disrespect toward the remembrance. Likewise reciting the Qur'an while lying on your side. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to recite the Qur'an reclining in the lap of ʿĀʾisha while she was menstruating, may Allah be pleased with her."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (297) and Muslim (301/15) from ʿĀʾisha.]]
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of reflecting upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, by His saying: ﴿and they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. But it is reflection accompanied by the saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾, not the reflection that aims only at acquiring material knowledge about the creation of the heavens. For that reflection, though it benefits a person in this world, does not benefit him in the Hereafter. This reflection must produce this statement and affirmation: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.﴾
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: if those who reflect upon creation are praised, then those who reflect upon the Sharia (sacred law) deserve it even more, because the Sharia is not something perceived by the senses. Reflection upon it is more powerful in faith than reflection upon creation. Creation is something perceptible that every person can grasp, but the wisdoms and secrets of the laws are not grasped by everyone.
* Among the benefits of this verse: seeking a means to Allah through His lordship (rubūbiyya) at the time of supplication. The most common way of seeking a means through the names of Allah in supplication is through His lordship, because lordship includes creation, sovereignty, and management. Therefore we find that most of what is supplicated with is lordship, either the name "Lord" or the attribute of lordship.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the negation of vanity in Allah's creation in an absolute sense. From where is this derived? ﴿You did not create this in vain.﴾ When vanity is absolutely negated, truth is established, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play (38). We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhān 38–39].
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of what the People of the Sunna affirmed, that among the attributes of Allah are those that are negated or are negative in form, by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.﴾ The principle among the People of the Sunna is that negated attributes are not intended as mere negation, but as negation together with affirmation of the perfect opposite, because the existence of the perfect opposite is what negates this attribute.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the acknowledgment by these rational people that Allah is the Creator: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.﴾ This is from the affirmation of which tawḥīd? The lordship (rubūbiyya) tawḥīd.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of wisdom in Allah's actions, by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾; for if He had created it in vain, wisdom would be negated. So when vanity is negated, wisdom is established. This is what the People of the Sunna and the Jamāʿa hold: that all of Allah's actions and laws are for a wisdom, and there is nothing in them that is purposeless in any way. What we do not know of their wisdom is due to the limitation of our understanding, not to the absence of wisdom in it. Do you understand this? Because Allah said: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 85]. We believe that Allah the Mighty and Majestic does not decree anything, neither by universal decree (kawnī) nor by predestined decree (qadarī), except for a wisdom.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exaltation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic above every defect and imperfection, derived from His saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾. What is exalted of Allah is two things: imperfection, and the second is what?
* A student: Defect.
* The Shaykh: Imperfection and defect; it is defect.
* A student: Resemblance to creatures.
* The Shaykh: Resemblance to creatures. Even in what is a perfection among creatures, Allah is exalted above resembling them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shūrā 11], and He the Exalted said: ﴿And no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qāf 38]. So every imperfection is one from which Allah is exalted.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the elite of creation are in need of supplicating for protection from the Fire, by their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of seeking a means in supplication through the attributes of Allah, from His saying: ﴿so protect us (faqinā)﴾. For they built ﴿faqinā﴾ upon their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, so protect us.﴾ Meaning: we seek a means to Allah the Mighty and Majestic through His exaltation above imperfection, that He protect us from the punishment of the Fire. Because we are believers who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, and who reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, and affirm that they were created with truth and for truth, and who exalt Allah the Mighty and Majestic above every imperfection and defect. And it follows from this that they made this a means for Allah's protection of them from the Fire: ﴿Glory be to You, so protect us.﴾ For it is well known in the Arabic language that the fāʾ (so) indicates what? That what follows it is a consequence of what precedes it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the Fire, which is the abode of criminals, sinners, wrongdoers, and disbelievers, by His saying: ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾

In the noble verse there are two words that may not be separated from each other. Where are they?
* A student: ﴿what You did not create this in vain﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿You did not create this in vain﴾. If you say: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this﴾ and stop, it gives a corrupt meaning. Therefore joining is obligatory: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.﴾ Like: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 43]. You must join it and say: ﴿do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. If you say only ﴿do not approach prayer﴾, the meaning is corrupted. And like: ﴿So woe to those who pray (4) who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Māʿūn 4–5]. You must join and say: ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾, because if you stopped, it would imply that the threat is for those who pray.

Did we parse ﴿in vain﴾ (bāṭilan)?
* A student: A ḥāl (circumstantial accusative).
* The Shaykh: A ḥāl from what?
* A student: From ﴿this﴾?
* The Shaykh: From what? From "dhā"? From "hādhā"?
* A student: From ﴿this﴾?
* The Shaykh: From (hādhā), ﴿this in vain﴾. It is also permissible for it to be an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: a vain creation. Yes indeed.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ This verse serves as a justification for the preceding supplication: ﴿protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, because whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced. ﴿Our Lord﴾ here is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been removed; the implied form is: O our Lord.

﴿Indeed You, whoever You admit to the Fire﴾: "inna" and its subject are in ﴿indeed You﴾, and the conditional clause ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ is in the nominative position as the predicate of "inna".

﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾: subject and predicate. The predicate is placed first and "helpers" is postponed; it is in the genitive by the extra preposition "min" ﴿from helpers﴾. The implied form: and there are no helpers for the wrongdoers. This is the i'rab of the verse.

These noble people say: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him.﴾ "Whoever" includes sinners and disbelievers. The sinners deserve entry into the Fire, and when they are admitted they are not wronged, since they deserve it. The disbelievers deserve it eternally and forever. Each of them, when admitted to the Fire, has been disgraced by Allah before all creation, meaning He has exposed and unveiled him.

His saying: ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, here the explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun, whereas the context would call for "and for them there are no helpers." It is stated explicitly in place of the pronoun for two benefits. The first: these people deserve this description, namely those who are admitted to the Fire deserve this description, i.e., being described as wrongdoers. The second: generality. Every wrongdoer, even if he is not admitted to the Fire, if Allah wills to punish him, he will find no one to help him.

There is also a third benefit in it: the affirmation of the cause for the ruling. If He had said, "and for them there are no helpers," it would not have been clear to us that the reason is that they wronged themselves. By describing them this way, He has stated the ruling together with its cause.

His saying: ﴿from helpers﴾ means: from assistants, because the helper (nāṣir) means the one who aids. Whether the aid is in repelling them or in rescuing them, no one will help them when they are admitted, to prevent it, nor will anyone help them when they fall into it, to bring them out. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqara 255].

* From the benefits of this noble verse, first: the understanding of these noble people of understanding, in that they stated the reason for their supplication that Allah protect them from the Fire, and that the reason is that the Fire is the abode of disgrace, may Allah protect us: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him.﴾
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the Fire, by His saying: ﴿whoever You admit to the Fire﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the wrongdoer has no helper, and this is in the Hereafter. As for this world, the wrongdoer may be helped, but the wheel of fortune turns against him. But in the Hereafter no one helps him.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that wrongdoing is a cause of entering the Fire, by His saying: ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ after their saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him.﴾

Then He said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed﴾, and so on to its end.

About ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard﴾ we say the same as we said about ﴿Our Lord, indeed You, whoever You admit to the Fire﴾ or ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾: it is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been removed.

﴿Indeed we heard a caller calling to faith﴾: they heard a caller calling to faith. The clause ﴿calling to faith﴾ is an adjective of ﴿a caller﴾, but its benefit is that it states what he calls to, since a caller may call to various things. So it clarifies what he calls to. It is therefore an adjective of ﴿a caller﴾.

His saying: ﴿that believe in your Lord﴾: "that" here is explanatory (tafsīriyya), because it comes after a clause that contains the meaning of speech without its letters. Every "that" that follows a clause containing the meaning of saying without its letters is called explanatory, meaning "namely." From it is His saying: ﴿So We revealed to him, "Construct the ship"﴾ [al-Mu'minūn 27], meaning: namely, construct the ship. So "that" here is explanatory.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, so forgive us﴾: the fā' here is conjunctive but indicates causation, because it conjoins one clause to another. His saying: ﴿our misdeeds﴾ is in the genitive ending (kasra) even though it is an object, because it is a sound feminine plural.

His saying: ﴿with the righteous﴾ is an adverb (ẓarf). Here the intended "with" is the "with" of rank and standing, not the temporal "with", because the deaths of the righteous differ.

They say: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling﴾. They said this as an expression of gratitude for the blessing of Allah in sending this caller. Their saying: ﴿we heard a caller calling to faith﴾: this caller originally means the one who calls out (muṣawwit), the literal meaning being "the one who calls out," because calling (nidāʾ) is raising the voice. But what is meant is Muhammad (ﷺ). Their hearing of him occurs in two ways: first, that they hear his voice directly without an intermediary; second, that they hear from others what he brought, hearing it from his heirs, who are the scholars. All of this is included in the verse: the direct hearing, which they heard from his voice, and the indirect hearing, which they heard through an intermediary from his heirs, who are the scholars.

The Lord, who knows what the commentary's wording means,

Ibn 'Uthaymin, *Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim*, on Surah 3, verses 189–193 (Part 4 of 5):

And His saying: ﴿calling to faith﴾. Someone might say: the expected phrasing would be "ila al-iman" (to faith), that is, "yunadi ilayhi" (calls to it). But He used *al-lam* (li-, "for"), because *al-lam* is more connected than *ila* (to). *Ila* indicates a limit (ghayah), and a limit must have something it limits (mughayya), and that which is limited is an endpoint, which implies distance. As for ﴿li-l-iman﴾, the *lam* indicates attachment (al-ilsaq), and it is more attached than *ila*.

And His saying: ﴿for faith, that believe in your Lord﴾. This explains the faith to which the Messenger ﷺ called. ﴿That believe in your Lord, so we believed﴾. Faith in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is: affirmation that includes acceptance and submission (al-idhan). It is not merely verbal affirmation. If faith were mere affirmation, Abu Talib would have been a believer, because he affirmed the Prophet's message. But it is not faith until it includes what? Acceptance and submission, meaning compliance (al-inqiyad). As for one who does not accept, or accepts but does not submit, he is not a believer.

And His saying here: ﴿that believe in your Lord﴾. Someone might say: Is faith limited to one pillar, which is faith in Allah? The answer: whoever believes in Allah believes in everything Allah has informed of, and among that are the rest of the six fundamentals: the angels of Allah, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree (al-qadar), both its good and its evil. Thus, faith in Allah includes faith in the rest of the pillars of faith. Sometimes mentioning them individually is for the sake of detail and clarification, not for specification, because faith in Allah includes all of this. ﴿That believe in your Lord, so we believed﴾ means: we affirmed that, with compliance, with acceptance and submission.

﴿Our Lord, so forgive us﴾, that is: by virtue of our faith, forgive us our sins. Forgiveness (al-maghfirah) is the covering of a sin and overlooking it. We say it is covering and overlooking because it is derived from *al-maghfar*, which is the iron helmet worn on the head that protects against arrows. It is known that this helmet provides both covering and protection. So whoever among the scholars says forgiveness is merely covering has an incomplete definition. Rather, it must be said: covering together with protection.

And His saying: ﴿so forgive us our sins﴾. The *dhunub* (sins) are the acts of disobedience. Their root meaning is "share" (nasib), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, for those who wronged there is a share (dhanub) like the share of their companions﴾ [al-Dhariyat 59], meaning a share like the share of their companions. But the term was specialized for the share of sins, and we seek refuge in Allah.

And His saying: ﴿and remove from us our misdeeds﴾. For the misdeeds (sayyi'at), they asked for their expiation (takfir), and for the sins (dhunub) they asked for their forgiveness, because the misdeeds are the minor sins, and they are expiated by what? By righteous deeds, by acts of obedience. Expiation by acts of obedience cannot happen unless the acts of obedience are performed in the most complete manner, because if acts of obedience are deficient, they are not strong enough to expiate misdeeds. A person may perform an act of obedience and gain from it only the discharge of his obligation, but it is not strong enough to expiate sins unless it is complete to the extent possible. For this reason they said: ﴿expiate from us our misdeeds﴾, through what we do of righteous deeds.

Then know that the expiation of misdeeds may be specified by the Law (al-shar'), that is, what expiates may be specified by the Law, such as: the expiation of *zihar* (a form of divorce by comparison), the expiation of homicide, and the expiation of intercourse during the day in Ramadan. This is restricted by the Law. It may also be general, such as the general expiation of misdeeds through prayer, through ablution, through Friday to Friday, through Ramadan to Ramadan, and through 'umrah to 'umrah. Thus, expiation is either restricted or general and unrestricted.

﴿And cause us to die among the righteous﴾. ﴿Cause us to die (tawaffana)﴾ means: take us to You. *Tawfiyah* means seizure (al-qabd), and from it comes the saying: "So-and-so took his right in full (tawaffa haqqahu)," meaning he seized it in full.

And their saying: ﴿among the righteous﴾. The "with" (ma'iyyah) here is not temporal togetherness, because it is impossible for the deaths of the righteous to coincide in one moment. Rather, it is a judicial togetherness (ma'iyyah hukmiyyah), a companionship in ruling, meaning that we be among them, in their group, even if we are after them. It is not "with" in the sense of simultaneous companionship, because the times differ between the deaths of the righteous, some after others.

*Al-abrar* is the plural of *barr*, and *barr* means one who has abundant good. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Barr﴾ [al-Tur 28]. Those of truth and righteous deeds are without doubt abundant in doing good, and they are *abrar*.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person should acknowledge Allah's blessing upon him without boasting of it before his Lord. This is from their saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith: that believe in your Lord, so we believed﴾.

* Among its benefits: the call of the Prophet ﷺ is a call to faith: ﴿calling to faith﴾.

* Among its benefits: the clarification that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ exerted effort in calling people to the truth, because calling (nida') is by raising the voice. It is as if the Messenger ﷺ were calling people with his loudest voice to faith.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: some statements may be understood by their content without detailing them. This is from His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed﴾, meaning in everything that must be believed. Everything Allah has informed of, when we affirm and acknowledge it, is included in faith in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of stating the reason, from His saying: ﴿that believe in your Lord﴾. The Lord is deserving that a person believe in Him, because He is Lord, Creator, Owner, and Governor, so the servant is worthy to believe in Him.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a person's mention of his righteous deed does not nullify it. If he says: "My Lord commanded me to pray, so I prayed," or "to pay zakah, so I paid it," or "to perform Hajj, so I performed it," this does not invalidate the deed, because they said: ﴿that believe in your Lord﴾, so what? ﴿so we believed﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of seeking a means (tawassul) in supplication through righteous deeds. This is from their saying: ﴿so forgive us our sins﴾, following their saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed﴾. Seeking a means through righteous deeds is also established in the Sunnah, in the story of the three men whom a cave closed upon with a great rock they could not move. Some of them said to others: "Nothing will save you from this except that you seek a means to Allah through your best deeds." So each of them sought a means through his best deed. When the first supplicated and sought a means through his best deed, the rock opened slightly. Then the second, a little more, but they still could not come out. Then the third, and it opened completely, and they came out walking.[[Agreed upon (Bukhari, 2272; Muslim, 2743/99), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and it is narrated here by meaning.]]
