So one of them sought a means through his complete kindness to his parents, the second through his complete chastity, and the third through his complete trustworthiness, and Allah relieved them (agreed upon; al-Bukhari, 2272, and Muslim, 2743/99, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar). Is it clear, brothers?

If someone says: "Seeking a means through this and what came before it is problematic, because someone may say: Is this not presumption upon Allah, and self-admiration and pride in the deed? It is as if he says: O Lord, I did such and such, and I did such and such, so forgive me, for example."

The answer is: No. Rather, this is from the aspect of humility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is from the aspect of humbling oneself before Him, and that I, O Lord, have humbled myself to You, and I know that You are the refuge, so I worshipped You and believed in You, and I ask You to forgive me, for example.

Sixth, seeking a means to Allah by mentioning the condition of the one supplicating. This is seeking a means to Allah by mentioning one's state, so that you mention your condition and say: "O Allah, I have wronged myself, so forgive me." The first was a *tawassul* through a righteous deed, whereas here it is the opposite, through one's condition. Among this is the saying of Musa: "My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me" (Al-Qasas 24). He mentioned nothing but this. This is a *tawassul* to Allah by what? By mentioning one's condition. Because when a person mentions his state, and that he is in need of Allah, this compels him to turn to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is one of the causes of the answering of supplication.

Seventh, seeking a means to Allah, exalted is He, through the supplication of a righteous man. Among this is the saying of 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan to the Prophet (ﷺ), when he said: "Indeed, among my nation seventy thousand will enter Paradise without reckoning and without punishment." He said: "Supplicate to Allah that He makes me one of them." He said: "You are among them" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari, 5752, and Muslim, 220/374, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas). Among this is the saying of a Bedouin: "O Messenger of Allah, wealth has perished and the roads have been cut off, so supplicate to Allah that He gives us relief." So he supplicated (agreed upon; al-Bukhari, 1013, and Muslim, 897/8, from the hadith of Anas). Among this is the saying of 'Umar to al-'Abbas: "Stand and supplicate to Allah." So he said: "O Allah, we seek a means to You through our Prophet, and You gave us rain, and we seek a means to You through the paternal uncle of our Prophet" (recorded by al-Bukhari, 1010, from the hadith of Anas).

The student should note, regarding this seventh type, what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed out: when you ask someone to supplicate for you, you intend by this the benefit of the one supplicating and his reward, because the one who supplicates is rewarded when he supplicates for his brother. He said this to guard against the case where the seeker wants only to benefit himself. He said: "This is the reprehensible request, that you say: 'Supplicate to Allah for me,' intending only the benefit of yourself. No, say: 'Supplicate to Allah for me,' and you intend that he also benefits from his supplication for you, because he is rewarded for his kindness to you, and because when he supplicates for you in your absence, the angel says: 'Amin, and for you the same,' or: 'And for you the like of it.'" This is when you want to ask a specific person to supplicate for you personally. But if you ask him to supplicate for the Muslims in general, this is not the reprehensible request, even if you do not consider his benefit. The parallel is that if you asked a man for a dirham for yourself, or said: "Give me a dirham for so-and-so the poor man," the first would be the reprehensible request, and the second would be a kindness to both the giver and the one given to, because you benefit the giver in the Hereafter and benefit the recipient in this world.

These, then, are seven types of *tawassul*, all of which the Sunnah has brought, and they are permissible, because each is in reality a cause among the causes. The word *wasīlah* (means) is in origin similar to *wasīlah* (a connection), and the letters *sīn* and *ṣād* alternate often, as in the saying: "Guide us to the straight path" (*ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*) and "guide us to the straight path" (*ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*) (Al-Fatihah 6). Both are recognized Sab'ī recitations.

So from this verse, "Our Lord, so forgive us," we take the permissibility of seeking a means through what? Through faith. And we digressed into mentioning the categories of *tawassul*.

Is the polytheism of the polytheists with their gods a form of prohibited *tawassul*, or what?

* **Student:** Something else.
* **Shaykh:** Something else. Yes, it is not *tawassul* but worship, because they say: "We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to Allah" (Az-Zumar 3). They intend worship. They call upon these idols, bow to them, prostrate to them, make vows to them, and slaughter for them. So it is not from the aspect of *tawassul* but from the aspect of intention and purpose, that these idols are worshipped.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: every person is in need of the forgiveness of sins, based on their saying: "So forgive us our sins" (Al 'Imran 193). So do not be deceived by the abundance of acts of obedience. The more a person's acts of obedience increase, the more he should fear for himself that these acts may be rejected and his deeds go to waste.

* From the benefits of this verse: the distinction among sins, that some are sins (*dhunūb*) and some are misdeeds (*sayyi'āt*). This is like our saying that they are divided into major and minor sins, and that major and minor sins differ in their essence and differ among themselves. Major sins include greater and lesser ones, and minor sins include some that approach major sins and some that are below that.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of asking for death in the manner of people of goodness, based on their saying: "And cause us to die with the righteous" (Al 'Imran 193). We mentioned in the previous lesson that this is not a supplication for a hastened death, but a supplication for death in a desired state, namely that one dies in the condition in which the righteous died. We mentioned parallels to this. Who recalls them?

* **Student:** The saying of Maryam: "Would that I had died before this and become a thing forgotten and out of mind" (Maryam 23).
* **Shaykh:** The saying of Maryam: "Would that I had died before this and become a thing forgotten." The meaning is: "Would that I had died before the calamity."
* **Student:** And the saying of Yusuf: "Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous" (Yusuf 101).
* **Shaykh:** Excellent.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the praise of the people of righteousness and goodness, based on His saying: "And cause us to die with the righteous" (Al 'Imran 193).

Then He said: ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ [Al 'Imran 194] Notice the repetition in His words ﴿Our Lord﴾, because they take delight in this expression, that Allah is their Lord. And if Allah is their Lord, then they are His servants, and a person's delight in his servanthood to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is evidence of the perfection of his faith; for the more humble a person is before Allah, the more perfect his faith. This is why they repeat: "Our Lord, our Lord," taking delight in this noble name.

As for His words ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us﴾, (ātinā) means (aʿṭinā, "give us"), unlike (ītinā), which means (jiʾnā, "come to us"). (ātā) means (aʿṭā, "to give"), and (atā) means (jāʾ, "to come"). What is the verbal noun of ātā? (ītāʾ). Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and giving to the kinsman﴾ [An-Nahl 90]. And the verbal noun of atā is (itiyān).

He says: ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. ﴿mā﴾ here is a relative pronoun, and its place in i'rab is a second object of (ātinā), because (ātā) takes two objects. What are their origins?

* A student: They belong to the sisters of (aʿṭā, "to give").

* The Shaykh: They belong to the sisters of (aʿṭā). That is, their origin is not a subject and predicate. The verb that takes two objects, if its two objects originally formed a subject and predicate, then it belongs to the sisters of (ẓanna, "to think"); if they did not originally form a subject and predicate, then they belong to the sisters of (aʿṭā) and (kasā, "to clothe"). This one belongs to the sisters of (aʿṭā) and (kasā).

﴿what You promised us through Your messengers﴾: ﴿mā waʿadtanā﴾ means what You enjoined upon us of the great reward for our deeds. His words ﴿through Your messengers﴾ may carry two meanings: first, upon belief in Your messengers; second, through the hands of Your messengers. He expressed "the hands of the messengers" by "the messengers," because the ones who made the promise were the messengers themselves. They promised the believers what Allah promised them, and they warned the opponents with what Allah threatened them with.

﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾: ﴿tukhzinā﴾ means You expose us and humiliate us. ﴿The Day of Resurrection﴾ means the day when people rise from their graves for Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. This day was named the Day of Resurrection for three reasons:

First: people rise on it from their graves for Allah.

Second: justice is established on it.

Third: the witnesses stand on it.

His words ﴿Indeed, You do not break the promise﴾ are the justification for their request; that is, "We ask You, our Lord, to give us this, because You do not break the promise," meaning the promise. The breaking of a promise is negated from Him only because of the perfection of His truthfulness and the perfection of His power. Pay attention: the breaking of a promise is negated from Him because of the perfection of His truthfulness and the perfection of His power, since breaking a promise happens either because the promiser lies, as with the promises of the hypocrites, or because the promiser is incapable, that is, he would fulfill it but is unable. Both of these are negated in regard to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He: I mean lying and incapacity. So, because of the perfection of His truthfulness and the perfection of His power, He does not break the promise. And this attribute is among the attributes of what? Negative. A negative attribute means an attribute expressed by negation.

We have established more than once that negative attributes are meant to convey two things: first, the negation of the attribute that is denied; second, the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite. That is, this is negated because of the perfection of its opposite. So when you say, "So-and-so does not lie," the meaning is that he is perfectly truthful, and no lie is found in his speech. For this reason we say that the attributes negated of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, are not meant as mere negation, but are meant to affirm the perfection of the opposite.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one who supplicates should frequently praise Allah, Exalted is He, by His names and attributes, because this is among the means of having supplication answered.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the perfection of these people's faith in Allah's promise, as shown by their saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us﴾, for if they had doubt they would not have made this request.

* Among its benefits: the messengers are the intermediaries between Allah and His creation, as shown by His words ﴿through Your messengers﴾. There is no doubt that the messengers are the intermediaries between Allah and the creation. And among Allah's wisdom is that He made them human, because harmony between them and mankind would not be possible if they were not of their kind. This is why Allah, Exalted is He, said in response to the disbelievers who said, "If Muhammad were an angel, we would believe in him": ﴿They say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not be reprieved. And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [Al-An'am 8-9]. In that case the problem returns to their own claim: ﴿and We would have confused them about what they confuse.﴾

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation that the creation has more than one messenger, ﴿through Your messengers﴾, since rusul is the plural of rasul. This is a known matter, known with certain conviction, for the Qur'an is entirely filled with the stories of the prophets.

If someone says: The plural has been used to mean the singular, as in His words: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 105], while it is known that the people of Noah denied only Noah?

The answer to this: we say that this verse indicates how many people were sent to? One. But since denying one messenger is denying all the messengers, He said ﴿the people of Noah denied the messengers﴾, because the intent is denial of the category, not of the individual. It is as if they denied the very category of messengership, saying that it is impossible for Allah to send messengers, just as He, Exalted is He, stated in describing the nations' denial, that they say to their messengers: ﴿You are only human like us﴾ [Ya-Sin 15].

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: these righteous people believe in the Day of Resurrection and in the humiliation and disgrace that people will suffer on it, as shown by His words ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

* Among its benefits: fear of Allah's punishment does not contradict righteousness, as shown by their saying ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Indeed, fear of Allah's punishment increases righteousness, because it increases one's belief in what Allah has informed of.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's truthfulness and power, which is derived from His words ﴿Indeed, You do not break the promise.﴾

* Among its benefits: that Allah, Exalted is He, never breaks His promise.

If someone says: This is contradicted by His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa' 48]; and Allah, Exalted is He, has threatened sinners with the sins they deserve, such as: "The one who engages in slander (qattat) will not enter Paradise" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6056) and Muslim (105/169), from the hadith of Hudhayfah], i.e., one who carries tales (nammam).

The answer: whenever we say that this negation is meant to show the perfection of Allah's truthfulness and power, then His pardoning of one who deserved punishment is not considered a breaking of the promise; that is, He is able, but this is perfection upon perfection, for pardoning instead of avenging while having the power is perfection. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿If you disclose a good deed or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent﴾ [An-Nisa' 149].

Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on Sūrah 3, verse 195 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I do not let the work of any worker among you be lost, whether male or female; you are of one another"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:195], "and so on to the end." *Istajāba* means *ajāba* (responded), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who responded to their Lord and established prayer﴾ [al-Shūrā 42:38]. So it means "response," that is, Allah responded to them. And His saying ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾: consider this gentleness toward them. He did not say "So Allah responded to them" but "their Lord responded to them," because they used to call upon "our Lord." That is, this Lord whom they had continually called upon has responded to them.

﴿Indeed, I do not let the work of any worker among you be lost, whether male or female﴾. ﴿I do not let [it] be lost﴾ means I do not waste it or let it escape. ﴿the work of any worker among you, whether male or female, you are of one another﴾, rather I repay each worker what he deserves. And His saying ﴿whether male or female﴾ is an explanation of the general term. For this reason we say: what is the meaning of *min* (مِن) here?

* The students: It is explanatory (*bayāniyyah*).
* The Shaykh: That *min* is explanatory.

And His saying ﴿you are of one another﴾ means: you are of one another in deeds and reward. You are one kind; what is established for the male is established for the female, and what is established for the female is established for the male. Reflect on how He said here ﴿you are of one another﴾ and said in Sūrat al-Tawbah: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are protectors of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:71]. This is because the meaning of that verse concerns support: every believer is a guardian and supporter of his brother. And in contrast to it He said about the hypocrites: ﴿The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:67], and they are not protectors of one another, because they, meaning the hypocrites, do not take one another as allies, unlike the believers.

* A student: Shaykh, (...).
* The Shaykh: Is it five times, this? In any case, Allah the Mighty and Majestic may respond even with less than this.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. I say: this... it may be answered with less than this. He may say "Our Lord, our Lord," but it requires reflection on the reality.
* The student: May Allah be good to you. Is a threat (*wa'īd*) ever broken?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: Is a threat ever broken?
* The Shaykh: Is it broken? Yes indeed, this is what gets broken; but a promise (*waʿd*) is not broken.
* A student: But, may Allah be good to you, the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic in Sūrat Qāf: ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants﴾ [Qāf 50:29], after He promised them the Fire and threatened them?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, because these people deserve the Fire for their disbelief, and the disbeliever does not have Allah break His threat against him.
* The student: Yes, so the disobedient person has his threat broken?
* The Shaykh: The disobedient person has it broken out of generosity.
* The student: But what is the evidence for the distinction, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: It is clear: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:48].
* A student: Shaykh, if seeking intercession (*tawassul*) through righteous deeds of people is permissible, for example regarding the people of the rock [the cave story], and seeking intercession through the supplication of a righteous servant.
* The Shaykh: Through the supplication of a righteous man.
* The student: This is permissible. For example, if I say to a man: "If you seek intercession through righteous deeds on behalf of the dead, this is impermissible," he says: "These dead (...)?"
* The Shaykh: Do the dead supplicate?
* The student: No, he says: "O Allah, forgive us through the righteous deeds of this servant."
* The Shaykh: He is seeking nearness to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, through his own righteous deed, the deed of the one making supplication, not of the one for whom supplication is made.
* The student: How?
* The Shaykh: If he sought intercession through the righteous deed of the one for whom he is supplicating, it would not be valid.
* The student: (...) is permissible.
* The Shaykh: That is, if you say, for example, at (...): "O Allah, this is Your servant, the son of Your servant, the son of Your handmaid, who has performed Your command, enjoined what is good and forbade what is evil, so forgive him," there is no harm in this. But if I say: "This is Your servant, the son of Your servant, the son of Your handmaid, who has performed obedience to You, enjoined good and forbade evil, so forgive me," making his righteous deed a means to Allah's forgiveness of the dead person, that is, of the one supplicating, would that be valid?
* The student: I understand; this is not valid.
* The Shaykh: This is not valid.
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, if I ask a person to supplicate for a specific group, such as saying: "Pray for the scholars, or for the students of knowledge," would this be among the disliked requests?
* The Shaykh: No, there is no harm in this, just as we say: "Give charity to the scholars or to students of knowledge" or the like.
* A student: Shaykh, the natural means (*al-wasāʾil al-kawniyyah*), what is the criterion?
* The Shaykh: The same thing. The natural means are what has been established by the Sharīʿah or by experience as a means by which one may seek intercession. For example, healing with honey: is it a means or not a means? It is a legislated means. And healing with black seed (*al-ḥabbah al-sawdāʾ*)? A legislated means. And healing with medicines that we test, which the Sharīʿah has not specified but which we know have benefited, this falls under seeking intercession through natural matters.
* A student: Does the *sīn* in ﴿fa-istajāba﴾ indicate a request?
* The Shaykh: No. Sometimes it indicates a request and sometimes it does not, depending on the context. Just as *istaghfara* (to seek forgiveness) indicates a request, *istakbara* (to be arrogant) does not indicate a request; *istakbara* does not mean "he sought arrogance."
* A student: Seeking intercession through the rank (*jāh*) of the Messenger, meaning that one believes in the rank and station of the Messenger; is this correct?
* The Shaykh: Why did he not say: "O Allah, I ask You by my faith in the station of Your Prophet with You"?
* The student: For brevity.
* The Shaykh: One should not be brief here, because it causes confusion. But most of those who seek intercession through rank, you find that they do not mean what you said. They mean the rank of the Messenger; they think that since he has rank, he will intercede for you. Just as you say: "This man has rank with the king, I seek intercession through him; I go to him and say: 'O so-and-so, you have rank with the king, I want such-and-such from you.'"
* A student: If his intention is, that is, belief in the rank of the Prophet, is this correct?
* The Shaykh: We say: if that is the intention, then between you and your Lord it is correct, but do not display it to people, because people do not understand this matter.
* A student: Shaykh, the hadith of ʿUmar and his seeking intercession through al-ʿAbbās. Someone might say: what is the reason that ʿUmar sought intercession through the supplication of al-ʿAbbās, even though ʿUmar is better than al-ʿAbbās?
* The Shaykh: What is the answer? He said: because he is the uncle of our Prophet. Clarify.
* A student: Shaykh, do not righteous deeds fall under the designation of faith (*īmān*)?
* The Shaykh: Indeed, they fall under the designation of faith; but in detail, faith is in the heart and righteous deeds are by the limbs.
* A student: Shaykh, what is the distinction between seeking intercession through faith and seeking intercession through righteous deeds?
* The Shaykh: And through righteous deeds; because the companions of the cave did not seek intercession through faith; they sought intercession through righteous deeds.
* A student: Seeking intercession through Allah's blessing upon a person (...), by what You have blessed me with.
* The Shaykh: That is not one of Allah's acts, no.
* A student: I think, may Allah pardon you, many people (...) the Messenger ﷺ said (...), and Abū Bakr was present, and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him and content him, did not supplicate against the Messenger ﷺ (...).
* The Shaykh: What? ʿUmar what?
* A student: ʿUmar did not supplicate to the Messenger ﷺ; he did not say: "O Messenger of Allah (...)."
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is known: if anyone says "O Messenger of Allah, help us," that is disbelief (*kufr*), this one.
* * *
* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I do not let the work of any worker among you be lost, whether male or female; you are of one another. Those who emigrated, and were expelled from their homes, and were harmed in My cause, and fought, and were killed, I will surely remove from them their misdeeds and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah; and Allah has with Him the best reward." (195) Let not the movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you. (196) A little enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place. (197) But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, as a provision from Allah; and what is with Allah is best for the righteous. (198)﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:195–198].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Tabāraka wa Taʿālā said: ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾. I think what preceded does not need repetition. Let us discuss His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿give us﴾ (*ātinā*)?
* A student: ﴿ātinā﴾, give us.
* The Shaykh: And *atina*?
* A student: Come to us.
* The Shaykh: Come to us. The verb *ātā*: they say it takes two objects?
* A student: In this verse?
* The Shaykh: Yes. In this verse and other verses it takes two objects. In this verse, what are they?
* The student: The relative *mā*.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And which of the two objects is this?
* A student: The first object.
* The Shaykh: Yes, and the second?
* The student: (...) omitted.
* The Shaykh: The second is omitted?
* A student: The first object is (*nā*) in (*ātinā*).
* The Shaykh: The first object is (*nā*) from His saying (*ātinā*). And the second?
* The student: The relative noun.
* The Shaykh: The relative *mā*. Correct. Do these two objects originally form a subject and predicate?
* A student: They do not originally form a subject and predicate.
* The Shaykh: Good. Then when do they originally form a subject and predicate?
* A student: Before the entry of (...).
* The Shaykh: Before the entry, before the entry of the governing word (*ʿāmil*), is that right?
* A student: The governing word?
* The Shaykh: The governing word that takes the accusative.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is it that takes two objects which originally form a subject and predicate?
* The student: *Ẓanna* (to think).
* The Shaykh: Yes, *ẓanna* and its sisters. Correct.

His Exalted saying: ﴿upon Your messengers﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿upon Your messengers﴾?
* A student: That is, through their tongues.
* The Shaykh: Through the tongues of the messengers and the hands of the messengers. What is it that He promised them through His messengers?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: To whom? His Exalted saying: ﴿and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾. What is the meaning of *khizy* (disgrace)?
* A student: *Khizy* means that He does not disgrace them.
* The Shaykh: That is, when it is said "Allah disgraced him," what does it mean?
* The student: That is, He turned him back from what he did.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: Shaykh, He exposed him.
* The Shaykh: He exposed him and humiliated him; *khizy* is exposure and humiliation.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, You do not break the promise﴾. Is this among the attributes?
* A student: The negative attribute; it requires...
* The Shaykh: Yes. Does it include?
* The student: It includes two things: first, the negation of breaking the promise from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and second, the perfection of the opposite.
* The Shaykh: What is the opposite?
* The student: Truthfulness and fulfilling the promise.
* The Shaykh: The perfection of truthfulness, and what else?
* A student: Power.
* The Shaykh: Power, correct. The perfection of truthfulness and power. Why did we say it includes the perfection of truthfulness and power?
* A student: Because the truthful... the liar (...), and also the one who is not able cannot fulfill what he promised.
* The Shaykh: Good.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I do not let [the work of any worker among you] be lost"﴾. *Istajāba* means *ajāba* (responded), like His saying: ﴿And those who responded to their Lord and established prayer﴾, that is, they responded to Him. And His saying ﴿their Lord﴾, and He did not say "Allah," because the context here calls for lordship (*rubūbiyyah*), and here it is a specific lordship; because Allah's lordship is divided into two kinds: general and specific. Both kinds are combined in His saying: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Mūsā and Hārūn"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:121–122]. The requirement of general lordship is absolute disposal, and the requirement of specific lordship is support, assistance, kindness, and other things that entail special care. Here, the lordship is of which of the two kinds?
* Students: The specific.
* The Shaykh: It is of the specific kind.

﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I do not let..."﴾: this is the explanation of what was responded to. What was responded to? He said: ﴿Indeed, I do not let the work of any worker among you be lost, whether male or female; you are of one another﴾. ﴿I do not let [it] be lost﴾ means I do not waste it, but I account for it.

His saying ﴿the work of any worker﴾. ﴿The work﴾ here is in construct form, so it implies generality; that is, any deed, whether small or great, Allah the Exalted does not let it be lost. This is like His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:7], and like His saying: ﴿And if it should be the weight of a mustard seed, We would bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:47].

His saying ﴿whether male or female﴾ is an explanation of *ʿāmil* (worker), so *min* here is explanatory, explaining the worker; that is, whether the worker is male or female.

Then He said: ﴿you are of one another﴾, meaning in supplication and its answer. As for support, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are protectors of one another﴾. But in the matter of work, response to them, and reward, they are of one another; there is no distinction between male and female.

Then He said: ﴿Those who emigrated, and were expelled from their homes, and were harmed in My cause, and fought, and were killed﴾. These are five attributes. ﴿Emigrated﴾ means they abandoned their lands and left them for the lands of Islam.

﴿And were expelled from their homes﴾: they were expelled from their homes either directly, by being driven out of the lands, or by being constrained until they leave; because expulsion from the lands may be direct, by being driven out, or it may be by constraining a person until he leaves. Which of the two is more severe?
* Students: The second.
* The Shaykh: No, the first. The first is more severe, because the second one can endure and bear it and not leave; he may hide at times, flee at times, and remain in his own land. But being driven out, being seized and expelled, this is more severe. For this reason the scholars, especially the Ḥanābilah (Ḥanbalīs), said regarding one who committed an act that requires a legal punishment, such as fornication or other things, and then took refuge in Mecca, in the Sacred Precinct (*al-ḥaram*), that he is not to be expelled from the Sacred Precinct, and the legal punishment is not to be carried out against him within it, because he sought refuge there: ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:97]. But he is constrained: he is not to be eaten with, nor given drink, nor traded with, nor spoken to, until the earth becomes narrow for him and he leaves. But to be expelled by force and told, "Get out so we can carry out the punishment on you," no. So there is a difference between those who were expelled in fact, that is, by direct force, and those who were expelled by means of constraint against them.

His saying: ﴿expelled from their homes﴾: ﴿their homes﴾ means the dwellings they inhabit, whether rented or not rented; for a rented house, for example, is still called a person's home.

﴿And were harmed in My cause﴾: that is, although they were expelled, harm came to them in Allah's cause, that is, in the religion of Allah, as happened to the Prophet ﷺ when he was prostrating beneath the Kaʿbah and some people of Quraysh went and brought the entrails of a slaughtered camel and placed them on his back. This is harm; it did not injure him, but it was harm to him. Much harm also befell many of the Companions, as is well known in the biography (*sīrah*).

﴿And fought and were killed﴾. Regarding this, I have: ﴿qātalū wa-quttilū﴾ is a reading. The second reading: ﴿wa-quttilū wa-qātalū﴾. So the readings are now three: ﴿qātalū wa-qutilū﴾; the second: ﴿qātalū wa-quttilū﴾; and the third: ﴿quttilū wa-qātalū﴾. The meaning does not differ greatly. As for His saying ﴿qātalū﴾, this means jihad: they fought the disbelievers. As for ﴿quttilū﴾, this means martyrdom: the disbelievers killed them in Allah's cause. As for ﴿quttilū wa-qātalū﴾, it is the same, but with the order reversed. As for ﴿qātalū wa-quttilū﴾ with the intensive form, it is more severe, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They were killed, killing extensively﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:61]; so the intensive killing (*taqtīl*) is more severe than mere killing (*qatl*).

﴿I will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾ and so on to the end. The clause with ﴿I will surely remove﴾ is the predicate of the subject in His saying ﴿Those who emigrated﴾, but it is a clause emphasized by three emphases?
* A student: The *lām*, the oath, and the energetic *nūn*.
* The Shaykh: And the energetic *nūn*. ﴿I will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾, that is, because of what befell them of these things: by emigration, by being expelled from their homes, by being harmed in Allah's cause, by fighting in Allah's cause, and by being killed, He removes their misdeeds from them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 195 (part 2 of 3):

We have already passed that the difference between forgiveness of sins (maghfirah) and expiation of misdeeds (takfir al-sayyi'at), when the two are mentioned together, is that forgiveness concerns the major sins (kaba'ir), while expiation concerns the minor sins (saghair), which are expiated by righteous deeds and expiated by calamities. ﴿Surely I will expiate from them their misdeeds﴾. What does "their misdeeds" mean?

The minor sins among their wrongdoings. It is also permissible that "misdeeds" here be understood in a more general sense, since it is not coupled with "sins" (dhunub) so that we would say each has its own meaning. This has many parallels: you find some words having one meaning on their own and another meaning when joined with other words.

And His saying: ﴿and surely I will admit them﴾. This clause also carries emphasis through the lam, the oath, and the nun, and it is coordinated with His saying ﴿surely I will expiate﴾, so its position is in the nominative, as a predicate of the subject, like the first.

﴿and surely I will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿Gardens﴾ is used in the plural, and sometimes it is said in the singular. When it is singular, what is meant is the genus in general; when it is plural, what is meant is the kinds of gardens. In the Qur'an, in the surah of al-Rahman, the kinds of gardens are how many? Four, and there may be other kinds that we do not know of. The point is that the plural is considered with respect to kinds, and the singular with respect to genus. So what are these gardens?

The root meaning of jannah is an orchard with many trees, and it is so named because it conceals whoever is in it, i.e., covers him. This root (j-n-n) all indicates covering and concealment. From it comes al-junnah, the shield of the fighter, which he takes to hide behind from arrows; and from it comes al-janan, meaning the heart, because it is hidden; and from it comes al-jinnah, the jinn, because of their concealment.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾. Flowing is well known, and ﴿al-anhar﴾ (the rivers) is the plural of nahr, and it is pluralized because there are four kinds mentioned in surah Muhammad: ﴿In it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muhammad 15]. These rivers never run dry, never diminish, and need no digging or construction of channels. Ibn al-Qayyim said in his Nuniyyah:

Its rivers flow without a trench,
Glory be to the One who holds them back from overflowing.

As for His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾: is the meaning "beneath the ground" or "beneath the shading trees"? The second is what is meant: beneath the trees and palaces there are rivers flowing continuously, yet they do not cause harm, because they submit to the command of their Owner. If He commands this river to turn right or left, it does so by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; if He commands it to stop, it stops.

And His saying ﴿as a reward from Allah﴾: I would like to know what made "reward" (thawaban) accusative?

* Student: A circumstantial accusative (hal).
* Shaykh: A hal? A hal of what?
* Student: A verbal noun (masdar).
* Shaykh: A masdar. Good, so what governs it? A masdar must have a governing element. The estimate?
* Student: "He will reward them with a reward."
* Another student: It is a substitute for the verbal noun (na'ib 'an al-masdar).
* Shaykh: A substitute for the verbal noun, how so?
* Student: Because the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) is a substitute for the verbal noun.
* Shaykh: The absolute object, but what is the governing element? What operated on it?
* Student: (adkhalna).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: A hal.
* Shaykh: A hal of what?
* Student: "Gardens."
* Shaykh: "Gardens, a reward"?
* Student: An object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi).
* Shaykh: No, nor a hal.
* Student: A masdar of a deleted verb.
* Shaykh: And the estimate?
* Student: "I will reward them with a reward."
* Shaykh: "I will reward them with a reward," this is the closest thing. Do you have a grammatical analysis of it?
* * *
* Student: His saying: ﴿and surely I will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. ﴿Thawaban﴾ is a masdar from the meaning of ﴿surely I will expiate﴾, emphasizing it. His saying: a masdar from the meaning of ﴿surely I will expiate﴾, i.e., "and surely I will send them." So the meaning of the whole is "surely I will reward them," so ﴿thawaban﴾ is a masdar agreeing in meaning, as if it were said: "surely I will reward them with a reward," and "reward" here means the act of rewarding, which is the masdar, although originally it is the measure of recompense. End.

His saying: ﴿thawaban﴾ has three possible analyses in its accusative case:

The first: it is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun, because the meaning of the clause before it requires it, and the estimate is: "I will surely reward them with a rewarding, or a reward-giving," so ﴿thawaban﴾ is placed in the position of one of these two verbal nouns, because "reward" (thawab) originally is a name for what one is rewarded with, as "gift" ('ata') is a name for what is given; then both may occupy the position of the verbal noun. This is parallel to His saying ﴿the work of Allah﴾ [al-Naml 88] and ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa' 122], in that both are emphatic.

The second: that it is accusative as a hal from ﴿gardens﴾, meaning "rewarded with them." This is permissible, even though it is indefinite, because it is specified by the descriptive clause.

The third: that it is a hal from the object pronoun, meaning "while they are rewarded."

* Shaykh: That is, either as a hal or as a masdar. But the masdar is problematic. He says that the governing element for it is ("surely I will expiate") and ("surely I will admit") on the basis that expiation and admission are a reward. There is something troubling about this in the soul. The apparent view is that it is a masdar of a deleted governing element, and this is the closest.
* Student: So it is not a reward, then.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...) the meaning would be.
* Shaykh: And His saying ﴿as a reward from Allah﴾: "reward" is used for the gift that a person is given, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 36], i.e., have they been given? It is also used for the act of rewarding, which is the act of the one who rewards. Which is the original meaning, the first or the second? The first: that "reward" is a name for what one is rewarded with, as "gift" is a name for what is given, and it may also be intended to mean the act of rewarding.

His saying: ﴿from the presence of Allah﴾: the attribution to "presence" here indicates the greatness of this reward, because a reward from the Great is great, as the Prophet ﷺ said in the supplication that he taught Abu Bakr: "Forgive me a forgiveness from You and have mercy on me" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (834), Muslim (2705/48) from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq].

His saying: ﴿and with Allah is the best of rewards﴾: this sentence emphasizes what preceded it, meaning that Allah, glorified and exalted, gives them the good reward, because this is what is with Allah; and for this He recompenses the doer of good with his good deed tenfold up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

* From the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of Allah's grace in answering those who made the supplication mentioned earlier, by His saying ﴿so their Lord answered them﴾.
* And from it: the establishment of Allah's hearing, since He rewarded them only when He heard their supplication.
* And from it also: that repeating supplication is among the causes of being answered.
* And from it, based on what preceded: that supplicating by the name of Lordship (rububiyyah) is closer to being answered than supplicating by another name, since most of the supplications mentioned in the Qur'an came with the name of Lordship.
* And from the benefits of this verse: the care of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for these righteous people, by His saying: what? ﴿so their Lord answered them﴾, because this lordship, as we said, is a special lordship.
* And from its benefits: that Allah perfects the reward in full, or gives the reward in full, by His saying: ﴿that I do not waste the work of any worker﴾. This negation implies an affirmation: if He does not waste the work of a worker, then it follows that He gives the worker everything he did, i.e., the reward of all that he did.
* And also from the benefits of the verse: the equality of male and female in recompense for good deeds, by His saying: ﴿whether male or female, you are of one another﴾.

If someone says: Did not the Prophet ﷺ say: "I have not seen anyone more deficient in intellect and religion who takes away the mind of a sensible man than one of you women" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (304), Muslim (80) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id], and he mentioned as a deficiency in her religion that "when she menstruates she neither prays nor fasts"?

We say: Yes, but if she prays at the time when prayer is required of her, her reward and the man's reward are equal. So if a woman prays the noon prayer and a man prays the noon prayer, they are equal in reward.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of emigration (hijrah), by His saying: ﴿so those who emigrated﴾. The scholars have said that hijrah is divided into categories:

The first category: abandoning what Allah has forbidden. The one who emigrates is he who abandons what Allah has prohibited, meaning that the emigrant is one who performs the obligations and avoids the prohibitions.

The second: emigration from a land of disbelief to a land of Islam, as the emigrants did from Makkah to Madinah, and this is the one in which the praise mentioned in the Qur'an applies.

The third: emigration from a land of immorality to a land of uprightness. Some lands are Islamic lands, in which the Islamic rites are established, the call to prayer is made, congregations are held, and Friday prayers are established, so they are lands of Islam; yet from another standpoint they are lands of immorality because of the abundance of sins and vileness and other things in that land, so a person emigrates from it to a land of what? Uprightness.

Let us consider which of these three categories is obligatory. We say: As for the first, which is abandoning what Allah has forbidden, it is obligatory upon every person, even in upright Islamic lands he must abandon what Allah has forbidden. As for the second, emigrating from a land of disbelief to a land of Islam, the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, say: if he is able to manifest his religion, emigration is not obligatory; if he is unable, emigration is obligatory. So if he is in a land where freedoms are restricted and Muslims are prevented from establishing the rites of their religion, such as congregational prayer for example, then emigration here is obligatory, obligatory, because the Muslim cannot manifest his religion. But if he is in a land that considers itself a land of freedom, then emigration is not obligatory; yet even so we say it is more complete and better than remaining. What did I say?

* Student: If the lands... if some lands prevent freedoms, must a person emigrate?
* Shaykh: If they prevent the manifestation of religion, emigration is obligatory upon him, even if he is from its people; if he is originally from that land, emigration is obligatory upon him.
* Student: And if they do not prevent that, and he is able to (...), then it is not obligatory upon him.
* Shaykh: Then emigration is not obligatory, but emigration is more complete, out of fear of trial.

The third: emigration from a land of immorality to a land of uprightness. This also has detail: if he fears for himself from trial, emigration is obligatory upon him; if he does not fear, emigration is not obligatory upon him, and perhaps his staying is better. If he calls to Allah, it may be that in this land of immorality his remaining is better and more beneficial, if he calls to the religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* And from the benefits of this verse: that expulsion from homes is a cause of expiation of misdeeds, by His saying: ﴿and were driven out from their homes﴾, and likewise His saying: ﴿were harmed in My way, and fought, and were killed﴾.

But if someone says: Is expiation dependent upon all five attributes?

The answer to that is: that making expiation contingent upon these five attributes is evidence that each attribute has an effect on the ruling; and were it not that each one has an effect, it would not be valid for them to be an expiation of misdeeds. This is an important benefit, because some disputants may say: the ruling is dependent upon five or more causes. We say: Yes, when it is dependent upon more than one cause, these causes indicate that each one has an effect; and if it were not that it has an effect, the ruling would not be dependent upon it at all. For if we say: number one has no effect, number two has no effect, number three has no effect, number four has no effect, the ruling would not be established. But when we say each one has an effect, yet it may be strong enough to bring about the ruling, or it may be strong enough only to bring about part of it.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, we said regarding ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾: "flow beneath their trees," and we did not say it is literally beneath them, beneath them literally. Why, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Because if they were under the ground, they would not benefit from them.
* Student: (...) and it is under the ground, so it is under the ground in some places, then it appears above the ground in other places.
* Shaykh: You mean they dig a well?
* Student: No, they do not dig a well; Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, makes the river flow in this way: in regions it passes through it is underground, and in places it is exposed, and this is a reality that exists.
* Shaykh: Yes, it exists in this world, but in Paradise its rivers are on the surface of the ground. This is like His saying, sometimes he says: ﴿the rivers flow beneath them﴾ [al-A'raf 43], i.e., beneath their feet, but they are on the surface of Paradise.
* Student: Is hijrah the form of mufa'alah (...), are they shared?
* Shaykh: Yes. The word fa'il (form) does not always imply sharing. Have you seen "safara" (he travelled)? There is no sharing in it. That is, the word fa'il does not indicate that two or more things must share; it is true that the basic meaning of mufa'alah is that it is between two or more parties, but it is not necessary.
* Student: Is it permissible for a person to supplicate by a righteous deed, to supplicate to Allah by it..
* Shaykh: To seek a means (tawassul) by it.
* Student: To seek a means by it. Shaykh, the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, after these deeds, that they were harmed in the way of Allah and emigrated and were killed, He said: ﴿surely I will expiate from them their misdeeds﴾. We said that the misdeeds intended are minor sins. So do these deeds not affect that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (...)?
* Shaykh: No, perhaps. We said just now in the same explanation that we do not assert these are minor sins, because they were not coupled with sins. In the previous verses: ﴿So forgive us our sins and expiate from us our misdeeds﴾; here it is necessary that the misdeeds be minor sins, but in this verse sins are not mentioned, so it may be general.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, regarding (...) "they fought you" ﴿were killed and fought﴾, does its meaning become clear, that if they fought you they would fight?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Did you understand?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: He says: As for ﴿fought and were killed﴾, there is no problem with it: they fought, then they were killed. But ﴿were killed and fought﴾: after they were killed, do they fight?
* Student: Shaykh, we said that the waw does not imply order...
* Shaykh: It does not entail sequence. This is one aspect; another aspect is that it may be distributed, i.e., some of them were killed and some fought and were not killed.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding those who emigrated from their homes, is the consideration the homes where they reside or where they (...)?
* Shaykh: The basic principle is that the consideration is only the land where one resides; this is the principle. But if we suppose that the land where he resides is equal to the lands near it, then he must leave the region.
* Student: Shaykh, some scholars say: a land in which there is not even one scholar, and it is an Islamic land, must be abandoned. What is the soundness of this view, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: That is, emigration is obligatory from a land that has no Islamic scholar?
* Student: A scholar, Shaykh, a scholar.
* Shaykh: What are you saying?
* Student: We did not understand.
* Shaykh: He says: some scholars hold that emigration is obligatory from a land that has no Islamic scholar?
* Student: That is not correct.
* Shaykh: It is not necessary; this is not correct. There may not be a scholar in it, but they know the rulings that bind them.
* Student: Does the saying ﴿they emigrated﴾ specifically refer to emigrating from sins and disobedience? Because after that it specifies: ﴿and were driven out from their homes﴾, so the hijrah is emigration from homes?
* Shaykh: The difference between them is that the emigrant left by his own choice, and the one who was expelled left against his will.
* Student: Is the difference in these deeds.. if he did one deed only, do we say that the reward follows, that his misdeeds are expiated and he enters the gardens?
* Shaykh: No, he is expiated according to what he did.
* Student: The same as the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make show, and withhold simple assistance﴾ [al-Ma'un 4-7]: meaning if he did only one deed, does he have woe?
* Shaykh: According to its measure; he has woe according to its measure.
* Student: (...).

**The Shaykh:** Yes. That is, when a ruling is attached to a set of attributes, these attributes have an effect on the ruling when combined. If they are all present, the whole ruling is established. If they are not all present, the ruling is established to the extent that they are present.

**A student:** Shaykh, regarding His words ﴿some of you are from others﴾, does this refer to action and response?

**The Shaykh:** It means that when they call upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He responds to males and females alike. That is, He does not respond only to males, but to both males and females. We also said that in action too, the righteous deeds required of each of them, they share in the reward. The male is not preferred over the female in reward for a deed they both perform.

**A student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** We do not need to say the same thing. ﴿Some of you are from others﴾ means that you are one thing.

**A student:** Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, if someone has an impediment to the acceptance of supplication, should he supplicate or should he leave off supplicating?

**The Shaykh:** If there is an impediment to the acceptance of supplication, it is obligatory for him to remove this impediment.

**The student:** Sometimes he insists on it?

**The Shaykh:** He fears. I say: he fears that it will not be accepted from him.

**The student:** He says: I know.

**The Shaykh:** Know what?

**The student:** He says: I know that I am falling into this prohibited matter, such as consuming usury?

**The Shaykh:** Good. If you know, refrain from it. If you want your supplication to be answered, then refrain from it.

**The student:** Do we not tell him: leave off supplicating, because that involves mocking Allah?

**The Shaykh:** No, no. There is hope in it. We say: you refrain from this prohibited matter so that it may be accepted from you.

**A student:** Shaykh, (...) in this there is an announcement from them of Allah's favour upon them and boasting of His blessing. That is, the word "boasting"?

**The Shaykh:** No. This expression should not be used; there is a question about it.

**The student:** But then, does Allah, glorified and exalted, intend boasting, or do the believing people boast of Allah's blessing upon them?

**The Shaykh:** Neither this nor that. It is not even appropriate, whether the boasting is from Allah regarding what He gave them, or from them regarding what He gave them.

All of these are causes for the expiation of misdeeds and the admission into Paradise, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿So those who emigrated﴾ and so on to the end of the verse. We have explained at length the difference between these attributes, and that some of them differ from others, although some of them entail others.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person gains reward by being harmed in the way of Allah.
* And it follows from this principle: a person should be patient with harm suffered in the way of Allah, as long as he expects reward for it, because whenever a person knows that he will gain a reward and recompense for being harmed, he must be patient with it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of fighting in the way of Allah, based on His words: ﴿and fought﴾.
* And among its benefits also: the virtue of being killed in the way of Allah, when a person is killed. It is well known that being killed in the way of Allah is one form of martyrdom in the way of Allah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: righteous deeds expiate misdeeds, that is, they cover them. This is because *kufr* (disbelief) is derived from *sitr* (covering). From it comes *kufrā* (the sheath that encloses the date-palm blossom), which in colloquial usage is called *al-kafūr* (the membrane over the palm blossom), because it covers it. Thus the covering of misdeeds by good deeds is called *takfīr* (expiation).
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted, gave a firm guarantee to those who possess these five attributes. He guaranteed them two things. The first guarantee: the expiation of their misdeeds. The second guarantee: their admission into the gardens. This guarantee is emphasised by three emphatics. The first? ﴿I will surely [la-ukaffiranna]﴾ and *la-udkhilanna* (I will surely admit).
* **A student:** The *lam* and the oath.
* **The Shaykh:** Yes. And the third: the *nūn* of emphasis.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: arousing longing for Paradise, so that a person becomes more energetic in working for it, based on His words: ﴿and I will surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. In the Arabic language, *jannāt* (gardens) originally means dense groves of trees, because they (i.e., dense groves of trees) conceal those within them, that is, they cover and shelter them.
* From this is derived: arousing longing for this great reward.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Paradise contains palaces, based on His words: ﴿beneath﴾ and "beneath" can only be in contrast to what? To "above," the high place. And that is so.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Paradise contains several rivers. Here they are stated in general terms, but they are detailed in Surah Muhammad, where they are specified as four: ﴿rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine delicious to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this reward is a recompense for them from Allah. Thus the favour is Allah's upon them, and they have no favour upon Allah through their deeds, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿a reward from Allah﴾. Had Allah willed, He would not have rewarded them, or He would have rewarded them with less than that. But by His bounty He made the reward for them this great reward: ﴿a reward from Allah﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the magnitude of this reward. From where is this taken? The indication of the magnitude of this reward? From His words: ﴿from Allah﴾, because a gift is magnified according to its giver, and a present is magnified according to its donor. So when it comes from Allah, this is evidence that it is a great reward, because a reward from the Great is great.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the best reward is sought only from Allah, based on His words: ﴿and with Allah is the best reward﴾, alone. So do not seek a reward from anyone other than Him, because however much reward the creation gives you, it will never be like the reward of Allah. The excellence of reward is with Allah alone.

In this sentence there is also an emphasis on the magnitude of this reward. When He said ﴿from Allah﴾, we learned the greatness of the reward from it. When He says ﴿and with Allah is the best reward﴾, we also learn the benefit of confirming what preceded: that this reward is a great reward, and that it is the best recompense with which a person can be rewarded: ﴿and with Allah is the best reward﴾.

* Can the exaltedness of Allah be derived from this noble verse? Yes. Some scholars held that whenever the expression "with" ('indahu) occurs, it is evidence of His exaltedness. But in some places this is not clear, while in other places it is clear, such as His words: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship﴾ [Al-A'raf 206], and His words: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 19]. Here the superiority is clear. But in a verse such as this one, it is not very apparent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 196–197 (part 1 of 2):

Then he said: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you.﴾ Have we explained this or not? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you.﴾

﴿Let not deceive you﴾: There is no doubt that ﴿لَا﴾ (la) in His words ﴿لَا يَغُرَّنَّكَ﴾ is a prohibitive particle (nahiyah). But someone will say: How can it be a prohibitive when the verb is in the fatha form ﴿يَغُرَّنَّكَ﴾, since the nun is the last part of the verb?

The answer to this: When the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) is attached to the present-tense verb, it becomes indeclinable and takes fatha, whether it is attached to it verbally and in meaning, or it is attached to it verbally but not in meaning, in which case it is not indeclinable. Example: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about the bliss﴾ [al-Takathur 8]. Here the emphatic nun is attached to the present verb, but only verbally and not in meaning. If it is not attached at all, the verb is not indeclinable, except when the feminine plural nun (nun al-niswah) is attached to it. So the present-tense verb is indeclinable in two cases: when the feminine plural nun is attached to it, or when the emphatic nun is attached to it both verbally and in meaning.

As for His words ﴿لَا يَغُرَّنَّكَ﴾, the address here may be to the Messenger ﷺ, and it may be to everyone who can be addressed. The rule we follow in tafsir is that if a verse may bear two meanings that are different but do not contradict each other, it is interpreted as both of them together. If it may bear two meanings, one of which is more general, it is interpreted as the more general, because the more specific is included in the more general and not vice versa. So here, if we say the address is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, we exclude the rest of the Ummah; and if we say the address is general to everyone who can be addressed, it includes the Messenger ﷺ and others. On this basis, the address here is general; that is, ﴿let not deceive you﴾, O observer who sees the going to and fro of the disbelievers in the land, let this not deceive you.

As for His words ﴿the going to and fro of those who disbelieve﴾: al-taqallub means al-taraddud (moving about), that is, their moving about in the lands, going from one land to another, and their going to and fro in trade and in various kinds of crafts and other things that Allah has opened to them. So this should not deceive you. The deception that may occur is that a person may be deceived by what Allah the Mighty and Majestic has given them, and so does the like of what they do, or he thinks that Allah's giving them this thing indicates that what they are upon is not denied; and if what they were upon were denied, He would not have enabled them to move about in the lands. On this basis, the deception comes from two aspects; so the deception is from two aspects:
The first aspect: he thinks that what they are upon is true, because he says: If it were false, Allah the Exalted would not have enabled them to move about in this way.
The second: that he does what they do, just as many people today have been deceived, thinking that the disbelievers reached what they reached because of their release from their religion, may Allah protect us. So he sees that adherence to religion is a cause of backwardness and decline. Thus the deception has two aspects.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, what is its aspect?
* The student: Some people (...).
* The Shaykh: That Allah enabled them to move about in this way, and if what they were upon were false He would not have enabled them. Good. The second?
* Student: The second is (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this is the first.
* Student: That he does the like of what they do.
* The Shaykh: That he does the like of what they do, thinking that what they did is the cause of this movement and expansion in trade and other things. The reality is that this does not deceive the believer, because Allah said in His Book: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for them. We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 178]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And those who deny Our signs, We will lead them gradually from where they do not know. And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'raf 182-183]. So do not be deceived; this is nothing but an increase in the regret that is upon them.
As for His words ﴿the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land﴾: is "al-bilad" singular or plural?
* Student: Plural.
* The Shaykh: And the singular?
* Students: Balad.
* The Shaykh: Balad. So al-bilad is plural, and the singular is balad, and balad is also pluralized as "buldan". In the lands. How is the going to and fro in the lands? They go from this land to that land, moving about in security and tranquility, trading and profiting whenever trade carries them from one land to another, so a person is deceived by that.
He said: ﴿a little enjoyment﴾. ﴿Matā'un﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimation is: it is matā' (enjoyment); their going to and fro is a little enjoyment. Matā' is that by which enjoyment is attained, whether it is psychological enjoyment or bodily enjoyment, and every enjoyment that is attributed to the world or to the disbelievers is enjoyment of what? Bodily; bodily enjoyment, as the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12]. So His words ﴿a little enjoyment﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject. Matā' is that by which enjoyment is obtained, and enjoyment is of two kinds: spiritual enjoyment of the heart, which belongs only to the believer, who enjoys the remembrance of Allah and what Allah has blessed him with of faith; and bodily enjoyment, in which humans and animals share, which is what the body gains of pleasure and delight and so on. He says ﴿a little enjoyment﴾: ﴿little﴾, is it little in its time, or little in its quantity, or in its quality? In everything. Its time is little and limited, which is a person's lifespan, that unknown span whose end a person does not know. Also little in quantity, because a person does not possess everything. Little in quality, because a person may be deprived of enjoying this world through illnesses that afflict him so that he does not enjoy it, or he may be deprived by losing some things. And Allah knows best.
* * *
* Student: ﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a provision from Allah. And that which is with Allah is better for the righteous (198). And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah. They do not exchange the verses of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in account (199). O you who have believed, be patient and endure and remain stationed and fear Allah that you may be successful (200)﴾ [Al 'Imran 198-200].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾. ﴿Lā﴾ here, what is its grammatical status?
* Student: Prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Negating?
* The student: Prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Good. How is the verb in the accusative with it when it is prohibitive, and the prohibitive jussives?!
* The student: This nun is attached to the present verb, the heavy emphatic nun, and the emphatic nun... So it is indeclinable with fatha.
* The Shaykh: So it is indeclinable, not declinable, and for this we say: ﴿yaghurrannu﴾ is a present-tense verb indeclinable on fatha in a position of jazm. Is that right? The address in His words ﴿let not deceive you﴾?
* Student: It is for the Prophet and the people.
* The Shaykh: If someone said: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, because the Quran was revealed to him?
* The student: It is also valid for the address to be to the believers.
* The Shaykh: But if a second person said?
* The student: We say: this is specific, and the general takes precedence over the specific.
* The Shaykh: Yes, we say: this is possible, but interpreting it as general is preferable because the specific is included in it.
His words ﴿a little enjoyment﴾..
Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a provision from Allah. And that which is with Allah is better for the righteous (198). And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah. They do not exchange the verses of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in account (199). O you who have believed, be patient and endure and remain stationed and fear Allah that you may be successful (200)﴾ [Al 'Imran 198-200].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran 196]. (La) here, what is its grammatical status?
* Student: (La) is prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Negating?
* The student: Prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Good, how is the verb in the accusative with it when it is prohibitive, and the prohibitive jussives?
* Student: The heavy emphatic nun is attached to the present verb, so it is indeclinable on fatha.
* The Shaykh: So it is indeclinable, not declinable; therefore we say: ﴿yaghurrannaka﴾... The address in ﴿let not deceive you﴾?
* Student: To the Prophet and all people.
* The Shaykh: If someone said: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, because the Quran was revealed to him?
* Student: It is also suitable for the address to be to the believers.
* The Shaykh: But if someone said: the second?
* Student: We say: this is specific, and the general takes precedence over the specific.
* The Shaykh: We say: this is possible, but interpreting it as general is preferable because the specific is included in it.
His words ﴿a little enjoyment﴾: what is the little enjoyment mentioned?
* Student: The little enjoyment includes bodily and sensory enjoyment.
* The Shaykh: But what is enjoyment? I am not asking about the meaning of enjoyment.
* Student: Enjoyment is that by which enjoyment is attained.
* The Shaykh: That by which enjoyment is attained. The intended meaning of "little enjoyment" is: their going to and fro in the lands is a little enjoyment. We said it is little in what?
The question: little in what?
* Student: Little in quantity and in quality.
* The Shaykh: And other than that? No, something else? We mentioned something else?
* Student: In duration.
* The Shaykh: Little in its time, its quantity, its quality.
What is the meaning of His words ﴿their refuge is Hell﴾?
* Student: We did not take it.
* The Shaykh: The Exalted said: ﴿Then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾. That is: after this little enjoyment, their refuge is Hell. He used "then" (thumma), and it indicates delay, to point out that however long they last in this life, their ultimate end is this wretched end, may Allah protect us.

Al-ma'wa means that to which a person retreats, so it is a noun of place; that is, the destination to which they will return is Hell. Jahannam is one of the names of the Fire, may Allah protect us and you from it. It was called that; it is said: because it is derived from al-tajahhum (frowning) or from al-jahmah, which is blackness. It is also said that it is a non-Arabic word, originally kahanam, but it was Arabized into jahannam, and it is one of the names of the Fire, so it is not derived. Whatever the case, it is one of the names of the Fire.

﴿And wretched is the resting place﴾: bi'sa is a verb of blame that takes a subject, and it has a subject and a specified object. The subject is "al-mihad", and the specified object is omitted; the estimation is: "wa bi'sa al-mihadu hiya" (and wretched is the resting place, it). The grammarians needed this estimation because al-mihad is other than the Fire, while the blame is directed at what? At the Fire; so it was necessary to mention an object of blame other than the subject of the verb, and the object of blame is the omitted pronoun, meaning: and wretched is the resting place, it. This is what the jurists estimated. Al-mihad is that which is a bed for a person, that is, a place of settlement for him, and from it is His words: ﴿He who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [Ta-Ha 53]. Mahdan means a place of settlement in which you rest.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse:
* First: the prohibition for a person from being deceived by the blessings and luxury given to the disbelievers; from His words: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾.
* Another of its benefits: that what Allah gives the servant of ease, abundance of provision, and freedom to move about the earth right and left is not evidence of His pleasure with the servant; rather, the measure of Allah's pleasure with the servant is the servant's following of the Law of Allah.
* Another benefit of the noble verse: that Allah the Mighty and Majestic may lead a person gradually by lavishing blessings upon him as a trial for him; as the Exalted said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbya' 35]. The way this is: Allah enabled these disbelievers to move about the lands as they wish as a trial for them, so that they would persist in what they are upon, and that would be an evil for them, may Allah protect us, as the Exalted said: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for them. We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾.
* Another benefit of the noble verse: that the believer is sometimes constricted in provision by Allah so that he returns to Him, unlike the disbeliever. I only say this lest someone say: Did not Allah say: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-A'raf 96]?
We say: The believers are the ones who are tested with adversity so that they may return to Allah the Mighty and Majestic; ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of that which they have done; perhaps they will return﴾ [al-Rum 41]. As for the disbelievers, the world is smoothed out for them and they are given what they want, and their paradise is their worldly life, unlike the believers.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: that however much of blessing a person is given in this world, it is a little enjoyment: little in its time, in its quantity, in its quality. But the Hereafter is the opposite. The Prophet ﷺ said: «The place of one of your whips in Paradise is better than the world and what is in it»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3250) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.]] Allahu akbar! The place of a whip, a whip is a meter or a little less, is better than the world and what is in it. The present world is not the only world before you; it is better than the whole world from its beginning to its end and what is in it, merely the place of a whip. To this points His words: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life (16), while the Hereafter is better and more enduring (17). Indeed, this is in the former scriptures (18), the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la 16-19].
* Another benefit of this noble verse: caution against the enemies of the Muslims playing with the Muslims, where they incite them with means of entertainment and open for them the means of amusement to distract them from what they were created for, the worship of Allah, and from what they should be upon of honor and dignity. These entertainment means are in reality poisoned bait for chickens. A chicken is deceived by poisoned bait: it finds a swollen, soft grain, rejoices in it, takes it with the tip of its beak and swallows it quickly, but it cuts its intestines. So likewise our enemies have opened for us the doors of entertainment from every side, so that we plunge into this luxury, with no concern except luxury, forgetting what we were created for, the worship of Allah, and forgetting what we should be upon of honor, dignity, and interests. From this verse is taken: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you (196), a little enjoyment﴾.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: that it is impossible for a disbeliever to enter Paradise; from His words: ﴿Then their refuge is Hell﴾. It is impossible that their refuge be Paradise ever, because they are disbelievers.

* One of the lessons of this noble verse: it points out that this comfort which they enjoy in this world will be forgotten. By what will it be forgotten? By this evil abode. If the abode is the Fire, they will forget everything, as came in the hadith: that "a man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection from among the most blessed people of the world" — meaning the most abundant in blessings and luxury — "and he will be dipped once into the Fire, and it will be said to him: Did you ever see any good? He will say: No, by Allah, I never saw any good." Why? Because he has forgotten it. This single dipping makes him forget all the blessings he had in the world, because he is brought from among the most blessed people of the world. "And a man will be brought from among the most miserable people of the world" — meaning the most wretched among them — "and he will be dipped once into Paradise, and it will be said to him: Did you ever see any evil? He will say: I never saw any evil."[[Recorded by Muslim (2807/55) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] Because he has forgotten it through this blessing, which lasts only a moment. Everything that befell him in the world of misery, poverty and harm is forgotten.

We believe in these realities, but heedlessness takes hold of us as if they had never come, as if they had never existed. We are in a state of intoxication — we ask Allah for well-being and that He awaken our hearts with His remembrance — we are in a state of intoxication, otherwise, if we returned to these realities and conducted ourselves according to what they require, much good would come to us. The intoxication of loving this world and preferring it over the Hereafter makes us forget this.

The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, due to the shock they suffered at the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), forgot some verses of the Qur'an, forgetting His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Muhammad is nothing but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ [Aal 'Imran 144], until the truthful one of this Ummah, the one most steadfast in heart during calamities, Abu Bakr, came and recited it on the pulpit, as if it had never been revealed.

So I say: In truth we forget these realities and do not feel them, but a time will come when a person will feel them. When the appointed term arrives, a person will wish that he had used his time in obedience to Allah, but how can that be? It is not possible for it to be delayed by a single moment from the appointed time. So we ask Allah to bless our lives, and yours.
