Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Then their refuge is Hell, and what an evil resting-place it is.﴾

* From the lessons of this noble verse: the ugliness, or the clarification of the ugliness, of this abode, because Allah praised it with the worst praise when He said: ﴿and what an evil resting-place it is﴾. This indicates the ugliness of the abode of the people of the Fire. We ask Allah for ourselves and for you safety from it.

And the Exalted said: ﴿And those who deny Our signs, We will lead them gradually from where they do not know. And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'raf 182-183]. So do not be deceived; this is nothing but an increase in the regret that is upon them.
As for His words ﴿the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land﴾: is "al-bilad" singular or plural?
* Student: Plural.
* The Shaykh: And the singular?
* Students: Balad.
* The Shaykh: Balad. So al-bilad is plural, and the singular is balad, and balad is also pluralized as "buldan". In the lands. How is the going to and fro in the lands? They go from this land to that land, moving about in security and tranquility, trading and profiting whenever trade carries them from one land to another, so a person is deceived by that.
He said: ﴿a little enjoyment﴾. ﴿Matā'un﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimation is: it is matā' (enjoyment); their going to and fro is a little enjoyment. Matā' is that by which enjoyment is attained, whether it is psychological enjoyment or bodily enjoyment, and every enjoyment that is attributed to the world or to the disbelievers is enjoyment of what? Bodily; bodily enjoyment, as the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12]. So His words ﴿a little enjoyment﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject. Matā' is that by which enjoyment is obtained, and enjoyment is of two kinds: spiritual enjoyment of the heart, which belongs only to the believer, who enjoys the remembrance of Allah and what Allah has blessed him with of faith; and bodily enjoyment, in which humans and animals share, which is what the body gains of pleasure and delight and so on. He says ﴿a little enjoyment﴾: ﴿little﴾, is it little in its time, or little in its quantity, or in its quality? In everything. Its time is little and limited, which is a person's lifespan, that unknown span whose end a person does not know. Also little in quantity, because a person does not possess everything. Little in quality, because a person may be deprived of enjoying this world through illnesses that afflict him so that he does not enjoy it, or he may be deprived by losing some things. And Allah knows best.
* * *
* Student: ﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a provision from Allah. And that which is with Allah is better for the righteous (198). And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah. They do not exchange the verses of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in account (199). O you who have believed, be patient and endure and remain stationed and fear Allah that you may be successful (200)﴾ [Al 'Imran 198-200].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾. ﴿Lā﴾ here, what is its grammatical status?
* Student: Prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Negating?
* The student: Prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Good. How is the verb in the accusative with it when it is prohibitive, and the prohibitive jussives?!
* The student: This nun is attached to the present verb, the heavy emphatic nun, and the emphatic nun... So it is indeclinable with fatha.
* The Shaykh: So it is indeclinable, not declinable, and for this we say: ﴿yaghurrannu﴾ is a present-tense verb indeclinable on fatha in a position of jazm. Is that right? The address in His words ﴿let not deceive you﴾?
* Student: It is for the Prophet and the people.
* The Shaykh: If someone said: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, because the Quran was revealed to him?
* The student: It is also valid for the address to be to the believers.
* The Shaykh: But if a second person said?
* The student: We say: this is specific, and the general takes precedence over the specific.
* The Shaykh: Yes, we say: this is possible, but interpreting it as general is preferable because the specific is included in it.
His words ﴿a little enjoyment﴾..
Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, as a provision from Allah. And that which is with Allah is better for the righteous (198). And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah. They do not exchange the verses of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in account (199). O you who have believed, be patient and endure and remain stationed and fear Allah that you may be successful (200)﴾ [Al 'Imran 198-200].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran 196]. (La) here, what is its grammatical status?
* Student: (La) is prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Negating?
* The student: Prohibitive.
* The Shaykh: Good, how is the verb in the accusative with it when it is prohibitive, and the prohibitive jussives?
* Student: The heavy emphatic nun is attached to the present verb, so it is indeclinable on fatha.
* The Shaykh: So it is indeclinable, not declinable; therefore we say: ﴿yaghurrannaka﴾... The address in ﴿let not deceive you﴾?
* Student: To the Prophet and all people.
* The Shaykh: If someone said: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, because the Quran was revealed to him?
* Student: It is also suitable for the address to be to the believers.
* The Shaykh: But if someone said: the second?
* Student: We say: this is specific, and the general takes precedence over the specific.
* The Shaykh: We say: this is possible, but interpreting it as general is preferable because the specific is included in it.
His words ﴿a little enjoyment﴾: what is the little enjoyment mentioned?
* Student: The little enjoyment includes bodily and sensory enjoyment.
* The Shaykh: But what is enjoyment? I am not asking about the meaning of enjoyment.
* Student: Enjoyment is that by which enjoyment is attained.
* The Shaykh: That by which enjoyment is attained. The intended meaning of "little enjoyment" is: their going to and fro in the lands is a little enjoyment. We said it is little in what?
The question: little in what?
* Student: Little in quantity and in quality.
* The Shaykh: And other than that? No, something else? We mentioned something else?
* Student: In duration.
* The Shaykh: Little in its time, its quantity, its quality.
What is the meaning of His words ﴿their refuge is Hell﴾?
* Student: We did not take it.
* The Shaykh: The Exalted said: ﴿Then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾. That is: after this little enjoyment, their refuge is Hell. He used "then" (thumma), and it indicates delay, to point out that however long they last in this life, their ultimate end is this wretched end, may Allah protect us.

Al-ma'wa means that to which a person retreats, so it is a noun of place; that is, the destination to which they will return is Hell. Jahannam is one of the names of the Fire, may Allah protect us and you from it. It was called that; it is said: because it is derived from al-tajahhum (frowning) or from al-jahmah, which is blackness. It is also said that it is a non-Arabic word, originally kahanam, but it was Arabized into jahannam, and it is one of the names of the Fire, so it is not derived. Whatever the case, it is one of the names of the Fire.

﴿And wretched is the resting place﴾: bi'sa is a verb of blame that takes a subject, and it has a subject and a specified object. The subject is "al-mihad", and the specified object is omitted; the estimation is: "wa bi'sa al-mihadu hiya" (and wretched is the resting place, it). The grammarians needed this estimation because al-mihad is other than the Fire, while the blame is directed at what? At the Fire; so it was necessary to mention an object of blame other than the subject of the verb, and the object of blame is the omitted pronoun, meaning: and wretched is the resting place, it. This is what the jurists estimated. Al-mihad is that which is a bed for a person, that is, a place of settlement for him, and from it is His words: ﴿He who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [Ta-Ha 53]. Mahdan means a place of settlement in which you rest.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse:
* First: the prohibition for a person from being deceived by the blessings and luxury given to the disbelievers; from His words: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾.
* Another of its benefits: that what Allah gives the servant of ease, abundance of provision, and freedom to move about the earth right and left is not evidence of His pleasure with the servant; rather, the measure of Allah's pleasure with the servant is the servant's following of the Law of Allah.
* Another benefit of the noble verse: that Allah the Mighty and Majestic may lead a person gradually by lavishing blessings upon him as a trial for him; as the Exalted said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbya' 35]. The way this is: Allah enabled these disbelievers to move about the lands as they wish as a trial for them, so that they would persist in what they are upon, and that would be an evil for them, may Allah protect us, as the Exalted said: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for them. We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾.
* Another benefit of the noble verse: that the believer is sometimes constricted in provision by Allah so that he returns to Him, unlike the disbeliever. I only say this lest someone say: Did not Allah say: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-A'raf 96]?
We say: The believers are the ones who are tested with adversity so that they may return to Allah the Mighty and Majestic; ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of that which they have done; perhaps they will return﴾ [al-Rum 41]. As for the disbelievers, the world is smoothed out for them and they are given what they want, and their paradise is their worldly life, unlike the believers.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: that however much of blessing a person is given in this world, it is a little enjoyment: little in its time, in its quantity, in its quality. But the Hereafter is the opposite. The Prophet ﷺ said: «The place of one of your whips in Paradise is better than the world and what is in it»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3250) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.]] Allahu akbar! The place of a whip, a whip is a meter or a little less, is better than the world and what is in it. The present world is not the only world before you; it is better than the whole world from its beginning to its end and what is in it, merely the place of a whip. To this points His words: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life (16), while the Hereafter is better and more enduring (17). Indeed, this is in the former scriptures (18), the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la 16-19].
* Another benefit of this noble verse: caution against the enemies of the Muslims playing with the Muslims, where they incite them with means of entertainment and open for them the means of amusement to distract them from what they were created for, the worship of Allah, and from what they should be upon of honor and dignity. These entertainment means are in reality poisoned bait for chickens. A chicken is deceived by poisoned bait: it finds a swollen, soft grain, rejoices in it, takes it with the tip of its beak and swallows it quickly, but it cuts its intestines. So likewise our enemies have opened for us the doors of entertainment from every side, so that we plunge into this luxury, with no concern except luxury, forgetting what we were created for, the worship of Allah, and forgetting what we should be upon of honor, dignity, and interests. From this verse is taken: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you (196), a little enjoyment﴾.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: that it is impossible for a disbeliever to enter Paradise; from His words: ﴿Then their refuge is Hell﴾. It is impossible that their refuge be Paradise ever, because they are disbelievers.

* One of the lessons of this noble verse: it points out that this comfort which they enjoy in this world will be forgotten. By what will it be forgotten? By this evil abode. If the abode is the Fire, they will forget everything, as came in the hadith: that "a man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection from among the most blessed people of the world" — meaning the most abundant in blessings and luxury — "and he will be dipped once into the Fire, and it will be said to him: Did you ever see any good? He will say: No, by Allah, I never saw any good." Why? Because he has forgotten it. This single dipping makes him forget all the blessings he had in the world, because he is brought from among the most blessed people of the world. "And a man will be brought from among the most miserable people of the world" — meaning the most wretched among them — "and he will be dipped once into Paradise, and it will be said to him: Did you ever see any evil? He will say: I never saw any evil."[[Recorded by Muslim (2807/55) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] Because he has forgotten it through this blessing, which lasts only a moment. Everything that befell him in the world of misery, poverty and harm is forgotten.

We believe in these realities, but heedlessness takes hold of us as if they had never come, as if they had never existed. We are in a state of intoxication — we ask Allah for well-being and that He awaken our hearts with His remembrance — we are in a state of intoxication, otherwise, if we returned to these realities and conducted ourselves according to what they require, much good would come to us. The intoxication of loving this world and preferring it over the Hereafter makes us forget this.

The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, due to the shock they suffered at the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), forgot some verses of the Qur'an, forgetting His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Muhammad is nothing but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ [Aal 'Imran 144], until the truthful one of this Ummah, the one most steadfast in heart during calamities, Abu Bakr, came and recited it on the pulpit, as if it had never been revealed.

So I say: In truth we forget these realities and do not feel them, but a time will come when a person will feel them. When the appointed term arrives, a person will wish that he had used his time in obedience to Allah, but how can that be? It is not possible for it to be delayed by a single moment from the appointed time. So we ask Allah to bless our lives, and yours.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Then their refuge is Hell, and what an evil resting-place it is.﴾

* From the lessons of this noble verse: the ugliness, or the clarification of the ugliness, of this abode, because Allah praised it with the worst praise when He said: ﴿and what an evil resting-place it is﴾. This indicates the ugliness of the abode of the people of the Fire. We ask Allah for ourselves and for you safety from it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 198:

Then He said: ﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ and so on to the end. Here someone may ask: what is the purpose of the corrective particle (istidrak) in this verse, ﴿But those who fear [their Lord]﴾? Istidrak (a corrective "but") is only used for something that might be expected to be included in what came before. For example, you say, "The people stood up, but so-and-so did not stand," where it was expected that he would be among those standing. So here, ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾: what is the point of the istidrak?

The point of the istidrak is that if those who fear their Lord were given the same worldly fortune as these disbelievers, that would not stand as a barrier between them and what is with Allah. In other words, believers may also move freely about the lands just as the disbelievers do, isn't that so? Would then the abode of the God-fearing be like the abode of the disbelievers? No. That is why He said: ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾. So the istidrak here is among the most subtle kinds, lest someone think that if Allah enabled the believers to move about the lands as the disbelievers do, they would miss out on what is with Allah. So He clarified that they will not miss it, saying: ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾.

﴿Those who fear their Lord﴾. Taqwa (God-consciousness, fear of Allah) comes up often. The best way to explain it is: taking a means of protection from the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is the most comprehensive thing said about taqwa: taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

As for His saying ﴿those who fear their Lord﴾ rather than "fear Allah," it indicates that Allah's lordship over them is a special lordship, through which He helped them to attain taqwa and granted them success in it. So His lordship over them is a special lordship belonging to them. (...) Like His lordship over some of the prophets, as in: ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ [al-A'raf 122]. It is a special lordship in which no one else shares.

﴿But those who fear their Lord, for them are gardens﴾ and so on to the end. When we return to i'rab (grammatical analysis) after understanding the meaning, we say: (lakin) is a particle of istidrak. Is it operative or non-operative? Non-operative. ﴿Those who﴾ is the subject, and ﴿for them are gardens﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the subject with its predicate is the predicate of the first subject.

﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Jannat (gardens) is the plural of jannah, whose original meaning is an orchard with many trees. It was so named because it covers (yajunn) whoever is in it, i.e., shields them. However, we do not explain the "gardens" or "garden" mentioned in the Quran, which Allah intends as the Garden of Eternity, with this explanation before the general public. If you explained it that way before the common people, their desire for Paradise would drop greatly; they would say, "That orchard over there is better than it, it has trees, palms, this and that." Instead, we say to the common people: Paradise is the abode that Allah the Exalted has prepared for the God-fearing, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. I believe that if you explained it to one of our old women by saying, "Paradise is an orchard with many trees and palms," she would turn away from you. Is that what Paradise is? Because she imagines Paradise as containing what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. But if you say, "It is an orchard with many trees and palms," what does she imagine? Everyone has seen that, everyone knows it. For this reason I say: the student of knowledge should explain the Quran according to its meaning, but if he fears causing fitnah (confusion or temptation), he explains it in a way that agrees with reason and does not contradict the texts. So when you say to the common people, "Paradise is the abode that Allah the Exalted has prepared for the God-fearing, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived," then this explanation is correct.

But when you speak with a student of knowledge who asks, "What is the meaning of jannah, and why was it so named?" we come to the root (j-n-n), and find that all of its derivatives indicate concealment. So you say: in origin it is an orchard with many trees. We may say that jannah in its original sense is this meaning, but it was transferred by the Shariah (sacred law) to the abode prepared by Allah for the God-fearing, just as salah, zakah, hajj and 'umrah were transferred to their legal meanings.

﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾. We have already noted that His saying ﴿beneath them﴾ indicates the height of their palaces and trees, and that the rivers are four, and that they flow without a trench and without a cut channel; they flow wherever their owner wishes, a canal branching from them or a stream leading from them that goes wherever he wills. Concerning this, Ibn al-Qayyim said in his Nuniyyah:

Its rivers flow without a trench,
Glory be to the One who holds them back from overflowing.

May Allah make me and you among its people.

He says: ﴿beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾. Khulud (abiding) means remaining, i.e., they remain in it. For how long? Forever, as Allah the Exalted said in many other verses: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ [an-Nisa' 57].

﴿As a welcome gift from Allah﴾. ﴿Nuzulan (as a welcome gift)﴾ is accusative as a hal (circumstantial state), meaning: these gardens are in the state of being a welcome gift.

If someone asks: how (...) and its owner is indefinite, because jannat is indefinite, and a hal cannot come from an indefinite noun; must its owner be definite?

The answer is: its owner is indefinite, but it is specified by the qualifying clause: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, and a specified indefinite can serve as the owner of a hal just as a definite noun can.

Another may say: (...) not a jamid (non-derived noun), and nuzul, which is the name of what is presented to a guest of food, is a jamid and not a derived noun?

The answer: a hal may indeed be a jamid but interpreted as a derived noun, meaning they are honored with this nuzul.

As for His saying ﴿from the presence of Allah﴾, it means this nuzul is not from so-and-so or so-and-so; it is from the presence of the most generous of the generous and the most bountiful of the bountiful, who is Allah. A nuzul from the Most Generous is great, noble, and abundant.

He said: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾. Ma (what) is a relative pronoun and cannot be a negation, because the meaning would be badly corrupted. If you said ma is negating, the meaning would become: "Nothing with Allah is better for the righteous," and that is false. So it is the relative ma: meaning "that which is with Allah is better," so it is a subject and khayr (better) is its predicate, meaning: what is with Allah is better than what has been mentioned of the description of the gardens. This is like His saying: ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35]. In Paradise there is more than what a person wishes for and more than what he imagines, and that is looking at the face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for looking at the face of Allah is the greatest of blessings. That is why Allah called it an increase in His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and an increase﴾ [Yunus 26]. The most knowledgeable of creation, the Prophet ﷺ, explained the increase as looking at the face of Allah[[Recorded by Ahmad (18935), and al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra (11170), from the hadith of Suhayb.]].

﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾. Al-abrar (the righteous) is the plural of barr, and barr (...) goodness, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Barr, the Merciful﴾ [at-Tur 28], meaning He is abundant in goods. So al-abrar is the plural of barr, and they are abundant in good deeds, by doing what Allah has commanded and abstaining from what Allah has forbidden. The mention of the benefits of this verse will come, God willing.

* Student: (...) (nuzulan) is a masdar (verbal noun) of a deleted verb, meaning "He lodges them in lodging."

* Shaykh: No, because nuzul here is what is presented to a guest; it is not from inzal (causing to descend).

* Student: So you mean: they derived it from it?

* Shaykh: No, that does not work.

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: What do you say in answer to this? Someone says: it is well known that the nuzul presented to a guest is only at first and does not continue?

The answer to this is: Allah made the whole of Paradise a nuzul, and it is well known that the nuzul presented to a guest, at its first presentation, is of the finest food and the most generous. So it is as if the whole of Paradise is like a nuzul, meaning its last part does not differ from its first. This is unlike the hospitality of this world: the guest, on the first day, is given good food, and the second day less, a little less, and that is the reality; the third day less, and on the fourth day we say, "Go in the protection of Allah." It is well known that the nuzul is best on the first day, so Allah made this whole Paradise a nuzul, and its last part does not differ from its first.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: That is correct, but when He mentioned the gardens He mentioned that what is with Allah is better than that. If the gardens are better than this world and what is in it, then what is better than the gardens is greater.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No, this is taken from other verses, but what is the good that is better than the gardens? We said: Allah explained it in another verse.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What does it mean?

* * *

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But those who fear their Lord, for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, as a welcome gift from Allah. And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran 198]. What is the benefit of this istidrak?

* Student: Lest someone think that whoever undergoes what the disbelievers underwent, moving about the lands, his end will be like theirs, so Allah the Exalted corrected that, until...

* Shaykh: That the end of the God-fearing would be like the end of the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾. What is the i'rab of ﴿what is with Allah﴾?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: A relative pronoun. Good. Then it is a subject, where is its predicate?

* Student: ﴿better﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿better﴾, good. ﴿The righteous﴾?

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: Plural of what?

* Student: Barr.

* Shaykh: And it means one abundant in goodness.

Is al-Barr one of the names of Allah?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. The evidence?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Barr, the Merciful﴾ [at-Tur 28].

* Shaykh: His saying: ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾ and so on to the end.

* Among its benefits: that the God-fearing, even if they move about the lands, their end is not like the end of the disbelievers; by His saying: ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾.

* Among them: the benefits of taqwa, and that among its benefits is what these God-fearing people obtained of the great nuzul with Allah the Mighty and Majestic, namely these gardens beneath which rivers flow.

* Among them: that the reward of these God-fearing people with Allah the Mighty and Majestic is far greater than what is given to those who move about the lands, because Allah said of those who move about: ﴿a little enjoyment﴾, whereas of these He said: ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾, forever and ever.

* Among them: the greatness of this recompense and reward that they receive, because it is a nuzul from the most generous of the generous, who is Allah the Mighty and Majestic; by His saying: ﴿as a welcome gift from Allah﴾.

* Among them: what some scholars deduced, that His saying: ﴿and what is with Allah﴾ indicates height, because it cannot indicate lowness, since that would be a deficiency from which Allah is exempt; so it is necessarily in the height: ﴿and what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾.

* Among them: that recompense is of the same kind as the deed. These people, being righteous and abundant in good, had with Allah the Mighty and Majestic this great nuzul.

* Among its benefits: that in the gardens there are rivers, great rivers flowing beneath their mansions and trees; by His saying: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Baqarah 25].

* Among its benefits: that whoever Allah favors with taqwa, this is part of the requirement of Allah's special lordship, since He said: ﴿those who fear their Lord﴾. So the specification of lordship here to these God-fearing people is from the category of special lordship.

We have often noted that the lordship of Allah the Mighty and Majestic over His creation is of two kinds: general and special. The general lordship encompasses all creation, and the special lordship is specific to the believers. Likewise, worship ('ubudiyyah) is of two kinds: general, which belongs to all creation, as in His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]; and special, which is the servanthood of the believers to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63]. Among this special kind is something more specific, as in the servanthood of the messengers, which is more specific than the general servanthood of the believing God-fearing; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1].

On this basis, in servanthood there is absolute generality and relative generality. Absolute generality is that which includes all who are in the heavens and the earth; relative generality is the generality of the servanthood of the believers, which is general in relation to the servanthood of the messengers but specific in relation to absolute servanthood.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these gardens beneath which rivers flow, if they are a nuzul, which is what is presented to a guest of honor, then what about what comes after this? It will be far greater good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 199:

Then He said: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them﴾ [Ali 'Imran 199].

In ﴿وَإِنَّ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ لَمَنْ﴾, *inna* (إن) is for emphasis, and the *lam* (اللام) is also for emphasis. So the verse contains two emphatic elements: *inna* and the *lam*. It is clear that the sentence has an inversion of order: ﴿مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ﴾ is the fronted predicate (خبر مقدم), and ﴿مَنْ يُؤْمِنُ﴾ is the delayed subject (مبتدأ مؤخر). ﴿لَمَنْ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ﴾ means: for the one who believes in Allah and in what has been revealed to you.

His saying ﴿وَإِنَّ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ﴾ refers to the Jews and the Christians. ﴿لَمَنْ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ﴾ and so on. Many of the Christians are of this kind, for many of them believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the Jews, they did not reach ten who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) during his lifetime. Among the Jews who embraced Islam was 'Abd Allah ibn Salam (رضي الله عنه), for he was one of their rabbis (ḥabr) and he accepted Islam. Among the Christians there were many, such as al-Najashi, the king of Abyssinia.

His saying ﴿لَمَنْ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ﴾: among what has been revealed to us is that they believe in the universality of the message, the message of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that he was sent to them just as he was sent to the Arabs. As for the one who says, "I believe in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), but only for the Arabs," he has not believed in what has been revealed to us. His faith in what has been revealed to us cannot be complete until he believes in Muhammad (ﷺ) as the messenger of all creation, and that he is a messenger to them whom they must follow. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) swore that: "No one from this nation (ummah) hears of me, a Jew or a Christian, and then does not believe in what I have been sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire." – meaning the nation of the call – "If he dies without believing in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, he will be among the companions of the Fire."[[Recorded by Muslim (153/240) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]

His saying ﴿وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْهِمْ﴾: as for what was revealed to them, it is evident that they believe in it. The Jews believe in the Torah, and the Christians in the Gospel. But if they do not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), they have not believed in the Torah or the Gospel, because 'Isa (ʿalayhi al-salam) gave them good news of Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when 'Isa, the son of Maryam, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad." But when he came to them with clear evidences, they said, "This is obvious magic."﴾ [al-Saff 6]. So His saying ﴿لَمَّا جَاءَهُمْ﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). After he came to them with clear evidences, and after he was shown to be the messenger whom 'Isa had given good tidings of, they said: ﴿This is obvious magic﴾, and they did not believe in him or follow him.

So the one who believes in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them – we say: his faith is not complete merely by believing that Muhammad was sent to the Arabs, or that the Quran is the speech of Allah, for example. Rather, his faith is not complete until he believes in whom? In Muhammad (ʿalayhi al-salam) as the messenger of Allah to all of mankind, and that he is obligated to follow him, and that he follows him as others do.

﴿وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْهِمْ خَاشِعِينَ لِلَّهِ﴾: His saying ﴿خَاشِعِينَ﴾ may be a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal, حال) of whom? Of ﴿لَمَنْ يُؤْمِنُ﴾. On that basis, the meaning is taken into account, because the word (مَن) is singular in form but plural in meaning, since the relative pronoun, although singular, can be used in a general sense. Moreover, (مَن) is one of the relative pronouns used for both the singular and the plural.

I say: ﴿خَاشِعِينَ﴾ may be a circumstantial qualifier of (مَن), meaning the one who believes while being humble, or a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of ﴿يُؤْمِنُ﴾, meaning he believes in a state of humility. The meaning does not change. Khushu' is submission, that is, humbling oneself before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: he believes in Allah while humbling himself and being submissive to Him.

﴿لَا يَشْتَرُونَ بِآَيَاتِ اللَّهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا﴾: "They do not buy" means they do not take, and do not seek, a small price in exchange for the signs of Allah. Here, purchase (ishtira', اشتراء) means taking, because there is no actual contract of buying and selling. But since the buyer takes the commodity seeking it and eager for it, those who take the life of this world in exchange for the Hereafter are treated as buyers. For this reason He said: ﴿They do not sell the signs of Allah for a small price﴾. This small price is this world, whether through leadership, wealth, status, or anything else.

In this there is an indication that among both the People of the Scripture and others are those who preserve their leadership, status, and wealth in order to disbelieve in the messengers. For example, Abu Jahl and the other leaders of the Quraysh – what prevented them from following Muhammad (ﷺ) was only arrogance and the preservation of status and leadership. For this reason they say: ﴿Why was this Quran not sent down upon a great man from one of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 31], meaning: why was it not sent down upon a great man so that we might follow him? They say this while knowing that Muhammad (ﷺ) is among the best of them, indeed the best of them in lineage, and the greatest and most honorable of them. Before the message, they called him "al-Amin" (the Trustworthy) and "al-Sadiq" (the Truthful). But when the message came, they associated partners with it – may Allah protect us – and denied it, and said: "This is from a contemptible man," just as Pharaoh said to Musa: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 52]. Thus these people said: ﴿Why was this Quran not sent down upon a great man from one of the two cities?﴾

﴿لَا يَشْتَرُونَ بِآَيَاتِ اللَّهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا﴾: the signs of Allah here refer to the legal signs (al-ayat al-shar'iyyah), because some people sell the legal signs for a small price. The meaning of "they buy a small price" is that they take status, leadership, wealth, and other things in place of the legal signs of Allah and following them. Allah described this as small because, compared with what is in the Hereafter, it is nothing, as is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than this world and everything in it."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3250) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd.]]

﴿أُولَئِكَ لَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: those are the ones who turned away from this world and did not take it in place of obedience to Allah and belief in Him.

﴿لَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: (أجر) means reward. Its attribution to Allah, ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾, indicates its greatness, that it is very great, for a thing from the Great is great, and from the Generous it is abundant. For this reason He said: ﴿They will have their reward with their Lord﴾.

His saying ﴿لَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ contains an indication, as will come – God willing – in the benefits (al-fawa'id), that it is lasting, because what is with Allah endures. For this reason the people of Paradise will abide therein forever. We ask Allah to make me and you among them.

﴿أُولَئِكَ لَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَرِيعُ الْحِسَابِ﴾: "swift in reckoning." Speed (al-sur'ah) is the absence of delay in a matter. Allah the Exalted is swift in reckoning in two respects. The first: this world is small, perishing, and swift, and it is only moments before it passes quickly. For example, Friday, or Saturday, or Sunday, or any day of the week, you take only a little of it and then it comes, quickly, until a person reaches its end and dies, and finds the reckoning before him. This is speed.

The second speed is on the Day of Resurrection, for Allah the Exalted will reckon all creatures in half a day, by His saying: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that Day will have a better resting place and a finer place of rest﴾ [al-Furqan 24]. Qaylulah (midday rest) happens only at midday, so it is so. From this it follows that Allah will reckon all creatures in half a day, such that each of them will rest in his dwelling and place of abode: ﴿Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: praise of some of the People of the Scripture, by His saying ﴿وَإِنَّ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ﴾, where "min" (from) here indicates partiality, and they are few.

* Among its benefits: the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in attributing virtue to its people. When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers and the reward of the believers, He said: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Scripture are those who believe﴾, thus attributing virtue to its people, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among its benefits: that those who believe in what Allah sent down to His Messenger (ﷺ), along with their belief in their own books, do so only out of glorification of Allah and submission to Him, not seeking worldly gain, praise, or the like; by His saying ﴿خَاشِعِينَ لِلَّهِ﴾.

* Among its benefits: showing the sincerity of these people, in that they did not believe in Allah and what was revealed to us for the sake of this world. They do not sell the signs of Allah for a small price. The verse, as we explained at first, may be understood to mean that those who disbelieve for the sake of this world (...) by this sentence. But we should say that it refers to those who disbelieved for the sake of this world and those who embraced Islam for the sake of this world. The second meaning is supported by His saying ﴿خَاشِعِينَ لِلَّهِ﴾, for it indicates that they are sincere in their belief in Allah and in what was revealed to them, meaning they do not intend any worldly thing, or status, leadership, or showing off.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those among the People of the Scripture who believed sincerely will have a reward, meaning a recompense in (...), even if they lose some worldly things because of their Islam; by His saying: ﴿Those will have their reward with their Lord﴾.

* Among its benefits: showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in the swiftness of His reckoning, where He said: ﴿Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾. Some of the Companions raised a difficulty with the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this meaning and said: "How can He reckon us in an hour when we are a multitude?" meaning many. He said: "Shall I not tell you about one of the signs of Allah?"[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (4731) and Ibn Majah (180) from the hadith of Abu Razin al-'Uqayli.]] meaning: from His signs that brings this closer to you. He mentioned the moon to him: the moon is one of the creations of Allah, and all people see it in a single hour, and they are not harmed in seeing it. If this is so for a creation of Allah whose light shines on everyone who sees it, and in which a number of the world shares that no one can count except Allah, then what about the Creator, the Majestic and Exalted?

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of reckoning, and that a person will be held accountable for his deeds, good for good and evil for evil; by His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾.

Let it be known that rights are of two kinds. A right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is built on forgiveness, pardon, and kindness. A right of creatures, by transgressing against them or against their honor, is not forgiven by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Indeed, the Prophet (ʿalayhi al-salam), when he sent Mu'adh to Yemen, said: "Beware of the choicest of their property, and fear the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and Allah."[[Agreed upon: recorded by al-Bukhari (1496) and Muslim (19/29) from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas.]] So to whom does the oppressed turn? To Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When he returns to his Lord, and he will surely turn to Him sincerely because he has been wronged by people, and when he returns to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with this sincerity, Allah, Glorified and Exalted, answers his supplication, and says, Mighty and Majestic: "By My might and My majesty, I will surely support you, even if after a time."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2526) and Ibn Majah (1752) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]] Therefore a person must guard against wronging himself and against wronging the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and against wronging others by transgression against them by word or deed. For this world will not last; it must pass away, and there must be a return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 200 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient, outlast (others in patience), stand ready (at the frontier), and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾ [Ali 'Imran 200] We always discuss His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and we cite the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "When you hear Allah say, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then give it your attentive hearing" (meaning, listen to it), "for it is either good that you are commanded to do, or evil that you are forbidden from."[[Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur in al-Tafsir (50).]] We have said that when Allah begins an address with this, it is a sign of the care given to it. Its reason: He begins it with the call that alerts the one addressed, ﴿O you who have believed﴾. Then, when the call is by the description of faith, it is a proof that what follows is a requirement of faith, because if it were not from its requirements, the address would not have been directed to those described with the word "faith." It is as if He said: O you who have believed, by your faith, do such and such, or, because of your faith, do not do such and such.

Second: It shows that opposing this is either one of the nullifiers of faith (nawaqid al-iman) or one of its deficiencies (nawaqis al-iman). If the matter is one of the foundations of the religion, such as ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa' 136], then opposing it is what? It is one of the nullifiers of faith. If it is in a branch of the religion, then opposing it is one of the deficiencies of faith, such as His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you are told, "Make room in the assemblies," then make room; Allah will make room for you﴾ [al-Mujadila 11]. If a person does not make room, we do not say that he is a disbeliever. Rather, we say he has opposed the command and his faith is deficient, because the requirement of faith is that one does what Allah has commanded, since Allah addressed him with this command by the description of faith.

Third: It conveys incitement (al-igra'), meaning urging a person and stirring him to do what he is addressed with, whether a command or a prohibition, because when a person is described by a description, that description spurs him on. If someone is told, "O generous one, be generous with this," the meaning is that you are inciting him, and that because of his generosity he must be generous. For this reason, when al-Mutanabbi was told, in the context of battle, "You said:"

*The horse, the night and the desert know me,*
*and the sword, the lance, the paper and the pen.*

He said, "Now you have killed me," and then advanced until he was killed. That is because the description a person claims and takes pride in, if he does not act upon it, makes him a liar in his claim. So it is as if Allah says: O you who have believed, by your faith, do such and such.

﴿Be patient﴾: Be patient with what? With everything that needs patience. Everything that requires patience, be patient with it. It is well known that what requires patience is what opposes the desires of the self. What opposes your desire is what needs patience, because it is difficult for you to bear. Obedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic is heavy on the souls, so be patient with it. Abstaining from sins is heavy on the souls, so be patient in abstaining. Pains and calamities that befall a person are heavy on the self, so be patient with them. The calamities that befall a person are themselves expiation for sins. If a person seeks their reward from Allah and awaits Allah's reward through them, then along with expiation there is an increase in good deeds. A person in this world must be tested, as the poet said:

*A day is against us and a day is for us,*
*a day we are made to suffer and a day we are made joyful.*

The world has never remained pleasant for anyone at all, ever. This is from the wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: He tests a person with blessings and tests him with calamities. Allah says: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial; and to Us you will be returned﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35]. So a person must be patient with everything that opposes his desire. Patience is heavy on the self and wearying to it, but when a person is patient, he looks to what lies ahead. What is the outcome? The outcome is good: ﴿Only the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [az-Zumar 10]. If he is patient, then let him be given good tidings. There is a saying: "Whoever is patient prevails." And in poetry:

*Patience, like its name, is bitter in its taste,*
*but its consequences are sweeter than honey.*

This is something proven by experience. Whenever a person is patient, he prevails, especially when his patience is joined with seeking the reward from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, for then it brings reward and a praiseworthy outcome.

As for His saying ﴿and outlast﴾ (sabiru): al-musabara (outlasting) happens between two parties, which is why it comes on the pattern fa'ala (the form of mutual action), like qatala and jahada. Sabara too requires another person who opposes you, so outlast him. The first patience has no one opposing you; it is something between you and yourself, that you be patient. The second is a person who opposes you, provokes you and transgresses against you, so outlast him, meaning overcome him through patience. This occurs in meeting enemies: the enemy outlasts you and you outlast him. Allah the Exalted has consoled the believing servants in His saying: ﴿Do not lose heart in pursuing the enemy. If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer; but you hope from Allah what they do not hope﴾ [an-Nisa' 104]. When you are wounded, you feel pain, and undoubtedly when they are wounded they feel pain. But there is a great difference: the one who hopes from Allah for reward for what befalls him, it becomes easy for him, to the point that sometimes he does not even feel it, due to the intensity of his seeking reward from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. So, patience is restraining the self, in the presence of something other than the one who outlasts it, and it occurs with what does not suit a person and what is hard for him. Outlasting someone is with a person who opposes you and is patient with you, bearing your opposition and your hostility, so you be patient and be patient. Allah the Mighty and Majestic has said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [ash-Shura 43].

As for His saying ﴿and stand ready﴾ (rabitu): ar-ribat (standing ready at the frontier) is more specific than al-musabara. That is, stand ready in acts of obedience. Among this is what the Prophet ﷺ explained when he said: "Perfecting ablution in difficult conditions, frequent steps to the mosques, and waiting for the prayer after the prayer; that is ar-ribat, that is ar-ribat."[[Narrated by Muslim (251/41) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] "Perfecting ablution in difficult conditions" means in the days of cold and freezing weather. When a person perfects his ablution, meaning completes and perfects it, this indicates his faith in Allah the Mighty and Majestic, his strong belief, and his hope for Allah's reward. The second is frequent steps to the mosques: when a person goes to a distant mosque that requires many steps, this indicates what? It indicates his standing ready in goodness, his persistence in it, and the truthfulness of faith in his heart. For this reason he goes to the mosque even if it is far, and returns to it even if that is many times. He returns to it at least five times a day and night, even if that is many times. This also indicates standing ready in goodness.

﴿Be patient, outlast, and stand ready﴾. Among standing ready is standing guard on the frontiers. However, this did not exist in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, because in his time there was no standing guard; the Prophet ﷺ would go out to the enemy, raid, and return. But after the conquests and the spread of Islam to the regions of the earth, standing guard came into being, and the Muslims needed it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "Perfecting ablution in difficult conditions, frequent steps to the mosques, and waiting for prayer after prayer; that is ar-ribat, that is ar-ribat," three times.[[Narrated by Muslim (251/41) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] This is because standing guard on the Islamic borders did not exist in the time of the Messenger ﷺ.

Then He said: ﴿that you may be successful﴾, meaning: in order that you may be successful.

﴿And fear Allah﴾: This is a command to have taqwa (God-consciousness) of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. We have mentioned many times before that taqwa means taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is taqwa. This is the best that has been said about taqwa: taking a shield against the punishment of Allah the Mighty and Majestic by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions; this is taqwa. Its being conjoined to what preceded can be explained either as the conjoining of the general to the specific, which is common in the Qur'an, or it can be said that what preceded are commands and taqwa refers to the prohibitions, as we say regarding His saying: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and taqwa﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2], that righteousness is doing good and taqwa is avoiding evil. When taqwa is mentioned alone, it includes both doing good and abandoning evil, and the two meanings do not contradict each other. So these four descriptions or commands, ﴿be patient, outlast, stand ready, and fear Allah﴾, all of them have a single outcome that includes one thing: doing the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

Then He said: ﴿that you may be successful﴾. The particle la'alla (that/perhaps) here indicates causation (lil-ta'lil), not hope, because the speech of Allah contains no hope, for He is over all things capable, and nothing is difficult for Him or burdensome to Him. Rather, it is for causation, meaning: so that you may be successful. As for al-falah (success), they said it is a comprehensive word, comprehensive for attaining what is sought and being saved from what is feared. This is success: that a person attains what he seeks and is saved from what he fears. There is no doubt that every one of creation wishes this, wishes to attain what he seeks and to be saved from what he fears.

* In this noble verse, Allah addresses the believers with the call, and from this is derived: the virtue of faith, and that the people of faith are the most worthy of people to be addressed, based on His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾.

* Among its benefits: a person should, in his manner of speech, use what moves him to do what he is asked or to leave what he is forbidden, based on His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient﴾.

* Among its benefits: encouragement to patience, indeed the command to patience, based on His saying: ﴿be patient﴾. It is in reality general: it may be obligatory, which is patience in performing what is obligatory, in abstaining from what is forbidden, and in painful afflictions; and it may be recommended, which is patience in performing recommended acts or in abstaining from disliked acts. Here patience is not obligatory, but it is more complete and better.

* Among its benefits: the command to outlast, that a person outlasts whoever opposes him and extends to him (his hostility). The outcome will be in his favor if he outlasts him, in compliance with the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, hoping for His reward and anticipating the praiseworthy outcome in which the turn of fortune falls upon the one who opposed him.

* Among the benefits of this verse also: the command to standing ready. Standing ready, if it is for an obligation, is obligatory, and if it is for a recommended act, it is recommended, according to what the one standing ready is standing ready for.

* Among its benefits: the command to taqwa, and taqwa is obligatory, because it is guarding oneself against falling into what is forbidden, either by abandoning an obligation or by doing what is forbidden.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the good outcomes for whoever carries out the commands of Allah, of patience, outlasting, standing ready and taqwa; and this praiseworthy outcome, that is, success, is what Allah the Exalted says: ﴿that you may be successful﴾.

* Student: His saying: ﴿and what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them﴾. The Muhammadan message requires belief in the earlier messages. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say, "We have believed in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to Abraham"﴾ [al-Baqarah 136].

* Shaykh: And "believe in what was revealed to them before the sending of the Messenger." That is, they combined two beliefs: belief in what was revealed to them and belief in what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ.

* Student: His saying ﴿and stand ready﴾: is the intended meaning the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about ar-ribat?

* Shaykh: Ar-ribat is more general, but the Messenger ﷺ explained it in terms that people understood at that time.

* Student: The verse you mentioned, O Shaykh: ﴿an accommodation from Allah﴾. When a guest arrives, he is honored upon his arrival. Can we say that Paradise has two gardens?

* Shaykh: No, not at all. We do not say that. All of them are an accommodation (nuzul), all of them are in the best condition from beginning to end.

* Student: (...) Now we have mentioned during the explanation the story of the Companion who asked the Prophet ﷺ how Allah the Mighty and Majestic will gather all creation in half a day. How is the gathering?

* Shaykh: They did not ask about the manner.

* Student: They asked how He would gather them...

* Shaykh: No, no, they asked about the quantity: how this amount can encompass or be sufficient for the reckoning of all creation.

* Student: This would be (...) a kind of the unseen.

* Shaykh: Even if it were, there is nothing wrong with it.

* Student: We mentioned that the Companions did not used to ask...

* Shaykh: Yes, they did not used to ask, but these asked about the quantity: how half a day can accommodate Allah's reckoning of all creatures. So the Messenger explained to them that this is not impossible.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, some scholars derived from (...).

* Shaykh: (...) ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah﴾. So the mention of belief here is in the present tense, indicating their continuing upon it.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: How are they among the believers? A believer who rules by other than what Allah has revealed!

* Student: An-Najashi.

* Shaykh: An-Najashi ruled by what Allah revealed, by what had reached him. I say: he would rule by what had reached him.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The ruling by the Qur'an had not reached him. He believed in Muhammad ﷺ, believed in 'Isa, and believed in the messengers, and this is what had reached him.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: These are special characteristics. He specially favors with His mercy whom He wills: ﴿Allah selects for His mercy whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 105]. So the humble ones, the burden is not heavy upon them (...).

* * *

* Shaykh: Is our being obligated to pay zakat and charitable expenditures a form of trial?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, it is a trial; a legislated trial.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: So here is a legislated trial, by our being charged to pay zakat, because some people do not pay zakat, and so there is harm to him in this.

His saying: ﴿much hurt﴾: is it from speech or from action? ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allah much hurt﴾.

* Student: (...) from speech.

* Shaykh: From speech? What is the evidence for restricting it to speech? What is the evidence that it is specifically verbal hurt, since it may be hurt by action, such as striking them?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: I want evidence that it is specific to verbal hurt.

* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture﴾...

* Shaykh: And what is heard?

* Student: It is speech.

* Shaykh: What is heard is speech. This is the apparent meaning, although it is possible that it could be hurt by action, and I may hear that this man was harmed, so I would be hearing about the report of physical harm.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things competent (189). Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾ [Ali 'Imran 189-190].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Where is the subject of (inna, indeed)?

* Student: ﴿in the creation of the heavens﴾: the prepositional phrase is the subject of (inna).

* Shaykh: Can a prepositional phrase be the subject of (inna)?

* Student: Then it is deleted.

* Shaykh: Deleted. What is the estimated (deleted) element?

* Student: ﴿signs﴾ (la-ayat): O Shaykh, it is postponed.

* Shaykh: That is the subject of (inna): ﴿signs﴾. What do you all say? Correct.

What is the meaning of ﴿for people of understanding﴾?

* Student: Those with intellects.

* Shaykh: Those with intellects.

Can it be derived from this verse that reason supports the Sharia, and that the Sharia develops reason?

* Student: Yes indeed.

* Shaykh: How is that?

* Student: When a person reflects on the creatures of Allah.

* Shaykh: But how do you understand from the verse that reason supports the Sharia?

* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿Signs for people of understanding﴾: none reflect on the previous signs except people of intellect.

* Shaykh: So the intellects support what the Sharia has brought, just as the Sharia develops reason and increases it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 3, verse 200 (part 2 of 2):**

Regarding His words: ﴿They remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾. Is this for variety (tanwi'), or for comprehensiveness (istighraq)? In other words, do they remember Allah sometimes while sitting, sometimes while standing, and sometimes lying on their sides, or is the intended meaning that they remember Him in all states?
* Student: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second. That is, they remember Allah constantly.

Regarding His words: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾. Is there a parallel in the Qur'an that supports what they said?
* Student: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad 27].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾. Correct. What is "in vain" (batil)?
* Student: Everything that does not conform to the Shari'ah is batil (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of the word batil?
* Student: That which does not conform to the Shari'ah.
* The Shaykh: No, no. I want the word only. I am not asking what is meant. I am asking the meaning of batil. The root meaning of batil in the language is that which is lost without purpose, lost, that which no one pays attention to or regards.

Regarding His words: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe﴾. Where is the subject of (inna)?
* Student: The clause: ﴿those who believe﴾.
* The Shaykh: The clause: ﴿those who believe﴾.
* Student: Only (man).
* The Shaykh: Only (man). So is the predicate a clause or a single word?
* Student: A single word.
* The Shaykh: (...) The estimate is: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe﴾. Do you explain (man) as: "for the one who believes in such-and-such"? Can you give an example of that? From the Jews?
* Student: 'Abd Allah ibn Salam.
* The Shaykh: And from the Christians?
* Student: al-Najashi.
* The Shaykh: If a People of the Book believed in what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), but said: "It is only for the Arabs specifically," based on His words: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2]. The question: if the People of the Book said, "I believe in what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), but it is for the Arabs specifically, not for the Children of Israel," based on the Most High's words: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾, is he a believer?
* Student: This one has not believed in Muhammad.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Student: Because he was sent to all people. As for the verse, it is informative and not (...).
* The Shaykh: How?
* Student: The verse is informative (...).
* The Shaykh: Sound.
* Student: Describing him as "unlettered" (...) is not a description of the message; it is a description of specification (...).
* Another student: I say: whoever does not believe in the Messenger has not believed in what was revealed to us or in what was revealed to them.
* The Shaykh: No. He believes in the Messenger. He says: "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," but only to the Arabs specifically.
* Student: But he has not believed in what was revealed to them, as 'Isa ibn Maryam said: ﴿O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of a messenger to come﴾ [al-Saff 6].
* The Shaykh: He also has not believed in what was revealed to us, because what was revealed to us is that he is a messenger for all people.
* Student: But he said: ﴿and giving good tidings of a messenger to come﴾.
* The Shaykh: My point is that he has believed neither in what was revealed to them nor in what was revealed to us. Not in what was revealed to them, because he did not accept the good tidings of 'Isa. Nor in what was revealed to us, because what was revealed to us was revealed as what? For all people. So if he says, "I do not believe, because he was sent to the Arabs," we say he has not believed.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Among the unlettered﴾. The meaning of the verse is that He sent from among them, that is, from among them. His mission began among the unlettered. They said: this is an indication that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) would not directly reach anyone outside the unlettered, because the conquests in his time did not extend beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Everything was in the Peninsula and its surroundings; they did not reach Persia or Rome.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: He is the One who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among them, as an emphasis. Or we say "among the unlettered" refers to the beginning of the message, as we explained: at the start of his mission it was among them, and then it spread.

﴿O you who believe, be patient and endure and remain stationed (for war)﴾. What is the difference between patience (sabr) and enduring (musabarah)?
* Student: Musabarah is from the pattern of mufa'alah. One is patient and makes himself patient (yatasabbar). The pattern tafa''ala for patience means making an effort to be patient, feigning patience. That is: if he is not patient, let him force himself to be patient.
* Another student: Sabr is sabr, meaning patience over the self that commands evil. As for ﴿and endure﴾, musabarah is what occurs between one person and another. It occurs through struggle (jihad), just as confronting the enemies of Allah occurs through struggle. A person is patient and endures against (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, you endure against whoever opposes you in your matter, because a person may be patient when no one contends with him, but when someone contends with him, argues with him, and debates him, he may not remain patient.
What does (la'alla) mean?
* Student: Causal (ta'liliyyah).
* The Shaykh: Causal. And it cannot be for hope (raja')?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Student: Because hope is not applicable.
* The Shaykh: It is not applicable with respect to Allah. Well done.
And what is success (falah)?
* Student: It is attaining what is desired and being saved from what is feared.
* The Shaykh: Well done, correct.

Regarding the Most High's words: ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾. What is the meaning of (istajaba)?
* Student: It means "answered."
* The Shaykh: And why did He say ﴿their Lord﴾?
* Student: Because this is a special lordship (rububiyyah khassah).
* The Shaykh: A special lordship, in that He granted them success in faith and in this supplication, so it is a special lordship.
Do you know that there is a special lordship and a general lordship?
* Student: General lordship belongs to all creation, and special lordship may be specific to the messengers or the believers (...).
* The Shaykh: What verse brings together both the general and the special lordship?
* Student: The Most High's words: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your earliest forefathers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26].
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [al-A'raf 121-122].
* The Shaykh: Yes. ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾. In this verse there is a subtle point, in that Musa is mentioned before Harun. What is it?
* Student: Musa is better than Harun.
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.
